We're aware characters have health or hitpoints, but Darkest Dungeon taps you on the shoulder and casually mentions that mental health also exists and makes you look like an idiot for not realising it was missing. Stress will play havoc on your characters if you don't know what you're in for.
Joe Schmo the Great enters dungeon, fights off fish men with harpoons and dark magic, steps on a trap twice, reads "Eldritch magic and you" because he can't stop himself (doesn't like it) and barely survives the journey home only to do it all again two days later. Pretty sure that would leave a mark, and Darkest Dungeon shows just how grueling a dungeon should be.
One of my favorite features so far is character "quirks" which are basically summed up as positive and negative traits. Your character could be a natural skeleton slayer but let the torchlight fade around them and they might become so stressed out as the fight rolls on that they will be driven to breaking point. They could either descend into some form of madness until you get them some help back home or they will rise to the challenge and encourage their allies to press on.
Rewards the player for experimenting with character skill combinations, preparing for the worst, and for making tough decisions. In the end when a quest looks like it will kill your characters, it is normally best to just cut your losses and get them back home to live another day. Yes, you didn't get the treasure or all the gold you wanted, but your characters could still prove themselves next time.
Great atmosphere, interesting character classes and skills. Also enjoyed the way the storyteller was used to bring you into the game, really effective. Really like the chosen art direction applied throughout with the graphics and cutscene animations.

A decent reimaging of an old classic.
While not a classic in its own right, or a master class in startaegy. Age of Empiers III is a decent strategy game that manages to bring update the franchises play style and strategy components.
To those who are familiar with the franchise its a lot of the same with a few interesting new additions.  To those who are not, its a pretty standard romp in real time strategy.  You have a city you build buildings, workers, gather resources-- pretty much what you'd expect.
The gameplay is solid and very, very similiar to its predesesor.  It does feel a bit stream lined.  There are less things to build and research overall.  In fact, they basically combined stone and gold into a single resource, only leaving the player to have to gather and manage three resources (food, wood, gold).  Far from a bad thing, it seems like these changes stream line the game and speed up the play.  Other new additions like trading posts which establish trade routes place emphasis on controlling the map at all times and further keep the player active at all points in the game.
The really new:  RPG lite.  Affecting the gameplay, but technically outside it, AOE III has introduced a RPG-esque elements that allow you to level up your different civilizations and build "decks".  Technically cards, they are a series of upgrades you can pick off several techs tree (some unique to your civilization)  that can then be activated in the real game using experience gained in that game by fighting and kiling units.  It's not the most well implemented system, but it is novel and I had a great time looking through it, planning things out, and seeing how each civilization could specialize.
Overall,  its a decent game.  The graphics and UI are up to date.  There are some novel additions to the genre.  It isn't a must play.  But as cheap as it is, you may want to consider checking this out if you are a fan of real time strategy games.

Q.U.B.E., Portal but different.
Q.U.B.E. is a wonderful little thing that takes a bit of inspiration from portal through its mechanics and setting and puts out a solid 3 hours of puzzling and interesting puzzles and plot. In this game you get plonked into a room wearing some form of suit that has the power of interacting with the blocks (Or should I say, Q.U.B.E.s) that you come across. There are various types with various applications and they make up the puzzles.
Gameplaywise, this game is excellent and makes you wish for more, as these mechanics feel like they could be expanded upon a lot, or complicated in a lot more ways than the game actually does. It never gets stale during the 3 hours or so you'll end up spending in it, and difficulty hikes up well. There is one puzzle that spikes in difficulty way too much, however, and it slightly ruins the pace of the game. The bugs this game has are minor, and none are gamebreaking. All in all, gameplaywise, this game is very solid.
Storywise, this game is lacking a bit. There's some nice storytelling done, making you question what to believe, but it also sets itself up for you to end it in the way you want it to. Unfortunately, the developers did not include a second ending route for you to take, and you're forced to go with one character's will. This little bit completely messes up the story, as whatever you do, whatever you think, it's all linear.
It's still enjoyable however, and the time you spend thinking about everything whilst solving puzzles is bound to be a great one if you're into these types of games.
The biggest issue I personally had with this game was the default pricepoint. I can live with 3 hour games, definitely. This game, however, charged too much for the 3 hours it can provide you with entertainment. It was priced at 20 euros, which is way too much. I much prefer to see it at its current pricepoint, and I highly recommend buying it.

The game is missing almost all of the promised features, so it's nowhere near beta. This is an alpha release advertised as a beta to increase sales. After months without any updates, and no significant updates at all since release, they're finally overhauling the game by making it more gated and linear than ever. Updates were still promised to be "thick and fast" until a month or two ago.
Fans will tell you "It's just in early access!" to excuse the detestable behavior of the developers, which has been to lie. Two of the screenshots on this very store page are from mock-ups; the art assets exist but are unavailable. Notably, the depiction of an underwater Hylotl city simply does not exist, because, almost a year since release, the Hylotl race still does not have any cities or villages. This game really shouldn't be allowed on Steam, since it uses fake screenshots to advertise itself even on the store page. Earlier versions of the website also featured hand-made mock-ups instead of screenshots, to deceive readers into thinking the game was farther along than it really is.
The procedurally generated enemies are boring to fight and the procedurally generated weapons are boring to find. Features announced as complete on the blog years ago, like the frozen ocean biome and the complex weapon generation system, are nowhere to be found, either having been simply removed during development or outright lied about. A system listed as "50% finished" on the Starbound Roadmap in December 2013 was only just being initially prototyped in September.
This game is a mess, and the developers are dishonest fools who do their best to censor all dissent. Don't give them any more money.

There are a lot of people complaining about this game so let me set the record straight. That being said, this game is not complete (though is more than functional at this point and has more content than most early access games) but it is CONSTANTLY being developed and EVERY SINGLE DAY I DOWNLOAD AROUND 200MB OF NEW CONTENT. The early access community sucks.

If they had, they'd realize exactly how much additional content is being added every day and would have no reason to downvote this game. The rest find it impossible to navigate to a beta selection tab and choose the nightly branch. That or it's too much trouble for their fat little trollhard fingers to carry their girth that far. , tracks the nightly development of starbound along the way with updates that range from small stability issues to massive additions of buff systems and items as well as dungeons and biome adjustments.

It pains me to do this, but I'm afraid I have to amend my original review. When Firaxis patched the game on November 8th, 2016 to add the ability to tour the Avenger with a controller (something I personally couldn't give a hoot in hell about) they broke the game so badly that it was literally unplayable. They issued a hot fix (which took a bloody week) that solved the targeting problem but have never fixed the interface problems on the squad selection screen, making it next to impossible to distribute your weapons and gear to your selected soldiers. Playing with the loot mods, which I particularly enjoy, compounds the problem exponentially.
Firaxis also introduced some nasty bugs with that patch. It crashes regularly on startup as well as during gameplay, and at least one bug is utterly game-breaking. The only time I attempted to play Ironman after the patch, the game froze during an alien turn phase and I had to reload the save. After reloading, the issue persisted. It wasn't the alien's turn but it wasn't my turn either. I couldn't select any soldiers or perform any actions and I lost the entire campaign after investing over 40 hours to it.
Breaking a game with an unnecessary patch is bad enough, since it demonstrates an astounding lack of proper QC testing, but then not fixing it for a year (and counting) is so outrageous that I'm obliged to withdraw my recommendation. My original review is below, but I can't continue to recommend a game that has been abandoned after being purposely broken.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
As someone who has played over 1,300 hours of XCOM: Enemy Unknown and XCOM: Enemy Within, I was understandably excited about XCOM 2. I actually preordered it, which is something I almost never do. In fact, the last game I preordered was XCOM: Enemy Unknown. They improved an incredible number of gameplay aspects. Concealment is interesting, collecting loot and modding weapons is fun, the overwatch and sight indicators help tremendously, and the new destructable elements add tactical options. They also added random continent bonuses, lowered the reload action cost, improved character editing, added a character pool, and embraced community modding. These are all very welcome changes to the XCOM recipe. They tried to randomize mission environments with a pseudo-procedurally generated system that kinda works, but environments now suffer from a generic quality that makes them all seem similar. Even though the hand-crafted environments in XCOM EU/EW tended to get repetitive, I prefer them.
Everything isn't rosy, however. They totally screwed the pooch with mission structure. Unlike XCOM EU/EW, timed missions are the rule rather than the exception, so they quickly become very tiresome. Enemy Within successfully added some urgency to missions through the countdown timers on Meld, but it was optional. The risk versus reward element pushed you forward, but the world didn't come crashing down if everything turned to sh*t and you had to forgo the juicy Meld to deal with a deadly tactical situation. It was a lot of fun. The few timed missions in XCOM EU/EW added variety and were enjoyable when they appeared, but you were generally free to deal with things however you desired. I thought Shen's Last Gift introduced some novel mission structure, but an endless series of time-limited missions aren't novel, tactically diverse, or even particularly entertaining. Keep in mind that this is criticism of the base game. Community mods can change the way timers work or even completely remove them, though I question how removing the timers would improve gameplay. If they aren't an integral part of the mission design then why are they there? To make matters even worse, a timer rears its ugly head in the strategic gameplay as well. Rather than being free to choose missions whose rewards would help you accomplish multiple strategic objectives, the Avatar Project ticker forces you to always choose missions that slow its advancement. As a result, strategic depth is severely curtailed.
XCOM 2 also failed with something less tangible that makes a tremendous difference. In XCOM EU/EW the world and everyone in it is threatened by an alien invasion. You are invested from the beginning and emotionally hooked. Here, rather than fighting a tooth and nail defensive campaign, you are fighting an offensive campaign. The shift from being a desperate defender to being an aggressor just doesn't work as well. Yes, you are still the underdog, but the emotional investment you have from the onset in XCOM EU/EW isn't here. The gameplay mechanics are better but I don't care as much, and ultimately that makes the first game better.
I have to recommend XCOM 2, as it is actually pretty well done, but it isn't what I'd hoped for. While playing I constantly find myself wishing I was playing XCOM EU/EW with the improvements from XCOM 2, and that makes me a sad.

This game not only exceeds the quality of the TV by a long mile, but the added tension of making decisions yourself will involve you in a way only videogames can. This is a point and click game where you control a character from fixed camera angles, walk around, interact with object, and talk to people. Action scenes involve a bit of QTE and clicking on the indicated points. This may not sound very entertaining, but trust me, it is. The dialouge in particular is extreamly engaging and well voice acted.
The action scenes and heated conversations are tense because you do not have long to react. In games such as Mass Effect you can wait forever before making a decision or deciding what to say. The Walking Dead forces you to make lightning fast decisions that will sometimes have a minor effect and other times have a significant impact. There is no way to do a perfect 'good guy' or 'bad guy' playthrough of this game. You will have to make many tough decisions, some of which you will regret, others you will not stop questioning yourself about days after you finish the game.
The art style is very reminiscent of the comics (but with colour) and does a good job at hiding the horrible texture quality which you will stop noticing after the first hour. The animations can be clunky and the framerate sometimes stutters, but you will forgive these imperfections quick.
People who are familiar with post-apocolyptic zombie fiction will have to stay through the first hour of the game before things start to get interesting. Most of us know how the zombie apocolypse starts out, how people first react, the cliques, the realisation of what a bite does, etc. Once that stuff is out of the way, the pace picks up fast and you get to deal with the situation rather than listen to characters dream about the military swooping in to save the day.
While I enjoyed the DLC, it was not as good as the 5 main episodes, but still worth it, especially if you intend to play season 2 (which you will after finishing the first season).
Fans of narritive games and post-apocolypse fiction must play this excellent game and also put season 2 on their wishlists for later.

Once again Artifex Mundi has handed us a really good hidden object game. They make these well folks, always.

This isn't part 2 of the story of Grim Legends 1, it's a second grim legend. If they ever make a third one I can easily imagine it will be yet a another different legend.
Pros
Nice music.
Well use of voice acting.
It's pretty. Just plain outright pretty to look at and watch.
Middle level gameplay. Spend a few mins and you'll rarely have to use the hint button.
Cons (of a sort)
Lack of gameplay inovation. It's just like nearly every other well made hidden object game. This isn't a bad thing but it's almost as if they used a formula.
Not really a mystery, if you rember the myth.
This is a really well made hidden object game. Definatly worth buying and adding to your collection.

This is another of the Artifex Mundi HOGs, with high production values, lots of puzzles, and not so many Hidden Object Scenes.  The story has nothing to do with the first game in the series, and is a loose variation on the seven swans. Some of the puzzles and actions needed are extremely obtuse, but most everything flows pretty well together.  The story is pretty incidental compared to some of the other games, but it works well enough.  The entire game (including the bonus adventure) took around three hours to complete, which is a little short for these kinds of games, but long enough for me.

I was told this game is "Dark Souls done wrong". I had no problem with that, I wanted to like it for what it offers on it's own. I didn't think it was fair to make the comparsion, despite the game clearly wanting to aim for the solid 2nd best position, trying to ride the fame and hype of a genre another game bringed back, lives and profits from in a quite dominant position. And I said, I'm okay with that, it can be a great game because what's inside is what matters the most, not the franchise name burnt on it's box. And still, Lords of the Fallen is just B- in everything on it's own, compared to no other game. You just feel in every moment of it.
I picked it up for 3,99 so no regrets here, mainly because I wanted a taste of what Dark Souls games are like and honestly it's only good for that. I haven't played any DS games, but I'm certain they must be better than this. It is a game that is never going to be finished (by me, it's a complete game tho), so overall I still consider it a waste if you buy this game for itself. I bought it for a taste of the DS experience, and it lasted 7 hours, and I feel like this isn't the way to make that work right. With no experience about the DS titles, I know THIS isn't the way to do it right.
For this reason I cannot honestly recommend it.
The game known as "poor man's dark souls". And I bought it to be that, so can't say I was disappointed with what I got, but the "poor man's dark souls" title speaks for itself. It wants to be something, but fails so, and has nothing else on it's own.
1. The combat is incredibly boring. You could say it is supposed to be tactical, but reality is that you have to use a few spells you get with every class, and it's almost always the solution. Or you can look at each other with both shields up and everyone bunkering down for 5 to 10 minutes. With a random filler enemy. Shielded opponent? Whatever class you pick you can either go a) invisible to backstab b) slow down time and walk around c) just send a firey clone of yourself in it's face to explode. You can do workarounds, try interesting special moves with all the weapons, but it gets repetitive incredibly fast due to..
2. the lack of cretivity. And this applies to EVERY aspect of the game. I think I have met about 4 types of opponents in the 6,6 hours I spent in Lords of the Fallen. Random "ork guy" with a shield, without a shield, jumping dog type that can breathe unblockable stuff, and crossbow guy. And variations of these, smaller, bigger, sometimes poison, sometimes fire, sometimes thin wizardey sometimes fat guardey, sometimes 4 legs sometimes none. But mechanically there is barely any difference between them and when a game is built like this, with the "less is more" in mind, so you have to fight a really small number of enemies compared to other similar games, the lack of creativity really shows. Same goes for the enviroment, it wants to be Dark Souls gothic so desperately, has a great looking engine to do so, but it just ends up being Darksiders with more blur. With the exception of the very few vistas (I think I've came across 2 under this ~7ish hours) and more unique rooms such as the temple hall at the first boss, it's always the same. Fortress, garden, cave, prison, royality rooms, even a different dimension,  battle hardened or brand new,  ALL looks the same. Not just the atmosphere, but the structural layouts, construction style, even the size of the bricks walls are mostly made of, everything is the same everywhere, and it gets boring. It wants to be Dark Souls, but every new room here is just like the one you came from instead of being something exciting, and outside areas are the same with the exception of not having a ceiling. And the bosses, oh the bosses. As interesting as they seem to be on first sight, you'll realize there is barely any challange there because they are SO BASIC mechanically that only your lack of patience can get you killed. All of them are like they exist in slow motion only, and just a bigger variant of some basic enemy with one or two extra spells and a really boring looks. Have you seen the first DS3 boss, the knight transforming to that darkness-snake thing? That alone has more creative design than everything and anything added together in this game.
If you are still interested, you should know that it is a solid PC version, no fps, crash or anything else issues happend. It's not particularly demanding, you should be fine somewhat above the minimum requirements to play it on nearly maxed out settings with good speed.

What an absolutley wonderful game. With a few modded classes added, even more wonderful.
The sound design is superb, and the music is nice and fitting. The voice-acting is amazing -- I haven't felt so enthralled by a video-game narrator since the likes of Arcanum. 5/5 Sound Design.
The visuals are pretty great as well. My low-end, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ computer can run everything (except for the opening cutscene) perfectly. The artistic direction perfectly fits the whole middle-ages/lovecraftian tone. And all the little details -- from meticulous little items hanging off each the characters' belts -- really make it special. 5/5 Visuals.
The gameplay itself is, while having a steep difficulty curve, pretty fair. Though, it can feel a BIT unfair at times, it's never so overwhelmingly so that it ruins the game. A few of the classes feel a bit lacking compared to others (for example, I find that the Man-at-Arms is really only good for guarding the weaker characters, and most everything else about him is done much more efficiently by other melee- or strongman-type classes). But, in the end, the positive FAR outweighs the negative. 4/5 Gameplay Mechanics.
The storyline, I honestly haven't given much thought to. And while it may seem trite to some to have the storyline revealed, bits by bits, via journal entires and ghostly narrations, it's important to keep in mind the theme. For a lovecraftian heavy game, having things revelaed through the mad scribblings of a madman warning others about the 'eldritch' and 'grotesque' monsters that have driven him mad GREATLY compliment the whole tone. So, while I haven't paid too close of attention to the story itself, I love the way in which it is told. 4/5 Storyline.
Now, I did get this game on sale just a few days ago, so as for value for the money I paid, $10 almost feels like a steal. This feels, to me, like a $30 game, so I feel $25 is definitely a fair price. 5/5 Value.
And, lastly, I don't think I could think of another game -- besides maybe the Civilization titles -- that compete to the amount of replayability this game has. Though, it heavily relies on how you view it. If you're looking for countless new characters and monsters, then you're probably not going to play it more than once. But if you're looking to mix-and-match the heroes, and try new combinations, and perfect your strategies, then you're going to fall into a bottomless pit of replayability. With the few mods I've added (from Actionjack), it's definitely added to the replayability by exponets. 3/5 Replayability.
Overall: Superb visuals, sound, and a great value at this price. Pretty great storyline and gameplay mechanics. And replayability if you're one that's into perfecting strategies and team-combinations. 4/5 Game.

As someone who's played and enjoyed many other games in similar genres, I was excited to play Darkest Dungeon, but found that it didn't hold up in comparison to the others I'd played.
The most obvious game to compare this to is Monster's Den: Book of Dread. Monster's Den is a free turn based game from 2008 where you explore a dungeon and fight enemies for rewards. There's no town, but the combat is incredibly nuanced and rewarding. Compared to this, Darkest Dungeon combat felt repetitive and clunky. The equip system was also not nearly as harrowing. There's generally only one or two characters where their equips will even *work*, so you don't need to worry about who gets the rare shoes and who gets cloth stockings.
Still, there's something to be said for simplicity. The modern XCOM games abstract a lot of your choices, leaving you with a 2D movement system and a few variations on 'fire', and are still formidable chance-based strategy. Darkest Dungeons is essentially the same thing, only with 1D movement. The problem is that 1D movement is a lot more constrained than 2D. There are only 4 positions in every battle, and players mostly stand in the same place to keep their attacks effective. This leaves just management (torches, looting, town) and attacks as the deep mechanics.
One of the most powerful draws of Darkest Dungeon is the 'roguelike progress', which invites you to feel like you're moving forward, even as heroes crumple at your feet. Adding story-style progress to a roguelike is a difficult yet emotionally powerful mechanic that's difficult to do right. Darkest Dungeon uses a RPG-style checklist as well as town management mechanics to motivate this. It's effective, but not an elegant solution, and you're prone to feeling sometimes that you're just slogging through dark halls, as opposed to participating in a story.
Another draw is the art style. Even if the mechanics of a game aren't as well oiled as they could be, that can all be made up for by a slick visual style. I have to admit that I don't know anything quite as striking as the stress and victory halos the heroes get as they fail and succeed.
Still, it's not as if this game is unique in that right either. As a top-down shooter, Our Darker Purpose is a bit different gameplaywise, but it still does far better at motivating 'roguelike progress', and equally good at putting out a visual style to make you question the dark nature of humanity.
In conclusion, if you look at Darkest Dungeon and say "a Cthulian-style roguelike management game? That's just what I've *needed*", purchase it, you won't be disappointed. If you're like me and say "Darkest Dungeon? I've heard good things about it, so it must be really great", then I'd recommend you think twice. There's not much here that hasn't been done better elsewhere.

This is basically  MOBA based on space combat. I'm playing this 4 days long now and I can say that I never get bored. The game is run by Unreal Engine 4, so details are awesome. Sometime I just love sit   watching jump animation of the ships. Can't complain about the gameplay too. I'm cheating on War Thunder( I'm typical war thunder player) but I've no regrets. I think I'm falling in love all over again. If you want to feel something new and fresh too, then welcome to Fractured Space!
There's two battlemodes as developers promised, but only one is playble as the game is in alpha phase.
There's three kind of ships - Attack, Defence and Support, three fractions(actually ships  builders) - USR(United Space Research), Zarek and Titan DS.
When I joined this game I though it's just typical space combat game with small spacecrafts, but be alerted, this game is about spaceships. Some people like fun shooter where they take a space fighter and keeping shooting around until match is ended, this game isn't for them. You have to keep your perception focused, because otherwise you would get defeated easily. You have to keep track of your map, ship and other players. If you compare it to Dota, you're going on right path.
There's only single map on current game mode ; Five possible 'fractured' sectors -  you can jump to, Two home bases, Two side sectors - Alpha and Beta, One combat buff - Gamma, it's the center of the whole map.
You would spawn on home base and can jump to Alpha, Beta or Gamma. Alpha - Beta got mine stations to capture. Capturing gives your team upgrade points, which you use to upgrade your ship in game. Oh I forgot, which by the way is really an important thing. Alpha - Beta got  forwading staions for each team. You have to capture one of them in order to access enemy base. Now, Gamma opens each 4 minutes. You can capture it in order to help team upgrade points. Home bases are ring shaped with defensive cannons and healing buoy for it's  team. In order to capture enemy base, you need get inside the base(to the center of the ring). Base shoots shells to you so, it's better to bring team members with you.
One good thing about game is - every ship is balaced in Attack and Defense, which means every ship can kill each other ; but don't know about Gladiotor, defense ship from Zarek, probably the best ship in game. Each ship have three main feature - Attack, Defense and Equipment, there's rating for this features, you have to choose ship by judging it. You need to assign a crew list to start playing PvP. I was stuck at that for some moment, so thought to share this on.
pros:
- balanced ships
- cool detailed graphics
- independent game mode to try each ship against each ship
- popular global servers to match make, e.g. EU, NA, SEA.
- non-toxic community(currently)
- free to play - as per,  may,2016 announcement
- you can win every match without spending a penny
- open development
- simple UI, options and controls, supportive for beginners
- MMR based matchmaking
- relatively small download size (~ 3gb)
cons:
- only available in PC (currently)
- playerbase too small, sometime had to wait 3minutes find a match
- takes time to load
- no singleplayer campaign
- only one game mode available currently(actually it isn't a con)
-  that's all!
Note: there's no explicit button for chat-to-all. you can use, right shift + enter or press enter then click left ctrl.
Note: Upgrading points can be used only to upgrade team ships, nor team base neither captured stations.

Call of Duty? Expansion? Impossible! Oh but it is and it was the only expansion ever made to date. Developed by Grey Matter Studios, Call of Duty United Offensive is an expansion to the original Call of Duty. It contains a new campaign split up into three smaller campaigns where you fight as a British, American and Russian soldier during battles spanning across World War II.
As an expansion it's pretty good. You got new locations and battles to fight in, some new weapons, and some tweaked gameplay. I forgot to mention how in the original Call of Duty the MG42 was quite hard to shoot at because the muzzle flash blocked out nearly the entire screen however they tweaked it making it much more useful to use in United Offensive. The best levels tended to be the starting and/or second levels of each smaller campaign. The American, British and Russian campaigns had really good starting levels however the last levels of the American and Russian campaign were quite annoying as you had to defend a specific location until help arrives and it was annoying getting shot at all sides.
I can't really say much more. It's more Call of Duty and has a decent campaign, sadly I still couldn't find a game in the multiplayer which was kind of dissapointing. If you're going to play the original Call of Duty then most likely you should pick this up as well in one of the bundles when it goes on sale. Fallout 4 is a wide expansive world that can be filled with rich backstory and replayable side quests - if you decide to mod that in, same with very high res textures, over the lesser quality and more storage intensive the 58GB free pack you get. Fallout 4 can be fun to play even without DLC, and for a first play-through, even without mods (which is a good thing, if you want to get achievments from this game). And well... talking about the mods, there is an extremely large selection of them on the internet, completely free of charge, including some which expand the bredth of the game beyond some of the DLCs which you can buy, however, there is one recent point of contention in the Fallout 4 community, and that is to say "paid mods" from the creation club. Bethesda claims that these mods (or "mini DLCs" as they want us to think of them as) are not paid for, as you utilise an ingame currency, called "Creation Club Credits" of which, you have to buy, in clunky packages which almost guarantee that you will over pay for the mods. Along with said mods being lackluster - what with free alternatives that are superior to the paid ones, you often have to go on a quest that dictates a very similar quest line of "go here, kill the things, get the item, leave" or just drops the item in your inventory - at whateveer time in the playthrough you are at, which can result in unbalanced gameplay, what with the player coming out of the vault at level two with a shotgun ready to kill everything in the wasteland. Of course, the paid mods would not be such a large sore spot if Bethesda hadn't already attempted to roll out paid mods and had them fail catastrophically, and with them attempting to edge their way into that market again, you can expect that the fallout and maybe even the elder scrolls series will fall under the drudgery of constant, endless micro-transactions to get that gun a bit earlier, a bit more mana to take down that boss or even just more carry weight, so you can fast travel back to your mountain of hoarded items which start to lag you out if you stare at it for too long.
all in all, I would have recommended this game before the 28th august, but now I have to sadly let it die in infamy, as the way bethesda is going, if we don't shut down their money grab now, well.. the next few games may be the ridiculous parodies that we laugh about, such as "the start menu DLC - £5.99".

Apparently, Assassin's Creed was suppossed to have ended at AC3. After that, the story, conspiracies, and well anything at all interesting or unique that made this game stand out was thrown out the window.  I didn't buy Black Flag once I had heard it was going to be about pirates and have nothing to do with the actual AC backstory or universe practically for that matter; I am unsure what compelled me to try Unity. I guess I thought the return to an urban setting would mean AC would be back on track. AC Unity just goes further and further of track. There is absolutely nothing about this game that is relevant to Assassins Creed when it comes to the detailed immersion in the brotherhood you have had before in past games, and their struggle/plight. ACU is just way, way, way to watered down to be appealing to long time fans.
The only accomplishment this game can attempt to claim is the super detailed and stunningly visual game world that IS better than any other AC ever. But it is totally glitched to hell, constantly repetitive in terms of side quests, random events you come across while roaming, and even the npc types and the interactions they have with each other.  And there aren't even shops anymore in the game. Only one hub to get ammo and gear from, which is either the assassins vendor in your HQ or the start button. YES, you can just click start and get what ever consumables you need. There is truelly no point to actually exploring and getting immersed in the game world, like in AC II for example.
I kept playing the game till I got about a quarter of the way through the story. I kept believing that I would end up playing a mission where my hopes would be revived and I would find a well designed level that was challenging and made me fell like a badass assassin again. Things only got worse, and worse, and worse as time went on. Eventually I found myself on a level where you had to listen in on and follow a target as they made their way through a mansion where there were just hordes of enemies crammed into each floor, just standing around. They didn't even have meanigful or well thought out patrol patterns. One cluster of three enemies walked infinitely around in a ten foot circle next to a flight of stairs. Unbelievable.
I  eliminated all of the outside guards before going in side, which was a breeze as enemies literally can not see what is happening directly in front of them if they are more than fifteen feet away, rooftop guards are especially like this. Once inside I was spotted quickly due to the cover system not allowing you to snap around corners, and then eliminated ten guards on the first floor, making loads and loads of noise in the process, there were even gunshots, and still I did not fail the mission or get penalized. I mean, the guards on the floor above which I could see with eagle vision were not even alerted. AT ALL.
Once I finished the mission, I exited the game and have not played it since. There was no point to. The only fun and somehwat enjoyable part of the game for me, going around the city clubbing random enemies over the head with my sharpshooter's musket, got boring fairly quickly. And that mansion mission was the last straw. There needs to be a "Lemon Law" for games, because ACU is just blatantly broken and unfinished. It is to the point that it is unplayable.

Another day, another Hidden Object Game. This time around it's Grim Legends 2: Song of the Dark Swan. I'm going to go ahead and say that this is easily the best HOG I've played yet. Admittedly, it doesn't sound like much since this is also only the fourth one I've played, but all the same. With its combination of spectacular art, great music, a solid story, and quality puzzles, I can't think of a reason for genre fans to avoid this title.
The plot starts off simple enough. You're a herbalist of some fame, and a king rolls out the red carpet, in the hopes that you can cure his queen's ailment. The queen can't speak and...eh well the rest is on you to figure out. There's a mystery to solve, a handful of twists and turns, and you're going to figure it all out and save the day. However, if you fail then...that would be silly! This is a HOG after all, the answer is always one click away. How you proceed is up to you. Skip through all of the puzzles to focus on the story? Or take your time and get your money's worth?
For those unfamiliar with the genre, a good Hidden Object Game is more than just finding trinkets. HOGs should also offer numerous puzzles, a compelling plot, and quality presentation. Like most adventure games, a HOG doesn't have much in the way of replay-value, so it's massively important that the few hours of game-play it offers are memorable. Grim Legends 2 is very successful in this regard. The art-direction employs some great usage of colors, and despite lacking 4k or even 2k resolution, can still astonish with its well-drawn environments. For the most part, the hidden object portions of this game are designed intelligently. The pieces are creatively hidden, and are sometimes unique, such as pieces of an elaborate necklace, or the parts of a magnifying glass. The difficulty is also well-balanced, so you'll feel that at least some effort is necessary. This makes progressing through the adventure more fulfilling.
As far as nitpicks go (don't act so surprised!) the NPCs can look rather strange. It's hard to describe. They have this uncanny valley when they speak to you. Perhaps that isn't the right term for it, but it certainly looks unnatural. Aside from being a blemish on the otherwise fantastic art-direction, weirdo NPC faces isn't a big deal. The herbalist's voice-acting is a little suspect at times, but again...nothing major. Everyone else in the game picks up the slack quite nicely.
All in all this is a great title to look into whether you're already fans of the genre, or a newcomer looking for a worthwhile entry point.

It pains me to do this, but I'm afraid I have to amend my original review. When Firaxis patched the game on November 8th, 2016 to add the ability to tour the Avenger with a controller (something I personally couldn't give a hoot in hell about) they broke the game so badly that it was literally unplayable. They issued a hot fix (which took a bloody week) that solved the targeting problem but have never fixed the interface problems on the squad selection screen, making it next to impossible to distribute your weapons and gear to your selected soldiers. Playing with the loot mods, which I particularly enjoy, compounds the problem exponentially.
Firaxis also introduced some nasty bugs with that patch. It crashes regularly on startup as well as during gameplay, and at least one bug is utterly game-breaking. The only time I attempted to play Ironman after the patch, the game froze during an alien turn phase and I had to reload the save. After reloading, the issue persisted. It wasn't the alien's turn but it wasn't my turn either. I couldn't select any soldiers or perform any actions and I lost the entire campaign after investing over 40 hours to it.
Breaking a game with an unnecessary patch is bad enough, since it demonstrates an astounding lack of proper QC testing, but then not fixing it for a year (and counting) is so outrageous that I'm obliged to withdraw my recommendation. My original review is below, but I can't continue to recommend a game that has been abandoned after being purposely broken.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
As someone who has played over 1,300 hours of XCOM: Enemy Unknown and XCOM: Enemy Within, I was understandably excited about XCOM 2. I actually preordered it, which is something I almost never do. In fact, the last game I preordered was XCOM: Enemy Unknown. They improved an incredible number of gameplay aspects. Concealment is interesting, collecting loot and modding weapons is fun, the overwatch and sight indicators help tremendously, and the new destructable elements add tactical options. They also added random continent bonuses, lowered the reload action cost, improved character editing, added a character pool, and embraced community modding. These are all very welcome changes to the XCOM recipe. They tried to randomize mission environments with a pseudo-procedurally generated system that kinda works, but environments now suffer from a generic quality that makes them all seem similar. Even though the hand-crafted environments in XCOM EU/EW tended to get repetitive, I prefer them.
Everything isn't rosy, however. They totally screwed the pooch with mission structure. Unlike XCOM EU/EW, timed missions are the rule rather than the exception, so they quickly become very tiresome. Enemy Within successfully added some urgency to missions through the countdown timers on Meld, but it was optional. The risk versus reward element pushed you forward, but the world didn't come crashing down if everything turned to sh*t and you had to forgo the juicy Meld to deal with a deadly tactical situation. It was a lot of fun. The few timed missions in XCOM EU/EW added variety and were enjoyable when they appeared, but you were generally free to deal with things however you desired. I thought Shen's Last Gift introduced some novel mission structure, but an endless series of time-limited missions aren't novel, tactically diverse, or even particularly entertaining. Keep in mind that this is criticism of the base game. Community mods can change the way timers work or even completely remove them, though I question how removing the timers would improve gameplay. If they aren't an integral part of the mission design then why are they there? To make matters even worse, a timer rears its ugly head in the strategic gameplay as well. Rather than being free to choose missions whose rewards would help you accomplish multiple strategic objectives, the Avatar Project ticker forces you to always choose missions that slow its advancement. As a result, strategic depth is severely curtailed.
XCOM 2 also failed with something less tangible that makes a tremendous difference. In XCOM EU/EW the world and everyone in it is threatened by an alien invasion. You are invested from the beginning and emotionally hooked. Here, rather than fighting a tooth and nail defensive campaign, you are fighting an offensive campaign. The shift from being a desperate defender to being an aggressor just doesn't work as well. Yes, you are still the underdog, but the emotional investment you have from the onset in XCOM EU/EW isn't here. The gameplay mechanics are better but I don't care as much, and ultimately that makes the first game better.
I have to recommend XCOM 2, as it is actually pretty well done, but it isn't what I'd hoped for. While playing I constantly find myself wishing I was playing XCOM EU/EW with the improvements from XCOM 2, and that makes me a sad.

Lords Of The Fallen™ - A game created by CI Games and Deck 13, some people compare it to Dark Souls. I got this game from a polish newspaper CD-Action (not expensive, like 2/3 of price I saw in a box version in retail shop). I will discuss some element and then summarize them to conclusion which will be an answer for a - nowaday important - question: "Worth buying at normal price/discount/stay away as far as possible?"
Plot (+/-) - Here we have a story or Harkyn, a prisoner released to stop some kind of invasion. Here I can compare it to Dark Souls, because campaign can be discovered also by hidden "audio logs" rewarded for a small amount of an experience, a matter which we can easily omit. However it is not impressive (sometimes silly) and i got 1 problem with voice acting - synchronization with facial expressions. It is done weak and can make you frustrated, because other more difficult things are much better prepared. Side quest are also done poor - things are said in a vague way and i mostly ignored them. :/
Graphic/Optimization/Stability (++) - For a 2014 title game looks brilliant. Animation (except facial expression) are well prepared, world itself/enemies/bosses/our hero - beautiful. Even better than some of AAA games. Concerning optimization - Everything is fine, no fps drops during 26,5 hours of gameplay. Stability - No crashes at all.
Game mechanics (+) - Even most beautiful game will be crap, if game mechanics are crap. However here, we do not have to worry about this aspect. For warrior we can feel a difference between weapons, fights are very dynamic. We can also perform critical hits (look strange to me), which for most part of a game means instant death for our opponent. Other aspect I will not reveal (you will have more fun disovering them) but I can say with ease that they are top+. Controls are simple and even newbie in genre will learn them easily using mouse and keyboard, what i know could be difficult in DS even for good players. Here I must mention 2 aspects (appears also in DS) - hitbox bugs and wallthrought attacks. Watch out, because till know this matter is still not fixed. There is also one element - lock on camera on enemy - but I have not tested it in a serious way, so I will not say anything on this topic.
AI (++) - Again comparing to some AAA titles like Advanced Warfare this element suits well the present time and every battle requires another approach, and enemy will not come like lamb for a slaughter. Especially well prepared boss fight, where game shows its true difficulty.
World Presentation (+/-) - Beautiful graphic and consistent world, however modest in content - some elements often repeat.
Music (+/-) - Well prepared, fits the battle, but with 1 problem - sometimes it doesn't stop, sometimes doesn't start. Problem appears even today.
Fun (++) - Playing this game - satisfaction. Beating a boss after 10/15/20 approach gives you joy which you can't met in most of games.
Summarize - Worth buying, even for a full price. Joy after victory, graphic, game mechanics, boss fights are done well. However, the game is not perfect and some bugs still exists. If you look forward to buy some games from From Software in the future or simply look for a good experience, Lords of The Fallen is for you. ;)

This review is being made after the April update that rendered the game Free to Play and introduced the case system. i should also put a disclaimer saying that I bout into the Alpha and bought the highest priced package at the time, so there might be some bias.
First of, I would like to respond to some of the more vocal fans of the game that are complaining about the case system and claiming it's now a pay to win game. No. Some try to mislead you by saying that all but the starter crew are locked off and that this is causing a huge imbalance as people who pay unlock different crew. They are correct, you can only get the starter crew and do need to grind or pay to get other crew, but this does not affect game balance in any significant way. All crew are side-grades from each other, and while ships work better with crew that compliment their abilities, the affect is minimal and any specialized ship will lose something for it's upgrades. Any specialized ship can still be taken down by a starter crewed ship easily if that ship is used right.
Now that I got that out of the way, onto the review. Fractured Space is a unique game, taking elements from MOBAs and vehicle battle games like World of Warships, and for the sake of adding it in, Hero Shooter like Overwatch and Battleborn with the latter having a higher resemblance. The game relies heavily on team work, the correct ship composition and very heavily on how good yo are with your ship. The game can be a grind as you need EXP and DNA to earn ships and crew, but the starter ships give you everything you need for a fair and balanced team that can hold of most teams. Ships can be earned with EXP, which you get by playing games in ships of the same tech tree, and crew are acquired as random drops that you get in crates that also require DNA to craft. While the crew system is abhorrent, it doesn't affect the game that much and is the only major downside and is not as bad as others will have you think.
For an Alpha game, Fractured space shows a lot of promise and already lives up a lot of praise it gets. The gameplay is solid, although the UI needs some tweaks before release, and it looks amazing with the Unreal Engine. If you're into it, you could easily lose weeks to this game, and it hasn't even come out yet! Of the games flaws, other than the crate system, many of them are not the games fault. There still appear to be a massive amount of new players that don't know much about the game mechanics and the tutorial is still in need of touching up so that player will also learn how to synergize with their team mates. The two game modes are fun, although I have not played any Frontline and am basing that opinion on what I have seen, and it is always fun to ram your colossus into a disabled enemy Ghost. Overall, I recommend you get this game.

THE PROS:
- This game looks AMAZING. The art style is pefect for what it does. The shadowy figures, the backgrounds, the lighting... It's such a minimalistic style compared to other games today, and probably looks better than most.
- The variety in combat is strong. Everyone's skills are used differently in every combat scenario.
- Every character is varied and well-rounded, for the most part. Everyone has skills that you don't think of using, and then when you do, you wonder where they have been your whole life.
- Enemies have some wild variants to them, ranging from walking skeletons with clubs, to massive pigs wielding flails and shields.
- The stress system adds another layer of management, making your characters go crazy or become heroic depending on the situation.
- The music is dark and menacing, just as it should be.
- The announcer? Absolutely NAILED it.
- A full progression system for your town and characters to get new upgrades and skills.
THE MEH:
- The RNG. Some people either love it or hate it. You will absolutely love it at times, when you swamp through a group of skeletons, and hate it another when that ONE PIG AT THE BACK PUKES ALL OVER YOU AND ALL YOUR PEOPLE GET SICK BUT HE'S TOO FAST TO HIT AAAAAAA
- The mods. Not going to talk bad about them, but if you're looking for character mods, you pretty much only have reskins of existing characters. Most of the other characters that are added don't have sound effects, don't have proper art sprites, their skills don't match up with descriptions, or their characters just don't look right compared to others.
THE CONS:
- Repetitive areas after a while. You can only kill so many skeletons before you figure out that they arrive in the same 10 patterns or so when you travel.
- Curio. Interecting with the world around you is fun. Really, it is. You're supposed to use certain items on certain things to make sure they give you good effects (ex: holy water on a confessional booth). The problem comes when you get an unreasonable quirk from something that makes no sense (ex: getting rabies from reading a book on a shelf).
- Stressful and poisonous enemies. They're good on paper, but the amount of stress and poison they deal out from ANY POSITION is rediculous. Not to mention that they can dodge your attacks like nobody's business. Be ready to deal with a lot of stress and poison in your characters. I just think that toning it down slightly would be nice.
- Trinkets. Things that increase your stats in one way, but decrease them in another. Doesn't sound bad, until that item that gives you +2 dodge also takes away -10 speed, making you the slowest knight in the history of slow knights. Sometimes, having an empty trinket slot is the right choice, which just doesn't feel right.
- Quirks. When you complete a quest, every character has a chance of getting a quirk to change how they work (ex: +20% damage against skeletons, or +20% stress in the ruins). The only problem, is that these things pop up for no reason. I just swamped a bunch of pigs without taking a scratch. Why is my character suddenly afraid of bandits? I just beat a boss for the skeletons, but I suddenly just "catch" rabies? It's frustrating at times when your whole party get negative traits when you just had one of the best runs you could think of.
OVERALL:
The game is great, but can be very frustrating at times (as it was made to be), but I feel the frustration comes from unintended outlets rather than the intended ones.
I would give the game an 8 / 10. Definitely as great, unique game that deserves a try, but the small things just dig away at you

Don't be fooled by the mixed recent reviews. Seems like pretty much all the negative reviews recently are due to the fact that some people can't be bothered to read what they buy. They paid for alpha access before others and gain various benefits even now, but apparently they should get their money back now that it's open for all when this game was always supposed to be free to play. Which apparently was clearly stated on store page when they paid for it too.
The game seems pretty polished for early access, and mostly seems to be lacking in tech tree and perhaps different maps/game modes, but that's to be expected at this point. The game mode in this is mobaish two-lane push to win tug of war where you try capture recource zones in order to gain levels, and prevent enemy from leveling. In the middle of the map there is an shared objective called gamma which comes online for contest every few minutes and give general buff for the whole team to pretty much every stat and every subsequent buff gets stronger. The main objective, as usual, is the destruction of enemy home base.
I have only scratched the surface, but the game feel pretty tactical and the ships seem quite balanced and have some paper/rock/scissors mechanics to them. You have to keep an eye out for overall situation on both lanes and for gamma objective, and warp around the map as situation calls for it. It's a mighty feeling to warp in middle of a big fight at just the right time to turn around otherwise losing battle to your teams advantage and then take an important objective or even win the game afterwards as a result of your timely arrival on scene.
The "grind" is gathering experience with different manufacturer ships and then unlocking ships how every you like. You may need to unlock some ship before the one you want if they are in a same development line. The ships aren't tiered so they should be all equal in overall strength. Although some ships require more exp and credits to get than others. Different ships mostly have different stats, specialisations, accessories(skills) and playstyles so there is no hurry to open anything in regards of gaining more powerful ships, it's more of finding a ship to suit your playstyle and your team composition.
Overall this game has been a very positive surprise. I barely installed this because of the mixed reviews(because I've come to expect that mixed/negative reviews on f2p usually mean p2w which isnt the case here at all) so I feel that I must recommend this to anyone who might be put off by the mixed reviews of reading impaired petty people too. The game is solid and free so give it a try. It may or may not be your cup of tea, but in my opition this is good for what it is.

Age of Empires III: complete Collection is a small compilation consisting of Age of Empires III and the two expansion packs. I already recommend buying this over the retail version since there was an issue with it. If one was to purchase Age of Empires III then War Chiefs and Asian Dynasties retail, it would only allow the use of Asian Dynasties OR War Chiefs. So, one pro is that both expansions can be played at the same time.
Gameplay
Age of Empires III is an RTS that is set in colonial times. What is most appealing about the game is the beautiful graphics for the time and the amount of replayability. The effort that was placed in each nation was specific and displayed the obvious strengths and weaknesses of each nation after some experience. For example, one nation might be unable to build a tower type build, but have a unit or another building that allows better protection against enemies. This also limits the player somewhat since not all nations can just wall up and defend well like in Age of Empires or Age of Empires II.
Story

United Offensive is a major expansion pack for the original Call of Duty game. It improves on a few of the issues from the original game and features some incredibly epic missions. The game's campaign is structered similarly to the original game with 3 seperate military campaigns starting with a largescale American battle in Bastogne (Battle of the Bulge), easing into a slow and painfully boring British campaign in Italy, and ending with an epic battle with the Russians at Kursk.
Once again, Call of Duty's american missions are based strongly on the events of the 101st airbourne as seen in "Band of Brothers." You are tasked with fighting off a larger Nazi platoon in the wintery forests of bastogne as you wait for Pattons tank unit to relieve you and there's plenty of artillery, tanks, and firefights. You then have to attack a village crawling with nazi soldiers by moving up with your squad from the forest to some haystacks just like in the show. These missions are some of the best missions that this game have to offer and they're a lot of fun. Unfortunetly, once again, you are stuck as a British soldier doing boring "stealth" based missions that require infilitrating enemy strongholds and destroying artillery guns or getting into incredibly frustrating on rails car chases. And then finally, the game picks up the pace again with another largescale Russian battle sequence, this time taking place at Kursk. This time, instead of landing on beaches with several other soldiers, you are all packed into large trucks and are crossing open fields while planes fly by and blow up your allies nearby. You are then tasked with reinforcing the trenchlines and repelling a major german offensive. The campaign starts to lose its pace after this though, as you start fighting through the streets to eventually hold off a German attack on a railyard that is impossibly difficult. There are snipers, tanks, halftracks, MG42s, infantry, and worst of all... player seeking airplane bombing runs. That's right... during your defense of this entirely open railyard, you are forced to relocate from cover while being shot by all the above because the bombing runs that come ever 30 seconds will always aim for you. It's an incredibly frustrating mechanic that really ruined the finale of the game. But other than that, the gameplay was solid and a significant improvement over the original game.
The graphics were improved also. The textures and models look essentially the same, but the smoke effects that would later become a staple of the series are finally introduced in this expansion and still to this day look fantastic, especially after a massive allied bombing run or after blowing up a tank with a bazooka. The lighting also appears to have received a boost, with interior fires casting a bit of an orange glow on the walls that I'm pretty sure didn't happen in the original game.
The gameplay mechanics also recieved some attention. A sprint button was introduced, but unfortunetly the sprint is incredibly short, allowing you to only sprint about halfway from one position to another before you have to start walking again. The health system is still incredibly stupid and enemies still home in on you as soon as you try and fight back. Some new weapons were added in that are given plenty of time to shine like the silenced sten submachine gun or the bipod mounted MG42 that you can walk around with. However, the latter came be annoying because it takes forever to deploy the bipod, and you have to keep the right mouse button held down in order to keep it deployed, or it will reset the animation, which can really ruin its effectiveness considering you generally need it when mowing down a large concentration of soldiers crossing a field towards you.
Another thing I feel I should mention is that the sound design is fantastic. Bullets will wizz and snap past you if they're close by and you can hear all the dirt and snow spitting up in your face after a tank fires nearby. Rain sounds accurate and realistic which is generally not even done correctly in games that come out today in 2015. So cudos to Infinity Ward for nailing the sound design way back in the early 2000s.
So overall, I recommend this game as it continues the 101st airborne campaign into the Battle of Bastogne and also features another cool russian campaign. However, just be aware that the graphics are severely outdated, the gameplay has plenty of issues, and the British campaign is painfully dull.

Despite hearing good things about this expansion for the first Call of Duty, United Offensive does not meet up to the praise. The biggest problem COD:UO has is the fact that this game is the one that experiences the most growing pains in the series. This is reflected in the first few missions in the American campaign where the player has to suffer through respawning enemies, limited health, limited ammo, and ridiculous objectives that force the player to do everything. If there is a tank, YOU must be the one to find a rocket launcher to destroy it. If there is an enemy bunker, YOU must be the one to charge in to conquer it. The list goes on and on. On a video game standpoint, this is perfectly fine, in fact, Wolfenstein uses this type of gameplay to enforce a good power fantasy. United Offensive goes too far however, to the point that teammates are rendered useless and the idea that the battle was won by a team effort absurd.
These following statements are going to be a bit controversial but please keep reading. The combination of respawning enemies and suicidal objectives may not have been so bad if your health was not limited or if you had a way to suppress enemies into cover. Call of Duty 2 has regenerative health for the player and smoke grenades that cloak your advancement on the battlefield. These solutions may be a bit overkill but they do a great job of keeping the action moving forward instead of the previous games where a stray bullet would make you have to backtrack through the level to find a medpack. The whole issue about health would not have been mentioned if it wasn't for the fact that COD:UO makes you do everything in a battle, to the point when you wonder if you are actually a Navy Seal disguised as a Private.
The game does have a quick save feature, which you may have to use quite a bit because the game has very inconsistent checkpoints. There will be times when you have already completed several objectives before getting a checkpoint. At the very worst, you may even get checkpointed while getting shot or having grenade land near by you (and no, you cannot throw back grenades). I do understand that quick saving has its purpose in PC games, especially RPGs, however, action games benefit more from carefully placed checkpoints rather than quick saves. If the developer is smart enough, they can place checkpoints in safe areas or segments past cutscenes that help with the flow of the action.  United Offensive assumes you are going to be using quick save frequently and the game definitely seems to be crafted that way. The first Call of Duty does not seem to suffer from this problem too much, at the very least not on Normal mode. COD1 was crafted in a way that it can even be playable on a console, where you can't quick save at all.
Not everything was bad in Call of Duty: United Offensive. The music was great, sound effects were great, and the British and Russian campaigns were interesting (You even take part in a bombing raid with the British Airforce in one mission). There are even light machine guns with deployable bipods you can use to defend areas (which become useless once you find out that you can't deploy them on sandbags aside from the mission sensitive ones). If you are lucky, you may even come across a flamethrower you can use for a few seconds in the early Russian missions. Unfortunately, I cannot recommend COD:UO because COD1 and COD2 exist. I get the impression that United Offensive got the praise it did because there really was nothing like it at the time but now that there is, the problems I mentioned earlier do not stand the test of time. Unless you are a completionist, you should avoid Call of Duty: United Offensive.

After Quake's 1996 debut, multiple trends of 3D First Person design came about, one of which was Valve's Half-Life in 1998. In opposition to other FPSs that focused on a more heavily arcade-influenced gameplay (secrets, par times, quick action), Half-Life was almost entirely designed around a linear first-person narrative structure, watching the events unfold around them through the eyes of Gordon Freeman.
Half-Life's blend of story and gameplay is what sells the game. You participate in this fast-paced horror/science-fiction/action journey through an enormous scientific complex and it feels incredibly satisfying to do so. Watching the enviorment go through various shades of Underground Laboratory Bunker gives you a real sense of scale at how Black Mesa is.
The weapons are a huge component of the game's atmosphere, with different areas giving you different weapons, all of them fun to use in some way. The game takes full advantage of its weapon selection not just from a story perspective but a character perspective as well. Gordon is a young, relatively inexperienced researcher who fights against the expected norms in this scenario by repeatedly fighting his way through Black Mesa backpacking all manner of experimental and unconventional weaponry. Learning how to use all of them makes a playthrough so much more satisfying than if you were to just sprint through with just the first four guns you grab.
The first Half-Life stands well apart from other expansions, mods, and even its own sequel. Opposing Force and Blue Shift, while satisfactory expansions don't maintain the uniquely original aura of the first game. Black Mesa, despite touting itself as a remake, really only succeeds in presenting a more modern and realistic setting. The rest of the mod is just poorly-playtested gunk. It's just not as fun to play as the original game. Ditching Xen to chase the multiplayer carrot didn't help either. Half-Life 2 just isn't as interesting a game as the first one. It manages to simultaneosly have worse gameplay, story, and artstyle than the first game.

Don't be fooled by the mixed recent reviews. Seems like pretty much all the negative reviews recently are due to the fact that some people can't be bothered to read what they buy. They paid for alpha access before others and gain various benefits even now, but apparently they should get their money back now that it's open for all when this game was always supposed to be free to play. Which apparently was clearly stated on store page when they paid for it too.
The game seems pretty polished for early access, and mostly seems to be lacking in tech tree and perhaps different maps/game modes, but that's to be expected at this point. The game mode in this is mobaish two-lane push to win tug of war where you try capture recource zones in order to gain levels, and prevent enemy from leveling. In the middle of the map there is an shared objective called gamma which comes online for contest every few minutes and give general buff for the whole team to pretty much every stat and every subsequent buff gets stronger. The main objective, as usual, is the destruction of enemy home base.
I have only scratched the surface, but the game feel pretty tactical and the ships seem quite balanced and have some paper/rock/scissors mechanics to them. You have to keep an eye out for overall situation on both lanes and for gamma objective, and warp around the map as situation calls for it. It's a mighty feeling to warp in middle of a big fight at just the right time to turn around otherwise losing battle to your teams advantage and then take an important objective or even win the game afterwards as a result of your timely arrival on scene.
The "grind" is gathering experience with different manufacturer ships and then unlocking ships how every you like. You may need to unlock some ship before the one you want if they are in a same development line. The ships aren't tiered so they should be all equal in overall strength. Although some ships require more exp and credits to get than others. Different ships mostly have different stats, specialisations, accessories(skills) and playstyles so there is no hurry to open anything in regards of gaining more powerful ships, it's more of finding a ship to suit your playstyle and your team composition.
Overall this game has been a very positive surprise. I barely installed this because of the mixed reviews(because I've come to expect that mixed/negative reviews on f2p usually mean p2w which isnt the case here at all) so I feel that I must recommend this to anyone who might be put off by the mixed reviews of reading impaired petty people too. The game is solid and free so give it a try. It may or may not be your cup of tea, but in my opition this is good for what it is.

I review games to help fellow gamers decide whether they should purchase a game or not.  With that said, although I consider Half-Life as a classical MASTERPIECE and possibly one of the greatest games of all time, I will still list down game mechanics from the past that some people may not enjoy today.
Think of it like this: everyone enjoys flying modern-day commercial jets like the 747, but it doesn't mean however that everyone would like to fly in a DC-3 built in the 1940s despite it being labeled as the 'most significant transport aircraft' in history.
Half-Life is a narrative-driven linear first-person shooter (FPS) action game and is the debut (and signature) title of Valve.  Hailed as one of the greatest games of all time winning dozens of awards on release, Half-Life revolutionized the FPS genre in a way that no other title has done since Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake. This game has since been the industry standard on how to make a perfect FPS game which combines realistic gameplay, fun puzzles mechanics, a narrative-driven single-player experience with fast-paced multiplayer action.
The game follows the story of Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist working for the Black Mesa Research Facility that is involved in Weapons Development, Research on Teleportation Technology and occasional cloning of a Security Guard named Barney Calhoun.  When an experiment with an unknown alien crystal results in a catastrophic accident that opened a portal to an alien dimension named 'Xen', Gordon Freeman, wearing the H.E.V. Suit, must now travel across the entire Black Mesa facility to reach the Lambda Complex where he must enter a portal to Xen and kill the creature that is keeping the portal open for the alien invaders. Fight against Invading alien monsters and, at the same time, US Military operatives who are attempting to stop the invasion but is also trying to silence any surviving 'witnesses' of the Black Mesa incident.
+ First FPS game to fully incorporate a Narrative-Driven story (as opposed to the industry standard of maze gallery shooters which was the Wolfenstein 3D / Doom mechanic)
+ Excellent level designs
+ Realistic combat mechanics (may be not as realistic now in 2015, but 17 years ago it was)
+ Fun puzzles
+ Great sound effects
+ First FPS game to incorporate scripted sequences for its level transitions rather than cut-scenes
+ Relatively advanced AI (back in 1998), with enemies actively dodging, tactically retreating and often times baiting you into an ambush.
+ Fun fast-paced multiplayer action that set the foundations for Counter-Strike which started as a mere mod of Half-Life
+ Mods; although Half-Life is not the first video game to be modded, it is the first to have several such mods become their own full games that still retain their Half-Life heritage
+ Challenging difficulty modes (but this is a given since most old-school shooters were challenging)
- Perpetual sprint with optional walking by pressing “Shift” (as opposed to today's standard which is the reverse)
- No objective tracker (players may forget what they were doing especially if they haven't played in a while)
- Melee weapon needs to be equipped rather than bound to a hotkey (though CS:GO players won't have a problem with this)
is the only word that best describes Half-Life in my opinion.  Although some of its mechanics may not necessarily be applicable in today's (2015) standard, the same can still be considered as part of its charm, much like how most of us still enjoy watching old-school movies and TV shows.
. I, however, do recommend you purchase the Half-Life Anthology if you already have Half-Life 2 but if you don't have it, get Half-Life Complete.
The advent of Half-Life was a turning point in gaming history, most notably, the First-person shooter genre.  Before this game, the only FPS standard to be followed was Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake, with the first two being plotless maze shooters and Quake being the first to implement a backstory but still retained the maze-like levels. With Half-Life, developers saw a potential for FPS games to combine intense action and gunplay with effective narrative story-telling through leniar levels (which is heavily abused by some FPS games today) and realistic game mechanics (a title, which most people agree, was held by the Metal Gear Solid franchise, a third-person action game)
Let’s put this in an analogy: Wolfenstein 3D is the Wheel (basically invented the mainstream FPS genre), Doom is the Horse-Drawn Carriage (Doom made FPS games extremely popular, accessible and widespread), Quake is the Steam Engine (Quake bridge the gap between plotless maze shooters and  plot driven FPS games
) and Half-Life is the Ford Model T Car (Half-Life set the standard for modern day FPS games who's basic and essential features still survives today.)

I've been trying games of this sort for a few days now and I have to say that 'Grim Legends 2: Song of the Dark Swan' is my favorite so far. One of the games I have tried is GL: The Forsaken Bride but I really liked this one better, everything from the soundtrack (which is amazing), storyline, characters was very well thought out.
In GL2: Song of the Dark Swan, you are a healer summoned by the king to check on the health condition of his queen. Without giving it away, let's just say that you end up getting more than what you signed in for ehehe. The story is interesting, much more than the Forsaken Bride, more so that at some point you even feel sorry for what is happening to some of the characters and that is something that I didn't feel while playing FBride.
The minigames/puzzles are quite similar to the one's on FBride so you won't feel much difficulty there if you managed to do them on the previous game. However, If my memory serves me, I think there are a few that are a bit different but still doable.
As I mentioned before the soundtrack is beautiful, it gives a special touch to the story and makes it even more amazing and captivating. The artwork is fantastic, the characters are wonderfuly presented with nice details.
Oh and lets not forget the little helpers! On the Dark Swan they are super cute and, of course, you'll get more than one. For those of you who don't know, on Grim Legends games you usually have little guys that help you advance in the story (don't worry they don't work as hints or cheats, etc).
The only thing that I liked a bit more on the Forsaken Bride than on Dark Swan was the Bonus Content. I felt that on FB it worked better as a continuance of the main story and I didn't felt that with the DS bonus content.
If you like games like this then I suggest buying it, being it in a bundle, on sales or at regular price, it's well worth the purchase :)
