"Grim Legends 2: Song of the Dark Swan" is a tough one to rate.  On one hand, Artifex Mundi (AM) has improved their Achievements so they aren't mutually exclusive.  In other words, we're not forced to make two run throughs to get all Achievements (yay!).  Also, the graphics seem to be a bit sharper and brighter than earlier games.  On the other hand, the voice acting is much worse than normal.  Some of the voice acting is on par with other AM games (i.e., tolerable).  But, the queen's voice acting is bad and the various children's voice acting is utterly horrible.  I cringed every time I had to click on those kids and listen to their "acting."  Ugh.  To go along with the bad voice acting, the story is even worse than usual for these casual adventure Hidden Object games (HOGs).  So, instead of an OK-cutesy story, this one tends towards the OK-silly side.  If it weren't for the dead bodies lying around, I'd even lean towards it being written for kids (especially in the Bonus Chapter).  I'd also like to mention that even though this game is classified as a HOG, most of the puzzles are NOT technically HOGs:  they're FROGs (Fragmented/Fractured Object Game).  Plus, most of the HOGs are of the type where you have to find a bunch of fairies or a bunch of flowers and not of the type where you have a hodgepodge of various items hidden among other miscellany.  Of course, that could be good or bad, depending on your tastes.
Unfortunately, I didn't properly record my actual game play time.  So, I can't give the exact duration of the game.  But, it took me about 8 hours to finish the whole thing with 100% Achievements:  a little over 6 hours for the main game and 1.7 hours for the Bonus Chapter.  So, with the pluses and minuses noted above, coupled with the slightly short game play, I'm recommending the game.  But, only if you can find it on sale.  I'd say you should buy it if you can find it for less than six dollars.

So I just finished this game and boy am I glad I bought it, despite the mixed reviews. People are constantly comparing it to Dark Souls, which is a franchise I absolutely love, when they should treat this game as a standalone game. Sure, it has many similarities to Dark Souls, which is the reason I bought it in the first place, but it also gives the players new challenges and possibilities when it comes to playstyle and gameplay. I would say this is a good introduction game for the Dark Souls franchise, in the terms this has a lot of the same mechanics but gives less frustration and easier opponents. Of course, I died now and then, but not nearly as much as in Dark Souls. Which can be a good thing if you`re not in the mood for the constant "heads up" and stressful fights. Don`t get me wrong, LOTF gives you plenty of challenges and tough battles, but if you use your experience points correct and your gear set wisely, your opponents will no match for your superiority.
I really enjoyed some of the boss battles, mostly the tough ones, since every boss has different moveset which needs to be learned in order to utilize their "recharge time". In these boss battles there are, unlike Dark Souls, room for mistakes. Which makes the battles seem "easy" because you can kill most of the bosses in one try, but it is only because you can make mistakes in the same battle and yet be victorious. And the loot reward is very satisfying, although most of the loot is strength based, some is agility and few are faith. As I went with agility, I also upgraded my faith to 20 which gave me the option to choose from balanced assasin to tank paladin. I therefore felt like I could change up my gameplay instantly and all new loot was always exciting!
Although I like the Dark Souls franchise better, this game does not deserve all these bad reviews. It was a solid game and I enjoyed it very much and it even exceeded the Dark Souls in the terms of graphic resolution and visual presentation. It looks amazing and the dark gothic world drawed me in and set the mood troughout the game. But one thing that I really liked was the design of Harkyn`s armor. He looked like an absolute badass and the design kept getting better and better. One time I simply had to change my playstyle just because that gearset looked so cool.
I absolutely recommend this game and although the story was a bit confusing to start with, the more I played the more I learned about the lore, the world and the realms. At the end I couldn`t lay it from me because the story was so intense and it ended with me beating the game at 06:14 AM instead of going to bed at 01:30 which was my original plan. And that my friends, is the definition of a good game.

For the mechanics, I love them. The skill upgrading, descending-mechanic when parkouring, it's all very clever and adds more to the game. I've also spent some time editing my outfit, trying to look badass, which was also fun for me. I've just completed all the 12 sequences, which was quite a lot of fun for me. The plot was a bit.. less than I expected, yet I still did enjoy it.
I've also had a lot of fun in co-op so far with my friends, just messing around, completing crowd events and just having tons of great moments with eachother. Co-op missions are also fun, trying to synchronise assassinations with your fellow assassins to gain more points and just having that amazing feeling when it looks so cool to take them out together like you were well-prepaired.
Notable
+ Skills
+ Parkour mechanics
+ Greater loadout customization
+ Co-op is very enjoyable
+ Active city, with change frequently
+ A lot of things to do (crowd events, side missions..)
- Bugs (getting fixed!)
- Framerate issues for most (getting fixed!)
- A lot of the same sort activity/mission
- Companion app neccessary for completionists
I'd give it an 8.5 when they end up fixing most important bugs and issues, for now.. a 7.

I'm not generally impressed by casual games or hidden object games, but this was really well done -- enough that I'm now on the lookout for other well-reviewed games from this company that go on sale.
It's an adventure game, in which you go from screen to screen looking for objects to help you on your quest, and along the way are basic puzzles to solve.  There is occassionally a hidden object puzzle, but not nearly as many as I was expecting.  It was a good pace, the art was great, and there wasn't any point at which I was really stumped.  More to the point, I was able to find all of the objects within a couple of rooms, and never felt like I was wandering all over the place trying to pixel hunt.
The story was interesting to follow, though obvious to where it was going.  Most of the voice acting was pretty good -- at least compared to other casual games I've played.  There was only one or two characters (younger boys) that I was taken out of the game by.
One minor note.. if you have a tablet, the games seem to be quite a bit cheaper there ($5 versus $10), but the steam sales can get down a bit further if you watch for them.

A number of games use a narrative as a framing device to tie their events together. Most however do so to justify taking the player between vastly differing locales. Bastion sets itself apart from many games in that the narrative follows along with the character during gameplay. Imagine for a moment that Morgan Freeman had the accent of a southern gentlenman. Logan Cunningham delivers an impressive performance the breathes life into a world long after it has been taken by "the calamity." The protagonist does not speak a single word and the narrator never puts words in his mouth making the character truly feel like an extension of the player. The developers quite literally thought of everything that could be reasonably be given some kind of  commentary and did so. Items, weapons, the in-game challenges. All delivered in a smooth fashion that makes you feel like you're listening to a campfire story. Gameplay is also very entertaining with excellent weapons and upgrades. Highly approved.

Pros:
Technically robust.
Aesthetically pleasing visuals.
Cons:
Frustrating, slow and unsatisfying game mechanics and puzzles.
Pacing problems.
Ham-fisted story.
Extremely annoying time buffers in the levels to accomodate audio narrative.
My biggest personal gripe with the design of this game are all the forced waiting periods between puzzles, such as slow-opening doors, slow-moving elevators or poitlessly long corridors, which don't adapt to the player's pacing at all and will force you to wait idly in silence if you stopped to look or explore while the audio-only narrative played out.
The audio narrative should've been playing during the puzzles, not in between!
Or at least speed up the arbitrary waiting points if the audio already stopped playing!
And to add insult to injury, the achievements indicate that there are hidden secrets in some stages, so exploration is both incentivized (with secrets) and punished (with pointless waiting if you lingered a bit between puzzles).
I can tolerate a pointless story, but not when it gets in the way of the game proper.
As for the core of game, I'd describe it as "Portal-esque, but oddly unsatisfying."
Most of the game is spent trying to guide balls or cubes through obstacle courses by remotely triggering fixed gadgets in the level, which turns out to be a boring, repetitive and frustrating task.
I imagine some people will love what this game has to give, but I was not one of them, and I generally can't recommend it.

8/10 - Here's why.
This is not your typical turn based game. In fact, I would go as far to say that, it mostly isn't a turn based game.
A large contributing factor to this game involves managing a town and I would say that if you see this game as a management style game, more than a fighting game, you will actually find it entertaining when the random number generator messes with you.
You, the player are the mayor of 'sh%t goes wrong all the time town'. Your role as mayor is to mitigate the damage from said sh%t going wrong. As the mayor you have a whole bunch of employees. Those employees, like people in real life, winge and complain about stuff. One might have a saw arm, so he can’t hit as hard. One might not like beasts, so he is scared of them more. One employee might have a bad case of mud bum and you have to send him to the doctor. So as the mayor, you have a choice. Do I spend money on my employee to help him? Or do I make him redundant and fire him.
And then some stupid bird comes along and steals all your stuff. So you have to deal with that. Then people attack your town...so much bad stuff happens. It’s all about the mitigation. You will lose stuff, it's just how much stuff will you lose? You may have to send one of your employees on a suicide mission to save heaps of other stuff. Or you can gamble all your best fighters in the hope you win and get the glory.
The worst thing you can do with this game is have this attitude; "I have a level 6 healer, I've named her Daisy and I love her and never want her to die". I'm telling you now. DAISY WILL DIE. You need to get out of this mindset and think more like the CEO of a major company. If your employee dies, just hire another one - life goes on, the wheels keep turning.
PROS -
- Unique game style. Mixes management with turn based combat
- Eerie atmosphere/graphics. It does well painting the picture of scary dungeons
- Real consequences. There is no scum saving here. Everything you do is permanent. So you have to think about every choice you make.
- Constantly on edge. I find that every time I go into a dungeons I am on guard. Generally, it isn’t the whole "beat heaps of trash and then fight a hard boss" scenario. Every encounter could mean your doom.
CONS
- If you are a defensive sort of player like me, the game kind of forces you into this survival mode where you just grind low level torchless dungeons, with higher level players in order to save up money. This can become repetitive.
- A few UI issues need improving. Eg, trinket management is very annoying as it stands now. I will often spend 2 or 3 minutes per dungeon sorting them out due to the UI.

Call of Duty United Offensive is an expansion pack for the first Call of Duty. Once again we will take on the role of three different soldiers from the USA, UK and Russia respectively. We start things off as the Americans in a snow covered Belgium. The snow doesn't make any difference to the gameplay but it is something that wasn't in the base game so it does give United Offensive it's own style. You will quickly find out that this dlc has much more fierce and unpredictable battles. It will keep you on your toes and raises the difficulty quite high right from the beginning. UO introduces a couple of new guns like silenced machine guns and flamethrowers for your nazi killing pleasure. They are uncommon unfortunately, I would have loved for more time to use the flamethrower.
Like the original you are nearly always accompanied by fellow soldiers and this time around they are a lot more useful. They can hold their own and are way more likely to actually kill the people shooting at them. It may be do to AI improvements or the fact that you will be spending a lot of your time in this dlc fighting close quarters. UO has much more fighting in villages and condensed spaces so carrying a weapon suited for that is a must. Unfortunately some levels spawn way too enemies out of the same locations which makes shooting them kind of tedious as another nazi will sprout out of thin air to take their place until it is time to move on. It also features far more moments were you must defend a location for a given amount of time which almost starts to feel like it's there to pad out the dlc.
It took me 6 hours to beat the dlc which is quite close to the what it took me to get through the base game.  No longer are the three Allies campaigns intertwined together instead you play through the whole American campaign then switch to the British when it is done. I much prefer it this way as it helps you keep track of the characters and makes the journey much more consistent than randomly teleporting your view to different events like in the base game. In the British campaign you will be riding in both a boat and a warplane. The plane section is pretty cool as it has you running in the interior to pilot different turrets and fix issues but it goes on too long and both vehicle sections just play out with you endlessly shooting from a turret.
Russian campaign does allow you to pilot a tank which was a fun distraction. It also lets you call in artillery strikes via binoculars at one point but you have to look at a very specific point and it comes off as nothing more than a gimmick. Fortunately the main bulk of the levels are very good and have been designed as to challenge returning players from the base game. Whether this difficulty is a good thing is up for debate but from my experience it kept it from feeling like this dlc is just more of the same even though it pretty much is. I don't believe it has any new additions to the soundtrack either which is disappointing as the composer is amazing.
Overall United Offensive tries new things but it is very much more of the same. If they would have toned down the padding thrown in to make the dlc seem longer I would say these campaigns surpass the ones found in the original. The multiplayer seems to have very few people left and some servers have bots to fill up the lobby. It is completely separate from the base game so the already small amount of people still playing CoD1 and UO have been split. You will need Call of Duty 1 to play United Offensive, this is not a stand-alone expansion pack. In the end of the day this is still a lengthy and exciting expansion pack that knows what made the original so good and made it better. Recommended to those that have completed the original and would like to take the fight to previously unseen countries like Italy and Belgium.

Every PC gamer on the face of the Earth will have heard about Half-Life, Valve’s first product, due to its immense popularity ever since its release in November 1998. Half-Life really is one of those games you have to play before you die. I unfortunately missed out on this classic as a child due to being predominantly a console gamer but have finally gotten around to playing it via Steam and I must say it was a pleasant and enjoyable game to play.
The player steps in the shoes of Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist employed at the secret underground teleportation research facility Black Mesa. In the due course of the teams’ research, experimentations and developments, something goes disastrously wrong and creates something called the Resonance Cascade which starts to flood the human world with alien-like creatures from a parallel dimension.
The game runs on the legacy Goldsrc engine and the gameplay reminded me of the styles I’ve observed in the original Thief games which used a completely different engine (Dark Engine). Initially, my impressions of the controls were that Gordon Freeman moved too fast, but I adapted to the game’s controls and this quickly subsided. The gameplay is a simple, intuitive and generic first person shooter (not generic in terms of Call of Duty) that plays out in a linear fashion. The linear world is by no means a negative aspect of the game because this game is best presented in a linear style due to its story. There are no inter-gameplay cutscenes and the player views the world uninterrupted through the eyes of Gordon Freeman. A arsenal of weapons are at your disposal to combat the feral Marine soldiers and alien creatures in any manner you feel comfortable. The signature crowbar is something best remembered from the series. The game provides a decent challenged on medium difficulty, but doesn’t provide an excruciating experience of pulling your hair out whilst shouting obscene things at your monitor with an evil frown.
With this game’s age in mind, one aspect of its design is its character models. Whilst, decent a lot of them are recycled and lack in variety. I remember about three typical Black Mesa scientists (an Einstein looking man, a black man, and a middle-aged white man). On the other hand, there is variety in the enemies which are conceptually intriguing ranging from leaping headcrabs similar to the creatures in the Alien films, ceiling dwelling Barnacles that suck you up with their tongues, as well as about a dozen more.
In a nutshell if you fancy having a blast from the past and either experiencing a classic for the first time or revisiting it, then grab a crowbar and get smashing headcrabs. That is, grab the crowbar in the game... not in real life.

While Grim Legends 2 isn't particularly inventive with most of its puzzle design, the presentation is fabulous and makes the game a joy to play. The puzzles are still fun, even if they stick a little too closely to the formula employed by the first game in the series, and by seek-and-find games in general. Most of the puzzles probably won't give most people pause, but they are varied and enjoyable for casual play.
The graphics are, by far, this game's greatest strength. They're sumptuously drawn, just like in the first Grim Legends. Progressing through the game is rewarded with eye candy in the form of beautiful scenery. You'll meet friendly, helpful creatures along the way, and one of the creatures even plays an unexpected part in the bonus chapter, which I thought was refreshing. I took my time, admired the art, and enjoyed this game's classic fairy tale atmosphere.

This game has done an incredible job capturing the spirit of hacking. Although by necessity, the procedures are highly simplified, the approach is rooted in practice and demonstrates how even secure networks can be compromised through a domino effect of lesser vulnerabilities. Topple the weakest link and the strongest will follow. Your target may be impenetrable at first. But what about cracking the defenses on an unsecured edge workstation -- breaking into an employee's laptop is far simpler. Once in, you can read the owner's emails, learn their passwords, snoop through files of mostly useless documents for the juicy bits, and finally, advantages and privileges under arm, launch additional attacks deep into the heart of the network. It's neat, and you won't have Interpol knocking at your door afterwards.

There's even chests that cannot be opened without a companion app (which doesn't work half of the time) and costumes locked behind their ridiculous AC Initiates system, which isn't even fully functional.
This game:
1) was released too early; should have had more testing done
2) is gameplay-wise & unlock-wise flawed; e.g. macrotransactions, weird unlocks
3) has annoying reminders that there's other things to do but play the game (initiates, companion app, uplay, etc)
4) has a rather disappointing story; e.g. Napoleon doesn't even appear more than THREE times, even though he was cites as a major character; some parts are good, some parts are just... boring
5) runs poorly; patches have been promised but you will most likely still need beefy hardware (avoid for now -- still poor performance as of patch 4)
It's not all bad. If you enjoy AC games, you might want to consider it down the line (if its issues are patched!). But for now, it was a major disappointment, and I wasn't even hyped that much. It's a beautiful game with a lot of flaws and annoyances. So, unfortunately, for now, I cannot recommend this game.

Artifex Mundi is a name that I associate with good quality games. I enjoyed the previous "Grim Legends", so I was really looking forward to this one.
The game has wonderful artwork. Very detailed and colorful.
There's a good variety of them and they are all fairly easy to solve. A tip for someone else: When you need to guide the princess wood piece across the map... don't drag the piece. Just click where you want her to go. I wish I knew that before raging because the piece kept jumping around and breaking the puzzle.
The hidden object scenes dosen't overload every scene with thousand of objects. All objects are clear and in a realistic size for the environment they are in. Everything is easy to find once you know what you are looking for. There were perhaps 2-3 objects which were a bit colorless that took a harder time to find.
It was unusually grim for a Artifex Mundi game. But I like that, it added suspence to the story and even if you didn't get to know the characters too well, you still felt very sorry for them. It deals with a lot of emotions of even the background characters, such as guilt, regret, pain and grief.
It isn't awful (except for the children), but it is the same woman as every other game. Can't they hire someone else? She is okay, but obviously still can't bother to do any form of shouting or screaming in terror. 2 out of 3 times she doesn't even bother, even though it clearly says "Ah!" in the subtitles.
The person you control is only known as "healer" and all she does is make healing brews out of herbs and solve the mystery. I just didn't like her for some reason. Usually I don't care that much about the anonymous main character, but this one was so dense. You figure things out long before she even puts anything together. I guess for the sake of the story she has to be dumb so the player can figure things out on their own, but most things are too obvious not to figure out on your own. She even finds a book that has the solution painted and she still doesn't get it! I can overlook this though for the sake of "story needing to unfold" and if the main character spoils it to early, it might ruin the pace of the story.

Grim Legends 2 is a beautiful fragmented object game set in a fairy tale land. It’s not as memorable as its predecessor, but it can be a great addition to the library of any Artifex Mundi fan.
Grim Legends 2: Song of the Dark Swan is a sequel in name only. The fairy tale setting remained, but everything else changed– including the sub-genre, which is now fragmented object.
The story is a spin on the Grimm fairy tale ‘The Twelve Brothers’: a heartbroken evil sorceress curses a kingdom, turns the seven sons of the royal family into swans, and their sister mute. You start the game several years later, after said sister married and had a child, whom is promptly kidnapped. Your task is, naturally, to save the infant and break the curse while you’re at it.
The fragmented object (and the few hidden object) scenes all have the usual high Artifex Mundi quality, whereas the conventional puzzles are a bit repetitive. The story uses a rather strange route with a lot of backtracking. This can make life pretty overcomplicated on the highest difficulty, but it can also give the game an unusually long play time for its worth.

Got this game about a month ago, as I've been waiting for a good discount on it.  I have played it obsessively since then and can honestly say I've enjoyed myself every step of the way through a normal playthrough and currently pretty deep into my second character in  'survival difficulty'.
- Its not a very good Fallout RPG.  If you compare this to the earlier games in the series expecting more of the same you will be disappointed.  There are very few meaningful choices to make that impact the story outside of choosing which of the major factions you will have to wipe out to finish the story.  I like the writing better than Fallout 3's, but it is still far behind the quality of 1/2 and New Vegas in my opinion.
-  Skills and perks are dumbed down and fairly standard fare compared to the pros and cons perks of the first games, or the 'wild wasteland' perk from New Vegas.
-  The recently added Creation Club.  This thing is an abomination.  Advertised as 'more like mini DLC than paid mods', this  thing lets you purchase overpriced basic mods such as backpacks, new colors on your pip boy or a new power armor suit.  Or the cringy Giddyup Buttercup Horse Armor.  What is even more egregious is that the service downloads and installs all the mods for sale even if you don't care about using any of them.  Even with the pitiful choice of mods for sale on CC so far, the install size of the game went up by over 2GB, and will only go up as more content is added to it.  This is such pathetically poor design it is almost physically painful to even think about how stupid the people in charge of thumbing this feature up are in the head.
-  Performance problems, in the busier downtown areas of the game.  My PC isn't great so I'm okay with this, but it seems to be affecting the vast majority of other players as well.  Sustaining stable 60 FPS in the busiest downtown places is but a pipe (gun) dream for most players, even on very expensive hardware.  Similarily, playing with highest quality shadows and godrays on also has a completely unreasonable performance hit.
-  As usual, as hefty injection of mods to fix bugs and improve various aspects of the game is required.  You will want mods for letting you know what your character will say during dialog instead of just seeing options for what kind of mood you want to reply with.  You will want mods for deconsolifying various aspects of the UI.  You want mods for disabling companion fall damage so they dont fall off highrises becoming 'downed' and and requiring a stimpack within a short time limit (literally impossible to reach in time, if you have to go through an interior or take run a ways to take a lift or such to get down to them) before they return to wherever they were recruited from.  You want mods for removing object limits in settlements.  You want a sorting mod, so you can actually look at a piece of gear and compare things in a practical way.
-  Mechanically, it is a FAR better action shooty game than FO3/NV.
-  The most interesting game world to explore yet in the Fallout series.  The Commonwealth is a big and exciting playground.  You also learn more about Boston and its history in this game than you did of the places visited in the older games, props for that.
-  Settlement building, while optional and ultimately a giant waste of time, are to me a very fun way to waste my time.
-  While this is not a great Fallout RPG, it is
.  I've had a great time getting sucked into the many stories of tragedy and morbidity, of the delicious alternate history post apocalypse Fallout world, yet again.

NOTE: United Offensive REQUIRES/NEEDS the original game to be installed to function.
United Offensive takes almost everything great from the original Call of Duty and builds upon it. New larger maps, a campaign as long as a standalone Call of Duty are on offer up-front. Behind these large offerings are smaller but notable additions, such as driveable vehicles and new weapons for each force in the game.
The campaign is slightly shorter than the base games by about 3 missions. The campaign itself is still about as long as, possibly longer than what is offered in Advanced Warfare, a definitely longer than Modern Warfare 2 and 3's single player. The American missions take you across France in large battles for control of towns, fields and ridges in the besieged countryside. The British missions start you in a RAF bombing raid as a plane gunner before switching to covert missions for the SAS. The Russian missions follow a small unit as they fight their way to Kharkov to liberate it from Nazi invaders. The campaign features the usual Call of Duty missions where you do slightly different things from the usual infantry boot work, such as drive-by turret sections, the RAF section and the Soviet tank mission which is similar to the tank mission in the originals Soviet campaign. Overall, the campaign is well made, the variety of missions under such a tight gameplay build is something that this and the original have that the modern games lacks.
This helps the gameplay factors. The lack of regenerating health means that you never feel like a super-soldier. You will probably want squad members to take point to avoid getting your face shot off by an unexpected MG42 gunner. The levels are built for PC players and the maps are built for vehicle traversing as well as on-foot movement, so a scale not present in later instalments is clear.
Visually, the game has aged. Animation looks hilarious sometimes, the faces look really bad. The environments look a little middy, but are large and grand. On higher settings (which I think a toaster can do now), the environments are more than passable. Forcing Anisotropic Filtering cleans up a lot of the problems with the games textures. Although the game is not beautiful, it is passable and the visuals never interfere with the game itself.
Audio-wise, just like the original, the soundtrack is brilliant and memorable, with the OST being pretty much identical to the original. The gun sound effects are decent, again being re-used from the original. The voice acting is hilarious sometimes, with the fake Russian accents being the most memorable. The German voice work is brilliant as well, with a few shouty lines being spammed across the whole campaign (This is re-used from the original). As with all the main instalments, the amount of chatter on the fields, screaming from soldiers to move and take covers enough to keep the player in the game.
Multiplayer-wise, if you can get on, people still play it. The maps are well-done. The use of mounted guns and vehicles means that the game is played differently from later games in the series. The maps are much larger than what is offered in later games, changing how multiplayer is played as they are far more open due to the different methods of play. There are some problems with weapon balancing however which is present in both this and the original game.
My only actual complaint would be within the campaign. Sometimes some objectives don't trigger themselves properly (well, it happened twice to me) and although the campaign is solid across the board, the Russian campaign could not quite beat the atmosphere shown in the original Call of Duty game during the Battle for Stalingrad, which is my personal highlight for the series. Despite this, the expansion pack goes above what many other games in the series attempt and is in my opinion, the best of the series. Any fan of the genre should definitely get it and any fan of the new ones should get this to see how Call of Duty should be done.

One of my favorite strategy games of all time.  It's almost a decade old, yet I still find time to play it.
Campaign:  8/10  The base game's campaign is broken up into three stories loosely connected via the characters.  The level designs are creative and the gameplay is always engaging.  For first time players, the campaigns are a good place to learn the intricacies of the game.
Skirmishes:  9/10  The base game has 8 or 9 "Home Cities" to choose from, each with unique units, buildings, etc.  Each Home City gains experience independently, so there is no shortage of game to be played.  The map selection is very diverse, especially if you indulge in the expansion packs.  The AI can be a little idiotic at easier difficulties, but challenging at harder ones.  The only fault I find with the gameplay is the lack of diversity among the units available.  Each Home City has access to a different combination of a dozen or so units, each with a specific purpose in your armies, so if you opponent is building mostly cavalry, you just build anti-cavalry units.  This can become stale after several games.
Graphics:  8/10  What can I say?  The game looks great, especially considering its age.  The building models are great and 'evolve' as you age up in-game.  The landscape and scenery are very well detailed, notably the water and trees.  The game even has some physics involved when you attack buildings and the buildings fall apart.  The only fault I find with the graphics are the character models, which dont have idle animations and have identical faces, uniforms, etc.
Overall, I give this game a solid 85/100.  You might get bored of it, butonly after many hours of rewarding gameplay.  By the way, the soundtrack is fantastic.

If you're itching to play something mechanically resembling (slow-motion) Souls, LotF is certainly that. I can even unreservedly say that the gameplay is quite polished (once you get used to the heft) and the boss encounters will satisfy you until DS3 comes out. However, if you're attached to any other aspect of Souls, steer clear.
Polished graphics cannot counteract a detestable aesthetic. How much you can stomach it will be highly dependant on your taste, but it's still puzzling that LotF would go for that overdesigned pauldron-fantasy look, given that it's aping a franchise on the very opposite end of the fantasy spectrum.
By the same token, correct grammar and competent voice-acting cannot hide the fact that the game's script was written by a non-native English speaker who refused to have it altered or localized - it's filled to the brim with cringe-inducing faux-idiomatic speech that only seems natural to someone unfamiliar with the language. Again, this is puzzling for a game that is aping a franchise praised by many for one of the best localization efforts in gaming history.
And even if you're fine with the script, you must still contend with a non-story about extradimensional orcs, characterization out of Call of Duty, a stunning lack of interesting things to say about the setting or lore, and an atmosphere about as thick as deep space. Which, yet again, is puzzling, since Souls is known for its lore, characters, and atmosphere.
To summarize, LotF is the gaming equivalent of trying to make crème brûlée by putting a torch to a hamburger.

Screw the haters.
Okay, here's the deal: the game is a Souls ripoff. It's also nowhere near as good as the Souls games. Does that mean it's bad? No.
Lords of the Fallen takes the Dark Souls formula and twists it a bit. You got interconnected areas to explore, you got respawn points to find, you got deaths to do, it's all there, but it's got its own additions to the system. It does magic really well - even the gimmicky-looking but fun spells like Mimic have use - and it has a really cool attitude to subquests: yeah, they're there, but forget tracking and a journal - you remember to do them, or you don't. This may sound annoying and backwards but given the rather small size and huge interconnection fo the game's world, it opens a lot of rewards for exploration: you get this mysterious item, wonder if that guy who alluded to it has something to say about it, better go talk to him - on the way, oh look, secret switches I missed and a whole new area filled with giant ♥♥♥♥ing spiders.
Completionists won't like it - or the fact that there's a bunch of choices with very definite consequences that can lock you out of rewards - but it encourages thorough approach and constantly being on lookout for secrets, and the game is chock-full of those.
Okay, the elephant in the room and what most people hate: combat. It's slow. In addition to good old souls' stamina, attacks just come out slowly even with fast weapons. It's not very stylish or action-packed and emphasises strategy over reflexes. I can't really speak for the people who hated it but here's a tip: try out the biggest ♥♥♥♥ing stick you have in your inventory. Wielding slow and powerful weapons has rarely been so satisfying and I maintain this game has the best-feeling warhammers I ever cracked goblin skulls with.
What else is there? The setting is obviously nowhere near Souls stuff and you will get tired of the endless snow, the story is really predictable (although the novelty of medieval audiologs helps with that a fair bit) and most of the bosses are variations on Big Guy In Armor. Mechanically they are mostly handed well (two exceptions aside) but could use a bit more creativity in visual department.
What it really comes down to is this: it tries to be Souls. It's not. But it's a solid tribute and definitely a good game for at least the one playthrough when you get all the magic of exploring harsh, unforgiving and content-packed environments. The real "failure" of Lords of the Fallen is that it doesn't live up to the source material - but when the source material is brilliant, being just good is nothing to be ashamed of. I wouldn't by it at full price but this game is a very solid sale pick.
Oh, and don't buy the DLC. It blows - about an hour long and ending with a boss that's just piling one idiotic design decision over another.

It is unfortunate to say this, but as great a game as Half-Life is, time has not been good to it. When I played the game, it was sad to see how old the game has become. Nonetheless, this is the game to shatter all games for almost a decade.
Video games have so much to owe to Half-Life, every single FPS that has come out since then, owes something to Half-life.

It was back at the end of the 90's when this game came out and changed my life forever. I was a little kid and my father used to play it while I was watching him, and I got caught by its great plot, its gameplay and its setting. I played this game over and over like more than a hundred times and it still takes me out of breath. Live the life of Gordon Freeman, take a look at how a normal day at work can be the beginning of the longest and the most intense journey of all times. And live it all throug the eyes of the mute orange-suited redhead hero who can solve any probem with his crowbar. No cut-scenes, no scripted sequences, not a single look at what Gordon Freeman himself could not see. You'll not be aware of what is really going on until the real end. Emotional, breathtaking, this is one of the game you must have. At its time, Half-Life totally changed the way videogames were seen, and even if nowadays actual games are based on the concept that Half-Life brought to the world of videogames, you will still see that this game has something unique, that will still take your breath away.
This game has also got a wonderful multiplayer deathmatch mode that even if it hasn't got many players as it used to have, it's still one of the funniest experiences you will have on a multiplayer game. Try it if you don't believe me.

Let me start by saying that this review is my opinion and in no way law with regards this game.
This game has been sitting in my playlist for over a year and I’ve been dying to like it. I have taken a few tentative steps on a number of occasions but never played past an hour or so (I’m an expert at the first area!). I heard this was ‘Dark Souls Light’ and I welcomed that as I was terrible at DS and would agree that is a fair comparison to be made. Then I discovered my character class rogue/fighter and the game opened up and became a lot more accessible. Finding the class that suits you is key and it has taught me not to just write a game off if I find it too hard.
The graphics are fantastic and puts me in the mind of the underrated Space Marine game if set in a high fantasy world that encouraged gruff voices and copious amounts of steroids. Scenery is beautiful and some the PhysX effects are great if you can have them on. The acting is pretty poor and the storyline isn’t going to be winning any awards but it is passable (if you use your imagination and fill in the gaps yourself) and you may as well just pen your own ending or steal one from your favourite book/film.
I realise that I’m sounding quite negative towards the game but I’ve given it the ‘thumbs up’ that’s because even though it has a menagerie of things against it, it’s fun. The combat is a flexible and you have to approach every situation carefully depending on what weapon you have equipped and who you are up against. I died…a lot, but this didn’t stop me from returning to the game again and again to get it completed. There was something addictive about the constant punishment and tough battles. I rage quit more than I care to admit but was back to it within fifteen minutes and determined to get past the area. That alone is something of a rarity in games these days, I went back to it and it wasn’t for the storyline.
Ultimately, this game should be commended for what it does right and there are a lot of things in that category. If this game is reduced then I would encourage you to pick it up in a heartbeat, look past the flaws and quirky story and you’ve got a gem of a game that shouldn’t be missed.

Lords of the Fallen really isn't that bad of a game, but I found it to be lacking in depth. It is praised as a "Dark Souls-like" but only really reminds me of Dark Souls on the surface. And in that way, it is just like any other game in this genre, so it really doesn't stand out to me.
My issue with this game basically boils down to one point, and that is this: All character builds are too similar. You have one build type, and that is 'bulky guy with big melee weapon'. Yes there are 'light' and 'heavy' armors but the difference between them is hardly noticable, visually or in action. In Dark Souls, if you put on lighter armor you get hit harder but are more maneuverable. Heavier armor has the opposite effect. In Lords of the Fallen, every armor class makes you roll the same and move the same. It's boring and makes me feel very limited in how I can approach the game. The Magic is incredibly lackluster as well; all it really is is buffs and debuffs, with one actual offensive 'spell' for each set. No matter what kind of character you try to build, they are all going to feel the same, whereas in Dark Souls a lightweight build or a heavy, 2h build or a mage are WILDLY different from one another.
If you don't like too many different genres and have already been through some of the other games in this genre then maybe this one is for you. But if you are hoping it will live up to any of the hype or really even compare to the other great games on the market in this genre, then prepare to be disappointed.

Cute and delightful, a little music adventure and a little bit of rhythm game. Story mode is pretty short (under 3 hours even if you're as bad at it as I am, yet the difficulty felt just right for me). There's leaderboards and extra challenges and composition mode, so there's some replay value too.
The music is what absolutely makes this game. The first few levels are maybe a bit slow, but then the singing starts and that's what makes this game great for me. Moonlight Bayou and Thunder Creek being my favourite levels.
The few negatives for me:  The story comics are cut off left and right on my non-widescreen resolution. The controls are a bit iffy -- I opted for controller, because the button presses were more responsive, although moving up/down with the stick wasn't quite as precise. Keyboard has more precise up/down, but I never could get the timing right for the "attacks".
Overall, I love it, and it was a steal at the summer sale price. The most similar other game I can think of is Ephemerid; if you liked this one, also check out that one.

I may not be as experienced as mainy of the other players and reviewers who have been involved with Fractured Space but I can say that with everything I have experienced within the 10+ games I have played, I Love This Game! Gamma station in the middle which periodically goes live and needs to be captured to gain your team a buff and then the 2 main bases where either team spawns with 5 turret generators to be destroyed and then the base to be captured to win.
This explination is far from the best but it\'s the best I can do in terms of making it simple, each ship has its own style of abilities and role to play in combat ranging from different offensive roles, defencive roles and support roles. The fact that it\'s free to play is also very inviting, I also feel that the game is far from pay 2 win because within my experience all the ships I have come across (3 starter ships and 7 other ships from different tiers) are all fairly balanced just rely on the player executing their role properly to do well in the game.
So anyways thank you very much for taking the time to read this some what amatuer review and I would definitely recommend this game if you love Big Battle Ships in Space! - 9/10

Ubisoft has filled the world fun little sidequests and collectables for you to nab ranging from tedious to geniunely interesting or fun. The customization is alright but it is hampered by the fact that Ubisoft thought it was a good idea to lock at least half of it until they decide to release a multiplayer game mode. It also suffers from collectables that are locked unless you have access to the companion app, which is just stupid. Not to mention their clearly forced in microtransactions that they must have tossed in there in the last five minutes. I will say that Ubisoft does not force anyone to buy these microtransactions as within 6 to 8 hours of playing you can accumulate a pretty substantial in-game fortune. While I do have these grievances with the game I would like to reiterate that I do actually enjoy it. I want to play it. But Ubisoft's broken release is actually now preventing me launching the game at all. I played for a good few hours with no glitches apparent, but then it started with the frame drops which I can't stand. So I stopped playing for several days only to hop back on today and find that the frame drops had disappeared. Then just an hour ago, I decided that I would play some more, but I was hit the ACUnity.exe has stopped working, and after trying all available fixes I have given up. It would be a crime to recommend the game in it's current state to others. The reason I am writing this review is because Ubisoft can't provide me with the product that I stupidly paid for. So instead, this time that should be spent enjoying my purchase is being used writing this review in hopes that I may deter at least one person from spending money on this product in it's current build so that they may not have to suffer my fate.

Q.U.B.E, aka Quick Understanding (of) Block Extrusion, is an action puzzle game where you control various rooms with blocks.
This Director's Cut version is a small, but needed expansion to the game. Some of the wording may be similiar from my Q.U.B.E review.
Graphics: The graphics is blocks. No seriously...what were you expecting me to type? Anyways, the majority of the rooms you go through will be made of opaque white blocks. The blocks you can control are in colors. Yeah, that's it. Just to put it short, it is simple.
Director's Cut Graphics: In my previous review, some of the stuff gave me motion sickness. However, some areas such as twisting rooms and the rotating rooms are fixed to accomodate that. Also, there are extra rooms and designs so that you won't be walking the same path over and over. Overall, a good improvement in this version.
Controls: The controls are simple. You use your mouse buttons to either pull the cubes up or to push them back in. Also, there is jumping involved. The gravity is a little higher than normal fps games, like from valve.
Gameplay: The goal of the game is to find a way to the next room or to solve puzzles in order for the next room to open. There are various puzzles in the game. The puzzles are simply climbing up to the next room, directing a ball into a hole, dyeing a ball a certain color and putting that in a hole, magnets to move blocks, and using your memory to note where blocks are in the dark. It seems like a lot, but luckily, the game walks you through from the beginner stage to the intermediate.
Director's Cut Gameplay: In my previous review, I mentioned about that super hard magnet puzzle with the four small blocks. This puzzle was removed-thank goodness! Also, the difficulty curve has changed a bit, but in the more easy way. There are new puzzles and some puzzles removed. Still, an enjoyable experience for those who played the original Q.U.B.E game, or for those starting new.
Story in Director's Cut: Finally! Some insight! The story has two people to guide you, the one to encourage you to complete and the other to stop what you're doing. However, the story is only in audio. However, there isn't much complexity in the story that will affect your gameplay or is required.
Music: The music of this game is mostly ambience. Now, depending for some, it can either be slightly annoying or relaxing. To me, it was relaxing (except when it came to that room I described above).
Music in Director's Cut: The music is a definite improvement. It's not just ambience this time, but actual music and beats to accompany.
DLC: The DLC, "Against the Qlock," is a small expansion to the current game with new puzzles with pickups to make it more fun. The goal for each puzzle is to complete it with as few moves as possible and/or as fast as possible.
Is this Portal?: While this game has an atmosphere feel and mechanics like the game, "Portal," it is not. The similiarities are, again the atmosphere and gameplay (excluding portals), using least amount of moves and completing the puzzles as fast as possible in the dlc, and the difficulty curve of the game. You may get a "Portal" vibe from this, but again, it is not.
Overall: Q.U.B.E is another great action puzzle game that is a great addition to your library that is recommended to all, even to those who enjoy "Portal" or did not enjoy it.Regardless of how bland the interface looks, the gameplay stands up and shines in this game. The difficulty curve is great, with an exception of that one room. While the design of the game is simple, the puzzles introduced can be complexed and require thought. However, with training and a good amount of thinking, you can surely be "Quick" in "Understanding" of "Block Extrusion."
Overall Director's Cut: Director's Cut is the much needed improvement from the original version of the game. With new puzzles, much needed fixes, music, and a story, this expansion is like reading the minds of the players who played the first game. While some people may be bummed out by missing the original game, there is no need for despair. It is mostly the same game, but with some modifications and new additions. Director's Cut is what Q.U.B.E should have been: An enjoyable, casual experience with various difficulty challenges for all.

This game gets a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I think it's one of the best RTS games I've ever played.
I played the singleplayer campaign, but I haven't ever enjoyed a single campaign from the dozens of RTS games I've played, so I won't say anything about this one.
There are about 1000 concurrent players on the ESO servers at a given moment, so it's a little rough to find a game sometimes but it's not that bad. People play 1v1s, the larger team games, and the custom maps. There are also unique modes for the conventional matches, like Deathmatch, Regicide, No Rush games, etc. People usually only play No Rush games if it's not a standard skirmish. The custom maps are pretty fun in this game, especially Lost, but I wouldn't buy this game for the custom games. Look into WC3 for that.
I mainly play 1v1s, and while the game has some balance issues, the flow of the game is great. It has a really good scale, each civ feels unique, and the shipment system adds to the customization of your playstyle. The economic and military sides of this game complement each other well, where it's fun to try to secure resources with strategic building placement and such.
One final note, there's an unofficial community patch, so if you get into the game, they've tried to balance it for competitive players, but a small subset of players actually use it.

It is unfortunate to say this, but as great a game as Half-Life is, time has not been good to it. When I played the game, it was sad to see how old the game has become. Nonetheless, this is the game to shatter all games for almost a decade.
Video games have so much to owe to Half-Life, every single FPS that has come out since then, owes something to Half-life.
If you played Half-Life rather thoughtlessly, you may think that the game is seriously overrated, but the story, the dialouge, and the characters in Half-Life are very subtle. Don't expect this game to parade itself as the best PC game of all time. It's modest that way.

So xcom 2 isnt an awful game per se, it just had a few glaringly awful design flaws.
1. Timed missions. I'll get this out of the way first. The majority of the missions are timed which really cuts down how "tactical" the game can be. If you have to rush to the objective, you don't have much of a choice of tactics.
2. Sectoids are not even slightly balanced. They can mind control your people which is a pain. But thats not the bad part. They can also resurrect anything that dies be it friend or foe. The main reason this is an issue is because they can do this through wall, with no chance to miss, and an incredibly (possibly unlimited) range.
3. The story and voice acting are both fairly poor and the narrator never stops talking. I've literally shut the game down because he was just talking on and on for 5 minutes and I couldn't skip it.

If it weren't for the timed missions I could get past the other faults, but there is point in playing a tactical game when you have no ability to use any true tactics

It was back at the end of the 90's when this game came out and changed my life forever. I was a little kid and my father used to play it while I was watching him, and I got caught by its great plot, its gameplay and its setting. I played this game over and over like more than a hundred times and it still takes me out of breath. Live the life of Gordon Freeman, take a look at how a normal day at work can be the beginning of the longest and the most intense journey of all times. And live it all throug the eyes of the mute orange-suited redhead hero who can solve any probem with his crowbar. No cut-scenes, no scripted sequences, not a single look at what Gordon Freeman himself could not see. You'll not be aware of what is really going on until the real end. Emotional, breathtaking, this is one of the game you must have. At its time, Half-Life totally changed the way videogames were seen, and even if nowadays actual games are based on the concept that Half-Life brought to the world of videogames, you will still see that this game has something unique, that will still take your breath away.
This game has also got a wonderful multiplayer deathmatch mode that even if it hasn't got many players as it used to have, it's still one of the funniest experiences you will have on a multiplayer game. Try it if you don't believe me.

You might get some enjoyment out of this game if you're a die hard Dark Souls fan. That's really the only reason I picked it up. Ultimately, it's just a failed clone. This game is one hundred percent a Dark Souls rip off. From the combat to respawning enemies to the refillable potions (estus flask) at check points, they blatantly attempted to cash in on the success of Dark Souls with this game. Which I would not have minded at all had it been a good game. Sadly, it is not. I would only recommend Lords of the Fallen if you pick it up on sale for super cheap and have an unquenchable thirst for Dark Souls game play. And even in that scenario, don't go in with high expectations.
+CONS:
-The story is weak. I just beat the game an hour ago and can't recall the plot if that's any indication of its impact.
-The characters are uninteresting. And instead of a custom made, mute protagonist (like DS), you play as Harkyn. A very boring, grumpy, unlikable big buff white guy.
-The controls are nearly identical to DS. Nearly being the keyword. They're so close that the few buttons they switch up constantly messed with me the whole game. There is no custom button mapping. Only two pre-mapped set ups you can choose from.
-The armors are dull. Finding new sets doesn't feel that rewarding when they all look almost exactly the same.
-The enemies are bland. Most designs are cliche and/or unmemorable.
-The combat is flawed. You'll often find yourself taking damage despite a very well timed dodge roll. They did a decent job of emulating DS combat overall yet it somehow ends up feeling not nearly as satisfying.
-The magic is wonky. You are forced to choose one of three builds (each with 4 specific spells) at the beginning of the game. But you don't really have any clue what any of the spells will do or how useful they'll be. So you're blindly picking and are then locked into that build the rest of the game. You can't change. Nor can you eventually branch out and use the spells from the other two builds. I randomly chose 'Rogue' and ended up spamming the 'Stab' spell the entire game. Your magic automatically refills after about 10 seconds so spamming is an accurate term here. Magic does far more damage than physical attacks. So you'll often find yourself running and dodging to kill time between OP magic casts.
+PROS:
-Pleasant graphics?
I did get *some* enjoyment out of this game. More so early on. However, finishing it became more of a chore. And the ending is extremely unsatisfying. If asked 5 hours into the game, I would have said it's decent. After finishing it, I have to say it's not really worth the time.

Let me just say that this game is quite an excellent game (especially considering the price). I have played this game a number of times ranging from its \"free weekend\" it had early on in development, to just last week. I have seen this game change in a number of ways for the better, and I think that this game is worth playing now, with even more potential and merit soon to come.
Granted:
This game might be a bit on the short side for now, but it is in early development stages. They currently have one PvP mode , a training mode, a ship testing facility, and a mode for custom games. That being said, they have a lot of room for improvement in that specific field.
To fix this for example:
They could add the ability to bring more friends into a given PvP matchmaking team (instead of the current 3).
They could add different maps to the current selection (with perhaps differently placed objectives).
They could make larger scaled matches (for teams of perhaps 7 or 8 on each side).
These are just a few suggestions, that I believe we will come to see in time.
As far as as the actual gameplay and ships go, there are also a few problems:
Ship scaling along a manufacturer tree is dangerously close to unbalanced (aka there is definitely a ship priority).
Premium ships can sometimes have unfair advantages.
Matchmaking only takes your previous performance into account, and matchmaking with friends can be hazardous.
Some (intentionally)  low performing people with higher-quality ships can be matched against new players (unfairly).
There is no easy banning system for removing players who throw games on purpose.
On the Pros side:
good flight mechanics
excellent combat system
appealing cosmetics
good play rewards
asteroids mini-game in matchmaking screen
replay value
ship design
upgradable weapons
customizable ship crew roster
free

I will describe and rate the key aspects of the game in this review, from a subjective view:
The music to this game is very good! You can clearly hear the passion Matthew Taranto, the creator of the game and music, had while writing it. And his music sheet BECAME the stage you are playing on, with the obstacles being the notes themself! But that is not all!
The music lines in perfectly with enemies in different themes of music and style, from Chiptune 8-bit stage to Crabs-and-snails western. There are also some twists in the core mechanics here and there for a neat surprise.
But be warned, this is not a rythm game per se. The core mechanic is that you dodge the notes that make up the music while collecting stuff, you are not required to press the keys all the time in rythm like you may know from games like Rythm Fever.
Sadly, this game is rather short. You can play through all stages in 1 - 2 hours, but the wonderful music and style makes them very replayable, so you can play them over and over again.
Also, this game features a in-game composer for your own levels, akin to Mario Paints composer but fit to the games style and mechanics. And with a Steam Workshop integration coming up, this means you will have plenty of more stages to play.
It costs 5 bucks, during the 2017 Summer Sale 1.25 bucks. That's somewhat as much as 1.5L of Coca Cola or some chips. But this game provides you with 1000x more fun than potato chips! Trust me, I did the SCIENCE!
Every frame is hand-drawn in a colorful, quirky art-style. The game plays in 60 FPS and obviously doesn't need much to run well. The games engine is Unity, so, yeah.
It can be quite challenging at times, but you can play through the game without dying more than 5 times in total. And I suck at video games. So, it's not too hard. But for that, there are "Challenge Flies", which can be quite a deal to collect! So there is something for the people who like challenges as well!
All in all, I rate this game a solid 9 out of 10 refrain-loops ;).

The short version:
Do you like rhythm games? Do you like retro homages? Do you like Brawl in the Family? Play this game.
The long version:
I discovered this game through Brawl in the Family. If you like Smash Bros. and online comics, check it out. It's ended now, but it's got some good stuff. Don't worry, this review will still be here when you finish. Anyway, I spotted the trailer for Tadpole Treble in the suggestions after watching their History of Nintendo music vid. I watched it, and thought it was a cool concept. It was also an indie, and as an aspiring game developer myself, I decided to cheer the game on. Since I didn't have my own credit card, I grabbed the game as soon as it came out on Early Access (which was actually the full game sans achievements). It was worth every penny--or peso, in my currency.
Tadpole Treble is part rhythm game, part "platformer" (without any actual platforms), and part music lesson. Levels are built on a musical staff with the notes as obstacles. Cymbals, reeds, and mushrooms add some percussion when whacked, while bubbles, sparkles, and food put some life to the background when touched. The general rule is dodge black, whack gold, and collect purple. The game starts off on a welcoming stage with a calming melody--perfect for learning the basics. The later levels vary in musical genre, theme, and, of course, difficulty. From the suspenseful snaps of Barracuda Cavern to the relentless munches of Piranha Jungle, from the soothing ballad of Midnight Bayou to the shocking chorus of Thunder Creek, from the retro beat of Chiptune Lagoon to the booming orchestra of Con--oh, wait, that's a secret. Anyway, each level is unique and has its own charm, and is worth beating a few times, especially if you're a completionist. Speaking of which, each level has five medals: one for completion, one for gaining an S rank (the highest), one for gaining an F rank (the lowest), one for collecting all the bubbles, and one for nabbing the level's challenge fly (a unique challenge for each level). There's no way to get all these medals in one go, since F and S are opposites, so you'll have to play the level at least twice, and possibly a third time after you unlock something special for gaining a specific medal. You'll probably also enjoy one level so much that you repeat it over and over again. And who knows, you might nab that #1 spot.
The plot isn't anything special, but it's still heartwarming. It's mostly about growing up and determination and whatnot, but it also has some environment stuff, which is something I feel everyone should learn from. Each level has its own miniature story, while finishing certain levels progresses the main. The way "cutscenes" are presented, in comic panels with accompanying sound, is positively adorable, and gives me memories of the old BitF. But hey, that's just me.
On a personal note, as I said earlier, I plan on making a game one day. And watching these devs, I can't help but wish for their success. So if that counts for anything, go support these guys. They're awesome and this game is awesome.
Overall, if you like music, rhythm, and/or Nintendo, go try this game. Trust me, it's worth it.

Song of the Dark Swan is the second installment of Grim Legends series. Thre previous installment of this series: The Forsaken Bride.
Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Music and Sound. The miscellaneous section has the following: Custom Cursor, Voice Overs, Difficulty Mode and Full Screen. Wide Screen is automatically supported in the game.
Game Difficulty Modes: Three game difficulty modes – Casual, Advanced and Expert.
Cinematic/Dialogues: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. Most of the cinematic scenes can be watch over again under the cut scene section the extras. There is an option for skipping the entire dialogue scenes without having sit through it.
Game Voiceovers: Nothing much can be said about the voiceovers asides from that they are well done.
Game Music/Sounds: Nothing much can be said about the music/sounds asides from that they both fit well with the game.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn with a painted feel to them.
Inventory Panel: There is a lock option for the inventory panel. Easy access for the items that are collected in the game.
Notebook: Objectives only.
Map: The map interactive with useful indicators; map icons/markers. The legend on the map explains the function for each of the map icons. The ability to fast travel to another location and back. The map can be access two-way via through the notebook or map scrolls next to the notebook.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Find “X” Amount, Fragmented items, Shadow items, Traditional word list with some and/or no interaction required. The hidden object scenes can be replayed in the hidden object puzzle section in the extras.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve.
Game Helper: Three critter helpers can carry out certain tasks that the players can’t complete themselves. Like retrieving items that are out of reach.
Game Ending: There is an ending for the main portion of the game. The bonus chapter portion of game is the pre-sequel to the main portion of the game.
Game Achievements: In game and Steam. Most of these achievements are featured in Steam’s achievement. There are three different sets of achievements to earn. Gameplay: 11; Collectables: 31; Story: 18. In total there are 29 achievements altogether.
Game Collectables: There are 31 Healer Sigils to collect within the game. They are scattered throughout the game.
Game Concept Art/Wallpapers: 12 concept art and 10 wallpapers.
Game Trading Card/Badge: This a special feature only available in the Steam’s version of the game. The game drops three different trading cards only once and the rest of the cards: Community Market, Booster Packs and Trading. The game badge can be crafted after having all the card in the inventory then it can be upgraded four more times.

So I stumbled on this game pretty randomly, but as I read more about it here and on other sites reviewing games of its type, it piqued my interest. It seemed like it was pretty quick playthrough, and for $10 I though "What the heck? I give it a try".
After installing it and getting through the tutorial, I was hooked. I beat it in about 14 hours, but that was doing all but one mission, and taking plenty of time to dig around and read every little easter egg I found.
To explain my qualifications, I am not a programmer or hacker of any type, nor is either a requirement for this game. I can certainly find my way around a computer, and figure stuff out if something goes wrong (often with the help of the great and powerful Google), but I have very limited programming experience and have never (sucessfully) used Linux or any other UNIX system.
I cannot praise this game highly enough. I grew up in PC gaming, and still do a lot to this day. I'm not the "go out and buy the latest AAA title" gamer; I feel I strike a balance between enjoying some AAA titles, like Mass Effect, Assassin's Creed, etc, Indie games that some of my friends throw my way, and Classics like the Half Life series. This game was incredibly unique in it's execution, and forces you to learn to play it in a new way. Even for those familiar with UNIX, I'm not sure how many have used a UNIX command prompt as their primary UI in a game like this before. I was a little nervous at first, but the tutorial for the game gives you more than enough of an understanding to work with to start, and there's tips snuck in throughout the game to help remind you how to do things. If you ever forget, you have full and ongoing access to everything you've previously done for reference. The game gives you all the resources you need to solve the puzzles it presents while still offering an exciting challenge. If you do get stuck, there's plenty of support on Steam discussion boards to help you get passed whatever has you stumped.
This game apparently has a multiplayer option planned, which is supposed to drop after the Mac and Linux versions are stablized. I look forward to that very much.
Simply put, this game was a hell of a ride, and has ranked among my most enjoyable gaming experiences. The story isn't super long, but it's long enough to be incredibly enjoyable without ever really feeling repetitive (regularly a bane of modern AAA titles). If you have $10 and a few days to spare, it's defintely worth it for something unlike a lot of what most people are playing these days. Something different, expertly done.

With the recent rise of Portal-like game, this is a decent indie approach to the genre. It has a simple yet effective art direction that the developers use cleverly: it may not have much variety in terms of the style of the environment of the game, but the layout of each new room and the transitions between them can really make a difference and break the monotony of seeing the same things again and again. The puzzles are okay, although sometimes they can bet a bit repetitive.
Between puzzle and puzzle we can sometimes listen to the narrative part of the game. There is a story, and I appreciate it being there... but, even though it is interesting, it has a very dull conclusion. I mean, I think it is okay if instead of a decision, there's only one path for the player to take. But then... do not make us believe there is another choice. Without spoiling anything, at the end, you are given two choices, yet if you don't choose what the game wants you to do, nothing happens and the game can’t go on until you do what you're “supposed” to do. What's even the point then! Make it a cinematic or provide another ending , but don’t you ruin it like that!
On another note, I’d also like to say that the voice actors are really great: AAA quality, seriously, Especially the voice actress. I really appreciate how well she played her role.  The game is, overall, fine, but just take it as what it is, a low-budget Portal/the Talos Principle wanna-be. It didn't quite appeal to me as those other games did, but it's an okay game nonetheless. It definitely deserves its shot if you're into this genre and besides it’s not that long or expensive.

8/10 - Here's why.
This is not your typical turn based game. In fact, I would go as far to say that, it mostly isn't a turn based game.
A large contributing factor to this game involves managing a town and I would say that if you see this game as a management style game, more than a fighting game, you will actually find it entertaining when the random number generator messes with you.
You, the player are the mayor of 'sh%t goes wrong all the time town'. Your role as mayor is to mitigate the damage from said sh%t going wrong. As the mayor you have a whole bunch of employees. Those employees, like people in real life, winge and complain about stuff. One might have a saw arm, so he can’t hit as hard. One might not like beasts, so he is scared of them more. One employee might have a bad case of mud bum and you have to send him to the doctor. So as the mayor, you have a choice. Do I spend money on my employee to help him? Or do I make him redundant and fire him.
And then some stupid bird comes along and steals all your stuff. So you have to deal with that. Then people attack your town...so much bad stuff happens. It’s all about the mitigation. You will lose stuff, it's just how much stuff will you lose? You may have to send one of your employees on a suicide mission to save heaps of other stuff. Or you can gamble all your best fighters in the hope you win and get the glory.
The worst thing you can do with this game is have this attitude; "I have a level 6 healer, I've named her Daisy and I love her and never want her to die". I'm telling you now. DAISY WILL DIE. You need to get out of this mindset and think more like the CEO of a major company. If your employee dies, just hire another one - life goes on, the wheels keep turning.
PROS -
- Unique game style. Mixes management with turn based combat
- Eerie atmosphere/graphics. It does well painting the picture of scary dungeons
- Real consequences. There is no scum saving here. Everything you do is permanent. So you have to think about every choice you make.
- Constantly on edge. I find that every time I go into a dungeons I am on guard. Generally, it isn’t the whole "beat heaps of trash and then fight a hard boss" scenario. Every encounter could mean your doom.
CONS
- If you are a defensive sort of player like me, the game kind of forces you into this survival mode where you just grind low level torchless dungeons, with higher level players in order to save up money. This can become repetitive.
- A few UI issues need improving. Eg, trinket management is very annoying as it stands now. I will often spend 2 or 3 minutes per dungeon sorting them out due to the UI.

This game is a freaking masterpiece. The gameplay feels extraordinary if played with a controller. The keyboard controls are far inferior for this. To me, the story makes perfect sense. I love every aspect of it, but I will refrain from talking about it cuz spoilers.
If you're a "hack 'n' slash" game lover, this is the perfect game for you. From an outside view, the gameplay may seem repetitive, but because of the ability to wield two sets of weapons at once (one set in your hands and the other functioning as high heels), your moveset can be customized to your liking. While some challenges are a bit absurd, it's a minor setback when looking at the grand scheme of things.
The gameplay is near-perfect, story is really interesting, and it's a fantastic experience. However, you may not want to play it if you are religiously sensitive, not a fan of massive amounts of blood, or drawn away from sexual characters. You play as one of the world's last Umbra Witches, who make pacts with demons in exchange for magic powers. In exchange, she has to hunt down and kill various members of heaven's armies. Her targets can vary from giants that fly around in tornadoes to humanoid female angels who have rather questionable body language. She kills all of her enemies in a flashy and bloody manor. While that in itself may be alarming, as it paints the angels and therefore heaven as the main enemy, keep in mind that it paints both the forces of heaven and hell as huge jerks. That's another aspect I like. It shows light and dark as not mutually good or bad.
Her finishing moves to kill her bigger enemies are by summoning her demonic pets to devour or tear them apart, all the while exchanging hilarious banter with them. There isn't gore, like guts flying out of them, but lots of blood.
As for the sexual content, that brings us to the biggest red flag that may be raised. There isn't flat-out nudity, as they always keep everything covered, albeit lots of the time hardly so. When summoning her demons, her outfit (which is made out of her own hair), disappears to form into the portal. Depending on the ritualistic dance she has to do to summon her demons, she ends in several questionable poses. I'm the type of person who finds humor rather than arousal in such acts. I assume some people think otherwise about it, though.
You know, I wrote WAY too much about this. If this sounds like fun to you, buy it immediately. Like, RIGHT now. As of when I'm writing this, the game and its two sequels are heading to the Nintendo Switch, and you KNOW I am going to buy them as soon as I can. Once you play this, you'll feel the same.

This game is truly amazing. It's coming close to my favorite game of all time, and that should say something as I am an old guy that is playing since the early 90's. I don't write many reviews, the reason I write one here (besides I find this game a piece of art) is to counter some badly argumented reviews that call out the bad side of RNG. Too many players can not handle the loss of heroes when a chain of bad events happen. It's a big part of the charm of this game. Good RNG is never called out, most players don't notice a 4 hero dodge chain but when a 4 enemy dodge chain happens they go look for the review button.
