"Will someone die of the curse because I didn't bring back enough blood?" "Should I take my best Highwayman even though he is wasting or craving and I have no blood left?". The tension feels so good. The curse can feel frustrating when heroes just decide to pass or attack one of your heroes at the wrong time, but oh boy does this make you feel stick to you monitor.
10 euro/dollar for this game in a sale is a crime, nothing this good should ever be so cheap. The one single hint I can give new players is : just accept heroes will die and are replacable, you will need this mindset to fully grasp this piece of art.

If you're a gamer and have never heard the name Half-Life, I'm sorry to say that you're either overly sheltered, willfully ignorant or just too young. For those of us who enjoy First-Person Shooter [FPS] games, Half-Life was just as influential to the genre as Doom or Quake (for those of you who have never heard of these titles, Wikipedia is your friend). Classics such as Halo: Combat Evolved and newer titles such as Bioshock: Infinite have been influenced by this game, and older games such as Counter-Strike were mods of Half-Life. In short, the entire FPS genre has been creatively influenced by the atmosphere and style of Half-Life.                          - FYI: Final Score is at the end -
- The Look -
Half-Life was released by Valve (the parent company of Steam) in 1998 for the PC. As such, the graphics are abysmal by modern standards. If you are a nostalgic gamer such as myself, though, the low graphics can be humorous and even add to the charm of the game at times. There are numerous texture packs available if you cannot handle such old graphics.
- The Story (Mild Spoiler Alert) -
You're a government agent/scientist who gets involved with some experiments on unknown substances. Through testing these substances, you somehow open a portal and unleash an alien horde into the testing facility. You must then find and fight your way out of the facility. Pretty simple and straightforward-sounding. Half-Life was the first-ever game to tell its story completely through scripted sequences (events triggered by certain programmable requirements) and as such has no cutscenes. This is a very nice element to the game as you retain control of your character throughout the entire game.
- The Sounds -
For some reason, Valve decided they needed to make everything sound like it was coming from the inside of an echo chamber. There is a lot of reverb on just about every noise if you are not completely outdoors. Again, this is an element where modern technology has progressed as to make this appear foolish and unappealing. Give it some time before you make any judgments, though. The effect enhances the scariness of some situations, in my opinion. If you ever play any of the other Valve games (Portal, Team Fortress 2, Portal 2, etc.), you will discover that a LOT of sounds and music in those games originated from Half-Life.
- The Movement -
You run. You run a lot. You run really fast. You have the option to walk and the option to sneak, but 98% of the time you will be running. Sometimes, especially for unfamiliar novices to the game, the speed is too much and you end up running into an alien patrol before you realize that you just passed through that hallway. You will eventually get used to it, though. Half-Life was one of the first games (if not the first; I'm not sure) to implement the "jump-crouch" concept. If you jump and hold the crouch button, you can actually jump onto higher platforms. Instead of lowering your body, jump-crouching raises your legs and feet, giving you more clearance to vault onto objects.
- The Combat -
If an enemy sees you, they will throw a grenade. Expect to be spammed if you are spotted. Half-Life is a quick-save/quick-load supportive game; you can choose to disregard this if you want a "purist" experience. Enemies in this game are rather easy to defeat in the beginning and get harder as the game progresses, but each new type presents its own unique traits that make it hard to kill. The weapon switching system is confusing to a modern gamer at first; it requires you to scroll (or press hot-key) and then left-click to actually arm that weapon. The left shift button, by default, switches instantaneously back to the previous weapon used, allowing for a much faster switch. Weapons and ammo are decently plentiful if you are conservative enough.
- The Mods and The Legacy -
Half-Life is the number one most modded game of all time. There are more mods available for this game than any other, followed by Morrowind and Quake. The mods have spawned entire new game series, as in the case of Counter-Strike and Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. Half-Life also holds the trophy for another gaming phenomenon: most-played for speedruns. If you are unfamiliar with a speedrun, the gist is that you attempt to start and finish the game as fast as possible.
- The Downsides -
Half-Life is an ancient piece of software by today's standards. With the advent of 2015, this game is now 17 years old (nearly old enough to purchase cigarettes!). Its age shows in many things. Several furniture items are completely cubic or square and have no roundness. Cockroaches are diamond-shaped. There are only three different models used for the human enemies and three for the friendly scientists. Each alien type has only one model/skin. The NPCs and enemies can get very repetitive at times, as such. Other than this, there aren't very many bad points to Half-Life. Its continued success and popularity speak for its quality and innovation.
- The Conclusion -
Half-Life is a classic in many gamers' opinions. I am of the same mindset. I completely recommend this game, despite its age and shortcomings, as a fun experience that will provide a decent challenge.
Final Score: 10/10

1. Timed missions. I'll get this out of the way first. The majority of the missions are timed which really cuts down how "tactical" the game can be. If you have to rush to the objective, you don't have much of a choice of tactics.
2. Sectoids are not even slightly balanced. They can mind control your people which is a pain. But thats not the bad part. They can also resurrect anything that dies be it friend or foe. The main reason this is an issue is because they can do this through wall, with no chance to miss, and an incredibly (possibly unlimited) range.
3. The story and voice acting are both fairly poor and the narrator never stops talking. I've literally shut the game down because he was just talking on and on for 5 minutes and I couldn't skip it.

If it weren't for the timed missions I could get past the other faults, but there is point in playing a tactical game when you have no ability to use any true tactics

Glitching mobs, that teleported through walls, projectiles moving through walls, getting hit by attacks while there are no mobs and crashes that make you redo a lot of your work. I can no longer recommend this game, although I loved a lot of it and it's taught me valuable gameplay lessons that will let me enjoy Dark Souls more now. Not being able to finish the game, because the end is full of bugs/glitches and crashes, ruins the entire experience for me.
Here's a movie of my last session (especially the last 3 minutes are 'interesting'):
I always found Dark Souls too confusing; what to do, where to go, who to kill, who not to kill? Those were all the questions, all the time... It eventually became just a bit too much for me, so I basically just stopped playing.
This game does a few things different, and even though it's not as deep as Dark Souls, it certainly is a good alternative for someone who needs at least a partial thread to follow. "Find Kaslo". I only half know who Kaslo is, but I shall find the old fool!
The combat feels good. There's quite a bit more to it then it seems, people who played Dark Souls with a controller should feel very at home with this game, most of the controls are apparently the same - I never played Souls with a controller, so this game is new to me. And for a new player, the tutorial is a little bit lacking. There are advanced moves, that you have to teach yourself, or find out yourself. Like, did you know you can kick? Or the Backstab? Well, I knew about backstabbing, but I had no idea how to perform it. It's a Light Attack from behind... After 5 hours of trying a Heavy Attack from behind, I was starting to think I had to progress through the story further to learn that skill (I'm an old Assassin's Creed fanboy), but nope, I could do it from the start, if only I knew the controls.
The bosses are tough, frustratingly tough even. They have their own mechanics and you'll want to go in and die a couple of times to figure them out. On the 3rd one, I spent about half an hour, maybe longer, dying before I gave up and looked up a tip on the internet.
I don't know how deep the character creation goes in terms of alternative playstyles, but there definitely is a huge difference between the slow but powerful warrior and the agile but squishy rogue. I play the latter and am having fun - check my playthrough for some more 'hands on' info:
I really like this game, and I recommend it for all of you who want to like Dark Souls but find it just way too confusing. Also, for all Dark Souls fans out there, this game is not Dark Souls. Don't expect Dark Souls, and you'll probably like it too.
Someone else already coined the term, but I'm using it too. This is a Souls-like, or Souls-lite.

A few technical problems with this one. If you are using an AMD graphics card, this game will likely slow down or run at sub optimum. The specs required are higher than suggested. It isn't super stable.
That said, this game is a solid experience. Like many people, I will compare it to Dark Souls since they fit in the same niche. This game is an odd blend of Diablo style leveling & loot collection (everything is randomized), and Dark Souls combat.
You can technically pick a class, but very quickly these have little to no difference, beyond the cleric having a heal. Weapon stats, damage, and speed are all random so a pair of shortswords can do more damage than a two hander, and be slower. You have a stamina bar, health, a limited number of health potions that refill at rest points, a block, parry, heavy attack, light attack, and roll.
The art personally reminds me of the chunky comic book style from Darksiders, so a big plus. It does repeat the Dark Souls 2 problem of most enemies being some variation of "guy in armor", but they all look impressive, and the rarer non-human enemies are quite cool. The story is pretty standard fantasy fluff, and isn't going to under or overwhelm anyone. For 20$ or less, you are getting 10+ hours of solid game to slake that thirst that -for me- only the Souls series really fills.

Tadpole Treble is a game about dodging notes and getting a high score. It sounds simple, and is. But the real fun of any music based game is in getting into the rhythm of a song. Tadpole treble has this in spades all due to it's clever level design. Point doodads and collectibles follow a certain flow, making the way you control your tadpole feel in time to the music. Each song has it's own art, events and theme which are seldom repeated and make each song feel unique. The music is written by the same guys who did the musical comics for Brawl in the Family (a now concluded web comic featuring Nintendo characters), you can find a few on YouTube if your are interested in sampling how good they are. It's a short ride, you could finish the game in a day if you power through easily and it's not difficult if you don't go for 100% completion, but it's a good one that I come back to occasionally for a few certain songs.

If you like the current state of Call of Duty, stop reading this.
...Okay, now that I've weeded out the plebs, let's get down to business. This is the definitive Call of Duty game. Great story, fun multiplayer, it's all in there, and better than the modern bullcrap that Activision is pulling out of their proverbial butt nowadays. Here's an overview.
The story in United Offensive is based on the happenings of actual battles of WWII. Throughout the campaign (which includes 15 missions), you'll play as Amercians, Russians, and the British. Instead of today's ridiculous "get behind cover to magically recover health", you'll be dealing with a health bar that can only be replentished with health packs. Instead of a one-man army, you have somewhat competent ai allies who can actually take down enemies (unlike another game I know...). There are one or two missions where you are on your own, but even then you aren't alone for long.
The multiplayer is fun, but sadly mostly dead nowadays. There is a greater variety of maps than there are in the new CoD games, some of which are large and have vehicles (Yes, I said VEHICLES, like, TANKS) and some of which are small and made for close-quarters. Guns have recoil, and the guns with the best range are single-shot bolt-action rifles. It takes more skill to be good in UO than it does in any game after it.
Sidenote: YOU CAN LEAN AROUND CORNERS. The same mechanic ironically was one of the key points of CoD: Ghosts E3 presentation last year. All they did was re-add a feature that had been stripped out.
Here comes everyone's biggest gripe: the graphics. I personally don't care how the graphics look, and I will say that even then they look better then certain "AAA" games nowadays. There are little to no physics, just death animations when you kill enemies. The voice acting is superb. The sound can also be commended for the time the game was released.
CoD: UO is worth buying. I would wait for a sale though. I think the battle chest which includes UO along with CoD and CoD 2 goes half off once in a while. Even if you are pleb, this game is worth playing as a reminder than CoD was not always a pleb game, and may in fact help cure your plebness.

The following is only representative of the single player campaign:
Surprisingly, this is the most scripted Call of Duty game/expansion ever produced.
At several points, any movement slightly off script will lead to an instant death from sniper fire, tank shells, or artillery.
As the levels are significantly longer than the first game, it is incredibly likely you will run into a scripting error. If you were several seconds late behind your captain in the first part of a mission, forget being able to rescue him when he is downed in the second part of the mission - the game assumes you were right behind him the entire time, forcing you to replay 10-15 minute sections to ensure you are in the proper position to continue with the level.
The objective marker has also seemingly been programmed by 45 different people that have never talked, emailed, or followed any project guidelines. The marker will sometimes point to where you need to go, where you need to run away from, where the weapons are to blow up the tank, where the tank is but not where the weapon is that you need to blow up the tank, etc.
Overall, this might actually be the worst Call of Duty campaign. Ghosts’ Campaign was run of the mill, but this is kinda straight broken.

For those who want to know a little more before getting this game, here is a basic overview of what is going on:
-The game is a 5v5 conquest style, the objective is to control key strategic areas in order to gain access to the enemys base and ultimatly capture it
-Strategys are very important, there are two left and right side wings where you must work up to the enemy side in order to capture a key jump base to get to the enemy base, this plays very well as they are effictevly two seperate maps.
-In order to get between the maps you must "jump" to them, it takes one jump to return to base and two to cross to the other side (ignoring the middle gamma for now), this is very similar to games such as league, where there is effictevly a time gap one can use to make pushes but also allows quick defense, depending on what the other team is doing.
-On each side of these two wings are resources you can capture to help buff your team (like a leveling system) - hence control on these is also important
-Behind these two wings are the bases on each side, which also act as basically seperate maps
-Finally there is a middle map, that every few minutes will open up. Capturing this gives your team a strong buff. Battles for these are often heated and are a great way of turning a losing fight around or making the final strike to win a battle. If your team controls one of the enemy's base jump points you can also jump directly to the enemy base.
The Ships
-You play with massive space ships (this is simply the coolest thing ever)
-There are three manufactures, each with thier own designs letting you pick/choose your prefered ships
-Each ship has a role, the basic three being defense, support and attack (With many permutations, but for simplisity these are the main three)
-At the begining of a match you can choose your ship and as well talk with your team on your prefered ship and find a suitable team composition
-The ships play very well, I find many enjoyable and balanced
Overall I am very impressed with what the devs have put together. I personally enjoy balanced competitive games where there is little luck or "dice rolling" involved and that victory is because you have played better than the other team. So far the community has been great as well, which is fantastic.
Final comments, the game is free and probably the best space game I have played in a while. Just awesome.

Its still an alpha game, with it comes bugs, structural changes (recently the crew system),  a product that doesn't run as efficiently as it could, and a bit of an anemic playerbase.  Doesn't mean its bad, just means that you will have to expect a bit of roughness starting out.
It does require grind to get more than the starter ships.  Its not all that bad though.  The starter and lower tier ships are all plenty usable and balanced against the higher tier ships when flown well.  A higher tier ship does not mean better, contrary to what a first impression may give you.  What it means is that the higher tier ships are more specialized and difficult to fly well.  The monetization overall is fair, money can accelerate your progress slightly.  The variety of cosmetics is alright, this is a developing thing of course.  While I wish more customization was possible (custom pain jobs, logos, ship 'bling' would all be neat to see someday) there are some really nice looking skins available for ships.
The game is a moba style game, capture mines, aquire resources, gain levels, win the game by pushing some sort of advantage all the way to the end.  The learning curve is steep, the tutorial is alright but there is far more to learn.  It is not a game where you can expect to do amazing the first few hours or days, but its very rewarding to get to this point.
The game has a dedicated playerbase, if a bit on the smaller side.  Poke around the forums a bit and show yourself to the community.  To get the best experience for anything more than a short playthrough this is where the most fun can be.  The veterans of this game are passionate and want to share what they know to newer players, they want to keep the fresh blood flowing into it.  Flying solo can be extrodinarilly frustrating but with friends can be amazing once you all have the basics down or have a helpful vet with you.
Overall, its a great game once you get past the larger and normal learning curve.  Its not all that gentle for a new player either.  The veterans want to share their love of the game and it makes it much better to play if you can put yourself in this.  The devs are pretty great too, they do pay attention to the community and you might even run into them in game too.

The line of sight is the worst I've ever seen in any game ever. Somehow enemies are able to see through solid walls and shoot my guy through a wall and two floors if my guy's face isn't pressed up against cover pointing just the right way. If there is an entire building between us, you shouldn't be able to shoot my guy. But since he's not hugging the right cover, he gets killed instantly.

I'm sorry but if the main mechanic of a boss fight is to stand on the platform to avoid magic damage (and an instant kill whole area aoe) then maybe it should work. Got the worshiper down to 1/4 hp, my best yet, good on hp and potions, etc. But I was on the steps of the platorm (literally the top step) and it still killed me. This game has so many things wrong with it, it's ridiculous. Artificial difficulty out the wazoo. I had to grind enemies to get anywhere near an acceptable build, and I'm still struggling. I beat Dark Souls 1 & 2 (note: on console), because they were challenging but not artificially. They had mechanics to learn which were consistent yet intricate. This game on the other hand? You think you know the patterns (roll now, now, now) but instead the boss decides *hmm, I think I'll wait 2 more frames for the last homing hit* and your pattern messes up, and you take 60 damage as "punishment." Honestly, this game is beyond annoying. I believe it might even have bugs, yet the forums suggest otherwise. Ex: when grinding, I farmed the baddies right after the commander boss (650xp + 280xp +280xp +200xp) and kept using the checkpoint to reset them to farm them again, after banking my xp. When coming to the worshiper checkpoint, however, suddenly the entire place I had explored previously, riddled with baddies, was a ghost town. Looking it up, I discovered that the way to make them come back was to load the game again. Didn't work. Another suggestion, which did work, was to leave the area and come back. This was exhaustive as I was nearing the end of that area, and all the enemies respawned. I got my xp farm back, it seemed, until I used the checkpoint again. It. Didn't. Work. So, yes, I believe this is some bug or some really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ design choice. Either way, ♥♥♥♥ this game. On a side note, Game Debate lied to me, saying my system could push Ultra at 1440p at 40-50fps, whereas in reality, it struggles to maintain 30fps on high at 1080p. It's a pretty game, but Minecraft has shown us graphics aren't everything.

The puzzles are inventive and while a lot are repeated from other games, they've been adjusted for this game's setting and feel new. System requirements are way too high for a unoptimized, inefficient game that provides the same kind of gameplay and repeatable missions without the cost of the season pass involved on top.

Your imagination is instantly peaked when you start to play as an alien blob-like thing. The Old Tree is a short game that takes very little time to complete, however, it inspires many different feelings throughout the course of the game.
Gameplay:
My playthrough took about 20 minutes, which I have noticed is about the average for most people. The moves encompassed the 'w,s,a,d' buttons (really, mostly just the 'a and d' buttons) and your mouse. For this game, those movements worked perfectly to get you from point A to point B.
Graphics:
The developers have done a very good job keeping your focus on the alien-baby you are controlling, with darker undertones for the background. This accentuates the vivid coloring of your character. I thought the graphics were well done with a sort of 'drawn on' effect.
Audio:
The music for this game is phenomenal! The melodies of course changed with different scenes, but did not take away from the experience in anyway. Instead, the music only enhanced the action!  The songs themselves did more for the general ambience of the game then everything else (gameplay/graphics).
Storyline:
This game has a very basic storyline that is really easy to follow. It seemed to me as though is was kind of a twist to the point and click genre. Your alien-baby is on rails throughout the game, and you only move ahead once you can sort out the puzzle. The puzzles are simplistic for the most part and do not take a lot of time to get through, so the overall flow of the game is not broken up.
There are so many ways to experience this game, and I think most people will have varying opinions on what it all is supposed to mean. To me, it started out symbolizing fear. Fear of the unknown, and what was to come for such a tiny creature. It then moved into more of a feeling of triumph, and the knowledge that one can do anything, as long as the will and the effort are there. With a game that takes under half an hour to complete, the playthrough is still a very pleasant occasion. Overall, I believe that this game is completely worth it, and I would highly recommend it, especially because it is offered for free.

With a limited number of actions/turn in this game, an unfavorable RNG roll can be devastating when facing certain bosses. It's not uncommon to lose 30 minutes of effort to a bad roll of the dice even when you take steps to mitigate risk. The classic "gnome with a wand of death" trope of roguelikes is okay when the opportunity cost is relatively low - insta death after only 5 seconds invested can be a fun story, whereas losing larger investments to RNG  can be insulting to the player. There's a lot of potential for this game to be very good with relatively minor changes to the mechanics, but as of the build I played, I can't recommend the stress upon a prospective buyer.
In essence, a 15% RNG roll shouldn't make the difference between flawless victory and total party kill. There are many, many such incidents where a perfectly well-off party encounters a seemingly non-interactive end.
Tl;dr:  If you are the type of person who enjoys the anguish of having your multi-hour save file corrupted right before defeating a final boss, you might enjoy Darkest Dungeon.

This game may have been beloved when it was released, but I can't imagine why people consider it a classic, it does NOT hold up.
It's fraught with irritating technical issues and tedious level desgn.
Freeman glides around like you're skating on an ice rink, continuing to run for a short time after you let go of the key. This gives the game a very imprecise, slippery feel, which makes trying to navigate the game's first-person platforming segments a nightmare. Platforming seems to be the main focus of this game, due to the game's crude geometry and physics you will frequently find yourself being catapulted off a pipe or a ledge because you approached it at an angle that the game didn't like.
Jumping is another big issue, it seems to me that jump commands only register about half of the time, meaning you're going to be failing jumps because Freeman just floated right off the ledge, in general jumping feels very unresponsive.
So already we have slippery controls and jumps that don't register, in a first-person platforming game...
I'm not exaggerating when I say the main focus of this game is platforming, actually shooting at enemies (which is enjoyable) has probably taken up about 20% of my playtime. The other 80% can be divided between the torturous platforming, and the tedious, unintuitive puzzles.
I hope you have a walkthrough open because it's the only way you're getting past most of these. In one puzzle it took me about 2 hours of trial and error and probably 40 reloads to get to what I thought was the button I had to push, I traipsed all the way back out of the facility only to realize that there had been two buttons in that room, not one, and subsequently had to go all the way back through the level to find it. The game is full of moments like these, and it makes you dread puzzles, because they're not rewarding, they're a roadblock you have to get around before you can go back to the enjoyable shooting.
I would describe this game as an interesting story with enjoyable shooting, broken up by insufferable platforming and puzzling and marred by basic control issues.

I started playing this game this very month, May 2016, and still couldn't figure out why there are so many recent negative user reviews. Since it is free for all, and the graphic is quite enjoyable, I guess there could not be any harm to try it out. There was a bit of a learning curve for me, because I was not used to 3 dimensional combat, but after that, the experience was quite intense, there were a couple times that our teams and enemy teams struggled to gain advantages over each other and makes the game time last quite long for games like this. Contrary to some review, this game is definitely not a pay-to-win game. There are some items and ships that can only be purchased by real money, and they do give you a bit extra advantages, however, those "advantages" are quite small under the setting of this game, I never see any other online competitive games that emphasizes on co-op this heavily: gaining upgrades (either the whole team get to upgrades or no one on the team get to upgrades), capturing enemy base (capture is the only way to win), all of these are down to how well each team members cope with each situation as a member of the team so that the team could reach its goals.
After all this typing, all I want to point out is that this game is worth to play, the waiting time would be a bit long (2-3 mins for match making), and since it is free, it could not possibly hurt you in any way. Other than that, compare the play time of users between those give positive reviews verse those negative ones, and you will be able to find out this is truly a decent game, even at its alpha stage.

The game mechanics are really good. Movement seems to be very fluid and easy and combat is now actually challenging. There is more emphasis on stealth, so it's finally an actual assassin game! Now let's go to the bad part, which is low frame rate and frame drops. One segment in the game I would have a solid 40-50 fps, and in the next sequence I would only get like 20 even though the scenary is still the same. The other problem with the game is the frame drops. Every few seconds, you would get a quick frame delay that makes you change your movement direction and pretty much messes up your entire gameplay expierence.
Now let's go on to the wonderful city of paris, which must be my new favorite game setting. The developers of AC: Unity made a beautiful and realistic looking city. It feels very realistic due to the little details that they added everywhere. One thing that makes the city look alive is the people. They are always moving and waving their flags, talking to each other, or stealing/insulting others. The problem with that though is I think it's partially the reason why the game lags because it requires intense CPU usage to process all those movements and characters, even though Ubisoft said that the number of people on screen dosen't affect frame rates at all, but that is something must people are calling B.S.
If the patches are going to fix the stutter and fram issues, I would rate this game a solid 9/10 and it would be my new favorite Assassin's creed game. However, in it's current state, giving it a 6/10 is a little generous of me. I would only reccomend buying the game when the game is actually patched.
I currently do not reccomend the game but when, hopefully, frame rate issues are fixed, i'm going to change to a reccomendation because the game is pretty fun.

On its own, this is a good hidden object game. Puzzles are detailed and beautiful, the storyline is well worked out and, while lifting on a well-known fairytale, still has twists.
All screens are partially animated, making the world feel alive, and the cinematic scenes are the developer's best work yet.
Compared to its predecessor however, Grim Legends 2 disappoints a little. Voice acting is of a lesser quality, with even cases where the subtitles and voice dialogue don't match.
Gameplay wise, there is only one kind of optional collectable to the previous games' two kinds, and you can no longer opt out of a hidden object puzzle for another kind of game: you now only have the option to use the hint button instead.
Fortunately both have standalone stories, so you won't necessarily need to buy "2" for story reasons.
Good is that the companion idea from the previous game returns, with now not just one critter helping you, but a new one per chapter. They are also used more, and feel more relevant to the story.
There is also more variation in the puzzles this time than just combine A with B or slide puzzles, so there is less idea of repetition here. You also backtrack less than in Grim Legends 1.
Overall Grim Legends 2 is a polished game well worth playing, but I feel more could have been done with it to make it a proper sequel to the first game. Taking it as a standalone though, I can definitely recommend it.

Tadpole treble is a game of notes. You must note down the music and most importantly your journey through to your habitat. You have to overcome various obstacles, (but mainly being eaten) in your journey to your safe heaven. On a personal 'note' I didnt enjoy the game even though the game has many positives to it.The reason as to why I didnt enjoy the game is varied.
To begin with the game is suitable (imo) for only certain age groups and not the older and more matured gamers. Secondly perhaps because I played this game on a wide screen desktop pc, whereas the playscreen of the screen is much smaller. Which kind of ebbed away the magic of the game. Apart from these the game is about a tadpole who is carried away by a bird from his natural habitat. Than the story begins as you have to survive and reach back to your place. The game has a musical tonocity to the game. As the music is generally enjoyble.
The game has twelve levels all spanning hardly three minutes, The music as mentioned enjoyable. The storyline rigid but with a sense of replayability.. The game has various levels through which you have to pass through and obtain ranks.Each level also has Challenge Flies you can collect by performing a specific task, and bubbles you can exchange for extras like bestiary pages of all the animals you encounter in the game.
All in all the game has many pros but relatively less cons. Some being :-
PROS
1.Engaging music
2.Easy on the pockets
3.Various ranks to be gained
4.Compelling storyline filled with suspense (created by play through)
CONS
1.Rigid storyline
2.Each level only lasts some three minutes
3.A bit monotonous some times
I give the game a 6/10 for all its unpolished efforts.

Pros:
-Minimalistic. It's a nice break from games with complex intricate environments filled with detail. There's not much background noise to distract you.
-Good puzzles. The hardest puzzles are a nice challenge but not super tough (imo). If spatial puzzles are your thing then don't expect to spend 30min stuck in a room.
-Short. Again, a good break from that drawn out campaign you're going through in that other game. You can explore everything in the main game here in 3.5h or less. Secret areas included.
-Against the Qlock. The DLC gives you a bunch of short challenges with a ton of achievements. They do have a stressful change of pace but you can play them in many ways.
-Those elegant hands and forearms. I feel strangely attracted to them.
-Cool environments. Not all of them but there's some screenshot/recording-worthy moments.
Cons:
-Slapped on story. This version is basically the original with voice acting to give you some sense of story. Personally it rubbed me the wrong way. I prefered the mystery of not knowing anything (in a Myst like way) rather than feeling like I'm in a bad stereotyped American film. There were so many things that made no sense, so many plotholes.
-Preformance issues? I'm not the only one. I'd like to see what the highest settings look like while still being able to have a good framerate (or is this just lag? I can't even tell). And this game doesn't demand much from the graphical part.
-Linearity. While I like games to be linear when they do have a linear plot, it was confusing to reach the only part where the other characters instill you to make a choice and yet... there's no choice to be made. You just keep going forward. It becomes irrelevant whom you trust because there's only one way to progress in the game. Even if that's against your wishes.
-Unpolished environment. Elements without collision. Invisible walls. Strange transitions in the secret areas.
-Unskippable cutscenes. But hey, at least they are short. Unlike the slow and painful elevator rides added in so you'd listen to the monologues. I get what the developers were trying to do but I believe they went a bit overboard.
All in all I enjoyed itt. The story, as bad as it felt, was bad in a laughable way. There were gorgeous rooms and corridors to be seen. The athmosphere was serene and somewhat mysterious. And the puzzles were accessible enough while still having some challenge in them that you'd feel accomplished. Yes, there's a bunch of things that could be better but they don't take the fun away from this game.

In Tadpole Treble you play as Baton, a tadpole who has gotten lost and must swim back home through a variety of different levels. The gimmick of the game is that the layout of the levels corresponds to a sheet music notation of their own music. As you go through the level, you dodge the actual notes of the music while collecting bubbles which unlock rewards as you collect more of them.
Speaking of the music, this game has some of the best music I've ever heard in a video game. It's honestly terrific, and really adds to the enjoyment factor. (Highlights: Chiptune Lagoon, Midnight Bayou, Thunder Creek)
The game is not without a few flaws, though. The framerate on some levels can struggle sometimes, seemingly at random, and the placement of objects in the levels sometimes seems a bit off - it seems like you can occasionally fall between the points you're usually locked at.
The cartoonish, hand-drawn artstyle of the game is also very nice and charming.
All in all, if you like rhythm games and good music, you should play this one.

Q.U.B.E. is a fun puzzle game that aesthetically reminds me of Portal, but overall functions differently. I'd give it a 7/10, and would only recommend purchasing if it drops to 3 dollars or less. The game is ridiculously short, and it took me about 2 hours to beat (Left it running in the background for 1 hour while I did some stuff). It's a great game out of a bundle, and I'd comfortably purchase it at 2 dollars.
The sterile environments in Q.U.B.E. are immediately pleasing to the eye, and the first thing I honestly tried to do was shoot portals from my hands when I began the game. Every new puzzle element you unlock is very fun to look at, every chamber opens in a cool way that makes me feel like I'm in a gigantic Rubik's Cube. The lighting is done fantastically, and lights the mood pretty well from chamber to chamber.
While the little beeps and boops aren't anything to write home about, they're spot on what they should be. The voice acting is actually done quite well, which impressed me. I'm not one for dramatic storylines in my puzzle games, but the actors were semi believable, especially towards the end. The only thing I'd wish they'd done differently is have a couple more sliders in the audio options. There's only a master volume slider for overall volume, which would be fine if they had normalized some of the dialog. It's not a huge problem, but you'll notice especially at the end of the game that the music is a little too loud and the dialog is a tad too soft. Overall nothing too worrisome, just my 2 cents.
Q.U.B.E. really tried its best to create a dramatic storyline where you are the hero, but all in all falls flat with the sheer absurdity of it. Don't get me wrong, the game's pretty fun, but at every moment that the story tries to reel you in, it immediately reminds you how ridiculous the whole ordeal is. Spoilers -

The biggest issue I have with the game is the idea that they plant into your head that there are two endings. There are not two endings. You have 2 people in your ear at all times telling you that there are two options, and there just are not. There is a point at the very end of the game where you are to literally walk into something that completes the game, and there is someone telling you to do something else. When you try to listen to him, nothing happens. I even looked it up to see if I was being stupid, and I was not (this time). The whole thing is ridiculous. Spoilers-
I'm not a puzzle game connoisseur by any means. I immensely enjoyed both Portal games and the Talos Principle, but I do not actively seek puzzle games out. That being said, the puzzles in this game were pretty simple. Although a lot of the base concepts were pretty fun and unique, they were all pretty easy to breeze through. There were maybe two or three times where I had to sit and think hard about the solution, and the rest was pretty much "ah, red here, blue here, green here". I think that most of the difficulty actually came via the player's own mechanical capabilities rather than using your brain to get through the puzzles. Oftentimes, I immediately saw the solution, but had troubles trying to press the buttons fast enough to get it to work. It actually would not be that big of an issue if the buttons worked
when I pressed them. Sometimes the buttons would pop when I wanted them to, sometimes there was a tiny bit of lag that between my press and the actual event occuring, which is beyond infuriating. Either way, that artificial difficulty only delayed the game's completion by maybe 20-30 more minutes overall.
I honestly feel that artificial difficulty is the way this game lasts as long as it does. It's not so much that the puzzles are super hard, it's just the tedium of trying to get everything to respond the way you want it to. Don't get me wrong, the game is NOT a laggy mess. It's done rather well, it just has a few minor issues that wear on you as you play. Beyond that, sometimes puzzles are just tedious to be tedious. Minor spoilers-

All in all, I would recommend the game if you enjoy puzzles and have a couple hours to kill one day. Again, I can't recommend it at full price, but is a great value in a bundle.

I have never played Q.U.B.E before.  But judging by my playtime I seemed to have been very good at it.  Maybe it's that I'm good at puzzle games.  Or it could be that I had a natural intuition for the mechanics.  Either way, I could imagine that some people who aren't as good at puzzle games as I am would have trouble and wind up having double the amount of playtime I had.  The most troubling thing for me is the pacing of this game.  I understand that part of that is for the sake of the puzzles, but it really could've been made a bit faster so that we don't feel like we're plowing through molasses.
What I don't understand is why people compare this game to Portal other than the fact that they're both first-person puzzlers (well, this game is more of a puzzle-platformer than a puzzler, but I digress).  Let's be clear: this game is
from Portal.  It has no portals, unlike Antichamber for instance, and it has no buttons and very few lasers, and so the puzzle mechanics are flat out
That being said, I will say that this game resembles Portal in its tiled and
environments.  But even there you'll find differences, I can guarantee you.
And speaking of game mechanics, there are 5 main mechanics in this game, but there are also plenty more underused ones, encountered in the latter half of the game.
Next up: the story.  It's a simple story told through two voices — not entirely unheard of.  At times it did make me wonder what the ending was going to be, but otherwise it only helped enhance the
environment in the latter portion of the game.
The UI was simple — perhaps too simple.  Even Antichamber (another UDK game) had more flexibility.  At least it had some basics.
Overall: 7.5/10

What a wonderful game this turned out to be. Tadpole Treble is the debut game by Bitfinity, which among others includes Matthew and Michael Taranto. The former of those two is the author of Brawl in the Family, a really good webcomic I urge you to read. It unfortunately ended before Tadpole Treble came out, so you can treat it as the comic's successor.
Now, I mentioned Brawl in the Family because it had a handful of strips where Matthew got to show off his skill at composing music, and his great singing voice. Since Tadpole Treble is a rhythm game - sort of - these two are both used to full effect. You play as Baton, a newly-hatched tadpole who finds herself abducted from her home at Tadpole Pond by Coda the Pelican (you may be noticing a pattern here). She escapes, but unfortunately finds herself at the tip top of Opus Island. To get home she'll need to swim through all of its waterways, and evade everything that wants her for a snack - which is a lot.
Gameplay is a mix between a rhythm game and an auto-runner, with the twist that you need to avoid the notes making up the song instead of hit them. It has a pretty forgiving difficulty curve, and there's usually multiple safe paths, not to mention a super mode you can trigger that lets you plow right through them (but not other obstacles) after it's fully charged. The stages have a great deal of variety, and all of them feel like they have their own identity. In one you have to deal with a barracuda pursuing you through a dark cavern, in another swimming backwards as you head down a waterfall.
And the songs! Not all of them are voiced, sadly, but they're as unique as the levels, and fit them all perfectly. I saw a comment comparing them to the Kirby series in how they evoke different emotions, and that's pretty accurate. These guys definitely have talent.
Tadpole Treble only spans twelve levels and they're all only about three minutes, same with the songs that accompany them. That's not a problem for me, since it's priced accordingly, the levels are fun, and there's a decent chunk of replayability to them as well. There's the obvious S Ranks you can acquire for perfecting a level, and uniquely, F Ranks you can get by skillfully being as bad at it as possible. Each level also has Challenge Flies you can collect by performing a specific task, and bubbles you can exchange for extras like bestiary pages of all the animals you encounter in the game.
I don't think there's a game on Steam quite like Tadpole Treble, and while it's not exactly a rhythm game I'd recommend it to fans of the genre anyway, or just to anyone looking for something colorful, happy and humorous.

Charming little game starring a teeny tiny tadpole in a big watery world filled with danger, adventure, romance, badgers, and of course, music!   Squirm your small squiggly self up and down the treble clef to fight off pelicans, lightning, bears, magical mayan deathtraps, horny tadpoles, obese amphibians,  and the supreme enemy of all things... a poor sense of rhythm!
Tadpole Treble is a short, but absolutely adorable game featuring one brave tadpole in her quest to return home / save the world / not get eaten like a bite sized frogsicle.    The core of the game is a rhythm-platformer of sorts;  As a tadpole, you swim up and down an underwater musical staff to avoid rocks and things that want to eat you, while collecting bonus bubbles and accenting the rhythm with tailswings in order to perform daring dives and Ecco-esque superjumps.
Every level in Tadpole Treble feels like a brand new experience.  Each area features a unique musical piece (in a variety of styles), along with new enemies and dangers - and often a playstyle gimmick to boot (from playing in darkness to swimming backwards to warping through Mario pipes and whacking Duck Hunt ducks in a pixellated wonderland).  The levels are all accompanied by charmingly catchy background tracks - some purely instrumental, others featuring pleasantly amusing lyrics.  Clearly, the developers put a lot of love into designing the different areas of the game as well as the thematically appropriate musical accompaniment.  Each and every level feels individually special, and playing through them is a joy.
The basic game is rather short (you can probably rush through it in an hour or two), but the online scoreboards and unlockable extras for performing certain feats and collecting ALL the bubbles may keep you coming back for more.  Additionally, there is a composition mode for those who wish to create their own musical adventures.  Currently the composition mode seems a bit awkward (both to use and to share your creations with others), but at least it's an option.  Additionally, the developers recently announced that they're looking into Steam Workshop share-ability, so it may be easier to find new levels to play through in the future.

Tadpole Treble will stick a smile on your face - and then continue sticking with you long after you play it.   There are a few minor negatives to the game (the controls felt a bit loose to me, the story mode is rather short, and some of the gameplay mechanisms aren't explained very well in game), but these are easily overlooked in favor of the unusually delightful experience that Tadpole Treble provides.

tl;dr–waited far too long to enjoy a title that has proven very, very difficult but not impossible (update: at 66.5 hr this title proved to be a thoroughly dissatisfying and near-complete waste of time and effort)
I actually held off on this purchase for roughly 2 years because of negative reviews.  Specifically, the content of many such reviews--even those published by trusted media outlets--led me to believe that the difficulty was simply too high, and that happenstance would too often rob me of the satisfaction of a good run (and ultimately render completion nearly impossible).  The art direction, sound design, and writing eventually won me over, however, and for that I am thankful.  The balancing seems about right, though I have some experience at navigating both RPGs and roguelikes.  Thus far, "radiant" mode has proved punishing and difficult yet far from impossible, and I appreciate the developers' attention to the issue over time.  Darkest Dungeon has been thoroughly enjoyable to this point, and its unique feel has compelled me to return again and again.  Check out the BaerTaffy or Northernlion playthrough videos on YouTube if you're on the fence.  If you find yourself imagining better choices while watching the second or third episode of one or the other, then it's fairly safe to assume that Darkest Dungeon is worth a shot.
~ ~ ~ UPDATE ~ ~ ~
After 66.5 hr of play, I have decided that I cannot lose any more time to a title that has proven impossible.  The events leading to my last lv. 5 battle exemplify several of the reasons:
(1) lv. 6 party members make it to camp in poor shape, but heal enough HP to give us a decent chance with the lv. 5 boss the next room over;
(2) ambush during camp which leaves party in worse shape than they were prior to camp; party disorganized and surprised, enemies landed crit after crit of sometimes 30 or more HP while member after member of my lv. 6 party missed time and again and experienced negative responses to crisis after crisis; and, finally,
(3) lv. 5 boss encounter with my battered lv. 6 party becomes a complete disaster during which control of my party was lost completely due to paranoia, hopelessness, etc.; naturally, these afflictions did not prevent my party members from taking action when called to the enemy Siren's aid.
Battles such as the one described had become the norm as opposed to the exception after most of the remaining quests were lv. 5.  Losing lv. 6 characters resulted in a 30- to 40-hr loop during which I leveled lv. 3 characters to lv. 6 only to lose them in lv. 5 dungeons, resulting in a complete lack of progression.  Reviews such as my own kept me on the fence for a very long time, and I only wish that I had stayed there.  If you're unsure because of reviews like this, then it is probably best that you take a pass.  Otherwise, you run the risk of losing a great deal of time with little to show for it.  It comes so close to greatness in so many ways, but so many of us found ourselves exhausted, frustrated, and thoroughly dissatisfied in the end.  Being unable to compete a title in which you have invested this much time, 66.5 hr, because of an unfair RNG algorithm that creates impossible difficulty spikes feels pretty bad.  I can never recover the time that I have lost; however, there remains hope that these words might lead another toward the decision to preserve his or her own.

This game has amazing style, and that's what it's best at. Dialogue, cutscenes, commentary, character and enemy design - it's all great. You collect Golden LP record shards that the devilish bartender uses to play in "hell" to lure enraged demons that he mashes into your next weapon. Some cutscenes play by like an oldschool film roll. They even have a between-level arcade-like shooter minigame!
Other than the style, if I have anything to say about it, it's FUN. The gameplay is stylish, flashy, fast, and has a lot of fun cinematics (whether the optional torture attacks on random angels or the dramatic take-downs of big bosses). Every major and minor boss is unique and interesting, and when you think there's no way the next one could possibly be any bigger or more dramatic or intense, they find a way to pull it off. This game has found a way to pair just enough comedic downtime with the action to make it seem like its constantly building and outdoing itself with insanity and action.
It's not all that hard to play, so you really can lean back, relax, and just enjoy the gameplay. If you're into harder things, you can put it on hard difficulty and equip the moon of Mahaa Kalaa to make all enemies auto-enraged. There's also infinite climax mode, which removes one of the main mechanics that makes fighting easier (witch time, which slows down time and lets you get a few hits on enemies while they're frozen), but you have to play through it first to unlock it.
It's also got great replay value, imo. The story doesn't change, but the gameplay is truly fun, and they've thrown in a few gimmicks to give you the excuse you're looking for to keep playing. Beating it unlocks harder difficulties, you get to keep your money/items/unlocked weapons, and it gives you an excuse to be a completionist and look out for the witch graves, crows, and Golden LP record shards you missed the first (or second) time around.
I played this with a PS4 controller via Bluetooth and it was flawless.
TL;DR: This game is stylish as hell, and so fun you could play it twice just to keep going. Play it because it's fun, not because you want to get nitty-gritty into complicated combos and inherently challenging gameplay (something it sounds like DMC has going for it). I've heard it said that DMC is hard, while Bayonetta is easy but hard to do well.

This game is good, but it is not as good as people often give it credit. There are numerous things that hold this game back from being a truly great game, and it is not as good as the Devil May Cry series. If you haven't played DMC3, DMC4, or DMC (reboot) you should go get those games first.
[1] The combat is too simple. [1.1] There are TONS of combos, but virtually no reason to choose one combo over another. For most fights, I just spammed the punch button and ignored kick due to lazyness. [1.2] The saving grace of the combat is the "witch time" mechanics. When you properly dodge an enemy attack, the game will go into slo-motion letting you beat the crap out of enemies. Witch time is an awesome idea and mechanic, but the game relies on it EVERYWHERE. There are enemies that you cannot melee unless you are in witch time. Thus, instead of being a fun, rewarding ability when you play well, it is a chore being forced to trigger it and waiting for an enemy to attack you. [1.3] One of the things that makes DMC's combat so good is the aerial combat. In DMC you can juggle enemies in the air and control your positioning in the battle field. Bayonetta has some moves that briefly knock enemies into the air, but no good way to melee most airbourne enemies. There is even a trigger that cancels witch time when you jump in most combat situations. The game forces you to stay on the ground the majority of the time. [1.4] Sometimes enemies will drop weapons that are a welcome addition, but they only last like 6 attacks. Why can't I just have an arsenal of weapons like in DMC that I can swap to/from on the fly? Decisions like this meant the entire games combat is too simple and focused 100% around the witch time mechanics.
[2] The game is cheap (on your first playthrough). [2.1] There are instant death quick time events during battle and cutscenes. And often good players will prevent the quick time event from appearing. For example, there are multiple times when the floor starts falling. And decent player who notices the floor falling will IMMEDIATELY jump. However, if you jump, it will prevent the quick time event from appearing and you will die. Instead the game intends for you just stand there on the falling platform and wait till it lets you hit a button. [2.2] Many of the hit boxes do not match the animation/visuals. Learning hit boxes in a game is never fun, and it can really kill your momentum. [2.3] The game gives you the ability to dodge in mid-air, which is faster than standard running. HOWEVER, there are tons of scripted sections of the game where it expects you to move at running pace (not air-dodging pace), and if you use the mid-air dodge during these scripted sections, you will die because the game will destroy the floor under you because you are moving faster than intended. This is EXTREMELY frustrating on your first playthrough to be punished for playing fast and using mechanics. [2.4] The game is just inconsistent. Sometimes there will be an invisible wall stopping you from jumping off an edge, but 5 feet later that will will disappear and let you fall to your death. Not all properly timed dodges will trigger witch time either. For example, dodging most enemy aerial attacks will not trigger witch time. Figuring out what does/doesn't on your first playthrough sucks♥♥♥♥♥♥and is annoying. [2.5] The camera can sometimes be a real pain especially is specific boss fights. For example, the "Fortitudo" boss fight has an upper area and a lower area, but having two areas in the fight causes the camera to get confused. The camera might zoom in to the point where you cannot see the boss to dodge his attacks.
[3] The games graphics are like a clone of DMC4, but less memorable IMO. The angels have a statue-like appearance with gold accents just like DMC4. The backgrounds are usually quite bland with poor textures and color palletes. But Bayonetta does have generally cooler boss environments/arenas. Often in Bayonetta you will literally be fighting on raised earth/buildings in sky against bosses.
[4] Bugs (on this Steam version). I ran into ~4 crashes while playing this game. It had something to do with the loading. It would completely stop the game and go straight to the Windows debugger dialog. Once this happened, I could not select "continue" after re-launching the game, because it would crash again when I did so. I would have to choose "load game" instead, which would remove all my progress on the current mission/level. Luckily I never had to restart the game from stage #1 yet, so it isn't too big of a deal.
[5] Story. Bayonetta herself (and Rodin for that matter) are really cool characters, but the story in Bayonetta focuses on the wrong things. They do the old cliche amnesia plot and make Bayonetta forget everything. And there is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ side character "Luka" that is a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor attempt at adding mystery and emotion to the storyline. Screw Luka, I want to know more about the angels. Who is Fortitudo? Why is Fortitudo in the human world? What has Fortitudo been doing since the opening cutscene of the game? How did the world react after Fortitudo literally turned that city into a lava pit? What do the angels do when they aren't fighting the witches? What hapened in Paradiso when you killed angels like Fortitudo? The game has really cool potential for an interesting story, but they don't go into most of the intersting topics IMO, and they give the main story (Bayonetta's story) a sour taste with that amnesia.
[6] This is just a personal preference but I don't like the still-image style of cutscenes they went with. Why didn't they just render the 3D character models and have dialogue bubbles like in Folklore (another dark-fantasy PS3 game from 2007)? I would have prefered that style.
Side Note: Give Folklore a look. It is one of those hidden gems that didn't appear to get much attention.
Anyways... Bayonetta is still a good and enjoyable game overall. It just makes me sad because there is real potential that got overlooked due to some poor design descisions that make the game frustrating to play at times. I mainly see myself returning to Bayonetta in times when I need a break from DMC3, DMC4, or DMC (reboot).

One of my biggest gripes, which had to do with the scarcity of certain resources in the overal progression has been largely adressed.
It is now that I feel comfortable recommending this game without any reservation.
Fractured Space, to sum it up in brief, is a team-based capital ship MOBA, where innovations in positioning, movement, and strategy help bring a sense of much needed fresh air to an otherwise predictable genre.
The only complaints I have are minor, and chiefly have to do with the out-of combat UI, which can be obscure and unintuitive for newer players. The soundtrack lacks variety, and can get a bit boring at times.
The selection of ships can feel a bit overwhelming at first, but the game allows you to try out each of them in order to understand how they play. This is a feature that I greatly appreciate, as some of the ships require a good deal of time in order to fully unlock. It is good to know what a ship plays like, so you not only know whether you wish to unlock it for yoursef, but also so that you understand the strenghts and weaknesses of your opponents.
The gameplay itself requires equal parts in-the-moment skill, overal strategy, and map awareness. I like the balance that the developers have struck here.
The map design itself is nice to look at, but honestly feels like it could use a lot more variation. There is very little in the way of difference when it comes to the different permutations of environments, both aesthetically and mechanically. That said, the actual level of polish is excellent, with no real complaints regarding the individual quality.
The controls feel tight and responsive, the general concepts easy to understand, but challenging to master.
I have greatly enjoyed my time with this game, and encourage anyone to give this game a shot.

I want to start this off, point blank. I paid for this game, via their founder system. And that this will not be a negative review. For those of you who disagree with me, please skip to the end, there will be a message to those of you upset with the now F2P model Edgecase Games implemented recently.
Allow me to start like this:
1) Fractured Space, made by Edgecase Games, is a (currently) F2P, Arcade, Space, PvP Shooter/MOBA. It balances early game ships which require low knowledge of the game, being easier to play for the newer players, against ships which are unlocked at the end of the tech trees, which may / may not require more direct knowledge of things like armor rotation, optimal ranges, AoE's etc. So in that sense, I would call it fairly A-Symetrical, though that does NOT make the game dull, or boring in anyway. Each match played can have a variety of outcomes, so please do give it a good effort before you give an opinion (:
2) Now while I only have just over 100 hours the game, this is due to some personal circumstances in which my time has become quite hard to spare on all of my games. I do feel I am able to say with confidence that I know a bit of the community, I've spoken to some of the Dev's in matches (love them to pieces by the way, quite a nice bunch so long as you are actually constructive on any criticism's you may have of their game), and I've given my 2 cents on some of the things I find right/wrong in the game. And I feel as though the small number of concurrent players at any given time often turns people off of the game, while in fact, I think it is a MASSIVE advantage because it means that the community is tightly bound by their love of this game, and this company. They are willing to help those in need and to try to understand / debate those who have things that make them very vocal via the Steam Disscussions page, or those who are just generally unaware of mechanics in the game since they are brand new to the game.
*Please do pardon if the Second point is a bit of a jumbled mess, But It is a bit hard to put to words at present, I will post an edit if the proper words come to me later (probably not though, so apologies again).*
Note to those who dislike the new F2P model of the game, please read the following part.
Edgecase Games made it very, very clear since I started this game (at least 2.5 months ago) that they wanted this game to be Free To Play from the get go. But they had the founder packs in order to a) help improve development of the game, the money goes to a good place, and b) in order to make sure people who played during the Early Alpha stages were people who were actually going to be willing to put in effort in improving the game. Once again, this includes bug posting, reporting issues, suggesting fixes/changes to the game etc. They most likely did want to appeal to a larger audience, but sometimes a large audience means you get less and less information that is actually viable or usable.
TL;DR
Fractured Space, by Edgecase Games, is a F2P Space MOBA with a fantastic community, and a team of amazing Dev's that are willing to listen and respond to their players as long as those questions/criticism's are constructive or at the least, not flaming others in the community. I would HIGHLY reccommend this game for those looking for a great space game that is both fun, looks fantastic, and also for those looking for a community to just fit in with some others.

QUBE proves that even if you have no design ability, no artistic skill, no programming ability, and no creativity whatsoever, you can still make a video game.  The basic gameplay loop is that you enter a white room, look for the three or four colored blocks, click on them in the correct order, and then move on to the next room.  It's basically a paint by numbers puzzle game where someone forgot to paint the numbers.
Aside from the utter lack of anything resembling artwork in the game, the puzzles themselves are pretty boring and pointless.  The block elements in the game don't really lend themselves to interesting or intuitive puzzles, and your interactions with the various blocks are limited to one of two actions.
Also, in the director's cut, there's some sort of thin, pointless story thrown on top.  It's totally disconnected from the game however, so instead of being mildly annoying like most pointless stories in video games, in QUBE it's actively distracting since you'll be scratching your head trying to figure out what the story has to do with the boring white room you're currently in.

What is the number one threat to the life of a tadpole? Come on, this is an easy question! Did you say Birds? Fish? Human children hunting tadpoles for their science projects? Nope you are completely wrong. The real number one threat to the life of a tadpole is those spiky music note rocks in the water! Tadpole Treble is the story of the life of a newly hatched tadpole that swam a little too far down river and was as a result, eaten by a hungry bird. Luckily, after a bit of a struggle and a few thumps and bangs, the tadpole was ejected back out of the birdies mouth and narrowly escaped the miserable fate of becoming bird food. Unfortunately, now because of her carelessness, the little tadpole was sadly lost and trapped far from her home pond. You must feel terribly sad and worried about the poor little thing. Won’t you take the job of helping the young tadpole find her way back home? You will struggle with the daunting task of collecting bubbles, challenge flies and dodging enemies such as the dreaded music note rocks!
A developer who was formerly a popular webcomic artist made Tadpole Treble. He became well known for “Brawl in the Family”, before retiring the comic series and turning his attention to game development.  Part of the charm of the old comic series is when the artist would break out into a song. Ode to the Minions is always good for a laugh and remains one of my favorite musical pieces. The song can really make you rethink some of your actions in games to date. How, without a second thought, you slay the various creatures you encounter for no other reason than they are there and they might have some money on them. Do you ever think or do you even care what you are doing to those creatures’ families… you really are heartless when playing a game. Tadpole Treble keeps this tradition alive by breaking into songs on a few of the stages as you play.
Tadpole Treble appears to be a rather simple, auto-scrolling, rhythm game on the surface. You actually only have three buttons to worry about Up, Down, Attack. That’s pretty much it. To complete a stage all you need to do is avoid hitting enough things that will damage you so that you can make it to the end. If you do a decent job as you progress, you will even charge up a meter. When that meter is released, it will give you temporary invulnerability that allows you to get revenge on those spiky music note rocks. You can also attempt to complete the various optional challenges on each stage as well. Collecting all the bubbles, smacking things with your tail, unlocking the challenge flies, getting a high/low score, etc. will yield you badges on each of the stages to see your past accomplishments and earn you most of the Steam Achievements as well. As you progress through the game, the stages get more difficult. Now you are no longer just avoiding the spiky music note rocks; you also have to avoid being eaten by various creatures who think you would make a nice appetizer.
There are not all that many stages in the game, but that actually isn’t such a bad thing. Each stage you play has its own unique theme and accompanying tune. You can see the five line music staff that contains the spiky music note rocks. You are able to move along any of the lines or the spaces between/above/below the lines in order to avoid coming in contact with the spiky music note rocks. As you pass them, they change colour and sound their note which accompanies the background tune of the stage. On occasion you can add to the beat of the stage by attacking optional gongs with your tail which plays their note and tosses you out of the staff for a while before returning. Sometimes you need to time it just right so you can keep out of the water as you fly majestically though the air over the obstacles in the water below.
If you are so inclined, there is even a level editor included so you can start making your own levels. It seems to be quite powerful too! They are currently looking to add Steam Workshop support so that people will be able to share their new stages more easily rather than having to use QR codes to share levels.
Presentation wise, the game looks cute. It has a colourful, hand-drawn, cartoon style to it that is absolutely charming. Each of the levels have their own separate background and theme so very little looks like it was recycled from level to level. The music in the game is all original content and passes through several genres. The notes of the theme being the obstacles you face made an especially interesting and unique twist for the game. It even has the added bonus that if you are handy with an instrument yourself, you could play along just by reading the spiky music note rocks on the screen as you watch someone else play.
Would I recommend you get it? It is incredibly short. My playtime was at 4 hours at the time of writing this. That included me playing each of the levels at least twice, attempting the single life challenge mode, sitting idle listening to the songs in the music player, making and trying my own levels and attempting to do some of the challenges to unlock more things. There is plenty of replay-ability and it will take me a while to unlock everything. This game was crafted with the intention that you will be replaying all the levels multiple times in order to truly complete the game. If you like rhythm games, Tadpole Treble is definitely one you will want to pick up because it isn’t really like any of the other rhythm games that I have tried. Tadpole Treble is unquestionably unique.

In some previous AC games, I haven't really felt like an assassin. In the overdone recreation of XVIII century Paris, I was able to sneak everywhere; plan my paths to my targets to minimize contact with the enemy guards; and even had time to safely retreat to safety, ressuply, and find an other way to finish the missions without failing and restarting over and over again.
I say "overdone recreation", because for the single player missions, most of Paris is surplus. Landmarks and monuments are of course really well done but it's a given since it's an AC game. Side quests are not very interesting. Well, I'm not much of a completionist, I did some murder mysteries, nostradamus riddles etc. but it seemed pointless aside for unlocking unnessesary stuff. And there is quite a lot of those side quests.
However, since we finally play a stealthy assassin, there was nothing like managing the Brotherhood, distrupting Templar's grip on the city by taking outpost by outpost or things like that. Capturing naval forts in Black Frag was very fun but not so stealthy and not so assassin-minded, so it's okay if this kind of gameplay is misssing from Unity.
The essential Parkour element of the game was finally something that can be qualitified as decent and fluid. Press this button to climb up, this one to climb down. Want to stealth? No need to look for pre-defined "stealth here only" spots, just press the stealth button and voila, you stay low profile, make less noise and can move from cover to cover to get to the perfect spot for a double air assassination.
For once, Ubi didn't took the player for a complete noob and forcing us to play a tutorial : Arno got his blade, fast forward a year, got his first real assignment. Want to train? Do the tutorials as a side-activity.
For once, Ubi didn't force-fed the "modern" story missions. Aside from the occasional useless and irritating shift to an other time period. You want to know what happens in the modern world? It's a side quest available on the map. Don't care? Well don't and play some other mission.
As is proper theses days, this big budget game was released unfinished and bugged. But, since I was able to play the game even with a graphics card below the advised minimum requirements, I can't complain much. I was just happy to play without dishing out $$$ for hardware. Just wait for patches and you should be fine.
Props to Ubi for the character Elise, and for the subtle Hobbit reference.

Assassin's Creed: Unity was, in my opinion, one of the most promising games of this year. It still is. Great, high-resolution graphics, amazing aesthetics, and a breathtaking world perfectly uphold, even surpass, the already high expectations for the franchise. Co-op play is a genius addition, and the interactive AI seem cutting edge.
However, this potential was immediately destroyed by severe performance issues and game-breaking glitches in almost every stage of the game. Instantly, the title screen peaked my frames per second at 2, which is, in retrospect, the best I got throughout the experience, despite my up-to-date system. NPCs teleported around me in the tutorial fights, and my character would randomly turn 180 degrees when running. I had looked through the reviews before purchase, but dismissed the glitches as the price of playing a new, unpolished game. However, this was not the case; the game is absolutely unplayable and unenjoyable. I realize that the team behind this game is working to solve these problems, and I do not blame them for the issues- but game is CLEARLY not ready to be released to the public. From the reviews, I know I am not the only one to be let down by this, and likely won't be the last. Until these MAJOR issues are solved, I cannot recommend this game to anyone.

I received a press code for this and had zero expectations for it. I heard it was a rhythm game (which I like) but saw the art style and characters and assumed it was made for kids. I was totally wrong. Tadpole Treble isn't a long game but I had an ear-to-ear grin on my face the whole time I played it.
The story is that you're a newly hatched tadpole who is separated from her family and must try to get back home. Your journey takes you through a variety of environments, each of which have their own original songs and level specific challenges. The songs were composed and largely performed by the game's developers, some even have lyrics and they're fantastic. They're cheesy and goofy but are purposefully so and that makes them endearing. They mix up genres and themes and every song and the level its associated with feels unique and fresh.
The game isn't super difficult if you're just aiming to get through the story but you do have a score and are graded on every level, plus there's additional challenges and leaderboards so if you want to replay it, there are reasons to. When you beat the story, there's also an endurance mode where you attempt to play the entire story non-stop to see how far you can get and how big a score you can obtain.
Beyond this, there's an entire composition and level editing tool included! You have all the tools the developers had at your disposal and they tell you right off the bat that you have full ownership of anything you create. The one glaring omission here is Steam Workshop support. You can generate a QR code for your levels that you can share on forums and stuff but come on, something like this is begging for Steam Workshop! I really hope they're able to patch that in later as I could see a real community forming around it.
Overall, Tadpole Treble is fantastic and one of my biggest surprises of this year. It's a rare opportunity when I can go into a game knowing zero about it and be so pleasantly surprised in the end. It's a bit short but the content is so good, I think it's well worth the asking price. If you like rhythm games, jump on this. I don't think you'll be disappointed.
