Tadpole Treble is an atypical rhythm game that puts you in the role of the guardian angel of a small tadpole named Baton who, through a series of misadventures, finds herself seperated from her home and family mere minutes after she was born.  Against the backdrop of a treble-aligned sheet of music, you must dodge incoming obstacles (which are usually notes directly from the background music) and collect points and bubbles (currancy) in order to survive...and make a high score, of course.
This game absolutely charmed my face off.  There's so much character within every nook and cranny of every stage, and even the menus and extras have a lot of love poured into them.  Clearly this was the work of someone who was developing a game that they absolutely had the most profoud respect for, and poured every bit of their goddamn soul into.
For a price of $10 (I got it when it was on sale for $7), this game promises exactly what it's going to give you; a quirky adventure through music and life that is infinitely replayable through the game's "Compisition" mode, which lets you create your own stages once you've 100%ed the game (and that alone is no easy feat).  I've heard that some people have some difficulties sharing levels, but at least you can show your friends your musical aptitude and level design locally.
If you're looking for something different, charming, and honestly fun, please give this game a try.

Q.U.B.E. is a first-person puzzle platformer that's drawn a lot of sorta-kinda-warranted-I-guess comparisons to Portal. You're an unnamed protagonist who wakes up in a maze of blocky little passages (all alike) without any real explanation of how you got there or why. A voice in your headset tells you that you're doing something of incredible importance to the entire human race—literally incredible actually, as seemingly all you're doing is solving block-moving physics puzzles and it's hard to see any direct correlation between making the green ball go in the green hole and humanity as a whole not dying this week. And the character communicating with you seems a little...unreliable. And then you realize you may not be alone in there...
Which makes for a really interesting, dark tone that maintained my interest throughout Q.U.B.E.'s 3-hour run time in a way that it might not have otherwise. Solutions are logical but not exactly obvious, so there's a sense of accomplishment as you solve each puzzle and move along to the next, progressively harder one—but there's also a fairly smooth narrative progression as well, at least until the conflicting radio messages reach a fever pitch of urgency just as the puzzles start to require serious thought to work out, which slows things down enough to undercut the immersion a touch.
But the biggest immersion break comes from the realization that but there's never any opportunity to explore an alternate path or flip the script. You either keep solving puzzles, or you turn off the game. Very meta, but a satisfying conclusion it is not. This all culminates in a final choice which—though the scene in which it occurs is very emotionally charged—you ultimately aren't permitted to make in a way that feels meaningful. The story here really isn't the point so much as the atmosphere of tension created by having to rely on a pair of dueling unreliable narrators, and it doesn't exactly ruin the game that came before it, but a cheap ending is a cheap ending.
Still, the puzzles are good and the game is visually very appealing, with a clean aesthetic and clear objectives that never leave you wondering where you're trying to get to. Late in the game there're some lovely mind-♥♥♥♥y moments to be had as the corridors start undulating and swirling around you like the whole place has come alive, which is pretty sweet. If you've already got Portal and Antichamber and want something else to scratch that itch, Q.U.B.E. is a worthy enough Steam Sale pickup.

An original, creative, and fun rhythm game - the music is catchy (I've still got Piranha Jungle's theme stuck in my head!), the art is gorgeous, and the score-chasing gameplay is addictive and fun. The game is short, but with so many challenges to try to complete in each level on top of trying to set a new high score on the leaderboards, there are plenty of reasons to come back to each level after you've beaten the game. That's not even to mention the easy-to-use song/level editor, which is really fun to mess around with, at least if you have music-reading experience. I've really only got two complaints: keyboard controlling is a little fiddly (I honestly didn't try to make any music puns in this review, but there we are!), and my computer lags quite a bit on the faster levels if I leave resolution and visual quality high (though my computer was about the cheapest one at Walmart, so I doubt many others will have this issue). These are minor complaints (puns again) about an otherwise lovely rhythm auto-scroller, and I'd highly recommend Tadpole Treble to anyone.
As a side note, key signatures and bass clef would be nice additions to the composition mode. (Though I guess it wouldn't be Tadpole Treble if it was in bass clef, would it? Baton Bass, maybe?)

Decent little game.  I enjoyed both the puzzles and the story.  The voice acting and visual style both impressed me.  Simple but polished.  Not quite on the level of Portal, but if you've played Portal and want more, this will likely suit your taste.
The controls are a weak point.  I'm going to talk a little about that, and I don't want you to think this means I didn't like the game, because I did.
In some parts, you have to aim very carefully (there's no auto-targetting help), fairly quickly, and the targetting reticle is often nearly invisible.  The shot cooldown is applied unnecessarily to all situations, including color-change targets which often need to be shot twice (shoot it once, click to shoot again, turn elsewhere, notice that your second shot didn't go through, turn back, find the first target...), so these parts of the game feel can very clunky and frustrating.  Jumping is never very good in a first-person game, and it's an annoyance here as well.  In particular, when you're standing on narrow platforms, and you have to walk toward where you're jumping, it does that FPS thing where walking into the wall at even a slight angle makes you slide along it.  Because of this, and because you can't see your feet, it's easy to accidentally walk off a platform, and also to miss your jump at a precipice.  At times you need to aim nearly straight up or straight down, and due to an overly simple polar coordinate control model the mouse control is very awkward at this; it makes sense, but doesn't feel natural or work well.
The main story mode is not, by any means, an action game, so there's no real enjoyment in learning to skillfully and precisely control it.  It's a puzzle game, and fiddly controls just cause annoying blunders and waste your time.  The controls are better suited to the timed-run bonus levels, but in today's market full of cheap, good games, I don't think the bonus content is a good use of anyone's time.
These things could be fixed with, I think, little effort, which makes them all the more grating in a project where so much was done with obvious attention to detail.

When I finally got the last achievement for this game and ALT F4'd out, it said it took me 26 hours, but with all the time I've spent doing other things with this game just running in the background, I'd say it took me around 20 hours total to get every achievement.
I have quite a bit to say about the game experience I had.
I discovered Kingdom Rush not too long ago, and enjoyed it. I was quite excited for this game as a continuation.
To make it a bit easier to digest, I'll make a pros and cons list.
+PROS:
+The new hero level-up system is great. Rather than having to level your hero from level 1 on each map, it's cumulative.
+Better towers that all feel viable.
+The addition of small comic strips before or after some maps.
+Some of the maps feel more alive. Sandpeople from star wars shooting random targets, giant plants that eat whoever gets too close to them, erupting volcanoes that force you to move your guys so they don't get killed. Those kind of things.
+They toned slightly down on pop culture references that their last game was too packed with.
+More achievements than the previous game, although some of these are a little grindy.
-CONS
-For a game with so few voicelines, its sad that they use so much from their previous game.
-Lots of reused sound effects, visuals and sprites.
-It feels like most of the creativity with enemies and maps was spent in the early levels and then just dropped later.
-Most enemies are just reskins of eachother without having anything special about them.
-Besides what I mentioned in the PROS section, they didn't really do anything new with the game.
-One achievement is to have a templar survive fatal damage 5 times in a row. This is calculated to about a 7% chance. Having a 7% chance to get an achievement is not fun.
With that out of the way, I want to add that this is a FREE mobile game. I think in the mobile version you have to use gems to buy new heroes, and these gems can be earned or bought for money. While in the steam version, you get all heroes for free when you clear maps. I was perfectly fine with this when I played the first game, cause everything was new and exciting. But now that they have recycled so many designs, sounds, visuals and voicelines while at the same time hardly did anything to change up the game, I can't really say it's worth the money.

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic dungeon crawler RPG in which you take some heroes and watch them ♥♥♥♥ing die.
Jokes aside, Darkest Dungeon is very fun. It also happens to be about as challenging as it is fun. Or perhaps not necessarily challenging - rather, the player gets very little extra power over the enemies. What I mean by this is that in other games the player often has a very clear edge over the enemies, whether that be more health, better equipment, special powers, or whatever else it may be. Consider something like Dynasty Warriors. I look at that game and I see it as the opposite of Darkest Dungeon (though I've never played it, so I could be wrong as I'm just judging by the looks of things). Not in terms of genre or anything, but rather in terms of how much of a threat each enemy is. In a Warriors game, you often see the player effortlessly sweeping large crowds of something like 20 enemies into the air and performing extravagant combos on them. In other words, it's clear that individual enemies are not much of a threat. In Darkest Dungeon, it's quite the opposite. You have to always be on the lookout. Every single enemy that shows up could ruin your entire plan. Maybe your party is doing fine in terms of hit points, but a single stress-based enemy could cause them all to go insane, causing your own heroes to start stealing items, attacking themselves and each other, performing their own actions, shuffling around your party orientation, skipping their turns altogether, refusing to be healed or further stressing your other heroes out. Or maybe you're doing fine in terms of stress, but you've got a couple of heroes on the brink of death, someone might be bleeding out and you're out of bandages, or maybe they've just contracted some horrible disease that might lower their health, or their resistance to poison, or it might make them need twice as much food, etc. In this game there are tons of things that can and will go wrong. That's how the game was made; there's even a few paragraphs that show up any time you start the game before the main menu that explain that the nature of this game is intended to beat you down and leave you to try to pick up the pieces of your team. It isn't about always winning, it's about learning to make the most of a bad situation, and I think it does that very well.
As for the overall aesthetic of the game - it's... well, dark. There's a deep-voiced narrator who comments on everything that happens with fantastically flowery language, with lines such as "Prodigious size alone does not dissuade the sharpened blade" or "Remind yourself that overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer" which really adds to the experience. The soundtrack is well done, though it's nothing particularly of note. The graphics are all absolutely fantastically done. Yes, the whole game does (visually) look as good as those screenshots.
I would highly recommend Darkest Dungeon as a game. The visuals are great, the feel of the game is fantastic, and though it beats you down at times, that just makes it all the more satisfying to succeed.

Having watched Battlestar Galactica and grown up playing X-Wing vs Tie Fighter, I always wondered what it would be like to actually control a Cylon Basestar or pilot a Star Destroyer. This game provides you that opportunity.
During each match, after demolishing countless ships with walls of cannon-fire and missiles, you will feel like a motherf***ing bad*ss.
Make no mistake: this game is definitely still in development. However, the gameplay is fun as hell - especially when playing with a friend over Skype. The variety of ships and the sense of control and strategy you have with each one makes for a competetive yet relaxed atmosphere.
The game has also come a long way from when it first started. Updates are constantly coming around and half the time I forget that this is still supposedly in the "Alpha" stage. What about the useless reviews commenting on how some ships are OP? Every ship has a counter and no player can dominate a battlefield in a team game such as this.
In conclusion: if you want to blow b******s to pieces in a massive spaceship, this game is for you. Highly recommend.

This game is what you'd get if you put Space Engineers, Minecraft, and Robocraft into a blender, and it's every bit as amazing as that makes it sound. You build a base, destroy enemies, and use their parts to upgrade your stuff. You explore the world and gather resources to make yourself bigger and badder, and the enemies just scale along for the ride. You can build an amazing plethora of machines. Giant harvesting/refining rigs? Check. Tiny, speedy buggies and planes? Check. Huge monstrosities devoted to flipping enemy machines and laughing at them? Yup. Crazy machines with shields, self-healing armor...all well within your grasp if you're willing to dream them up. Even in early access, the game already has an amazing amount of content, only compounded by the community interaction. Remember in Spore how your creation could appear in other people's games, and theirs in yours? Yep, TerraTech does that. Enemy contraptions can 'invade' your world, forcing you to face off against other machines similar in size and power to your own, crafted by mad scientists and explorers the world over. 10/10 experience, highly recommended. If any of this sounds pleasing to you, try the demo (but don't judge too harshly just based on the demo, it's missing a -lot- of features.)

You awaken stranded inside a structure made from millions of interlocking cubes with no memory of how you arrived.  A woman's voice sounds over a radio.  "Fingers crossed you can hear me. You are in a large ship in space headed for Earth. You are humanity's last hope for survival.  Solve some puzzles, destroy the cube."
As the story progresses another voice crackles across the radio in your suit.  "The woman is lying. Her fingers are crossed behind her back. They stole your memories and trapped you in an underground test facility.  Do you really think solving tests will somehow save the world?"
The puzzles are fairly simple in design, though solving them can and does become very complex by the end of the game.  You're limited to 5 abilities: red cubes expand and contract, blue cubes bounce objects into the air, yellow cubes transform into stairs, green cubes create blocks that can activate switches, and purple cubes rotate sections of the room.
The game is fairly short, which is good since the mechanics don't really allow for much variation in puzzle design.  The solutions become more convoluted as the game progresses, but ultimately you're doing the same thing over and over again on a grander scale each time.
Aside from the new story, the director's cut also includes 3 beta puzzles that were note included in the original game.  These puzzles are essentially 3D tilt labyrinths and they add a tiny bit of variety to the game.  There are also some speed run levels to see how quickly you can click your mouse on colored blocks as you run forward through a level, but I don't much enjoy those types of challenges.

Hacknet is an excellent hacking simulator. Its user interface is very convincing and sleek, and there is just enough recognizable computer-jargon to make it somewhat realistic without making it boring or too dense to understand. Using the command terminal is way faster (and way cooler) then just using the GUI and makes you feel like you're the real deal.
Downsides to the game are the occasional spelling mistakes and the lack of explanation at some points in the game. My biggest issue with the game, however, is the complete linearity of the game. It never feels like you're interacting with a bigger world around you, just a pre-determined set of servers you have to hack, which is a shame. If it could be expanded somewhat to include a more dynamic 'internet' for you to explore, and more leeway in how to approach missions, this would've been the new standard in hacking sims. As is, it's a great game, but Uplink still holds the title.
The best art style they've done yet and a somewhat more serious story line make this possibly my favorite from this developer.

It'll say on my review that I recieved this game free, which is half true; I got it for donating to the kickstarter.
A creative spin on rhythm games with a charming hand-drawn artstyle. While this game has probably a few too many bugs (not counting the flies and mosquitoes), given that it's BitFinity's first game and it's still fun to play I can look past that.
The gameplay revolves around moving Baton the tadpole up and down the music staff, avoiding the notes of the song playing on that level. There are collectibles among the notes, such as healing petals, bubbles for unlocking bonuses, and bonus points if you want a high score. You can also do a tail slap to interact with certain parts of the levels.
Each level is a different style of song, and Baton must conquer them all to get home to Tadpole Pond. There are "boss" levels, but with one exception, you never actually fight the boss, just outmanuever them throughout the level and escape. The boss levels generally play like a regular level with a few extra hazards.
The soundtrack, as should be expected, is excellent. My favorites are Midnight Bayou for being a rather novel addition to a video game, and Thunder Creek for the excitement factor. Other highlights include the winter themed Snowfall lake, and the suspenseful Barracuda Caverns. Given all the different themes, however, I hesitate to call any of them better than another.
To summarize, Tadpole Treble has a few minor bugs, but more than enough content for a $10 pricetag and is an overall memorable, enjoyable experience. I give it 9/10.

Offensive is just superb and even hold up on all levels today.
The game has three campaigns that run between America, England, and Russia. You play as three different faceless soldiers, but the environment is the main character here. Each campaign has an amazing opening scene as well as some memorable moments like the escape on a Jeep in the American campaign, the gripping plane scene in the England campaign, and the tank scenes in the Russian campaign. There is never a dull moment in Offensive and everything from sound, great voice acting, and realistic sounding war effects bring together a riveting experience that I truly have not found in any other WWII game (even in later CoD games).
Instead of trying to pack every scenario into one game (including weapons) we get some long battles that feel challenging, but not terribly hard. Some scenes can last up to 20 minutes (like the plane scene in the British campaign), but it holds you out just enough to make you feel the terror of war and a little helpless. Some battles require waiting a certain amount of time before reinforcements arrive and then a wonderful orchestral soundtrack picks up and makes it that much more intense.
The gun play is solid and feels great with favorite weapons like the MP40, M1 Garand, MP44, and the Springfield sniper rifle. We’ve used the weapons dozens of times but each weapon feels different which includes power, accuracy, and mechanics of the gun. I feel the grenades still have no weight, but there are a variety of them. Each level and scenario feels different and gripping, but you never get attached to any characters because the environment is the main attraction.
Mutliplayer would keep you coming back, but due to the age there is no one playing online ever so you have to stick to LAN. War games just aren’t like they used to be, and United Offensive shows how to put across the feeling of war as well as realistic feeling weapons. United Offensive stands up graphically as well thanks to tiny details. The only thing dated are the low poly models, low resolution textures up close, and some static lighting. Most of the time you won’t notice because you’re sucked into the experience too much. If a game from 2004 can suck you in after playing modern war games then that really shows how much a games stands up.
--Score: 8.5/10

A fun game with lots of unlockables. If you love devil may cry youll both love and hate bayo. Reason being one of the main aspects of the game is the fact that tons of different combos are available from the start, so unlike dmc you wont be using the same 4 moves early in the game until you buy enough new attacks. The main problem with the game is also the fact that it throws a huge amount of combos at you early in the game. Theres some 50 or so different possible combos to learn. The comboes arent as difficult as say a fighting game, but memorization and muscle memory are a must of you want to ace the game. So long as you understand how the basic combos work, such as stringing punches and kicks, holding buttons and making pauses between attacks to change the combo, you can somewhat button mash your way through in normal mode. Some attacks as mentioned previously are purchasable, but are usually flashier moves that in and of themselves dont translate well into a combo, such as a teleport dive attack or more utility such as an air dodge. Additionally, different weapons have their own combos and mechanics but i didnt delve to far into then.
One complaint i have personally is the way enemies are treated in the game. The game doesnt have quite as many bosses as other action games normally have, with about 8 different bosses not counting rematches and an unlockable boss. To make up for it some normal enemies are much tougher and require more time to take down and fought either alone or in very small groups of the same enemy, such as flying snake angels where you fight no more than two at a time with out any smaller angel enemies. Id prefer more varied enemies on a single screen like dmc.
Personally the difficulty seems a bit skewed at times. Despite playing in normal mode ive found myself getting comboed by certain types of enemies for a quarter and up to half of my total health and a distinct lack of healing drops when killing enemies. I dont recall dmc being so stingy and brutal, just something you have to get used too in not dmc.
The game also makes use of witch time, where time slows down for a few second after a successful last minute dodge. This is great and all but for some fights the mechanic is almost required to get by on top and not half way to the grave. This is especially tue of enemies that are on fire, where you can only damage them while in witch time and take damage yourself when not. Im still not to sure how to get around this effectively since higher difficulties remove the witch mechanic altogether. Perhaps my skills have dulled over the years having not played a game of this genre for quite some time.
Anyways, this is a great game if you got time to kill and want a nice fast paced action game to play over a weekend, and an even greater game if you take the time to master the mechanics.  20 dollars well spent

"A deceptively addictive, wholesome adventure into a land of strangers that feels like home." - 9/10
Like most indie titles, Stardew Valley's genre is hard to put a pin in. It's part choose-your-own-adventure, part resource management, part RPG, and part trying to figure out if the Wizard is Abigail's dad or not.
The progression system will feel slow in the first few weeks, but the sense that you are moving toward improving yourself will become a captivating, intrinsic motivation to continue playing. You'll be compelled to unravel the mysteries of the Valley, like what's wailing on rainy days, what's at the bottom of the mine, or the various personal histories of the townspeople. Or, you know, showing the dullards at Joja how to *really* run a corporate empire with a ruthlessly efficient blueberry-based economy.
Some players may be off-put by the relative lack of tutorial, however the controls and gameplay are very intuitive for anyone who's played a PC game before. WASD to move and left click to interact. While it is possible to sleep immediately after tending to the farm, much of the game's longevity stems from interaction with the townsfolk. Stardew manages to make a single-player world feel like it's alive, a feat unaccomplished by most titles today.
I can not praise this title highly enough. It is one of only a handful of games I would eagerly accost a friend to purchase at full price. The developer has his heart in his work, and it shows. I have played ~6 farms over the course of 315 hours to date, and each time it has felt like an entirely new and different adventure. Just remember to always keep one of everything and don't buy the coop on year one.

This game uses real UNIX commands. For those of you new to the coding world (I guess?), it won't be hard to pick up; the tutorial does a good job of introducing the commands, and the 'help' menu will always be there to help you. For those of you who are familiar with the UNIX command prompt, you will be pleasantly surprised. The animations you get when hacking is pretty cool too. The best part of this games\ is that there are some systems that will start tracing you once you start your hacks. You have 100 seconds to do whatever you need to do and GTFO the system, or else (I don't actually know what happens because I have never failed doing so). You can, disconnect midway to cut the trace short and come back in the system again to do your stuff (again) at a later time, but hey, where's the fun in that? Along the way of making yourself a name in the hacking world (in the game), you will encounter files that are seemingly unimportant (like IRC log files, random text files, etc.). You are half right,
of these files are unimportant. They may contain jokes and the stupidity of internet friends chatting together; but the rest may contain passwords that will make your life much easier when attempting to access some systems or useful information on your target's location.
There are decent puzzles in this game that happens in a specific scenario, but the contracts you get are pretty repetitive:
. New commands are introduced every now and then, but those have instructions along with them, so it's pretty easy to do whatever you need to do after. Basically, it's not very challenging (unless the devs add a "No x-server" mode to force you to use the command prompt throughout the game, that would be really fun, devs pls read). The last thing that this game lacks is the ability to adjust the SFX volume. Me clicking things actually shocks me sometimes because trust me, the SFXs are loud.
In conclusion, Hacknet is a good hacking sim with a decent storyline and a bit of realism. Would I recommend? Yes. Would I play again? Yes.

Ah, Tadpole Treble. A game I have been waiting for since BiTF finished quite a while ago. As somebody who highly enjoyed the musical strips, I was looking forward to see what Taronto would do with his own game. And what do I think of it?
First off, lets talk about the absolute best feature of the game: the music. It's such a wide variety of genres, and yet EVERY one sounds good. All of them. I suspect witchcraft was involved. Obviously, being a music-based game, this is fantastic, as you're going to be hearing those tracks a lot. Which brings me to...
The Gameplay! It's all well and good having good music, but is the game itself any good? Well, I think so. The main gameplay revolves around obstacles and items being placed according to the music, much like other rythm games. What separates this rythm game however is that it effectively takes place on a musical score, with the things being placed according to their note. You move your tadpole up and down the score, and can occasionaly attack things in front of you with your tail.
So that's the basic gameplay, but each stage has its own gimmick that makes it unique to play. It could be going backwards, or being chased by Pirahnas, or losing health in the salty water... you get the idea. There's also a lot to do in each level. Each level has 100 bubbles for you to collect, which are the main collectable of the game, a challenge for you to complete, and several medals for you to achieve. And of course, you're scored in each level - with both high scores and low scores being recorded. Trust me, there's a lot to do.
That is, if you're going for completion. This brings me to my first gripe with Tadpole Treble: it's pretty short. I completed the story in about 1 1/2 hours, only really getting stuck on one stage. Beating levels is pretty easy for the most part, so bear that in mind.
The second gripe I have is with the controls. They're simple enough: up, down, and attack; but (at least on my keyboard) the movement felt very loose. I had to tap super quickly to make sure they only moved one layer, which became particularly egrigious when I was forced to carefuly manouver through dense layers of obstacles.
The final gripe I have is with the final boss level, which was very unclear as to how you beat it. I only beat the first phase completely by accident after I'd wasted several minutes waiting for something to happen. The second phase was admittedly fine, but the third phase... I'm still not sure if I was always doing it right and it just took an inordinately long time, or if I was doing something minutely wrong then got it right by accident. Oh well, at least I don't have to return to that level any time soon.
Despite my gripes, I still had fun with Tadpole Treble, and will likely play it again to complete some parts of it. I feel it's definitely worth the price, as long as you enjoy rythm games.
Oh yes, and the art is adorable. :)
EDIT: On replaying to try and complete the game I found out why I was having so much trouble with the Pirahna level: it lags like crazy. This not only makes controlling slippery, but sometimes it can even muck up the scripted cymbal events. Seriously, the second cymbal causes me to hit an obstacle when I land a majority of the time. And this isn't an isolated incedent - I've seen plenty of other people having the same problem. This kills the replay value, since it makes it impossible to complete the game. Which is a shame, as the rest of the game is really fun. I still recommend the game overall, but it's a shame I can't fully enjoy it. :\

The review:
If you’ve heard the name “Matthew Taranto” before then you must be a fan of his Brawl in the Family webcomic series. I know I certainly am, so I was one with that crowd when it was announced Tadpole Treble would be Matt’s (and his brother Michael’s) direct entry into the development part of the industry. It doesn’t have Kirby eating something funny or comedic shots of Solid Snake’s butt or Waluigi’s horrendously drawn face. However, what it does have appeals to my love for cartoons and music in a truly mesmerizing manner.
Graphics
Given how adorable the Brawl in the Family comics look, it’s no surprise that the Tarantos would deliver a similarly charming original world.  What makes Tadpole’s presentation stand out is just how kinetic and synchronized the action is. It almost felt like I was playing through a cartoon musical; there are events that would time themselves with the music. The backgrounds are fully loaded with animation and scenery. Tadpole Treble is the most visually interesting game since the day Parappa the Rapper birthed the modern conventions for a rhythm game.
Audio
Oh…my…God. This soundtrack. THIS soundtrack! It partially seems to be there to complement the stylistic gameplay, providing melodies that people could hop on board with. It’s not a bad thing by any means, since the general compositions fit the concept like a glove. However the highlights of the soundtrack come around when the music goes above and beyond to be as diverse and catchy as it could. Each level has a unique piece, and the instrumentals can range from piano melodies to drums and bass to full-on lyrics!
The music is in complete control of what goes on in the game, and players have no choice but to go with the flow. Because they’ll be having fun anyway. If anything, there is one level that (while the song is still solid) has a portion in which the mood changes rather abruptly. It kind of makes the song lose its momentum the tone had prior to the moment it changed. Other than that one nitpick the audio is an A+ in my book.
Gameplay
The gameplay is easy to grasp. As the plucky little tadpole, you move up and down to avoid the black notes and instead collect the purple bubbles. Sometimes you’d need to whip your tail at particular timings for extra points or to keep away from certain level-specific dangers. While rhythm games often rely on the music to be the basis for mechanics revolving around matching button presses, Tadpole Treble‘s gameplay is pretty much in the music’s hands. It’s fun to keep at the given pace and collect the bubbles as they are synced with the background piece. The graphics also come in to play in the form of surrounding animated animals serving as unique gameplay obstacles. There is life created through the musical gameplay and it does a darn great job at embracing it.
You too can embrace the lively musical cartoon vibes as well via the game’s Composition mode.  You can even make your own levels! And since this is a music game, that means you can make your own songs and share them with others. This is where the game’s inspiration from Mario Paint becomes a lot more evident. That’s because the music creation is intuitive and fun, much like Tadpole Treble‘s own levels. The tools are easy to learn, and the results are ultimately effective.
Verdict
Guys, I freaking love this game. Heart and soul is visibly poured into every detail of Tadpole Treble and all I can really think to do is obsess about those details. It’s like my interests in music and cartoons had a night out and partied at a multimedia theater. As much as I’d want to dish out a couple nitpicks (which I just barely managed to do), I have had too much fun mentally dancing along and playing through the game to care. Seamlessly synchronized and filled to the brim with charm and personality, Tadpole Treble is unquestionably a must-have for your Wii U. I can’t wait to see what else the Super Taranto Bros. will come up with in the distant future.

Lords of the Fallen is an action RPG that goes with a playstyle like the Souls series.  However, the combat is slower, and the story is clear.
This game has gotten quite a poor reputation due to some of its imperfections, I found myself annoyed at the fact a shield-bearing enemy's block couldn't be broken by normal means (In that they'll instantly recover to block again), and that when a large boss swings past you, once it finishes it's animation it instantly turns towards you.
Despite these problems that make the combat slightly less smooth, I found the game enjoyable.  Many secrets are around the world, which rewards exploring, as well as special challenges, which rewards backtracking.  Some of the bosses are fun to fight, each having their own mechanics you have to play around.
The enemy variety is admitably lack luster, though each enemy type is different enough in that the best strategy to kill one usually isn't the same to kill another.  Weapon variety didn't seem much better, many of the weapons I got were the same style/type with just a stat upgrade in some way.  Though, this may be due to me simply missing the unique weapons, as there were several doors I never found the way to open and secrets I never found.
Overall, I'd certainly play this game again.  If nothing else but to try out the other styles of play, and find the secrets I missed.

Putting that aside Age of Empires III ensures that the Age of Empires is one of the best RTS series' on the market. The new card and shipment system has brought in an extra level of strategy. The cards can be instrumental between a massive victory and a crushing victory, and i have often been involved in battles decided by who has the better cards. They can be the decider in who rushes the quickest, or who has the strongest military, or assist in establishing a stable econonomy with resource cards.
Trade routes and native training buildings also bring in more strategy, with the ability to train cheap, effective native troops who have no impact on your population (but still have a build limit). Trade routes pretty much replace and improve on relics and allow you to collect more than just gold from them and can be a good resource provider.
Units have been improved from 2 and nearly every unit has a strength against another type of unit, but for every strong unit, there is always a counter of some sorts. Although unique units from castles has been removed, you will find that in the base game, some civilisations will have access to some units while not having access to others.
Artillery has been improved (organers from AOEII would destroy every unit in a battle, friend or foe alike) and the artillery can play a much bigger role in deciding the outcome of a battle.
Ship Combat has also been refined and has become more fun to engage in, with access to ships that can train units, and having more than one ranged DPS ship designed specifically to destroy other enemy ships from a distance.
Overall, Age of Empires III is a great game and is my personal favourite out of the series. I would recconmend it to new players and veterans of the genre who have played the first 2 and are looking for something new. Although be warned, stratetgy masters from the first 2 games will also have to learn the new mechanics; you cannot just pick up where you left off in AOEII and think you'll be just as good in AOEIII, and vice versa. It will feel alot different when you go back and play the first 2 games.

Everybody knows by now that the launch of the highly anticipated Assassin's Creed Unity was - to say the least - a disaster. Tons of millions of bugs scared the customers and serious frame rate issues on every platform caused broken hearts.
A long story of patches, new ridiculous bugs and not working features followed the launch (which caused the shares of Ubisoft to drop about 10% at release date), a story no one had expected from a big company like Ubisoft and such a triple-a game.
A story which is too long and too churning to be told in this review.
Nowadays Ubisoft apologized by making the Dead Kings DLC available for free and giving those, who already ordered the Season Pass an additional free game combined with a hidden oppressive contract. Thanks for that! Plus, they granted us a fourth patch and finally the game is playable with far less problems. So let's focus on the game on its own at the beginning.
Assassin's Creed Unity is set during the French revolution in Paris and does a great job showing the tumults and split society. It's love for detail is incredible (the player can notice tons of different animations, from apple picking over dancing to book pressing) and it's graphics are stunning. The city of Paris is really big (maybe even a bit too big) and, applause, the most important feature of Assassin's Creed is back: beautiful architecture to be climbed.
This time the game features quite a lot of interiors that are ranged from generic to beautiful and impressive arranged.
The story of Assassin's Creed has a hell of potential, having a really amazing setting - a potential, no game can even fulfil and neither does Unity. The player takes control of Arno, a young Parisian whose father is killed as he was a boy. And there we go with the lamest motivation of all time, which sadly lowers the quality of the story enormously: Revenge. Please Ubisoft, how about Revenge, leading to idealistic deeds?
While Arno does have ideals and tries to save humanity, it never feels like he is aware of what he's doing. In conclusion Arno is a much weaker character than Ezio or Altair, and his story can't fascinate the player by far as much as Altair's or Ezio's story could.
There are tons of optional quests, but sadly they don't have anything to do with the main story. It's more like occupational therapy than an addition to the story on which the impressions could grow.
The game immersion has to suffer from another thing: A lots of game features.
The game has several features worth mentioning:
Overall there are lot of features in Unity that barely work to enrich the game. Some are fun at least, others are nothing but insolent.

United Offensive is largely more of the same from the first CoD, but with the spectacle ramped up a bit in spots and a really nice bonus with the B-17 bombing mission.  If you played the first CoD then it's back into play as the ordinary soldier again as you're pushed around to different setpiece battles where you face off against hordes of cloned German Nazis. You can choose which guy you kill, but you mainly feel like you're biding time until you're allowed to hit the objectives because otherwise the Nazis respawn endlessly to make life tough.
The B-17 mission is standout because it's got such a neat vibe; you're VERY MUCH playing whack-a-mole, but the variety of gun turrets at your disposal makes for interesting times, and the damage your plane suffers is uniquely more interesting than the other moments ingame where you're strapped to a moving vehicle and have to shoot stuff.
UO is an older title and has no reason for costing $20, but a sale of $10 or less is worthwhile.

This game has actually inspired me to begin watching `The Walking Dead' TV series - which I know I am very late to the party but I am enjoying that, too.

Anyway, if you're looking for a story-rich rollercoaster of emotions and a bit of a scare now and again, this is your one.

Whether it's your best friends son getting bitten and him being in denial until push comes to shove as he has no choice but to put him down and you have the choice of doing it yourself to spare him of his pain or to force him to do it. The Walking Dead puts you in charge of a girl named Clementine and she is the most innocent little girl, you care for her and you have to teach her how to survive and stop her from getting hurt or killed. Overall this game is a masterpiece that defines a true gem in the point and click genre, One of the most somber, Immersive, and down right disturbed atmosphere and relatable characters. Before, I did not like this game because you were required to rebuild yourself every time you fought and I really had no idea what I was doing. I posted a review of this game disliking it however even after uninstalling it I actually really wanted to play it again. So I reinstalled it no less than 24 hours later and found I had completely misjudge it's FTP model. The game is completely free to play however unlocking ships feels slow as of the moment because there are simply not that many ships in the game however within time it's clear they will be more ships that are easier to unlock. I'm not a space combat enthusiast however it's clear that the combat in this game as been at least in some respect streamlined. It's kind of like MechWarrior online and how they simplified the simulation game down a bit. For example I remember one of the star wars games had a system in which you could divert power form say your left shield and put it in the right shield because you knew you were going to be in the right side at that time and so on. That level of micromanage is not present in this game and that honestly a good thing it makes the combat more action pact and allows players to focus on moving and working with their time and timing there abilities. There nothing like that in this game and while that level of micromanage may have been present in order space simulators this game forces on its combat. And that's where it needs to shine if it wants to be a MBA style game. And it really does each ship has its own abilities that make them feel different from one author and they also feel different controlling. Overall the game shows great promise and it's free to play model isn't anything out of the usual the problem is as of writing this there isn't that many ships and some are the last line in a tree of ships so it jumps form say 4000XP to 72,000XP needed but that will change as the game is grown. Overall I'd say this game is more than worth your time espcially if you liked EVE online.

Got this game back when it was in early access and left a scathing review. But I have to switch that after playing the final product.
The basic gameplay loop is as follows: land on a planet, analyze artifacts of the local civilization to figure out where their species is hiding a plot progression item, play a constructed level and fight a boss and get that item, advance to a new planet with greater threats and better materials.
This leads to a surprizingly well consructed feeling campaign, despite every planet being randomly generated. The new planets you visit will have different crafting materials and be different biomes depending on what type of star they orbit which creates a difficulty curve that the player gets to decide. You can improve your character by getting upgrade materials for your Matter Manipulator (pickaxe), your home ship, and movement abilities. These upgrades require specific items you can only get by completing quests for locals or exploring planets, which gives you a good reason to explore the planets beyond the "analyze artifacts" step. And again, lets the player decide the difficulty they want to play at.
My only major criticism of the final version is that there isn't really anything to do in the post-game. There isn't any kind newgame+ content, so once you beat the final boss all you can do is visit planets with inferior materials or build up hotels to meet new NPCs.

7/10 (buy it on sale $10-15 range)

Disclaimer: Backed the kickstarter, fairly long-time reader of Brawl in the Family.  So I might be a bit biased!
One of my favourite things about videogames generally is the music, and while some of it took a little while to grow on me, the more I've played this game the more I love its soundtrack.  I guess that's the nature of game music - it really helps to hear it in context, at least at first.  And since this is a game where you have to really think about the music to play the levels well, that probably goes double.  I've had a soft spot for Chiptune Lagoon ever since it featured in the demo, but for me there's also a great stretch of level music for the levels from Snowfall Lake to Thunder Creek.  Then again, ask any fan of this game and they'd probably pick out their own faves.  I dunno.  Music.  It's good stuff.
The gameplay is solid, with a good difficulty curve.  I'm not generally a fan of rhythm games, but the decision to make it a game about dodging the notes (for the most part) rather than hitting them allows for a lot more freedom for the player - and creativity for the level designer.  The gameplay varies nicely, with some levels focusing on gimmicks and others just focusing more on hitting you with increasingly complex songs.  There are even boss battles every third level or so!  The main game is quite short, but there's plenty of replayability if you want to gun for challenges or high scores - which also adds to the good feel of the difficulty curve.  The game is easy to learn, reasonable to beat (heck, I've beaten it, and that's saying something) and pretty darn hard to master.
The art style is simple, cute and effective, and the game's writing has some nice humour, as you might expect from Matthew Taranto - make sure to chat to Etude whenever you get the chance :).
As it stands, the game's only real weakness is with Composer mode.  It's a brilliant idea - a toolset that allows you to write your own tunes and, in the process, design your own levels for the game.  The way that you transfer your saved levels to other players - QR codes - seems really clunky though, and if you try writing a long or high-tempo piece of music you quickly exceed the game's ability to generate QR codes for sharing.  Steam Workshop integration would be a huge deal if it could be implemented.
Other than that, the game's a pretty great deal.  I don't often write Steam reviews, but Tadpole Treble feels like it could use some more publicity, so I'm poking my head over the parapet for it.
PS: one great little joke in Composition Mode: the symbol for bass (the guitar) is a bass (the fish).  Well I laughed, anyway.

The gameplay, while not necessarily unique or revolutionary, is fast paced, moderately challenging, and fun. There is a solid selection of very unique weapons that are fully upgradeable, letting you experiment and create very different play styles.

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic dungeon crawler RPG in which you take some heroes and watch them ♥♥♥♥ing die.
Jokes aside, Darkest Dungeon is very fun. It also happens to be about as challenging as it is fun. Or perhaps not necessarily challenging - rather, the player gets very little extra power over the enemies. What I mean by this is that in other games the player often has a very clear edge over the enemies, whether that be more health, better equipment, special powers, or whatever else it may be. Consider something like Dynasty Warriors. I look at that game and I see it as the opposite of Darkest Dungeon (though I've never played it, so I could be wrong as I'm just judging by the looks of things). Not in terms of genre or anything, but rather in terms of how much of a threat each enemy is. In a Warriors game, you often see the player effortlessly sweeping large crowds of something like 20 enemies into the air and performing extravagant combos on them. In other words, it's clear that individual enemies are not much of a threat. In Darkest Dungeon, it's quite the opposite. You have to always be on the lookout. Every single enemy that shows up could ruin your entire plan. Maybe your party is doing fine in terms of hit points, but a single stress-based enemy could cause them all to go insane, causing your own heroes to start stealing items, attacking themselves and each other, performing their own actions, shuffling around your party orientation, skipping their turns altogether, refusing to be healed or further stressing your other heroes out. Or maybe you're doing fine in terms of stress, but you've got a couple of heroes on the brink of death, someone might be bleeding out and you're out of bandages, or maybe they've just contracted some horrible disease that might lower their health, or their resistance to poison, or it might make them need twice as much food, etc. In this game there are tons of things that can and will go wrong. That's how the game was made; there's even a few paragraphs that show up any time you start the game before the main menu that explain that the nature of this game is intended to beat you down and leave you to try to pick up the pieces of your team. It isn't about always winning, it's about learning to make the most of a bad situation, and I think it does that very well.
As for the overall aesthetic of the game - it's... well, dark. There's a deep-voiced narrator who comments on everything that happens with fantastically flowery language, with lines such as "Prodigious size alone does not dissuade the sharpened blade" or "Remind yourself that overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer" which really adds to the experience. The soundtrack is well done, though it's nothing particularly of note. The graphics are all absolutely fantastically done. Yes, the whole game does (visually) look as good as those screenshots.
I would highly recommend Darkest Dungeon as a game. The visuals are great, the feel of the game is fantastic, and though it beats you down at times, that just makes it all the more satisfying to succeed.

I really wanted to like this game...but it's just an unplayable mess.
First: The primary issue is that it's a pretty good tactical game that let's down by its execution. It's very common to have: enemies be able to shoot you where they cannot see your units, it's nearly impossible to guage what a move from your soldiers will allow them to see after the move (there's an undocumented feature that's terribly executed that helps a little bit with this, thanks to a mod it's pretty usable most of the time), enemies can take shots through walls / terrain / etc (this helped somewhat by mods), it's impossible to tell how far a unit will be able to move on the next turn (there's a hacky mod that kind of addresses this), it's impossible to tell the hit percentages of a shot until after the move is made, concealment is a joke and doesn't work right or the AI will just patrol right into you if they can spot a square inch of your toenail from 5 miles away (again helped by a mod), etc.
Sensing a pattern? The modding community has gone to extraordinary lengths to make the game playable, but they can't do everything.
The last straw came from a known bug that corrupted my latest game, as caused by the DLC Shen's Last Gift. It's been known about for months with no fix in sight, if you're curious look for: "pure virtual function call..."
I really wanted to like this game, but it fails in the same way the first modern XCOM failed and the modders had to do their best to fix that game with Long War, but couldn't do enough to make it playable either.
This will be the last purchase of the series until the developers can demonstrate they can address these issues.
UPDATE:
Long War 2 (LW2) came out recently. It's modifications make the game MUCH better in every way (better tactical combat, better story, better strategy, etc). I love LW2 to death. It was a labor of love and it shows.
Unfortunately it's built on top of XCOM2, which is still a buggy piece of crap in almost every way. Thankfully mods address most of the core game play issues (most notably stealth, which is just as awful as ever). It's so bad late in the game that you have to play with the console open just to fix the issues, so you can continue to play and so that game breaking bugs don't ruin your game. That's right, you have to cheat to play right!
Most of them are just screws ups of the core mechanics: enemies will commonly shoot you through walls and positions from where they can't see you and don't have squadsight, enemies will patrol directly into you during stealth (the LW2 devs thought they had addressed this, but in my play testing the obnoxious behavior of the AI to walk directly over you no matter where their patrol path is, is still there from XCOM 2), the LoS system is screwy and unintuitive, the system that shows flanking and the location of who is visible is broken fairly often (often you'll start a move because the system showed you had a flank shot on an enemy, only to get there and find out it was bugged and you don't have the shot, necessitating a reload or a console command to fix), etc.
Then there are some LW2 specific annoyances, but it looks like the LW team is doing their best to address (at time of writing, before 1.3), which is more than I can say for XCOM 2.
TL;DR: XCOM2 is still a buggy piece of crap, despite how awesome Long War is. Don't play.

I've been playing since the wipe back in January, and even as a relatively casual gamer have put in over 300 hours into this amazing game (and probably close to that on the forums).
On the surface, Fractured Space seems like a relatively simple MOBA style game, only
a lot of classic MOBA content such as Creeps and in-game items have been culled. And therein lies it's charm (well, besides the fact that your flying huge♥♥♥♥♥capital ship around!) For a new player, the game is fairly easy to come to grips with. Cap stations to give you resources in order to level up your ship, and open up the forward stations to allow entrance into the enemy Home Base while simultaneously defending your own. Cap to win.
But as you play more, you begin to get a sense of the depth of strategy and tactics involved. Each ship plays very differently, with different abilities and flight models. Engagements will vary wildly depending on the ships involved, and there are many ship to ship interactions that aren't immediately apparent. Then there's each teams ship composition to consider, and how that can drastically alter the approach needed to win the match.
Add in the frequent Gamma Lane all in brawls for the gas power-up, and you witness some truely cinematic moments.
Those who are worried about microtransactions- DONT BE! There is no need to spend a single dollar on this game if you dont wish to. Money does not give you any advantage against your opponents- only practice and experience will do that.
For those who do like throwing down a bit of cash, there are options to by some great Ship Skins, Premium Ships (which are identical in performance to their non-premium variants in every way except for credit/exp making potential), as well as some ways to speed progression via credit and exp boosters. But once again YOU CAN NOT PAY FOR AN IN GAME ADVANTAGE. No pay to win here.
There are a few things that need to be considered.
-AS polished as it may seem at time, this game is still in ALPHA. That means that it's very much still in development, and things can, and do change, especially if feedback on the forums is overwhelming on a certain aspect, such as the recent crew system. Use this as an opportunity to help shape the game.
-While there is a matchmaking system in place, it can only work with the number of players it has. You will get games that pit you against differnt skill level/rank players, as there just simply arent enough players yet for matchmaking to work 100% all the time.
-New player- GET INVOLVED ON THE FORUM. If you're having issues with a particular ship for example, ask for advice. I assure you that, for the most part, all ships in the game a balanced agaisnt each other. When you working through the ship tech trees, you aren't working towards better, more powerful ships, your working towards MORE COMPLEX ships with a higher skill floor, and the "grind" is to give you experience in game with more friendly ships before jumping into something less.
Overall this is an amazing game, that looks and plays amazing, even though it's still in Alpha. Would highly recommend giving it a fair go. After LoL, I was majorly put off anything remotely MOBA, but this game really is something special. The art, the pace, the strategy, and the cinematic nature makes this a game I had no idea I wanted so badly.
Also, giant space ships. Yeah, nuf said.

The Walking Dead by Telltale Games tells (excuse the pun) the story of Lee a convicted criminal, and Clementine a young girl in the aftermath of a zombie apocalypse. The story is broken up into 5 episodes, much like a TV series and I think it works well for a point and click game, building tension and excitement for the next episode.
Gameplay: You control Lee using a mouse or preferable a gamepad, as you would any other game. However, the game is limited in its action, consisting of interacting with the environment and pressing a button to choose a specific dialogue. There are moments interspersed throughout the game where you can aim a weapon and shoot, although it is very simplistic and scripted.
Graphics: The graphics of The Walking Dead is reminiscent of a graphic novel or comic book and works well to immerse players into a dark, brooding and ultimately, a world devoid of hope. They are not the best visuals in the business but are adequate.
In summary, The Walking Dead is not a game I would normally play. However, the survival story that you as a player encounter throughout Lee and Clementine's eyes is too interesting to pass.
Overall score: 8.5/10

Q.U.B.E: Director's Cut is a first person puzzle game that is as much Portal as it is NaissancE.
It functions essentially like Portal, with sequential, and well defined puzzles. However, when moving from one puzzle to the next, you encounter some pretty huge monocromatic structures, very much like NaissancE.
The difference between this version and the previous, is the addition of a story, through voice-acting... I don't think the story is very well put together, in the context of the game, though. It's not
, but I don't think it is very important, aside from giving the player a break between puzzles.
The puzzles are rather eclectic, drawing from several different types of puzzles. It certainly keeps things varied and interesting. Unfortunately, there will inevitably be sections with puzzles that many players may not like.
A specific example I can give is some of the physics-driven puzzles... It's always the same problem: instead of very clear cause-effect, you sometimes get weird interactions that make the puzzle much harder and confusing than it should be.
I'm also not a fan of sliding puzzles, of which there were a couple.
Overall, nothing too bad! Most of the puzzles were pretty good! I liked it. Not much more to say about it, though.
The visuals are great, and the music sets a nice atmosphere. It's around 4 hours long to beat the main campaign, but there are some time-challenges and other secret puzzles hidden around that may let you take something more out of the game.
Finally, I mentioned the story. Not to spoil too much, it's mostly trying to get doubt into the player's mind, by having 2 people trying to tell him different sides of the story, seemingly leading to a decision in the end. Unfortunately, the game was designed as a straightforward puzzle game. As a result, the story is literally a few lines of voice-acting between areas. It never affects the gameplay. The player never actually chooses anything. Never questions anything. Never explores around to find clues. Nothing.
It's just there! And what could be a cool thing, ended up being nothing at all.
It's purely a distraction.
But hey, this is all subjective. These were my impressions after playing through it.
Although not as striking as either Portal nor NaissancE, it does manage a nice balance of both, and it's definitely a good game! Worth a try if you're looking for a first-person puzzle game.

This game has been a big part of my life these last five days, as I have spent more time in a week playing this game than most americans spend working, one bout of playing it having kept me up more than 24 hours. 65 total hours in five days.
-Gameplay
During those hours I found myself challenged, having to adapt and learn, while also benefiting from my creativity and ingenuity, be it making my base be a sentry-base hybrid so that my one sentry would always turn to be be between my important stuff and trespassers, or using massive hover propellors to lift the front end of a vehicle for angling a long range artillery shot with those big, beautiful, EXP mortars. Creativity, ingenuity, planning, and knowing when to be bold or be careful are key, as this world is relentlessly relentless. It even has a good combat system that rewards those who plan their tactics and vehicle out in relation to their foe(s)!
-Graphics
Going into the game, the graphics were good enough for me, but yet I always found myself using the fastest setting due to how resource intensive big bases can be. Besides, I never focus as much on the eye candy so much as the actual, playable content.
-Audio
Simple, and still lacking sounds for many aspects of the game, with only two tracks I know of that I nickname "Cowboy" and "Drunken Cowboy Broken Beer Bottle Brawl". I don't mind too much, as they're probably focusing on bugs instead for the time being, this game itself being early access.
-Controls
Forward, backward, left, right, shift for hover pads/rockets, click'n'drag, and double click another of your vehicles to switch to it. 'Bout it. When it comes to how your vehicle controls, it's all on you and how you design it.
As for the stability of this game, I'd say it's best to relax, have some patience, or wait for them to fix up what's going on in the background. Early access and all that. Regardless, I've found a fun platform for unleashing all my little, devilish vehicles upon all the unsuspecting victims, "Invaders" included, as they get flipped right over by creations half their size, then have their bellies gutted so I can mount their 'parts' on my car. Who knew a game appropriate for kids could be so wonderfully vicious?
I find this game thoroughly fun, and quite replayable. Also, why does the yes recommendation have only a one thumb option? Oh well, I give it two thumbs up anyway.

Better visuals and music, a more grandiose story, and the same old cast make sure that The Book of Unwritten Tales 2 is not only a worthy successor of the beloved point ‘n’ click adventure game, but even manages to surpass it.
The Book of Unwritten Tales 2 brings us back to the magical land of Avantasia to meet our stalwart heroes one more time, who may have gone their separate ways since the events of the first game, but a new sinister plot quickly drags them back to adventuring.
As expected from a sequel, everything is now a little bigger and even a little better; this goes especially for the breath-taking graphics and the soundtrack. Only one thing got smaller, the time we spend with former protagonists Ivo, Nate, and Creature, as they now serve a secondary role to the little gnome mage, Wilbur.
The writing got darker, especially in dialogues and characterisation, and touching a few grim subjects—the humour is still there, but in smaller doses, with only a token amount of geeky in-jokes. The puzzles reflect this nature, as they are closer to traditional adventure game mechanics, where we can catch some of the genre-defining moon logic, but for the most part, they are only there to serve as some form of gameplay between plot elements.
Said plot is incredibly intricate, to the point where it could even stand as the story of a complex RPG. It has one crucial flaw though: it leaves quite a few threads hanging, and ends in a gigantic cliffhanger. Considering we have not heard of a sequel for years, be warned: you can get a wonderful adventure game, but one where you end up with more questions than answers.

Tadpole Treble puts a fun twist on the rhythm game genre.  Typically, in rhythm games, the goal is simply to time you're button press correctly.  Games like Guitar Hero, Rockband, and Rhythm Heaven are great examples of this.  The other way these games usually play is having you move around.  That encompasses your DDRs and Just Dances.  Tadpole Treble doesn't fall into either of those two categories.
In every level of Tadpole Treble, your goal is to dodge the notes as you swim down the river.  You can ascend and descend the scale to avoid danger, nab collectables/health, or simply to position yourself.  It's an incredibly fun way to play, and every stage has it's own way to keep things fresh and interesting.  A few worth noting are travelling in reverse, changing the theme to 8-bit, and giving you a tadpole partner who serenades you as you swim.  These gimmicks give every level its own unique feeling.
The aesthetics to this game aren't overly complicated, but they're pleasant to the eye.  Colors are well used to contribute towards the mood of each area.  Everything you need to know is quickly communicated to you, with enough time to react accordingly.
The music is excellent.  If you've seen Matthew Taranto's work on Brawl In The Family, or the Ace Attorney Musical, then you'd definitely see this coming.  I don't know much about his brother Miechal, but I'm sure they both contributed greatly to the final product.  The songs have very nice rhythm, and match their areas perfectly.  My personal favorite is Midnight Bayou, as it has vocals by Matthew (He has the voice of an angel).
This game is definitely worth purchasing, even in the early access phase.
UPDATE:  For anyone who cares, I personally recommended this game for the “I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award” Award.  I feel that this game deserves it more than any other I played this year.  I encourage everyone to do the same.

There has never been a game I have sunk so many hours into as XCOM 2. Over 400, to be precise.
So yeah, it's pretty damn good.
What really makes this game shine are the various insidious ways in which Firaxis makes you care about your characters. And yes, I call them characters rather than units, because if you're anything like me, you'll be spending at least as much time fastidiously picking their hairstyle, tattoos and jewellery as you will sending them to their likely deaths in the field. You'll never be prouder in a video game than when you're seeing the beaming faces of your underlings, slapping their knees in triumph as the dropship rockets them back home from a successful mission. You'll never feel more devastated than when they're cradling their heads in sorrow, mourning the loss of a comrade who bit the dust because you couldn't be bothered to find them some solid cover to hide behind.
Firaxis understands how to make success feel like a full-on, fist-pumping, champagne-popping triumph. From the deliciously satisfying death squeal of an alien stormtrooper as he gets ragdolled halfway across the map by a shotgun blast to the head from the kudos you'll receive upon returning from a flawlessly executed mission, this game will give you all the feels.
Also, I highly recommend adding Long War Studio's superb content mods, as well as the plethora of voice packs out there. Struggling against an alien occupation becomes that much more light-hearted when you have the entire cast of Futurama and Archer on your side.

Let me start of by saying I am a great fan of the Series and have been a Supporter of Ubisoft for many years now. I've foolishly preordered the game a few months ago and I have given the Devs some time now to fix the game so here is my Review on it so far:
Graphics: The game can be amazingly beautiful. The Artist did a superb job of creating a realistic and wonderful Paris, unfortunetly most players won't see it. The required Specs are really high and even if you meet them there are a bunch of graphical bugs and problems ruining the scenery. (Not even mentioning the problems it had at launch, which now have been partially fixed) (3/10 on release) 6/10
Sound: Excellent choice of music and voice actors, all quite well. No Problems here, nothing grandios either. 9/10
Balance: Fights have gotten a lot harder in my opinion but are still managable, if you don't happen to face a couple of well placed snipers who seem a bit OP. I'm really glad they fixed the alarm system, getting caught no longer means mission failure in stealth. The Assassinations can be performed differently now with a open approach on how you get to and kill the Target, although the secondary objectives are a bit too obvious in my taste. Then there is the microtransaction. This is a full price release, there shouldn't be microtransaction in it. Period. 7/10
Atmosphere: Paris is alive, there are people everywhere going about their daily business, you feel the uprest in the Citiziens and the tension between Guards, Fanatics and the Assassin. The districts are diverse and all sides of the city. The main story however is (as always) told in the present, which more then ever is more annoying than enjoyable. The jumps in history and "Simulation" seem like a quick way to throw some exciting stuff in but makes it hard for me to immerse myself into the world. 8/10
Controls: As always in AC best played with the Controller but Mouse and Keyboards works alright. The menues are obviously designed to work on consoles but are not terrible on the PC. But as always there are the weird problems with the free-running and climbing, getting stuck on weird places for no reason. 7/10
Extent: Paris is a large City, filled with the usual treasure and collectables, but some of the treasure is only accesable through playing the Companion App or Browser Game. There are many secondary missions (some of which are refreshingly new and interesting like the Murder Cases) so you'll be busy even though the main story is not really long. Now here is the real problem though: Save games are not save. When released saving the game was pointless and even though it was fixed for a time, many players still have problems with this including me. I had about 45% of the game when it got patched, now this save game is broken and I can't save anymore. (Was 6/10) 2/10
AI: Decent enough AI, the enemies have different approches and don't all wait their turn to be slaughtered like they used to in the older games, even though the regular guards are still easily overpowered. Allies are helping out ok, civilians are behaving like they should though sometimes a bit too late. Some guards have spotted me where they shouldn't have and not spotted me where they should have, and (especially in Co-Op) NPCs tend to have problems navigating.
7/10
Weapons and Skills: Costumization has gotten a lot of love in this game. There are many different Outfits, Clothes, Colours, Weapons and Skills to unlock and you can make your Assassin look unique. Sadly most Outfits must be unlocked (again) via the Companion App or Browser game. Also many of the Skills players have gottten used to as standart must be unlocked again. Some of the Skills and gadgets seem useless in the end game. Speaking of Skills, there is no way to get all Skills unlocked in the game. This is terrible as in the first playthrough you don't even know which skills are gonna be useful. 6/10
Story: As always the historical context and playing with the historical events and people is a lot of fun. Some Characters are great but sadly come to short in the story (Napoleon or de Sade) while the story focuses on a dull and obvious love story. The twists and the end are very predictable, and no veteran of the Series should be suprised. Sadly the ending is not only obvious but also seems unfinished and rushed. There is no real resolution as the game again only tells you about the love story not every other part of the story. Arno is an overall ok character but doesn't really have anything motivating him except for the love interest. I expect Ubisoft will provide more story and explanation in the coming DLC's and sequels but Unity's story leave me dissapointed nontheless. 4/10
Multiplayer: Lets put the first few days of Server troubles behind us and look at the Coop. The Idea behind it is great to me and it feels awesome to climb, jump and fight around as a team but the realization is again the problem. The Uplay servers still have problems, the gameplay is laggy, the NPCs are having difficulty and take way to long to follow protocol. Plus communication with your team (which would be very helpful) is impossible which makes it weird as most players don't like to follow each other around. 5/10
61/100
Summary: Do NOT buy this game in this state. Last time I've preordered from Ubisoft. They need to fix their game, which is a shame because at the core the game is really fun but it was released too soon. Maybe pick it up the Defenitve Edition when all DLC's and Patches are out.

If you played the Dark Souls series and loved their combat, don't think this will be like it. Well you can just ditch all your knowledge and the observating mindset. This game is not without its flaws (and there are a LOT of them - mostly to do with the horrid interface), but it needs to get noticed by more gamers. Why, you ask?
1. It's the only game of its kind for MMA. No other management sim comes close.
2. It's a statisticians wet dream. Every single fighter in the game has a unique profile, dozens of different attributes, and a fight history that develops over the course of the game.
3. Each fighter is also represented by some very nice artwork. (And many of the women are hawt!)
4. Even though it is a text-based game, the fights seem like they're happening right in front of you. If something exciting is happening in the ring/octagon, you'll get messages such as BIG STRIKE! appear in bold red, and it brings the events to life.
5a. The main reason why I love this game is the editor, which allows you to completely customise the entire database of fighters, companies, TV shows, etc, to your liking. Why other management sims don't do this, I'll never know. It adds a tremendous amount of value, (thus the hundreds of hours of play time.)
5b.  There are loads of brilliantly made fan mods available out there.
