Game was extremely frustrating at first, only because I'm not used to playing this type of combat style. This game actually got me to play Dark Souls just to see the connection everyone was talking about, and I'll agree it definitely was inspired, but its so different from DS that honestly the only relevant link I can make between them is the combat style. A few key things to note about this game would be:
- Every action you take animation locks you. Light weapons like daggers/fists are very short locks if you don't get snagged in a combo attack, and larger weapons like greatswords and maces have a longer lock (approx. 3-4 seconds per special attack swing). This is also effected by the type of armor you're wearing. Wielding Heirloom (elemental hammer) and wearing all light armor I was able to swing and dodge attacks significantly faster.
- Know your enemies! This game is 90% about knowing your enemies and how to handle them. This isn't the type of game where you get in and steam roll through trash mobs to the boss. You need to wait for your enemies to give you an opening and move in for the attack. The more you play this game & the more you die, the more you'll get better at noting openings in your enemies. Once you get the timing down to make hits in the sweet spots, the enemies drop like flies.
- Leveling. I found it insanely helpful to level grind for a while in order to progress to the area past the 3rd boss easier. The good news is that there's an experience modifier you gain from killing multiple enemies in a zone without going back to the crystal and healing. This modifier makes it insanely easy to level up and I recommend taking full advantage of it. (side note: bank your experience when you get the chance, it won't reset the modifier and you'll be thankful you didn't have it on you when that 1 mob decided to eat your face off in an area way far off from your last crystal touch).
Things I would like to see them improve on with this game:
- Combat system: swing/hit lag. There's been numerous times in a fight where I got hit by a swing that was actually 4 feet away from my face, as if the weapon has an invisible hit box on it that extends past the actual model of the weapon. There's also the enemies that swivel around to cornhole you when they should be stuck in an animation lock.
- Combat system: heaviness. I enjoy how heavy combat feels here, but to an extent. I've fought quite a few enemies wielding a huge great axe with a heavy shield on that come at you swinging a mile a minute AND have time to swivel on a heel turn and block your attack with that big shield that begs you to question why this is kosher when it takes you 3-4 seconds to make that swing and sticks you in a deadly animation lock. If combat is going to be this heavy I would highly recommend making sure all the monsters suffer the same penalty.
- Expansion to multiplayer/co-op. I really, really hope to see this game develop further into a state of being where other players can come in as other characters and assist. I realize at the moment everyone plays as Harkyn, so it's a bit unlikely, but this game has a ton going for it in all the right places and I would love to get the opportunity to play it with friends instead of having them watch me play. This game starts out a little raw in the beginning, so it'd be nice to have the ability to walk through it with a friend that's new to it and encourage them to keep going/show them the ropes.
- Map. This game would have benefitted GREATLY from a map or at least a compass that points you towards lost experience points like the loot compass if you're really against maps for forcing exploration (I'd argue there's no reason you can't just have people unlock the map by exploration as they go though). I had no problem memorizing where to go and how to get there after a few runs of zones, but whenever I died I wasn't particularly paying attention to the exact location I was in and I'd have to run around for a while to figure out where I dropped exp. There was also a time where I died at the entrance and dropped 6k, but when I respawned the experience wasn't there, even though I still had 100% (6,438) on the screen waiting for me to pick it up. I had to just take a dive because I had no clue where it put it.
Comments:
- I would have loved to see the story developed a little further. We know very little about Harkyn, but are continuously reminded of his reputation. This may be intentional, leaving the player to their own imagination, but it makes it feel a bit impersonal. Also, the ending was....disappointing. I just wasn't really ever sold on this game story-wise. I played it for the challenge and the audio clips were intriguing to say the least, but that was about it. It could have benefitted from a little more world immersion, cutscenes, and an ending that's better than just a re-cap of what you accomplished and a snippet of story about Adyr.
The ending feels rushed honestly, or like someone got burnt out and just needed to meet a deadline. It bums me out because of how awesome the game was otherwise -- but perhaps we'll see more great titles that improve upon this? :)
I would love to see some worthy content addition that adds more areas to play in so we're not stuck in just this one castle. While there is one other area you gain access too, most of the game is played just in a single area with multiple zones you're entering into. It's huge, don't get me wrong, but I would love to see more.
TLDR: I highly recommend this game and will be continuing to play with ng+ and ng++. It frustrates the crap out of me when I die but, I'm constantly challenging myself to beat bosses without taking any damage at all or meeting legendary requirements to make it harder on myself and taking advantage of every slow-mo death blow I deal while adding a "BAM" vocally for enhanced enjoyment, as is mandatory. Game takes a while to warm into if you'r'e new to it's kind, but stick with it and you'll get your monies worth.

A great experience, though awfully short. The game presents pleasantly sterile puzzling environments, while still succesfully introducing a plot and some story development to the player. The dialogue is very well written, and the little nudges to cause the player to think about the scenario a little bit are welcome and often provide a great base for further thought, beyond the game's scope. Throughout the game, little bits of information are fed to the player at regular intervals, but they provide more questions instead of answering them and serve to build up to a powerful conclusion, without becoming boring on the way. The puzzle mechanics are nice and mostly function correctly, although they're not very complex and might quickly become boring to puzzling enthusiasts. In addition, the sphere-based puzzles leave quite a lot of consistency to be desired. Any additional difficulties or factors are properly introduced and the player is quickly made familiar with them, making for a smooth playthrough without entirely being stuck on a new mechanic. Q.U.B.E.'s soundtrack acts as the atmospheric centerpiece of the game and perfectly accentuates the dialogue and the plot's setting, taking the player into a harmonic, yet isolated world all by itself. Ranging from smooth ambient soundscapes to rough, but continuous drone-like backgrounds, this game's score not only fuels its amazing atmosphere, but also makes for a great puzzling experience, both inside of the game and outside of it. With the right tracks for the right mood, Q.U.B.E's soundtrack is great for studying, work, or even more puzzling. Overall, I absolutely recommend this game to anyone with even a slight interest in first-person puzzlers, or games that require thinking in general.

Before you think that I am recommending this game because I found no flaws with it whatsoever, I did. It overheated my computer after 24 minutes.
Granted this is mainly a personal issue, stemming from the fact that my own computer's quite old and should probably be replaced soon.
I've played many 2D games (because that's apparently the bulk of what my computer can handle without dying), and this is perhaps the only one that's so far made my computer overheat. She Remembered Caterpillars, for instance, is another 2D game with detailed art with a comparable filesize (though obviously that's not everything), and it ran on my computer just fine. In short, I think the game hasn't been well-optimized, and because of it, I'm refunding the game. When I get a better computer, I'll definitely be interested in buying this again.
However, from the 24 minutes that I played, it's a very fun game with pretty neat puzzles (though with slightly frustrating but still tolerable execution). You control a man-- Oh wait, you don't. You control
a man, primarily by ringing bells, which makes the man try to go to certain spots on the map, and by turning lights on and off, which makes the man try to avoid any turned-off lights. By cleverly blocking off some paths on the map and allowing others, you have to make the man run over switches to open doors, access cabinets (containing keys to be used on locked doors).
Later levels add timing-based switches (which will only keep the door for a short time) and movable giant blocks (which will block off certain paths from the man).
Verdict: Fairly good game (I think), but not optimized well enough for people with older computers to play it.

HOOOOOOO boi. What a game this is. So if you're looking at this review then you're probably wondering, what is The Walking Dead? Well, it's a 5 part episodic game made by TellTale Games based on the comic series "The Walking Dead". That was a mouthful, but yeah basically, this is a game where your choices affect the story. How, you ask? Well, simple enough. I'll explain it to you. Imagine that there are two people and you need to save one, who would you save? Guy A or Guy B? Who you choose will affect certain outcomes in the game but it doesn't change that much here. Stuff like will you save this guy or not? Basically those things. Moving on, it's time to start the review.
Story: ( I won't spoil much)
You are Lee Everett, a man convicted of killing a man who slept with your wife. You are sentenced to life time to serve in prison, you get in the car with the police officer, everything is all right. However, as the car is moving the police officer hits someone and as a result, the car crashes. You gain consciousness and find an exit out of the wrecked car. You see the police officer dead on the ground, you get his keys and uncuff yourself. He comes back alive, however not the state you'd want him to be. You kill him and go into a house you see after escaping from walkers. You find out that this house belongs to a family of a girl named Clementine. As you investigate through the house, you slip on a pool of blood and a walker attacks you. You have to kill her with the help of Clementine. It works, and she dies. Then you have to decide if you'll go find help in the dark or in the morning. (summary ends here)
The story is pretty great, there were a lot of twists I wasn't really expecting on the way. It gets better and better every episode, more so with the final one. I loved Episode 5, it was really great imo. Perfect execution and ending. TellTale nailed it with the story.
Characters:
I for one would say that the characters in this game are really fleshed out. They feel real and can leave an impact on you. You might be asking yourself, "why would Lee go out on his way to protect Clementine all the time?". Well, that's quite a question but it's easily answered. He takes care of Clem because he wants to be there when her parents aren't, and adding up to that, he always wanted kids of his own. Going back to the characters. There's one character I didn't like much. Particularly Lily. I won't go into detail but, you want to care for her and understand her but then she does something really really bad. I didn't forgive her. Another character that isn't liked much as well is Ben. Why isn't he liked? Well, he gets a lot of people killed and is the cause of a chain of events that happens inbetween 2 episodes. He puts the group in danger because of his clumsiness and cowardness. He's a good guy but he's not really dependable.
Sound:
The gunfire sounds are pretty good. The sound of hitting stuff is good too. The sounds the walkers make are believable I guess. I don't know much about the music since I didn't really put my attention to it but that ending song is great. The one thing I know that is good is the voice acting. The voice actors really did a fantastic job in voicing their characters. Everyone's voice was pretty good, all scenes were acted really well.
Graphics:
I love the art style of TellTale so I like the cellshaded graphics that they did for it. Graphics aren't that amazing but they're good to me. They put a lot of work into the art and I can see that well. Overall great graphics.
Gameplay:
Not that much gameplay since it's an interactive story game but I like the gameplay. It's simple point and click. The shooting parts were fun too. As for the choices, TellTale again did a good job by making me pause for a while and think of what to do before choosing.
And that concludes my review of The Walking Dead.

I got over the moments when I couldn’t figure out a solution to a puzzle with considerable ease, as I allowed myself to sink into the meticulously made visuals and music of Pavillion. It may seem like I am completely overlooking the puzzling, the one gameplay element that should be the most important part of a videogame. That’s not the case, though. The puzzles are varied enough. Their complexity grows as the game progresses and, save for a few moments when the solutions bordered on the arcane, they are showcases of competence and understanding of pacing. However, as well done as they are, my attention glided primarily towards the music and the art style. The second part is due to come out this year, however, even now, I’d heartily recommend Pavilion to any gamer that loves puzzle games. More than that, I’d also recommend it to everyone else, for the overall experience of passing through a brilliantly designed world, while having a wonderful soundtrack as faithful companion.

I don't play a lot of shooters. Black Squad is your typical lobby shooter. You goto quick match, choose team death match and there you go. I found myself getting shot from around a corner at times even with my ping saying 40 ms. Things like that did not happen to me in BlackLight Retribution or Warface.
The tutorial is minimal. There are also some things that look like cover but do not stop bullets. You can be shot through them. It makes sense as they're flimsy wooden boxes but it took me a few deaths to really learn which ones they are.
Then there are the maps. The majority of the maps turn into massive spawn camping fests as the TDM's last about 150 kills. There is only a handful of spawn points, usually 2 for your team that are both easily camped with the, I believe it's 8 v 8 matches. There is also a bit of balancing in TDM with some of the guns. The sniper rifles for example, at least the M10 is pretty much a 1 shot from full HP no matter where you're hit. You also don't have the options  of classes in TDM, at least not from what i've noticed. That means no strategic planning like claymore mines or the like when in a normal match.
All in all, I think Warface does it better than this game. The netcode is shoddy and honestly the gunplay just isnt' fun. It seems like it takes a billion bullets for me to kill anyone with an SMG while 2-3 bullets from a rifle pretty much ends me instantly. I've already uninstalled but don't really plan on picking it up again.

A timeless classic. The story may be convoluted and hard to get behind, but the visuals, gameplay and general design are outstanding.
While Bayonetta is more than seven years old, the console versions felt ahead of their time. The visuals were simply too much to run at more than 720p and 30 frames per second. On the PC, however, the game can finally show off. The results are nothing short of spectacular. The game's age actually works to its advantage - even a midrange PC can easily run it in full HD. And unlike many older games, the visuals hold up on a 4K screen as well, thanks to an incredible amount of detail in the 3D modelling. The enemy design in particular is some of the best I have ever seen, easily on a par with the Dark Souls series.
Combat is fluent, responsive, and has such a wealth of combos and possible moves that it hardly ever gets old. The difficulty options offer a large amount of replayability, covering everything from "cake walk" to "inhuman". Despite this, the game never feels cheap. You always have a fair chance, and apart from a handful of overzealous quick-time events, skill is consistently rewarded.
Overall, this is probably the best example I know of a game ageing well. Considering the expectedly low price for such an old game, Bayonetta is a real bargain. If you like melee action games in any way, this is a must-have.

I am a typical lover of great RTS ttiles. I started with AOM and kept exploring new and fresh titles in the RTS genre slowly stumbling upon turn based RTS games like Heroes series. I learnt about Xcom via internet reviews and decided to purchase the original along with the expansion series. When a sequel was announced, I was really excited and always wondered what could be improved upon an already perfect turn based RTS game. I was pleasantly surprised with the new changes in battle modes especially the timed quick hit and run style missions which came alongwith Xcom 2. I found this really intriguing because I prefer the turtling strategy in my RTS games and apart from the limited bomb defusal missions in Xcom I took my own sweet time in completing Xcom missions. Here I was encouraged to completely rethink my strategy and reconsider my initial and late game playstyles. Apart from the new strategy changes I adopted I found new and more difficult enemies to defeat. With the release of Alien Hunters DLC its an absolute nerve wracking joy to pit your whole squad against an elite berserker queen with insane health and the ability to respond to each and every action of your squad including taking cover. It was more like trying to battle in a slowly drowning battleship against a colossal destroyer not entirely hopeless but each and every move you take has to be well planned and researched. I absolutely enjoyed the new DLC missions and am hoping that Firaxis will bring in more such awesome content in the future. There are a few wrinkles though, I killed my Berserker Queen by sheer luck, a repeater added onto one of my squad member's shotgun killed her instantly. While I got a great kill with literally no collaterals the easy kill spoiled the whole alien elite ruler boss thingie. I am a core single player and rarely play multiplayer. Xcom 2 can be played multiple times each with its own different experiences. I also love the fact that there are multiple community supported mods for Xcom which can enhance the gaming experience by many ways. I only hope that a mod similar to Long War in the original Xcom would be released for this one. I purchased a physical retail copy of the game for a much lower price than the Steam edition (Steam price Rs 3349 or 52$ for Digital Deluxe while I purchased a physical copy for Rs 999 on ecommerce websites. I purchased the bundled DLC for Rs 499 so the total cost is Rs 1500 or 24$). The price point is a sore thumb especially for markets like India where piracy is rampant and internet speeds average around 0.5 MBPS with ridiculous capping on data download limits. I have a 200 GB cap @ 100 MBPS speed followed by unlimited download quota @ 10 MBPS so I registered the physical game on STeam and downloaded the whole content. I would recommend this game for all those who are looking for a good Turn based Strategy game, both noobs and veterans. Noobs will get addicted to the great storyline and gameplay dynamics while veterans can enjoy the replayablilty factor and also enjoy multiplayer. One of the gems of my collection.
Finally there are very few games in my colection which have the privilege of being in both my PC and console library. Xcom was the first game to earn this honor.

This sequel is "more of the same", in a positive way.  Some new tower types, enemy abilities, and map designs will have you thinking in new ways.  For example, Necromancer towers let you raise your foes as undead to act as temporary blockers, and enemy spellcasters can shield their soldiers from damage, requiring focused fire or an antimagic totem to nullify them.  These new wrinkles keep the old formula fresh.
There are more Heroes to work with this time around, and "levelling up" is now permanent, instead of only lasting for a single map.  Some like this change, some don't.  I do; it gave me a little bit of extra leverage when retrying a tough map with a slightly stronger Hero than before, but it never led to steamrolling.  Some players will choose one or two favorite Heroes and stick with them; I rotated through the whole roster, and by the time I finished the last map on Iron difficulty, everyone was at maximum level.  Satisfying.
The original game was very punishing on the final expansion levels;
eases off a bit.  It's still hard at the end, but never seems to require "one true configuration" of towers as its predecessor did.  The previous game was a bit more hard core than I liked - once I was able to 1-star the last level on normal difficulty, I called it good.  Here, I was ultimately able to max score every level on every difficulty, and enjoyed myself the entire time.
Bottom line, this is another outstanding entry in the tower defense genre.  Enjoy!

First of all before my actual review: It was announced from day 1 when the game got on Steam, that it would be a F2P title.
The review:
I've played this game before the game went F2P, there where 2 things that holded me off to play much: 1- Small playerbase, 2- No ability to party up with friends. Issue 2 got fixed a few updates ago and issue 1 got fixed because the game went F2P. Yes the playerbase ain't huge, but So far I didn't had to wait more then 1.5 minutes for a match.
Unlocking ships ain't that slow like people try to suggest, yes you have to put some decent hours into the game to get to the last ships in a tech-tree. And no, you don't have to do that. Each ship has it's own playstyle, they have their own pro's and con's. An USR Venture (one of the beginners ships) is just as viable to pick as an USR Guardian (currently one of the ships at the end of the USR tree) depending on the situation.
Also you can get "Drops" from completing missions, so far I've got Platinum (premium currency) and Credits (in-game earnable) currency from those drops. But you can also get crewmembers and DNA (Points to unlock crewmembers) out of said drops.
I've 1 small complain though: The way how premium ships are handled... Premium ships are just reskins of free ships (which is a good thing, and yes I've checked this fact). The only thing a premium ship has an advantage off is the fact that it grants a 10% XP and Credit boost. But since there is a special place to buy boosters and skins for free ships, it gives a very wrong and strange first impression about how the premium ships work.
EDIT: This part ^ is not relevant anymore, they've changed this. Premium ships are gone.
Overall the game runs smooth for an Alpha game (it runs at about 55-60~ FPS at max settings with a GTX 760 (OC'd), AMD-FX6300 and 8 GB ram).
Also, if you don't like MOBAs: Still give this game a shot. I don't like LoL, Smite or Dota but I do like this game. Mostly because it doesn't feel or plays like a MOBA to me.

Fair warning: if you haven't played BOUT1, I don't recommend starting with the sequel. You will probably be more than a little confused with the story. Critter Chronicles can be skipped if you want, though I still plan to play it, if for no other reason than I need a third game in this wonderful franchise ASAP.
While the narrative is very connected between games 1 and 2, this one takes things up several notches. You can see it immediately in the production value, particularly in terms of the beautiful visuals. In just about every way, the look and feel of the game has stepped up in effort and budget by a substantial and noticable amount. The first game feels instantly dated once you play this sequel.
Gameplay-wise, the games are pretty identical. The puzzles are some of the best the genre has to offer, often based on the interaction of multiple playable characters which you swap between freely. There is very little, if any moon logic. But there's just enough challenge to make it cerebral enough for puzzle addicts like me.
Then there's the story. While the first game was a fourth-wall breaking comedy, the sequel is a 'dramedy'; serious and soulful AND filled with laughs. Coming from being a fan of darker stories like Gabriel Knight, I appreciate a story that makes me care this much without resorting to melodrama.
This is a classic in the adventure game genre, and I cannot recommend it enough. If you ever want proof that these games haven't completely died, here it is.

I wasn't looking for it to succeed Dark Souls, but I did expect it to at least be a satisfying experience in its own way. It's not and if I hadn't left it running idly while I did other things and accrued a play-time in excess of 2 hours, I'd have refunded this game even though I only paid $10 for it.
The combat is painfully slow, the enemies/environs tiresomely monotonous and the controls as unresponsive as a vegetable.
I knew the combat would be slow going in, but actually experiencing it is another matter entirely. Imagine the movement and mechanics of Dark Souls were universally reduced to half speed and suddenly the collision detection was off. So you have daggers moving like greatswords, axes moving like ultragreatswords that you don't have sufficient strength to wield, and anything bigger moving like glaciers across concrete. Top that with getting hit for 48 damage by the first boss even though every visible part of your character is half a foot away from his sword and you have combat in Lords of the Fallen. Why would you make everything slower instead of maintaining a wide and interesting variety of speeds? How could you fail to ensure that collision detection was working perfectly in a game where nothing else matters? These are the questions...
The Steam screenshots cover the extent of enemy/environmental visual design. You have your spiky-pauldroned guy with winged helm and axe...then a spiky-pauldroned boss with winged helm and sword/shield combo who only 30 minutes later appears in miniature as a standard enemy...then there are some blorchy zombie-mutant whatsits and some spiky-armored hooded guys with swords. Yeah...
Dark Souls did the boss as a standard enemy thing too...but the first time you see that is much later in the game and it gives you a tremendous sense of how far you've come. Seeing a boss as a standard enemy 30 minutes after you beat him gives you a tremendous sense of "what the ♥♥♥♥ is this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t".
As for aspects less mechanical...
Many people said the voice acting was competent. I say that's at most partially true. I don't know if it's poor acting or poor writing or both...but I know for certain that the near comically exaggerated animations certainly didn't help. The exchange between the player character and the woman on the cusp of throwing some priest over a wall made me wish I was the priest and that she had followed through to completion.
The music is generic and lame. The menus are barely serviceable. The different armors don't have any sense of uniqueness because their sizes all conform to the beefy frame of your character. The enemies continue to make annoying sounds 5 seconds after they're dead. Objects/textures sometimes appear to be clipping through each other. etc...etc...
But none of this would matter at all if the game was fun to play. And that is Lords' cardinal sin.

Pavilion is a hand-crafted audio-visual experience purposefully devoid of dialogue, text, and tutorials in an effort to express its story through visual cues and observations. Physical progression of the main character (MC) through his mysterious world filled with puzzles is dictated through interactions and manipulations of the environments themselves, providing only indirect control of the MC (you can not directly move him). This describes the game's ambitious "fourth-person puzzling adventure", and although Pavilion created a novel experience, it is encumbered with weak execution, ultimately denying potential for true greatness.
As a game whose goal was to tell a story using only visual cues and relying on puzzles as its only form of gameplay, Pavilion does not manage to perform exceedingly well with either aspect. Very little time is spent on developing the characters themselves, making it very difficult to form any sort of emotional attachment whatsoever. The environment and progression is so abstract and surrealistic that it can be very hard to discern what is going on. Throw in an unresolved ending to be revealed in Chapter 2, as a separate DLC to be released in 2017, and ambivalence towards continuation is what you’ll get. Even though I was able to see the the developers' train of thought at the end of Chapter 1, all I can really remember about the game are the baffling puzzle mechanics.
Extremely aggravating character pathing and speed puzzles that rely on precise timing ruin the novelty that Pavilion was trying to portray with its fourth-person concept. When you know what you have to do, but the character won't path the way you want, adding that subtle difficulty layer of figuring how to control the path doesn't provide any sort of challenge, just frustration. For example, most of the puzzles will have 2 bells in order to attract the character's attention. The idea behind this is that the player will have to ring certain bells in a timely, or specific sequence in order to attract the MC towards one of the ringing bells; however, there are moments where the MC makes a weird turn or moves away from the ringing bell. Add in step pads (with a timer) that require the MC to move in a certain path and the product is a fist-clenching experience. There are definitely times when the fourth-person puzzle solving manages to succeed in an innovative "ah-hah" sort of way, but those moments are very far and few between. Most of them can be solved within minutes, and the variance of puzzle mechanics barely differ with each other.
With a weak story and problematic puzzle mechanics, Pavilion does exhibit great art design - its major saving grace. The hand-painted level design made the game really immersive in its eerie, supernatural sort of way. Upon closer inspection, there are some interesting choices of horror aspects incorporated throughout the environment, such as: howling wolf-head mounts, faces carved into crystal walls, and ghastly apparitions taunting the MC. With no dialogue or text utilized throughout the game, minor reactions between the MC and his surroundings do a great job expressing a sense of terror inside the guy; a feeling that all he wants to do is get out of this crazy mess. His fear of the dark, whimpers of pain, and reflexes into fetal positions elicited a small sense of pity from me, even though I didn't particularly care about his survival.

I haven't felt so conflicted about recommending a game in quite some time. Most games have a strong tendency to lean towards one side of the is-it-worth-it scale, and for the ones that don't, there are usually aspects of a game that are either likeable enough, or distasteful enough, to provide some sort of conclusion. Pavilion is the type of game that is mostly aggravating, but pretty neat. Many may dislike it, but many will also enjoy it. A strong YMMV (your mileage may vary) candidate. I felt annoyed through most of the game, but thought that it was still worth playing. It's a terribly worded verdict, but all that I can come up with. With so many weak aspects and an incomplete story, I can only recommend this game to anyone that wants to try a new puzzling experience with some pretty eye-candy.

Pavilion has you playing as a man. A rather ordinary man at that. He has no super-powers, is scared of the dark and is also relatively unadventurous. The whole world is a mystery and even the gameplay can prove to be a bit of a conundrum. There is no text tutorial or beginning explanation. All you are given is a man, a gorgeously drawn environment and a cursor that is controlled via the keyboard. The cursor is there to help this man navigate his away around puzzling labyrinths.
Puzzles generally require you to create a pathway to an end goal such as a door, moving platform, archway or other such method of progression. To do this successfully you’ll need to prompt the man to move by ringing bells. Each bell is connected with a symbol on the floor that the man will run to when the bell is chimed. Sometimes there will be obstacles between the man and the symbol on the floor that will require moving, other times there may be lights that need to be turned on. As I mentioned previously, this man is scared of the dark, so he won’t run through areas that have no light.
The puzzles in Pavilion are really well thought out and are rarely too hard that you start to get frustrated. This is a good yet bad point depending on how you like your puzzles. Some people might find there is a lack of challenge that is instead replaced by long-winded requirements. Other people (like yours truly) will find the puzzles are quite satisfying to complete, especially when lateral thinking isn’t your cup of tea.
A lot of the mechanics involved in solving the puzzles are very imaginative and well planned. One such example of this is when you come to a point where your cursor is “upgraded” and can start to reflect light off reflective surfaces like crystal formations. The light provided will allow the man who is afraid of the dark to proceed. Other small nuances like being able to smash your way through wooden planks with an elevator are quite entertaining.
Along with moving the environment to allow the man to proceed are smaller puzzles inside chests of drawers that activate doors etc. Also you’ll need to make sure the man accesses some drawers in order to retrieve a key to progress.
So the gameplay keeps you hooked but does the story? To be honest, I had no idea why I was doing what I was doing. At one point near the beginning of the game you see a woman in white running around in an area you can’t access. Who this is, is a mystery. But to be honest I didn’t really care, I just wanted to get to the next puzzle so I could continue to test my brain! Of course there is a lot of mystery surrounding the story of the game, but that’s completely intentional. Curiosity is a powerful thing.
Stepping away from mouse and keyboard controls, Pavilion takes us back to the days of only being able to control a game using the keyboard. Here’s where a few people might kick up a stink. The cursor feels too slow when moving it around with your arrow keys, and sometimes when moving blocks around the fourth person plane, you can easily get confused as to which keys you should be pressing to get it to move in the direction you want.
However, personally I can see exactly why the game is controlled primarily via the keyboard. Often you will come across puzzles that give you a short time limit to activate the next required object. If you were able to move the cursor quickly with your mouse, the impact of needing to hurry would be lost. Controlling the cursor with only your keyboard adds that much more of a challenge to an already brain-bending game.
Each environment and it’s accompanying objects are lovingly handcrafted and provide the bulk of the pleasure to be derived from the game. Of course the puzzles are the main hook, but when a game has graphics this beautiful, it certainly boosts the entire experience.
Sound-wise, I really didn’t enjoy the background music or sound effects. I preferred to keep the game’s volume down to a minimum whilst playing. Some puzzles will have you scratching your head for a while, so you can imagine that the music would become quite repetitive and frustrating.
It’s always great to see unique indie games being released, and when they involve challenging puzzles and handsome graphics, it’s definitely a plus. The current version of Pavilion contains the first of two chapters, the second chapter to be released in 2017. And for the price you pay, the length of the first chapter is actually quite satisfactory. Depending on how good you are at solving puzzles, the game could take anywhere from two and a half to five or more hours to finish.
Pavilion is a nice little game to add to your library if you’re a puzzle fan, but if you’re looking for an absorbing story, sadly you won’t find it here. The main points of playing Pavilion are it’s puzzles and graphics, so if you’re into eye-candy and tricksy puzzles, you’ll get a nice experience from Pavilion.

Bayonetta is one of those games that comes around every now and again, and while it may never get massively popular, it develops its cult following with its loyal fanbase for a variety of good reasons. I know that less than 10 hours isn't enough to beat the game on Steam, but I played it before on xbox, so my memory of late game may be fuzzy, and as a result I won't be discussing the story of the game, but it is a great experience.
Right off the bat this game comes off as an over the top, blockbuster action game with Platinum's signature Mach Jesus playstyle. The beauty of it is that's almost exactly what you get. Bayonetta is a sexy, sassy, and shameless woman who will stomp pretty much anybody into the ground with her high heels if you get on her bad side, and is also a surprisingly lovable character despite her uppity first impression. The game doesn't take itself too seriously both in its cutscenes and in it's combat, and that's not necessarily a bad thing. The over the top fights, the wide variety of very well designed enemies, the wealth of combos and abilities at your disposal, as well as Bayonetta's quippy self as she dances around her enemies really lighten the tone, which is done especially well by the campy, upbeat soundtrack during its combat sections.
Now since the game has been out for a good while, its visuals, while still pleasant to look at, are nothing special compared to other games Platinum has put out since (NieR:Automata, MGR). Personally though, not my biggest concern. The gameplay is where this game excels, and it does so with flying colors, albeit a few minor hiccups here and there. The controls are tight and responsive with an easily grasped combo system and an easy way to evade attack, although the camera can sometimes get itself into 'unfavorable' positions which can obstruct your view of the screen. The difficulty is a healthy challenge, but there are some enemies who will quickly put you in your place if you're not quick enough with the dodge or the heavy attack to stun them. Thankfully the game has a very gracious checkpoint system which restarts you before that specific combat scene so you don't have to replay half the level again, and again, and again. There are three ways to succeed in Bayonetta and get those platinum trophies, be fast, be stylish, don't get hit. On the downside, a couple really awkward driving sections could definitely have done well with a bit of a rework.
TL;DR: Bayonetta is a great experience with great controls, good challenge, a colorful cast, a great soundtrack, an interesting setting, and a unique and interesting storyline. Highly recommended and well worth the 20 bucks for the time spent.

Oh boy, where do I begin?
Half Life, such an iconic game to me and so close to my heart, being one of the first real games I enjoyed playing and went back and finished numerous times. In my opinion it's one of the best games of the 20th Century, and dare I say it, of all time (and I'm sure many will agree with me).

There has never been a game I have sunk so many hours into as XCOM 2. Over 400, to be precise.
So yeah, it's pretty damn good.
What really makes this game shine are the various insidious ways in which Firaxis makes you care about your characters. And yes, I call them characters rather than units, because if you're anything like me, you'll be spending at least as much time fastidiously picking their hairstyle, tattoos and jewellery as you will sending them to their likely deaths in the field. You'll never be prouder in a video game than when you're seeing the beaming faces of your underlings, slapping their knees in triumph as the dropship rockets them back home from a successful mission. You'll never feel more devastated than when they're cradling their heads in sorrow, mourning the loss of a comrade who bit the dust because you couldn't be bothered to find them some solid cover to hide behind.
Firaxis understands how to make success feel like a full-on, fist-pumping, champagne-popping triumph. From the deliciously satisfying death squeal of an alien stormtrooper as he gets ragdolled halfway across the map by a shotgun blast to the head from the kudos you'll receive upon returning from a flawlessly executed mission, this game will give you all the feels.
Also, I highly recommend adding Long War Studio's superb content mods, as well as the plethora of voice packs out there. Struggling against an alien occupation becomes that much more light-hearted when you have the entire cast of Futurama and Archer on your side.

Kingdom Rush series again managed to deliver a solid Tower Defense game. If you are itching for a casual and dynamic tower defense game look no further. This comic-esque game is similar to the predecessor with quirky dialogue and paid its tribute to some of the biggest games and movies titles in history such as Mortal Kombat, Indiana Jones and etc is guarantee to bring back some memories.
The gameplay and towers upgrade structure is the same as the previous title but a whole new tower specialty upgrade. There are no single way to win a level. DIfficulty is scalable and does not affect yours unlockables or stars earned. There are also no pesky leveling or tower upgrading outside level.
Heroes, however now has persistent level meaning experience and levels gained are permanent. Heroes are free to choose from once they are unlocked (by progressing in game). Levels can be challenging but also rather forgiving. There are many enemies type and the levels are spanned across several theme each with its own traits and strategy.
The length of the game is simply enough to keep things interesting without getting too grindy or repetitive. For achievements chasers, don;t be put off by the long list. Once you've completed the game entirely, surely most of them have been unlocked so put no mind to them when playing. Game is balanced and levels can be short enough to pick up a game or 2 casually if you won't want to sink too many hours at one go.

Fractured Space is a  5v5 teamdeath match type game, where each player uses 1 of 3 factions  Capital ships to capture specific points that allow you to warp to the enemies base. The maps are set out in a "moba" factions with 2 lanes and a jungle in the middle. in the lanes there is a warp point that connects you to the lane and your base, if that is taken the other team can then warp to your base and start caping it. On the other end a point leads to the enemies base and you can cap it and then be allowed to warp to their base. A zone is also located in the middle where at certain times a point will be availble to capture and if you do it will grant a damage bonus to all allies making it useful to push back enemies.

I am long overdue for writing a review to this game clearly as indicated by my hours played. I'm not very good a objective reviews but I'm going to try my hardest to do so.
So Fractured Space is a free to play game about big old capital ships duking it out in a 5v5 situation. It has amazing visual and audio effects for all ships, though I will admit some are more fitting than others. The gameplay is extremely compelling and involved and you really have to do your research if you want to get good at it. This game is not for the faint of heart or the ones that easily give up. It's a very hard game at the start and can be very punishing. Each ship you can play feels unique and perfectly distinguishable both visually and in a gameplay sense. The game also has a great community behind it and i've made many good friends playing it.
The major negatives I can think of are all mostly excused by the fact that this game is still in development but that doesn't mean it shouldn't affect your decision. The game has a lot of minor glitches and bugs, most of them don't make the game unplayable but for the nitpickers it can be a little irritating. The game is also really not optimized so those with potatoes for computer might not have a lot of luck with this game. I hear a lot of complaining about the servers from others but I have fine responsiveness and performance from them despite having an average of 200 ping. The game is also currently not in an amazing state of balance in terms of the ships themselves but Edgecase (the makers of the game) is not currently invested in ship balance because they are focused on putting all the systems in place before they are 100% functional. Balance is still on going but it isn't a priority for them.
On the side of more good things I can say that this game is genuinely a bundle of fun. It rewards the skillful and encourages teamwork. It's very tactical and really drives you to think about every action you take. The map is separated in to five sectors that you have to use a jump drive to access. The game is also filled with a variety of brilliantly designed and voiced crew members that provide bonuses to your ship. Something else to note is that the developers are very responsive to player feedback on the forums. They read almost everything even though you might not think it.
I apologize if this review feels a little jumpy and all over the place, i'm not good at structured writing. The big thing I want you to take away from this review is that the game is a ton of fun and while it may have some problems, they will most likely be fixed in the near future.

Got this game back when it was in early access and left a scathing review. But I have to switch that after playing the final product.
The basic gameplay loop is as follows: land on a planet, analyze artifacts of the local civilization to figure out where their species is hiding a plot progression item, play a constructed level and fight a boss and get that item, advance to a new planet with greater threats and better materials.
This leads to a surprizingly well consructed feeling campaign, despite every planet being randomly generated. The new planets you visit will have different crafting materials and be different biomes depending on what type of star they orbit which creates a difficulty curve that the player gets to decide. You can improve your character by getting upgrade materials for your Matter Manipulator (pickaxe), your home ship, and movement abilities. These upgrades require specific items you can only get by completing quests for locals or exploring planets, which gives you a good reason to explore the planets beyond the "analyze artifacts" step. And again, lets the player decide the difficulty they want to play at.
My only major criticism of the final version is that there isn't really anything to do in the post-game. There isn't any kind newgame+ content, so once you beat the final boss all you can do is visit planets with inferior materials or build up hotels to meet new NPCs.

Hacknet is certainly worth the $15 list price (and if it's on sale, even better).  The gameplay is highly atmospheric with an engaging storyline.  If you have a four or five hours to set aside, I'd recommend playing through in a single sitting - I did, and I found it made for a very immersive experience.
The game does an excellent job of progressive puzzle solving.  I was reaching back trying to remember what tools and strategies I used in earlier hacks in my attempts to complete increasingly complex contracts.
On the downside, the hacking itself can get repetitive.  Around the 40th time I ran SSHCracker.exe, I found myself wishing I could just get to the next plot point in the story.  However, the game isn't too long, so the feeling of repetition doesn't turn into a feeling of grinding.  Additionally, the game progresses at a fast enough pace that it wasn't too long before I encountered a new type of defense or a new way to break into the system, and the "side quest" contracts are punctuated frequently enough by unqiue and highly engaging contracts.

This adventure offers around 20 hours of entertaining gameplay : probably the lengthiest point & click that I know of. Gladly the kind humour remains the same, with so many references of Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones, etc. This game made me smile and laugh so many times I stopped counting. The gameplay is intuitive, but there are complex and challenging puzzles or actions nevertheless.
From an artistic point of view, the game is simply astonishing : the graphics are gorgeous and colorful, sometimes you just take a minute to admire the background and the details ; the soundtrack regroups elements of the first game and adds some new splendid musics (surprised myself humming after playing) ; the voice acting remains impeccable, at least in English.
I would advise to play
first in order to get familiar with the story and the characters. In my humble opinion this game deserves more credit : it's a must-have for comedy / point and click lovers. Let me cross my fingers for a Book of Unwritten Tales 3.

Nice, but not as good as its predecessor(s)!
The First BoUT took me by surprise and I ended up simply loving it. It had clever humor, nice references and fantastic characters. The "extension" named Critter's Chronicles didn't quite live up to the first game, but was still quite fun and still had that quirky humor that I loved in the first one. When it comes to this installment I'm slightly disappointed. Don't get me wrong. I still think it is quite good and well worth playing if you are into adventure games, but to me it falls a bit flat and thin compared to the others.
Firstly, it has to be said that this game is probably one of the lengthiest point & click adventure games I've ever played, and that should be a good thing. Only, I feel like the story and plot has been stretched just for that reason, to be lengthy. This makes portions of the game feel a bit dull and unnecessary, and I hate to say it, but it could have gained a lot by shortening it a bit to keep momentum up. This caused me to get a bit bored with it all and I had to take some breaks from the game to do something else and then come back to it. Something that is unusual for me to do.
You get to play the same characters as you do in the previous titles and they are all very familiar, though I found it to lack a bit of the fun banter they had in the first game. For the most part the voice actors on both the main characters and the NPC's you meet on the way are done well, but is at times a bit monotone. Wilbur especially seem to react pretty much the same way to every situation. At times it feels a bit more read out loud voicing instead of acting while voicing. I'm however more surprised about the voicing of some of the NPC's as some of them are really good. I also like that you get to meet a lot of the characters you met through your first adventure in this universe, and more than a handful of new ones as well. Sadly my favorite from the first game was nowhere to be found here (Death).
When the game finally came to an end it felt very anticlimactic to me. A bit rushed even, which seems odd seeing that everything else seemed stretched out. It definitely leaves you on a cliffhanger with hints to a 3rd book coming eventually. And, even though I felt this was a step down from the first, I hope there will be another one. There is a lot of talent in this team and I want to see where they take it next.
Artistically the game is brilliant. It looks absolutely stunning. The scenery and backdrops are highly detailed and has a lot of fun elements to them. The characters and their animations are well designed and suitably quirky in the way they behave. You're bound to fall in love with several of them.
The music is also very well made, and clearly inspired by the works of John Williams. Already in the main menu did I feel like I was going to go on an Indiana Jones adventure. I would however have liked a bit more sound effects in the game itself. Some ambient sounds and the like to build up the atmosphere of your surroundings, and also maybe some more dramatic build-ups to certain events. However, I do understand that one does have to cut some corners to make budget.
There are some technical issues too. I did not experience any crashing or game-breaking bugs, but I had quite a few losses of audio. More a slight irritation than anyhing as you also get text to read, so you don't necessarily lose much. It also seemed a bit unresponsive at times  and I had several occations where I had to click several times on an item for my character to interact with it and even to walk to certain places. I also found the inventory a bit clunky to deal with, but that could possibly just be preferences.
All in all it is mostly a good game but it failed to really engage me. After completing it I felt a bit unfulfilled, and I was left with several unanswered questions. Let's hope that they continue the story and ties up all the loose ends there and go out with a big bang. For an adventure fan there is still a lot of worth in this title and I would certainly not want to miss it, but it does not feel like a game that would make many new fans of the genre either. By this time the game should be pretty easy to get on a sale, so if you are looking for a lengthy and cheap adventure you might want to look into it. It would certainly be worth getting on a discounted price.
I'm ending up giving this a 6/10 rating which might be a bit strict. At least compared to the overall ratings here at Steam. But to me it is slightly above average. It is of course a subjective opinion and if you read this as a tool to decide to get the game or not, be sure to check out several reviews and not base it on this alone. Even though I didn't find it to be all that good, your opinion could differ a lot from mine. And clearly a lot of others found this to be very very good. Thanks for taking the time to read my review :o)
Happy gaming!

As a fan of "Brawl in the Family", I might be a bit biased, but I will say that this game is incredibly well-done, as well as fun. Yes, the main story is small (I could probably have finished it in about an hour had I not gone back and replayed many of the levels in order to get at least an "A" rank on each one), but the addition of "Composition Mode" is really fun to play with, and there are plenty of online levels that can be played if you scan the QR codes. Not the most efficient system, but I'd say it works for now.
Also, I'll probably end up buying the soundtrack at some point. The music here is top-notch.
Anyway, despite the short length, I'd say this game still justifies the $10 price tag, and I do indeed recommend it. If rhythm games aren't your favorite or you don't really enjoy music-centered games (there is at least one person out there like this), I would still say to maybe wait until the game goes on sale and then give it a shot. It is definitely worth it.
Afternote: This game is indeed a finished product, despite the "Early Access" tag. This is not a scam or a trick to get you to buy the game before it has all of the gameplay features; the game is complete and surprisingly polished.

Age of Empires 3 is basically Age of Empires 2, but with less content, less gameplay options and better graphics/visuals and AI. I guess they had to sacrifice some for the others, but we seldom know what happens behind the curtain. The gameplay experience is practically the same, but with some changes. In this game, as you build your city, collect resources, build an army and lead them to conquest, you gain experience points, which then grant you cards from a premade deck or a deck of your choosing, each card granting you a perk. Basically, it is an RTS with RPG elements. I don't think this feature is either worse or better than the original RTS experience, but it is certainly interesting and can turn the tide of battle, especially if you have a better deck than your opponent. This being said, the game definitely feels less balanced than other RTS  games, along with a handful of specific units that are obviously a bit overpowered.
I'm recommending this game because it is still fun, but was certainly lacking content and gameplay options, is not better than AoE2 and definitely not better than Age of Mythology.

It seems many do not understand why some of us would dedicate our time and show our love to Age of Empires 3. While some might say it is old and “dead”, no – in fact far from it. With the help of a friendly online community known as ESOC, this classical RTS gem remains as a popular choice for younger generations. Far from “dead”, the server population has been slowly but steadily increasing every year (of course the number of people playing may fluctuate depending on the time).
Surely, there is a glaring issue with the design, but there is a way to overcome. A big minus to new players is the pain to grind home cities – getting to certain levels just to unlock new cards and politicians, and create optimal decks for home cities; however, with the use of XP mod, and the support provided by the aforementioned community, it takes just a matter of minutes to get all the home cities to a certain level that the full experience of the game is possible from the very beginning.
Other than that, there are no outstanding design issues. Of course, it has been a while since the game was released and updated, encountering a few minor bugs and issues occasionally would be almost inevitable, but none of those should annoy anyone except for the sound bug that can happen once in a while.
This game really does deserve more love and understanding from many others, especially from the Age of Empires community. Last year I nominated this game the “Test of Time” award on Steam, and this year the “No Apologies” award. It is really a classic gem with a friendly community, and even if I leave it there for a while, I always come back to it.
The normal price can be quite expensive to some, but it is on sale right now with 75% off. For those who haven’t got the game, but are still thinking about it, I would say, why not give it a try?

I've put more hours into this game than just about any other. I've played it since the first version was relased and found each version a nice step up from the previous. This version isn't the newest either, but I've still played this one more.
First off, this game is going to appeal to the gamer who wants to be an owner and matchmaker for an MMA organization rather than a fighter. This is not one of those take over a guy and see how high you can get him games, it more strategy and sand box than that. Think of Sim City meets UFC.
Graphics are not present in the game, and the fight play by plays can get repetitive after a few thousand fights, but that doesn't change the interest in the fight for me. With this being more of a sandbox game you have the option to watch the world unfold, or to actively grow your company. You can choose to stay small and thrive or go for broke and become the top company in the world.
It's still too easy to become financially sound in the game, so some house rules might need to be in order, but the fun factor isn't impacted. Fights themselves can be "watched" or simply simmed with the results shown afterward. Once you've become accustomed to the world it's easy to get locked into that one more turn feel. Setting up your next matchups, developing young fighters or deciding to let your icon leave because he just can't do it anymore are all choices you'll have to make.
You'll also have the opportunity to tweak the rule set for your company and that can have a massive effect on what guys are going to perform best for you and your relevance in the larger MMA world.
Overall, I'm very happy with this game and have no problem recommending the game for people who love MMA and contol over the business aspects of the sport.

I had the biggest, stupidest grin on my face between booting it up and letting the credits roll. It's just that charming.
I've been a big fan of Matthew Taranto's work for a few years now-- Brawl in the Family was one of my favourite webcomics,  and I've stumbled upon some of his musical work as a result of it. When he announced that he was working on a game of his own, let's just say, the hype was real.
I'm glad to say that my faith was not misplaced. The game's art style and music are top-notch, as to be expected from Mr. Taranto and Co. Perhaps more importantly, however, the game is incredibly well designed.
It's one of those games that's easy enough to beat, if all you want to just to rush to the end (aside from the last couple of levels). But for those wanting to see everything Tadpole Treble has to offer, it's got just the right amount of challenge for old salts like me. It's like the lovechild of Audiosurf and the musical sections from Rayman Legends, and it nails the blend perfectly.
Have I mentioned the grin I was wearing from beginning to end? The game has TONS of character, and even more heart. It's clear that this was a labour of love, and love is the operative word here. Charm oozes out from every pore, the artstyle is adorable (as to be expected from the hand that brought us Brawl in the Family, one of the best gaming comics of all time and easily THE best family friendly one)
If there's any complaint I have so far, it's that, occasionally, the screen comes across as a bit "busy." With notes to avoid, bubbles and health to grab, stage specific obstacles to navigate, and often some other sorts of things to keep an eye on, it can be a little difficult to keep track of it all. It's also a bit short-- clearing it will only take a bit over an hour, though completionists will have a field day and the level editor should help it last longer.
Tadpole Treble is a great game in its own right, but as a first foray by an independant studio, it's absolutely fantastic. BitFinity is going to be a studio to keep an eye on in future years, and I, for one, am looking forward to every step they take.

This is probably the weirdest game I've ever played. It's a surreal game with beautiful music. Very surreal, I spent much of the time wondering what was going on. In a good way, I should add.
A few comments...
* No mouse support, which is weird at first since you're only controlling a cursor. I can see why though, since in some of the puzzles it'd be more difficult to use the mouse, but in  those cases perhaps using wasd or similar would have been a good complement.
* There is no predefined steam controller button for bringing up the menu, you have to press ESC on the keyboard. Other than that, the game works fine with the steam controller.
* The puzzle mechanics can be a bit slow. The speed is good for the atmosphere though, so I wouldn't actually want it to be faster.
* This is a short game. Apparently I finished it in less than 3 hours.
* The ending is somewhat underwhelming. Be aware that this is only part 1.
* Some people have complained about bugs, but I didn't notice any, which is nice (running on Linux).
* In some places, some of the stuff on screen was blurry, a bit like if you were taking a close up photo with a big aperture. Not sure if that was intentional or not, but I didn't like it.
* You only need to understand the language for the menues, so if you're not good at any of the available languages then you shouldn't have much problems anyway (although you'll probably not understand this comment in that case... oh well...).
Most of these points may seem kind of negative, but the negativity is actually pretty much just nitpicking. So, in conclusion, I liked the game and I'll probably buy both the DLC and the next chapter (when it's released).

I really loved this game. But it could have been so much more. I have not played any other fallout game, but from what i have heard and seen all over the place, this game really don't have much on earlier games.
Good aspects of the game tho:
1. Nice graphics, but nothing too special honestly.
2. Awesome gun play and a good combat system in general.
3. I liked the perk system.
4. A lot of base content.
Bad aspects:
1. The settlement building just felt really really forced and completely useless. And let's not even talk about the physics (not that i really had anything against it, it just does not make any sense)
The only part i enjoyed about the building system was building my own "base" where i store all my crap n scrap. Apart from that, i never payed too much attention to settlements. Sure sometimes i got into it, with settlements such as The Castle and Hangmans alley. But once i was done with that and had everything set up with food n water n beds. I never went back and took a second look at it, because i really had no use in doing so.
2. The RPG elements. Now i am not that much of a rpg person, but in the beginning of the game, i quite enjoyed it. It gave me more of a chance to play of my own morals. But the more i kept going into the game, i really just noticed how dull it really was. Sometimes it did not matter what dialoge option you chose. The outcome was the same. But in the end, it was not the worst.
3. The story the plot and the ending (Insert spoiler warning here)
Again, not the worst thing in the world. But it could have been done sooooo much better. Especially the ending(s).
Throughout the game, you get to know of 4 factions (that matters). The minutemen, BoS, The institue and The railroad. Now i constantly had issues with choosing which one to go with. In the end i had to go with the railroad/minutemen. Because they were the ones that actually had some humanity in them. While BoS and the institue were just bigots.
But even then, i was really disappointed in the ending i got. Like, it made no sense to blow the institue up, it was so unsatisfying. Sure, i was not a big fan of their ways. But even then, not only did ya endanger an entire city by blowing up a nuclear reactor. But all the technology just thrown away like that. Tech that actually could have helped humanity instead. Why not just push the institue out of the ground instead and take over the facility?
Also, when the plot about Shaun (your son) was unraveled. It was just a big "ok, now what?" moment. It really did not add anything to the story itself after it.
4. The DLCs.
Did i enjoy Far Harbour? Big yes. Did i like the little Automatron added? Yeah. But when it came to Nuka-World. It was just so dull. The dlc itself was good if ya went all in into the raider side. But if ya went with the "good" side. You really did not get anything worhtwhile out of it.
But the worst thing of it all, are these "workshop" dlcs. They should have just been free, because they really add nothing of importance or fun. They are not like Far Harbour, they dont add any story,  only some hours of screwing around (Some people enjoy it of course, but still). But the most insulting part about those small tiny dlcs, are that they include achievments. It's a massive middle finger to people that actually want to hunt achievements. "Oh, you want to 100% this game? Well too bad, ya gotta spend another 15€". I get it, sales are a thing, but even then, greedy move.
5. CREATION CLUB:
Do i even have to say anything? I think we all understand how scummy it is and that it really does not add a single thing to the game worth having. And the things they expect us to pay for are already there as free mods. FREEEEEE MODS. Sure, i can get behind that modders deserve some credits for their work. But out of donations, not actually having to buy their mods.
" Their most ambitious game ever" at least they know how to joke.
But all in all, you will most likely enjoy the game if you buy it, especially with mods, they really just make the game live longer. But personally I enjoyed the base game.  But there are just so many things that♥♥♥♥♥♥me off about it. So i'll have to give it thumbs down for being a disappointment in the end, because when I play a game, I expect satisfaction when it is over, this game did not deliver it.

Let's begin with a disclaimer: Bastion if really freaking hard to describe.
At its core, it's a top down action game with RPG elements, and at that, it does its job. The game plays like a charm, and most of the weapons are fun to use (even if I found myself liking the ranged options more). The whole game feels extremely tight and polished.
Where Bastion really shines, however, is its story AND the way it is presented. Every action you take, even some really meaningless ones (being hit by an enemy in the first level, breaking crates) are commented by the ever present Narrator - if you ever played Portal and liked how GladOs reacted to your actions, you'll like this, too. The story is very good, too, and among a plethora of brown and bleak post-apocalyptic scenarios, I feel the colorful fragmented world of post-calamity Bastion is a refreshing spin on an over-abused genre.
With how little it costs, seriously, you just owe this game to yourself. And your friends, possibly.

The heroes add an interesting twist to the TD game because it's not just about placing and upgrading towers, especially since some of the heroes' abilities can enhance tower's stats. Some heroes can fly, for instance, while others can burrow underground or teleport. Some heroes can buff towers, while others do massive area damage when they die. Choosing the right hero for a stage can be the difference between winning and losing, and sometimes I found I needed to try the stage a number of times with different strategies while levelling up my heroes to meet the challenge. The graphics and sound are charming with subtle pop-culture references ("it's on like Donkey Kong!").

I am long overdue for writing a review to this game clearly as indicated by my hours played. I'm not very good a objective reviews but I'm going to try my hardest to do so.
So Fractured Space is a free to play game about big old capital ships duking it out in a 5v5 situation. It has amazing visual and audio effects for all ships, though I will admit some are more fitting than others. The gameplay is extremely compelling and involved and you really have to do your research if you want to get good at it. This game is not for the faint of heart or the ones that easily give up. It's a very hard game at the start and can be very punishing. Each ship you can play feels unique and perfectly distinguishable both visually and in a gameplay sense. The game also has a great community behind it and i've made many good friends playing it.
The major negatives I can think of are all mostly excused by the fact that this game is still in development but that doesn't mean it shouldn't affect your decision. The game has a lot of minor glitches and bugs, most of them don't make the game unplayable but for the nitpickers it can be a little irritating. The game is also really not optimized so those with potatoes for computer might not have a lot of luck with this game. I hear a lot of complaining about the servers from others but I have fine responsiveness and performance from them despite having an average of 200 ping. The game is also currently not in an amazing state of balance in terms of the ships themselves but Edgecase (the makers of the game) is not currently invested in ship balance because they are focused on putting all the systems in place before they are 100% functional. Balance is still on going but it isn't a priority for them.
On the side of more good things I can say that this game is genuinely a bundle of fun. It rewards the skillful and encourages teamwork. It's very tactical and really drives you to think about every action you take. The map is separated in to five sectors that you have to use a jump drive to access. The game is also filled with a variety of brilliantly designed and voiced crew members that provide bonuses to your ship. Something else to note is that the developers are very responsive to player feedback on the forums. They read almost everything even though you might not think it.
I apologize if this review feels a little jumpy and all over the place, i'm not good at structured writing. The big thing I want you to take away from this review is that the game is a ton of fun and while it may have some problems, they will most likely be fixed in the near future.
