This is my first Steam review, mainly to warn other games of the potential catastrophe that is Assassin Creed Unity.
Graphics: 9/10
This game is visually stunning, if you have a rig that can run it. The textures for the roads, rooftops, walls, interiors, paintings, and even some NPCs are some of the best in any genre. The clothes actually have a softness look to them that make them seem like they are clothes. Although a minor complaint there is that your clothes never get wet, but thank you for allowing the grotesque blood stains when we get injured. There is a weather system, but like the clothes the attention to wet surfaces also seem to be ignored. I am running a EVGA 970 GTX at ultra settings, an upgrade I made specifically for this game due to low performance on my previous Sapphire 7850HD. The lag is not very noticeable at all with my new setup and I probably average 30-40 fps at 1080p. When the game is working, it is a visual experience very few other games can even come close to deliver. But the overall lack of some of the realism elements, such as wet textures, are a deal breaker for me so I cannot give this a 10/10 since many other games have implemented this sense of immersion, including Ubisoft itself with Watch Dogs for example.
Game Play: 3/10
I can say with some degree of confidence that the game play is one of the most annoying aspects of the game. Ubisoft finally added a long overdue game play element to allow for better vertical traversal of the environment, but it is equally annoying as it is helpful due to awkward camera placement during the animation. In fact, the camera in general is something that I am constantly fighting while indoors or in small corridors as well. As for the fighting aspect, it was a little hard to pick up initially, but ultimately this is the one piece of the game play that holds up well despite the departure of previous games' fighting mechanics. This is the part of this section that makes up the entire score I have assigned. As for the rest of the game play goes something like this: constant crashing, NPCs acting glitchy, falling through the ground, getting stuck between a table and a chandelier, losing game saves due to cloud or saving strategy issues, general lack of online components and sometimes even online support itself, the number of features that say “Coming Soon”, and poor performance for those without a $1,000 PC to play the game... seriously I feel for you if you have anything less than a higher end 700 series GPU and a quad core processor. I can only imagine how horrible this game would run on the consoles, and I have been reading some of the complaints. Overall I would also bring down the score even more due to missing game play elements from previous games that should have been included. Transportation, transportation, transportation. Where are the horses? Where is my flying machine? Where are the zip lines? Underground rail systems? Something... at least Arno will be in great shape having to run everywhere, I guess. Which actually brings me to another complaint, is it just me or does Arno jog in places where he should sprint? And is it also random when he decides to run or sprint? I know getting up to speed can be an issue on the ground dodging all of the crowds I guess, but when I have not run into anyone seriously, sprint please...  I will be running close to a crowd and he drops to a jog, and when you are running everywhere it gets quite annoying. Long story short, Ubisoft update this issue and sprint when in doubt if you have not run into anything.
Sound: 5/10
The music score pretty well sets the scene in most cases. It does feel natural and dynamic, when it is available, but I did notice that there was an overall lack of music unless something is going on. This is not necessarily a bad thing, to be honest it makes the moments where you are actually doing something feel much more engrossing. The ambient sounds is where we start to take a hit though. I feel like a lot of sounds are just plain missing, like sometimes they are there, and other times they are not. Kind like shooting a gun and expecting to hear the gunshot, but for many different things in the environment like dropping a bottle, getting pushed into a wall, NPCs falling, etc. . It's like the crowds of people are suppose to keep us from noticing the overall lack of ambiance that is not coming from a NPC. The NPC do seem to talk for 30 sec loops in some cases. I camped out near a set of NPCs just to see how much animation was given to them and the dialogue that was associated with those animation. Overall, it seems as if everyone is repeating the same routines. Some people probably just walk in circles all day, never stopping in for a drink at the tavern, or going home to sleep. I often see people pouring out of walls and closed doors without any sound, due to day/night cycle changes I am guessing??? In my opinion it is this lack of immersion elements and ignorance to these types of bugs that hurts ACU the most.
Online: 3/10
I was able to get online with a friend to play some of the online play. Of course by the time we were set up and going my PC crashed. That pretty much concluded our online session. Unfortunately this section takes a hit due to constant Uplay issues. After spending nearly 20 hours on the game my save game disappears and I seemingly have to start over. Even when I do, and I restart the game my progress is lost. Even if I set up a local save and ignore the cloud service, my game will continue to lose my progress. Between this issue and the constant crashes, this game is unplayable. No one with a life could hope to sit down and finish this game without being able to save your game. I put this here since it seems to have to do with the cloud save feature, but when you can get an online session started and your game does not crash it can be quite fun. If I could access my previous game save I might be able to play online again. I do feel like the online play could be promising, if the game worked.
Story: 1/10
Well, here is my two cents on the story. Overall, who am I again? Of course I am one of the disgruntle gamers who cannot even finish the story due to an unplayable game. Maybe sometime after the second memory sequence you actually get to see a reason to get invested an any of the characters, so far I am not very invested at all. By the time you start getting attached to someone they are out of your life by either fast forward years on end, or separating due to Arno's choices. Some character development would be nice, but I am too early to even know.  Guess this takes a hit since I cannot even play the game anymore without losing all progress.
Overall score: 4/10
This is probably the most unfinished game I have played to date, maybe from any developer, and in fact it is now currently unplayable for me due to losing progress on restart of the application. The online game play is promising, if Uplay servers could actually handle its gamers.  Overall ACU feels incomplete, with only game play and graphics holding it up, and only when the game actually works, or you have a rig that can run it. Otherwise it is impossible to overlook all of the issues with the games. Ubisoft should definitely step back and take a long look at themselves.
My advice to you, wait 6 months or a year until they can iron out all of the bugs, then maybe it will be the ACU that we were all looking so forward to. I am betting many folks at Ubisoft are wishing for a do-over right about now. A suggestion you may want to consider is maybe that you should stop selling this broken and incomplete game.
My overall feeling towards my purchase is that I feel I have been taken for granted as a returning customer. The scrutiny in which I use to judge Ubisoft games from here on out will be far worse due to this installment of AC.

Hope everyone picks it up during this holiday season and dive into the adventure of Nate, Willard, Ivo and Critter.   Very highly recommended.

Lords of the fallen is a great game if you like harder arpgs where your attacks are a commitment, and timing is important. Lords of the fallen is trying to make an entry into the same genre as Dark Souls, with a lot of similarities,
but also some cool differences.
I have more than 600 hours in Dark souls 1 and 2. Lords of the Fallen has fun bosses, weapons, armor, and the labyrinth DLC adds a fun puzzle. As a dark souls 1 and 2 onebro, I actually think doing a level 10 LOTF run would be harder, if you are worried it will be too easy of a game, Please support this game when it is on sale, and allow for the rest of the world to enter the HCARPG market without a unwarranted fear of failure. EDIT: I did a lvl 10 run, and it was challenging, but not as much as I thought, but still very fun.
Pros
+ Great graphics
+ Different builds play and feel different, add replayability
+ You feel like a badass, but a mortal badass
+ Combat is always fair, you should only die to an enemy once if you can learn.
+ Bosses have interesting mechanics (not all but most)
Cons
- lots of people complain of crashes (not me)
- World is large, and well made, but only consists of a few kinds of environments
- Some combat is forced in small corridors and the camera makes this hard to see what you are doing (only a couple spots)

I was in two minds whether or not to recommend this or not.
Initially I started with KDM FC, which are an Asian based MMA organisation.  They don't make much money, they have virtually no attendee's and inexplicably have a world class fighter on $500,000 per fight - which is guaranteed to bankrupt the organisation.
After a few in game months of running the organisation into the ground, I started to lose hope.  But I restarted and chose one of the bigger federations, and after a year I've made quite a bit of money and feel like I am actually 'competing' with the other top companies.
It is not entirely clear what you are doing when you start out, what you are aiming for and what your immediate goals should be - especially if you don't take the easy option and go for a top federation.
I feel the game is missing quite a few features that would attract a wider audience.  In one sense, it reminds me of a beta run of the original Football Manager game - but a bare bones versiona at that.  Databases full of 'ever so slightly different looking' fighters are one thing, but there need to be more actual features the user can use in order to feel they are actually influencing the path of the gameplay.
In many ways, this game is for me "Joe Silva (UFC head booker) MMA contract and booking simulator" instead of WMMA3.   And the contract system is WOEFUL.  Why on earth you have to have a time delay on signing talent - especially unemployed fighters - is beyond me.  Well, not really.  It's clearly a way of filling space in the game where nothing happens between events.  That to me hints at a lack of a finished article to me.
What I would have liked in the game is more focus on training facilities/gyms that you can invest in, media events to send fighters to, sponsorship deals, drugs scandals, a more developed in-fight text display with a greater variety of descriptions (eventually incorporating some kind of graphical display). greater interaction with the fighters, inter - federation matches, and more.  But I do appreciate that you have to draw the line between a text based engine and a sports game such as the UFC Undisputed series, as you can't really have the depth of detail and the sports sim in the same game.
Ultimately though, I do recommend the game and I have enjoyed playing it.

I usually go the a game's reviews looking at the negative, and then positive ones separately, for this game I had to:
Step 1: go to the negative reviews.
Step 2: disregard any review with the word "souls" on it.
Step 3: read the 2 ramaining review.
But seriously, the negative reviews on this game are crazy, its an ok game to grab on sale, user reviews should read mostly/very positive instead of mixed, (when the game released it was mostly negative), dark souls fanboys are to blame.
Now the obligatory good vs bad:
The good:
- The game runs well and seems well optimized.
- M+k fully supported as well as controller; the ingame prompts change depending on which you're using.
- Well implemented mouse camera.
- Pretty graphics, nice locations.
- Good level design.
- A variety of weapons and armor as well as trinkets to equip.
- Good sense of progression (equipment and stats).
- Nice looking, viseral and interesting combat.
The bad:
- Some of the wepons are ridiculously slow (seriously); most strength weapons swing like thy're been used by a 4 year old, terrible design choice.
- Some bosses take too long due to their high amount of HP and few windows of oportunity.
- In some boss fights the hit boxes are too small and the collition detection tends to fail (your weapon will go though them but no hit, so you gotta get even closer).
- Enemy variety is a bit lacking.
In general a very good game, reminds me of games like Enclave and Severance: Blade of Darkness, or more reacently, darksiders but with viseral combat instead of spectacle combat.
Recommended.

The Walking Dead Game was a surprise to me because i'm not and still aint a true fan of the point and click type of games, but this game is the closest that any game will ever get me to be a fan of this type of gameplay. The Walking Dead is one of the most emotional games ever. I'm not a fan of the TV series so i wasn't excited but i heard that it was based on the comic book so i gave it a shot when it was 75% off in a steam sale and god i poared in days apon days to finish every chapter and if i made a bad decision i would rewind to fix it because i didn't wanna screw up my decisions with people i cared about. This game makes you feel the characters around you and makes them feel truely real. Whether it's your best friends son getting bitten and him being in denial until push comes to shove as he has no choice but to put him down and you have the choice of doing it yourself to spare him of his pain or to force him to do it. The Walking Dead puts you in charge of a girl named Clementine and she is the most innocent little girl, you care for her and you have to teach her how to survive and stop her from getting hurt or killed. The world is so dark and disturbed, people's spirit crushed, people before your very eyes killing themselves before the zombies can make them turn. on a story and emotional immersive connection, this for me almost tops Majora's Mask on that department. The gameplay is decent but sometimes glitches can occur but some are funny. My only real con is that the servers are really glitchy and a lot of times you start up the client and when you try to connect you never do, i found myself, many times stopping my game client and restarting hoping that the game connects to the servers correctly but besides that the game is flawless and it is a very easy game to run it's mostly on your cpu so this game could even run on a high quality phone if you turn down the graphics a little. Overall this game is a masterpiece that defines a true gem in the point and click genre, One of the most somber, Immersive, and down right disturbed atmosphere and relatable characters. I loved every minute of it, yet The Walking Dead doesn't win anything in the client department. Walking Dead Season 2 fixed that though. 9.2/10

Glitches, bugs and performance issues aside (since with help of creative people and my own skill I was able to push game to a more or less playable state) I still would not recommend this game, unless you are eager to see beatiful city of Paris, consumed with revolution, use it as a playground and do coop missions, which are quiet fun. If you are looking for a story of an assassin, that turned the tide in the eternal war - then you might want to consider skipping this game.
The main story is dull and full cliches. I knew exactly how the story is going to end after tutorial section and I also knew which mission will lead to what conclusion. I was especially disappointed on how the antagonist has been revealed and how he's been played (i hope revealing his gender isn't much of a spoiler =) ). The game tried to make a surprise out of it, but ended up making protagonist look stupid in the eyes of player. The Assassin's brotherhood feels like unnecessary addition to the game, even with the drama inside. I barely remember the names of the counsel members, since they've been just sitting on their arses all the time and just barking. There is no development in the characters at all, the young protagonist, starting as a careless boy that does not think much of consequences, keeps staying that way till the very end, when suddenly, just before credits roll, he makes a 30 seconds speech that supposed to make us feel he grown. "real life" section also a letdown. you start as a noname, suddenly becoming an assassin, because this girl asked you nicely, and given a task to find something inside Helix virtual reality (new animus), but during gameplay you barely remember about it, you're being remind like 3 times maybe when servers are shutting down. And there is no conclusion in it, because when you find the thing you've been looking for - nothing happens. not with you, nor with the team, that you've been "working" for. just credits.
This game is either just that bad at main story, or it will be heavily DLCed. this game has reminded me of original Assassin's creed game, but even story of Altair looks much more deep and well developed in comparison with story or Arno.
to sum it up - a waste of really good voice acting (english of course, don't even try russian, if you value your ears and brain) on a poor text writing.
few words about gameplay - at the beginning, game feels really challenging, especially if you're going to spend your first time in there exploring areas and doing sidequest. if you see a difficulty of 5 starts - be prepared to face enemies, that will probably kick the crap out of you. unless, of course, you feel confident that you will be able to avoid conflicts. and of course you can also use a cheat - spam smoke bombs and kill enemies while they're stunned. work all the time. just don't forget to replenish.
the most annoying thing i found though is the challenges (optional objectives in the main missions). they simply make little sense most of them time and probably implemented to make easy missions more challenging for no particular reason. e.g. - why do you have to sabotage all alarm bells that are all over the courtyard, if you plan to enter the building from rooftops, which is much easier and makes more sense?

As a huge Dark Souls fan, I was bitterly disappointed by Lords of the Fallen. The visuals are beautiful, and certainly better than anything the Souls series has produced as of SotFS. That's the one good thing I can say.
The gameplay is slow and frustrating- even at light load, you move slower than 'fat rolling' in DS. The enemies are fast and attack quickly, while you have a choice of attacking at glacial speed for good damage, or attacking quickly and doing almost nothing.
The map design is terrible- all the beautiful environments and objects are mashed together in similar ways to make it very difficult to navigate, and you are frequently required to go find a door which opened several areas away. The objective hints are always vague and never helpful. The storyline is poorly written, very lacking in any content, and leaves you utterly unaware and uninterested about what is going to happen next. It would barely cover a demo of a Souls game- implicit storytelling is so, so much better than bland storytelling (such as the sidequest in which there is a SASSY WOMAN who has BREASTS, and you FIND SOMETHING for her to receive PLAYFUL BANTER because she's the WOMAN! And it's one of the biggest and most fleshed out sidequests!)
But by far the biggest failing is the bosses. Every one of them is about the same size, uses the same moves (barring a few palette swaps and pyrotechnic effects), moves predictably, hits hard, and has roughly 10,000,000 hp. This means that what should be epic and exciting encounters are always beaten by 1) lock on 2) circle strafe 3) hit them once when they do the move which leaves an opening 4) repeat 200-300 times. This is a stupefyingly boring way to spend 20 minutes (per boss), and if you get hit a couple of times you start again.
In short, this is exactly what would be produced if you took a 16 year old who had watched some youtube videos for a Souls game, gave him an unlimited budget/large production team, and flattered his ego to the point where he believed he could direct a competent Dark Souls clone. It looks good, but has all the charm, depth and satisfaction of snorting wet cardboard until you asphyxiate.

I am not quite sure what this game is trying to be. It is kind of like Dark Souls, but not really, which is not exactly a bad thing. It is not like Dragon Age at all which is a bit of a dissapointment. And it is not like Kingdoms of Amalur either, even though I have heard it compariered to all three. However, this is one of the most boring, monotonus, and overrated games I have seen in years. And here are three reasons as to why.
1 The Basics: gameplay, graphics, mechanics ect.
For starters, it is a hack and slash job, meaning that the gameplay is going to be a johnny one note eventually once you hit a stride. This is not always that bad, Dragon Age could be argued as a hack and slash but it is so good that it over comes that querk. What lets this down for me on that end is the way you fight. Once you figure it out, combat is down to this formula, block, stab, dodge, counter attack, rinse and repeat, rinse and repeat, rinse and Zzzz, Zzzz. There is not other truely effective tactic regardless of class used, not that the classes are all that different mind you. It will not matter which you choose, I will get into this later but it is quite bland. To make things worse, you cannot choose what your character will look like so you are stuck with one ugly SOB with a shaved head, bad beard, and stupid tattoos all over his face. Give up any asperations of running for government office. Not that you ever see it that much, the camera control is pretty much locked up to you rear end both in and out of combat, the only time you can ever see what you look like is in conversation, which is only marginaly better than the one found in Kingdoms of Amalur. Not that this matters either because the graphics are a big let down for a title of this price and rating, and this only came out a little over a year back.
2 There is no F***ing castor class!!!!!!!!
In Dragon Age, I prefer mage, Mass Effect, Sheperd is a Sentinel, and I go full Battlemage in Kingdoms. Three guesses which class I like, hint it sure as little green apples ain't here. The class system here is a little confusing, you begin by choosing three "magics" that have nothing to do with magic in any respect with the exaption of prayer, maybe. Next you choose which of three weapon and armor types that leave you in the same place, heavy armor, big weapons, and no finesse. In total, there are nine classes that can be chosen, first time I went out I came up with Ranger,the second, Paladin, third, Brawler. All three felt exactly the same, no kidding, the exact same gameplay, I gave up on each just a few minutes in due to sheer bordom. If you are like me, avoid at all costs.
3 This kind of thing has been done to death, ressurcted, and done to death again.
Big picture, massive evil army of death dealing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s out to kill everything in sight. Dark Spawn, Reapers, Uruk, Dreadic, Thalmor, whatever, they are the smae thing now they are called the Rhogar. Top points for sounding like the noise I make when I have bronchitis. Long story short, the market for this kind of this is saturated to a point where it is raining bits of archdemon in my house. You would think something like this would work to seperate itself from the pack with something, but if you look at it closely, Lords is a Frankenstine's Monster. Bits of gameplay and stories have just been cherrypicked around from other games. It is official, the guys here have less imagination than the guys who draw the bodywork for Porsche.

WMMA3 is a wonderfully complex (and yet quite simple in its basic principles) simulation of managing an MMA federation. Although the basic premise is, well, basic - you have to book events that feature fights between your company's fighters - the gameplay is very engaging as you try to decide how to draw in fans, who to promote, who has the potential of becoming a superstar, how many fighters can you have before you are unable to make them popular enough to carry you financially, who to hire and who to let go etc.
However, the thing that makes it even better are emergent storylines and emergent world. Just as in, for example, Paradox Interactive grand strategies or football managers, half of the fun is not in the strategy and planning but in seeing how various decisions and random factors converge into narratives - the fighters, with their gradually scouted skills, fight histories and pre-MMA backgrounds, become almost real people whose careers you watch, who you cheer for (or against), whose successes you celebrate and failures mourn (or shout at the monitor about). You begin to notice personal quirks in the fighting (which is described to you purely by text - but in a dynamic and entertaining way), you start to like or dislike certain fighters, you plot a favourite youngster's rise to fame by a series of easy matches and weep as he gets beaten down by weaker but more experienced employees, you carefully consider whether your nostalgia for a former champion is strong enough to extend his contract even when he's way past his prime, you plot an ideal title match by giving enough exposure to the contender (or, as I once did, seek for a fighter who would be able to fight the belt away from that jerk I stupidly gave a shot at the title only to discover that he's good, but he's a sucker who wins fights by masterfuly smothering the enemy against the cage wall for 5 rounds straight which puts the crowd to sleep) and rejoice as your plan comes to fruition, you contemplate the fall of another federation - and then race against the competition to grab their best stars...
This game is by no means perfect. Its interface takes a lot of time to get used to, and even then it's basically just not good. (WMMA4 seems to be much better in that department - but it's not on Steam. :() The fight descriptions can become a bit repetitive and boring if you play for many dozens of hours (although even then you can be surprised and entertained when a match goes in a direction you'd have never thought about). The character pool could be bigger (although there's a healthy amount of mods on the developer's page that can help with that). But once you get sucked in, those flaws don't seem big enough to discourage you from planning just one more event, staying just until the TV station sends its reply about your new show idea, fast-forwarding to the beginning of just one more month to see the new recruits in the MMA industry, seeing your champion defend his title just one more time...

Pavilion is a fourth person puzzle adventure, where you are thrown into a world that neither you or the character know anything about. This the first chapter of a two-part series.
At first, I was confused by the term ‘fourth person’, but in this game, you don’t actually control the main character. The character moves on his own, from one area to the next. You control certain objects in the environment, solving the puzzles in the correct sequence, to influence his movement, and guide him to the next objective. The puzzles vary in difficulty, but overall, I found them to be enjoyable.
The game took me about 2.5 hours, but that time will vary depending on the player’s puzzle solving skills. Pavilion is a beautifully crafted game, with enjoyable (but not too difficult) puzzles. Manipulating the environment to guide the main character through is interesting, but the character pathing could use some minor tweaks on a couple of the levels. I do wish the game had been a bit longer though. I would have also liked to know more about the story because I wasn’t really satisfied with the little story there was. I liked the puzzles and game design though, so those alone are enough to make me want to play the next chapter when it releases next year.

The greatest selling point of Tadpole Treble is that it's absolutely oozing with style. Every little detail of this game has obviously been carefully hand-crafted, and you'll find little tidbits of style to enjoy all throughout Baton's adventure. (If you're not aware, one of the primary developers of this game is Matthew Taranto, creator of the webcomic Brawl in the Family, and the style of that comic has very much carried over into this game.) I found myself smiling at little details like how Baton's facial expressions would change in response to events in the level around her, or little moments of synergy between the level design and the music.
The music deserves special attention, as it's one of the primary focuses of the game. I personally highly enjoyed the soundtrack throughout - I never had the impression that a song, or even part of a song, had been composed as filler, sound to fill a space where it seemed sound should go. Note that this is not the typical electronic-music heavy material you tend to get from music games on Steam. I would actually peg this as closest to high-quality children's music, not unlike the music of old Disney films or one of Sandra Boynton's albums.
Tadple Treble is short, but offers considerable replay value - and it's in that replay value that the gameplay is at its best. Your initial runthrough of the game's 12 stages will likely take you a little over an hour. Most of my deaths on my first playthrough came from an unusually punishing scenario involving shaking off a pack of piranhas - otherwise, simply completing the game usually just requires staying out of the way of obstacles. The interesting challenges come when the game requires you to start taking risks to meet more completionist-style goals.
It should be noted that Tadpole Treble is Bitfinity's first game, and it ocasionally shows in small rough patches - an occasional not-quite-intuitive menu, or a loading screen where it seems odd that the game should need one. Composition mode probably shows this most clearly, with understandable but less-than-ideal limitations to sharing levels, and controls that work well enough but fall a little bit short of a smooth level/music-creating experience. Overall, however, these issues are small, and shouldn't dissuade anyone interested in buying.
Long story short, if you were a fan of Brawl in the Family, enjoy music games, or even just think the screenshots look appealing, Tadbole Treble comes highly recommended.

An excellent Rythm game that mixes in a bit of SHMUP bullet hell to keep things interesting. It's full of personality, the characters are adorable and hillarious in turn, and the soundtrack would be amazing even on its own. (Thunder Creek is my new favorite song.) The Treble Charge mechanic is tricky to pull off, especially in the faster paced songs near the end, but it's very rewarding to be able to plow through everything that's giving you a hard time. The final boss battle is a joy to behold, if a little confusing your first few attempts. The art and musing being from the genius who gave us Brawl in the Family is just the icing on the cake!
Sadly, it's not without a few flaws. Despite the obvious amounts of polish that went into this game, there are a few bugs that can't be eaten by Etude. Firstly, I noticed a few times that a cymbal would project a location, only to send me a half-step just above or below where it was listed. In a game where positioning is everything, this can very easily wreck a run of a song. In Piranah Jungle, this happens consistantly on the second cymbal, completely preventing you from grabbing all the bubbles! This needs to be fixed ASAP! Also, I noticed occasionally while talking to Etude that his text would bug out and skip a line of dialog. This isn't too bad, as that option is just there for fun and flavor, but it is frustrating to miss the setup to a punchline.
Another little detail is that it can be somewhat tiresome on the later songs to sit through their intros whenever you have to restart, due to missing one lousy bubble. That's more a problem with trying to be perfect in rythm games in general, though, and the songs are so good, It's not like it's a chore to get to hear more of them.
Overall, definitely worth the money. Just fix up the bugs and you've really got something special here, Matt!

I enjoyed this game and played it all the way through in two sittings. It very much has a Portal 1 feel to it in both storytelling and aesthetics.
On aesthetics: cubes everywhere! Cube walls, cube lifts, cube lights, broken bits of cubes, all the cubes. At one point there is a pillar that is a cylinder, it gives you a new gameplay mechanic which is exciting, but I found myself suddenly confused by the cylindrical column trying to work out if there was more of a hidden meaning behind it as it wasn't a cube.
I found the puzzles were at just the right difficulty, with some just being deeply infuriating rather than hard to solve. But these were few enough to be bearable and actually did increase the satisfaction of completion. The puzzles themselves introduced new elements and variations in each zone keeping things fresh. The puzzles were not done to death, and thinking back I find myself wishing that there were more of a certain type of puzzle rather than being annoyed because it's "another one of these ones"
I actually quite enjoyed the story; it was pretty un-intrusive and nicely tied the puzzles together. And I thought that the ambient music did a really good job of adding suspense and uncertainty. I really couldn't quite decide what the truth really was, which I suspect was the point, and I changed my mind more than one or two times
There were some pretty long corridors and lift journeys carefully placed so that long monologue could be played whilst not doing puzzles, unfortunately I spent some of that time looking for hidden doors which did leave me to walk them in silence quite a lot.
Technically, my aging computer handled the game quite well, although the mouse was a little jumpy on the menu & pause screens, and my computer certainly struggled in the final sequences. I also found that the transition from the play and the "cutsceans" was not particularly smooth, and was noticeable. At one point I was all ready to be super smug about finding a broken bit of texturing only to turn around and discover that this was in fact a secrete puzzle and it was supposed to be like that. I'm not sure if I liked that or not, but I happily got frustrated with all the puzzles, so all good.
All in all great fun puzzle game. I will now be playing the speedruns to try and get all the medals.

One of the greatest games of all time. In 1998 Half-Life took everything that was great about the FPS and revolutionised the genre in a way Half-Life 2 did in terms of story-telling in 2004.
The graphics don't hold up well in terms of today's standards, however the gameplay, story, and AI certaintly do. The story whilst cliched was told in a revolutionary way, showing how a story could be done in games without the need for cutscenes and thereby allowing full player immersion. The gameplay never stays the same and showed other developers how to vary the gameplay in each stage, introducing new weapons/enemies, allowing you time to experiment before unleashing a number of enemies at you. The latter stages of the game are a bit of a let-down in comparison to what came before, but it barely detracts from an awesome game.
The AI holds up just as well as the gameplay and story. The aliens are standard fare, but know when to charge and when to hold back if injured. It is in the Marines that you encounter where the AI shines through. The Marines know how to flank, take cover, throw grenades to get you out of cover, place traps when running away, and fall back when injured. Rarely will you encounter AI as intelligent in most modern games.
If you want to play a game that many recognise as revolutionary in 1998 and had a profound effect on the games you play today then play Half-Life.

First and foremost is your camera, which you will spend more time fighting than any of the game's enemies. The game loves to take camera control away from you, particularly angled down toward the floor and straight forward from wherever you entered a given combar arena, regardless of where you're moving or what direction enemies are in. The downward angle is enough that you often can't see enemies on the ground three feet away from you, yet not enough that you can see anything below you while you yourself are in the air. It also has a fixed distance away from you during combat, meaning that it never peels away to give you a better view of the action, especially for the game's larger arenas or oversized enemies.
While the game is mechanically sound and the dodging is fantastic, all of the major fights tend to be against enemies that are far larger than your screen and as your ranged combat isn't really an option, you'll spend fights mashed up against the big bad's model and randomly guessing when to hit your magic backflip button - they might have tells for their attacks, but the camera doesn't let you see most of them. The unfairness level is incredibly high due to what I can imagine was simply an old PS3 hardware limitation where they could only render so much.
The problems with cinematography aren't just gameplay, however. Most of the cutscenes comprise of mostly static models superimposed with dialogue, almost like a VN but they didn't spring for portrait art, which is as boring and lifeless as it sounds. The cutscenes that are actually animated are fine until any action kicks up, at which point they do hard cuts multiple times per second to wildly different angles that leave the viewer more confused about what's happening than anything else. For a game that revolves entirely around bullet time, you'd think they'd actually apply that to lend impact to more of their action sequences, or at least understand on a basic level how not to shoot an action sequence, being the supposed kings of the genre and all.
It's just as confusing why they thought the game needed a crafting system. There are three types of consumable here, your life restorers, mp gauge recovery (which fills up quickly as long as you're not eating hits and is rarely relevant on bosses anyways), and a short-term damage buff. Each one uses a different material to craft, but each item used counts as half a death as a penalty to your score, meaning you're only ever going to use the health recovery items and the rest are a totally pointless waste of time and screen real estate that you'll never touch. I get why the score penalties are there and that harkens back to classic DMC, but if you're going to institute a mechanic that invalidates a different mechanic then there's no point having those items in the game at all.

ONRAID is a game that looks good in principle,  but just pulls it off poorly.
At first glance it looks ok, especially if you go from the trailer, but not long into the game you'll realize the visuals seem a bit... "cheap." You'll be fighting a lot of the same enemies over and over, through a lot of very similar looking levels (which are mostly tiny) using characters that aren't even really animated. They're just made up of still images made to hover around and move to give the illusion of animation. Heck, none of the characters even have arms or legs. It definitely feels like there wasn't a lot of budget/time/effort put into that side of things...
Then we get to the controls. Arguably the single most important part of a game like this, and in ONRAID the controls are... kinda...meh. I've seen worse, but these really aren't good. The jumping action seems floaty and odd, the characters themselves seem oddly heavy, almost locked to the ground until you hit that jump button. It all feels very sluggish and unrefined. SImply put, things just don't move in the way that you would expect, or want.
I'm not going to go into PVP and playerbase in the game, as I don't have much experience with that. I played with another friend and we mainly stayed in the "campaign." Some people say the player base is gone, but I wouldn't know.
To sum everything up, even though I was playing with a friend, we were both fairly unimpressed, and even a bit frustrated with the controls, etc., and decided we'd had enough of this game and would rather move on to something more fun.

Hacknet, Uplink's spiritual successor.
Developed by a one-man studio called Team Fractal Alligator, Hacknet is a terminal-based game that implements real UNIX codes and commands to bypass and/or shutdown firewalls, proxys, ports, etc., to gain access to other peoples' computers and eOS devices (game's parody of smartphones) for their information or information in general and retype false info for a cilent to help him, steal the infomation and expose it to light, or destroy the user's computer server.
The story for me so far is surpisingly good. To avoid spoilers, I'll keep it short. It involves a notorius hacker named Bit. He fails to reconnect to his system for 14 days, his failsafe kicks in, sending instructions in automated emails to you. It's up to you to find out why.
You can get jobs from different entites, such as CSEC, to receive hack codes and malware injectors to help you along your cyber hacking adventure. Sadly, unlike Uplink, you don't earn money and you can't upgrade your computer, RAM, CPU, etc.
Lots of little secrets here and there, some computers have little chat logs from other users for a fun read. The music is good, nice tempo beat to it.
Overall, it's a fun terminal-based hackers game with a modern day retouch.

*DETAILED REVIEW*
fun free to play shooter, but don't be expecting a high skill ceiling.  there are too many zero recoil weapons to make gameplay as fun as i was expecting.  sure you can just aim at the head to tap him out quick.  that becomes an issue when you can get prefired by a rifle with extremely low recoil.  i would recommend the ability to restrict certain weapons for more competitive play.  the movement and accuracy within blacksquad reminds me of counter-strike: source.  headshots feel just as rewarding while using the ak47 and desert eagle.  you have the option of aiming down a sight, but this doesn't mean hip firing isn't as accurate.  they are equal.
now as for the maps.  the maps are too busy for a demolition style of gameplay.  for every bomb site there are a minimum of four different ways to enter.   this is a great idea when you're quickly scrambling to create a map for player, but in practice there are way too many angles for one to three players to be watching.  the goal should be to have a decent sized map that is simplistic beauty.  another issue i find is the 40 second bomb timer being too long for these demolition maps.  due to the small size.  i would rather a 25 to 30 second bomb timer because the rotations are so quick the planter(s) get walked up on within 10 to 15 seconds.  most gun battles last an average of five seconds.
the community is exactly what you would expect for any shooter.  with this title being free to play you've got the typical join lobby, play, leave, join another lobby, rinse and repeat players.  these players have no patience and want constant action.  my favorite is the 'f5 f5 f5 f5' or 'gogogogogo' or 'start plz'.  and, some of them fully don't understand how to play a demolition style game mode.
*SIMPLE REVIEW*
all in all the game is worth checking out.  you can wall bang certain boxes and almost every door.  there are cool cosmetic items you can earn and spend money to obtain.  interesting game modes to be played.

Project Juno... Best. Mission. Ever. You start with an IP address, you go and poke and come up with a link or another IP address hidden in some memo, or even a password to something you can't hack and you basically explore the net and look for a solution while nobody knows if a solution exists (well, it does, since this is a game, but you get the idea). The final mission and dtory outcome feel a bit underwhelming, but all-in-all, very nice game of holywood hacking.
The only thing that sucks is the music. Not a fan of techno, but most hacker games seem to have it. Is this a thing? Like another stereotype of hacker = shy, socially awekward nerd with zits and dorky glasses, who listens to techno? Anyway, that doesn't drag the overall experience down. If you liked Uplink, get this. If you like hacker movies/games, get this. If you type like a toddler, go practice, then get this.

Pavilion is a fourth person puzzle adventure, where you are thrown into a world that neither you or the character know anything about. This the first chapter of a two-part series.
At first, I was confused by the term ‘fourth person’, but in this game, you don’t actually control the main character. The character moves on his own, from one area to the next. You control certain objects in the environment, solving the puzzles in the correct sequence, to influence his movement, and guide him to the next objective. The puzzles vary in difficulty, but overall, I found them to be enjoyable.
The game took me about 2.5 hours, but that time will vary depending on the player’s puzzle solving skills. Pavilion is a beautifully crafted game, with enjoyable (but not too difficult) puzzles. Manipulating the environment to guide the main character through is interesting, but the character pathing could use some minor tweaks on a couple of the levels. I do wish the game had been a bit longer though. I would have also liked to know more about the story because I wasn’t really satisfied with the little story there was. I liked the puzzles and game design though, so those alone are enough to make me want to play the next chapter when it releases next year.

Note, that this is not a glowing recommendation. Very far from it. But Lords of the Fallen is a pretty interesting attempt at creating an aRPG that follows on the formula of Dark Souls, but with a more Enclave and Blade of Darkness feel to it. Where it succeeds it does things very well, where it fails it fails pretty hard.
A lot of mechanics and even controls work pretty close to how they do in Souls series, but Lords of the Fallen is a lot more restrictive in ways you develop your character and how you play. While the game differentiates three classes, in actuality they seem to work more like variations on a warrior class - one that focuses just on pure brute force, one that focuses more on quick moves and one that focuses on mixing magic and weapons. There's only one ranged weapon you get and it can get elemental damage and the "spells" work more like active skills, usual to aRPGs. Those spells are quite similar between classes and if you play the New Game+ and then ++ you will be able to get all the class-specific magic spells, if you want.
What feels most off about the entire game is, probably, that the game feels much more script/premade animations heavy, than Souls games and the classic Blade of Darkness. Enemies track you with absolutely perfect precision, even when they run around like crazy, unless they are in the attack animation, they can get into block or attack animations (that hit/block) even sometimes right after standing with their back turned to you (I once got hit by a projectile of an enemy that was looking in the opposite direction and lots of ranged enemies will turn and shoot without missing a beat and always hit) and most projectiles track you insanely well. All of those CAN be avoided in most cases, but they still look and feel like player input reading AI perfect creations, rather than creatures who exist in the game's virtual world. Which is very unlike Souls games, where enemies feel much more "flawed" in a natural way - like fighting another player, not a computer. Another huge issue of the enemies in the game is that lots of them sit in full defense mode most of the time, requiring you to wait till you can backstab or parry/riposte them, with enemies 100% controlling the rhythm of the fight. Which, more often than not, actually feels boring, because enemies rarely feel unpredictable.
And the predictability even goes with the bosses. You don't learn to counter their different moves that they can mix in various ways. With most bosses, you learn one, yes ONE, pattern they will always follow, slowly but surely chipping at their health and doing the same thing over and over until they finally die. There are exceptions, but usually bosses are more frustrating and boring than any fun.
What about the world and the story? The design of the levels (and there are distinct "levels" in the game with loading in-between, but you can go back and forth) looks good, as does the art design of most of the game, but they are actually rather boring. Especially when you realise, that even if you do explore them early and completely you will still need to redo that again and again after, because some things will just appear or change, sometimes without rhyme or reason, in them. You found a locked door behind which is just one square room with a chest and can't open the door? You will be able to get the key to it only by the end of the game. Even if you don't even need to go back there, even if the item you get isn't really worth it, there's no story reasons behind it - it's just that. And story itself is, actually, pretty dreadful and told via voice acting that ranges from passable to pretty bad. Which is sad - game actually has some potential to tell some interesting and variable stories and the NG mechanic even seems to hint that maybe something similar to Eternal Darkness replayability. But nothing like this is here and even those variables that can change the ending sometimes glitch out.
Lords of the Fallen has some good ideas, it's actually rather fun to play, but it's questionable decisions keep annoying you and by the end part of the game, they can build up so you might want to drop it. Sadly, there might not be a sequel that actually improves on the game's ideas, because this was a pretty good first try.

WMMA3 is an Mixed Martial Arts Tycoon-style game. You are playing a powerful executive in a UFC-style company (not a fighter!) who is in charge of hiring fighters and scheduling matches (like Joe Silva). There are two game modes available: the standard "Career" mode, where you pick a suit, choose his skillset and control a company, and "Quick Fight" mode, where you can easily pair two fighters and see the fight. The career mode is deliberately made less deep than Football Manager's, for instance. I'd rather not call it a Manager game at all. Financial management is limited. The emphasis is on filling your events with attractive matchups and watching the gameworld unfold. You can adjust the rules to be more like PRIDE and can even host legendary UFC 8-man tournaments. It's all up to you. Just watch out to keep your finances positive and that you have some ethnic diversity on your roster.
Gameplay comes down to scheduling fights and scouting potential fighters based on skills, popularity and hype. Will you sign the charismatic ones, the superskilled ones, or will you populate your company with average joes to make your stars look good? There's some weight class management as well. Fighters' stats are quite deep and reflect the game of MMA very well imo. There's things like 'punch power', 'low kick speed', 'muay thai clinch elbow technique', 'killer instinct', 'leglock submissions', Altogether this makes 85+ stats that directly impact the fighter's performance, which is amazing. These stats are constantly progressing as fighters visit camps to train. Once they reach a certain age, certain skills start to deteriorate. Older veterans, however, are often more popular given their history. Will you make them look good as look as possible, or feed them to younger talents?
The game really shines on the part that comes after the gameplay. You don't even have to play to enjoy the game and can turn over control to the AI anytime or watch other AI companies. Afterwards you can sign their stars and pit them against yours. Just don't forget that Japanese stars aren't as popular in the USA as they are at home. When fight night arrives, you get to watch all the fights you want, which is often a trilling experience if you bring yourself to care about the characters. Information hits the screen on a play-by-play basis: every action gets mentioned until you press 'space' to continue to the next. Upset victories have you jump up from your chair in disbelief.
There's also a sandbox option for the people who just want to hire people and have them fight. You will never get fired, run out of money or have matchups refused. Fighters also won't need to prepare in this mode. Either way, the game has limitless replay value as it just keeps going, creating a new fighter whenever one retires. One of the best things about the game is the support for modders: There's real life mods, there's expansions for the fictional one that comes with the game, there's a video game characters mod, etc. Anyone can easily mod the game during gameplay or make new characters and importing them into your existing game is child's play. More games should have this kind of support.
While I really enjoy the game and have spend hundreds of hours on it, there are several things about the game that could potentially frustrate you, so consider this a warning:
* Due to the resources used to create the game the resolution of this game is fixed, so there's no full screen mode. There's no 'fix' for this. On my 22" screen it takes about half the screen. If this somehow bothers you, try the demo first on their official website. I personally decorate my desktop with MMA-style graphics to counter this. I suggest you do the same.
* It's a text-based simulator so there's few graphics: there are (often quite nice-looking) renders of all the fighters, and there's promotion logo's and banners. During the fights, there's no visual representation. Personally, I think that's great as you can imagine the fights taking place without visual restrictions. However, this obviously requires some imagination. And to imagine it you also need some MMA knowledge. If you've only watched a couple of UFC events you might get lost in the positions and interactions. You don't need to be an expert or a practitioner: just a fan who watches regularly and knows what an 'americana' or the 'north-south position' is.
* There's actually an advanced version of the game available called WMMA4 on the developer's website. This game has more options and tweaks to fix some problems mentioned in other reviews (like the contract signings). I think it's a great improvement but the difference is not so groundbreaking to wait years before it finally comes to Steam (if you don't want to buy directly from their store).
If you are not bothered by these things and are a fan of MMA, I'm pretty sure you'll enjoy the game. I posted a small guide/tutorial to help you book your first MMA event. You can even run it with the free demo on the GDS site. If the outcome doesn't excite you, maybe text-based sims aren't your thing. But any MMA fan owes it to himself to try. :)

Much like The Book of Unwritten Tales, this sequel is a good choice for people that like comedy point-and-click adventure games. But not so great for those that want a more serious game. The comedy is really great in this one, and personally I feel it is better than the first one. Since the reference humor and fourth-wall-breaking comedy doesn’t get quite as hard-handed as it did at times in the original.
There are a lot of characters from the first game, so if you like them you are most likely going to like them here as well, as their personalities haven’t changed too much.
The only character that seems to have changed a bit is Ivo. I found her role in this game to be particularly funny this time around, especially since I had gotten to know her as an athletic adventure seeking young elf in the first game. And to be honest the only one that truly seemed to belong on a dangerous quest of the four playable characters. To see her being in a gilded cage and wearing a pretty dress was for some reason strangely amusing to me.
There are also plenty of other side characters returning, as well as some new and fun characters thrown into the mix.
As for the puzzles. For the most part they are still great and challenging, however not all of them are equally easy to figure out. There were a few where I had no idea what I was supposed to do, because they just had such an odd solution, that I hardly believed it even after it was done. Like before it is often a good idea to go back and talk to characters you have previously talked to, in order for them to give you the item you need to progress. But it is consistent throughout the game, which is better than being a surprise just once.
The game keeps up the cartoony and charming style, which fits the very comedic and light hearted atmosphere of the game.
A great adventure game and I hope they make a new one. (Even if I hope Critter and Nate won’t be in it. As I dislike those two a lot. But you might like them, and they don’t really affect my view on the game, since they weren’t that terrible. Just preferred if it had been only Ivo and Wilbur.)

The final boss battle is a joy to behold, if a little confusing your first few attempts. The art and musing being from the genius who gave us Brawl in the Family is just the icing on the cake!
Sadly, it's not without a few flaws. Despite the obvious amounts of polish that went into this game, there are a few bugs that can't be eaten by Etude. Firstly, I noticed a few times that a cymbal would project a location, only to send me a half-step just above or below where it was listed. In a game where positioning is everything, this can very easily wreck a run of a song. In Piranah Jungle, this happens consistantly on the second cymbal, completely preventing you from grabbing all the bubbles! This needs to be fixed ASAP! Also, I noticed occasionally while talking to Etude that his text would bug out and skip a line of dialog. This isn't too bad, as that option is just there for fun and flavor, but it is frustrating to miss the setup to a punchline.
Another little detail is that it can be somewhat tiresome on the later songs to sit through their intros whenever you have to restart, due to missing one lousy bubble. That's more a problem with trying to be perfect in rythm games in general, though, and the songs are so good, It's not like it's a chore to get to hear more of them.
Overall, definitely worth the money. Just fix up the bugs and you've really got something special here, Matt!

I've barely scratched the surface of the game but I feel I've got enough under my belt to post a review.
I can sum this game up as what happens when Dark Souls 2, Darksiders, and a touch of Dragon Age produce something from their unholy orgy. That said I enjoy it so far.
The art style is something I've always been a sucker for, however it does remind me of my experience in Darksiders, where everything is either a mass of flesh or muscle covered in plate mail. It does get old after a while when EVERYBODY resembles a member of the Adeptus Astartes. But I digress, let me break it down easily.
Pros:
The art style, audio quality, and "feel" of the game is fantastic.
Actual story to progress through, while cliche is always nice as it drives the player forward.
Combat is Acceptable. Nothing outstanding but unlike a lot of reviewers I like how slow your swings are with some weaponry. An Axe should be slow and devestating, a haymaker swing with it should remove a limb if that helps put it in perspective. The fact that Harkyn is strong enough to roll in full plate or even move is a testament to his physique, thus slowing some weapon swings down further is understandable.
Bosses are unique enough to pose a threat without being so over the top you can't adapt to combat quick enough to survive AND learn how to defeat said foe (Looking right at you Dark Souls).
The world has a unique mix of linear maps with the ability to "Roam" them freely so long as they're not home to a major piece of the plot you haven't unlocked yet, and backtracking is actually fruitful for those completionists.
Cons:
As almost every other review has said, it's trying SO HARD to be a Souls game and it just isn't. The timings for dodging and even attacking can range from horribly forgiving to WTF level wiffs and misses (Sometimes hits).
The weapons by and large only offer attack speed differences, there's not a huge purpose to the variation of attacks, they all seem to be frontal and are either blocked or not, no grazing hits. The Souls charm came from every weapon feeling like it was suppose to, having differing amounts of penetration and stagger that you just don't see in a lot of other games.
The Shields are from what I can tell, again dumbed down versions of the Souls variety they want to be. Granted a lot of familiarity there with Poise and Block Damage percentages but It doesn't feel like the enemy variety is high enough to really matter.
The magic system also feels like an after thought, a dumbed down after thought (So like Souls only dumbed down).
Lack of ranged weaponry is disappointing but it's not a huge deal.
While pretty and runnable, I find the game to be horribly unoptimized. Running the game at max settings consumes 4GB of VRAM and 9GB of System RAM. Not saying the game isn't pretty but I've played games that looked a lot nicer that didn't require that much system resource. (Disclaimer, it runs fine on 2 970s in SLi so long as the board it's on is aftermarket and actually has 4GB of usable VRAM i.e. eVGA SSC2.0 ACX 970s)
Final Thoughts:
I'm satisifed, not excited or fangirly about it, just satisifed. This game should hold anyone over until DS3 comes out or the Gods see fit to pillage Sony for the rights to a Bloodborne PC port (XD). I wouldn't buy this at full price, I was able to snatch it for 10$ and I'd say it's easily worth $20 USD but it's not a bad game and it's a valiant attempt to honor the Souls tradition of unforgiving punishment and challenge.

Welcome to perfect dodge simulator, happy dodging
As a pretty big dmc fan, i felt obliged to pick up it's &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥edition" just to find a completely different experience. A good story and AMAZING characters kept me going even when gameplay took an obscene dive, level desing, variety, creativity never fall short and the game presents new features all the way to the very end and extends it. I have just ONE single serious complaint about this game apart from some negative personal views, everything else is at least good overall.
I REALLY need to praise this game's characters, art, cutscenes, progression and design, it's simply amazing and make the game a must have experience, do yourself a favor.
Now, i didn't like at all witch time, instead of perfect dodges being something extra, it feels like the whole game runs around that feature, filling up the purple orbs out of witch time is a pain, connecting hits is also way too hard out of witch time, you will thrive more in the game by using two buttons (RT and Y) than you will by learning combos and apllying them and that defeats the whole purpose of a fast paced hack n slash, playing agressively gets you punished, HARD, if you're not focusing on those perfect dodges, you're gonna have a bad time since enemies are hard to stagger and you're vunerable through every frame of every move, on top of that, there are few combos in wich you can move, there is a dash forward and a pop up move but that's about it, wanna move? You need to dodge, wanna make your dodges count or do damage in the process? You need to perfect dodge, no other good alternative is given.
The soundtrack really didn't catch on to me, there is just a certain number of times you hear a "fly me to the moon" remix untill it gets old and it plays nearly on EVERY chapter including the tutorial, you'll be hearing quite a lot of the same beats for the majority of the game but still, it adds to the game's feel but the slight lack of variation is missed.
The only last thing i didn't enjoy about it is how everything in the game feels like a turbocharged 35 years old wooden roller coaster, nothing is really explained and the game's pacing as a whole is all over the place, not to say it isn't fun but when you work your a$$ off to buy an acessory, equip it and most of the time it doesn't even take effect for no explained reason or in some battles it just disables witch time, the damn core mechanic of the game, even throwing in a timer along for the ride makes for a feel that you're rarely in control, while playing it, i barely thought about anything, i was just reacting to whatever was thrown with a dodge mostly or a random combo instead of figuring out wich combos are faster, wich do more damage, wich are safer or what connects with what. I felt like the game punished me for experimenting and just obligated me to perfect dodge stuff.
The game is a fantastic experience with some of the most amazing characters i ever saw, a ludicrous amount of easter eggs and clever lines, amazing art, awesome design and cool and fresh mechanics and features, even though the gameplay kinda shambles around at times and it's centered around features that not everyone will enjoy fully and also a bit of compatibility issues, it's quite an experience.
And for a price THIS LOW, it's one of the best deals you will find around, if not THE best.

Original Kingdom Rush Review
Probably the best Tower Defence game I have played.  Don't let my steam hours fool you, I have a whole lot more on my tablet, where I originally played this.  Very addictive gameplay.
Each level have a set amount of points you can build towers on and you can choose to build one of 4 towers.  The basic towers are
Barracks provide troops that do damage but also engage mobs, preventing them from advancing down the late.
Archer Towers provides ranged dps, high rof but low damage, good for weak swarm mobs and magick resistant mobs.
Wizard tower provides ranged dps, low rof but high damage, good for armored enemies and slow enemies.
Artillery towers fire explosive rounds that do aoe splash damage, great for swarm mobs.
Now each of these towers can be upgraded multiple times and each have two unique upgrade paths.  Once fully upgrades they will have 3 additional bonus you can purchase with 3 levels each.  They have this for each unique upgrade path provide plenty of variety in your tactics.
In addition to your towers you have a hero that you can upgrade throughout the game (all heros are available on PC verssion).  Heros are powerful units that can help hold the line against the unrelenting tide.  You also have troops (seperate from baracks) you can spawn at any location on the map.  These can be ugpraded throughout the game as well.    They are great to deploy to help hold the line or as a last ditch effort to stop a mob from hitting your base.
Each level has 3 version.  You have the standard campaign level, then you have two more difficult versions.  These prevent you from using certain skills or towers and are tough but a great challenge and give good XP rewards which you can use to upgrade your towers (these ugprades are passive abilities).
The two main differences I remember from PC version and Tablet version is you cannot purchase buffs on PC version and all heros are unlocked.  On tablet most heros need to be purchased with real money.
Highly Recommended.

Review For The Old Tree
You may see that I've only played this game for 30 minutes... that's how long the game is. You may be thinking, wow, a half hour game, how dumb. You sir, are wrong.
Alright, so you may or may not be this alien, you are definitely following it. There is no story, no background story at least, you are just this alien that is trying to get back to space. Now, what do you do? Control the alien? Nope. You are controlling the environment around him or her, which is surprising cool.
The graphics don't need to be good, but they are, well at least the environment is, especially in the cave areas. Basically, the alien moves to a certain point and you have to try to find a way to get him/her to progress the level. It is a puzzle game, but it's a point and click puzzle game. Some of the puzzles are really simple, leading to a 3 second progression time and others had me for as long as about 10 minutes (the water one especially) and the puzzle difficulty are the right level, which is the best. It's a free-to-play game, so you can't beat that and it takes about 1 minute to install, this game is fun. No music however, but sound effects which makes the game a lot more mysterious.
You don't grow any bond on the alien but you do feel bad for him, you have that part where you're despirately wishing that he will find a way home. 30 minutes worth of gameplay is enough for this game, no story and just a ton of puzzles for maybe an hour more would be a little boring. No multiplayer neither a title screen, if there was one complaint I had about the game was that there are no options or title screen, that would have been nice to mess around with. There's no title for the game when you are playing either however, an Adobe 11 message is what fills your screen.
For a free-to-play, 30 minute, puzzle game (no spoilers) but a quick but enjoyable ending, point and click, no music but errie feel, alien loving, bee crushing, soup making, water cranking, bee-water-carrying, this game will give you nothing less than a fun and good time, is it replayability worth? Yup, I do have to say.

I've barely scratched the surface of the game but I feel I've got enough under my belt to post a review.
I can sum this game up as what happens when Dark Souls 2, Darksiders, and a touch of Dragon Age produce something from their unholy orgy. That said I enjoy it so far.
The art style is something I've always been a sucker for, however it does remind me of my experience in Darksiders, where everything is either a mass of flesh or muscle covered in plate mail. It does get old after a while when EVERYBODY resembles a member of the Adeptus Astartes. But I digress, let me break it down easily.
Pros:
The art style, audio quality, and "feel" of the game is fantastic.
Actual story to progress through, while cliche is always nice as it drives the player forward.
Combat is Acceptable. Nothing outstanding but unlike a lot of reviewers I like how slow your swings are with some weaponry. An Axe should be slow and devestating, a haymaker swing with it should remove a limb if that helps put it in perspective. The fact that Harkyn is strong enough to roll in full plate or even move is a testament to his physique, thus slowing some weapon swings down further is understandable.
Bosses are unique enough to pose a threat without being so over the top you can't adapt to combat quick enough to survive AND learn how to defeat said foe (Looking right at you Dark Souls).
The world has a unique mix of linear maps with the ability to "Roam" them freely so long as they're not home to a major piece of the plot you haven't unlocked yet, and backtracking is actually fruitful for those completionists.
Cons:
As almost every other review has said, it's trying SO HARD to be a Souls game and it just isn't. The timings for dodging and even attacking can range from horribly forgiving to WTF level wiffs and misses (Sometimes hits).
The weapons by and large only offer attack speed differences, there's not a huge purpose to the variation of attacks, they all seem to be frontal and are either blocked or not, no grazing hits. The Souls charm came from every weapon feeling like it was suppose to, having differing amounts of penetration and stagger that you just don't see in a lot of other games.
The Shields are from what I can tell, again dumbed down versions of the Souls variety they want to be. Granted a lot of familiarity there with Poise and Block Damage percentages but It doesn't feel like the enemy variety is high enough to really matter.
The magic system also feels like an after thought, a dumbed down after thought (So like Souls only dumbed down).
Lack of ranged weaponry is disappointing but it's not a huge deal.
While pretty and runnable, I find the game to be horribly unoptimized. Running the game at max settings consumes 4GB of VRAM and 9GB of System RAM. Not saying the game isn't pretty but I've played games that looked a lot nicer that didn't require that much system resource. (Disclaimer, it runs fine on 2 970s in SLi so long as the board it's on is aftermarket and actually has 4GB of usable VRAM i.e. eVGA SSC2.0 ACX 970s)
Final Thoughts:
I'm satisifed, not excited or fangirly about it, just satisifed. This game should hold anyone over until DS3 comes out or the Gods see fit to pillage Sony for the rights to a Bloodborne PC port (XD). I wouldn't buy this at full price, I was able to snatch it for 10$ and I'd say it's easily worth $20 USD but it's not a bad game and it's a valiant attempt to honor the Souls tradition of unforgiving punishment and challenge.

Unfortunately this is currently by far the worst Assassins Creed. Eventhough we were able to notice a few steps towards this in Black Flag it is impressive how bad this game really is.
Ther performance of the game is quite terrible. I would say I own an above-average rig right now, but I can only play on the lowest details available to have the game run smoothly. Unfortunately even the first Assassins Creed looked better (of course on high details, but it's Assassins Creed Unity on lowest details looks like it came straight from 10 years ago). As a result: The textures look like mud.
A big argument for buying the game was the new Coop-Gamemode, but unfortunately Uplay is Udon'tplay since the servers keep collapsing all the time and as a result I am almost unable to play the Cooppart with friends, but only with random people.
In Combat you now ONLY have ONE weapon available (No more daggers or other fast weapons, no more fighting with the hidden blade and no more fighting with your fists only.) and basically what you have to do is simply click left as fast as you can until one enemy gets a yellow healthbar instead of a red one and then you have to press E to parry it or sometimes you have to dodge it by tapping Space. Later you can also learn to perform heavy attacks or to shove into the enemy staggering him and that's it. You can't grab the enemy anymore, you can't disarm the enemy and the countering has also gone overboard somehow. So the fighting is boring at best and annoying the rest of the time due to enemies you can't parry since somehow they do not count as in your fight or whatever. And a question to Ubisoft: What the hell was wrong with the fighting in AC III? That was perfectly fine!
Another thing: The freerunning. I really like that they added the ability, to choose whether one would like to go up or down while freerunning (This is the ONLY change in gameplay I found enjoyable). But unfortunately I experienced a (I would call it heavy) bug for the first time in the series. I got stuck inside walls nummerous times, when Arno grabbed the side of a window sill and thereby transferred half his body into the wall.
The story: Sometimes within Unity one gets the feeling that Ubisoft simply left out huge parts of the story, that you have to pick up from cutscenes. Also everybody seems to know about templars and assassins and last but not least: The entire background story (Outside the Animus) is missing. All you get are a few cutscenes telling you a little bit about what you are looking for, but it's more of an excuse then a real story.
And sometimes it's just the small things: Sometimes when Arno pops out the hidden blade in a cutscene there is simply air and blade (Notice the "sometimes" because other times I can see it) or in a cutscene Arno picks someone up who just lost a swordfight, but the person's sword is magically in the swordbelt again. The reload time for the pistols and muskets is also quite interesting. Everyone in Unity is worldchampion in speedloading ancient guns... Also: Why has the ammo you can carry for your pistol/musket been reduced to almost nothing? I mean I was able to carry 8 shots in reserve in the end, which pretty much made a musket as weapon ridiculous.
My conclusion: Sadly I recommend buying other games instead of this one. For people new to the series: Take Assassins Creed III or if you only want the freerunning and assassinating: Shadow of Mordor offers that too and that game is running smoother, looks better and the combat is quite enjoyable. I really enjoyed all parts of this series up to AC III with increasing joy and Black flag was also still a good game, but Unity is unfortunately garbage, since even if Ubisoft manages to increase the performance by patches the combat will still be worthless.

This game only further improves upon the ground laid by "Enemy Unknown". The story is gripping and actually drops you into the pressure of saving the planet from aliens developing a world-ending technology with its "avatar countdown" system.
Every stage is a methodical tactical test - Some combining this with a turn-based time limit, and others even adding in capturable VIP's to further increase the tactical challenge posed by the game.
The research and construction element of the game balances how you proceed through the progressively more difficult campaign system, and is nicely controlled with time limits relating to available appropriate area staff members you have acquired. Side missions to gain materials, recruits, and income help use time effectively between campaign-critical missions - And the game doesn't feel as if it drags or becomes weary in a vanilla playthrough. Mods significantly amplify both the challenge and the fun in the game, but it is a game that can quite easily attain merit without needing any of them.
