You've probably heard about all of the DLC, tie-ins, and technical nonsense that has been plaguing the launch.  But even looking past those things, it's hard to find the silver lining here.
For a series that is supposed to be about climbing, stealth, and combat, this latest installment of the series somehow made those things worse.  My strategy toward the end of the game was (1) run into middle of several guys, (2) spam attack, smokebomb, and health.
They said they improved combat, but they made it worse.  Let me explain: once you've triggered combat, you can't do any low-profile things anymore until your alert is lowered.  So trying to easily perform an assassination when you aren't necessarily in the midst of combat is impossible.
Due to the new death physics and fancy 'finishing' moves (why were these added?) you can't do a dang thing until that body hits the ground and stays there.
Climbing is as awful as ever.  Here's the big, beautiful city of Paris, and here you are stuck to a wall unable to move like a freakin' idiot.  The whole accidental jumping thing doesn't happen anymore.  You just get stuck to the wall.  Let me tell you, when running from guards, I would prefer to take that leap of faith (no pun intended) than get shot at.
The stealth hasn't advanced at all.  There's really no incentive to do it, because you can always kill everyone in every scene.  Unless it's a mission requirement or bonus achievement, there's no point to it.
The side missions are boring.  There's nothing new and exciting to do, except for the mystery missions, which don't make a whole lot of sense and require a lot of running around.
The modern day plot has been put on hold - you're just playin' a virtual reality game, getting tips from modern day assassin's.  There's no point to it.
The actual (historical) plot's pacing is absolutely awful.  And there's not enough to make any sense of it.  It's a revenge story where you meet some historical characters in the process, but they never play any meaningful part.  The assassin's aren't the cornerstone of the story, or even the age-old Assassin v Templar narrative.  Even the main character doesn't play a meaningful part.  I barely cared until 20 hours in, where it finally took an interesting turn.
The voice acting doesn't help.  The main dialog is all in British, while some conversations heard are in French.  The main dialog, strangely, still throws in French-isms like "merci".  If you played AC3, this game may trigger your PTSD.
There is some time-travel fun to be had.  You climb the Eiffel tower during WW2, and go back to midieval times.  Unfortunately, these are short sequences and simply remind me of other, more fun games - The Saboteur and the original Assassin's Creed.
Now, the less crappy stuff.
The companion mobile app does not have an option to be played in-game like AC4.  I tried pulling out my phone.  It's annoying and not worth the effort.  Unfortunately, these locked blue chests in the game will taunt me forever.
There are new missions that can only be played multiplayer and there are lockables that only unlock if you multiplayer.
There are chests that only open if you have the other games.  I have the other games.  The chests did not open.  I presume that will be fixed.
They let you 'hack' upgrades by paying real money.  Honestly, this doesn't bother me so much, except for the fact that I can't imagine anyone getting into this game enough to want to pay more for it.
In summary, AC:Unity feels like a really bad indie game with huge budget.  The graphics are great!  There are tons of useless minigame-like things!  But where's the beef?  It feels like nobody is making sure the game is coherent as a whole.  Ubisoft has kind of cornered themselves here: they can't make a game this big as polished on a yearly release schedule as they did earlier games in the series, but if they make the game smaller or the release schedule longer, they face other consequences.
In the future, Ubisoft needs to: (1) polish the core mechanics of the game, (2) pay for good writing, (3) put someone in charge of pacing.  If they can't fix these things, the series is going to fall apart and stop being a cash cow.
Pros:
* Another AC game!
* Paris!  Graphics!
Cons:
* Everything.  This game died a death of a thousand needles.

Trove is an MMORPG that heavily borrowed stylistic elements of minecraft and similar games. Besides combat and crafting there is a minecraft-like building system that can be used to build small individual homes or large "club worlds". Most of your goals in Trove will be to collect building materials, item "styles" and mounts and basically become the biggest hoarder.
While it has a fairly fun setting and pretty smooth gameplay, Trove lacks the depth that can be expected from most modern MMOs. End-game content is simplistic, combat usually revolves around spamming one or two skills, there is a lack of variety in enemy encounters and the story is pretty much non-existent. While games like WoW or TES-online favor storytelling, teamwork and pre-made worlds basically everything in Trove is just about collecting things and the grinding that precedes it.
The "styles" mechanic works well and gives some nice, if limited, character customization options not found in other MMOs. As you collect more items you destroy the ones that don't have the stats you want in order to unlock their specific look. Any item style unlocked this way (only hats, masks and weapons) can be used to replace the style (but not the stats!) of your current item. That means that you are not forced to walk around with items that you think look bad. A downside of this mechanic is that outward appearances only marginally reflect a characters' power and level of progress.
There is a good ammount of original classes available but since they all have only three active skills and one passive skill the play becomes repetetive within just a few hours. New classes can rarely be unlocked by basically collecting enough to raise your "mastery level" (corresponding to the ammount of stuff you collected) but will usually cost you real money to buy.
For an MMO Trove does a lot of things right, especially in the pressing addiction buttons in your brain department. As for teamwork, storytelling, variety and mindful gameplay... there is too much that Trove leaves unattended. 5/10

I don't write a lot of reviews, but it seems criminal to me that Lords of the Fallen's current Steam average is "Mixed," so I'm doing my small part to tip the scales. This game isn't perfect, but it's a lot of fun and I highly recommend it if you can catch it on sale (I bought it for $9.99).
My PC isn't top-of-the-line by today's standards, but I was able to keep visual settings pretty high and maintain a solid framerate. The environments are beautiful, your character looks like a total badass no matter what weapon or armor combination you equip, the common enemies are well-designed and intimidating enough, the Lords are terrifying, and the animations are smooth. There was never a moment in-game where I was disappointed in the visuals, but I guess if I'm digging for a "con" here, I'd say that there wasn't a huge variety in the environments.
Sometimes, music and sound effects can make or break a game experience for me, but this wasn't one of those times. The theme song is great and there were a couple of times when the music crescendoed while I was fighting a Lord (which was cool and added to the "badass" factor), but for the most part, I didn't notice the music at all in this game. That's okay, I guess. The sound effects were impressive, especially the growls and roars of enemies and the impacts of weapons against shields and walls. The one thing I really wished as I was playing through the game was that enemy footsteps were more audible. There are times when you find yourself navigating corridors where enemies are patrolling, and you should be able to hear that big dude with the axe stomping around just down the hall...but you can't.
The voice acting was well-performed throughout the game. Some were better than others, but for the most part, these people did a good job (the most cringeworthy line in the whole game is probably Harkyn's "My vow of defiance!" in the opening sequence).
Okay, to be fair, the story isn't what will draw you into this particular game, but it is well-crafted, and so many minor details are revealed through picking up scrolls, which activate voiceovers that describe enemies, experiences, or locations. Even if you don't find yourself caring about the lore, you learn more and more through the words of characters that you haven't even met...and this is often a rewarding experience. You learn more about this world and its history if you care to, but it feels more alive, regardless. There were people here before you, and you get to hear their stories and connect the pieces for yourself.
This is it. This is why you start the game, and this is why you continue it...even after you've been killed 30+ times by the same enemy and you curse so loudly that you wake up your wife and fear for your marriage. The gameplay is just. So. GOOD. Okay, okay, with the boss fights, it sometimes feels less like you're exploiting weaknesses and more like you're just memorizing patterns, but for some inexplicable reason, it's still fun. Blocking, dodging, rolling, slashing, thrusting--it all feels so...right. Now, granted, it takes a while to get there, and it takes even longer if you're experimenting with different weapon types, but once you get the hang of it, this combat experience is beautiful.
My first piece of advice: don't just spam your attack buttons. This took me a while to figure out, but each weapon type has a narrow interval after each swing (slash, thrust, etc.) when you should activate your next attack for a quicker follow-up, with less of an impact on your energy. You can even practice this without enemies around--just try out different combinations and watch your energy bar. It will flash with each perfectly-timed attack.
Also keep an eye on your equipment and Endurance. If your Weight score is green, you'll move and execute combinations more quickly (this may be less important for warriors wearing heavy armors and shields, but I played primarily with short swords and daggers, so speed was extremely important).
You have quite a few customization options as far as character development and equipment, but you need to keep a few things in mind. This is a combat RPG with a
emphasis on melee combat. Your ranged attacks are limited to spells and your gauntlet, which also uses up your magic. In general, you won't be fighting or killing enemies from a distance. You also won't be collecting tons of loot and trading/selling items. It's just not that type of game. Personally, I was okay with that...lately, when I've played some other RPGs, I've hoped that the enemy I just killed didn't drop anything, because it felt more like work than play to be constantly managing my inventory.  There are runes that you can equip to weapons and armor, and there are attributes that you can improve as you progress, but this is not nearly as involved as, say, Skyrim or Diablo or even Borderlands.
To sum things up: Lords of the Fallen is an excellent combat RPG. Just know what you're getting before you get it. You'll die (probably a lot), but the combat is amazing, and you'll feel a sense of accomplishment with each enemy that you defeat.

So I played this game before I played Dark Souls. Here are my pros and cons.
Pros:
- Reasonable difficulty level. Each enemy has its own strategy to defeat it, but mistakes are punished hard.
- amazing graphics
- non linear world/map layout. lots of things to explore
- no minimap or map in general. you have to look twice to find everything ( i have missed several treasure chests because of rushing through an area)
- easy to learn, hard to master combat system
- few class options but significant changes in playstyle ( equipping another weapon could feel like a whole new class )
- advanced equipment system needs you to care for things like weight or poise
- lots of non randomized gear
- rewarding experience system ( the more enemies you kill without dying/saving the more exp you'll get from a kill)
- the game runs very stable. i had no crashes or something in over 30 hours playing
Cons:
- heavy backtracking. this whole game basically takes place in one giant keep and most of the doors are locked until later in the game
- story is very standard. dialog choices are mostly irrelevant
- magic is very buggy. it misses often
- descriptions of trinkets are often unclear. look them up to see what they are doing
- no new weapons in "new game plus" or above
I had a lot of fun with this game and i recommend it to everyone who likes action-rpgs and overcoming challenges. And I also recommend to finish this game at least twice to find all items.

After playing this game for a few hours, I felt compelled to write a review.  I play a lot of the mainstream types of games, but when I saw Hacknet on sale, I figured that it wouldn't hurt to broaden my spectrum.  What I got was a great text based game, where I actualy felt the exhilaration of hacking.  Am I really hacking like real hackers do in the real-world?  Probably not, but that's ok, because it feels like I am, and that's not a rabbit-hole I wish to delve into.
The beginning missions do just enough to teach you what you need to know without holding your hand too much to the point where you go looking for the toggle switch to "turn off hints".  Sure you hack into computers and you feel cool, but it's not until the first hack that you're being traced and there's a timer ticking, that the adrenaline really starts to kick in.
The puzzles are just difficult enough that you don't want to look to a guide, and feel rewarded when you succeed.
I can't tell you much about the story, as I feel like I'm still in the phase where the game is making sure I'm ready to venture into the story, but I'm having a blast just thinking about all the trouble I'm about to get into.  It's a game I have a hard time putting down, and an even harder time being away from.  Whether you catch this game on sale, or pay full price, you'll definitely feel like you've made a solid purchase.

Good god I wanted to like this. Despite the negative amount of reviews for the game, the positive ones said it's under rated. And I honestly felt that way until I got further in.
Mechanically it very similar to a souls game, which is why I wanted to and for awhile was liking it. Sure the story was kind of generic and the gear didn't feel like it had the same variety of souls gear, but it felt solid. The magic system was Meh but it worked.
It even had a couple of nice ideas - the risk reward system for XP was awesome. A lot of the gear and weapons looked awesome, even though variety was so-so.
But it has 2 serious areas of shortcomings.
(1) General Design issues: Bosses are generic and not fun or very memorable. Some of them just look like gnarlier versions of the base guys. Some enemies are extremely annoying to fight leaving usually one exact way to end them quickly (standard mobs, not special mobs or bosses btw). Many of the weapons are pretty much useless, you'll go from one to the other instead of in DS where I would often rank up 2-4 different weapons and switch depending on situatuion, you'll just sick to the playstyle + strongest. Also one of the larger issues with the game - Hitboxes and targeting are effed up. Half the time you roll completely out of the way you still get hit. Your blows may not land even though they clearly did. Hell the infiltrator boss I had to one-hand my weapon instead of two handing because even though I didn't lock on, the two hand attacks would target the center of him at the lock on point(the strong spot) even if I started the attack facing one his legs (the weak spot).
(2) Technical Issues: By far my largest issue with the game. I have rig more than capable of running it at any settings. I'm not talking dual GTX 980 with 16 GB of ram, but I can run stuff like Battlefield 4 and Far Cry 4 on ultra. So even after tinkering with some settings as people recommended online, there are parts where there are just random♥♥♥♥♥pop-ins and chuggy frame rates. But most unforgiving are the random crashes. I haven't had a game crash this much since Vanilla WoW. I got to the point where one specific boss, it always crashes roughly at about 33% of life left. Every time. And its known issue they didn't bother to fix. I literally cannot progress anymore, tried seven times. Every time, about 1/3 life, crash. Even had it memory leak on me once in general and gave me a blue screen of death crash.
If they had made better bosses, and polished the bugs I'd recommend it in heartbeat. The core is good. The idea is ok. The execution is BULL♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ When a game tries to emulate the style and difficulty of something like a souls game which are renowned for the hard but fair play, the amount of crashes and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hit detection is unforgivable.
Wish I could still get a refund. I mean if the bugginess prevents me from finishing it, I wouldn't have bought it in the first place.

X-Com 2
Simply put, it is a turn based strategy game set with Invading Aliens. You’re a commander of the eponymous military organization. You take over a mobile ship sending your forces out in missions to complete to gain certain aspects of the game that you can use to make weapons, research advancements, and new technologies, you can recruit and build certain facilities all within a story based format. It is a vast improvement to X-com with beautifully done cut scenes and story action sequences. A must have for strategy lovers. However, it has some solid pros and cons to look over before buying if your unfamiliar with the previous incarnations, which you don't need to play.
PROS
•	A: Vastly improved Real Engine 3.5 allows for great cut scenes within the actual battles, so you see terrific end moves to your actions. Wonderful story cut scenes.
•	B: With the Workshop, you can custom everything from weapons to looks, you can make them into super hero costumes, classic characters or your own mad creations. Voices, Weapons, Armor all to your specific look. Long War 2 all brilliantly done.
•	C: new concealment system can help you stall but not make much a difference. Still cool to have
•	D: Fun difficulty settings and wonderful modding tools.
•	E: I am sure more expansions will continue to enhance the game story and levels down the road.
•	G: Still the best Animation end sequences of any Isometric turn base game out.
•	H: Expansions to get and build off this template.
CONS
•	A: A serious one is your computer compatibility. You must look at the requirements, better the machine better output, but the game has been plagued with failing files and some hiccups. However, matching the minimum requirements will be risky. Poor performance on systems is an issue I do think they will get a handle on.
•	B: The fact that you must play the game in a progressive format like the first few games, does not allow you to build and enjoy your creations for long endeavors. It seems like a waste for example It will not allow to deviate long from moving forward with the story. Sort of like playing RISK wanting to build up, when all you must do is complete the story itself to get to the result. Long War different story.
•	C: It is confined by the old game battle mechanics. The Workshop mods help with adding abilities, but still restrict you to past mechanics
•	D: Careful of the DLC releases, some good, some a waste. Expansion has its own merits and grading.
•	E: Must have your men on Overlook all the time and positioning can be frustrating and you will miss a lot. This can upset players who put a lot into their creations.
OVERALL
In my honest assessment, XCOM2 is a great game that as I said a must have for strategy lovers. Wait till for a holiday sale before buying but make sure your system can handle it. You can try X-COM enemy within first if you’re not sure. Go to the VIDEO in the discussion section to watch others play and then decide if it is for you. This game has more to like than dislike, but be clear that I did stay objectively in adding those cons. X-COM2 is fun, will keep you engaged. I give this a positive for the entire game scope, but not without flaws. RATE 3.9 out of 5 stars.

I really wanted to like this game. I REALLY DID, but everywhere I look I find things they screwed up on. The frame rate is awful (which makes picklocking much harder than it needs to be), I've gotten stuck in hay baskets, fallen into buildings or just through the ground altogether, and even lost items that I had already unlocked. In addition, there are chests everywhere you can't open unless you download their stupid app and play it a bunch (and the app is awful). THEN they also have in game currency that you can BUY with real money called Hack (up to $99 worth. Seriously?). And don't even get me started on Co-Op. Connection is terrible, host migration takes forever, and gameplay wise, it's difficult to properly communicate with teammates. You are limited to targeting something (mind, you can't REMOVE a target once you set one, so at some point there are just targets everywhere) and a "Let's go" command. I can't tell my teammates to throw a cherry bomb, or use their phantom blade, or tell person A to go there and person B to go somewhere else, or even tell them what I'M going to be doing. The whole thing just ends up being a big mess as you try to predict what your teammates are going to be doing. I honestly end up treating co-op missions like solo missions, paying little attention to what my teammates are doing and not working with them at all.
As far as things the game does RIGHT, I can say that the story is...ALRIGHT. It's not fantastic but it's not bad either. I like the changes to combat. Instead of couter attacks you have parry, which will render the enemy defensless for a short period of time, rather than just instantly killing them as you string together counter attack after counter attack like pervious games. It goes really well with Co-op, because with 2-4 people you'd consider just charging into an army and taking them on. However, with combat more challenging (and guns nearly one shotting you with basic armor) it makes you think twice about your strategy. They brought back magic medicine which heals all your health at the push of a button which I actually don't like at all. I liked health rejen out of combat much better because then I could get in little fights all around town and if I got hit once or twice it didn't matter much. But now, I'd have to use medicine after every little fight to keep my health up. I also like the skill system. In co-op it lets each player bring somethign different to the table. One guy might have lots of health and melee skills, another might have ranged skills, and the last two have stealthy skills. It spices up the gameplay nicely. (ALSO I REALLY LIKE THAT YOU CAN HAVE A RIFLE AS A WEAPON. JUST FREAKING SMACK PEOPLE WITH A RIFLE. SWORDS? TOO EASY. BULLETS? THOSE ARE FOR SCRUBS. JUST BASH THEIR FACES IN WITH IT)
Overall, I would NOT recommend this game at this point in time. MAYBE when they fix frame rate issues (I know I didn't talk about this a lot but believe me, IT'S A BIG ISSUE), and the various bugs the plague the game get sorted out my opinion might change. I realize the game hasn't been out long but that is NO excuse for all these issues. When you release something, it should be as perfect as possible. I understand they can't catch every little bug but this is just unexcusable.

I had no idea what to expect when I started this game, I was just in a mood to try something new. If I had gone by the description I might have never played it, yet here I am dozens of hours in and I'm really glad I did. It's not the style of game or specific gameplay elements that make this game great, it's the obvious love and care that went into making it and the surprising depth for what seems to be a relatively simple game on the surface.
You have a lot of freedom to approach the game in different ways - if some elements aren't your thing you can simply ignore them for the most part. For example, there are periodic festivals or events that you can attend or just skip and go exploring a cave instead. You can work on friendships and romances or not bother. Spend any day farming, fishing, foraging, crafting, exploring, mining, or whatever you feel like.  I haven't "finished" the game yet and am not sure if there is any sort of ending (I'm assuming it's just open-ended play), but I think I've experienced all of the different aspects of the game. I find some more enjoyable or better executed than others, but there's plenty of variety for different play styles.

The top of the pinacle of hack and slash Platinum-over-the-top-ultra-action-all-over-your-screen games, Bayonetta may not be suit for all but is surely a must for those who like this kind of games.
The gameplay, as expected is extremely fluid and varied, there's plenty of combos to learn and they all are intuitive for you to discover them on your own without sitting through the list to get the best ones, enemies are a great challenge for the player to test skill with such move set, and a big set of weapons that can be combined with one another to make all kind of overpowered and querky combinations before facing any foe, this game really makes it feel like dancing through the battlefield... that's once you get a hang on the difficulty.
The story, though superficial and seemless at first glance, is a whole universe contained behind the jokes and hilarious scenes, it's meant for you to research it only if you really want to know, and its deep and explains every single bit and reason on why Bayonetta behaves in... such a peculiar way, super powers included; but if you don't really care to know the details, you'll get just enough context to start beating up foes without feeling unmotivated.
The design on this game is masterful, the enemies, the levels, the art concept that inspires everything is so detailed you could spend several hours just watching the surroundings or character models, since most angels and demons are based on real life mythology, they reflect how much thought is behind them just on their looks. Long story short, it's eyecandy
The  music is another really good part, a 5 cds soundtrack that contains songs for the biggest actions scenes to keep you pumped up all the way through the end, songs for relaxed ambiance before the battle, there's a song for every ocasion in the game and maybe even outside it for those who like game ost.
As a conclusion, Bayonetta is probably one of the best hack and slash games produced by Platinum, maybe the appearance is a little excentric and might turn away those who are aware of what would their friends think if they saw you playing games with sexual inuendos of women dancing partially nude, but if you are like me, you'll end up with a 40 minutes monologue explaining why they behave like that and how it's not offensive towards women but intead empowering

You loved the original Kingdom Rush and want more!
Very much what you want from sequel... everything that made the original game great, but with enough new content to keep it fresh and exciting. A completely new set of new enemies, new heroes and 22 new levels... more than you can shake an oversized Dwarven bombard at (or at least enough to shut you up for a good 20-30 hours).
The Tier 4 towers have also undergone an overhaul, providing a new set of tactics and toys to play with; from assassins, to battle mechs... and, most deliciously, a freaking
. Finally... Now
the one who gets to summon armies of the undead! The new towers feel well-balanced and have a diverse range of special abilities that seem to promote a much stronger focus on synergy than before, at least from my experience (though the Necromancer can feel a little overpowered on lower difficulties).
The only major change (which is hard to say if better/worse) is that the heroes now retain their exp between levels. Where, previously, they'd go from 1-10 in a single level - you now level them up throughout the game, adding earned points into to cool abilities and passive upgrades. Whilst it adds a nice RPG element to your favourite heroes... it can equally add a grind factor if you wish to play with the full range on offer, as you'll need to level them up individually. And obviously, if you wish to try any new heroes, you'll need to level
up to the same as your current ones to be able to provide a meaningful comparison. So swings and roundabouts really... But the hero you use is more for your own fun, so it's not like you're hindered from finishing the game if you only wanted to stick with a handful or even just the one - in which case this isn't a problem at all.
Other than that: Same loving attention, same cracking array of challenges and same humour... What's not to love? And at 60 fps, it looks smoother than ever before.

Few sequels live up to the original, but this one comes pretty close. Just like the first Book of Unwritten Tales, the sequel is full of fun, funny puzzles, full of tons of pop culture references (D&D, World of Warcraft, Lord of the Rings, Doctor Who, and the obligatory "Guybrush Threepwood: Mighty Pirate" dialogue option, just to name a few). Unlike a lot of fantasy adventure games, which try to make you invested in them because of epic storylines while having brain-breakingly evil puzzles, these puzzles are fun but still challenging, taking some ingenuity but not a lot of trips to a walkthrough. There are your traditional "combine every item in your inventory to every other item in your invetory" puzzzles, but there are a lot more interesting onces, too, involving math, dance, and the optional gambling dice game. Add to that the same great characters you met in the first installment, some great new ones, some unexpected plot twists, hilarious dialogue, and even some genuine heart and emotion, and you've got one amazing episode in an already amazing franchise.
10/10. Would adventure again.

If you are a Dark Souls fan, you may enjoy this game. If you are not, then you will definitely not like this game.
The graphics for this game are great. Each location is highly detailed (What few locations there are) and have a great deal of depth. The character’s equipment also show great detail. The monsters in the game are quite inventive but suffer from re-used graphics so they do not stand out as much as you play through.
There are parts of the game with graphical glitches. As you kill the boss and absorb their energy your helmet and glove will randomly disappear. The scene will start off with you having them on but within a few seconds there gone. This happens on several but not all boss encounters. Other than a few things like that, I would say the graphics were extremely well done.
The sound in the game is also quite good. If you have a 5.1 system or better, you can really hear the weapons moving and clanging from each attack. As you run through caves with water you can almost feel the mugginess around you. Even the blowing wind is convincing.
Then we have the storyline and side quests. This was one of the downsides to this game. You have been released from prison to stop an invasion. Your first task with the monk who set you free is to find Antanas. Right at the beginning you find out that the monk you are with is injured and needs medical attention. As you meet the first boss, he is thrown across the room. After your fight you go to help him out only to find him gone. So now you are on a quest to find this injured monk through a castle with switch enabled gates, monsters, archers’, and other various nasties. He must have had some potions of invisibility, levitation, and invulnerability to get where he did! With that said, the rest of the game and many storylines have overly farfetched concepts or things that are half explained.
Now we have the most important part of the game The Combat System. The game lets you choose between a Cleric, thief, or warrior style combat. Nothing special here but it does not need to be. Each type still revolves around the hack and slash concept but varies it up by their additional benefits.
Weapons and armor have a weighted feel to them. You can easily become encumbered and slow down dramatically. Each type of weapon has its own animation and attack. However, the larger weapons feel way to slow. Anticipation is the major factor of this game, however when you have to initiate a swing well before the enemy gets to you just so they walk into the attack is just ridiculous.
While I am on the mechanics, LEDGES suck or rather the jump mechanic. Several points in the game you find locations that you will be able to jump. If you walk up to them, you will fall. If you run up to them and are not in the right position you will fall. I was towards the end of the game and was looking for the next location. I ended up jumping on a pathway and was shot by archer’s. The same thing happened the second time. The next 9 times I could not jump and kept falling.
You have probably read a lot about the backtracking. There is a decent amount of that where creatures have respawned and have gone up in skill/level just like you. That will in fact make things a bit interesting a very welcome. However, you will do more backtracking looking for where to go next or getting lost. The game needs a map. If you plan on playing this go online and download one of the many maps and saver yourself hours of running around in circles.
The game has a lot of promise but is definitely not worth the full price. If you are a Dark Souls fan, pick this up when it is 50% - 80% off. It is a decent game that requires a lot of polish. If you are not a fan of the Dark Souls game style stay far away as there is almost nothing here for you.

Didn't like it. No matter what I did I couldn't get out from behind the massive 8-ball this game puts you behind. The blunt reality is that your heroes are not good enough to do what the game demands of them. Its very well tuned to keep you from realizing that right away. Theres plenty of gimme fights that make you feel powerful. Even gimme dungeons that make you feel like you're making progress.
The truth: you're one bad encounter away from everyone dying and your finances being crippled.
Thats the other big complaint. I felt like most dungeon runs cost more to embark on than they brought back. Even runs with the antequarian barely put me in the black. The economy of the game is stifling. Sitting there on 20k gold and in order to build my party the way I need it to be i have to blow half of that on upgrades and skills before they even set foot in a dungeon. Then i have to provision and suddenly I need this run to earn me over 10000 gold just to break even. To top it off unless I'm very lucky I have to blow a further 3000 on de-stressing some or all of the heroes after the run.
Look, I can get into a hard game. I can get into a brutal game. But after nearly 50 hours played I was still running in place. No matter how hard you want the game to be, surely at some point you want to reach a position from which you can beat it.
I'm sure that point exists in this game, but for whatever reason I couldn't reach it and i simply burned out. A shame. This game is covered in polish and character. I just can't do it anymore.
I'm thumbing this up because its a game everyone should experience. Just don't expect it to be one of your all time favorites by the time you're done with it. If you're like me, the brutal ten steps forward ten steps back reality of this game will eventually make you lose interest. But before that happens its an experience worth having.

One of the things that most people forget about video games, though we do like to prop them up as art for the world to see, is that your experience with them can be heavily influenced by where you're at psychologically at the time you participate in them.  Psychologically, emotionally, and more.
Hacknet has been, for me, one of the best experiences I've ever had playing a video game.  I often struggle with the concept of my potential and for a few hours, I was living to the fullest.  I was a master of my domain.  I had power over others, able to subvert their plans and see what they tried to keep private.  No longer was I underappreciated at work, no longer was I just some peon struggling to make someone else rich.  I did what I wanted, went where I wanted.
I couldn't tell you one way or another if this is actually what it's like to "hack" in the real world, but it felt like it to me.
Pick up this game if you, like I did, have a long weekend and want to get in some quality gaming time.

ONRAID is an online competetive game 4v4, but it also has your typical campaign for loot, where you can cooperate with other people.
It is a 2D Sidescrolling platformer shooter. However, be AWARE THAT THIS GAME IS ONLY COMPETETIVE. There are no CASUAL MATCHES. That means, even when you just meant to farm gear for your set, you'll get ranked, unless its campaign.
I would press no for recommend, but... to be fair, and of course to write something everyone in general could go by (and not my scale, because clearly, I won't waste my life farming on a game NOT having fun.. So I'd rate a game as bad if it enforced farming, but wasn't consistent in gameplay to make it seem natural).
ONRAID isn't bad for a FREE TO PLAY. It just has its moments, but they aren't as bad as let's say... Other games with RNG.
This game is influenced mostly by the gear you have and equip. It is influenced LITTLE by skill (How do people keep dying even when someone mashes dematerializer the moment they see you... Just walk away for a bit, like damn!).
Is it fun? No. Being grouped with at least 1 cruddy teammate every time you enter the CASUALLY RANKED MATCH isn't fun. That one person on your team dying 15 times, forcing you to lose and plunging your rank isn't fun. What makes it worse? The game seems to do it EVERY TIME. EVERY GAME. Unless you're lucky, you'll have decent people on your team that realizes that the game is so dumb to the point where casuals got mixed with ranked. Then they'll actually play like they have some sort of sense...
Does this game have its good sides/upsides? No, of course not. It's overshadowed the moment you enter the main menu for your first time, by "Legendary" gears, and boxes you can just pay for if you don't want your rank messed up before you hit level 15...Oh cool, you can change equipment... After you're lucky enough to have played long enough to farm it, or through random drops.
As I know about how video games are made, I also have to go on and say I'm unimpressed. The moment I see a freaking Destiny box, or be forced to farm for even♥♥♥♥♥♥♥10 minutes to level (Like Nioh, where you're forced to farm levels just to play through campaign regularly, and farm gear that won't drop for you.. Even if you DON'T DIE, you'll be forced.) ..., It's a hands down 1/10. Obviously, I won't give OnRaid that score, but let's leave it at 6/10, for merging ranked into regular games mainly... I would put Destiny at a 0/10 just because of... Ugh, your wallet... Glad I didn't spend on it... (It's repetitive anyways.), and Nioh at a 2/10 because it's just bad period. Felt like an Xbox age game with farming added, and didn't even PROPERLY rip-off the game it was supposed to rip-off, and filled with artificial difficulty.
I enjoy OnRaid and understand that obviously they have to make money somewhere (Because armor/skins in this game give you actual stats, they had to make chests drop them..). It also doesn't seem like your weapon/armor effects too much, but, if you really think that, bring your flimsy poison dagger against some epic one and see what happens when you withdraw and lose half your HP instantly...

X-Com 2
Simply put, it is a turn based strategy game set with Invading Aliens. You’re a commander of the eponymous military organization. You take over a mobile ship sending your forces out in missions to complete to gain certain aspects of the game that you can use to make weapons, research advancements, and new technologies, you can recruit and build certain facilities all within a story based format. It is a vast improvement to X-com with beautifully done cut scenes and story action sequences. A must have for strategy lovers. However, it has some solid pros and cons to look over before buying if your unfamiliar with the previous incarnations, which you don't need to play.
PROS
•	A: Vastly improved Real Engine 3.5 allows for great cut scenes within the actual battles, so you see terrific end moves to your actions. Wonderful story cut scenes.
•	B: With the Workshop, you can custom everything from weapons to looks, you can make them into super hero costumes, classic characters or your own mad creations. Voices, Weapons, Armor all to your specific look. Long War 2 all brilliantly done.
•	C: new concealment system can help you stall but not make much a difference. Still cool to have
•	D: Fun difficulty settings and wonderful modding tools.
•	E: I am sure more expansions will continue to enhance the game story and levels down the road.
•	G: Still the best Animation end sequences of any Isometric turn base game out.
•	H: Expansions to get and build off this template.
CONS
•	A: A serious one is your computer compatibility. You must look at the requirements, better the machine better output, but the game has been plagued with failing files and some hiccups. However, matching the minimum requirements will be risky. Poor performance on systems is an issue I do think they will get a handle on.
•	B: The fact that you must play the game in a progressive format like the first few games, does not allow you to build and enjoy your creations for long endeavors. It seems like a waste for example It will not allow to deviate long from moving forward with the story. Sort of like playing RISK wanting to build up, when all you must do is complete the story itself to get to the result. Long War different story.
•	C: It is confined by the old game battle mechanics. The Workshop mods help with adding abilities, but still restrict you to past mechanics
•	D: Careful of the DLC releases, some good, some a waste. Expansion has its own merits and grading.
•	E: Must have your men on Overlook all the time and positioning can be frustrating and you will miss a lot. This can upset players who put a lot into their creations.
OVERALL
In my honest assessment, XCOM2 is a great game that as I said a must have for strategy lovers. Wait till for a holiday sale before buying but make sure your system can handle it. You can try X-COM enemy within first if you’re not sure. Go to the VIDEO in the discussion section to watch others play and then decide if it is for you. This game has more to like than dislike, but be clear that I did stay objectively in adding those cons. X-COM2 is fun, will keep you engaged. I give this a positive for the entire game scope, but not without flaws. RATE 3.9 out of 5 stars.

A puzzling adventure similar in premise to portal but with focus on cube manipulation rather than portals. The game uses several different cube types, all designated their own colour to quickly and efficiently let the player know how to interact with them. Red cubes can be extracted or retracted three times, allowing for you to build bridges or tower-like structures with them. The yellow cubes form a ladder when interacted with, the side you choose to left click will always be the longest with the other two nearby cubes forming steps. Blue cubes work as trampolines and can send both you and other cubes or objects flying. Purple cubes rotate the area they are attached to, this includes other cubes. Finally, green cubes form a boxlike object which you can push around or transport with the help of other cubes. Think of it as the companion cube from Portal but with less personality.
There are also some puzzles which use balls that are sent rolling as they spawn, in these circumstances you are to transport the ball throughout a maze, often by making it go through different colour cubes to change its colour and thereby making it react properly with a certain coloured goal. Colour mixing and laser puzzles do also appear but in limited quantities.
What sets this Director's Cut appart from the original Q.U.B.E is the narrative. The standard edition had no focused story at all, and was instead simply a collection of puzzles taking you through an unknown and strange place eventually bringing you to the game's climax. Here however, the developers hired a writer and some voice actors to formulate a narrative story piece fitting the game's gameplay and pacing, and hopefully bringing the player a deeper satisfaction as to why he/she would complete these puzzles in the first place.
Does the narrative succeed with its goal? I believe this is highly subjective, and I've seen both much positive and negative feedback regarding the story. A lot of people are calling it bland, and I certainly can't say it matches the story of Portal 2 in terms of character development or pacing, but it is there and it somewhat does its job. The story, without spoiling too much, tries to give your character, well; character. You are told that what you are doing is for the purpose of saving the world, and that you may not remember anything because you have been out for far too long. Soon however another voice appears and tells you not to believe "their" lies. The player gets more and more information the longer the game goes, and the more puzzles you solve the more hectic the whole situation seems to become. Before you know it you got two sides calling each other liars, and you are to choose who to believe.
The unfortunate thing is that, although I rather liked the story itself, and it did make the game more interesting for me personally, the ending was very poorly implemented for the story. I think that they should have either changed the ending and given you more options as to how to end the game, or rewritten the story's climax to better fit the game's ending. In the end it feels like no matter who you choose to believe, you are simply left with no choice but to follow the game's "canon" ending, which makes no sense at all if you believed the other side.
If the game's climax had made more sense as regard to the story, or at least given you two choices as to how you wanted to end the game I would definitely recommend this. As it stands however; the payoff is really a letdown. And I therefore believe you are more likely to enjoy the standard edition, which has no story at all, and make up your own story instead if you wish, rather than playing along with their story and being forced down one path despite the game hinting towards two endings throughout the entire experience.
I recommend you try out the original Q.U.B.E instead. It is an excellent puzzle game and the only real gripe I have with it is that the physics engine sometimes seems to malfunction slightly which can lead to frustration and having to redo puzzles. Overall, a great game which should satisfy your puzzle-itch for a few 2-3 hours.

The unforced tension, the muted soundtrack that can suddenly crescendo and have you frantically pressing keys and muttering cmon cmon cmon, the beautiful scenery that takes from graphic novels and interactive media, and fighting like dairy farmers. This game has it all.

I've played this many different times with many different friends and watching people fall in love with it is just as great as the first time I realized I loved this game. I'm one of those people who have fervently defended Bethesda in the past. I don't write this review happily, or without hesitation. However, in light of recent circumstances, I'm crashing the bandwagon that is negatively reviewing a game to show a dissenting opinion.
Creation Club started out as a bad idea. As of the time of this review, it's even worse than I thought. I have put over 3000 hours into Skyrim and almost 800 into Fallout 4. I have both modded and placed on my SSD, and have carefully managed that space with patches and archives to allow it all to fit. However, with the latest patch, I had to remove Fallout 4 in its entirety. I cannot have both games currently. It automatically puts all the files associated with CC content on your computer. Supposedly this is so that it cannot fall under console limitations that might otherwise cause its removal. On top of that, it forces the script extender to update, which means existing mods that require F4SE or SKSE64 in the future will consistently break, forcing you to play cat-and-mouse with updates and script extenders. So there's the technical side.
On to ethics. Mods have always been a free and creative platform, where we interact and develop mods together for the betterment of the game, free of charge outside optional donations. Yes, this has shafted mod developers in the past, but mods have always been a labor of love rather than profit. And developers still get shafted under CC rulings, since they're paid the same amount regardless of whether they developed the top mod or the lowest performing one. This new content in no way adheres to overhaul mods, and under CC regulations, cannot be patched for it. So if you have a PA overhaul or bullet physics addition, weapons and armor added by CC cannot be patched for it under their guidelines. So there's the ethical side of things.
So in this reveal of the creation club, it established four very important things: users get shafted by its implementation in the worst way, developers get shafted, nothing on the creation club is worth the asking price and it sets a dangerous precedent for mods moving forward. If you feared that the creation club would be bad, it turned out to be even worse. Somehow, despite having access to our concerns over the past three or so months since CC was announced, Bethesda managed to confirm every single one and invent new ones in a single move. This reveal, in its entirety, has been, in my mind, the worst move for Bethesda in its history. As a PR move, it is disgusting. As a profitable option, it is laughable. As a gesture of respect to mod authors and the modding community at large, it is tantamount to a calumny. Bethesda fans and modders alike are being laughed at with this reveal.
This action was inexcusable. And it pains me to see my favorite publisher do something so sickening without any forethought.

So, clearly this game has gotten quite a bit of negative press from fans and professional reviewers. I for one, have played for over 30 hours at the time of this review, and I honestly haven't experienced a single one of the reported issues.  The city looks beautiful and the game mechanics have been (generally) improved from previous iterations of the series.
This being said, the game is very hardware intensive. It takes a pretty powerful system to be able to rock this thing on "ultra" graphics. I personally believe, (but cannot confirm) that many of the issues that people are experiencing are for this exact reason. If you are unsure as to whether your machine can run the game without any issues, then it probably can't. I guess Ubi capped the FPS at 30, which caused a sort of♥♥♥♥♥♥storm amongst the community, but I haven't really noticed or cared. I haven't had any frame rate dips on my computer, and the visuals look great to me, so /shrug. Oh! Also, the game download is a staggering 55GB, so if you have limited hard drive space, keep that in mind.
The story is engaging as ever. It does seem a bit rinse and repeat to an extent, but I've enjoyed it thus far. They said that the player character would be less "godly" but the combat is very much the same from the previous games, and once the best gear is unlocked, it is quite difficult to die. Speaking of, I enjoyed the ability to customize your character. It adds a bit of personality to how you prefer to play the game.
The ability to free-run down a building is a welcome addition. The NPC's feel much more alive, and they are frequently seen doing any number of activities as you're walking through the streets. The buildings are well designed, and you can travel through many of them, so there are naturally more ways to get from point A to point B. The map is very, very large, and as far as mechanics go, I would say that this is the best AC game to date.
I haven't played any co-op missions with anyone yet, but I have solo'd a few in private and they seem to be pretty good.
All in all, is it a must have in your collection? No. Is it the best AC game that I've played? No, comprehensive consideration causes me to give that award to Black Flag. Is the game woth picking up if you are a major fan and you have a rig that can run it? In my honest opinion, absolutely! It's been quite a bit of fun and I'm glad that I purchased it.

Bastion is a somewhat short but completely enjoyable action RPG. The story is compelling but not critical to the gameplay's mechanics- that is, you're not beaten over the head with the interesting story. The story is delivered through a voice which describes your actions- in essence, this voice is recounting your story as you make it, which is an interesting point of view to play.
Power progression feels meaningful without pushing numbers on you too hard, so it's a lot friendlier than a gear-based action RPG. You get weapons and can unlock more abilities with various items you find in the world. Once you've unlocked a 'tier' of abilities, you can switch back and forth between those two cost-free, allowing you to customize your weapons to what you want them to be. Playing with the large number of weapons makes interesting gameplay- as you can only have 2 weapons on you at any time.
The achivements are challenging but not absurdly difficult to complete.
This game plays equally well on controller and mouse/keyboard, though I think aiming with the K/M is a lot easier for certain weapons.
I haven't had any crashes or technical performance issues at all.

Many brain training programs on steam which are far or few inbetween aren't always the most straight forward.
This one is brand new and seems to still be in progress (as far as further development is concerned).
My main suggestion for this is a type of progress tracker where you can view your progress across each day of each month. For example, I could see my best time for "Fastest" during the month of october and what day it was on, my best time ever, and etc. It would be nice to see how progress is going as one continues to use this program to improve the areas of training it provides.
I enjoy it so far but I feel a type of tracking system such as what I mentioned above would really help one monitor all of their improvements and what areas they are excelling in and what areas they need a lot more focus within.

I really didn't like this game. There's 3 parts to the game, but you have to marry the royal to get to part 2. My plan to seduce the queen failed, so I didn't get to the 2nd part. However part 1 was so bad I have little to no desire to play again.
Cons:
-I found the characters to be very one-dimensional.
-I had high hopes for intrigue, but there wasn't much at least in part 1.
-I had high hopes for romance, BUT THERE IS NONE. You just pick the best option and the other person throws themself at you. There's none of the flirting, tact, or humor you'd expect to find in a romance.
-The game rewards you for being agreeable and waiting for a chance to scheme behind the scenes. I found this dull and unimaginative. I thought there should have been more options to intimidate your rivals in the open, create misdirection, and just make your character more interesting.
-I assume you get to the good stuff by romancing the royal, so why are there other romance options? One is a the non-conformer who seems interesting, but you learn next to nothing about her before you have to decide if you'll marry her  or never see her again. The other is described as old and very unattractive, but buys you expensive gifts and wants peace so is considered "kind" wtf?
-Your stats don't seem the mean much. My lowest skill was charm, but I was exceedingly charming, a great actor, and the best dancer EVER.
Pros:
-Life mages and death mages. Made for some interesting court dynamics and greatly helped the world building.
Final Verdict:
-I may play again to see if the game can salvage anything in parts 2 and 3. But part 1 was so bad, don't buy this game.

This is both a review and a PSA of sorts. This story is meant to be played as a female protagonist. I don't see anything in the description saying this (quite the opposite, in fact) and while you have the option to play as a male it is clearly not the way it was written.
The fact that the story is much more believable and conducive being centered around a female progatonist is not, in and of itself, a bad thing whatsoever. But I DO think that there should be a PSA on the store page informing the consumer that while there is an option to play as a male, the story fits better and makes more sense if you choose female. Instead, I felt I experienced a story as a puzzle piece that didn't quite fit into the puzzle. I will steer clear of using pronouns and describing things as being overtly 'masculine' or 'feminine' for fear of inciting the wrath of the PC police, but I will just say that my choice to play as a male protagonist really clashed with the ability of the story to maintain a believable narrative, despite it changing various pronouns from 'she' to 'he' and vice versa. In addition, there were a number of typos that cropped up (primarily in chapter 1).
While my personal experience of this story was not positive, I do believe it is still a decent entry into the Choice of Games catalogue, but the decision to omit a simple "Best played as a female protagonist" line in the description is unfortunate. At the same time, anyone who tries to distinguish anything as being gendered in any way is likely to be publically shamed so I'm almost understanding of why they chose not to incude it. My hope is that someone who reads this at least has a heads-up. Have a nice day!

After approximately 30 hours of mostly very good gameplay, I've finally finished the BoUT2.
Almost everything about the game is excellent. The graphics are wonderful and the animation and sound is good. The story is interesting and the jokes are amusing, some are even laugh out loud funny, which is very rare.
Voice acting is good to excellent, with maybe a couple of minor characters not being very good.
The only negative are the puzzles. The vast majority of the puzzles are fairly simple and fair. Unfotunately there are a handful of more difficult puzzles that are very frustrating. Some of them are frustrating because of errors in where objects are labeled and where you actually have to click to interact with the object. In one screen where your movement is very restricted your character blocks a key item you have to interact with so I missed the object until I had to resort to using a walkthrough.
Despite this, overall I highly recommend the game. It's one of the best adventure games of the last few years. I hope another sequel is produced.

Starting from the place I left the last time… the performance is still subpar (Vsync in particular TANKS my FPS… turning it off gave me +50fps on average Oo) but since the last time I’ve changed my processor and that seems to have sorted out the hard crashes for whatever reason. There are still some enemy types that make the game a bore to play (namely shielded ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s) and often times I feel like I’m fighting against the game rather than the enemy (camera angles + GIGANTIC shoulder pads + tight TIGHT corridors + instant spawning enemies RIGHT BY YOUR SIDE =  well… not that fun) which is not ideal to say the least.
Coming from DS I’m always looking for epic bosses but they’re nowhere to be found here. Personally I feel this is superior to the original on a few merits.
1. The worst puzzle in the game is gone.
2. The DLC is bundled with the main game, so it's a cheaper price for the same content.
Otherwise, it realy is the same game.
The main game I've discussed before but I'll talk about briefly; it's a competent enough Portal-clone with a variety of decent puzzle ideas but little in the way of originality, it uses standard puzzle logic and you'll have no problems figuring things out, it's on the easy side of things. Unlike Portal, Antichamber, etc. there's no original mechanics introduced, just... sliding blocks. Not that it's a bad thing! What it does, it does well, and some of the cube constructs look pretty neat.
The narrative feels kind of forced into the game and some of it they actually had to add slow-moving elevators for, apparently, dragging out the puzzle-less sections even longer. Fortunately the narration also fills in what were previously dead sections and gives some context. There's an interesting theme of faith vs. doubt going on the whole way through but the issue is that, as Q.U.B.E. is a game with one ending, there's no real weight to it especially if you've played through the game before, because you know how it's going to end either way. I don't mind it and I don't have a preference between the lonely atmosphere of the original and the narrative of this version. It's fine.
The DLC levels attempt to make the game more like a speedrunning game, while still retaining a lot of the elements from the main game. It becomes a puzzle to figure out how to get all the time-saving pickups and figuring out the fastest route through levels (or puzzling out the route that uses the least moves.) The levels all have some flavor to them and do really interesting things with the game's mechanics, I was pretty impressed by the level design.
UNFORTUNATELY. The game's mechanic's also aren't very well suited to this kind of speedrunning thing. There is a pretty decent delay between any input you make, the base character speed is sluggish, and the cursor is tiny. One slight miss can completely destroy a speedrun attempt and it gets rather frustrating rather fast. Especially when it looks like you hit the powerup/block/switch you were aiming for (with the glow that appears showing right on an edge) but the game says you haven't. I think it would've been in their best interests to alter the mechanics slightly for the DLC, because the main game on its own is fine, and the DLC's content itself is fine, but the mechanical flaws of the main game don't suit the DLC levels very well.
There's also the issue of having quite a number of grindy achievements that basically don't respect the player's time at all. Play 500 DLC levels? The shortest still takes some 40-50 seconds, so that would double my playtime just to do, practically. Walk 100000 meters? I only barely made 10% of that going for all the main achievements, I wouldn't dare imagine how long hitting 10000 would take; over 150 plays of the last level, I guess, which sounds like torture (and would also take some 2-2.5 minutes per run... also quite a lot of extra playtime. 10000 pickups? Again, I barely made 1000 going for all the main achievements. These kinds of achievements are pointless time-wasters not in the slightest worth grinding it out for, kind of irked that this will forever sit as unfinished simply because I refuse to waste that much time on this game.
The problems are kinda nitpicks, yeah, but they matter to some people (like myself) and overall it's still a good game, though not a great one.

Unfinished and lacking innovation. I very much enjoyed Black Flag, my first and only AC so far. I brought Unity because I liked the predecessor and the new setting was interesting and the looks were impressive. In particular the large crowds. They really make the city feel alive. The level of detail of houses, their interiors, the streets is an eye catcher. Perfect to just walk about and enjoy the scenery.
However, I have had many graphic glitches. For instance characters completely in low-res textures standing right next to me. Low-res textures on objects here and there. Flickering inside buildings, like white dots on edges. Colored, glowing squares randomly appearing on the character in my character menu (this started after the second patch). And all this with a GTX 970 on ultra high settings.
I also experience game freezes every once in a while. I have no idea what causes them. After a few seconds, the game continues as normal. Very annoying.
I lost several hours of game play because it was not saved properly. The very same problem I once had in Black Flag. Apparently, it was not addressed in this game either. Lost game play is an absolute no-go. I suspect it has something to do with Uplay. Why I even have to have another additional software aside from Steam is beyond me. It's extremely annoying I have to run two different softwares to start a third software.
Regarding the lack of innovation. It was advertized that due to the lack of a ship like in Black Flag, the character itself would now be the focus and could be upgraded. This is true to a certain degree. The available upgrades consist almost entirely of abilities which the character of Black Flag had from the very beginning of the game. In Unity, however, I have to unlock them with points I receive from the main quest. For instance, in Black Flag I could blend in by sitting down on a bench next to an NPC. The very same ability in Unity has to be unlocked first. Throwing money on the ground to cause a distraction; in Black Flag a free ability, in Unity I have to unlock it. Plus, one has to buy money pouches to throw them away. Doesn't make any sense to me.
In short, they did not add a substitute for the missing naval action and abilities. Instead they just cut the whole thing and simply made already existing abilites unlockable. That's no innovation at all; it's two steps backwards.
Then there are the controls. I took me a while to get used to the Black Flag controls, but then it was fun and I could get everywhere very fast and easy. The controls changed and are now more complicated but without benefit. When I'm in Free Run and want to get over a table, for example, I have to hold B in addition to the left stick and RT. In Black Flag I don't have to push any additional button to get over or under obstacles; it was cool and smooth movement. To just run on roofs and jump from house to house is less enjoyable and less easy now. I often get stuck somewhere. Stop right infront of a wall instead of climbing it, stay on the edge of a roof instead of jumping to the next, or jumping from a view point to my death instead of doing one step forward to the sync point. The controls are certainly not as smooth as in the last game.
The fighting system has changed too. Enemies are greater threats now when they have higher level and come in larger numbers. This is a good thing in my opinion. Unfortunately, the controls come into play here. On several occasions I was fighting and had to parry an attack. An indicator shows when best to do that. I hit B when the indicator was showing and nothing happened. Several other times the same thing occurred. Hitting B repeatedly doesn't help. My input was simply ignored. As a result I died several times, even though I would not have if not for the controls. It makes fights much less enjoyable and I don't have the feeling of being this highly trained, deadly assassin.
The story is ok from what I can tell so far. I hope there will be a few (positive) surprises waiting for me further down the story line and I definitely hope there is not so much of this Abstergo stuff. At least this is better than in Black Flag. There it was a hassle every time when I was pulled out of the Carribean and put into a dull company setting with sluggish controls.
Perhaps I'll get used to the changes at some point, even though I will still miss my ship. I won't be buying the next AC so fast and I don't recommend Unity at this point. The game came out 4 days ago, there are already 2 patches out and there are still many bugs and glitches. Not worth it.

To start the game is way WAY too hard, even on easy you will often find the random chance means your whole team gets wiped even if you haven't made any major mistakes and from then on you are fighting a losing battle as you lose an experienced squad member permanently plus the resources invested in them. Although you can save your game you will have to use this function to reload and replay missions as part of the games design to stay relevant with the ever increasing difficulty. There aren't enough inventory spaces to use the options you develop so you have to know exactly where to spend your resources before you have any idea what the research might uncover and you aren't given enough time either in mission scenarios or outside while exploring the world to complete the tasks you need to stay relevant.
While very pretty, the game mechanics haven't moved on any from the last X-Com and the new features such as exploding objects seem to ignite and explode randomly, meaning another tedious mission reload and retry as your team gets wiped out by a burnt out car they were using as cover.
The ridiculous stealth function gives the opposite side an advantage rather than helps you plan an ambush as you get spotted at random despite the pointer tiles which then interrupts your turn and gives the Aliens essentially a free round of attack, in addition if one of your team triggers one of the in mission scenario squares an event will spawn a load of new aliens and give them a free turn to kill your team - queue another reload retry tedium. Even more frustratingly there isn't an option to reorder your teams actions meaning you have to waste a whole round waiting on one team member if you want him/her to trigger your ambush.
I imagine that the out of mission date timers and in mission turn timers are supposed to give the game a degree of excitement and tension, unfortunately they serve to degrade the game experience so that it becomes more and more frustrating as the game becomes more overwhelming and your team becomes untenable. So you end up playing a mission until you hit the pretriggered event and get wiped and learn where it is and what triggers it so you can plan for it when you reload and retry to get past that trigger point until the next one - rinse & repeat.
The whole game plays like a bad rerun of the film The Edge of Tomorrow, and unfortunately given the medium of a turn based game there is little in the way of skill development and just a tedious learning of each mission making the difficulty setting a complete waste of time.

Performance (as of Sep 2016) is reasonable on my old PC (Core2 Quad, 4GB of RAM, GTX560ti) with mixed low/med settings and will no doubt be much better (or look much better) on more modern equipment.
Mod support is supposed to be a lot better than for XCOM EU/EW, so I look forward to a new super-mod like Long War for EU/EW for XCOM2 and modding will no doubt give the game extended life like it did for EU/EW.
Overall I'd give the base game 7.5/10 (as of Sep 2016) rising to 8/10 with the addition of Shen's last gift, which is the only DLC (as of writing) that improves the game in my opinion.

Following on from the monumental success that was Age of Empires II, this third installment brings the franchise into the light with jaw-droppingly amazing graphics and a style of gameplay that is a dream to play. The attention to detail is astounding, from everything to cracks in a townhouse just about ready to crumble, to the wide range of sound effects ranging from hilarously stereotypical comments from Isabella of Spain to Frederick the Great of Germany, to the sounds of canons such as the Falconets. Even the different environments manage to evoke a sense of belonging, as if one is truly standing in the snow in Siberia, or sweating bullets in Caribbean - not an easy feat for a strategy game to achieve. The fact that no major installment have been released since (Age of Empires IV anyone?) is simply a testament to the replay value and endurance of one of the all-time greatest strategy games released.
VERDICT: 10/10

Now that Fractured Space has gone free-to-play, I figured I should put in my two cents on why it's worth getting into. FS is the first "MOBA" I've ever really gotten into, so this review should be taken with that in mind, and while I have decent previous experience with the game, I've only started getting back into it recently as of this writing.
First, I put MOBA in quotes above because FS plays with many conventions typical of the genre, if not outright breaking them. To enumerate a few:
1. No minions or destructible towers
2. Three lanes, but one of them is less important in the early game and a potential tide-turner later on
3. No creeps: resources for leveling up come primarily from capturing and holding mining stations and secondarily from player kills.
Next, I think the one aspect unrelated to the MOBA genre that sets FS apart from other games is three-dimensionality. Ships can freely move in the X, Y, and Z axis, and you would be foolish not to take advantage of this, because three-dimensional combat is enforced by:
1. Giving many ships different amounts of armor on different sections
2. Giving many ships different preferable angles of attack, such as broadside or head-on
3. Having ships turn at varying speeds to present the best armor or number of guns
So, what else is there to like about this game? Well, several things:
1. A small but generally friendly and supportive community
2. Active devs who listen to player feedback and respond appropriately and promptly
3. A good selection of unique ships, most of them viable
4. The game is free-to-play, not pay-to-win; some advanced ships can be bought with real money, but they are statistically identical to their normal counterparts
5. Teamwork is vital to success, and a victory earned through working together is incredibly satisfying
However, much as I love this game, there are some things that could be improved on or are simply lacking:
1. Wait-times for matchmaking can range from 2-5 minutes plus the possibility of having to restart matchmaking if both teams can't be filled, and while the devs have stated this is being worked on, at least one aspect they can't forcibly change is-
2. -Low player population. I've seen the number of players online slide between 300 and 500 on a weekday, and with each match taking 20-25 minutes average, the number of people actually looking for a match at any given time is going to be low. While this means you can repeatedly be grouped with the same competent, friendly players, the opposite is also true
3. Teamwork is so vital to success that if one player disconnects or decides to do their own thing, the team they're on is pretty safely doomed - definitely try to group up with friends *and* communicate with your entire team
4. The system for acquiring new crew is a major grind, especially for new players who don't get all their original crew gifted to them, and while this isn't insurmountable, it is telling that buying crew with real money is rather prominently promoted
5. The game takes a commitment in time, especially with the new daily missions which give rewards for completing 2, 4, and 6 matches a day, which is a large obstacle for people who might have an hour or less to play per day and is made worse by the aforementioned problems with matchmaking
6. As should be expected for a game that is both in Early Access and features a large selection of ships, some ships and combinations are simply superior when skill levels are similar, the main example being the Colossus, which is by far the best defensive ship due to its health, damage output and crowd control abilities
7. The pace of the game may be slower and more tactical than what some players may be interested in
8. A small complaint, but the inability to freely pitch or roll your ships feels like it limits some of the fun that could be had with the game
Despite that list of negatives though, I still highly recommend Fractured Space to players looking for a unique MOBA-esque experience featuring space combat in large ships.
Finally, if you do decide to play, here's probably the most important tip to help new players:
Capture the mining stations. Unless you're using a frail ship meant for sniping, assassination, or healing your team, take every opportunity to capture mining stations that you can, and even if you are using those ships, you can still capture mining stations when it doesn't get in the way of fulfilling those duties.
