Bayonetta is and will remain, for a lot of gamers, a nearly genre defining title.
Frantic paced beat-em-all with a rococo twist, the game lets you control Bayonetta, a witchy witch which witches with her hair, a couple of familiar demons, and the most deadly high heels since the ones that twisted your ankle last summer.
The game's ambition is to offer a cinematic experience while concerving the nervousness and grit necessary to dismember flock after flock of avian themed angels (yeah no, don't ask me, that's the story).  It delivers almost flawlessly, but its over the top, cut-scene heavy art direction combined to uneven difficulty and capricious camera will deter newcommers and less patient players.
Recommended for completionists and beat-em-all fans.
Not recommended if you don't have much time, or patience.
+Excellent combat design
+Excellent enemy design
+Great choreography
=The story is a hit or miss
=Visuals won't please everyone
=Camera can get pretty annoying
=Uneven difficulty
=Needs a serious time investment to be fully enjoyable
-Quick time events. Whut?
-Cut scene constantly break the pace
-Voice acting / acting direction is horrendous
From the get go, players will feel that the combat is extremely fun (which it should be, since it's the focus of this genre). There are dozens of ways to defeat your opponents, from commanding a hair dragon to swallow them whole  (it looks less dirty than it sounds), to crushing them inside an iron maiden. Combos are aplently, and even vary depending on the equipped weapon. Witch time, a bullet time triggered by evading an attack at the last moment, is a great addition to the mix, and allows some strategising, since everything from timing to range is important, and enemies don't take turn to attack you. The enemy design is also spectacular, with very few opponents feeling cheap or rushed, all having their strenghts, weakenesses and particular moveset.
The core gameplay, thus, is done as right as it comes. But there's a but. Well, a couple of (hairy) buts.
The camera, to start with, tends to err way to much in certain situation. There is a lock-on button that can help in some cases, but in others, I have found myself grinding my teets while trying to look for my foe. Some players won't mind - I, do not like it, especially given how crucial the timing gets while confronting some enemies.
Then, there are the quick time events. They barely have a place in the gameplay, and result in an instadeath if done wrong, which is extremely frustrating.
The difficulty also feels somewhat unbalanced. More than once, I have felt than fighting standard variations of enemies was tougher than some bosses. This isn't too bad, the game is long enough to allow you to git gud, but still, with the camera getting in the way, and the very nasty habit the game has to force the player through previous sections after losing a tough fight (yeah, okay, I like corridors and all, but can't we just? Thanks), it might get irritating.
Passed these technical considerations, a point must be made regarding the art direction of Bayonetta.
To begin with, not everyone will like its over the top aspects, from voice acting to caracter design. You'll like the visuals if, like me, you have a thing for your grandma's finely chiseled antique silverware or a thing for enemies looking like they were born from the combined nightmares of the Monty Pythons and H.P. Lovecraft.
You will deeply loathe the voice acting if, like me, you like your characters sounding like... whatever is in character as opposed to what a 10 year-old would think is in character. I've heard my little cousin play dolls once, and I swear her inflexions wheren't far from Bayonetta's (or maybe that child is irreparably broken, I wouldn't know).
I really emphasize on this aspect because, well, as I wrote in the begining the game wants to be cinematic and inserts a cartful of cutscenes which tend to completely ruin the pacing and are, for me, the most cringe I've had in a long time (and I've played Killer Is Dead). Don't watch them and you'll be completely missing the point of why Bayonetta is doing all the iron maiden pressing, watch them and you'll need weed (but then you won't be able to play while on weed, the rococo will get you first).
To conclude, Bayonetta does fighting perfectly, but the general experience is tainted by many little details which can seriously reduce the overall fun, especially if you aren't the patient type.
I would recommend it for its fantastic enemy and combat design, but again, only if you're patient enough to withstand its flaws.

After over 900 hours played sense tech-alpha, I think I have a fair grasp of the game. My turn for one of these:
TL;DR If you like giant space ships and MOBAs, you need to be playing this yesterday.
Fractured Space is, at it's core, a simpler MOBA game. However, many of the more well-used MOBA bits and bobs have been thrown out, and for the better. There are no shops to comb though, builds to learn, creeps to farm and keep track of for pushing, or ultimate abilities that completely change the power level of things once level X has been reached. You have everything at the start of the game, as it should be.
It's just you, your team, your ships, and a few stations to battle over. You may think that would make things simple, but you would be wrong.
Instead, the complexity is moved to the ships. Each ship has a set of abilities, with loadout options you can get to alter those abilities slightly(WIP), armor facings to manage, and ways to complement your allies.
This is what makes Fractured Space great. You don't get stuck having to do tons of learning just so you can have a good time with the game, you just have to take a few minutes to understand what everything on the map is for, what your ship does, and you will be set. That is not to say that there is not a deep, deep dive into things to be had if you want to get into more competitive side, but you don't have to spend hours combing through guides to at least be alright. Low skill floor, very high skill ceiling.
If you want to spend some cash, you have plenty of options. Tons of skins at various price levels, some premium ships that look fantastic, and boosters that you can apply WHENEVER YOU WANT! None of that “Well, you had a booster running for X games and they were all♥♥♥♥♥♥ suck to be you!” If you had a baller game, you drop those boosters on that game, and can save any others for the next time you carry the team on your broad, meaty shoulders.
All in all, Fractured Space is the game I did not know I wanted, and am honestly happy to be existing at the same time as.

I'm not going to waste your time with a real long review. If you want nitty gritty detail I'm sure there's deeper reviews out there than mine, I'm just going to give a laymen's perspective.
Is it Fun?
OH HELL YEAH.  This game is one of those ones where you can put it on easy and just button mash your way to psychotic combat victory, or crank up the victory and debate whether you want to throw your controller in a fit of rage, or bring the heat and show that Boss who's the true Lord of Funky Town.
Is this game for me?
That depends on what you're after. It's a rhythm and timing combo-stacker combat game. The storyline is crazy over the top, but highly entertaining. The cinematics are amusing, the characters are whacky, and the situations are pure "What the ♥♥♥♥ were the writers smoking and where can I get some?"
If you're cool with wild stories of witch craft and angelic warfare, and you enjoy a game that's ostensibly simple but has an engaging combat learning curve you'll probably dig it.
If you're looking for something more down to earth, with a deep, engaging story, and a lot of emotional depth this probably isn't the game for you.
Personally I give this one an 8 out of 10. Gameplay is solid, story is entertaining, music is AWESOME, and I played it to death when it first came out on consoles. If you didn't get to play it back then it's certainly worth picking up now.

Kingdom Rush Frontiers is a fine tower defense game, but its relatively standard gameplay does little to set it apart from its competitors.  If you are looking for a tower defense game to play, I would recommend Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten instead, because it does much of what Kingdom Rush Frontiers tries to do, but better.
Particularly glaring in Kingdom Rush Frontiers is the lack of a fast-forward button, which has become standard in the genre for a reason.  The game has little downtime, but levels can take 15 minutes or more to complete, so replaying them for a better score at 1x speed can be annoying.
The four tower types are unique, but I thought some of the tower specializations were underpowered.  The numerous heroes have a good variety both thematically and gameplay-wise, and were enjoyable to discover.  It would have been nice to be able to more actively control them, because you are given only two spells to affect the battle with in real time.
Kingdom Rush Frontiers has fewer but longer levels than most other tower defense games I've played, but the enemy and map variety keeps things interesting enough.  One highlight was the iron challenges, which disable certain tower types to provide a short but focused challenge.
For the most part, the tooltips are of acceptable quality, though sometimes they refer to having "a chance" of an effect rather than giving numbers.  The metagame is pretty barebones; it mostly consists of upgrading your towers along a linear path.
The story is essentially nonexistent, which I have no problem with.  Don't expect any real characterization or plot developments.
Kingdom Rush Frontiers held my interest, but unfortunately, I see no reason to recommend it over Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten.  I enjoy standard tower defense games, but the sad truth is that if you fail to innovate, you run the risk of someone else making the same game, but better.
Buy and play while waiting for the next one.

If you're not into replaying (like myself) to get different achievements, it might be a bit short. But I'm very satisfied even with just one playthrough because it's such a well-written choose-your-own-adventure. Decisions feel realistically complex - no good v evil, but struggles between self-interest (from personal gain to mere self-preservation) and morality. I especially like the inclusive-style of plausible gender and sexuality equality in an otherwise feudal setting.
The one massive flaw is one that I didn't experience because I selected the 'right' option. Namely that, apparently, you fail to proceed from the first 'Act' if you choose the wrong suitor. This is disappointing because surely a King/Queen's favorite consort could cuckold their partner, whilst still having land and riches bestowed on their family. Surely there could have been an option where lack of marriage raises the risk/reward stakes, whilst marrying for family/wealth or love, still allows for seducing the monarch but without being able to makes claim upon certain... endings. A disappointing design choice.
Nevertheless, there is still a well-written, thoughtful choice trees that (minus the aforementioned hiccup) accomodate a broad range of roleplay- a sincere lover to the monarch; a ruthlessly self-interested Machiavilli; or an ambitious but pragmatic social climber (with or without moral convictions).

After 30 hours of playing I must say that I am real happy with Lords Of The Fallen™. I decided upon this game mainly because it is based off of the Souls style of gameplay which is most fun. Due keep in mind this is my frist review so take it with a grain of salt.
Brief Con
Though the game is extremely fun it had its major downfalls. It will be different per person but the most common Con was the many, many crashes within the game. 15 hours into playing my game began acting up and failing to play. After 2-3 hours of research I found, in my opinion, it was due to NVIDIA. This problem was fixed after some time but after hours of trying to fix game it had me expect more bugs and crashes. After more research I have found that the crashes have been a common problem with other players. I cannot tell you which of the methods I have done that fixed the game because I honestly don't know which one worked. I believe it was AFTER I downloaded __PhysX-9.13.0604-SystemSoftware-Legacy___ for NVIDIA. For me this was the only problem that I went through that made frown upon the game.
Brief Pro
With the top CON out of the way now for the fun part. The game was absolutely fun and challenging. Being a Souls fan I was very happy to be playing  Lords Of The Fallen™. Through my time playing the game I didn't find any sort of bugs or gamebreaking glitches that would end my fun (other than the crash). The gameplay ran smooth and the bosses were satisfying to kill, especially after finding an attack pattern to deal with them. In my humble opnion if you like the Souls game then you would enjoy  Lords Of The Fallen™. But don't expect it to be exactly like the Souls games because it's not. What makes  Lords Of The Fallen™ it's own game is the semi slow pace of the action. As you start off fresh you cannot simply run in and think you can backstab or hack everything down. The enemies have some pretty good defence and offense. Which is a challenge for beginners like me.
Final report
Lords Of The Fallen™ is easily a fun game and recommend the game to even people who do not know the Souls series. But PLEASE PLEASE Keep in mind that the game could have a chance of crashing and failing after some hours.

This game borrows heavily from Demon Souls and Dark Souls, but compared to those games this one is far less frustrating but also not nearly as challenging. To me it was the perfect balence between challenge and fun gameplay and without a lot of the frustrating grind that is in Dark Souls.
The Good:
The Graphics and visual design - This is a truly gorgous game, great textures and enviroments comes to life with some awesome Nvidia effects and some great physics. Armor design is really good and they look really nice with the amazing clothing physics. You mostly travel through dark corridors and smaller open areas in this game, but they are very detailed and I never found the game lacked variety when it came to the world. Character lipsyncing and such is not that good though, but on the whole the graphics is outstanding. There are also some really cool looking monsters in the game.
The Combat - I played as a Paladin type character focusing on Heavy Armor and Weapons and with some magic mixed in, such as healing. The game focuses on melee combat compared to most RPGs like this game and the game does it really well. Though the combat is very similar to the combat from Dark Souls.
The Exploration and Loot - Throughout the game I loved exploring all corners finding new loot, especially since every new armor or weapon had a distinct look and very nice visuals. They are very stylized but very fitting to the setting the game takes place in.
The Average
The Boss Battles - There are some very cool and fun bosses in this game and I had fun taking most of them down. But some are a bit on the easy side though and they can seem a bit samey at times. Don't really have to change your tactics much. The bosses are not even close to as hard as in Dark Souls as I managed to take down most of the bosses on either my first or second try. But they are still fun to fight. It may be a much harder game on New Game+ but I have not tried that yet.
The Bad
The Story - The story is average to bad, the main character is your typical anti-hero gruff sounding bald guy who has very little interesting to say. You meet a few characters in the game but they don't really have much depth. There are some interesting aspects to the game but nothing that truly stood out. And some bad lipsyncing and presentation when it comes to dialog does not help. That being said it at least has a story and gives you a purpose for doing what you are doing.
Lack of Information - This game has no quest log, so when you pick up a quest you pretty much have to remember where they say you should go. And most of the time you get no info at all so you pretty much have to find out by yourself. This is really tedious and very annoying. Hate having to resort to checking out a walkthrough just to find out where I have to actually go. And there are many items and such that lacks any info on what they actually do.
Well that is that, it is a good game with some flaws. But I do recommend it for anyone who likes the combat in Demon Souls or Dark Souls but find those games to frustrating. Or to annyone who just want a pretty new world to explore and fight some cool looking bosses, and of course find that sweet sweet loot.

I approached this game after reading a lot of hateful reviews on how "this game is not a souls game so don't buy it, it's just an imitation".
For the love of God people, a game is not an imitation of another one just because it shares some mechanics or controls.
These are not the central characteristics of a souls game. It's the dark, misterious and challenging atmosphere, mixed with the frustration following you troughout the game. Yes, I'm a great fan of the Dark Souls saga, but I liked this game nontheless, and not because it reminds me of dark souls. I liked because is a good game, for different reasons.
Lords of the Fallen has a beautiful story and background (no spoilers): during a raging war between humanity and the brutal armies of a fallen god, defeated from humanity itself ages ago, a monk sets a dangerous criminal free to fight fire with fire.This plot is strenghed by architectures and the optimal character design, although I think they could have developed it better in the finale.
The level design is amazing, very detailed; the environment was not a mere scenario, but a concrete element f the game (for example, I found myself struggling with the falling snow clouding my view during battle, costing me victory mre than once) and the combat system does not present any sensible problems or bugs; enemies are very aggressive and hard to defeat (good AI, various moveset and a relentless desire to follow you everywhere), in particular if you're not in one to one duel, but there is not a wide variety of them. The bosses in particoular are one of the best perks of this game. They are strong (like, a lot) and you can't hope to defeat them mindlessly swinging your sword around. besides, the boss fights are epic as f**k.
Always about the combat system, I liked in particular the fact that I could really feel the weight of armour and weapons at every level, so that I was forced to choose the right time and distance to land a blow. Weapons and equipment are costumizable only with runes, but there is a good range to choose and every kind of weapon has it's fighting style (plus some special weapon completely unique).
So, in the end, Lords of the Fallen is a game that I definitely reccomend to every lover of the action rpg genre, and not beacuse it's similar to another game, but because, with his pro and cons, it's beautiful standalone.

This is a hard game to review. There's some elements to it that I love, then there are some that I hate so passionately it beggars belief.
If you liked the original (which I did) then initially you are in for a treat. The mechanics are the same albeit more streamlined and the graphical upgrade is very welcome. The stealth addition works suprisingly well and the change in storyline and subsequent game mechanics also feel fresh and well researched, although once again a little light on the details in comparison to the original XCOM.
What I HATE though, is the lack of immersion and the funky 'logic' the game uses. If you can accept that this game is based on a framework of stats, numbers and percentages that will over rule the in game logic then you should be fine. I wasnt. When im standing 3 feet away from an alien with my assualt rifle up his jacksy, I dont expect to see %65 chance to hit.
The game is designed to pummel you, you WILL lose people and there will be NOTHING you can do about it. I understand this is a design decision, but it ultimately ruined the game for me.
In summary - this is a great game if you can deal with unfair spawning, nonsensical 'logic' and frustration.

I'm one of those people who have fervently defended Bethesda in the past. I don't write this review happily, or without hesitation. However, in light of recent circumstances, I'm crashing the bandwagon that is negatively reviewing a game to show a dissenting opinion.
Creation Club started out as a bad idea. As of the time of this review, it's even worse than I thought. I have put over 3000 hours into Skyrim and almost 800 into Fallout 4. I have both modded and placed on my SSD, and have carefully managed that space with patches and archives to allow it all to fit. However, with the latest patch, I had to remove Fallout 4 in its entirety. I cannot have both games currently. It automatically puts all the files associated with CC content on your computer. Supposedly this is so that it cannot fall under console limitations that might otherwise cause its removal. On top of that, it forces the script extender to update, which means existing mods that require F4SE or SKSE64 in the future will consistently break, forcing you to play cat-and-mouse with updates and script extenders. So there's the technical side.
On to ethics. Mods have always been a free and creative platform, where we interact and develop mods together for the betterment of the game, free of charge outside optional donations. Yes, this has shafted mod developers in the past, but mods have always been a labor of love rather than profit. And developers still get shafted under CC rulings, since they're paid the same amount regardless of whether they developed the top mod or the lowest performing one. This new content in no way adheres to overhaul mods, and under CC regulations, cannot be patched for it. So if you have a PA overhaul or bullet physics addition, weapons and armor added by CC cannot be patched for it under their guidelines. So there's the ethical side of things.
So in this reveal of the creation club, it established four very important things: users get shafted by its implementation in the worst way, developers get shafted, nothing on the creation club is worth the asking price and it sets a dangerous precedent for mods moving forward. If you feared that the creation club would be bad, it turned out to be even worse. Somehow, despite having access to our concerns over the past three or so months since CC was announced, Bethesda managed to confirm every single one and invent new ones in a single move. This reveal, in its entirety, has been, in my mind, the worst move for Bethesda in its history. As a PR move, it is disgusting. As a profitable option, it is laughable. As a gesture of respect to mod authors and the modding community at large, it is tantamount to a calumny. Bethesda fans and modders alike are being laughed at with this reveal.
This action was inexcusable. And it pains me to see my favorite publisher do something so sickening without any forethought.

At this time, I cannot recommend this game -- it is buggy, it is poorly thought out in many places.  While it is entertaining, Ubi went out of their way to tick off players on many aspects of the game.
For example, there is a "join in progress silhouette" for "hey, join my co-op."  This is implemented, when playing with a controller, on one of the primary buttons that you use for other actions.  And so what happens is you get thrown into a co-op match you have no intent of actually playing or participating in, in the middle of a mission.  Entering, it saves your inventory and if you quit -- it resets you to the start of the sequence you're doing.
Thats not so bad, but it also resets your inventory to where it was when you started the co-op -- and so you might have to visit a vendor.  Keeping in mind, that I had no intent of actually participating in the co-op in the first place.
Most of the features are poorly thought out and/or implemented like this.  I'd give them until February or March to fix the issues.  The game has so much potential, it's a shame that they aren't yet delivering on it.

This review is based on my first impressions...
First of all, this game looks great. I'm fortunate enough to have a fairly meaty PC for it, and the ships look like the awesome, kilometre-long juggernauts of space death that they are. The weapon effects are nice, too, and give a nice impression of the amount of laser/missile/energy stuff the ships fling at each other, and the resultant damage.
Gameplay-wise, it's fairly straightforward: float around in big starships, unload weapons-based punishment on each other, and capture control points around the map, with the aim of capturing the enemy's home base (while they do the same to you). I was understandably not very good in my very first game, but it's fun enough to make me want to keep playing and get virtual medals, promotions, crew and ship upgrades as I strive to become un-useless. However, I like to think that I and my 6000+ crew members all died noble deaths. Again. And again. Like in Edge Of Tomorrow, but without the learning process.

TLDR: One of the best point & click adventures, worth getting at full price
+ Great graphics, the best I've seen in a point & click adventure
+ Great voice acting (I played it in English)
+ Great writing, very funny and self aware.
+ Very long play time. The trailer claims 25 hours, but it's more like 15. I did click through most conversations since I finished reading before they were done talking.
+ Needed a hint only 3 times, and only one of those times was actually justified. This was mainly due to the ability to display all important locations on the screen, so I didn't need to go pixel hunting.
- Sometimes the game freezes and you may lose some progress, but not too much since autosaves are frequent.
- There are some audio bugs that don't really affect gameplay since everything said is also written, but still annoying.
- Most NPCs were characters that came back from the first game. There are some interesting new characters like the gnome bounty hunter, but they don't get enough story.
- Too many story threads are left open at the end, with many things that are hinted at but not shown in this game.
- No replayability value. I won't play the entire game again just to get the few achievements that I missed

I have 50 hours in this game. I feel that it will soon transform to 100 and hundreds more after that.
The thing about this game that makes it annoying is there is so much encouragement to keep playing, keep grinding, keep fighting, keep upgrading, keep crafting, keep collecting, keep exploring, etc.
With the new expansion coming out, "Mantle of Power" that will essentially double the amount of time it takes to max out a class makes the game more compelling and exciting, with more biomes, abilities, item rarity, mounts, levels, and classes, right now is a great time to pick up Trove.
First of all, there is so much this game hands to you for free. You start the game with one class you may choose. This is not a game that restricts any classes in the beginning. You can play any class you want. However, getting new classes costs Credits, the game's premium currency, but this is not a problem.
With the game's feature of a player market, many items that may seem "Pay To Win" or "Premium" can be bought and traded for via community, such as Class Coins and Cosmetics. It simply is not right to call this game pay to win. A better way to say it is pay to advance. The game has a very fun sense of progression, and limitless amounts of items to farm and grind for. If that's not your type of thing, simply buy advancement.
There are many biomes and types of dungeons to grind with your friends it seems like my life is starting to slip into the abyss. All I know is Trove.
Combat is not too intuitive, but still fun nevertheless. Professions really make the game grindworthy, such as ringcrafting, runecrafting, gardening, and crafting. Another fun feature of the game is Mastery Rank, which measures how much experience you have in the game. Your mastery rank stays the same as you switch between classes.
Overall I think it would take you over 70+ hours to max out a class in the game. There are 14, and with the new expansion coming out that expands class level limit, It's going to be one hell of a grind.
So, in conclusion - Trove is a well polished voxel sandbox MMORPG definitely worth downloading and playing. Very grindy and time consuming, and contains the ability to switch in between classes without having to make a new account, reducing repetetive gameplay and enhancing the game experience.

Don't expect any groundbreaking changes to the series, with this one; Kingdom Rush Frontiers is the first game, again, just with more creative level design. If you're like me, though, that's exactly what you want. If you've finished KR Classic, and you feel like you could use another 21 levels of it, then this game has what you're looking for.
There are eight new towers, but they replace the eight original towers, so although they're fun to unlock and use, you don't have more towers overall. There are new enemies, but half of them are just reskins of the classics, so only the latter zones really feel noticeably different. Apparently there's also a small improvement to graphics, but I didn't notice.
The only obvious difference, to me, was the introduction of the leveling mechanic for your heroes. This time, they start off at a lower level, and you have to grind them up to lvl 10, and choose which powers to upgrade along the way. Since they all end up the same at lvl 10, however, your individual choices don't really matter in the long run; just grind your favorites to 10, so you can use them on the hard stages.
Like I said, though... I didn't want anything different, and I don't suspect that you do either. I loved the last game, I wanted more of it, and that is exactly what KR Frontiers delivered. The only complaint I have (without spoilers) is the final boss. I feel like he broke one of the unspoken rules of Tower Defense games, and I did not enjoy fighting him at all.

With a heavy heart, I have to give this game a thumbs down. I greatly enjoyed certain aspects of this game, I've been playing it since the early access, but the core mechanics are just too flawed.
Lets start with good ... no, great things :
1. Art. Pretty much everything in this game is wallpaper material. Heroes, monsters, backgrounds. It has a distinct, brilliant artstyle of a dark fantasy.
2. Music. It's dynamic, but even more so - subtly dynamic. As your light level gets lower you'll notice the changes in music as well, untill all hell breaks loose in complete darkness. Music sets the mood greatly.
3. Voice acting. There's only one person talking, your Ancestor, but pretty much his every quote will ring in your ears.
4. Characters and abilities design. You'll simply love to use certain abilities, just because they look so awesome.
And here comes the bad ...
1. Grind. Don't get me wrong, I like the grind. There's something pleasant in getting rewarded for your hard work. But in this game, you need to grind just to recover. You'll need to throw hundreds of nameless, faceless lvl 0 heroes into the meatgrinder, just to fund your next heroic expedition.
2. Random. This is a tactical, turn-based game, where you rely on careful planning the most. And even one dodged/missed/resisted stun can completely screw you over.
In the end, it feels completely unrewarding to wade through the dungeons of this game. I'm not winning anything, I'm just paving the road to victory with corpses of my heroes.
But at least they're free to hire, so technically you can not lose.

I don't typically do reviews. But for all things I felt I should for this game. If you do not want spoilers do not expand this review.
8/10 Would get frustrated at the story again.
First off I do like this game, and unlike several of the top helpful negative votes, I have not played the previous version with no story.
However I do very much agree with their complaints vs. this rather plot-hole filled story line. One plot-hole of which bothered and irritated me so much I literally could not finish the game for a whole extra thirty minutes as I did everything in my futile power to try and stop the story from going the direction I was predicting. I will get to that and other cons later though, I will first explain why I still recommend it.
Pro's:
Q.U.B.E. is a really brilliantly put together 3D Platform Puzzle game. It manages to make really visually interesting environments with the majority of it being made out of same sized cubes. It's lighting effects and background music & sound effectively change how one feels about being in such a strange place throughout the game. Making the place feel oddly interesting to explore at first and then gradually becoming more and more unsettling and foreboding.
The puzzles are rather somewhat simple to figure out throughout the game (for me personally at least) however they did become more challenging at a good pace and were all still very fun to solve. Some were more difficult to a degree due to some quick switching you needed to do in order to get things where you wanted them. This was rather hard to do sometimes since your abilities are kind of slow to act. Its a good thing though because that slow activation sequence makes you rely on puzzle solving more than quick reflexes.
The controls are smooth and simple. It also doesn't explain any of them or how your powers work. I have this as a Pro because I find it rather annoying in games where they give you so much explanation on the controls it make you feel as if the game is mocking your intelligence. This also adds a small level of solving to the puzzles as well through trial and error.
Cons:
The main story game is a little short, however this isn't much of a Con considering that there is a bunch of added stuff to do and the story wasn't all that well put together.
The story Is likely the biggest Con. I will go a bit in depth as to how it goes so don't read further if you don't want to know. It was an interesting Idea, but it came out rather painfully terrible.
So the story is you have no memory of who you are or why your here and two people who contact you throughout the game periodically try to influence you to either continue or stop. This is all rather moot though because the one who wants you to continue makes no sense and sounds like a liar from the get go, and the others demand is that you don't listen to her and do nothing to save your life. I say its moot because this really all wouldn't affect you in this situation anyway. You would solve the puzzles anyway because doing nothing wouldn't get you anywhere so the one argument you would never listen to and the other one doesn't need to try and get you to continue.
There is a point in their rather almost random poking around that they suddenly focus on faith and it suddenly becomes the whole thing the "story" is about afterwards. This all rather becomes annoying at the end because they make it off as a "Who do you trust?" only to make it so you can't choose. Not to mention the message this story conveys is that you should have complete blind faith in someone you don't really know. For reasons. It almost feels like you completely confirm that what you have is a gun in every way possible without actually firing it and then being told to shoot yourself in the face with it because that will save billions of lives including your own somehow. By the time you get to the end they create a logic conundrum. If you want to complete the mission, realistically in your mind, you would have to accept the person who has been trying to get you to complete it has been lying to you which, in turn, would make you not trust them enough to complete the mission. However as I stated you get no choice in the matter because there is only one route. Well there is only one route due to invisible walls and the developers lack of wanting you to fail the game. The last part is likely done because almost everyone who would play the game would fail it due to the fact you would likely not choose to complete the mission out of distrust. All in all the story is rather annoying, though interesting idea, that make the game frustrating at the end of the story.
Apologies, that last part ended up a bit of a rant. but that is how terrible the story is. The game is still good, it just has a painfully bad story. So if you like 3D Platform Puzzles like Portal then you would definitively like this game's mechanics.

An excellent game in its own right. Valves first masterpiece which inspired the sequels (HL2, Ep 1 & 2) and countless mods throughout the series, such as the acclaimed Team Fortress 2 and Portal.
The player starts of as a researcher in Black Mesa running late to work. After the Gordon Freeman, the character the player controls, reaches the test he is supposed to participate in he is immediately put to work. This has cataclysmic consequences, and Gordon Freeman is then forced to defend Black Mesa from an alien invasion and, eventually, the military, all the while being followed by the mysterious G-man.
In terms of gameplay, Half-Life is very simple. You have health and suit power, a variety of guns and hopeully some aim. Starting with a crowbar and ending with a laser, you will shoot your way through Black Mesa, solving simple puzzles and navigating sometimes complex coridoors.
The plot is simple yet effective, as is the gameplay. Overall, a very satisfying game, and worth checking out regardless of reviews, due to its impact.

This game is an amazing Rune....
Almost no game is completely perfect.  This game is not perfect by any means of the imagination.  However, this game has some amazing maps, monsters and difficult challenges.
Pros - The graphics are super sweet!!  I played this at 2560x1440p with a G-sync IPS  monitor and averaged between 80-100 FPS most the game.  The game looks fantastic
- The monsters in this game are really fun to fight (not to mention they have cool names).  You fight people like the Beast, Champion, Annhialater, Worshipper, Guardian, etc... and they range in difficulties, but are all fun to fight!
- The controls are good.  Some people complain that sometimes you hit someone and it doesn't register.  This is true, but it doesn't happen very often.
- The loot system is nice because you can carry endless amounts of items.  However, you still have to be careful how much you are actively carying, because this will cause you to become overcumbered.
- Once you beat the game, you restart and can select a different area of magic and you keep your XP and weapons, abilities, spells, etc.. and play again.  This time the monsters are really difficult and it really feels like you are starting over!
- It's not Dark Souls
- Got this on sale for $9.99 (worth every penny)
Cons - When I first started playing this game, it crashed on me a few times.  When it crashed, I lost an hours worth of saved XP and almost rage quit the game completely.  After the first few stages, it never crashed again!
- In two of the portal (challenge areas) areas, I immediatley died when going in there and my XP simply vanished!  I was so upset, that I found a youtube video to farm experience to get my XP back.  Take that game!!! - Lesson learned, be careful when going into the portal challenge areas!
- Voice acting is laughable.  The story isn't very good either, but you will meet fun people along the way that help you stay engaged throughout the story.
- Not really a con, but sometimes you will get stuck trying to find an objective and you will run around for long times trying to find out where to go next.
Summary - Buy this game if you want to have an awesome experience in an open world RPG.  Yes it does have its own issues, but if you like Dark Souls, then you will like this game.  It's great!  I'm really hoping they make a Lords of the Fallen 2!!!!

This game is pretty controversial, and I've been with it from the very early days before it was even available on the Steam platform. Whilst it's true that the developer has pretty much stopped working on the game, with the last update being on the 22nd of November, 2016, after a loooong time with absolutely nothing changed, I would disagree that the development has stopped because he "took the money and ran" or is "a coward" as some other reviewer has said.
Overall, it's a nice premise. A little bit obscured because of the sheer amount of very-similar games that had a lot more advertisement behind them, but the game has a certain charm to it. Developed by one man, who ultimately stopped development because he has other priorities in life. This game is a plethora of randomly grabbed royalty-free assets (Which I can excuse because it's developed by one guy who, as far as I can tell, doesn't have any art experience) on top of a clever idea. The programming is pretty solid, though lack-luster. The modability of the game is great and it's very easy to take almost every aspect of the game and edit it using Lua scripts and other easily editable files. I'd love to somehow get a hold of the source code of the game and see what it's written in, and continue its development as a hobby project.
Whilst I'm giving this a positive review, there is very little to actually do in the game itself -- But I feel the developer deserves some support. There's a lot of negativity in the reviews here and some of them are pretty harsh and said with no investigations or evidence. Really, it's not about the money for this guy -- He didn't get much to begin with, and the sales for the game never improved. It's more about "He worked on one thing then went on to do other things in life", which is something absolutely anyone who has ever started any project in life will do at least once. This developer was fortunate enough to get his game all the way to Steam, through the OG days of Greenlight when votes weren't rigged. I'd say, for a small scale project he just wanted to work on because he had a good idea, that he got pretty successful for a man with no team and no financial backing.

Affairs of the Court: Choice of Romance, is one of Choice of Games' first games, and also one of their best. In it you play a young noble going to court to find love, money, and power. You can do this in a variety of ways, role-playing very different kinds of characters, which can result in widely varying outcomes.
The world is interesting. It's a magical fantasy counterpart to medieval Spain, with another counterpart for Al-Andalus/Granada. There are different kinds of magic, Life Magic and Death Magic, which is primarily wielded by nobles like yourself. Life Mages can do things like healing and some forms of genetic engineering, and some forbidden arts like mind control. Death Mages mainly use offensive magic, like fireballs and death curses, and also lead the armed forces. Unfortunately one of the few choices you can't make is which one you want to be; you're a Death Mage no matter what. Still, magic jousting can be fun!
Without spoiling much, the first chapter, Choice of Romance, is primarily based on finding someone to marry to secure your position. Once this is done, Choice of Intrigue is all about court politics and trying to navigate different factions and create an heir, and heavily features the conflict between Life and Death Mages at court. Till Death do us Part is about the monarch's later years and further political machinations, while also dealing with some new and extremely dangerous threats to their rule. There are many different paths and endings, and almost none of them are unambiguously happy; if you get the best ending, you've really earned it. Because of all of this, the game encourages several play-throughs.
It should also be noted that you can only go on to Part II if you romance the monarch, which is the canonical path.
If you're unsure if you'll like the game, the first Part has been available for free on the Choice of Games website for years. I highly encourage you to try it out. In any case this has always been one of my favorites in their line, so I'm very happy to see it finally come to Steam.

Writing a review for this game is difficult as while it is enjoyable its also fairly frustrating. As someone that has played Dark Souls 2 for hundreds of hours, I can see how this game can be compared to that game on the surface. This game allows you to lock on enemies and circle them like in souls and also requires you to understand the attack patterns of the enemies to determine how to beat them. Having said that this game is really quite a different experience from Souls. While the non-boss enemies are almost too easy with simple attack patters, the boss enemies can be ridiculously difficult if you don't have the correct stats/weapons/armor set up for that boss. Rather than skill, beating the bosses really just requires knowledge of a particularl character configuration suited to defeat the boss. While some bosses took me 20 plus attempts to beat, I mostly felt frustrated rather than satisfied when I finally beat them. Its a fun game to get on sale, but don't expect the satisfaction of a Souls game where any particular configuration can defeat the enemies if you are skilled enough.

A rather short game, pleasant and at moments tense and thoughtful... But with a number of glaring flaws that leaves me unable to recommend at full price. I've narrowed it down to two points.
My largest complaint would probably be the illusion of choice presented in the first chapter. You simply cannot continue onto the remaining 2/3rds of the story without picking one specific romance option out of three romance options. The game presents each option as having their own merits and demerits but the moment you choose to deviate, the game will wrap up your story with a "try better next time" sort of ending and urge you to pick the correct choice.
Assuming you proceed to the rest of the story, which is, as I said, a rather pleasant experience, my next complaint rears it's ugly head and strikes out of nowhere. You see, in the beginning of the game, you set up a character of a certain gender, interested in certain things in his or her romantic parter; this helps you build an image of the character who's fate is in your hands and helps to build the immersion. However, while you were given the illusion of choice in the first chapter, the second and later chapters strip even that! I could be playing a stoic, dour, and decidedly heterosexual courtier, interested only in a single and sole true love and... still be forced to read lines where my character's heart is a flutter, his emotions for his beautiful and loving partner swept aside by a single passionate glance from his friend, a character I had been treating something like an annoying uncle. I consider myself knowledgeable about adventure games. Since the first Simon the Sorcerer game, this genre has been a favorite of mine. Although after a while, it all becomes a bit repetitive.
Matching yesterdays' quality (Deeponia),  relying too heavily on scenario and forgoing the polishing (Dreamfall Chapters), or betting it all on funny oneliners (Broken Age) just does not cut it for me anymore. Don't get me wrong, all the games I named are good.
Yet none are as polished as BOUT2. The effort and attention to detail truly shows in this game. You can see that they paid extra attention to character animations. It may sound unimportant, but makes a huge difference in how you view the characters.
Scenario and comedic relief wise, BOUT2 is as good as the best of them. Especially that Library scene is a work of sheer genius. The election cycle is a well thought parody of American politics. Quite frankly, this may be the best adventure game ever.
If you are remotely interested in adventure games. This is the game to play. Just make sure this is not your first adventure game as any game you play after this will look lacking.

Third installment of the fantastic series and a truly fantastic game. The graphics are stunning, the voice acting is great and the soundtrack is nice to listen to. Thankfully, the puzzles are slightly more challenging than in the first game, but still never frustrating. The story features all of the well known characters from the first two games and is again filled with puns and references to other games/books and films we all love.
The only downsides I can think of are:
- The new inventory is a step backwards. The old one where you just had to move the cursor to the bottom of the screen was way easier to use.
- A few bugs with the speech audio files (especially in the German version, some parts are not voiced or the volume is completely off)
- The movement of the characters sometimes feels too slow and it can be annoying when they are stuck in animations that force you to wait.
What I miss:
- Having chapters or acts with rendered movies in between them would be great because it feels so rewarding when you hit those points in the game.
For fans of the classic point&click adventure genre this is an absolute must have, but I would recommend this to anyone really, since it is such a fantastic game and probably the only game of the genre that has the look and feel of a AAA production. Finally, the game is also good value because even as a veteran adventure player, resorting to a walkthrough guide a couple of times and not always waiting for audio to play out, the first playthrough took a full 24 hours.
PS: Do not play it with a controller, you will regret it.

Much like the other Choice of Games stories I have, this one is decently written. But, only if you follow a specific path.
My very first playthrough, I was Dona Yin de Castillo, a prodigy Death Mage of high intelligence who wasn't particularly charismatic. My goal on going to the capital city was to find love, and I found it in the form of Gabriela de Mendosa, an enchanting young woman of great intelligence. My aunt wanted me to marry into money, but her choice for my suitor was bland and uninteresting to me. My uncle wanted me to gain status by wooing the Queen, but I didn't care about status.
So I eloped with de Mendosa. And the game ended immediately and told me that, while I lived happily ever after, if I wanted to experience the other two parts of the story, I would need to "survive and marry the Queen."
I was a little annoyed by this, but I started up a second game as Don Orfeo de Pena, who was more studious than Yin de Castillo and only slightly worse at magic. I wooed the Queen, leaving de Mendosa alone completely, and entered the second part - but I didn't marry the Queen, I was just one of her affairs (though she apparently loved me enough to ignore her husband). And then, de Mendosa appeared. If she was going to show up in part two anyways, why did my first game end abruptly when I married her? Why not have Yin de Mendosa arrive with her wife to the castle, and carry on from there? (Incidentally, I made it to part three, but died because I was too busy info-gathering to stop myself from being assassinated.)
So, while the story is fairly well-written, there's a huge railroad involved with becoming involved with the Queen (I haven't tried the third route, because nothing about that character appeals to me. I can't even remember her name!) that didn't have to be there.
It's fairly enjoyable, but that one lack of choice really turns me away from the game. I'm not sure if I'll play it again. I might, but I don't know.

XCOM 2 is a really fun tactical strategy game. There are many additions to XCOM 2 that improve things over Enemy Unkown/Within. Little things like making reload only one action. Or making weapon attachments like scopes not take up inventory slots, make you feel like you have more control than before. Being able to customize your soldiers and their weapons even more than before makes you far more attached to them. Things can get really emotional when you hand over the weapon of your fallen champion to the new blood. A large variety of enemies keeps things fresh through the game, nd a very simple but fun story with some cool science fiction concepts also keeps you playing.
My biggest complaint would probably be that even though you're supposed to be taking the role of an on the edge resistance instead of an internationally funded organization, the gameplay feels almost exactly the same. This mostly comes down to still having to kill all enemies on the map to achieve victory instead of the "Hit and Run" tactics you'd expect to be performing as an underground rebelion. In general the game just feels a bit too easy. Once you hit the second tier of weapons and armor, it because a little too easy to start steamrolling through the game. I've beaten it on the 2nd hardest difficulty "Commander" twice now, and since I've heard Legend is mostly the same thing but the enemies have more health, I'm not super interested in something that's more tedious than hard, and doesn't force me to think on new strategies.
However almost all of these problems are offset by the developers fierce and comprehensive support for the Modding Community. The workshop was fully open from day 1, and since then thousands of mods that change balance, add new enemies, weapons and levels have been added, making XCOM 2 a good game that's only going to get better as time goes on.

Bastion is the perfect example of how non-major market video games can stand up to and even surpass their major market counterparts in terms of presentation and gameplay. This game is a textbook case of where concept meets execution.
The narrative story telling mechanic is what caught everyone's attention on its release. In addition to that, a perfectly realized game world and an impecably paced soundtrack make Bastion the high water mark for presentation in the independent games scene.
On the gameplay front, you get a fairly typical hack-n-slash game, but with nicely paced action and some really fun weapons and weapon upgrades. If you aren't laughing like a pyromaniac when you get the flamethrower, something is wrong with you.
And lastly, Bastion adds something that I think is sorely missed in modern online gaming; a single player score online leaderboard. It's fun to see how your campaign run-through stacks up agaisnt other gamers out there.
In sum, a 100% must play.

I had to find the game on steam and download it there to finally be able to write a review. Not sure if the time I've spent grinding my way through this game will appear above my review or not, but I was one of the lucky few to say they were there when it started. You created an account, hopped over a hole in the ground, and went off on your adventure.
I was a naysayer at first but man, this game blew me away. There were a few things that got monetized, but it wasn't too big of a deal. Just mounts and classes basically, and you could get them with the currency you earn by playing. The community was astounding, most of the content in the game had been created by players. Looking at all the weapons and armor, you could see the individual credited for it's creation.
After some time, it was pretty obvious Trion spent much more time figuring out how to make the money and not how to properly code the game. A company needs money to survive and to keep delivering quality content to it's customers and Trion is known for only the first part. They have turned an incredibly addicting game into a paying simulator. Saving up for that awesome class with cubits you've earned by playing? Sorry little buddy, you have to spend money to get the classes now. So not only will the development of the classes be much slower (it already took forever for a new class to come out) but you won't be able to obtain them without spending money.
There's your link. It's truly upsetting to see Avarem post such a thing and I really see the game dying off because of it.
Some old players who already have everything unlocked will be absolutely loving it, because people like it when they have things others cannot get. And they will insult the people who don't have these things already and claim it's the greatest thing ever. But I can tell you, as an OG, this truly killed any hope of me coming back/continuing to play trove.
I know Trion, and their reputation for ruining their games (which are actually great by the way) just for money seems not  to be going away any time soon.
The absolute worst part is the bulk of the players are very young and just don't know when they're being screwed over and they'll only be bashed by the people who have everything when they finally step up and say hey this game sucks because I can't get anything. I will miss it, but I believe this to be wrong. Companies should not to these things to their customers and I truly believe the ratings for this game on steam will plummet for it.

ADDED MORE NOTES..
Just to add that since the latest pacth (Patch 3) I have noted some improvments. Frame rates are coping better on TSAA but since playing around witht he settings some more I have found FXAA to work so much better now than it did before. I got the 25-35FPS swing pre patch on TSAA with all on ultra high, since patch 3 I was still getting the same swing but the frames are more stable so a bit smoother to play. Also the cutscenes where not lagging stuttering as much.
With FXAA though I am getting 30-45 FPS with slight swing and very smooth gameplay. Cutscenes are smooth at 20FPS minumum other than the previous 12-15 FPS I was getting before.
The patch hasn't fixed everything but it has solved some issues.
I still say this is a good game, and if your system is having problems and your machine is high spec, then I think you got something going on because my machine is not as high powered as what some people are claiming doesn't work and I am working just fine...so... I don't know what thats all about really.
Personally I think people get crap motherboards because they think so long as they have a monster CPU, RAM and GPU the PC will be awesome, however if your bus speeds of your motherboard are bottlenecking the performance then it will run like crap.
I spent money on a decent motherboard so perhaps that is what makes my system different from these i7 GTX980 systems people claim are not working??
As for the game itself, the story of the game itself with Arno is OK. Typical assassins creed plot, seeking revenge trying to find out what the templars are up to etc but still fun to play through. Lot's of side missions and other content to keep you busy also. There is some more detective and riddle type missions on this game which I like for a bit of a change. Some of them are a bit of a wild goose chase but if you pay attention and think about the clues, then its pretty rewarding once you figure something out. I quite like this part of the game even though it does not relate to the main story.
The control and game mechanics are a littel different but not so much as to think 'whoa this is so different to any others'.... its mainly things like being able to jump launch from wall to wall, i.e. looking back and jumping across a gap to a parallel wall is not something you can do in this game. I think its a bit rubbish but not a terrible loss.
The downward free running is pretty good once you get the hang of it between this and dropping off as we used to. You can still drop off platforms but if you are like me, I tend to press the run button by habit and this makes Arno jump down somewhere instead of just hanging of an edge for example... just need to get used to it.
The eagle vision works a bit different as it times out faster than before. This is a skill which can be effected by the gear you choose.
The gear and weapons is crazy customizable... perhaps too much so, and I am not entirely convinced the stats really make that much difference unless you put on gear that changes them quite extremely. It is still nice to personalise Arno to your playing style though. Some gear costs a lot of credits, and you can upgrade items to get extra stat boosts. There are things called hack points which means you can upgrade by hacking instead of paying which is kinda pointless in some ways but you are grateful when your low on coin and you have a load of hack points saved up so you can still boost your assassin.
Graphics and the overall feel of the environments etc is amazingly good. The map is huge but each section gives off different vibes and atmospheres while walking though the streets. The rooftops pretty much are the same anywhere unless you come across a land mark but the perpective view is incredible.
I still say people should play this game. Ubisoft may have made a booboo from undertesting this product on different systems but PC gaming will fade away with these titles if people can't get their systems to work properly or just slag off every game which has a glitch. there are so many variables in PC machines that I can totally see why game companies would rather write for consoles with consistent hardware and OS. PC gaming for me is mostly about tweaking things to get games looking their best and playing right. I rarely finish playing games these days as I enjoy the look and feel, I tweak my system settings to get it running sweet, then I am satisfied.
If you don't want to tweak and tinker or possibly upgrade your PC once you hit a limit you know is hardware related then don't game on a PC. If you just want to play games a console is a better choice and the consoles are looking pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥hot these days. I got a PS$ myself purely to play games I can't get on PC which happens but then i do tend to play the game more and not worry about the tweaking side of things, but as I said for me, the tweaking is part of the fun. ...
Anyway I say buy this game, tweak your PC and enjoy it.

So I got Fractured Space a long time ago in a sale, because it looked cool. I played now and then about 10 games for 2 months. No grand choice of ships, just Protector, Hunter, Colossus, Venturer and maybe 5 other ships. Also the bases weren't painted or detailed.
I expected all of this from an Early Access game in it's alpha.
What you saw 4 to 5 months ago raised your expectations for this game and then I started playing again a month ago:
There are now very detailed bases in each sector with 3 or 4 different asteroid maps to battle in, the ships are absolutley gorgeous (except the ghost which reminds me of southparks a*** probe) and the effects are beautiful.
The Shiptree (or Character tree) now counts 26+ ships from 3 different manufacturers with unique looks and weapon systems.
I myself favor the Titan Defense Systems [TDS] because their ships feature an often sleek and well shaped exterior with awesome beamweapons and Smartguns [they're locking on to the enemy in a limited angle and do not make that much damage]. The TDS tree also offers some of the most potent healers [e.g. Protector, Paladin].
As far as I can tell most ships are pretty balanced, some are more or less annoying depending on which ship you fly.
All ships are accessible via playing the game and for most of them you need like 10 games.
BUT the 3 starter ships are completly sufficient and count to the [IMO] better ships.
You can customize the stats of your ship to a certain degree with specialized crewmembers [damage resistance, multiplier etc. pp. in the range from 4-10%]
Everything gameplay relevant is FREE TO PLAY [yes you can buy ingame currency and with it ships, but hey where's the fun with that; also there aren't any ships that are completly over the top good so you have no real advantage].
The ingame market sells only cosmetics and xp- and creditbooster [the latter you can aquire by lootcrates (so called droppods) which you get for playing at least 2 games at one day].
The general goal of the game is gathering as many resources through occupied mines in 2 sectors as possible, engaging in epic space battles at the main mining station in the middle of the map and ultimately capping the enemy base while destroying every enemy ship on the way [or vice versa :) ].
So I can only recommend this game to all people who like capitalspaceships, explosions, strategy and to a certain degree MOBA's.

With a heavy heart, I have to give this game a thumbs down. I greatly enjoyed certain aspects of this game, I've been playing it since the early access, but the core mechanics are just too flawed.
Lets start with good ... no, great things :
1. Art. Pretty much everything in this game is wallpaper material. Heroes, monsters, backgrounds. It has a distinct, brilliant artstyle of a dark fantasy.
2. Music. It's dynamic, but even more so - subtly dynamic. As your light level gets lower you'll notice the changes in music as well, untill all hell breaks loose in complete darkness. Music sets the mood greatly.
3. Voice acting. There's only one person talking, your Ancestor, but pretty much his every quote will ring in your ears.
4. Characters and abilities design. You'll simply love to use certain abilities, just because they look so awesome.
And here comes the bad ...
1. Grind. Don't get me wrong, I like the grind. There's something pleasant in getting rewarded for your hard work. But in this game, you need to grind just to recover. You'll need to throw hundreds of nameless, faceless lvl 0 heroes into the meatgrinder, just to fund your next heroic expedition.
2. Random. This is a tactical, turn-based game, where you rely on careful planning the most. And even one dodged/missed/resisted stun can completely screw you over.
In the end, it feels completely unrewarding to wade through the dungeons of this game. I'm not winning anything, I'm just paving the road to victory with corpses of my heroes.
But at least they're free to hire, so technically you can not lose.

After Combat Arms got infested with Hackers, I had no other choice but to search for another similar shooter to full fill my need. I tried a couple of them, such as Warface, Phantomers, Dirty Bomb. I was considering buying CSGO until I found Black Squad. What caught my attention was the "NO-pay-to-win" headline, and I'm really glad this is actually true.
At first, the game give me really good impressions, specially the graphics and gameplay, but after 2 months playing everyday, I can finally give my "final" analysis.
The Graphics: They are good and runs smoothly in my laptop, tho they aren't impressive or revolutionary. The character model is really interesting and well done. Tho, the scenery lacks of detail, in most of maps we have those huge, flat, corridors with little detail. There is also not much happening in the background.
The Gameplay: I really enjoy the gameplay, but comparing to Combat Arms, I found harder to control the gum while shooting. I was used to shot in burst mode instead of full-auto, that give my shooting much more precision (in Combat Arms) But here in Black there isn't the same, it's not that big of problem, but affects me a lot. Also, the lack of ladders, tilt aim and climbing edges really bothers me.
The modes: I really love "Capture" mode, it's so much fun. Sometimes strategical, sometimes like a real freaking war! Hahaha! It's really too bad we have only two maps for this mode. Also, the Korean version have more modes I want to try out, such as Airborne. The other modes are the same you expect from an arcade shooter. TDM is cool, tho the maps don't help much.
The Maps: They are the lowest point of the game unfortunately. There are some few good maps, but most are really boring and unimaginative. Mirrored maps help balance the match, but it's so boring! It's really sad, cause the game is cool. I mentioned that Capture Mode has only 2 maps, both nice maps but you can get tired pretty quickly. I wish there was more maps for Capture mode, perhaps with two Capture points! (that would be hell on earth, but interesting). Combat Arms had much better maps, I have to say. Hope they fix this by adding more maps in the future.
The guns: No complains, tho there are really few shotguns and pistols. I wish there is an option to customize your gun, adding scopes/sights or hand grips to improve stability. I also miss some of my favorite guns, like the FN F2000.
The paid content: It's not pay-to-win, but there is paid content, in form of skins for weapons and characters. These paid content doesn't give any advantage to the player, it's purely cosmetic. Witch is really nice! Thanks! But, I really wish I could just go and buy the stuff I want, instead of those annoying random boxes (yep, you buy loot boxes).
The Verdict: It's a really nice free-to-play online action military FPS. The best part is not being a pay-to-win game. Isn't perfect, tho it's really competent, I'm sure they will add more content in the future, and things will improve significantly.

I am primarily writing this review to do  my part to improve this game's review score. Many play this game, expecting it to be like Dark Souls, and while this is not untrue, there are two key differences that I have observed in my limited time playing.
- The combat is slower. Dodging, attacking, and other aspects of Dark Souls muscle memory must be overcome before you can get far. Dodge early, and you will be able to avoid most attacks.
- The story is bluntly presented. Dark Souls presented its story in subtle way, rewarding those who took the time to explore it. This is not the case in "Lords of the Fallen", and that is not something I like. The story is also less "serious", and more action-hero-oriented. The atmosphere is completely different.
In the end, I enjoy playing the game, but it does not provide the experience I had hoped for. However, I still think it is a worthy purchase at $30 or below. I am happy to have given it a chance, and I think people are being hard on the game because they come in with high expectations.

I love fallout, playing throught fallout 3 back years ago on the Xbox 360, aswell as New vegas. Fallout 4 i sadly went into knowing it was a downgrade from 3 and NV, but i tried to not let it get to me.
I like the story and lore, its good and i had fun playing through it, there are four factions in it, The Commonwealth Minutemen, Brotherhood of Steel, The Railroad, and lastly The Institute, all being seprate, however the story arc of all of them in terms of quests are simular. The new gravity mechanics are awful, and basically just add a requirement when building spaceships. Without gravity, a spaceship is completely unflyable because you can't stay on the floor, which means that if you get into a spaceship without one and fly up, you'll lose control of it and not be able to land it.
Because of this, my main game, which had been saved while in space, couldn't be played any longer. As soon as I loaded it, my character floated off the floor and couldn't take control of the ship. I lost a ton of progress. Also if you saved on an asteroid, you're similarly out of luck, because one jump sends you off into space.

On top of that, world generation takes a ridiculously long time even though the whole star system is smaller than a small fraction of other voxel based games that load lightning fast. Having too many planets makes the system impossible to play, though I'm not sure why that would make a difference since any competent code would only be loading the planet that you are currently on. It's pretty obvious that the programmer does not know what he's doing.
Additionally, the game freezes for about 10 seconds seemingly at random about every 5-10 minutes.
Also turrets are completely useless since if an enemy gets behind something of yours, including the house or ship that the turret is attached to, it will shoot right through it. I had a turret destroy my spaceship while trying to kill a snake on the surface of the planet beneath me.

If you're debating whether to play this or the original, they're both fantastic games. The main difference in this one is a new soundtrack and a story. If you're only playing it for the puzzles, the original might be a better choice.
*STORY SPOILERS AHEAD*
I liked the story at first, but it was obvious that it was somewhat shoehorned in, as there are a large amount of inconsistancies. The man Jonathon Burns managed to convince me that I was underground, as he actually made some good points as far as the symbols on the walls being recognisably human, and there being no windows. I was actually looking for something else to do other than take the escape pod at the end. It seems a shame that his paranoia actually made more sense than the rest of the game. Now that he is pointing these thing out, we can't dismiss is as "video game logic", they now become serious flaws in the game's story.
*END SPOILERS*
With that being said, the delivery of the story is well done. Both of the main voice actors did there jobs very well, and the writing was spot on as well. It's almost like they set up this story to fail, as if they had spent a little more time on it ironing out inconsistancies, maybe making an alternate ending, it would have been a really great game. In it's current form though, I would recommend the original over this one, but both can certainly be enjoyed for the puzzles.
It's OK, if you are in too shooters, but if you are looking for a role-playing game this isn't for you. Also, with the Creation Club, you better have several terabytes of space.

So I have something of a love hate relationship with this game. On initial release I picked it up on PS4 (before seeing the glorious volumetric light of gaming PC goodness!) and tried my best to enjoy the game but hated so many aspects of it. Those aspects still apply but seem mitigated to an extent on the PC version.
The other reviews you can see here pretty much cover the pros and cons quite extensively so I won't go to far into them but I'll give you a rundown of the issues I ran into and how I overcame them.
To start with the main issue plaugeing this game is the sheer frustration caused by frustrating enemy design such as enemies apparently being able to rotate on the spot and track you when you strafe around them even if they're mid attack. This means tougher enemies can give you a really irritating experience and having to plough through them every time you replenish your potions is a nightmare and not in a good Bloodborne nightmare way. However once you come to terms with this niggle you can soon just deal with it and get on with the game.
Some bosses either seem to rely on mobs or healing capabilities to make them challenging which is dull to say the least and mind bogglingly frustrating at worst.
The character design is okay but I personally don't much like the whole 'fat chunky 40k space marine' look that the game has gone for with their 1D main character. Controls on the PS4 also seemed a bit clunky with the 30fps refresh rate.
Playing this game on a PC at 60fps seems to have improved my experience somewhat in that the controls feel a lot more fluid and the game in general just feels a whole lot more appealing. I feel like games of this nature should attempt to aim for 60fps no matter what in the future (if mgs v can do it on xbone then dark souls like games surely can!)
Anyway I'm running on a 6600k core i5 running at 4.0ghz with a gtx 960 2gb and 16gb of DDR4 ram and it runs well on high settings.
I'd recommend playing the game if you can move past its flaws which can be quite substantial depending on what you value in a game.

I really have to say: I like this game. I play on Commander difficulty and soon I will start on Legend difficulty.
Now some pinpoints:

+very interesting story
+great tactical challenges
+good (but not great - no micromanagement) possibilities of the base management
+random generated maps (the lack of this feature really brought down 2012 X-Com's replayability)
+some timed missions but always enough time if you know what you are doing and how to play
+fully generated maps also apply to the MP, so there is no more type of gamer "I will learn by heart where to put my troops on "bar" map.
- STABILITY ISSUE - sometimes game randomly crashes during combat (it happens even more often in multiplayer mode)
- PERFORMANCE ISSUE - even with 8 GB of RAM and almost all possible software disabled or turned off (including of course all browsers) I'm experiencing some RAM related issues and long loading times
-with time you will get a band of super, uber-human never dying squad of heroes with incredible skills (similarlly like 2012 X-Com) - it's far from reality and real combat situation (classical X-com had this feeling - soldiers would die in a combat with aliens all the time as they would normally do and no "inhuman" skills were present; just some stats improvements with higher ranks)
-no micromanagement AT ALL (again classical X-com had plenty of it - you had to make sure that you didn't forget to take ammo for your soldiers for the mission, you had to account for available space in Skyranger, you had to make sure that you have enough living space in a base for your personnel and storage for gear and items, and you had to even account even for travel time - if you recruit new soldiers they will not magically appear at your base in no time just like they were already walking impatiently around by the entrance just waiting to be enlisted...
-if you lose your entire squad of super heroes for any reason you can expect to lose the game (campaign) in general.
-unfortunately most of the tactical activity (with the exception for alien rulers) can be summed up in this simple scheme: move a soldier in your squad, trigger "combat situation" with 3-4 aliens, deal with them (kill them all or at least most of them - it's your turn), repeat unit success...
-in multiplayer you can build your squad only from predefined characters now - there is almost 0 customization now, not even armor type or weapons. You can choose only from few items (vests, granades etc) - it's a big step back comparing to the 2012 X-Com (oversimplification)
In general it's a great game and I had tons of fun with it. It may not seem that way after reading all those negative remarks but please be advised that I'm very demanding person. I would give it 82% if I was a professional reviewer. I would love to see next X-com with more connections to the classical game (more ambitious, better designed, more challenging, micromanagement) but of course with all bells and whistles of the current age and graphic cards possibilities.
