This game is actually nuts, but in all the best ways.  You're a angel-slaying witch whose clothes are her hair, and also her hair is sometimes used to channel demons to eat angels when they're particularly large.  Also sometimes very large fists or shoes for huge demon-punches/kicks.  Also it's nut-crushingly difficult.  10/10 would have Bayonetta crush my nuts again.

Some of the bosses are quite difficult, requiring a level of "twitch" capability that is difficult to achieve on a PC ... definitely easier using the hand devices of a console. The game saves only in certain places so you often have to go through several iterations of the same combats to get back to the boss. This gets tired really quickly. One could kind of cheat though by staying near a spawning/save shard and leveling up significantly before moving on. However, this kind of defeats the fun of the game unless levelling is important to you. And the PC keyboard-mouse combination just doesn't seem to respond quickly enough.
Perhaps the intent was to compel players to purchase the weapon upgrades that make the player powerful enough to face these tough bosses. Whatever the case, the game designers may have thought that making the game tough and constantly repeating was good game design but I've found it to be frustrating and a disappointing experience.

I can only truly recommend this game if you've played the original.
There's controversy that this could have easily been released as DLC, but I'm not reviewing the politics of game admissions.
With the Director's Cut of this game comes a brand new narrative as well as a new soundtrack. They are both welcome additions to the game, alongside reworked puzzles, new secrets, and the previously released DLC. There's not a lot of extra things to see or do, but for a returning player who wants a bit more of the Q.U.B.E. universe, $5 isn't a big hole in the pocket.
However, the reason I prefer the original over this version is based on two things; the first being the actual lack of story in the original. There was almost a haunting mysteriousness to it, in the sense that you never truly understand the game as a whole. You pick up bits and pieces of things, formulating and speculating the who and what and where and when, but in the end, there were no concrete answers. These are the elements that made the game enjoyable for me beyond the gameplay. It was the time I spent wondering, "what really is behind all of this?"
The second reason being the soundtrack. The original game has a much more upbeat, ambient electronic score. It's catchy, it's fun to listen to, and I found myself listening to it even outside of the game. While the new soundtrack isn't necessarily bad, as it has been tweaked to fit the new found atmosphere that coincides with the added narrative, it simply just isn't as memorable. There were a few tracks that I did enjoy, but in the end it cannot compare to what was.
If you haven't played Q.U.B.E. do yourself a favor and track down a copy of the original. It's a short, simple, but entertaining and involving. If you're a returning fan who doesn't mind throwing a fiver down to replay and re-experience the game in a different light, go for it. It's not the best five bucks you'll ever spend, but I personally don't have any regrets. It gave me an excuse to have some fun with it again, and most importantly enjoy myself. After all, isn't that the point?

A really nice game, recommended if you have a powerful PC (and no mainboard integrated graphic card).
- One of the better feeling game in the recent voxel dig/craft/build genre attack
+ feels more complete in comparison to games like Blockscape, StarForge, Xenominer, Vox, Realm Explorer
The good:
- as usuall -> lots of digging, searching for resources, building and crafting
- a well thought building system
- nice skill points system - the more you build the more points you get (to unlock skills/perks/cratfables)
- not bad graphic (compared to pixel voxel games)
- perks/skills to swim/build faster, etc. Also to unlock new crafting items.
- cool game modes in development
- build a spaceship and fly do another planet!
- cool water system /pipes, pumps
The bad:
- very demanding on pc (poorly optimised, memory leaks/etc)
- crashes are often, some people cannot get the game to start
- still in development -> patches are not very often, can break things. The Dev is deploying hotfixes though.
- not much to do yet once you unlock all craftables and fly to planets
- small planets
In overall, a recommendation from me.

TL:DR This game is absolutly worth downloading and atleast trying, Its a blend of League of Legends and Battlestar Galactica in one title: and who would say no to that.
I originally got this game during "The Mighty Jingles" promotion. Stopped playing it for a while because of performance issues. Played again during the free weekend in Jan 2016 and forgot about it again. Started playing after the May update and immediatly remembered why I was so interesting in it. (Even whilst disliking the majority of Moba style games.)
Firstly - the game looks im hesitant to say beautiful but it looks good for a game in alpha, the effects look like they actually came from the weapons you fired and not some b movie looking stock flak effect.
Now that the game is out. This game is absolutly gorgeous I cannot fault a single visual effect present within the game. The ships are stunningly pretty, with a varied designs even within the 3 ship manufacturer asthetics.
Second - the combat: It feels heavy, its very much like Battlestar Galactic in that the ships don't float about like their made of nothing, they all have inertia, they take time to slow or turn (especially with the larger, tankier ships like the Leviathan, Gladiator or Colossus). When you fire your guns (especially on Destroyer) they feel weighty, they feel like they should for a capital class warship, they have presence that so many games fail to achieve.
Onto the monetization of the game: There is premium time for more exp and credits, cosmetic skins and premium skins that provide even more credits per game
Third - the unnecessarily feared drop system: Its effects are minimal on the game. Drops range from credits to crew, Elite xp used to level up/ unlock crew and you can even earn premium currency and premium skins.
On to something Ive noticed in other reviews, People complaining about it being p2w (which is completly untrue as there is no paid for only items in the game that have any effect on gameplay
The "grindy" nature of Fractured space isn't a new system. Its been present in plenty of other games without complaint. Fractured space needed a monetisation system, and the one they have implemented is easily one of the most generous systems i've ever seen in a game like this.
Overall you should at minmum try this game its free to play after all, and if you enjoy it please play it. Edgecase games deserve far more players for a game that rivals the largest Mobas in gameplay and features.

There's a lot of nerdrage being thrown around about Chucklefish, the rate of progression, "broken promises", and the game being unfinished. The critical gamer should be wary of customer reviews, as there's very little accountability or objectivity among the gaming public. Furthermore, many complaints demonstrate a definite lack of understanding of the game development industry.
Here are a few of the more common complaints - and the problems with them:
1.
If someone makes this claim, the first thing you ought to do is look at their hours played. It's hard to imagine someone spending hundreds of hours on a game without content. The fact is that even the current stable build has 10 technological tiers, four bosses, 16 planetary biomes (ie. planet types), 35 mini-biomes, hundreds of furniture items, countless vanity items, infinitely diverse weaponry, and 17 techs that give the player unique abilities. And that isn't even a comphrehensive list of everything in the game, nor does it reflect the
changes in the works for the next update, which promises to be a big one.
2.
This statement is inaccurate. The stable build hasn't changed much since that time (though there have been some additions, such as directional melee aiming); however, the nightly version of the game gives players a chance to taste the changes being made on a day-to-day basis. The current nightly version is worlds apart from the stable version in terms of content and mechanics. Upgradable ships, a shipboard AI, a much expanded mission system, a re-working of game progression, and a combat overhaul are just some of the features which have been demonstrated in nightly. The team also makes daily posts on the front page of their website, detailing their activities that day and showing off some of the upcoming changes.
3.
Okay, right off the bat - CF is only making
games: Starbound and Witchmarsh. Both games have separate and distinct dev teams, meaning that work on one is not slowing progression of the other. Chucklefish is
several other games, which is a completely different process which makes use different skill sets and personnel. Publishing games is not hindering the development of Starbound in the least.
As for the fact that some of the money being used was earned from Starbound sales... well, yeah. When you have made millions of sales at $15 a pop, it's not possible, efficient, or reasonable to be expected to re-invest every dollar in the game. Some of that money goes into paying your talent, some goes into paying for physical resources such as office space and hardware, and some will inevitably be re-invested in your company, so that you can be sustainable in the long-term and continue developing games. That's how corporations work.
4.
...really, dude? You (or perhaps your parents) purchased an early-access title. Your complaint is invalid.
5.
Okay, my position here is a bit more nuanced. I was heavily involved in the "nay" side (neigh side?) during the great Horseboob wars of July. I didn't like the fact that the devs were hinting at the possibility that my favourite race would have a creepy ship AI that made very little sense within the lore of the game. Admittedly, there were some fumbles by the devs during this process... they tried to play down the seething intensity of the forums by making some horse jokes during their daily updates, which were perceived by many as mocking dissenters.
At the time, I was among those who took the devs to task for their handling of the situation. However, in retrospect, it's clear that they were attempting to lighten the mood, but had badly misjudged the response they would receive. They made a mistake. It happens.
One or two of the moderators may have been a bit too loose in their interpretation of their powers during this time (I should note that at least one of them is now an ex-moderator). However, moderators are not Chucklefish employees, and while they are vetted by the devs, they do not necessarily represent the company's position. It is equally important to note that another moderator, Izzabelle, did a
job of maintaining a centralized thread for debate on the issue. Unlike the aforementioned "bad apple" mods, Izzy did not let her personal opinions on the matter (she was against Horseboobs) distract her from her primary duty of keeping things civil. Because of her hard work and countless hours of unpaid service, we managed to have a 50+ page dialogue on the matter, and, in the end, find some common ground.
Apart from the Horseboob Wars, I have yet to see an instance of the devs or moderators acting unprofessionally, or in bad faith. They have gone above and beyond to be transparent in their work and actively communicate with their fans (and critics, provided they make their points respectfully). And therein lies the most important fact that the Steam critics never want to tell you: 90% of the folks unhappy with the devs decide to make their point with foul language, threats, and personal attacks. When their threads are locked, they go on Steam and scream bloody murder about Chucklefish suppressing dissenting opinions. However, the 10% of critical threads that are made calmly and respectfully often blossom into some of the most productive discussions the community has.
---------------------------------------------

First things first, I loved the slick layout and visuals Hacknet plays quite nicely.  Music is pretty damn good too!
At first I really liked Hacknet as it feels like what Uplink should be in the modern gaming age.  You get cool looking interfaces, some psuedo-unix commands and maniplulations and a feeling of pressure as you hack your way past traces and logs.  However, thats where it falls apart a little.  You realise that logs are redundant and apart from an active trace when hacking some systems there are no repercussions to breaking log chains.  Except for one scripted event you dont need to worry about the men in black knocking on your door.  It was this attention to detail and consequnce that, in my opinion, gave Uplink its amazing gameplay.  I felt like the game needed that next level of complexity and difficulty to really come of age.
The major thumbs down however is game breaking bugs.  At time of writing this review there is at least one huge bug that is preventing the game being completed.  An attempt at fixing the bug was done but it did not solve the problem.  Cudos for the Developer at rushing to solve the issue but after one attempted patch there has been no communication on the status of the bug for about a month now.
Bottomline.  Its a fun little game but becomes one dimentional and easy once you realise there is no real way to lose apart from letting an active hack trace get you but even that is easily bypassed with one click or command.  The killer at this stage is bugs and more bugs.  I hope the game gets fixed and expanded, it could be a very nice game one day.
UPDATE:  The major bug has been fixed and I was able to finish the game.  Thanks to the Dev for fixing that up.
I have left my recommendation as negatvie which I am sad about as the game is pretty good.  The problem still is that its too easy once you realise there arent any repurcussions to not covering your tracks.  A little more depth would make this game a killer title!

Amazing game, well worth getting for fans of the first game and it's expansion. It's also a bit more difficult compared to the first game. And that's actually a good thing, because of lot of the higher difficulty comes from more (less predictable)  factors that affect a battle and the strategy involved. The randomisation of certain elements of the levels also works just awesome in terms of better variation. I did notice some bugs or glitches in this generation though, but it's usually very very minor stuff. And no, don't worry about this game losing it's fairness. It's still very much the same risk-management you'd do in the original XCOM Enemy Unknown, but just made more interesting for longer play.
I did notice the game takes quite a bit longer per turn for the enemy AI (and sometimes hangs a bit). There also seems to be an occasional bug in terms of ending turns automatically vs manually ending turns. The game sometimes forgets to start the next turn automatically it seems. The AI does respond in smart ways, so it's not much of a issue. It might also be due to higher hardware requirements to run the game. Having said that, the game looks gorgeous.
The game is also filled with a lot of new features, new abilities, new and stronger enemies and so on. Even people who are a bit burned out playing the previous XCOM game will find a lot of new things here that significantly refresh the old formula. The game also quickly introduces a lot of these new enemies and whilsts you will encounter certain types almost every mission, it never gets boring. New concepts like being concealed to lay ambushes and such are really welcome additions. In many ways this is the XCOM game they might have originally envisioned making in terms of those new features, specifically in terms of replayability. There's also a good story with interesting characters. Easily better than the first game.
All in all it's easy to recommend.
Oh and I do think Shen's Last Gift is a mission worth getting the DLC for, but the other cosmetic stuff is really quite mediocre. It lacks polish the original content has. The new mission is absolutely great though. Challenging and with a great story to it. I still think DLC is best bought at a discount though. I've gotten the XCOM 2 game with DLC in a recent sale and must say this game has plenty of value to be worth full price even. Great game.

I actually couldn't bring myself to finish this game. It's an alright attempt at a Souls clone, considering the fact that it's the only other game to attempt to compete with From Software's fabled series. But I actually stopped after failing my second attempt to kill a boss later on in the game, not because it was challenging, but because it felt like I was playing Monster Hunter or something. The boss has unavoidable attacks, too much health, and only one attack combination, with the ability to replenish health. I'm comparing it to a Monster Hunter boss fight in that it takes forever, and feels boring the entire time.
The iFrames while rolling are off, so rather than being legitimately capable of dodging an enemy's every attack, you're forced to treat the game more like a character action game than anything, tanking the attacks of your enemies, and being forced to endure the damage they're dealing to you. Oddly enough, there are also only two control schemes, with none of the simulating the controls of Dark Souls all that well. I almost wonder if the developer couldn't figure out how to bind two actions to a single key or something, as sprinting can only be found to clicking in the left thumbstick for some reason, rather than the "B" button on your controller.
Hitboxes are also off by quite a bit, making the issue with rolling iFrames far worse. I can't tel if it's better or worse than Dark Souls 2 in this area.
The world design is nothing like that of a Souls game. Rather than making everything interconnected and allow progression through shortcuts, the developers threw the "bonfires" of the game everywhere. I guess it's also similar to Dark Souls 2 in this vein.
Bosses are the worst part of the game though. Despite advertising boss fights as being phase-based and all that, they hardly ever are. Bosses have an even smaller moveset than your standard enemies, and oddly enough, almost no downtime. Rather than rewarding you for managing to dodge every attack with an opening in the boss' defense, you're greeted with the same moveset on an endless loop, so as mentioned earlier, the game isn't treated like a Souls game in this aspect, but a character action game. You just keep mashing "RT" and hope that you have enough potions to last you the entire fight, which in my case, I don't, so I'm not going to keep playing this game. The boss fights have this epic music playing in the background that doesn't actually match up with what you're doing. They feel really poorly handled, and I don't think there's a single boss in the game that's better than the worst boss in the Souls series, excluding Bed of Chaos of course.
Parrying is far better than it was in Dark Souls 2. I'll give them that much. In Lords of the Fallen, the window for parrying is much more forgiving, and the actual animation for parrying makes much more sense. Riposte works a lot more frequently, and backstabbing deals damage more similar to that of a riposte.
The weapon/armor variety is one of the points where this game shines. It's really easy to swap between different weapons, and I felt like I was actually earning something by looting a new weapon or piece of armor, rather than just filling up my inventory with useless equipment like in all of the Souls games. The issue that the Souls games have is that you only get so many upgrade materials, so often times you might loot a weapon or piece of armor that's technically better than what you're using, what you're using is already upgraded, and you won't be able to make that new piece of gear better unless you go back and farm the materials necessary to improve it. I've probably already used more weapons in this game than throughout the entire Souls series. The weapons and armor also look really impressive, with a wide variety of unique attack combos and ripostes.
The story is horrible, and the voice actors are horrible.
The visuals are also far more impressive, most of the time, and so long as you turn off chromatic aberration. Textures looks great, particle effects look great, and the geometry looks great. Unfortunately, the game's missing some really basic visual features, like water splahing when stepped in, dust/dirt/snow particles when walking around on surfaces made of those materials, and the footsteps left in the snow you walk in are poorly done.
The audio is disappointing. While the soundtrack is actually really great, everything else is pretty bad. Enemies don't stop making sound if you kill them, footsteps are either too quiet, or bugged and not making any sound at all. Plus, even if I wanted to listen to what any of the characters are saying, dialogue audio often bugs out and skips entire conversations.
Despite everything good about this game, I couldn't possibly recommend it to somebody looking for a Souls game. Wait for Dark Souls 3, or pick up a PlayStation 4 for Bloodborne. Maybe the devs of this game will be able to improve upon what they've already established with a sequel, but as it stands, Lords of the Fallen isn't worth playing.

This game on the surface looks beautiful, but unfortunitly it has at least three major flaws (besides the known technical issues) that really take the fun out of the game.
1) The big issue for me was the combat. In Lords of the Fallen, all, and I do mean ALL of the combat is based off of timing. This means that combat moves pretty slow and feels clunky and one tries to position the enemy into just the right spot and then waits to swing the weapon. Weapons are fairly heavy in this game and so they take a good amount of time to swing, which means one has to mentaly calculate how long it is going to take you to swing your weapon, how long your enemy is going to take to swing his, and then determine the window of oppertunity. This leads to an awkward period in which on is trying to judge all of these things...in really slow time since the weapons are heavy. I know other games do similar things to this, but once agian the apparent weight of the weapons makes this feel like it is going on forever.
2) The second big issue for me was the weapon leveling system (and really the whole leveling system in general). The only way to improve a weapon in this game is to add a ruin to it, and hope that the weapon you want to add the ruin to is one that you can add a ruin to. See why this is annoying yet? What makes it worse is that the ruins only add special effects, and don't really do much to the damamge base damage of the weapon. My problem with this, other than it being anoying, is that it doesn't really allow you any good or even decent way to grind, work, or attempt to make personal approvements to gear up for a boss or tough enemy. The leveling system doesn't help either as the complex load out and multitude of essentialy useless options means there are plenty of places to put skill points but very few that seem to help.
3) The story. Its just bland and at times can be a bit hard to follow. I know I didn't get terrebly far into the game, but after three bosses, you would think one would at least have a vegue idea as to why one is trying to fight these bosses. Or at least why one fought the bosses I did fight. I watched the cut scenes and all I know is that nobody likes monks and demons are bad. The story just bores me.
Despite the beauty and great graphics of this game I just can't recomend it. I should also not that I never experianced any of the technical issues many other users have, but I'm using an MSI GT72 Dominator Pro so...that may be something to think about. Anyway, I just don't think its worth the hassle.

Compared to other Platinum games, or even just Bayonetta 2, this game is actually kinda mediocre. The colors are drab and bland, the story is pretty bare-bones, and some enemies are just BS. However, what Bayonetta does best is the titular character herself.
Bayonetta is just a fun, bouncy character. She's over-sexualized, but to the point of irony, though there's still probably somebody out there looking up the Rule 34. While she may not be the most characterized, even in her own sodding game, she's definitely one of those characters that just makes you feel... Happy. Like Yahtzee once said, Bayonetta would be one of those people I'd want across from me on a long boring train ride.
And everything in this game reflects that. Her fighting style, her weapons, even her walking animation all reflect the essence of sheer fun. The game can never take itself seriously, and that's fine. It still builds that atmosphere of joyful energy. And that's not to say Bayonetta is a 2-dimensional character. She certainly needs expanding, but the game still does a good job of giving her motivations and weaknesses. If only the rest of the game and characters weren't so brown and lifeless. Except Jean. She's cool.
So in closing, buy this game if you have no other Platinum games left to buy or if you just want to see Bayonetta as a character. The combat is fine, not Platinum's best, but still a blast. The environments and enemies are still pretty dull for the most part, which compromises the tone of the game. Buy Bayonetta 2 if you can, but buy this if you can't.

First things first, I loved the slick layout and visuals Hacknet plays quite nicely.  Music is pretty damn good too!
At first I really liked Hacknet as it feels like what Uplink should be in the modern gaming age.  You get cool looking interfaces, some psuedo-unix commands and maniplulations and a feeling of pressure as you hack your way past traces and logs.  However, thats where it falls apart a little.  You realise that logs are redundant and apart from an active trace when hacking some systems there are no repercussions to breaking log chains.  Except for one scripted event you dont need to worry about the men in black knocking on your door.  It was this attention to detail and consequnce that, in my opinion, gave Uplink its amazing gameplay.  I felt like the game needed that next level of complexity and difficulty to really come of age.
The major thumbs down however is game breaking bugs.  At time of writing this review there is at least one huge bug that is preventing the game being completed.  An attempt at fixing the bug was done but it did not solve the problem.  Cudos for the Developer at rushing to solve the issue but after one attempted patch there has been no communication on the status of the bug for about a month now.
Bottomline.  Its a fun little game but becomes one dimentional and easy once you realise there is no real way to lose apart from letting an active hack trace get you but even that is easily bypassed with one click or command.  The killer at this stage is bugs and more bugs.  I hope the game gets fixed and expanded, it could be a very nice game one day.
UPDATE:  The major bug has been fixed and I was able to finish the game.  Thanks to the Dev for fixing that up.
I have left my recommendation as negatvie which I am sad about as the game is pretty good.  The problem still is that its too easy once you realise there arent any repurcussions to not covering your tracks.  A little more depth would make this game a killer title!

This is the best Age of Empires game and one of the best strategy games of all time. Ships are big and beefy, cannons are cannons that do huge damage and splash and each civilization is unique.
In AoE 2, you have crossbowmen shooting arrows at stone walls, battering rams hitting farm fields and making them burn, and swordsmen using their swords to beat down structures. In AoE 3, units have their own siege attacks and animations which fix that problem. Every civ's Church or religious building is a different model. Every civ has their own unique units and tech trees.
The Explorer is your colony's leader and sort of a hero-like unit from Warcraft 3. You get to explore the map, fight neutrals and claim treasures during the start of the game, which makes games less repetitve and more fun in the beginning.
The Home City part of the game is awesome. You can send shipments or technologies from your mother country to your colony. Every civ has a ton of different strategies.
Each map is different enough. Most maps have Native people and settlements that you can trade with or ally. Your mother country will give you additional support on some maps, like early shipments or free economic starting buildings. There are also trade routes that you can establish.
The game has good balance, almost rock-paper-scissors, with various types of infantry, cavalry and artillery. Also, farms and plantations do not need to be 'queued' like in AoE 2, fixing any annoyance from that game.
In conclusion, AoE 3 is the most improved and well made Age of Empires yet. Every civilization is unique and all the annoying or bad features from the previous Age of Empires series games have been fixed. Each time you play will be different and every civ has different strategies. The maps are all different. My favorite part of the game is the sound of distant artillery, which echoes far! This is a great game and I am glad it is on steam, now it will continue to be supported!

I would really, really like to say that I enjoy this game.
I would like to say it's fast-paced, fun, and tactical all at once.
I would like to say that the matchmaking is good, and ships are balanced.
Unfortunately, I can say none of these things about Fractured Space
TL;DR, It's a losing grind-fest of a "pay-to-grind-slightly-less" title with a tiny community of people willing to put up with its BS, and you should play literally any other game before playing this one. Seriously.
Here are the pros and cons of the game, as I see them:
Pros:
Cool ship designs
Good graphics
Unique weapon systems/combos
Cons
Game runs poorly, as framerate and connectivity are both less-than-perfectly optimized
Matchmaking is slow
Controls are sluggish and ships have inordinately long response times
Group tactics, while important, are ignored by the community because of their opacity
No ranked mode

Lastly, there is one major con I haven't mentioned yet because of how incredibly frustrating it is: the XP/credit system
Let's break it down.
1. Some ships are CATEGORICALLY BETTER than others.
2. Said better ships require approximately 35k XP to unlock, on average
3. After supposedly UNLOCKING those ships, you then have to PURCHASE them with CREDITS at about 100k each

This same system is used for ship components.
Here's why this is a problem. On average, you'll recieve about 2000 credits for a good match, as a frontline assault ship. As a support, you may get 500 from a good match. This is unfair to begin with. Next, halve those for an OK match. Now halve that again for a losing match. This means that, early-game, it may take you up to 60 matches, at about 2 minutes of matchmaking time and at least 15 minutes of play time to unlock your first ship.
That's 15 HOURS of gameplay time to unlock your FIRST ship. Furthermore, for the ENTIRITY of those 15 hours, you will be losing at least 2/3 matches to players who already HAVE either purchased premium ships or grinded to the best ships.
Save your money, save your time, save your sanity. Don't buy anything related to this game, or waste your time playing it.  Go buy Rainbow SIx: SIege, or No Man's Sky, or DOOM. Something fun. Because this game isn't.

They had the right idea with convenant switching, but there's literally only like 5 convenants and two of them do the same thing and still aren't fixed since launch IIRC. Kinda sucks.
Most players won't even notice these things, let alone care, but it matters to me enough to at least say it.
All in all it's a great game, it's the obvious fanservicing and nostalgia pandering take away nearly all its sense of identity. You'll probably enjoy it! I still think Dark Souls 1 is the better game, but this game has one thing it doesn't; polish.

Dark Souls 3 is a great game, but I understand that many people, like I was, are turned off by its difficulty. Everyone just says "git gud", and, in a ridiculous recent trend, calls every game with frequent death (however un-punishing) the "Dark Souls of (insert genre here)". It's in the marketing too. "Prepare to Die", "Stronger than Hell" and other intimidating stuff.
I recently beat the base game completely solo (I'm about to do the DLC too). It was a rewarding experience, and if you have the time and energy, I highly recommend it. Beating a game that doesn't treat you like an inattentive koala is a precious novelty which is sadly quite rare these days.
However, I just want to let people know you don't have to be a hardcore gamer to have fun with this game (though some would argue otherwise). You can get help from other players on every single boss except the first one, which SEVERELY impacts the difficulty of the game. If you can't play online, the game even gives you NPC allies (who you sometimes have to earn), which aren't as smart as people, but even just having someone else for the boss to attack can make a huge difference. Don't be ashamed to look up guides for leveling or ask a friend for advice. Also, don't expect to have a perfect playthrough the first time. The game is cryptic, even in its systems, but there are lots of sources for basic tips and information. Oh, and get a cheap USB controller if you don't already have one.
The game is daunting at first, but there are literally at least thousands of other people ready and willing to help you every step of the way.
Otherwise, if you insist on challenging yourself, I'd recommend playing this game during some kind of sabbatical, brief or otherwise, like I did. If you play games to relax, don't stress yourself out over this game. Winter or summer break, a lengthy vacation from work, or hey, just retire. I guarantee you'll feel accomplished every time you reach a new bonfire or beat a boss, and not just the first time. It's even more satisfying seeing yourself improve as a player when you start a new character and breeze past the stuff that used to hold you back for hours.
Besides all that, it's just a well-made game, clearly put together with love and devotion. The environments and music are beautiful; the story, while cryptic, is engrossing; and the gameplay, while punishing at times, is by far the best and most engaging gameplay out of every single action RPG out there.
So, for those sitting on the fence, I completely understand. This series is famous for its difficulty, and that might mean you won't have fun, which would totally defeat the purpose and be a waste of your time and money. But don't be afraid of this game! You can get help with the hard parts. But I also truly do believe that anyone with enough patience can "git gud".

There are clear influences from Uplink, but Hacknet stands on its own two feet for many design decisions.
Hacknet requires a lot of typing due to the text console. This brings a level of realism which is enjoyable, and the countdown timers do not seem to require the player to type at 200 words per minute. However, a few actions can also be initiated by mouse using a graphical user interface. The use of the mouse is a bit incoherent: those features which can use the mouse and those which cannot feel arbitrary and without obvious design merit.
There are a number of little bugs here and there. Head over to the discussions and check the bug report thread. Many of the valid bugs reported actually have more to do with polish. It's unfair to call them bugs, but fixing the issues could enhance the game's polish and lead to better immersion. There are a few actual bugs that can lead to gameplay issues, but they seem to be few and far between.
The story is a bit linear. I have found it hard to explore the networked universe outside where the missions take me. Compare this to Uplink, where there are a great many ways to find and access computers by goofing around. Computers tend to have random snippets from
, which are humorous logs of conversations that reportedly happened on IRC. It's a nice touch as a reward for looking at systems and it makes them feel a little more fleshed out, yet the contents tend to be disconnected from any of the game's context. The snippets simultaneously help and hurt immersion.
Creative expression is available in small doses, but I do not consider this any kind of sandbox game. The potential for such a thing is there. For example, there are computers which run web servers. You can modify the HTML, and when you visit the web server, your changes are visible. It can be amusing to deface a virtual server even if no other living being will see it. However, if you delete all the system files from a computer and then forcibly shut it down, it should prevent the system from rebooting. This would destroy a system. In Hacknet, if you do this, the system will disappear from your network map for a little while and then come back (while still lacking system files). As a related polish-bug: you can immediately connect to any computer "destroyed" this way using the command console, even if the network map does not show the system as online.
The music is electronica-themed to suit the stereotype of a computer hacker. The sound track brings good ambience. I personally start to notice the repetitious nature of the music after playing 2-3 solid hours, but that's usually a good time to take a break anyway.
The recent release for Linux/Mac is welcome, except that has introduced a number of new bugs that need to be squashed. Save game interoperability is a current problem that needs to be resolved at the time of this writing. Linux/Mac support has its own thread in the game's Steam discussion area. I'm sure those problems will be resolved soon enough, but they are worth reading through before purchasing if you plan to play on Mac or Linux.
Overall, I'd say Hacknet is a fun puzzle game with a solid computer hacker theme. It could use more polish and the design decisions regarding keyboard or mouse interfacing could use some rethinking. As a professional programmer and IT person, I cannot really say with certainty if this game is accessible to non-programmers or non-IT people. I suspect the game is approachable enough to anyone who has ever had to type commands into anything instead of clicking glittery UI buttons.

It could have been one of the best, if not the best, Assassin's Creed yet.
I had no problems with the performance on day 1 even, but the game just itself isnt worth 60€/$/whatever. Maybe on sale.
Lets get to the review before this is longer than the LoTR trilogy:
Up and down parkour works sometimes perfectly, and would be perfect addition to AC series, but it is about luck. Arno will not follow your orders at all sometimes. Even in the new cover system, Arno will choose the cover he prefers over the cover you chose, and is very clunky. The counter button does not everytime work, Arno's decision not yours, so you will die every now and then, because it was Arno's wish to die.
Combat took a massive leap backwards, it was better in AC3 and that should be saying something. The counters dont work, as I said, but not the biggest problem. The biggest problem is the gunshots. You cannot counter them, you cannot always dodge them, and they can happen even when you are in middle of finishing move. Yeah, and two or three shots is enough to kill you when you have max health.
A rare plus here tho: I like how when one enemy sees you, they dont have shared vision anymore, so the rest dont. The enemies are individuals, and not controlled by some overmind.
Ubi advertised their new customization a ton, but the truth is, it doesent change anything all that much, expect belts (more ammo) wich were in previous ACs too. They are mostly cosmetic changes, and there are only 3 or 4 different armors, and the rest change just one button of the shirt or so. Then there are the good looking ones, but you have to compete in Club Competetive to win those. And even after that you have to save a ton of money to get it, or you could always ''hack it'' with ''hack currency'' that you buy with real money. Yeah, a pay to play pay to win game.
What did I like about the game tho? The small, very small, customization and the up and down parkour as ideas, seemless enterable buildings and the new assassination missions. If Assassin's Creed is going into this RPG direction, I feel it is the right one. And playing with friends is almost always more fun than alone. Just ditch this ''seemless multiplayer'' crap, it ruins singleplayer for the singleplayers and multiplayer for the multiplayers.
I hope that Assassin's Creed will go the original Tomb Raider path, that another studio would buy the series, and make the series what Assassin's Creed used to be.

I'd like to address the major complaints most people have about this game:
1. This is not a walking simulator. The amount of time you spend simply walking compared to in combat or preparation is negligible.

Yes, you can do everything perfectly and still lose the expedition because of bad luck, but you can always recover from any way RNG might screw you over with loot-and-retreat runs, even if you have no money left. The factor of luck makes experiences in this game a lot more unique and for me makes it more exciting.
3. Yes, the developers were ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and censored criticism for this game. That was entirely wrong of them. But how does this affect the game? The game is still just as good as it would be if the developers did not censor anything. That should not be factor in whether you should buy a game or not: only how fun the game is should be.
I would recommend this game. It kept me hooked with a great atmosphere and a fun experience. Unless you cannot stand a lot of RNG, you should buy it, especially if you are reading this during the summer sale while it is 60% off.

THE GRITTY DEETZ:
The biggest success from this dev team is a mobile game. Not that mobile gaming is ALWAYS terrible, but it usually is just a cash grab market. This is the type of game I would expect from someone successful in a cash grab market.
I thought this game looked like fun when I picked it up. I gave it an honest try, but I ultimately cannot get behind this game at all. The gameplay is missing a lot of what makes a game fun. It is more like they took an idea for a game and did the bare minimum. There's no love in the design, just a lot of half-hearted content created for the sake of content.
The character design feels like a direct pull of Team Fortress, Overwatch, and World of Warcraft. Enemy design takes from a plethora of different games. The Loot boxes are a reskin of Hearthstone Packs. The "crafting" system (I use that term lightly) is the new LoL system. There is no narrative, just a bunch of mindless missions. It's depressing how unoriginal a lot of the art choices are for this game, because the artists did a pretty good job on the assets themselves.
The balancing in this game, both PvP and PvE, is virtually non-existant. Instead of balancing PvE they just put as many healthpacks and checkpoints in the game as they could get away with. In PvP, it's "Everyone is OP, So Nobody is OP."
The Character Selection is run like a MOBA with a free rotation and the option to purchase characters. Alternatively, with the right amount of time sunk into it, it appears you can unlock all of them without spending anything. That said, the odds are stacked against you when it comes to equipment. The only likelihood you have of getting the Legendary gear (which will end up dominating Rated PvP) is to buy as many loot boxes as possible in the hopes of getting the right amount of hero tokens to buy what you want. I take the biggest issue with this, as Pay-To-Win games are absolutely unfun for anyone unwilling to shell out a small fortune on RNG.
On the bright side, I can recommend this to anyone with exactly 2 friends who want a mindless hack and slash game to play in their spare time. The Skins/Gear don't mean as much in PvE so the Pay-To-Win aspects of it don't tarnish the value in that respect. If that's your thing, go wild. I, personally, will look elsewhere.

One of my favorite games. Has a somewhat steep learning curve, especially if you're unfamiliar with the genre. Once you figure it out, it's a lot of fun. There is some RNG, but there's a lot of things you can do to mitigate it - which is part of the skill of the game. The only similar game on steam I could compare it to is Tharsis.
Gameplay: You start with 6 dice. Each die can be spent to perform an action - build a building, gather a resource, make more dice, etc. You also get 3 cards every turn that can be used to perform or augment actions (tip: try to use all 3 each turn). Certain actions score victory points (randomized each game) and you need a certain amount of victory points to advance to the next stage. Win 3 stages to win the game and advance to the next rank.
If you like board and/or dice games, you will like this.

[Note : This review applies to both Season 1 and Season 2 taken together but applies to each one individually]
Before buying this game, I didn't expect anything special. I knew it had good reviews and that's why I tried it.
It turned out to be by far the BEST COMMERCIAL PRODUCT I've ever bought in my LIFE, better than any movie, game, book or anything else I've ever bought so far.
The game genre is said to be a "Point'n'Click", but in fact it isn't that much ; there is no puzzle, there is just the story, and you implicated in it.
I couldn't say this is a "game" though, you won't play, but you will be told a story, a beautiful story in witch you will be emotionnaly implicated as long as it speaks you to.
Basically, I could say that the game is a big cutscene that you influate by your actions (by what you say in fact, choosing how to answer to the main characters). I KNOW that it sounds strange or bad, but it isn't, there is no way to properly describe how good this "game" is.
To be a bit more clear, I would only see 3 reasons why someone could not like a game like that :
● They don't like cell-shading graphics (look at the screenshots)
● They absolutely hate stories that take place in a Zombie Apocalypse environnement
● They don't have a good English Level or don't know how to Install translations (2nd Season is in Full-English)
Pros :
+ Incredibely good voice-acting and credible characters
+ The way you are emotionally implied in the story, never had I seen that before in ANY game
+ The possibility to "influence" the story and that you always feel that what's happening is because of your choices
+ The whole story is intense, everything is useful, there would be no part to scrap down, I wasn't bored a SINGLE SECOND.
+ Clementine as a deuteragonist (Season 1) and protagonist (Season 2), Tomboys as a main character FTW. :heart:
+ The story is in NOW WAY predictable, you never know what will happen next.
+ Incredibly good "filming" and animation and character facial expression, as good and even better than most TV Series.
+ The end... really... only time I cried in a Video Game.
+ Good Music (special mention for the End Credits)
+ Simple controls : WASD + Mouse
+ There is no need of a Gaming PC to run this, most computers will do the job
+ You don't play this game, this is the game that plays you
Cons :
- It has an end... no really... NO CON
(-) Can have some resolution problems that can be fixed by the simple addition of a line in the start options on Steam
(-) Translations in other languages than English are fan-made, the one for Season 2 isn't included with the Game ; play in English if you could for maximal effect.
Conclusion : A MUST-TRY (at least in Sales, and at least for Season 1), 11/10 : best "game" and product I've ever purchased in my life ; I know that every game I'll play for a decade will surely not be as good as this one ; this was a once-in-a-lifetime experience, THANKS Telltale Games =) + please, Clementine again in Season 3 :beg:
PS. There is absolutely no need to know the Comic Series or the TV Series "The Walking Dead" to enjoy this game, the story is an original one based on the Comics.
PSS. You will certainly need a little time to fully enter in the story, try to play at least 2 hours before saying that you definitely don't like it or you could miss something.
PSSS. You need to play this "game" ALONE for a maximum effect.

I think this game is highly underrated. While the graphics are simple, the gameplay is pretty deep. After you advance a few ranks, your decisions really start to matter, and one slip-up can make you lose the game. But don't worry! The game's rank system means you will always be presented with an appropriate challenge, so the game never becomes too hard.
I do think the gameplay is a little too mathematical. You don't have to do any math to play the game, but if you want to play it at a high level, you'll need to do some arithmetic to make sure you get the most value out of every move you make.
My other complaint is that the endgame is almost always far easier than the opening. By that point you've usually got the game pretty well locked up and you're just going through the motions. Maybe that becomes less true at higher ranks, though.
Still, I think these are quibbles in a game that's definitely worth giving a try if you're into turn-based games at all.

"This is my opinion so you cant Critique is" ok so now that we've gotten that out of the way I would like to admit that when it comes to real time strategy. Age of Empires 3 has always held a special place in my heart. I've played since the first AOE so just liking what I have is not a thing here. I genuinly see this as an improvement and large innovation in the series. The pace is nice, and the fact that resources gather so long as your settler are gathering is a nice change that speeds up the game. the addition of deck and shipments is also very fun allowing multple builds for nations and different ways to play your nation no matter what you play. The base nations alone are also well made. some balancing is an issue as it is with most unsupported games but each nation feels different and has a new way to play and thrive. IE Russian= numbers over strength, France= cavalry and defense. There's quite a few ways to play your nation so don't be too focused on the "meta". Trade routes and native alliances make a nice change as well, most native upgrades are helpful and give you a reason to explore the map and find native settlements. Frankly the game I see here is great and I wish the community was larger rather than focusing on the past of AOE 2. The changes are well done and keep the game fresh.
If you're a fan of RTS's I would highly recomend playing this game. especially is you found AOE 2 to be a bit slow and lacking.

Absolutely fantastic game if you are a fan of building games (Civ etc.) and the elegance of chess. You build a little town, making your build choices differently based on variations in the layout of the terrain and the victory point conditions that vary in each play-through. It is consistent enough to appeal to (former) chess player in me, but random enough to be exciting and new each time. Random cards and "dice" (types of "people" you can use each turn to take various actions) keep it exciting, forcing tactical adjustments every turn, but largely without upsetting your larger strategy.
It has its limits. Once you have really mastered it (I am 5th on the leaderboards) it is pretty much done. You cannot play it 20 totally different ways for 10 years like the best Civ-type games of all time. But the subtleties of tactics and strategy are absolutely fantastic to figure out along the way despite what look like incredibly simple mechanics. So it is an wonderful puzzle game wrapped in a tactical game that is wrapped in a builder game. While I am pretty much done with it, it will stay in my memory as one of the best games I have ever played.

Hey everyone and this is my review about the game!
This is a Turn based board game.
There are not many resolution sizes available.
You can play the game in fullscreen mode or windowed mode.
There is a sound volume slidebar available.
There is a music volume slidebar available.
You are able to toggle the quick move button or practice mode.
They will offer you a tutorial (if turned on).
Well this game is interesting to say the least. You are playing on a small map/board which is randomized each time that you play. Each turn a dice will be thrown and you will get a couple of action cards. Each action card has a different purpose. You are able to get a worker, Gatherer, Builder, soldiers and many other things. At the top you will see some Scroll tabs and completing on of these requirements will gain some victory points. You will have to complete 3 scroll tabs in order to complete the game and everytime you are advancing to a new scroll, Something will happen on the board. You will have to become victorious before you have been destroyed by barbarians or you no longer have turns available.
are the one that creates the productive things, Such as chopping wood or mining stones.
are looting the resources from the workers and store them to safety.
are used to make new buildings, There are 3 contruction tabs that your able to pick from.
is a very useful card to make more action cards. Have 2 of these reproduce on the same location and place a new one on op top of them to gain some extra cards.
The game could be difficult to learn at the start but it will not take a long time until you will know the basics. You will have to place a worker/gatherer inside of a house and you will move the worker to a resource location to start working. To perform an action you will need to put a worker card on the other worker that is standing on resource spot. Then you will have to send a gatherer to obtain the loot and once again you will have to need to place a gather card on the other gather unit that is standing on top of the resources.. The resources should be used for making new buildings while food is needed to deploy action cards to the board. There are 2 types of movement. Save movement or instant movement. Each Card that you end up keeping when you are ending your turn will be transformed into save movement. Which could be to move units. If you need to move an unit straigth away, you will have to place a card into the left bottom corner that say x2. Scrolls (on the right side) could be useful to activate something quickly without spending food. You will have to defeat those barbarians by recruiting soldiers out of the Guard towers. Barbarians are able to destroy an entire resource spot instantly and all resources on that spot will be lost. If you have manage to destroy all of the spawners and barbarians before they are becoming a pest. Then You no longer have to worry about new spawners or barbarians. Once gone, is always gone.
Game is randomized even in taking turns.
Everytime a new small board.
Pretty addictive.

I really enjoy playing Trove with my friends. I started a little while ago, got off for a while, then came back. It has fun gameplay, soothing graphics, and a friendly community. But recently it has gone a little bit too pay to win. Many others in the community agree with this, as classes are now behind a paywall. They used to be free, with a bit of work. Sadly that is no longer the case. Simply spending money will get you everywhere. It has also become a lot harder for new players to get anywhere. You need a currency, Flux, to upgrade your weapons. However it is also the currency that is used mainly for trading with other players. Grinding for flux is incredibly difficult. Doing a dungeon, as a low level, will get you maybe 30 flux. Buying a Class Coin with real money and selling it will get you 100,000 flux. I still love this game to death, but it is breaking my heart the direction it is going. I hope the devs see the negative backlash from the playerbase and backtrack quickly.

1.0 Update (edited 8/6/2016):
The game is at the core same as before. Yes, there are a bunch of things that I personally don't like with the 1.0 changes, but there are mods for that and I see where chucklefish was going with what they did. Fun game, bunch of new stuff, progression is a bit wonky because there is no handholding and you just have to figure out what to do. This can make is real hard to learn the system, but once you do it's very self consistant. I still definately recomend it if you want an exploration/building game.
At the heart it's still very much a game where if you like bulding and exploring you're in for dozens of hours of fun. If you want lore you can go read books in villages and dungeons for even more hours. And then you can use those things you collected to uild your own awesome stuff to show off. Contrast that though to if you want to do combat and "story" progression. If you do the game will get old pretty quick.
The game is "like" Terraria in style and genre, but the focus and core gameplay is completely and absolutely different. It's like saying Smash Bros and Tekken are the same style and genre and then trying to compare them directly. They're very different types of fighting games, just like Starbound and Terraria are very different types of tile sidescrollers or w/e you call them.
A lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥you see trashing the game is about how the Devs haven't lived up to their promises, which in some aspects they haven't, and in some aspects the game feels disjointed in it's design (lack of tile protection in some RNG dungeons). But they have stated they're comitted to developing post 1.0 content and the scope of their original kickstarter/early access was on the scale of Starcitizen's scope, which is honestly absurd to hold them to. Sure they should not have made the promises they couldn't keep, but equally to blame are people who expect them to keep absurd promises they made 4 years ago when they were fledging developers and didn't know just just how much work creating an engine from scratch and all the assets would be. I would rather the game be in a decent state and pushed to 1.0 than have it be perpetually 0.8-9 trying to chase stretch goals that are not worth the implementation effort to get into the 1.0 build.

Oh boy, this is a hard one. I 100% love XCOM to death but this time I can't say yes. XCOM 2 has so many problems I can't figure out where to start and I'm sure the other reviews will help better. Overall I enjoy it but I can't support a broken game where the creators sit there and turn their heads.

Bugs (note: this version of the game has been patched twice already)
-Sudden corrupt saves taking away several hours spent in playing the game. This can happen from quitting the game during multiplayer or just plain anywhere else. Confirmed a common problem.
-Bugs and sudden lag spikes which is annoying, and sometimes can cause your death.
-Flickering corners in every object inside your headquarters or many other interiors with a high performance PC in any anti-aliasing settings, especially the lowest one.
-And a lot more glitchy stuff you see in other people's reviews, too. They're geniune, not complaints.
Gameplay
-Combat improved with the parrying system and realistic difficulty and AI, re-ruined by it's sluggish approach.
-Free-running made easier by new up-or-down system, but also causes new navigation problems where you still press the right thing and jump to your death/the wrong place.
-Stealth smoother than in previous games, made better by the crouch system. Broken cover system, lack of whistling, and sometimes being detected while hidden brings it back down.
-Controls still as broken as ever!
The co-op is pretty useless and occasionally annoying unless you have actual friends to play with. I got more done doing the missions on my own.
Didn't believe the majority on the Internet, I thought it was just haters being haters. Nope. The game is actually broken, which is too bad. The characters are less forgettable than in the previous games, the story more engaging, and the missions are actually fun, and there is some pretty decent customisation in this game. Either wait for a lot more patches to come out, or just don't buy the game.

And with that, my heart is broken. Fallout 4 gets uninstalled.

I'm going to be comparing this game to Dark Souls since it is VERY similar to Dark Souls except not as good.  It's so similar that the controls are virtually identical when using the "alternate" control scheme.  Even the special moves have the same controls, ie parry/riposte, jump attack, backstab, rolling attack.
The world is a decent size but pretty small compared to Dark Souls, and it all kinda looks the same.  Maybe equivalent to about 3 areas in Dark Souls.  The game does encourage you to go back to old areas to find new items and open doors that were previously locked, but when you go back most of the enemies are trivially easy to defeat so it's not that great.  The combat is pretty similar to Dark Souls too.  You can use shield+weapon, or dual hand weapons for more powerful/faster attacks.  I found the strength based weapons painfully slow to use, but the agility based weapons behaved a lot more like Dark Souls.  It also has the Dark Souls system of fatroll vs fastroll depending on what % of your carrying weight you are using.  The enemies have a decent variety although nowhere near what you'll find in Dark Souls simply because it's a much smaller world.  The animations and hitboxes are a bit off sometimes though.  You get used to it but it's nowhere near as "crisp" as Dark Souls.
The game also has a system of weapon/armor upgrades where you place runes into slots, but a lot of weapons don't even have any slots for runes, and even the ones that do usualy only have one slot.  Because of this most of the runes don't actually make a huge difference.  Sort of like upgrading a weapon to +5 or something in Dark Souls, instead of being able to go to +10 or +15.  You can also add things like poison/fire/magic to your weapon but because most weapons only have one slot you are sacrificing physical damage to use those runes.
The story in the game is pretty generic and boring.  That's not the reason I bought this game, but even so this is one of the areas where if differs from Dark Souls the most.  Dark Souls has a very subtle/mysterious story and lore that you could totally miss if you weren't paying attention, whereas LOTF hits you over the head with it.  Luckily there isn't a ton of dialogue/cutscenes but still a lot more than Dark Souls.
This game also has no multiplayer at all.  No PVP or co-op which really limits the replayability of the game.  I would also say it's easier than Dark Souls as long as you have the right weapon for your playstyle.  Maybe that's just because I've played a lot of Dark Souls though.
Whatever performance issues the game had when it was first released, they seem to be sorted out now.  The game ran perfectly for me.  I think it's worth getting on sale for someone itching for some more Dark Souls-like gameplay.  Just realize before buying it that you probably won't like it as much as Dark Souls.  I hope more devs in the future try to create games like this though, hopefully with some more original ideas in them too.

Trapped in a monster filled sewer littered with keys, it'll take a lot of clever box pushing action to navigate to safety.  The lack of a windup animation before pushing a crate makes it way to easy to slip up and slide a box unintentionally.  The isometric visuals are a bit too askew often creating confusing when it comes to walking behind objects.
The monster AI patterns are unpredictable making navigating around them incredibly difficult.  Often it's best to sit and way for long periods of time for them to eventually path away, which is not a fun way to accomplish goals.

The combat:
The combat feels rather slow-ish but very impactful. The movement is very weird. Rolling feels kinda wrong. Even fast rolling  seems slow. Walking away seems more effective but rolling generates alot of invincibility frames. It's overall really strange. And in addition to that, there are no running attacks making boss fights a bit more difficult and anoying.
Overall, not to shabby, not great either.
Map design:
The map design is a bloody mess. Alot of corridors look exactly the same and alot of objects blend into the enviroment.
I overlooked NPCs aswell as the paths where i was supposed to go. Also, there is no teleport system. While you can acess the blacksmith from alot of different stations, you can't do that with the monk who enhances your potions. Alot of backtracking is involved in this open world game. Shortcuts open up rather often so its not to terrible but it's still no good.
Also, you never really know where to go. Since all the paths look the same you run around in circles alot and if you get lost. That's beyond anoying. Its especially terrible in the later sections of the game.
Item distribution:
The beginning seems solid. They give you alot of variations that all look nice. However, at the later stages of the game they just throw at you plenty of epic weapons and armor that are twice as good as the ones you used before. That felt awefully off.
Difficulty:
It's solid. I managed to do a couple of bosses on my first attempt. Some not. Overall, still challenging.
Graphics and Performance:
The game performs finely. 60fps @ highest settings with a gtx 970 is nice to have. Overall it looks impressive. Only the hair of characters look aweful. Also, the game crashed twice within 10 hours and the voice acting is all over the place.
Conclusion:
I'm in love with this genre. And because of the lack of games that adopt this genre i am willing to overlook all of its flaws and play more of it. If you are like me, thirsting for more games like Dark souls then you can pick it up. If not, stay away from this game.

TL;DR: Excellent boardgame-inspired dice-worker-placement/town-builder.  A bit rough around the edges, but well worth the price of admission if you're a fan of planning-heavy strategy games.  8/10
You start with a pool of 6 'workers' represented by dice, two houses, three ability cards, and a board with resources and light danger (barbarians, of course).  These are well-established tropes in boardgames, and they're put to excellent use here, with a little bit more dynamic action than you'd find in something like Agricola or Troyes.   You have a wide variety of activities you can engage in to win (card + worker creation, base building, resource collection), but the game requires a good amount of flexibility in approach.  Matches last 20-40 minutes.
It's quite a bit like FTL in that you have some situations which seem impossible or are just barely winnable and you have to get yourself out of bad situations, with meager resources, eventually coming out the other side with a nice victory rush or a feeling of "that was super close, I can try it again and get it next time".  And there will be plenty of 'next time's and opportunities for tuning your strategy.  I'm 35 hours in and still tweaking my standard build order.  Sometimes your win conditions will be easy, sometimes they'll kick you in the teeth and you have to kick back.
The sound and graphics are pretty barebones, but functional and unobtrusive.  The gameplay starts a bit rough, but smooths out after about a dozen games once you get the hang of the systems and the buildings involved.  I'm about 35 hours in at the time of writing and am hovering around rank 30.  It's still very challenging and I will lose every third game or so, but it will almost always be very close.
The developer is very active and still updating the game.  If you have an issue, post on the discussion board and it'll be addressed in fairly short order.  It would be nice to have the game fleshed out a bit more: lots of the buildings seem "samey" and there's only one game mode (for example, adding a zachtronics-style challenge mode where you have a set starting situation to overcome and are trying to beat not just those challenges but also the results of others would be a welcome change of pace).
Overall, I really dig the game.  I'd dig it more if there was a bit more meat on the bones.  It can also be a bit overwhelming to dive in and have a list of 15 buildings to choose from, especially if you don't have prior experience with boardgame equivalents.  But overall, for an indie effort, it really is a good value and I hope the developer continues to show the game some love so that it grows some real legs.

Axes and Acres is a single-player digital board game about building up little civilizations over the course of a few dozen turns.
A single turn in Axes and Acres begins by rolling a set of dice that will present a set of workers for you to use. These die can be deployed to the board, or spent to activate special cards or dice that are already on the board. Most of the actions you take drive you towards earning victory points, and you must earn a fixed amount of points before a turn limit expires to win.
Like most board games, you're going to need to spend a little bit of time just getting to understand the systems. You might spend a couple of matches feeling a bit confused and frustrated, but if you go through the tutorials and stick with it for just a little bit, you'll find a tremendously rewarding little gem of a game waiting for you on the other side.
Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm going to cozy up under a blanket and enjoy a few more rounds of this wonderful game.

Whether or not you liked the original Kingdom Rush will determine whether or not you like its sequel.
There's nothing really different about the mechanics - there's just new, fun variants on the old theme. The tower specializations have differed (and are quite interesting) but the basic purposes are still the same. The enemies are different but the general premise is unchanged. There are new heroes, but the purpose of having a hero on the field is the same. So if you liked KR, you'll like KRF; and conversely if KR wasn't your thing, KRF is not sufficiently different that your opinion will be altered.

Great and fun game as well as addicting. It does have bumps on the road however and can be incredibly frustrating, especially with the introduction of the Sand Wraith, an upgraded version of the enemy spawn unit from the first one.
The pro's of this game have been listed by many people, maps are enjoyable, able to find and click things for a bit of amusement, and towers are a ton of fun to figure out which works and doesn't. Feels like the old one but with updated and new versions that feel at home in this game. Which is weird to see someone list that as a con but honestly a Paladin guild would not fit in a desert setting as opposed to a assassins guild they have in this one.
The main cons of this game that I feel are the hero's, introducing a very grind system into the game that should not be a part of it especially since you can only use  your hero's on the 'campaign' parts of these maps, they're taken away during heroic and Iron situations. The hero's themselves are enjoyable and appear to all be unique and fun but very weak as well to the Desert Archer swarms which can be a bit difficult to handle if somone is new due to how fast they can rip the hero apart. The other part would be the Sand Wraith. The first game had a Necromancer which did a similiar thing of spawning 4 skeletons peroidically while having a ranged attack but easy to handle due to how far into the game they're introduce, giving the player a chance to be able to handle them. The hero's as well were capable of beating on them due to progressing in levels during the campaign, not a grind mechanic this one has. They work with spawning a coffin at a random location, ahead of them, in the samel lane they are (so yes they can spawn past your militia barracks). This is a huge problem as they'll also spawn more than just 4 mummies so easily able to get swarmed and suddenly over burdened. This wouldn't be an issue if they were somewhat squishy but they have half as much health as an Executioner who's supposed to be the Ogre (except he has one hit kills majority of the time) with 1400 health. The Sand Wraith's stats are HP: 700 DPS: 30-60 ranged AR/MR: none MS: Slow and thankfully only take 1 hp away. The bad part though with its slow MS it spawns more than enough tombs to release a swarm of mummies and towers will focus the mummies over the Sand wraith which you have zero control over. They'll also kill your militia quickly if you try and move them to handle it. Early on Hero's will not be able to handle it or help as well. I did the mistake of not leveling up my reinforcements and meteors apperantly as that's the only way I find to slow them down and when the wraiths are distracted with melee attacks they'll still spawn mummies. This is something of a huge turn off for me as i've actually RQ now due being so quickly being overwhelmed by 3 wraiths who spawned in close succession (without rushing the next wave in).
Outside of those two things this game is once again incredibly enjoyable and a very welcoming feel to the TD genre. It can be frustrating, especially with tower placements at times, but that's the challenging part of it as well. Finding the best ways to maximize your Militia and defense towers range/damage. No tower is better than the other as each one is required to beat a map, the hero's are a welcoming part (in my mind) to the TD genre. The upgrades can feel a bit forceful in what you have to get first in this one however but make the game give a reason to actually get more stars and do better.  I still recommend the game, even though the Sand Wraiths are a huge turn off as well as the grinding feature in a TD game.

My favourite game of 2016.
Plays like a town building worker placement board game with some deck building on the side.
You are racing to meet your Victory Point target before you run out of turns. If you are successful you move on to the next phase where you keep all the infrastructure you have built, but the actions which give you Victory Points change. After you beat all three phases you win the map and increase one rank.
Each rank you go up increases the number of Victory Points required to beat the next map, however if you lose two maps in a row your rank decreases by one. This does a really good job of making sure things never get too hard or too easy for you.
Definately a good game, but there is not much to do atm. Would recommend to pick this one up post-beta.

I just want to begin by saying I am basing this off my "personal" experience and understand that plenty of people are having technical issues however I am not 1 of them.
This game lacks some of the story depth of previous assassin's creeds titles but makes up for it in my opinion by the sheer scope of the game world, Paris is huge and full of collectables and side missions that can keep you occupied for quite some time.  The games new combat system seems well received by what I've seen however I personally do miss the instant death counters of previous games, but not having god mode does make you approach missions with a more stealth frame of mind then the old run and stab approach (atleast until you get better gear).  The game does lack the fun and quirky side characters of previous games however i do enjoy how smooth the main character is.  The new parkour system works a treat after you get use to it with less moments of getting stuck on a wall then previous titles.
Pros
- Massive and beutiful city
- Lots of side quests and collectables
- Plenty of item customization including being able to spec for different play styles.
- Fun multiplayer co-op missions
- Beutiful graphics
- Improved parkour
Cons
- Reported issues with frame rates (personally i dont have this issue)
- No instant kill counters (personal preference however a lot of people like this change)
- Story doesn't have the depth of previous games (still pretty fun though)
- No quirky side characters (as in Leonardo from 2 or blackbeard etc from BF)
- Some clipping issues etc (pretty sure they have been fxed in a patch)
Conclusion
If your one of the people who really enjoyed going around ac2 collecting every little thing and doing side quests I strongly recommend this game, the game does have it's flaws however the sheer scope they aimed for is magneficent.  Even the story while worse then some previous titles is decent and i much prefer the game as a whole to say AC3 haha.

Age of Empires 3 is a classic RTS that pits towns against each other in a race for resources and ultimately, military domination. The varied maps and civilizations allow many playstyles to be possible. On a desert map, trees may be scarce, creating a struggle to control the limited timber. Or, on a swamp map there may be very little land suitable for construction, leaving you to build several tiny bases instead of one fortress and leaves you vulnerable to attacks. An Ottoman empire can churn out villagers to gather resources quickly until they can build the civ's crown jewel, the great bombard, a massive artillery cannon. A Dutch empire can build banks that spawn gold, an important currency to build advanced units. Once you think you've played a few matches and think you've learned the best way to play a civ, you learn that you can bring a deck of "cards" in each match. These are free units or important upgrades that can be spawned throughout a game. Winning matches earns experience, which can be used to unlock new cards in a tech tree fashion, largely unique to each civ.  Some sivs might seem weaker at first, but unlock a bit of their tech tree and they become incredibly powerful. The graphics and physics engine were far ahead of their time and although noticably old, are not an eye sore on this brilliantly fun game. Age of Empires is at its best with friends, so I highly recommend convincing a couple pals to buy it with you. The single downside is that you cannot make more than two teams, so you can play 3v3, but not 2v2v2. This is a minor blemish on an older game that does little to get in the way of enjoying this lovingly crafted strategy game.
