Axes and Acres Review
The review below, and others, can be found in my Announcements page
This is the second game (Steam, Apr 2016) by a small indie developer, BrainGoodGames.
. They had a great hit with Militia (on Steam Dec 2015),  and just released a new game (Skyboats, Steam Aug 2016). I'm a bit behind the Steam  release schedule; I only got around to picking up A&A this month. In the past two weeks,  I've put 46 hours into A&A, and can strongly recommend it.
For the record, I would recommend Militia as well. Although they're both turn-based  strategy (TBS) games, they each have a different vibe. Militia feels like the kind of  game an RTS player would like, whereas A&A feels more like a base-/city-builder. If you  preferred Dawn of War 2 to Dawn of War 1, then Militia's probably your game. But for fans  of Caesar, Pharaoh, Stronghold--games in which dealing with your city's growth and  development is the critical task, and dealing with armed invaders is only a passing  concern--A&A is definitely for you.
Building on the square-grid based, minimalistic art style of Militia, Axes and Acres is a  solid turn-based game with randomly generated villages and objectives during each round  of play. When a new round begins, three sets of sub-objectives are rolled, representing  three distinct phases of play. I believe the developers (BGG) refer to these as early,  mid, and late game phases. With the update near the end of August, victory points  required for the completion of each phase have been rebalanced to ensure equal strategic  difficulty during each phase. Complete all three phases, and you move up in difficulty.  Fail twice at a difficulty level, and you drop down to the previous level.
Militia felt more like a game of chess or checkers: the board is the same size each time,  and each piece moves and attacks in well-defined ways. A&A expands on this model in  several ways. Each 'Peasant' in your village is represented by a d6. You begin each round  with six peasants; reproducing to grow your population is a critical strategic point. While each Peasant die has the same faces (two Work, two Build, one Gather, one Reproduce which I like to call 'Heal'), the dice are rolled at the beginning of each of your turns, so your strategy in in part dictated by the faces that you roll each turn. Placing a die onto the board requires Food, one of three resources you must manage during each round. Do you spend this turn focusing on food gathering? Building? Gathering other resources? Your strategic decisions are made based on the number of VPs you need, how many turns you have left in each phase, and unexpected opportunities or hindrances provided by which faces your dice roll each turn.
Managing your resources in A&A actually feels a lot like Star Ruler 2--there exist a multitude of ways to transform one into another. At the beginning of a round, you start with five 'Motivation' cards. Building the higher-tier buildings in your village can provide you the opportunity to gain more cards. So it turns out that you have two additional resources: 'Moves' and 'Cards'. Six resources total: three literal (food, wood, stone), and three strategic (dice/people, moves, and cards). Like a card-building game, you want to keep your card stack strategically lean, because you must spend all of the cards in your stack before the stack reshuffles. Many cards give you two opportunities to use them, to use dice, and to interact with your board and other resources. But if you need to kill rampaging barbarians, having a glut of build cards won't help you!
At those advanced buildings, you have opportunities to train your peasants (and other dice) to become more advanced positions: woodsman (two gather faces, one wild), priest (three crusade faces, one wild), mason (three build faces, one wild, one stone), actor (always rolls wild, can be deployed as work, gather, heal, build, or crusade), and noble (two VP faces). Some phase objectives award you VPs for having two advanced peasants. Or perhaps your strategy requires more build faces than you've been rolling. In the later difficulty levels, the number of VPs required to finish the third phase become so high that you may just want to build a castle and convert your peasants to nobility, and brute force your way to victory.
Being used to playing 4X and Grand Strat games, the simplicity of A&A's interface put me off initially, but I warmed to it. I also thought that I'd eventually tire of the gameplay loop--it's a game of raw mechanics, not much story, not much customization, only a handful of buildings. I likened it to Star Ruler 2 earlier; I'd say that the two games have a lot in common: tightly intertwined mechanics, adoption of new strategic elements when the current situation demands it. I have found the mechanics compelling enough to keep me playing all month--my intrinsic motivation has become enthralled with the experience A&A provides!
Axes and Acres could just as easily be a solo board/dice game--BGG should probably consider kickstarting a hardcopy version.  :)  The use of the computer medium is less important for A&A than it was for Militia. However, the user interface, while simplistic, is not explicitly designed for mobile/touch devices. It could probably make use of keybindings, but it does give you hover-over information, and uses both left- and right-click commands.
I give A&A a solid recommendation to fans of strategy mechanics, minimalistic interfaces, and/or somewhat casual strategy themed games! I'm looking forward to reviewing BGG's newest game!

Notes before reading:
I purchased the game during a Steam Sale for $7.36 CAD, and the game time for a single playthough of the game is about 3-6 hours (depending on how you complete the game).
Review:
This game really makes you feel like a hacker without making the gameplay incredibly long and boring. The hacking in this game is no Watch_Dogs, you truly feel like a hacker sitting in front of your computer taking over the world and then completely destroying it. The introduction to the game is nice, and the tutorials are comprehensive enough. I got stuck on one mission, but there are complete guides on every mission if that does occur. I have already completed the game (not in the hour listed when writing, Steam for some reason did not calculate my play time correctly. The game is longer than that), and am now replaying the game to find the secrets I have missed, including a lot of missions which are hidden from players who aren't experienced with the game yet. (Secrets of which I happened to find on my second playthrough myself from the fury that arose when someone Forkbombed me and made my system BSOD).
No, this game does not have you writing code to take down enemies, but unless you are a programmer yourself, that would make for the most boring gameplay (Although, I hear else heart.break() does this gameplay well, not sure). This game does however simulate the feeling of a hacker without boring the player.
Highly recommended!
PS: Dev's have previously said that Modding and Multiplayer is on their to-do list. Seeing as the game is still being worked on, as Mac and Linux ports were just released a few weeks ago from the time of writing this, I have faith that the developers (developer?) will finish these tasks. In which case, the game will totally be worth the price!

It was once one of my favourite games. Imagine Minecraft, with mounts, dungeons, classes, less time consuming and less grindy.
The classes were great. There were so many options, each for a different playstyle, and it took about a week or two to get a new class. The great thing about that is that you don't rush a character, and you get the most out of that class. You get a feel for it's style, and then you can quickly change to a different class if you dont enjoy it.

The bosses are difficult, but not so difficult you get mad and annoyed. As long as you play it right, you can beat any boss. The dungeons are balanced, and the loot is balanced aswell.
Now: Why do I not recommend this game? I made it seem so amazing! Well, if you noticed at the beginning of this review, I said "This was ONCE one of my favourite games." You didn't need to pay money for it, and paying didn't give you a big advantage. You could obtain most items without paying, and those you needed to pay for, there was most likely an alternative. Well, now classes are only the premium currency. Classes seemed like the core part of this game. You'll get bored of one character too fast for it to even be worth paying real money to get a class, if you can only get one character, and then what are you gonna do? Spend money? In 90 hours, I didn't spend a single penny and had a blast with those 90 hours. The last 1.6 hours, though, were boring and bland because there was no way for me to get new characters without spending real money.
In my opinion, this game could've been one of the greatest, if it didn't demand you spend money to have a good time with it. Looks like another great free game was ruined by the lust for money. Don't get me wrong, the developers need to make money for the time and effort they put in this game, but there were plenty of ways they made money from it, including new classes

The game is Early Access, though in this case; That also means there has been hardly any promised updates since release.
If you do want to play this game, I would wait until its 'finished' according to the devs or else you're paying for a whole lot of promises instead of actual features.

My unfortunate Plague Doctor, Faintree, was the only one to survive a horrendously mismanaged and under-equipped trip into the dungeon. She has spent three weeks at the brothel, refusing to leave, and I can't blame her for that.
This game really is great. The art is great, the narrator (and the sound direction in general) is great, the gameplay is great, and the RNG goes both ways (which is great). Sometimes my heroes are critting for double digits, sometimes the enemies are the ones who get to do that. I never feel like the game has been unfair to me when one of my heroes dies, because hey, everybody's luck runs out eventually. Darkest Dungeon isn't the kind of game where you can just grind for a while, make the perfect squad, and then just win win win no matter what.
There's often a lot of planning that goes into another run at the dungeon, and sometimes maybe you forget to bring the things you really needed to survive effectively. Do you soldier on and hope the dice continually land in your favor, or do you stress out your heroes by escaping the dungeon, and remember to provision the proper supplies next time? Darkest Dungeon lets you play it incredibly safe, but it also never lets you feel like you can be perfectly prepared for every possible outcome, and that's what I love about it. You WILL lose your favorite heroes to something terrible, and your goal in Darkest Dungeon is to stave off that inevitability for as long as possible.
I've experienced no bugs or crashes, either, which definitely helps me feel positively about the game. Overall, a very polished experience that is well worth the $10 I paid for it during the sale. If I have one complaint, it's that some classes do feel a little underwhelming when compared to others--the Grave Robber in particular feels mostly like an improved Highwayman, for example--but that might just be because I haven't yet put in the hundreds of hours I can already feel I'm going to spend playing this game.
This game is a true 5 out of 5 for me, and I will definitely support the developers (Red Hook Studios) in the future.

(Performance Review)
So, just to start off with, I have a BELOW minimum requirements PC:
GPU: GeForce GT640
CPU: i5-3330 @ 3.0GHz
Memory: 8,00 GB RAM
After a few minutes of tweaking for the first time of running this game I find it amazing looking even with all the graphic options at "Low". With the new patch the cinematics run great and the whole game is what I call pretty playable. As for now, no overheating, the proc. is usually running at 60% of the whole capacity, no crashes AT ALL and co-op is running just perfectly. Not to mention I did get the latest NVIDIA drivers which got some specific stuff for AC: Unity to run a bit better and I'm glad to say it did work.
So, you got a few options here. If you have a minumim spec. computer you'll sure be able to run this game without lots of issues. Yes, I'm not playing at 120FPS or something and I'm not playing with maximum settings (I mean, is that really necessary for a game?) but hell I'm happy my low setup is able to run a decent playable version without issues compared to the "High-End setups" that keep crashing all the time.
If you want to have fun with a great game and you got a decent setup, get it. If you don't have at least a decent video card, you are probably going to struggle a bit. Like I just exposed, mine is nothing above minimum specs. and still can play without any sort of issue at all.
If you are only looking for the graphics and FPS and you don't have a decent/maximum setup, don't get it. You'll regret it.

Ok, ok, this review has gone through a few iterations so bear with me people.
When I first played LOTF, I absolutely despised it.  Being a big fan of the Souls games, I was looking forward to some Souls-esque but-without-getting-stomped-by-overpowerd-invasions fun.  But dang, Harken was slow and seemed to spend about 10 seconds winding up his attacks before actually throwing them, and I quickly grew bored of this game and its unresponsive controls.  So, my first review was rather scathing, and lo many a fan boy/girl posted some rather immature and insulting comments, most of which have been deleted.  I’m a stoopid noob and I should go back to candy crush saga, apparently.  I also need to 'git gud' even though the difficulty of this game (which isn't much) was never an issue...
Being a cheapskate and wanting to get my money’s worth out of the game, I forced myself to complete.  And you know what?  LOTF is not a bad game.  I might even have enjoyed it a wee bit.  But I would not recommend this game unless it is on sale – because there are much better games (i.e. Dark Souls) which do everything LOTF does only much better.
Still, LOTF is bloody gorgeous, looking like Todd Macfarlane and Warhammer Fantasy got together to make a Cannibal Corpse album cover.  The armour and weapon designs are so ludicrously spikey and evil that I want to break out my old Slayer albums.  Sound is also great, with satisfying clunks and crashes giving combat a satisfying feel.  The bosses are super cool too.  I also particularly liked the system up upgrading weapons and armour with runes, which is very simple but kinda nice anyway.
However, I found the controls to feel really unresponsive.  No matter what class you play as, there’s a significant lag between actually hitting the attack button and Harken swinging whatever oversized spike metal thingy he is carrying.  It lead me to a lot of frustration, as I signed in vain while the enemy would rush off for a cup of tea, do the washing, then come back and put their shield up in the time it takes Harken to wind up his attack.  Second, the game is not really challenging, and it doesn’t have difficulty settings.  Most enemies can be overpowered just by circling endlessly and button mashing, and many of the bosses can be easily beaten on first try once their attack pattern has been seen a few times.  I understand that NG+ is more of a challenge, but I’d already lost interest by then.
In summary, my opinion, which you don’t have to agree with, is that LOTF is an ok Dark Souls-lite game, but I wouldn’t recommend it because Dark Souls, even Dark Souls 2, does EVERYTHING infinitely better aside from graphics.  Furthermore, if I’m in the mood for some fantasy hack and slash and I’m not in the mood for Dark Souls, I’d play Devil May Cry, Darksiders 2, Dragons Dogma, Revengence or something long before I’d go for LOTF.  but hey there seems to be a lot of ppl who really loved this...what does a stoopid noob like me know anyway? git gud or go home...
Edit - Now that Dark Souls 3 is out there is no need to even contemplate this game.  Or go with Salt and Sanctuary if your a 2d indie hispter - that said, if they make a sequel i'd give it a look as, if they got the gameplay right, this could easily be the Slayer album cover made flesh the never-dying 12 year old inside me is always looking for.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Redemption
Update Version: Initial Release
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Gameplay footage:
It has been a while since I have picked up a semi-brawler on the Steam store. Most of the time I worry about weak combo systems or cheap enemy attacks bogging down the experience and end up avoiding the genre all together. This time around, I didn't really have the opportunity to research the combat system and decided to charge in blind. I can safely say that the game has some interesting ideas, but fails to really present anything extraordinary at this point in Early Access. This doesn't mean the game itself is terrible, just dull for the most part.
Visually the game is competent, but overall bland. The environments are restricted to a post-apocalyptic desert or a ruined factory cluttered with destructible barrels and oversized boxes. NPC models look rough with some decent costume designs for the playable characters. Enemies range from mutants to insects, including one or two modified appearances to each enemy type. I didn't notice any real texture abnormalities outside some clipping issues with doors and will say the attack animations do feel relatively fluid. This allows combat to remain responsive, which is more important than next-generation graphics. If you came here for aesthetic, you will be pleased with the texture quality and character models at least. This contrasts the sound design, which has a few metal and techno music tracks. Basic attacks and skills produce sound to help with hit feedback and the enemy does respond with painful groans, but the characters don't produce sound.
If there is a story at this point, I haven't seen it. The game begins with your character saving a young woman from a jetpack clad goon only to abandon any notions of either one of them soon after. You inevitably run into the goon again later in the form of a standard boss, leading me to the conclude the story aspect just hasn't been added yet. None of the residence are fleshed out, the player characters lack any biographical information and the setting has no bar rings outside the name. A story isn't really a concern for a brawler, just don't expect one going into it.
I am rather conflicted on how to rate the available content in the game. Out of the sixteen total heroes, only six of them are playable. Each one has a unique set of skills and have a different feel to their basic attack. I managed to reach level 11 with the young lady using the mini launcher in four hours, completing the eleven stages currently out. Once you do finish the last level, Hard mode opens up and you can progress over the same missions in greater difficulty. There is also another difficulty setting following it as well as challenge modes (2 at the moment) and deathmatch PvP from 1v1 to 5v5 (I was unable to find anyone though). Design wise, each level is filled with corridors occupied by a set of enemies that must be killed to progress to the next area. A boss tops off each pre-made level, making the enemy numbers and layout the same every time you enter. The game is missing the necessary variety to keep things interesting, instead opting for difficulty and leveling to pad out the game while they add more levels.
Like any ARPG, nothing is more important than the combat system built into it. This is, unfortunately, still a weak point for the game. You have six unique skills that you learn (the final skill is acquired at level 9) and a basic attack to round out the entire combo system. It has the Y button listed as well, but no matter how hard I tried, I couldn't get it to activate. The skills do pack a punch and carry some artistic flare in delivery, but they require mana to use. This makes the basic X spamming your primary function. Enemy AI is average with plenty of telegraphed moves to help you dodge (Z) out of the way. They have a tendency to chain attacks if they catch you at a bad moment, causing your HP to descend rapidly. Ranged turrets also cause a knock back while some of the little gremlins can stun you with their projectile. It can feel very cheap at times, but the strategic aspect of rounding up the enemies into a good position does help offset the underutilized combo system.
Inventory management is shared across all characters. Gold, equipment, crafting materials and even consumables are carried over whenever you switch. The only time consumables won't carry over is if you have the items hot-keyed to the quick actions bar. This makes it extremely easy to trade off equipment that you find on one character without the hassle of a secondary system. You can purchase items, but thankfully any item can drop during your progression including gold and crafting items. As of this writing, there is no crafting system so anything related to it can either be sold or kept for when it is finally implemented.
Problems are plenty though ranging from minor to absolutely frustrating. Crashes are frequent and make the next issue exceptionally annoying. If you disconnect from the server, switch characters or quit the game, any experience you gain during a level's progression will be lost and reset to 0. Items can become unobtainable if an enemy is killed in a corner or up against a wall. Attacks also have the chance to elevate in the same manner, which will cause it to miss any nearby enemies due to range discrepancies. Bosses can be forced against the door frames, rendering them unable to give chase and allowing the player to eliminate them from a safe distance (mostly possible with the Technician). During certain boss introductions and cutscenes, you can become vulnerable to attacks and risk death. The ground pound from the stage six boss will hit you after the cutscene ends and any enemies still alive during the stage 11 main boss fight will be able to kill you during the exit cutscene. I understand this is early access, but some of these can be detrimental to reliable progress.
At the end of the day, I found Redemption to be a good introduction. It is still a proof of concept, but the combat feels smooth with a great deal of feedback to complement it. Plenty of problems hinder the overall progression of the game which hopefully will get ironed out sooner rather than later. Unfortunately, some of these problems make it rather difficult for me to recommend Redemption at this time. I wish I could say otherwise, but for now I recommend watching to see how it evolves before jumping in. I will return to these barren wastes in the next six months to hopefully change this decision.
Pros
- Visual quality isn't bad with some nice costume designs
- Combat animations are smooth with plenty of visual and sound feedback
- Unique skill sets for each character
Cons
- Combat is lackluster (no real combo system)
- Crashes frequently
- Content is rather thin at the moment (can be offset with the increased difficulty)
Additional note: Requires you to be online to play

I'm going to recommend The Old Tree, but only because:
1. You play it in 15 minutes.
2. It's free.
That being said, it is not a great game, nor is it exceptional in atmosphere. Escorting the tiny alien baby is a rather nice concept, but in my opinion not enough is done with it, and not enough is shown. Of course, out of a 15 minute puzzle game you can't expect any wonders in gameplay (and indeed, none are delivered), but the limited art we're shown for the most of the game failed to impress me. The ending was pretty, at least, but saying that it's an atmospheric game and then give us very little music in mostly black corridors feels very odd.
Comparisons to both Samorost and Machinarium are wholly unfair to the two, as they are in all regards superior games with superior atmosphere. The only thing The Old Tree has that is (arguably) better is the faster play time.
In short, I wasn't impressed by The Old Tree as many others seem to have been, but perhaps I'm just grumpy. Come for the free game, stay for the cute alien, I suppose.

[Note : This review applies to both Season 1 and Season 2 taken together but applies to each one individually]
Before buying this game, I didn't expect anything special. I knew it had good reviews and that's why I tried it.
It turned out to be by far the BEST COMMERCIAL PRODUCT I've ever bought in my LIFE, better than any movie, game, book or anything else I've ever bought so far.
The game genre is said to be a "Point'n'Click", but in fact it isn't that much ; there is no puzzle, there is just the story, and you implicated in it.
I couldn't say this is a "game" though, you won't play, but you will be told a story, a beautiful story in witch you will be emotionnaly implicated as long as it speaks you to.
Basically, I could say that the game is a big cutscene that you influate by your actions (by what you say in fact, choosing how to answer to the main characters). I KNOW that it sounds strange or bad, but it isn't, there is no way to properly describe how good this "game" is.
To be a bit more clear, I would only see 3 reasons why someone could not like a game like that :
● They don't like cell-shading graphics (look at the screenshots)
● They absolutely hate stories that take place in a Zombie Apocalypse environnement
● They don't have a good English Level or don't know how to Install translations (2nd Season is in Full-English)
Pros :
+ Incredibely good voice-acting and credible characters
+ The way you are emotionally implied in the story, never had I seen that before in ANY game
+ The possibility to "influence" the story and that you always feel that what's happening is because of your choices
+ The whole story is intense, everything is useful, there would be no part to scrap down, I wasn't bored a SINGLE SECOND.
+ Clementine as a deuteragonist (Season 1) and protagonist (Season 2), Tomboys as a main character FTW. :heart:
+ The story is in NOW WAY predictable, you never know what will happen next.
+ Incredibly good "filming" and animation and character facial expression, as good and even better than most TV Series.
+ The end... really... only time I cried in a Video Game.
+ Good Music (special mention for the End Credits)
+ Simple controls : WASD + Mouse
+ There is no need of a Gaming PC to run this, most computers will do the job
+ You don't play this game, this is the game that plays you
Cons :
- It has an end... no really... NO CON
(-) Can have some resolution problems that can be fixed by the simple addition of a line in the start options on Steam
(-) Translations in other languages than English are fan-made, the one for Season 2 isn't included with the Game ; play in English if you could for maximal effect.
Conclusion : A MUST-TRY (at least in Sales, and at least for Season 1), 11/10 : best "game" and product I've ever purchased in my life ; I know that every game I'll play for a decade will surely not be as good as this one ; this was a once-in-a-lifetime experience, THANKS Telltale Games =) + please, Clementine again in Season 3 :beg:
PS. There is absolutely no need to know the Comic Series or the TV Series "The Walking Dead" to enjoy this game, the story is an original one based on the Comics.
PSS. You will certainly need a little time to fully enter in the story, try to play at least 2 hours before saying that you definitely don't like it or you could miss something.
PSSS. You need to play this "game" ALONE for a maximum effect.

The action story boards never have truely divergent paths.  Some people argue that while choices made cannot change the ending, but that they do change the way the story plays out. Hardly... Thin veil games do the minumum work possible, provide a reasonable story that might even be considered good to people who dont read often. Real choice would require writing a lot of material that may potentially go unseen, there is maybe 2% of material that may go unseen in any thin veil game and this is generally limited to minor changes in dialog.
To truely simulate the stress of group dynamics in a survival situation you absoloutely need to include elements of AI. The look and premise of the game seemed interesting enough, however the game has one significant flaw, and that is complete lack of written documentation and/or wiki. Instead, you are given a tutorial that does not explain anything, only orders you to do certain action (that is NOT the way I want to learn about games), and lengthy tutorial video that of course cannot be consulted when you want to explore a particular feature of the game.
This would not be such a problem in case of an established genre like point and click adventures that are simple enough to pick up and play. However, this particular game has very unusual conventions, even grasping what exactly are actions available to players and what are their use and impact on the game. For example, you spend workers to move other workers. How the heck you should "discover" this peculiar mechanic without a proper manual?
The interface is a haphazard mixture of buttons of various sizes, with vague descriptions like "Build 3". Build 3 what? Compare this to games like Renowned Exploreres that create a set of distinctive symbols representing knowledge, renown, supplies, etc, that simplify the understanding of the game quite a lot. Yes, there are tooltips, but they are very inconsistent in the way they provide information.
Axes and Acres may be even a very good game, but I will never know. Fearing that I will not have enough time to decide if I like it due to the necessary battle with  the interface and lack of explicit explanation of the game fundamental principles, I have requested a refund.

The screenshots for the game may make the game look simple. That’s because the surface layer is pretty simple. The old adage holds true – don’t judge a book by its cover and never judge a game solely by its screenshots. Once you dig beneath the surface what you will discover is one of the deepest strategy games to be released in 2016 – indie developer or otherwise. Axes and Acres is a step by step dice and resource management game.
This is not the type of game that can be judged by its graphics. They don’t need to be any more advanced than what they are. Where the game is to be judged is in its game play. This is a nearly flawless board game. In fact, I was more than a little surprised to find that this wasn’t a board game before the game was launched onto Steam. I can see this being the type of game that strategy buffs could sit at a table and spend countless hours playing. This is the type of game that is designed to be played endlessly (number of rounds or individual games) and it serves that style perfectly yet each round can be played and completed in under an hour. It’s the perfect game for those who are limited to short play sessions as well as players who are wanting to dedicate themselves to a specific game.  Where the game is lacking in graphics the music by Doctor Turtle makes for an inspiring choice for the game.
The aim of the game is to gain a specified amount of victory points within a predetermined number of turns. You are set tasks to complete in order to obtain these points. For example, you have to create X number of houses, Y number of roads, kill X number of creatures/barbarians, etc. Each game has three phases with an event taking place between phases. I have only played at the lower difficulty levels and so far have only noticed positive events but I am certain that if you were to play at higher levels of difficulty you would find a mix or worse.
Where most players will have difficulties in absorbing the play is the steep learning curve. The game has a tutorial but even with the explanations and the detailed work going into it the game is still rather difficult to learn. Therefore it may not be as accessible as what I would have hoped for. Players who lose patience or don’t have the time to dedicate to learning the depth of strategy required to be successful in this game will quickly turn away and move onto something else.
If you’re a fan of strategy games you are going to want to get your hands on Axes and Acres. At under $10 it’s a bargain if you’re ready to commit to it in your gaming schedule.

V1.01a Review, based mostly off of 1.00 gameplay — 21.4 hours logged
tldr: Step-by-step thinking dice and resource management game with clean graphics and somewhat steep learning curve.
Recommended for those with the time and patience to learn the game.
Short Review
------------------------
Axes and Acres is a strategy dice/card game with survival elements. You manage food, wood, and stone resources to deploy dice, construct buildings and other actions to gain enough Victory Points to win and progress to a harder rank.
Careful management of your resources is needed, and using your dice as a resource is part of the fairly steep learning curve. You start with 6 dice and spend them not only for their face value (building, gathering, working, and reproducing more dice), but also one die to "confirm" each action, and one die to move 2 spaces. You also use cards to perform actions more efficiently to save on dice.
Graphics are clean and well done. Music is relaxing and sound effects sparse in a good way.
Recommended for strategy gamers with patience for the learning curve.
Long Review
------------------------
Axes and Acres' menu is very simple. You have some tutorial levels, a teaching video I didn't watch, "Play" mode, and an options menu with some basic sound and display options.
(The tutorial has been improved in V1.01, but I have not tested it yet.)
V1.00's tutorial may be very confusing and frustrating even for seasoned strategy gamers as myself. I had to restart some tutorial levels several times just to pass them, and I still didn't really get the game's basic mechanics when finished.
The main mode of the game, "Play" mode, starts you out as rank 1 and will progress you 1-2 levels on a win, and decrease your rank on I believe two losses in a row. This flow is actually very nice, and has kept me playing for hours trying to get better at the game and achieve a higher rank. Maps are procedurally generated.
Axes and Acres is a strategy game with some very concrete, step-by-step thinking involved. Careful management of your resources is needed to succeed, and using your dice as a resource is part of the fairly steep learning curve. You manage food, wood, and stone resources to deploy dice, construct buildings and other actions to gain enough Victory Points to win and progress to a harder rank.
Your objective is to achieve a certain amount of Victory Points (VP) in a certain amount of turns. VP are gained through completing the phase objective on the top of your screen (ex build a road, have 4 houses, hunt an animal, kill a barbarian). Harder ranks require more VP relative to the amount of turns given. Each game has three phases with a VP threshold required to meet phase two and three. When the phase changes, an event happens (positive event on lower difficulties, negative on higher ones) and your three phase objectives change as well.
You start with 6 dice and spend them not only for their face value (building, gathering, working, and reproducing more dice), but also one die to "confirm" each action, and one die to move 2 spaces. You can't save up extra moves gained this way, though dice left over at the end of your turn do add 1 move to a pool you can use anytime. You also use up to 3 cards a turn to perform actions more efficiently to save on dice. This detailed management may seem tedious to many players, but after playing this fun game a while you will get used to it, and is all part of the strategy and fun of Axes and Acres. :)
The player starts out a match with just two houses by a river. They must expand their infrastructure over the course of the game to gain enough VP in time. Axes and Acres features 15 buildings that will let your dice navigate the map, collect resources easier, "upgrade" your dice, generate powerful cards to your deck, and more! It takes hours to realize the potential of buildings and their effects.
Graphics are nice and simple, with a large and clean interface. Don't confuse simple with lazy — the graphics are very well done and all fit a cohesive art style. The music is doable, there's two or so acoustic-y tracks that play and serve as some good background music, though about half of the time I like to listen to my own. Sound effects are simple but nicely done, nothing over-the-top or annoying and fit in well with the relaxing atmosphere (minus the stressful thinking involved :P) and minimalist style of the game.
Overall, I would recommend Axes and Acres for those with the time and patience to learn the game. There is great fun to be had for those that enjoy step-by-step thinking and setting both short and long-term goals for a level.

Each time you win, you play the same game again, but with fewer turns to reach your goal. The path to victory changes a bit each time, as does a few bonuses. The map also changes, but I find this to be of minor importance, as I love building roads.
After a few games it gets a bit boring and repetative, but this only lasts a few hours, as I find myself draw back to this simple, yet well crafted game.
There are so many ways that this game could be expanded, with new challenges, more variety between missions and unique challenges. I hope the devs will look into this, to keep me comming back for another swing with my axe, out there on the acres.

Based off of the player-base passion, I have tried every iteration of Dark Souls. I keep thinking I'm overlooking something, but I think the problem for me is, having poured in hundreds of hours in Dragon's Dogma Dark Arisen, and in particular the post game content featuring the single best dungeon crawl experience I've ever encountered (Bitter Black), to then come to Dark Souls is such a massive drop in quality of gameplay and game design. The movement mechanics are far more clunky in Dark Souls, and the playstyle absolutely and utterly limited to timing dodges and healinig potions. The thing about Dragon's Dogma is, you can have that dungeon crawl experience, but then you can also go back out into the massive, open world and it is just so much more expansive.
If you want the challenge of Dark Souls in Dragon's Dogma, you can actually create a character that is intentionally limited to only being able to do what you can do in Dark Souls (Just with far better movement mechanics and animation fluidity) and then select "hard mode", then complete the first phase of the game to unlock the post-game world, which is much more difficult, and let me know how that goes for you.
Pros:
Bosses that hit very hard and don't die easily
Decent crawl layout (though I think the first version was the most ingenious of them)
Good fight mechanics (undermined by lumbering and clunky movement mechanics, which can be made to seem even worse if you prefer to play with keyboard and mouse as I do), with huge emphasis on timing, which actually takes something resembling skill to implement successfully.
cons:
Not as great a port as you would hope for, at least not from a big franchise game, especially if you're a keboard/mouse person.
Graphics are disappointing given the recent release date.
World is not immersive, it's more like an arcade game.
Fights are too repetative. The bosses themselves are very unique, but you are not. At all.
Too dependant on pain = satisfaction. In other words, if you die a lot on a boss, once you finally kill him you feel as if you have achieved something. This is appealing to many gamers, which is why the game "getting over it" is selling so well. It's the exact same concept. You go through hell to get to moments of victory, but they are only moments of victory BECAUSE you had to go through hell.
I can't fathom spending that much time doing the same thing over and over, regardless of whether or not the game is on sale.
Incredibly fun dungeon crawling, excellent soundtrack and narration, endless replayability.
A rather primitive mobile port with badly adapted controls. It could've been worse. But I don't see how.

WARNING: THIS GAME IS NOT FOR MOST PEOPLE, WHICH IS WHY I AM NOT RECOMMENDING IT!
This game is the prime example of tone becoming gameplay, the overall tone being despair. This overwhelming sense of despair asks the biggest question in all of gaming: what makes a game good?
Darkest Dungeon is a hardcore lovecraftian turn based dungeon crawler where the only thing that is guranteed is failure. You are the inheritor of your uncles estate which has been overun by monstrosities and its up to you to save the lands from otherworldly horrors, well, its up to a group of four beaten and war-torn adventurers that you send into the dark dungeons on your behalf.
They wont complete the quests a majority of the time. Most will die, either from a deadly blow from a vile creature or a heart attack from too much stress. Those who come back, victorious or not, will be both physically and mentally scarred. They will beg you not to send them back in, but you will do it anyway because they are better fighters. Sometimes even the best of fighters will be overwhelmed and struck down, wasting countless hours of leveling and alot of money you spend on their equipment.
You will lose. That should be this game's motto. No matter how skilled you are at this game, most of the time the odds arent in your favor. Thats just how it is. This game captures the feeling of despair perfectly. You will feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥playing this game, and whatever hope you have will be taken away at the next adventurers death. So back to the question of what makes a game good. Is a game good because it is fun, or is it because it captures a tone so well that you will be mentally drained after playing a few minutes of it? Seeing as a majority of people are looking to play a game to escape the despair of life, they won't like the overwhelming despair that this game gives. They won't understand the true lovecraftian feel that the game gives off, and even if they do they won't want to play it again, so I can't recommend it to them.
This is why the 'yes' 'no' system doesn't work, because people wont read into what people are actually saying. They will just see 'mixed' and say "Eh, mixed, guess I wont buy it.". This is a game purely for those looking for a true lovecraftian game, a pure feeling of dread and despair. If you enjoy that then I implore you to buy it, but I can't recommend it for most gamers.

Arno goes on a trip with his father, meets a pretty young girl, and soon finds his deceased father lying dead at his feet. He grows up into a roguish man with a fondness for getting himself into trouble. His bad boy ways catch up with him as he tossed into prison after he is framed for murder. Coincidentally, he is placed in prison with a man who served with his father as an Assassin. With this new knowledge he takes on the role his Father once held and starts on his path to revenge.
What we liked
Splendid Visuals - France is beyond gorgeous, and this is easily one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. The detail of each of the buildings is superb. The increased number of civilians are what truly steal the show, with over 100+ NPC’s crowding the streets and causing havoc. Each of the main characters are painstakingly detailed and have accurate and convincing facial expressions to match. This is easily the best looking and detailed Assassin’s Creed title to date.
Stealthy – I always thought that for a game all about Stealth, Assassin’s Creed had one of the absolute worst systems for doing so. Someone using the Animus has played a little bit of Splinter Cell, because Arno has finally learned what other Assassin’s haven’t… how to sneak around and use cover. It isn’t perfect by any means, but at least the options have expanded significantly.
Wealth of Content – Unity makes sure that you don’t ever have to worry about running out of things to do. There is so much content that exists in the game that it can be a bit overwhelming at first. Once that map opens up and each of those quests and collectibles appear on the screen, you’ll wonder if you will ever complete it all.
Cooperative Play – I’ve been dying for an Assassin’s Creed to allow for some true cooperative play. Unity does a great job at setting up missions for up to four players, or allowing them to free-roam and take on the world with their pals. If only the game wasn’t a mess in pretty much every other way.
What we didn't like

Buggy – What would an Assassin’s Creed game be without bugs? From people sinking into the floor and regularly popping into view, to the odd appearance of textures forming in the background. This title is full of all sorts of nonsense that will surely create many a YouTube Blooper Reel.

Not Optimized – I have a GTX 980 and this game has all sorts of issues playing the game past the high setting. The frame-rate sporadically dips from 60 to 45 during cut scenes or anywhere there are tons of people standing around the city. This game was clearly was designed for a graphics card that will only appear when we get warp drive technology. It makes it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to configure for both looks and performance, and the random leap between frame-rate can get in the way of the experience.

The PS4 version on the other hand is filled with muddy textures, and basically becomes a slide show in most areas. This actually impacts combat and movement responsiveness which made it harder for me to parry attacks. The game had the nerve to freeze up randomly in some areas as well, while still sporting all of the buggy issues mentioned on the PC version. The console version is an absolute mess.

Terrible Story – The plot relies on the tried and true revenge trope and a lot of convenient moments so that Arno can kill people. Unlike the previous games in the series, assassinating a Templar figurehead will emit a wave of memories for Arno to pick up with his ESP or whatever godlike ability he possesses. The problem is that for some reason the story is led by his sudden visions and nthe meanderings of the Assassin’s running the animus from the outside.

The story outside of the animus highlights the Assassins finding a random hacker, and asking him to help them beat Templars. He has no choice but to help them of course, and that’s the whole back story. You play a random guy who has to stop the Templars from stealing history… go you! I feel like I’m playing a random episode of Carmen San Diego or something, nah… that would be cool.

Stiff Combat – There are a few changes that have made the life of an Assassin much harder. Enemies strike with a bit more precision and can kill an under-geared assassin in one or two shots. Other than that the combat remains strikingly similar to previous games in the series, and in some ways it takes many a step back. Arno can get hit while trying to finish animations, or fail to properly lock-on a target to attack someone at his back. He will often flail about attempting to fight, and the overall feel of combat feels slower and less refined. It looks bland in comparison to games like Shadow of Mordor, which proves that sword combat can be fast, fluid, and visceral.
Parkour fail – Assassin’s Creed games are notorious for ignoring the problems with its automated navigation system. In fact, Ubisoft promised that Unity’s climbing system was “overhauled” for the Next Generation. If by overhauled they meant they add some pretty animations and kept the awkward loss of momentum issues… I’d agree. Anyone expecting quick and fluid animation as shown in E3 video will be sorely disappointed.

Outside content – Assassin’s Creed Unity has a collection of content within the game that cannot be accessed without other apps. You have to download the companion app and sign up for the initiates’ website to access certain chests in-game. So unless you feel the need to get all these excess programs, you won’t be able to enjoy all the content.

Conclusion
As it stands as of the very first week of release, Assassin’s Creed Unity is a technical mess full of bugs and performance issues on every platform. When you can get around the frame drops and the glitches, the gameplay doesn’t make great strides improve on the tried and true formula. Assassin’s Creed Unity earns a Fans Only from Geek Citadel. This franchise has taken a spiral due to the lack of attention paid to creating a working game.
The most volatile part of the problem is when well-known video game journalists like IGN, Kotaku, and many more don’t let us know these problems exist. They wait until we’ve all started boohooing after we purchased the game, but they have clearly had their hands on it a week ahead of schedule. Right after that they want to make an article saying “You should stop buying games early,” so they can fit into the mold. No guys, you should have created an article stating that this game is awful before release.
I know a lot of these “video game journalists” are afraid to lose the free games they receive from companies. Yet people on YouTube go out of our way to buy a game, play it, and create a review without a handout from publishers. If we can take our time and do that without fear of being blacklisted by these companies… why can’t Gamespot, IGN, and Kotaku? They get paid to do this stuff, so where is the journalistic integrity when we need it most? Don’t be afraid to say before we spend $60 on a game that it is garbage.
Publishers also seem to think they can just push a game out the door because it “should be released by now.” That’s an easy way to push garbage onto us people who are paying for these games. It’s an unforgivable practice to ship a game as retail in such a broken state. Assassin’s Creed Unity is a game I want to like, but the more I try to play it the more the flaws hold back my experience. For a game branded as a full release, it absolutely feels like a game that belongs in Early Access.

There are only two games I consider to be perfect; Bayonetta and DOOM. No review of Bayonetta will do this game any justice, you'll just have to experience it for yourself. The combat is amazing and is the most fun combat system I've ever experienced. You don't need to know every single combo to succeed, all you need to know is when to dodge. You basically rewarded with everything that you do. If you dodge right when an enemy attacks you enter something called Witch Time which slows down time and allows you to unleash a bunch of attacks and combos on enemies. I accidently restarted a chapter (which yes can happen if you're not careful) and wasn't even upset about it because the gameplay is just that good. The story is great and actually holds my interest, it's another thing that drives me to keep playing the game. It's not the most complex story but it isn't♥♥♥♥♥♥either. The writing and comedy is outstanding and is the funniest game I've played so far. It never fails to give a good laugh when it tries to. If you didn't already know, this is a VERY sexual game. There is no nudity, but it gets real damn close to it. If a sexy witch that does all sorts of sexual poses isn't your thing than DO NOT play this game. With all that being said, this is a game you simply have to experience to understand where all the love is coming from. The port is also amazing, with the only issue I'm encountering being that when I press ALT + Z (to enter GeForce Experience) GeExp will sometimes just close itself and then I can't move or access menus or ALT + Tab or anything. I can still do flips and attack but I can't move. The only thing you can do when this happens that isn't related to the game is to CTRL + ALT + DEL. You can collect records and notes in the game, that can help you out later on. They aren't invasive and don't require you to look around every single corner or do obnoxious grinds just to get them.
This game is the definition of perfection and I suggest everyone reading this to pick this game up at full price, and if it's on sale than buying this is truly a no brainer. Even if you didn't like DmC Devil May Cry from 2013 you will definitely love this game. Platinum did a great job making this and they definitely did a great job porting this.

1.0 Update (edited 8/6/2016):
The game is at the core same as before. Yes, there are a bunch of things that I personally don't like with the 1.0 changes, but there are mods for that and I see where chucklefish was going with what they did. Fun game, bunch of new stuff, progression is a bit wonky because there is no handholding and you just have to figure out what to do. This can make is real hard to learn the system, but once you do it's very self consistant. I still definately recomend it if you want an exploration/building game.
At the heart it's still very much a game where if you like bulding and exploring you're in for dozens of hours of fun. If you want lore you can go read books in villages and dungeons for even more hours. And then you can use those things you collected to uild your own awesome stuff to show off. Contrast that though to if you want to do combat and "story" progression. If you do the game will get old pretty quick.
The game is "like" Terraria in style and genre, but the focus and core gameplay is completely and absolutely different. It's like saying Smash Bros and Tekken are the same style and genre and then trying to compare them directly. They're very different types of fighting games, just like Starbound and Terraria are very different types of tile sidescrollers or w/e you call them.
A lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥you see trashing the game is about how the Devs haven't lived up to their promises, which in some aspects they haven't, and in some aspects the game feels disjointed in it's design (lack of tile protection in some RNG dungeons). But they have stated they're comitted to developing post 1.0 content and the scope of their original kickstarter/early access was on the scale of Starcitizen's scope, which is honestly absurd to hold them to. Sure they should not have made the promises they couldn't keep, but equally to blame are people who expect them to keep absurd promises they made 4 years ago when they were fledging developers and didn't know just just how much work creating an engine from scratch and all the assets would be. I would rather the game be in a decent state and pushed to 1.0 than have it be perpetually 0.8-9 trying to chase stretch goals that are not worth the implementation effort to get into the 1.0 build.

These days it's extremely rare to see an original game design within the realm of video games. It's also hard to find elegant strategy games that are easy to learn and unfold their depth by the combination of relatively straight-forward rules. Axes and Acres delivers on both fronts!
The game resembles an economic solitaire board game, but uses the digital format to take full advantage of randomization (map, cards, goals, dice) to keep every playthrough fresh. All of the randomness happens before the player is making decisions though and can be mitigated in various ways, so it never feels unfair but more like a set of conditions you have to make the best out of every turn.
On top of that, the game uses a ranking system to dynamically adjust the difficulty to the player's skill every match. It's a feature far too few single-player games use.
All in all this is, so far, probably the most interesting game I've played this year.

English:
As shown, I have only spent little time so far with this gem, but I think I have made up my mind far enough to give it a thumbs up.
The game will appeal especially to fans of abstract board games, puzzles and solitair games. The idea is based around making the best of each situation, using the given tiles on board, the dices you throw each turn and the individual goals for each level. It will award people who are good in planing ahead and are a little creative. Brain-wise I found it pretty demanding. There is an interactive tutorial and a link to a You-Tube video explaining some concepts to get you started. You will still have to do some trial- and error though, but I did like this exploring side of the game, trying to learn the mechanisms by yourself and how things work together.
The further you will get, the more it will count to make the best out of every single move, as the goals become quickly quite demanding.
The developer seems to be a nice guy and is interested in feeback, so I'm sure the next update isn't gonna be far.
Some negativ issues as well:
- I have encounterd once some graphical glitches in the tutorial missions and only there. I was not able to reproduce it. So probably it was some very rare event. I have contacted the developer about it already and he will look into it.
- It's strictly English only. That might be a problem to some.
- The music won't set you on fire probably.
- I can't say if the game will become repetitive after 15-20 hours. Right now it's very exiting and I can't wait to give it another try.
Deutsch:
Ich habe bisher nur wenig Zeit mit dem Spiel verbracht, allerdings gefällt es mir bisher, so dass ich mich entschlossen habe eine kleine Empfehlung auszusprechen.
Das Spiel wird sicherlich insbesondere Freunden abstrakter Brettspiele, Puzzelspiele und Solitärspiele zusagen. Es geht im Prinzip darum, aus dem Würfelglück, in Kombination mit den Begebenheiten auf dem Spielplan und den gesetzten Zielen eine individuelle Strategie zu erarbeiten. Gefördert werden die Fähigkeiten Planung und (ein wenig) Kreativität. Nach so einem Level, dampft einem ganz schön der Kopf. Das interaktives Tutorial bereitet einen in drei Stufen auf das Spiel vor, ein You-Tube Video gibt es auch dazu. Danach kann man loslegen, muss aber am Anfang mit einigem an "trial and error" rechnen. Ich selber fand es aber spannend mich mit den Details der Spielmechanik vertraut zu machen und wie alles zusammenspielt.
Je länger ich das Spiel spiele, umso mehr offenbart sich mir die Tiefe des Spiels. Es geht ums optimieren jedes Zuges. Über einzelne Levels wird der Spieler in immer anspruchsvollere Ziele herangeführt.
Der Entwickler ist sehr engagiert und ich bin mir sicher das nächste Update kommt bald.
Negative Aspekte seien auch erwähnt:
- Im Moment habe ich vereinzelte Grafik-Bugs festgestellt, bei denen die Wüfel auf dem Spielplan nicht richtig dargestellt werden. Allerdings konnte ich es nicht mehr reproduzieren. Kann also sein, dass es eine Ausnahme war. Der Entwickler ist auf jeden Fall informiert und interessiert.
-EDIT: Bisher stellten sich die Grafik-Bugs nur im Tutorial dar. Im Spiel selber keine Bugs bisher festgestellt.
- Die Musik ist relativ eintöniges gedudel (zumindest für meinen Geschmack), ich habe schnell die Mute-Taste betätigt.
- Alles ist auf Englisch, dies mag für manche ein negativ Punkt sein
- Bisher unklar ist, ob das Spiel nach 10-15 Stunden anfangen könnte sehr repetetiv zu werden. Bisher ist es noch sehr packend.
Addictive and good time-killer if you are bored!

Even though it is a turn-based-strategy game there are only very few games out there, that are more exciting. Thats mostly because of the cool cinematic action-cam-shots whenever your guys or the enemy is doing an action and because of how much u get attached your squadmembers over time.
You require good foresight and strategic decisionmakeing to get your guys through the missions. The dificulty of this game is quiet tough and useing the vast variety of special skills and researchable equipment of your soldiers in the right situations is a must. Fortunatly u can take your sweet a$$ time to plan your moves every turn and you are going to do so.
Beside the missions u also have a homebase, the Avanger. A huge Aircraft that pretty much looks like the Ship from the Movie "The Avangers" - Coincidence? Defenetly Not.
There you can build new facilities that help your soldiers and research new badass stuff like EXO-Suits, or Railguns. There is nothing over fieldtesting a flamethrower the first time at some ugly a$$ Xenos! But even thoug you got full controll over everything that is going on, the resourses and time are limited and u just cant do everything you would like - that keeps you motivated over the game and always confronts you with new problems that cross your initiate planning. You will be stumbling from one greyzone-decision to the next. The feeling of beeing a commander fighting against an overpowered enemy gets deliviered in every single second of the game. That most of these situations are not artificaly created by story twists but by random events increases the replayability of the game immensively.
Last but not least you have a very powerfull Character-Editor where you can customize the siht out of your Veterans. This will get you even more attached to your soldiers. Loosing a Highleveld-Sniper-Captain is bad of course. Just from the Gameplay Point of View as he/she had to survive lots of missions to get there and has really powerfull skills that you are going to miss in the folowing missions. But you are not only missing a nameless soldier. You are going to loose Angela "Reaper" Lombardi, an Italian Elite Sniper, that once solokilled a Sektopod with a 15% shot and prevented you mission from an epic fail, and all your soldiers from a painfull death.
You are going to loose a "friend" on whom you spent 15 minutes in the Chracter Editor to make him/her look unique and badass. And DAMN they can look unique and Badass in this game. If you have the imagination that i have, you are going to get as (mabey even more attached) to your top soldiers than for your Crew in Mass Effect f.e. Knowing that there is nothing preventing them from Permadeath but your wise decisions makes this game even more exciting than it already is just from the Gameplay Mecanics.
So if you think that you just somehow can have fun playing a turn-based game in 2016 and have that imagination that creates a story out of the gameplay you wont regret any Cent and any second u spent on this game. It is totaly awesome.
You can also buy X-Com 1 if u didnt do so already which is cheaper and also one of the best games in my libary.
But appart from the turn limits in like 50% of the missions, X-Com 2 is a fully successfull improvement to X-Com 1. And a awesome game that gets an even more awesome sequel is rare these days.

It was bad in v1, it remains bad in v2 and here's why it's really a bad and annoying game:
1. the mechanics are totally primitive: 2 moves, 1 action per soldier. Like move, move, shoot. Once you shot the soldier's turn is over. You can't shoot twice instead of moving, no sir, just move 0-2 times and 1 shot. Oh, there's a moronic ability that will let your sniper whip a pistol out and fire it in addition to a normal sniper rifle shot. Makes sense? No, but many things in this game make no sense.
2. the game is supposed to be like hard. While this might appeal to some, most people I know play such games to relax and have fun, not to experience masochistic pleasure, but mostly to relax. In this broken game you lead a small squad that you can improve by developing their abilities (through enemy kills). However, once you loose a squad member your squad is much weaker, so you don't want to have any losses. This is simply broken mechanics, trying to emulate a Hollywood story of 4 pals vs. the world, but then it meats a like of JRR Martin and your heroes are gone. Are you happy? Neither am I.
3. in order to add insult to injury there are usually timers added to objectives. Kill 12 opponents with your 4 soldiers plus do it in 8 turns. What on Earth? This makes you rush and it's no fun at all, just forcing you to rush a silly game that otherwise becomes painfully shallow in it's simplisitc mechanics.
4. have I mentioned simplistic combat mechanics? Run, run, shoot. Run to the enemy and slay him with a sword. He's got a gun pointed at you but no avail, you're immune to overwatch. Of course enemies have tons of close combat units that really benefit from this.
5. totall lack of tactics. It all revolves around hitting the enemy or not. One character can not really kill two opponents in a single turn (unless he uses an explosion, which are relatively weak damage wise). Also, due to the small squad size you got you'll have to reload a save every time your important squaddie gets shot.
6. Reloads take a long time. Maybe this works into the inept mechanics, but it just serves to punish you some more.
7. Lying stats. 48% to hit. Shoot. Miss. Reload from save. Shoot. Miss. Releat 6x. Not a single hit. Killing game client from the task manager.
8. No freedom. You think that you'll choose your battles and which way to develop? This game is not a shadow of original Xcoms that allowed you to feel in control. Here it's a tunnel: do this, almost done, popup, go do something else, two more popups, red/black mission, whatnot. Total chaos. No fun, just annoyance.

Some dark forces invade, again. Some guy is released from prison to fight the aforementioned dark forces, again. We don't know what exactly is happening, again. We have to fight an kill every one, again. We die, the sector is repopulated and we try to kill everyone, again. You probably see where I'm getting at, the game is a pretty and somewhat polished collection of clichés  with an emphasis on 1 on 1 (maximum 1 on 3) sword/axe/hammer/etc fight and some magic.

Cons:
•	somewhat glitchy controls and camera
•	no map (yep, you have to memorise the locations)
•	battles become systematic once you learn the enemy types
•	boss fight are often frustrating because of controls, and become easy once you figure out bosses' fight pattern
All in all this is a solid mid-tier action RPG, it is not worth the full price, so I can only recommend it for $20-25 if you have 12-20 hours to kill.

It's only worth it on sale, maybe not even that. Marred by issues, the pros don't outweigh the cons.
PROS:
* Gorgeous cutscenes, and the graphics are nice when they're not bogged down (which is unfortunately more often than not).
* Very interesting narrative and story setup.
* Highly customizable units.
CONS:
* Graphical stutters and lags unlike any game I've played on this machine. I'm sure tweaking the settings would bring it up to speed, but this is unacceptable, my rig should not have to turn down anything for this.
* AI takes an obnoxious amount of time to respond sometimes. You could end up waiting up to, say, 15-20 seconds before that last alien makes its decision on what it's going to do. Maybe even longer. I've gone AFK sometimes. That's also unacceptable, and combined with the graphical stutters makes for quite the chore.
* On the whole, it's too damn difficult. It feels like I'm fighting against the game makers and they're like "a-HA! gotcha AGAIN!" like they're torturing ants. Or more like, bullying children. Because "oh, it's too hard for you? You're weak, git gud! Hahaha! Have another Codex thrown at your squad!" It's just obnoxious.
* On that note, the RNG is very much NOT reflective of itself. I don't know what smokescreen they're trying to pull, because "idk, it's random! you could just have bad luck!" but no. This ain't no bad luck. And early on, getting hit literally once could spell doom for the rest of the mission. Oh wait, that's later on too.
* And of course, walls only sporadically work for line of sight. You *could* argue that they're shooting through walls if you've already given away your position--which is fair--but not fair when one squaddie gives away everyone else's position everywhere. And for the rest of the mission.
* Stealth/ambush/whatever element makes no sense contrasted with the time limits and "rescue X amount of civilians" elements.
I wanted to like this game. A LOT. But frankly it feels like a chore after a while--too much work for not enough pay, so to speak. I'm not about to throw myself at the same missions for hours just to end up being left with a (loaded) dice roll against me as usual and likely a dead squadmate or three if I *happen* to get any luck. I took similar issue with the previous title, but that was significantly more tolerable than this mess.
See, these difficult RNG games *can* be fun, I'm all for them, but the problem here is that victory just isn't satisfying enough. You're quickly going to be thrust into a new mission again with a now-broken squad and very little, if anything, more to show for it. So what's the point? To just continue watching my squadmates die while I replenish them with recruits that just end up dying too? Oh, my reward for this mission is a scientist and a smattering of resources? Hardly makes up for the dead and injured.
I might seem a little salty--and I am--but it's largely because I got this game on release, and now that I've waited months to try picking it back up again in hopes it's been tweaked to be more fun and technically sound, I'm instead greeted with some weak DLC. Difficulty and gameplay issues aside, it's the technical issues that really just kill it for me, that just adds insult to injury.
Overall, while I love the game's presentation, I can't recommend it, but damn it I wish I could.

Dark Souls had a baby with a WRPG and it came out a little premature. I enjoy some of its design decisions but it's incredibly short (with DLC it took me under 9 hours), and I can only ascribe so much of that to my experience with similar titles. However, it has actual useful kb/m controls, and is a solidly programmed title on this platform, so that's a huge plus over the aforementioned's PC edition.
I'm incredibly fond of its risk/reward mechanic: the longer you go without laying down a save/dying, the higher your XP multiplier becomes. XP functions as currency and level-fodder, but can be gained also via exploration, sidequests (yes! those exist in this!), and a "checkpoint" system which lets you choose a new respawn point/effectively quicksave, without resetting the multiplier. The multiplier only applies to combat-given XP, but that makes perfect sense, and it's not like that doesn't make boss encounters more tense as you try to take them out in one so you can turn them from one level up into four.
Other positives: bosses all have a specific kill condition to upgrade their drops (which is hinted at in some of the lore or notes) for further risk/reward and playstyle changes, you get a shotgun (or just projectile weapon, but I liked using it as a shotgun) which can be used offensively or defensively if you want to make that your build, and the various spell schools allow for some drastically different play, if you want straight offense, healing, or a more subterfuge-based style. I'm all over this and I hope some of its systems get lifted for future titles, because apparently lately I only play evolutionary dead-end titles.

This game was inspired by Dark Souls, with emphasis on the combat execution, sharp controls and tough enemies. I liked that this game is fair, so whenever you got killed, you were aware why that happened. Also the game does reward the more curious and determined players by having plenty of secrets, or several tougher side-quests. Your choice of magic and weaponry does affect the gameplay significantly, I found myself testing out different weapons against different enemies, because the different weapons have different moves. Your agility is also affected by how much you are burdened, so playing as a dual-knife-wielding rogue in cloth armor feels very different from a steel-clad knight waving a giant polesword.
Graphics and enemy design are very satisfying, sometimes stepping into the grotesque, but nothing that breaks the atmosphere. Detailed textures, particle effects, good animations - all present. As you play along, you get to know each enemy type and how to beat them. But sometimes the bad guys synergize in a killer combinations and then you have to pull them from the pack and dispatch them one by one.
Level design is also inspired by Dark Souls, using a hub-like system with interconnected locations, where you unlock shortcuts as you progress, eliminating the need for fast travel system, as everything is relatively nearby. This can lead to confusion at times, because the in-game objectives are quite vague, so once or twice I needed to take a look at a guide to see what to do next.
Overall, I cannot avoid comparing Lords to the Souls. This feels like a love letter to Dark Souls, but is a good game on its own. The missing piece, why I won't be playing it over and over again, is the absence of multiplayer, which added so much to Dark Souls - observing, how others beat the boss, checking out different builds and movesets. Here you are all alone.
Yes, I would buy it again.

Bastion is a beautiful looking game, with great music and a engaging storyline that'll pull you in until the end of the journey. If you're not used to running around on 3D planes, it can take some getting used to as there are no invisible walls bordering the map (luckily, the game only take off a small portion of your life you happen to fall off) However, once you get used to the controls, gameplay and battle feels very fluid.
The game gives you a variety of weapons and skills to take out your enemies; each one succeeding in feeling very unique from the other.  There are also special challenge areas designed to help you learn how to make the best of a particular weapon, rewarding you with upgrade items and new skills for completing them.  And while many of the skills are heavily relient on what two weapons are currently equipped, there are also a handfful of useful skills that can be used with any weapon,
I highly reccomend grabbing the soundtrack along with the game.

After 12 levels, I'd say God Game: The Odyssey is a surprisingly fun little game. The player can use wind and water currents to guide a herd of ships to their destinations while avoiding various perils, Due to the force of the elements, the ships are very hard to steer in an exact manner, so the player can only be successful if he thinks a bit forward and plans sweeping fleet movements ahead. Good multitasking is also an advantage as many of the perils can be negated by divine (ie. player) intervention, but leave the ships to their own devices for more than a couple of seconds, and they're bound to stray into their destruction.
All the levels so far had adequate solutions - sometimes you can get away with being a bit clumsy if you're lucky, but luck is not required.
God Game: The Odyssey is simple but fun, quality entertainment for a few hours. It's worth your money even at the full 2.5EUR price.

In the unlikely event that you read my review for the previous Firaxis X-COM, then I can tell you that it reads much the same as this one will.
First and foremost, the game is buggy beyond all belief. Minor things like broken or repeating animations are common enough to occur on every turn, load times are extremely inconsistent (your CAPS LOCK key will magically shorten them, somehow), and textures will randomly vanish. Major issues also occur frequently enough that I have to wonder if the playtesters were listened to, or if such a team ever existed in the first place. Manually backup your saves, especially if you're playing an Ironman run, as this game gobbles up saves like a free buffet. The movement planner will also sometimes just give you the middle finger: "Yeah, there's an open door there to get to that good cover three tiles away, but I'd rather your soldier walk outside through this fire, this overwatching enemy, and this poison cloud in a dash that consumes both turns!". Sightlines are horribly busted; an enemy will regularly be able to see your concealed team through two floors and a wall and fire at them, but you'll not be able to retaliate against the unknown enemy. In a tactical game, sightlines are everything. I don't know why Firaxis let two games release whose basic mechanics don't work more often than they do work.
Balance-wise, the early game when you're still building up from rookies and trying to get some basic research and building done is the most miserable part of the game, by far. A giant wall of enemies with much better accuracy and one or two-hit kill weapons who can dodge your poor rookies' point-blank shots will prevent many runs from ever properly starting up. Once you actually have some leveled up soldiers and all of the basic facilities built, the game becomes almost laughably easier.  Only a few aliens or robots with particularly nasty abilities or stupidly large health bars will ever pose a serious threat to an armored squad of corporals or above. Oh, just remember that all enemies still get their BS free move when discovered, so you will have to slowly and carefully crawl your way across the map to avoid having your squad get flanked by the free movement and then shot apart on the upcoming enemy turn; well, you would be smart and avoid rushing, except many missions have very strict time limits where you will have to dash on a couple of turns to make it to the objective before instant mission failure occurs.
DLC addendum: the DLCs make the early game even harder and more unfair, if you play the associated story missions. I actually recommend dropping down from Commander difficulty if you want to play the story mission for "Shen's Last Gift", because it is a long, painful grind against endless waves of armored robotic enemies followed by a boss fight against a special Sectopod. If you do this mission as soon as it's available in the early game, then your poor squaddies are not coming back. You can get the moderately useful SPARK units without playing this mission, thankfully.
Consider getting this game once the deluxe bundle is on sale for half off, and only if you think you can handle the early game frustration and the potential occurence of game-crashing glitches or save disappearances.
