I'm glad to see that the developers of Kingdom Rush are sticking to what I consider to be the quintessential tower defense game. This title is "more of the same" but I can't stress enough that this is absolutely a good thing.
Often, a sequel entirely overshadows its predecessor to a point of invalidating any reason to return to the first game - in this case, I'd strongly recommend picking up both. It's perhaps better to see this game as a gigantic expansion to the first, protected from accusations that it should have just been DLC by the first game's colossal amount of extra content existing beyond the main campaign and within the base game and the large number of variations that Frontiers has made to tech tree progression, enemy types, and map interactivity.
What it boils down to is simple - if you like tower defense games, buy both of the Kingdom Rush ones. If you're unsure about the genre, I'd strongly recommend either of these two as a great introduction to the genre.

Alright, for those of you who will actually read this, let me start off by saying that these opinions are my own and my perspective is coming from playing the PC version (Finished both the Singleplayer and played about 13 hours of Co-Op already). So, that being said, let's get started. I will be writing my review in a sort of a listing format, being mixed with both pros and cons:
Singleplayer/Storyline:
The storyline was good, but it seems like they rushed it a bit in some key areas.
Arno becomes an Assassin out of nowhere, it feels.
Arno had a very similar backstory to that of Ezio, even though Arno seems to be a bit higher class maybe? Seems that way but it wasn’t explained too well.
The outside forces (the modern day Assassin’s who are helping you) play no role whatsoever other than saying “Hey, do this because we think it’s important”. We have no connection with the person controlling Arno. Even though we had basically no connection with the one in Black Flag either, at least you got to roam around and understand why you were there.
Arno has become one of my favorite main Assassin’s. even though it’s hard to pick whether I loved him or Edward Kenway more. Maybe if there were more developing missions for Arno’s character I would have cared.
Unity has been the most nostalgic game to me since Brotherhood, so I do give it credit for giving me “the feels.”
I liked the addition of the Rift missions. Even though they had no real purpose other than attempting to give the outside forces more developing storyline. Being able to play in occupied France during the Second World War was amazing. But it just shows how a more modern Assassin’s Creed would NOT work.
Absolutely NO importance is placed on the Sword of Eden, making it just another cool collectable to get for finishing the game. Unlike the pieces of Eden in the other games where everything is based around them.
The only motive you have in this game is revenge. You can argue that the motivation comes from Arno trying to keep Elise, but when she is out of  the picture (both when you don’t have any contact with her during the game and when she dies ) you don’t feel anything for either her or Arno.
I like how no naval missions are in this. I like them and they worked well in the previous games, but it wouldn’t have for this.
The ending was unoriginal, easy, and quick.
Main story line was not very long. I thought for a huge, hyped up game like this it would take me around 10 hours to complete, not 3 or 4.
Poor quality of side missions, leaving you with not a lot to do when you’re done with the story.
Let’s be honest, you will have little to no idea who is on who’s side. Little to no understanding of what is happening in the world outside of Arno.
Open World and Random Others:
I love the environment of Revolutionary France (well, Paris and some other locations).
Having random scenarios happen around you was a cool addition. I like seeing some random person get mugged, people standing around a recent murder, crowds showing off their revolutionary rights, or anything else you see.
Gotta love the crowd chants you hear every now and again; it really immerses you into the environment around you.
I hate how there are only about 6 cafes you can fix up. In previous games, I enjoyed be able to renovate tons of places and especially the Villa. The renovations are cheap and the missions are quick and easy. The renovations are pointless because they serve no  real purpose to the story line.
The Companion App is a cool addition but it’s more than annoying to have to basically play a whole other game just to get some rewards and open chests.
No whistling system? REALLY?
I have to buy the ability to throw my money on the ground? HAHA.
I understood not being able to double assassinate people in previous games until you got two blades, but not being able to do it until you buy the ability is rather pointless.
I like how the buildings are now explorable, rather  than just running through them in a sequence. Their design is very well done, too. Some of them are beautiful.
The climbing system was very good, for the most part. The controlled descent is what made it the best system so farm.
The Eagle Vision is also the best so far. You can easily move around in the world while viewing through it.
The soundtrack is very good. Not the best, but not the worst.
No weapon wheel, which was a very good part of the AC games.
You can’t pick up rifles, so if you want to use one, you will have to buy one and sacrifice the use of your sword.
We have to wait for Club Competition just to unlock some Legendary gear?...
Similar to the more recent AC’s, there are no blacksmiths, banks, or anything like that. Just one shop that you can get everything at. I find that a bad thing.
Murder mysteries are easy and quick.
Nostradamus Enigmas missions are fun and a cool way to unlock armor, but they can be difficult.
- No horses :(
Tons a different regions, which is awesome. You can be in swamps, farmland, villages, rural middle class areas, high class areas, industrial, ports, and shanty towns just to name a few.
The combat system is terrible. I understand they geared it towards being more stealthy than the other titles, but it’s still awful. Especially the parry system.
I like the mini map. It’s larger and more visible than others in other games.
There is no pickpocketing unless it’s assigned in a mission, which is stupid.
I like the propaganda/graffiti that’s in this game. You can tell the people are going through a revolution without having to shove it down your throat.
The amount of NPCs in this game is amazing. It pays off mostly with crowds, showing just how chaotic the time period was.  But it becomes annoying in the streets when all you want to do is run a straight line and end up getting caught up on every single one of them.
Co-Op:
Singlehandedly the best part about this game. Really fun to get a bunch of your friends together and do missions.
The upgrade system is well done, forcing you to play a lot to unlock good gear.
The customization is also well done. You can choose what type of play style you most prefer by upgrading and customizing your character in a certain way.
Some of the missions are too easy, like the heist Ancient History, for example. It’s a 5  star difficulty yet you can solo it easily with weak gear.
The heists are easily exploited for easy money. One of your friends can stay behind as one solos it. Do it again but changing the order of who does what, and you can earn the most amount of money in 2 goes.
Huge amount of issues with connection.
Huge amount of issues with disappearing players, enemies, and mission markers.
The missions will glitch every now and then, unallowing you to advance. For example, in Women’s March, the two women will just not move. You will have to quite, and then re-queue just for the mission to work.
There is NO way of communicating to other players in the lobby (if you aren’t in Skype, or whatever, with the).
A lot of attention was paid to the environment, you can tell. The buildings were accurate replicas and looks marvelous.
Mechanical Issues:
This is what REALLY brought the game down and has been the worst PC release out of any Assassin’s Creeds.
I have a computer the well meets the minimum requirements, yet it forces me to play on Low (I can run Revelations, which was the most demanding AC to me, on high).
If you change your settings you need to restart your game or else it will skip  every 5 seconds.
You will randomly fall throw the map and desync.
If the enemy you're killing is killed by someone else, your character stands there for a couple seconds before being able to move again.
Sound cuts out at times.
A very beautiful game, if you are able to play it on higher graphics.
The loading screens are unbearably long.

I held off on this game for a looong time after complaints about issues with the game surfaced right after its release. I am glad I waited. I got it for about 25 dollars on a weekend sale including all DLC. The game is definitely a love/hate relationship. The reward system is not random like I would have preferred. The combat and magic system are interesting and fun. You really feel the hits in the game. Make no mistake. This is an insanely difficult game to learn initially. You basically have to play long enough to understand every enemy in the game so you know how to approach them. They all have a weekness. The same goes for the bosses. I found it very useful to run around at different ranges to feel out the boss for the first time until I figured out their tactics. Once you figure that out, it makes the game much less difficult. The lack of energy at the beginning of the game makes combat very difficult. You get maybe one or two swipes with a weapon with enough left for one dodge to get back out of melee combat range.
All of that being said. This game is about grinding, grinding, and grinding. The longer you can grind without saving the better your rewards. The experience multiplier goes up with every foe that you defeat without saving. You can save without healing or resetting your xp modifier just so you don't get pushed back to an area that is too far away to get back to where you lost your xp. You can get your xp back by fighting back to your ghost or by using a gem that allows you to restore your xp ghost without fighting your way back to it. I don't know if those are things they put into the game after release or not, but they are there none-the-less.
Graphics are superb. I had to turn my camera sensitivity almost all the way to max to get the game to allow me to move without feeling like I was stuck in quicksand.
Final rating: B+
Due to the grinding nature of the game, difficulty, and lack of random treasure drops, and no map feature meeans I had to lower its rating. Eventually that stuff starts taking its toll out of you. The game really isn't that long as far as the story goes. But, getting lost intially is easy to do. With no mini-map or world map to help you navigate, it is difficult for new players to keep their bearings.
I suggest making the wiki site for the game a favorite in your web browser. You will be using it a lot initially to figure out where you should go next.

I would recommend this game, and for people who truly enjoy strategy games, science fiction, strategy, and cheesy storylines, I would still recommend it - but for numerous reasons, to the general rpg and strategy player, I simply can't provide my recommendation of XCOM2. Here's why.
First of all, the game is incredibly demanding on PC resources - so much so that even with a near top-of-the-line air-cooled rig, I run it on low settings. It is buggy and crashes occasionally. There are frame drops and hiccups. I had issues with the cinematics when it was first installed - sound would play out of sync, and sometimes the cinematics wouldn't show at all.
Secondly, it is overpriced for what you get. The DLCs add very little to the game, and the rewards from completing them are quite hefty from a resource-cost standpoint. Even if you forego all of the DLC, on Commander+ difficulties you will find yourself grinding missions simply to get more resources before the final assault. Throw in the DLC rewards, and you will very quickly realize just how much of a grind XCOM2 can be.
Third, there are no *real* choices in XCOM2. When you have access to three guerrilla operations, you are merely choosing between the best reward in most cases (which is typically fairly obvious.) Outside of that, your only choices will be whether or not to spend intel to buy a weapon upgrade on the black market, or spend resources on your ranger shotguns instead of sharpshooter sniper rifles. Missions are completely linear, and some missions are literally impossible to complete thanks to cheating AI and random spawn locations. (One time I spawned on a map with four alien groups that triggered simultaneously the following turn, even if I didn't move.)
There are no alternate endings besides success and failure. Missions do not change much even on new playthroughs - you will meet new aliens at approximately the same times and in the same order. There are only three or four game-progress missions that *require* completion. The rest are time wasters and provide a slow trickle of resources...which are the only real impediment to your progress. Player skill and good decision making will not impact your completion speed much - only the random rolls for whether or not you get downed UFO missions will influence that.
It becomes painfully obvious eventually - 95% of the missions are simply obstacles to your progress within the game, and barely feel like they *are* the game. They're more like a house fly that won't stop landing on your arm. Your actual success or failure depends not on completing these missions, but rather on whether or not you have the resources to obtain region contacts to reach the missions you *need* to progress. This lack of importance makes 95% of the game - the mass of meaningless missions - feel like the filler on a one-hit-wonder music album.
If I were to rate XCOM2, I'd give it a 6/10. It's not a terrible game by any means, and I know a lot of work went into it, but it seems like they never finished it. Maybe they expected the mod community to do the work for them...maybe they figured they'd make their money back and some more, and that'd be enough. But the lack of RPG-type customizeability on soldiers, the apparent meaninglessness of most missions, and the on-rails story really ruins what would otherwise be a solid turn-based strategy game.

I got this game free about a year ago and I although i didn't play it a lot at first it was still a fun and decently fleshed out game and since then it has been improved dramatically with better visuals, game balances, and new ships. Now I can't get enough of this game. Its technically in Alpha still but I'd consider it a fairly complete multiplayer game for $10. It is very well balanced. There is definately a counter and a weak spot to every ship in the game it just takes an expierenced player to know where they are. And you definately learn with time. There's definately not a ship that is simply better than another.. they all have thier specialties and their roles to play which makes each unique. What i like the most about this game is how team driven it is. Your team can literally make or break your match but reguardless of the outcome there is never a dull moment and players are always respectful.
Which brings me to the community. The community is definately small. Some people say this is a downside to matchmaking but I've never spend more than 5mins searching for a match (maybe you consider that long).  Players are, for the most part, always helpful, understanding, and there to just have some fun which is a somewhat underrated aspect in multiplayer games. You do occassionally get a player who is toxic and just wants to throw a fit about losing but that happens in most online competive games. And you will lose A LOT! But thats just part of the game.
Devs are always making improvements, adding new ships, balancing, etc. What I like most about the development is the devs keep the players very well informed on changes and updates.
Overall I definately reccommend this game. This is my first time writing a review for a game, but with me talking about it constantly and having put 140 hours into it, I guess it's the best game for me to write a review on.
The main thing i love about the game is the variety in how the ships play. Unlike other games, you can't buy one ship and overpower everyone by just buying the most expensive ship. They all have their strengths and weaknesses, and your play style must adapt to what ship you have and what situation you are in.
They all have distinctive weapons, sounds, looks, and abilities.
There's no many good space combat games out there, so I believe it would be safe to say that this is the best in it's category.
Now, that's not to say that it's absolutely perfect.
While they have had patches and updates, the matchmaking is flawed. Because of the slim amount of players, they can't quite match everyone up by rank. This somtimes ends up pitting newer players into more skilled people. Another issue from the lack of players is that it can be a pain to find a match, god forbid its late at night.
But if you're looking for a space combat game that isnt pay to win, has good graphics and gameplay, this is the game  you want. It's a bit of a learning curve to get used to having to position and maneuver your ship to keep your armor between you and the other ship as well as your guns, but once you get past that and learn how the enemy ships work, this game can be a blast.
Out of all the games i've played, i'd have to recommend this the strongest.

Also, it'll take up as much of your time as you would expect of a $10 (for $7 if you got it on sale like I did) game.
But these two problems are not at all enough to keep me from recommending this game to others. The story is really engaging, the puzzles are interesting and rewarding (not too straightforward while also not being impossible), and the music and style of the game is on point. If you come from a programming background (specifically using the linux command line), you'll probably be disappointed that this perfectly realistic, but it's obviously not meant to be. It makes you feel like a hacker, it's not an educational tool.
My point is that is game is amazing. This was both my first hacking and text based game, and I still loved it. Please do yourself a favor and play it. 10/10.
Note: I never had any game breaking bugs like many of the negative reviews reported. There were some things that worried me, like aborting a story mission and not knowing if I could pick it up again, but after a quick google search it appeared finishing the mission I aborted for made the mission "spawn" again, so everything was fine.

Let me start by giving the folks at Chucklefish a huge round of applause for drawing me in to this game.  The trailers, videos and other media for this game all looked epic.  Here was a true adventure game!  Something to revigorate that awesome Terraria feel, but even better!  An amazing tale of discovery and rebuilding!
And then you bought the game, started playing, and realized - it was all a facade.
Starbound has one of the worst put-together progression systems I have ever seen in a game.  It goes like this - find materials, combine materials, fight boss, next stage.  Rinse and repeat for not 2 tiers, not 3, but 10 FRIGGIN TIMES.  And after the fourth teir, there aren't even any more bosses.  Dreadful.
Mining is useless, since caves are incredibly rare and usually contain nothing of use.  And anyways, you can find everything - yes, everything - you need just by walking around on the surface.  So that's almost 70% of the world that is simply useless.  Dungeons are huge and...that's it.  They contain almost no loot, and present no challenge since almost every room is the same.  Just fighting my way through Terraria's single dungeon was more fun than all the dungeons I have gone through in this game put together.  Dreadful.
And, quite possible Starbound's worst offense?  Let me give you the fast version.  In a game with an insane, morbid cult, a devastated human race, and a race of mutated apes who are under threat of extinction, there are ten times as many terrible jokes, fourth wall breaks, and other things that ruin your experience.
DREAD-FUL.
Simply - do not buy this game.  Go spend your 15 dollars on Terraria, or Minecraft, or any other sandbox you can think of.  Don't let Starbound's clever advertising get to you - this game is nothing it says it is.

God Game: The Odyssey is... difficult to give a standard genre category... the popular tags are: Action, casual, strategy, indie, simulation. But I would create my own genre called "Phone app games" or "minimalist computer requirements."
God Game: The Odyssey was developed by Liquid Dragon Studios and released in 2015, you play as the Greek Goddess Athena, your goal is to help guide Odysseus's fleet back home by controlling the wind, and water currents.
Story: God Game: The Odyssey follows the story of Odysseus returning from the Trojan Wars.
As the story progresses, you hear more about Greek mythology, which introduces a new mechanic/NPC that you must learn to combatant to successfully pass through the next set of levels.
Game Play: There are two core controls in guiding the ships through the various puzzles: Controlling the wind, and controlling the currents. When you use wind, the ships will try to sail directly to the end goal. This sometimes works in your favor if there are no obstacles obstructing your path... if there is something in the way, you will need to click and drag to create "water currents" to guide your boats.
As the game progresses you need to face giants, tornado's
, Harpies, Lotus
, and much more. The game is very good at pausing and explaining just why you should avoid _____ because _____.
you move the ships with two main functions: currents and wind. As the game progresses there are new mechanics that build off these core controls... mostly new mechanics to just frustrate you though.
Achievements: There are no achievements for God Game: The Odyssey. But I have seen some forum posts requesting achievements. You REALLY don't want achievements for this game, the only people who will try to get them all are maniac-achievers like myself, and please don't make me get perfects on each levels, that's just madness.
This is a sample of what it looks like to complete a level, if you do very well you'll get a "perfect" or "excellent" star rating for getting enough points.
Price God Game: The Odyssey is priced at $4.99, I personally like having my games last an hour for every dollar I spent, however, this game started to grind me down after playing through several puzzles. I think it has a fair amount of content, and a fair amount of replay value... but it's best on a mobile device, rather then on a computer.
Conclusion: In conclusion... not a bad game, but not a game I personally won't be spending much time playing it. If Achievements are added, I'll be forced to return to Odyssey ...and wish for death because the game can be agonizingly painful at times. However, there is a sense of pride when you complete a puzzle in Odyssey.
I recommend this to people who enjoy "app-style-games", as well as anyone looking to support an indie game publisher, and lastly people that play games on mobile devices.

I would recommend this game, and for people who truly enjoy strategy games, science fiction, strategy, and cheesy storylines, I would still recommend it - but for numerous reasons, to the general rpg and strategy player, I simply can't provide my recommendation of XCOM2. Here's why.
First of all, the game is incredibly demanding on PC resources - so much so that even with a near top-of-the-line air-cooled rig, I run it on low settings. It is buggy and crashes occasionally. There are frame drops and hiccups. I had issues with the cinematics when it was first installed - sound would play out of sync, and sometimes the cinematics wouldn't show at all.
Secondly, it is overpriced for what you get. The DLCs add very little to the game, and the rewards from completing them are quite hefty from a resource-cost standpoint. Even if you forego all of the DLC, on Commander+ difficulties you will find yourself grinding missions simply to get more resources before the final assault. Throw in the DLC rewards, and you will very quickly realize just how much of a grind XCOM2 can be.
Third, there are no *real* choices in XCOM2. When you have access to three guerrilla operations, you are merely choosing between the best reward in most cases (which is typically fairly obvious.) Outside of that, your only choices will be whether or not to spend intel to buy a weapon upgrade on the black market, or spend resources on your ranger shotguns instead of sharpshooter sniper rifles. Missions are completely linear, and some missions are literally impossible to complete thanks to cheating AI and random spawn locations. (One time I spawned on a map with four alien groups that triggered simultaneously the following turn, even if I didn't move.)
There are no alternate endings besides success and failure. Missions do not change much even on new playthroughs - you will meet new aliens at approximately the same times and in the same order. There are only three or four game-progress missions that *require* completion. The rest are time wasters and provide a slow trickle of resources...which are the only real impediment to your progress. Player skill and good decision making will not impact your completion speed much - only the random rolls for whether or not you get downed UFO missions will influence that.
It becomes painfully obvious eventually - 95% of the missions are simply obstacles to your progress within the game, and barely feel like they *are* the game. They're more like a house fly that won't stop landing on your arm. Your actual success or failure depends not on completing these missions, but rather on whether or not you have the resources to obtain region contacts to reach the missions you *need* to progress. This lack of importance makes 95% of the game - the mass of meaningless missions - feel like the filler on a one-hit-wonder music album.
If I were to rate XCOM2, I'd give it a 6/10. It's not a terrible game by any means, and I know a lot of work went into it, but it seems like they never finished it. Maybe they expected the mod community to do the work for them...maybe they figured they'd make their money back and some more, and that'd be enough. But the lack of RPG-type customizeability on soldiers, the apparent meaninglessness of most missions, and the on-rails story really ruins what would otherwise be a solid turn-based strategy game.

2. Hit or miss chance is heavily skewed towards the computer. You will miss a LOT, even when you have a shotgun shoved under an alien's nose. Shouldn't really be possible, but it is. The computer on the other hand will hit you from near impossible ranges and crit you to boot. I have found that grenades are way more reliable than any gun in my arsenal.
3. Cover doesn't always mean much. It seems the more complex the cover gets, the more it fails. Think you are safe hiding inside that train? Tough. Watch helplessly as your guys get slaughtered through walls and floors.
4. Upgrades. It may just be me, but it seems like resources and upgrades are far more difficult to get a hold of this time. You rarely get anything new, and when you do it just doesn't seem quite worth all the resources you had to dump into it.
Those are the most glaring problems I have found while playing, however, as I said I still enjoy the game and think it's worth the $30 I paid for it. If you enjoyed the first one and don't mind the downfalls, you will probably enjoy this one too. However, if getting stabbed through full cover and crit from across the map with a pistol makes you want to break your screen, steer clear.

Half-Life is a true classic. It's one of the first shooters to actually tell a coherent story.
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is really good! It's a semi-linear FPS with a good variety of weapons. There's a variety of enemies, both alien and human. You can ask security guards and scientists to follow you, and they will do their best to help. Security guards will shoot enemies, and scientists will use medicine to heal you, making the combat gameplay more interesting. Overall, gameplay is this game's strongest suit.
PRESENTATION: The graphics were pretty good back in 1998, but they haven't aged well. The colorization is kind of bland and ugly. The textures are, of course, low-resolution. However, there's lots of big explosions and stuff falling apart, which is visually satisfying to watch. The sounds are good, and the voice acting is decent, too. Most importantly, however, is that this game's soundtrack widely held to be one of the best in video game history.
STORY: The story isn't that great by modern standards. It's not bad, but it's just doesn't have alot of depth. You play a a regular old guy named Gordon Freeman who goes to work at the lab only to participate in an experiment that would open a portal to a border-world named Xen, allowing hostile aliens to enter the Black Mesa Facility. The government sends soldiers to contain the mess by killing everyone in the facility. The story helps, and it never gets in the way of gameplay, ever.  There's no cutscenes. Remember, this is back in the days of Duke Nukem 3D when "the president was kidnapped by ninjas" was considered an acceptable storyline.
It's a good purchase for any classic gamer.

AoE 3 is a pretty decent historical fiction RTS.  The game takes place mostly around the frontier days, with the exception of the Asian Dynasty pack.  I'll be talking a lot about that expansion because it's vastly different from the rest of the game.  Voice acting is decent, as are the stories, predictable though they are.  The music is catchy but highly repetitive.
85% of the game has no chill.  While it's not really all that challenging on Normal difficulty, most of the missions in the game have some kind of time or mechanical constraint that prevent them from being standard "build then destroy" affairs.  Normally I wouldn't complain about this, but themes are re-used so much that they quickly grow old.  "Oh, I don't start off with a base again."  "Oh, I can't get any villagers again."  "Oh, I don't get any resources so I have to use trading posts again."  So on and so forth.
The UI is kind of bad.  It eats up a third of my screen on 1080p, and hotkeys (of which there are many) aren't discernible via mouseovers of the buttons, so you wind up having to go back into the Options menu repeatedly if you want to use them.  Attack-move seemed not to work properly for me, which was very noticeable but not a dealbreaker.
Asian Dynasties involved very different mechanics.  Minus the UI, the production value, and a couple of buildings/progressions, it was almost different enough to be another RTS.  Some of the alterations were neat, others were bizarre.  If you play the Chinese faction during Skirmish mode, they can't build any common soldiers until they Age Up (upgrade the town hall), only siege units.  I'm sorry, what?  Whose brilliant idea was that?
You see, although there are many factions, there are really only four styles in the game:  European, Japanese, Chinese, and Indian.  It's not merely a difference in units, or buildings, but the fundamental mechanics of how they work.  Because I didn't spend a lot of hours in Skirmish mode, it's impossible for me to say if the game is balanced, but I doubt it.
Something that appealed to me were the farming/shipment mechanics.  There's food, wood, coin, and a separate export resource if you're playing Asian Dynasties.  The way it's handled, however, you can build farms or receive shipments that are slow, infinite pools of any of those things.  If you run out of wild animals to hunt, build a farm or raise livestock.  If you run out of gold, plantations or rice paddies are infinite.   Wood is more difficult, but Asian Dynasties allows you to plant groves, or you can receive shipments in any case.  As a result, resource-management in the game is a lot less stressful than pretty much any RTS I've played.
Another thing that stood out is the ability to train stacks of five.  If you have the resources, you can train five troops in one building at once, and when it's finished five will pop out.  The need for multiple barracks is basically absent.
That's about everything that stood out for me.  I wouldn't pay 40 dollars for the game, wait for a decent sale, but it's definitely worth picking up for RTS fans if you don't mind historical backdrop.

I gave this game a positive review originally, but the last five or so matches have made me realize how unbalanced and unplayable this game really is.
Controls are clunky. Holding the jump button (W by default) doesn't result in an auto jump when you land. Instead, you have to press the key every time you want to jump over even the smallest raised bit of terrain (which can stop you in the middle of a chase and make things even more unbearable). Trying to move in midair is slow and sluggish, and you'll spend a lot of your time just trying to get up to the next platform because you keep missing it.
Gameplay is standard PvP fare: Point Cap, CtF, and an irritatingly unbalanced crystal harvesting gamemode. Whichever team has the most number of strong characters wins, though, no matter what gamemode you play, so prepare to get one-shotted by weapons dealing over 500 damage in a single hit, while you can only deal 100 or so in the beginning. Want to reach these players' levels of salt-inducing 'skill'? Spend the next several hours grinding away for metal and gold. Unless you just need the gold, in which case you'll be grinding for the next week or so.
That brings me to the money system in place in this game. You get literal *pocket change* when you win: 20 coins for every PvP win. You get *nothing* if you lose, except for a very sour taste in your mouth, and an urge to flip off everything onscreen. You spend money to unlock characters and buy loot crates. But, and here's the real kicker, *new characters cost 12000 coins to unlock*. Loot crates only cost *2000*, and even *that* is extremely high up there in price, especially since what you get from them is pure RNG.
The game also fails to mention a number of things. Firstly, *skins have an effect on your stats*. Most players don't really bother with skins, unless they want the aesthetics, but you'd never know that a new skin will affect your character's stats unless you look at the skin. This raises a number of issues, as there are players using the rarests skins and rarest weapons to essentially steamroll everything in sight.
This leads to my next issue: Balancing. Team balancing is completely random. Players aren't sorted by player or character level, or by character type, or even by your stats. Instead, the game just picks people at random, throws them into a game, and punts you out the door. What doesn't help is that people who team up before the game starts usually do so with the intention of doing what I call 'bulldozing'. They run together as a group, and they grind through everything in their path, making every gamemode a nightmare. There have been enough occasions where my team just couldn't do anything because the whole enemy team was dominating us with this tactic.
Lastly, and this is something I can't stress enough: *There is no incentive to play for any longer than an hour or so at a time.* You get pocket change for winning matches, and your dailies require a boss to be defeated (almost impossible to do by oneself), or a certain number of players to be killed (which is painful enough to slog through). You can get coins by leveling your characters, but it's only going to be a few hundred coins, which doesn't really put much of a dent in the wall that is the price of a new character.
I regret even putting time into this game. Unless you're some salt-craving lunatic, don't bother trying to play.

Gameplay is still fun as ever, and the horrid matchmaking system is slightly better with the larger playerbase offered by making the game free-to-play. The maximum wait time I have experienced, thus far is 2:35; which is significantly down from the 6:00 - 7:00 I would wait before the free-to-play update.
However, as the game is now free to play it has many microtransactions that just seem annoying. These can range from ships that seem very over-powered and unbalanced with other ships to drop pods that offer little to no rewards.
The new crew system is absolutely atrocious, but it is survivable. The current system means that the players must unlock the genetic pattern for a crew member to synthesis them. Sounds cool, right? Well, you get these genetic patterns from drop pods, which are occasionally unlocked and you are literally given a spinning wheel with a small chance of getting a drop pod. Once you actually get the genetic patter, you need to accumulate enough DNA (The third form of currency) to actually create and use the crew member.
Ships are painfully slow to acquire, some ranging in the millions of XP and Credits required to unlock the ship, then even more to buy the ship. This systems is a very tedious grind that isn't very fun, as you will experience getting destroyed by the ship you are trying to get several times.
The actual match is fun, but can be very dull and repetitive depending on your ship choice. Occasionally, you will be against a team that has the perfect counter to every one of your ships and it will just be a devastating loss. Losing results in many of your post-game rewards being limited as well, which causes the game to have been almost worthless to play.
I really want this to be a great game, it is very fun to play and the effects and graphics are just beautiful, but several issues prevent it from being as great as it truly can. Hopefully the developers (who do listen to the community, regardless of what most people say) take a look at these reviews and fix some of these issues if they can.

This game is an absolute pleasure to play, both from a gaming standpoint and an artistic standpoint.  First off, the graphics are incredibly beautiful.  I have played a ton of space games for the longest time (Freelancer, DarkStar One, Elite: Dangerous, Star Citizen, Etc.) and this game tops all of them in terms of ship design and textures.  The explosions, ship fires, and weapon trails look gorgeous whilst for the ships themselves, their aesthetic is unique and alluring. Secondly, the gameplay is fun.  It's simple and easy to pick up, but so very hard to master.  It is much slower than many modern "action games" but that doesn't mean that it can't have a frantic space battle in the midst of a match.  If you only like doing 720noscopes#420blazeit, this game is not for you as trying to do a 720° turn in the middle of battle will A) Take 5 minutes and B) Undoubtedly get you killed.  If you, however, enjoy space, enjoy 5v5 strategy (Moba), enjoy fighting in humongous capital ships with ~2,000 people on board (All of whom die if you explode), and enjoy yelling "Ludicrous Speed!" when hitting the "Boost" button on your ship, this game is for you (No joke, that crap flies fast).
Notes:
-This game is in Early Access and currently unavailable unless you buy a Founder's Pack. HOWEVER, it will be free to play when it releases. It is in no way (I mean it. In NO WAY AT ALL.) a Pay to Win. You can't even buy ships you haven't unlocked with XP with money. And you only earn XP by playing.
-There are some occasional matchmaking bugs, but that doesn't detract much from the whole experience.  The devs know about the bugs and are working to fix them. But, let's be real, if you win a 4v5, you feel pretty freaking awesome, so don't be afraid to try (You do get a 30% respawn timer cut).
-The community is small (~300ish people on at any given time) but the game is not dead.  As previously mentioned, it is in EARLY ACCESS and unaccessible unless you have the game already/bought a Founder's Pack.  That will change once it becomes a F2P.
-There is a bit of a grind to get some higher tier ships, but that doesn't mean that the "higher tier" ships are any better than the starter ships.  The game is actually incredibly balanced (Not perfect, but few things are), and playing with the starter ships is completely viable even in higher level matches.  The other ships are not better at all, they are simply different.
-NOT P2W.
-Ugh I can't get over how beautiful this game is.
TL;DR - Game is beautiful, fun, balanced, free (soon) and not P2W.  Few matchmaking bugs hurt a tiny bit, but they're already known and being worked on.

I want to make a post addressing all of the new bad reviews for dark souls 3, as they fit neatly into 4 categories.  The first is that the game is too hard.  This would be understandable from new players, but I've seen people who claim to be veterans say the same.  I am a newish player.  I only got into the souls series in the last couple of months.  Dark Souls 3 is not hard.  I am not saying this to be facetious, I am being legitimate.  It is challenging, but there is a difference.  Like all souls games, if you find yourself doing really poorly over and over again, there is probably an easier way to do what you are trying.  For example, I see many people playing ds3 with their shield up and just circle strafing.  That works well in ds2.  In ds3, the dodge key is your friend, and your shield will betray you.  Try a more active playstyle.  I hate to say "git gud," but if you are playing passively and haven't noticed how fast the enemies are in ds3, you are either new, or have no idea how to adapt.
The second argument people have is that the controls are poorly optimized for pc.  To these people, I have to question if you actually play on pc.  The reason is it should be obvious that you can rebind keys.  It took me no time at all to find a configuration I enjoyed.  For those saying go to console... I have to question your sanity.  You have a pc.  You can plug in a controller if you just can't be asked (though I can confirm the game is way easier on keyboard and mouse once you set the keys right).  I will even point you in the right direction.  set 'q' as interact, and 'e' as both back out and use items.  It works wonders.  Also, if your mouse has extra buttons, use them for power attacks so you can pull off weapon arts easier, as those are the only thing awkward with keyboard controls.  You can get a cheap 4 dollar mouse from cyberpower pc of decent quality for gaming that has two side buttons, so cost shouldn't be an issue.
The third issue people have is graphical.  I'm sorry, but ds3 is a graphically intense game.  You might not be able to run it on ultra settings.  It isn't an optimization issue, you just have your settings too high.  I can pretty much garauntee that if your card fits the minimum requirements for this game though, that you can at least achieve console quality.  Obviously you can crank it up far above that with better cards.  Stop saying go back to console, you have the better version, its bad advice.
The final issue I have seen in the reviews is people saying "too many cheaters, go back to console," or "too much lag, go back to console."  I group these two together for a reason.  I have yet to come across a single cheater.  It is exceedingly rare, because the anticheat software for this game is very good.  People seem to think that just because its pc, it's easier to cheat.  easier is relative.  It's still extremely difficult, and will still get you banned REALLY quick.  As for the lag, I hate to tell you this, but it is just as bad everywhere.  Every youtube video I see for pvp has at least one lagger, no matter the system.  There is no magical "lag free" system, because people all over the world play this.  I can say that ds3 will probably in the long run have the least lag on pc, because pc gamers tend to latch onto games longer and play them after the console market has moved on (this has to do with the way marketing is done to console gamers, as well as backwards compatibility in many cases).
In other words, stop blaming these issues on the game, it's brilliant. It has its flaws, but these are not them.  You need to, and I know you saw this coming, git gud scrub.

Reaction to this game has been laughable. I guess most people need to brush up on their French history and world history for that matter. First off, I find it silly that I have to explain that the world wasn't in 1080p until 1962, but that must be before your time. Unity surprised me by accurately showing Arno dropping through the ground and into the white abyss that exists under the real Paris, even to this day. Finally, there is the non-issue of pop-in... God Game is a casual puzzle game inspired by "The Odyssey" (you know that famous old greek myth!). Your goal is  a simple yet getting progressively more difficult one: Get your ships safely to the exit by manipulating wind/air currents. To finish a level you have to have saved a certain number of ships; stretch goals include an expert rating (save more ships) and a perfect rating (save all ships). While it is pretty easy at first to get perfect rating, pretty soon the difficulty steps up by introducing environmental hazards like sand banks, reefs and even enemies e.g. Cyclops, Harpies (the later can even be used to your advantage and you will have to utilize them at times).
The game itself is nice to play in between or to relax. My only gripe is the lack of incentive to go back to levels and try harder at getting expert/perfect rating...achievements would definitely do the trick here.

So this review was planned to be targeted towards those people that think it as negative that this game plays seemingly alot differently than the previous two games. However, I don't know where this review will be going as I am typing spontanously.
First off, this game does play differently. Alot, actually. From what I have seen, the gameplay from Age of Empires 2, especially online, solely consists of spewing out as many villagers as possible in a short time, hamster all the resources to build yourself up quickly and just make a ♥♥♥♥♥on of units, preferably cannoniers and siege cannons.
However, in Age of Empires 3 this is simply not possible, as the population cap is already at 200; considering that unit types [e.g. Musketeers as light infantry, Helbardiers as Heavy Infantry, Light Cavalry, Ranged Cavalry, etc.] it is mandatory to have a balance in your army, as the quantity is limited. In this game it is necessary to think about the numbers of Helbardiers to defend your ranged units against enemy melee soldiers, the numbers of Skirmisher to strike down enemy infantry, the number of cavalry to attack the enemy's ranged units, additionally the number of cannons who are deadly agaist masses, and so on, and so on.
Personally, having to think about such things instead of spamming units seems way more fun.
Same thing is to be said about the buildings.
Unlike Age of Empires 2, in this game most buildings can be build limited times only; you cannot build a wall of towers anymore to defend yourself, you can only build 11. You cannot build a Fort (basically AoE3's version of a Castle) in front of the enemy's town because for one, you cannot build things too close to the enemy's town centre, and for two, most civilizations can only have one or two forts in the entire game which can only be built by special wagons, making the risk of losing a fort far more tragic.
These special wagons can only be sent by home shipment cards, along with other things that make your resource gather rate higher, send you a certain number of units, resource crates, and wagons which build towers/forts/town centres for free.
This seemed to be a thing that could have confused fans of Age of Empires 2 at first (the only reference I have about this is my cousin who didn't like this specific mechanic, don't bash me), I mysel thought the game to be too complicated, although this turnt out to be entirely false as the home shipment system is far more simple than expected.
Most civilizations in Age of Empires 3 differ alot from each other; Chinese can only build "armies" which are essentially packs of 2 different soldier-types; Ottomans produce villagers automatically and for free, however this takes longer and the production process has to be sped up with upgrades; they lack melee infantry and instead of having a musketeer unit, they use a more expensive and stronger Janissary unit. I could go into more detaill into the different civilizations like the Aztecs which only have Infantry, but it is best to discover all these things for oneself or just googling it, as this review would take too long.

The legendary skins are better than the epic ones and if you want legendary stuff then you better grind a lot or pay for it. But there's a lot of grinding to be done to get even one complete (character + weapon skin) for one character because the hero tokens are random and you need 20 for that * 9 characters = 180 boxes = 360 000 gold. If you also want to unlock 9 characters that's 135 000 more gold. I'm not sure you'd have the metal to unlock those things by then thoguh .. The game is pay or grind to win, if you have legendary stuff then you'll got lots better equipment than those who don't.
And the game reward the players who already got the best stuff with even more stuff. The top ranked ones receive a legendary skin + weapon at the end of the season and those in the two leagues below that receive legendary weapons and the rest receive nothing. So if you are on the top you get rewarded with even more stuff which help you stay there and in the mean-time you own all the players below you because they don't have that gear and you aren't competing at an equal level.
The game-play is just fine but it would be better if it was equal.
That you can unlock stuff may pull you in to playing more of the game but the grinding become slower and slower the higher level your characters are and hence less rewarding. The missions give some gold and XP and those could have helped but at most time they have been very hard and ATM they are instead very easy in general with some pretty hard challenges. There was one level which could be grinded and rewarded "plentiful" of XP and gold but that was "fixed" so now that one is very hard instead.
Technically and in game-play and variety the game is an achivement.
The monetizing and grinding design of it totally ruin it though.
It want to be competitive but since it's an unfair game to give benefits tho those who play it or already is on top or pay for it .. well..

Recommended -> with some caveats.
After 32 hours, I'm writing this review.  I'm not (was not?) a bus fanatic.  I like fps games in general.  i saw a youtube video (nerd cubed ) quite some time ago and the game looked so ridiculous that I had to try this thing for myself.  I purchased the game and got bored/frustrated after about a half an hour.  There the game sat in my queue.  I picked it up more recently, more determined to get through the hard learning curve.  I still don't know a lot. But I see a lot of folks frustrated with graphics, and I may have some information that helps, so here goes.
The game is hard.  It may take you a half an hour to even start the bus.  It may take you a few attempts to get through the introduction, since the intro sequences will stop you from proceeding even when it's not clear what you button you need to hit (it should at least flash, blink, or tell you explicitly what button or key to push).  You'll have to read the manual for help, but when you put enough hours into the game (10?) you'll have an easier time with this.  You may want to use a bogus driver "login" because you'll be terrible at first.  You'll miss stops, you'll be late, especially if you're counting money.  I started with the money, but you can turn this off if you want to focus on the bus driving first before adding things that will cost you time (making you late).  I picked the same bus each time for awhile, because you'll need to figure out stuff that will be harder if you keep changing buses (i.e. you have to try to keep the bus comfortable for people and, if you're not used to Celcius, you will be).
I'd recommend these things for new players, although people's thoughts will vary on this (I did this with money-counting and I had an OK time with that).   AI traffic - the traffic will hit you wildly and you'll have to stop and call in the police (thereby making you late).  I turn that off, and I try to drive properly even though I don't "need" to (I can simply drive through cars at this point).  I'd turn the money off to start, or maybe simplify it.   drive through the tutorial in Grundorf (note that you only get the tutorial here) and drive for awhile there, as that's a simple map.  It's still fun.
Graphics -> this thing is a monster and badly needs optimization.  I see lots of people complaining about this, and what i found to be helpful was to scour the add-on DLC manual pages and follow their recommendations (they differ, so compare them and test).  I have a 4790k  i7 intel cpu and GTX 750ti (not the fastest but not awful for games of this era).   I was able to double my framerate by following the steps in some of those manuals.  Right now I set it to 30fps, I lowered the other settings as recommended in the manuals, and I set up filtering via my nvidia graphics card settings for the game.
The game is fun (oddly, despite its flaws).  The mouse controls are actually quite easy to use for steering and acceleration.  You need a full numeric keypad to use turn signals (easily, but you could reprogram to another key).  It's humorous, even when it shouldn't be (the people move like robots and look barely human at times).  I wouldn't recommend turning down random streets.
The learning curve is extremely difficult.  After 30 hours I can manage getting through routes on a few buses on two lines.  But it's relaxing, kind of like a truck simulator with some busy work to do.  The DLC is not inexpensive, and I'd recommend research --  a lot of reviews show some difficulty with some of the addons.  The game should have been much more optimized and should be running much more smoothly at this point-- hopefully, following some of the graphics settings as prescribed in the newer manuals will help.

This game has its pros and cons. I'll recommend it because I spend a lot of time on it but decide for yourself if its worth it.
Pros:

Freeware mods are great, and there's a very wide range of them.
Wide range of DLC available. Good ones are good.

Cons:
Badly optimised. Unstable and relatively low FPS even on conservative settings. Stuttering and crashes can be common.
Payware/DLC is expensive and quality of some of the DLCs can be very poor.
Long load times into maps. Really really long.
Not very user friendly. Controls can be complicated to use given the lack of a tutorial. Easy once figured out, but it takes awhile.
Despite its age, it's still more buggy that I'd like.
End of the day, I still play it, so I'd recommend it, but do consider these pros and cons and make the decision yourself! :)

Like the first Kingdom Rush, this is a well balanced tower defense game.  It seems a little repetitive in some areas, I.E the winding map layout, with the same level layout, 1 standard mode, 2 (of the same) challenege modes per level.  The hero system, tower upgrade system and even tower building/tower types have more or less remained the same, as well as the special (#1 and #2) abilities.  What I notice to be relatively good improvements over the first, are the tower upgrades have changed at least (however the 4 base types are still there), but also the hero system has been somewhat improved with a leveling/perk system, which is cool.  This gives all the newly designed heroes a unique feel, where they can all be exploited for maximum effect depending on your playstyle.  The visual portion of the game engine also appears to be a lot more crisp, and/or sharp in this game, it seems to flow a lot more smoothly than the first game.  This game also seems to have ramped up the difficulty (for me at least) since the first game.  Like the first game, I'm playing on Normal mode, and I just can't understand the formula in this game sometimes.  It's nice in some ways, and frustrating in others, I am not new to tower defense games at all, but I had a few roadblocks in the first game, and seemingly more-so in this game.  I wouldn't blame this entirely on the game however, but what I'm getting at, is it makes the game feel very "linear" in a sense, where only 1 type of setup will work (in certain levels, Not All.).  For example the Level 4 Iron mode, I have tried many different tower layouts, and just get destroyed seemingly very early in the level, I just cannot for the life of me figure out how to make any progress there.  Or, the center jungle level (where the "purple" enemy first shows up), I have tried many different layouts and heroes, and can get almost to the end but just get overwhelmed every time.  So, things like that make it seem there is 1 "key" I cannot find that makes these levels passable.  However, while this game seems repetitive in some areas, overall it is an improvement over the first in every way, as well as worth the price of admission, or at best, on sale.

There are goals to keep you motivated and invested and collections you can make, but it's really all up to you. The music is pleasant, the enviornment is beautiful and changes with the seasons, and the townspeople are not flat characters. Pros:
+ A tense (at times) simulation of hacking
+ Interesting missions
+ Abundant hints that helps move things along without excessive hand-holding
Cons:
- A bit short
- Some technical issues, most notably unresponsive keyboard entry (at least on the Mac OS X)
- Missions are scripted, making replayability questionable
Hacknet is a scripted version of Uplink... I think that's the best way to describe it. Where Uplink offers a plot, you can completely ignore it and treat the game as an open-ended simulation. Missions in Uplink are pretty much generated on the fly, which gives you an endless supply of it at the cost of things being repetitive after awhile. Hacknet's missions are more tightly scripted, making it much more interesting but I do question its replayability.
Both Hacknet and Uplink offers stylized view of hacking. Hacknet is slightly more realistic with the fully functional console (which those of us used to working with Unix-like commands will find completely familiar). If I have one complaint against Hacknet's art is that it seems to be schizophrenic: it can't decide whether to go for a completely realistic look or a completely stylized one; the mix-and-match style somehow feels a bit of a mismatch. Another complaint is that I sometimes find that the keyboard input is unresponsive: characters are sometimes ignored, the Enter key not properly recognized, etc. This can be very frustrating when you are trying to hammer in commands as quickly as possible before you are traced... this does make for some tense moments, though, and makes me wonder whether this is a bug or a feature.
In all, Hacknet provides you a pleasant distraction for a couple of hours, and it may look cool to bystanders when you seem to be frantically typing commands into your computer to hack into some mainframe. It's got its tense moment, provide a moderately challenging puzzles and some laughs (be sure to read some of the text files scattered in the servers you are hacking into).
Recommended.

Let me start by giving the folks at Chucklefish a huge round of applause for drawing me in to this game.  The trailers, videos and other media for this game all looked epic.  Here was a true adventure game!  Something to revigorate that awesome Terraria feel, but even better!  An amazing tale of discovery and rebuilding!
And then you bought the game, started playing, and realized - it was all a facade.
Starbound has one of the worst put-together progression systems I have ever seen in a game.  It goes like this - find materials, combine materials, fight boss, next stage.  Rinse and repeat for not 2 tiers, not 3, but 10 FRIGGIN TIMES.  And after the fourth teir, there aren't even any more bosses.  Dreadful.
Mining is useless, since caves are incredibly rare and usually contain nothing of use.  And anyways, you can find everything - yes, everything - you need just by walking around on the surface.  So that's almost 70% of the world that is simply useless.  Dungeons are huge and...that's it.  They contain almost no loot, and present no challenge since almost every room is the same.  Just fighting my way through Terraria's single dungeon was more fun than all the dungeons I have gone through in this game put together.  Dreadful.
And, quite possible Starbound's worst offense?  Let me give you the fast version.  In a game with an insane, morbid cult, a devastated human race, and a race of mutated apes who are under threat of extinction, there are ten times as many terrible jokes, fourth wall breaks, and other things that ruin your experience.
DREAD-FUL.
Simply - do not buy this game.  Go spend your 15 dollars on Terraria, or Minecraft, or any other sandbox you can think of.  Don't let Starbound's clever advertising get to you - this game is nothing it says it is.

In this game you play as the goddess Athena, who's job it is to guide Odysseus' boats to safety. You do this by altering the wind strength, which always blows toward their destination, and by dragging your mouse through the sea to create currents.
This sounds simple enough, but you also have to prevent the ships from hitting rocks and sand bars, and avoiding other dangers like a cyclops throwing rocks at them (you can catch the rocks by clicking on them with the mouse). Additionally you need to direct the boats to statues to unlock gates and there are also bonuses to pick up along the way. Naturally it gets harder as you progress, with newer dangers and more difficult maps to negotiate.
Although the graphics are pleasing, the resolution is only 640x480. You have a choice of full screen or windowed.
To be honest, it's not my type of game and it didn't hold my interest for very long, but it's by no means a bad game. It wouldn't appeal to everyone, but it's fairly challenging and I'm sure some gamers would enjoy it.
Conclusion: a decent casual game ideal for a quick play when you don't have much time to spare.

Game is broken and unbalanced, and central mechanics are treated as a formality. Yes, the enemy will have a penalty to hitting you when you stand next to a stack of bricks, but it doesn't affect the line of sight in any way. Zombies will melee you through walls, and vipers will snatch you with their tongue from the other side of a parking lot and drag you through every single car on the way, or from the top of a building, hidden behind a railing. As soon as you lose concealment, every active enemy on the map knows exactly where every single unit you have is located. I say "active" because the only thing keeping the entire map from coming after you is the fact that some groups of enemies are braindead until YOU see THEM.
It's ridiculous how a well positioned and entrenched squad gets decimated because a viper and a lancer works together and uses unfair range to snatch, crush and incapacitate a unit in one round. Sectoids apparently don't even need a direct line of sight to use their abilities. I've seen them posess people and raise zombies (I don't know if they have an upper limit for how many they can raise)  from the other side of a building, halfway across the map and out of reach for my squad.
"Well just git gud" you'd probably tell me, or tell me to take my time and use positioning and conservative tactics to carefully cross the map, but in most cases where some unpredictable element doesn't rush out of nowhere and ruins your day in one round, the mission timer will force you to be reckless. You got caught in a prolonged battle in the middle of a street, but you have to push past the enemy and risk getting shot in the back just so time won't run out and your whole squad goes MIA.
I don't recommend the game, and I see no point in buying DLCs for a rushed and broken game.

I never preorder games, but I loved Firaxis' reboot of the XCOM series, I was excited by the concept of fighting a guerilla war against invaders who had already conquered the world, and I wanted to support good old PC gaming, so when it became available, I went ahead and preordered XCOM 2 with the Reinforcement pack. I regret that decision, I regret buying the game at all, and I will never again make the mistake of ordering a game before there are significant numbers of user reviews.
The game does some things right; there are some changes from the last game that are genuine improvements, but the flaws in the game overshadow these and make playing the game a chore. For starters, there are the performance issues that still plague the game months after its release. The game has much more demanding hardware requirements than XCOM: EU, has trouble running on many systems that exceed its recommended specs, and yet, in the end, does not look significantly better than its predecessor. And what is the deal with the ridiculous load times before and after a mission? What exactly is being loaded? I could understand the load times before missions if they were being used to generate the mission map (though that's apparently not the case), but why on earth do I have to wait 5 minutes just to get back to base? I can play three or four games of XCOM:EU in the time it takes to play a single game of XCOM 2, not because the campaign is longer, but because of all the stupid load screens and unecessary delays in the gameplay.
The worst flaw in the gameplay itself is the number of missions with a turn limit. The problem is not with the turn-limited missions themselves—it's not that they're too hard or unbalanced in any way—no, the problem is that there are just so many of them that they become dull. The bomb disposal missions in XCOM:EU were a welcome change of pace, and I found myself wishing there were more missions like that. In this game, however, I breathe a sigh of relief whenever i get to play a mission that doesn't have a turn limit.  The developers have stated that the turn limits were designed to speed up the pace of gameplay. In reality, they slow it down. Because each move is more important, you have to spend more REAL time scrolling around the map and carefully planning your moves and less REAL time shooting aliens and having fun.  Again, if it was only a quarter to a third of the missions that had these timers, I would love them, but when it's over 90% of missions, it just gets boring.
I won't review the DLC here, but suffice it to say none of it was worth the cost.
The biggest problem, though, is the constant bugs. They make it impossible to play ironman. Even with the latest patch, I've had soldiers who got stuck after opening a door, soldiers who were injured by elements they were supposed to be immune to, soldiers killed by explosions in squares they had already moved away from, mission objectives that suddenly went from full health to zero in a single turn with no one shooting at them, and many many others. Granted, not all the bugs have been in the aliens' favor: I did once have a soldier who was killed, but was still somehow able to shoot (though not move). The game has also been crashing on startup with increasing frequency. I can fix this by verifying the game cache and letting Steam download the files that fail to validate, but lately I've been having to do this every time I want to play the game. I'm writing this review now because I just unistalled the game fully intending to reinstall it and see if that fixed the problem, but now that I've removed it, I've realized that I don't really WANT to reinstall it.
I preordered this game because I wanted to support PC gaming, but if this is the kind of crap we can expect from developers, maybe it would be kinder to let it die.

Let's start this off by saying that I love this game. It's free, there is NO pay to win aspects (though you can buy weapon and tool skins and cosmetic items from the marketplace. You can also earn such items simply through playing the game), and the modding community is quite extensive. I love where this game seems to be heading, and I'm always excited when Nelson, the single developer running Unturned, posts information about new content. There are plenty of maps to keep you entertained until a new one comes out, each with their own personal touches. The housebuilding, though slightly limited, is fun and easy. The art style is very friendly and easy on the eyes, giving the whole game a casual feel. The game is very noob-friendly, perhaps too much...
All that being said, there are a few things that I personally think could be, and hopefully will be added or improved on. I will begin with talking about the singleplayer, and then the multiplayer. Please keep in mind that I'll only talk about my personal issues with the game, and that I completely respect the opinions of other players. Singleplayer can be fun at times, and boring at others. When first starting the game, It's very fun to explore all the maps, complete quests, build unique houses, and collect all the goodies that the game has to offer. Once you've learned the basics of the game, however, the game becomes much easier. I'm personally able to get military gear after getting nothing but a hammer to defend myself. After getting such gear, raiding towns for things like food, water, and materials becomes less of a hassle, and soon I'm able to craft seeds, water barrels and planting boxes to sustain an almost infinite amount of food and water.
Simply said, after a certain point, it's not a point of survival, it's about getting better guns and finding creative ways to slaughter hordes of zombies. this is where multiplayer comes in. PVP servers are about finding the best vehicles and guns before anyone else, and then simply ganging up on the guys who logged on to the server 7 minutes ago. PVE servers are about building a cool base with a cool layout and getting a nice vehicle before everyone else steals and locks them all. Arena servers are about aiming, which most players kinda suck at because they spend so much time building bases and killing zombies that quite literally have no brains. If it were a bit harder to loot up your survivor, maybe things would be a little different.
I also wish there was some vehicle customization. Paint color maybe, or vehicle parts that you could use to upgrade a ride, such as different horn sounds or things that actually change vehicle performance. Nothing too complicated, considering the player community mainly consists of tweens or adults that act childish (nothing wrong with either group!). Despite all this, this is still one of my favorite games, and I'll continue playing this game for many more hours. I highly recommend Unturned to any and all gamers!

I have seen a few reviews saying this game has a confusing story/poor story element, yet all I ever hear is praise for Dark Souls when it's story is basically "you're dead, kill these people and it might help". While despite playing Dark Souls several times it couldn’t hold my attention, and I have beaten Lords of The Fallen. But I digress...on to the review.
I like Lords of The Fallen in most areas. I think the combat is reminiscent of Fable on the original Xbox which in my opinion was responsive and fun. Locking on has some quarks but is easy to get used too. Spells and the gauntlet add some diversity to the combat but do not break the game, like in Dark Souls where magic is easy mode. (It may seem like I am bashing DS but I’m not. I like DS but it is the only game I have to compare this one to as it is obviously inspired by DS.) Bosses do lack visual diversity in a since but their skills are varied enough to make each one feel like a new experience.
I absolutely love the art style in this game. It is rare for the lead character in a game to not only act like a badass, but to look like one as well. Harkyn is certainly both of those things. He looks inspired by Ragnar Lothbrok from Vikings and is just as hardened. It is refreshing to get away from the stereo typical "why did this happen to me" lead, and see one man up to the task without whining about it. The game is grainy and dark in tone for a mature feeling.  Gothic and Viking inspired architecture is pleasing to the eye and feels ominous. Armor and weapons seem to have been inspired by the dark ages mixed with the absurd scale used in Warhammer 40k; making you feel indestructible and enemies look menacing.
The difficulty in the game at first is frustrating. Never on the same level as DS but early on you will die frequently to even standard enemies. But by endgame Harkyn can tank blows from even the final boss and carries more than enough potions. Some people do not like the feeling of godliness in a game, but I enjoy it as it satisfying when character progression feels like it has payed off. Leveling up and gaining new gear can make you unbeatable, and I feel like every game should allow the player to become a god of death if that is how they want to play.
Overall I think Lords of The Fallen is a solid game. It lacks some polish but the important mechanics feel good, and most major bugs have been patched by this point. I did not experience even one crash during my play through, and the hit detection was spot on. Every time I died it was my fault. At around 20 hours to beat with all side quests and secrets I do not think the game is worth $50, but if you can find it on sale at half that or less pick it up.

In many ways, XCOM 2 is an improvement upon the already excellent game XCOM: Enemy Unknown from 2012. The strategy layer has been made a lot more interesting than just "scan for activity", the soldier classes feel a lot better and more unique because each class has their own secondary weapon, the aliens are generally more diverse and have more interesting abilities (like the Codex' clone ability or the Archon's blazing pinions). The randomized maps also add a lot more variety to the game and make no two missions the same (although some generated maps can be pretty bland).
The game certainly has it's problems: The performance still seems to be quite poor for a lot of people, but for me personally it works perfectly fine (and has since release). However, this might be an issue for you.
Additionally, the game still has problems with explosion animation and damage animation not being synchronized or sometimes the game seems to hang for a bit before it continues. For that reason, I'd certainly recommend using the mod "Stop Wasting My Time". And the developers have stated that they are still optimizing the game, so this situation will probably improve in the future.
Also, the DLC has not been received very favorably. I'd say that this is understandable for Anarchy's children, which adds some rather weird cosmetic options to the game. There is mods to make them look a little more in line with the game's general tone, but I don't think it is necessarily a must have. The other DLCs add very interesting gameplay mechanics but they are also not mandatory, in my opinion. It's important to keep in mind that a fully fledged expansion pack like Enemy Within is still in production.
I hope that future expansions will improve the game in the areas where it's not yet reached it's potential, like the strategy layer or mission objective diversity. But this does not mean that the game is not already a very enjoyable experience.
The game has been a ton of fun to me and I am still playing it today. But that is mainly not because of the vanilla gameplay itself, but because of the tons and tons of mods that are available. Most prominently, there are the mods by the Long War Studio that make the game a lot more interesting and add a lot of variety, but then there's also mods like A Better Advent or Grimy's Loot Mod by lesser known modders that look professional and freshen the game up a lot. It is really the modding that provides the game with hundreds of hours of replayability.
Almost every problem that you could have with the game can easily be modded out. Don't like the turn timers? There's a mod for that. Don't like the weapon balancing? There's a mod for that. Think some aliens are unfair or maybe too weak? There's a mod for that (in fact you can easily adjust these kinds of things yourself with no programming knowledge required). Don't like the design of some weapons or armor? There's mods for that.
If you like turn based strategy and like a good challenge, then XCOM 2 is a great game for you. If you get into modding, you can sink hundreds of hours into this game.
