And if it isn't their developers, it is the fourm mods, which have banned people for even critique.
Usually ends up like this: 'I think X is bad, because Y' ( BANNED. Reason: 'bad'. )
Before a wild fanboy appears, you can literally google this. I will not hold your hand, do it yourself.
Game is not going anywhere, they're already working on another game too.
( Apparently it's another team in the same company, as if there even was anyone working on it in Starbound in the first place. )
EDIT2.0: It's been a LONG time and yet still none of the promises were expanded upon, and the game's current population are fanboys or people who are angry, still waiting for a product.
-REVIEW-
Starbound is very linear, with no real goals on what to do other than: 'Collect stuff, make better stuff.'
There is no real incentive to play beyond that, as building is mostly pointless as you will leave worlds behind, as you should be travelling across the whole galaxy of space and whatever.
The quest system is very under-utilized ( as of which, they have stated that they will add more for 1.0 )
and even if they do add more quests, the question changes to: 'Will it ever be worked on far enough to be interesting and add value to the game?'
Outside of it's initial charm, which comes from the 'immersive' part of the game, the game can get old rather quickly, as there currently isn't enough material to keep you interested in the lore of the game, and there isn't enough quests/dialogue to keep you wanting to stay around the towns/villages/airships, which again, comes down to lack of content. There are plenty of descriptions, which are a nice touch to the 'immersion' factor, and the player will actually move as if they were talking. There's also a ton of references, which will entertain some. Some references are VERY obvious, while others are a bit more subtle, however, still obvious.
But that isn't enough to keep players interested for long.
There's survival elements into this game that require you to eat, be warm, and of course, remain in good health ( so nothing completely ruins your day ).
However, this adds to the linear part of the game.
You make armor, it protects you, you make better armor, it protects you better, and now you are a bit more warm. As for food, you can get food almost anywhere, making it more of a annoyance than an actual survival element. And I do mean anywhere, you can kill animals on the moon if you needed to.
The combat works in a good concept, it's actually better than Skyrim. You'll need to actually attempt to stay alive, as enemies are dangerous enough to overwhelm you, until you are geared.
There are various types of weapons in Starbound.
Spears - Good for poking
Swords - Good for stabbing
Guns - Good for shooting
Bows - Good for Hunting
and various other tools of violence, all at your disposal.
Currently, the enemy isn't programmed far enough to actually require tactical use of the weapons.
The best use is simply to get a ranged weapon and kite the opponent.
If an opponent could require certain use of weapons, ( perhaps teamwork )
then this would be very interesting.
Shooting a monster, while it turns to deflect you, while an ally stabs it in the back with a spear, avoiding it's protruding spikes and toxic clouds.
There is the standard mining. Not much to explain there.
Cutting down trees actually falls over. Rather than combusting. +1 Immersion.
Items; they are everywhere.
There are plenty of items and upgrades within Starbound that really change the game.
However, your luck is based on whether you go to the right planet or not.
Whether you got lucky with the RNG, or maybe you looked for a good planet on the internet, there will still be many pointless planets in which you do nothing but look for a giant monster that has red particles near it. Then you kill it and get a weapon with special properties, which are pretty fun to use. My personal favorite was the bonehammer, which let you slam with a melee attack, while at the same time, launching bones at the enemy.
Speaking of items and upgrades( called techs ); there are some pretty cool finds that let you do certain things.
Using a quick dash, or maybe creating a bubble to help you levitate, those help with the game's combat, adding a bit of excitement. But, again, there simply isn't enough to use, losing out on any potential diversity.
The game's modding scene is extremely good, but, as this is a review of the base game, we will not discuss mods as part of the game. The modders of Starbound have done some excellent work and have added many things that players have wanted. If you did pick up Starbound and regret it, you may have a chance using the player created mods, which would help you gather some value out of the game.
Now, you have all of those cool stuff in a sci-fi world. 'What more do I need?' - No one, ever.
There's the giant problem of the game not being finished, and not currently having enough meta-game. The lack of content really strains the game, a moment where dynamic missions would be very influential. Right now, the only real content there is, is based on the sole existance of player creativity, and mechanics. Once a player has exhausted either, ( which they will, unless you have a never-ending supply of drugs. ) they will then have nothing to do. Yes, there are quests, but how long will those really last the player? Will they be lengthy enough to continue playing, and will they successfully hook the player? The lack of a true meta-game really shows after just beating the first boss, and is very evident after you get to the last sector.
'Oh, you can uh-uh-uh build a b-b-base!'
But what purpose does it serve me, other than for more storage?
Other than searching for dungeons ( then raiding them after hopefully finding one )
and beating all of the bosses in the game and crafting the linear-upgrades of items, what more can you REALLY do?

Now... before I start this, probably meaningless, review off, I would like to say that I do enjoy the difficulty of the game. For the same reason I enjoy other games like Xcom. Its fun to be in high stakes battles, and the the game delivers spades in that particular department. While it is down to random chance, the fights feel beefy while still avoiding the pitfall of having "bullet spongy" enemies. The bosses are unique, and while at times frustrating, are extremely satisfying to kill. Its a fun game...
However...
This "however" isn't about the new dlc, in fact I don't even own it. No, this is about a certain radiant quest added as free dlc that snuck its way into my save file called the Brigand Vvulf, along its associated town event.
Lets start off with the basics, It is a level 6 end-game content level of difficulty, and yet it can trigger if you have at least four level 5 characters. It pops up a menu about "If you don't comeplete this mission the town will be damaged!" without specifying "how" much your town will be damaged.
Spoiler alert! it's two upgrades, but you would've never known that unless you've checked online...
It's a mission similar to the final level as in, "If you abandon this quest we'll randomly kill one of your party members even If your only at the start, because REASONS"
It's trash mob's are slighlty more annoying versions of the standard endgame enemies, mixed in with weaker level one enemies, and the boss isn't too shabby either being a cool mix of the prophet and brigand eight pounder. It seems fun... If your at the endgame. If your not, and are... lets say roughly sixty percent through the game? like I was, then your not going to have a good time.
I didn't know anything going into the fight, but initially, I thought that If I didn't then all my buildings would lose all thier upgrades, as that would seem the logical outcome given the games track record. I went in with level 5 guys, mostly un-upgraded to top tier due to me trying to get my other guys geared up. I went in, and got mostly destroyed, but I persevered and got all four of my party members to the boss so I could go and do something more fun. I got mostly destroyed, but I was able to kill the boss, after of course three of my party members become paranoid freaks. I was ready to move on and- wait... why arn't his summoned guys dispersing?
I got hit with a critical slice and dice, the stress"wave" hit my party twice.
My man at arms had a heart attack, and died. With my healer, refuseing to do what I say, I decided to retreat, I mean I killed the boss it should... It reset the ecounter... to top it all of the "retreat stress" caused the rest of my party to be pushed over the brink and have heart attacks as well, I failed the mission...
I proceeded to ragequit, HARD. Save. deleted.
Maybe I wouldn't have attempt such a mission at such a under prepared level, but the game was vague on the consequences of not completeing the mission. I can forgive RNG fails, but throwing endgame content at someone randomly spikes the difficulty and isn't fair. You could defend it by saying "THATS DARKEST DUNGEON BABY"...
HOW-EVER
The game designs CHOSE, to implement the possibility of this happening to someone who's unprepared, has only four level five's, and is maybe even new to the game. Also, the chance of it happening begins when you first get four of the level five variety hero's, and the chances of it happening increase by 4% per week, and yes, I checked this on the official wiki. So the game litterally FORCES you to encounter the event...
Maybe It's just me, but this, it isn't "fun"...
Up untill they fix this, rebalance or remove it entirely, I'm not going start playing the game again anytime soon... but, to everyone who might want to buy this game. It WILL throw curveballs at you, It WILL ramp up the difficulty without warning... and It WILL leave you feeling cheated.

Kingdom Rush Frontiers, the sequel to arguably the best Tower Defense game ever made.

+3 Bosses, more coming in the future
+Lots of heroes (8 at the moment)

+Lots of levels. The main campaign is 15 levels, 30 if you count the Heroic and Iron challenges
+More levels are coming in future updates

+Tons of easter eggs. Even more than in the original one. From Predators to Wilhelms you are gonna have fun trying to find ´em all
+Amazing sound track. I would recommend finding the OST on YouTube and listening it, especially the Boss Battle soundtrack
Cons:
-Bosses are too easy. Maybe it´s just the fact that I have completed each KR like 5 times, but these bosses are ez to slaughter.

-The new hero system is a bit annoying. It took me 22 levels just to level Mirage (one of the starter heroes) all the way to max, which annoys me so much. I want to experiment with different heroes, but that is too annoying when a hero can´t get even one level up from one stage.

I love the KR series. Like I said, I have completed all the games ATLEAST 5 times on veteran, all stages. Overall I also appreciate the devs behind the games. Like for real, the amount of detail, secrets and easter eggs on these games is mind blowing! Like I mentioned earlier, each leve has something unique in it, usually even more than one thing! These devs just put so much work into their games and I am going to
buy KR:O if it ever comes out, alongside with Iron Marines.
Would I recommend it? ♥♥♥♥ yeah. It is gonna be worth those 10 bucks, specially if they are gonna add something "special" like they hinted. So, prepare your upgrades, rally your troops, place your towers and get ready to head into a new Frontier!

- it's shorter than the original. There are more stages coming in future updates though.
- "tap to..." don't do that. I know it's a port but this is PC.

Is Lords of the Fallen a good game or is it a bad game? Well, it depends. It's most certainly not a terrible game. It's not that great either. It's like if you took Dark Souls and played it on 1/3rd of the speed, and the game (including the uninspired and monotonous bossfights that hardly ever present a challenge) is mostly pretty easy and boring/tedious. The visuals are pretty nice, though, even if the artistic direction is kinda generic (as is the disjointed and bland narrative and lore), but rather demanding from a performance point of view.
My bottom line would be – if you try to make a clone of Dark Souls games (which is what this game clearly and undeniably is, even if some people get really mad when you mention this), changing things here and there just for the sake of not being a direct DS clone without really understanding what really makes Dark Souls such a great series might not be the best idea. I would very much like to see a Dark Souls game with the visuals of LotF. I'd rather not see LotF game with the visuals of Dark Souls, if you get what I mean. Nice graphics really isn't the most important thing to look for in a game.
In the end, I give LotF recommended, but an unforgettable instant classic like Dark Souls it ain't. Take it as a 6/10, if you will.

tl;dr: It's quite nice. Has very little to do with hacking, but still a fun game to play if you're apt with a shell.
Summary:
Hacknet is a game in which you do various tasks for various people for various reasons. You delete files, fetch passwords, etc. See it as a puzzle game, of sorts.
If you're a bit familiar with InfoSec, you'll find several references to real-life tools like nmap, or real life ♥♥♥♥-up's (like Apple making "alpine" the default password on every iOS device).
Cons:
However, you'll likely be disappointed that the in-game shell isn't nearly as powerful as any comparable real shell and that a lot of realism has been cut away for the sake of gameplay.
Further, a lot of details simply don't add up. Why does the whole world run UNIX with an open SSH port? Why do they have .dll and .exe files on UNIX? And why does it bluescreen? Why do "binary" files contain 1's and 0's when cat'd, instead of the actual ASCII representation? If you're really out for realism, I suggest you to start a real shell and get cracking - but hey, it's just a game, so enjoy.

I backed this game. I liked its concepts, and I thought it would work really well, and had high hopes for it.
Sadly, I cannot recommend this game.
Basically, you are playing a "space" Moba, with ships that have different "powers" or skills, stats, and so on.
On to the meat of the matter.
Pro's
- Variety of ships. The sheer amount of different types actually make it interesting, especially since you have to play against other players. This means your skill, as in, how well you know your enemies ships, and how well you know how to play your own, is a huge factor.
- Team play. Unlike most Moba's I have seen, Fractured Space will actually force you to play as part of a team. You CANNOT just "run off and do your own thing, and hope it works". If you do, your team will loose. Fast. Its quite suprising how quickly a match can go from "tied" to one side completely dominating in under 2 minutes, but teamwork actually matters here, which is both a pro, and a con.
- Space Physics/Enviroment. Honestly, this is one of the things that drew me to this game. Space ships duking it out in space. It handles...like you would expect a space ship to handle, slowly, and precisely, though the "larger" the ship, the slower it manuvers.
- Player community. This one is hit and miss. Sometimes you'll find players that will help new players, and then...you get the trolls as well. Like I said, hit and miss.
Sadly.....there are more negatives then positives right now, which is why I had to change my review from a positive recommendation, to negative.
Con's
- Same map. No matter what ships you play with, no matter what your team is, your basically going to be running the same map. Over. And over. and over......and....over....I know this doesn't seem like a big deal, but when you replay the exact same map for months on end with no break, it can get..a tad annoying.
- Same ships. While there ARE indeed a variety of ships, most you will never see. Because the ships themselves are Horribly unbalanced. To put it bluntly, same ships are a LOT better at killing enemy ships then others, which means players tend to ONLY play these specific ships. So you end up fighting the same 3 or 4 ships nonstop. Also, as a  new player coming in against these powerful ships, its not fun. You get slaughtered, basically nonstop. Good example of this was when I played the ship that "stressed" defense, with high health, and resistance to damage. I was killed in under 10 seconds by 1 of the enemy players. And usually, battles happen with 2-3 ships at the same time on each team duking it out. Not really a "good" learning enviroment for trying to get a feel for how to play the game.
- Complete lack of guide. Now, this has changed, there is a "base" guide explaining how the game works, but sadly, this guide confuses players more then helps. The game itself is actually quite complicated, with 4-5 factors determining who is "Winning" the match. Sadly though, the guide, while walking you through what each thing "does", doesn't explain WHY you should use them. As an example, there are 6 "resource" points, that, if your team has any of them, will give you "resources" that you can then use on an upgrade. (aka, gives you exp). Now, the goal of the game, is to take over the enemy station. Not destroy. Take over. When you enter the enemy stations "field" it starts hitting you. Hard. And of course you can't regen while in that field, though the enemy can. The more you die, the longer you have to sit in "time out". There is also a "special" gas station, that gives you a boost in the center to damage. Problem is, resources can counter that. It becomes a waiting game, of trying to kill your opponents, so they can't spawn quickly, holding resources, and taking gas when it triggers (about every 2-4 minutes.) LIke I said, the guide doesn't actually explain why you want to hold these, its more of a "hey, do this because reasons!" sort of thing. Granted, its better then letting a player walk in blind, but still sucks for a new player just starting.
- Player community. Sadly, this one is hit and miss. Sometimes you'll have a really helpful team/players that will assist a new player. Then others, you have the guys that are twice the level of players just starting, and targets the new players explicitely, going out of their way to "stalk kill" them, even letting other players shoot them to hell, JUST to kill the new players, because they know the new players can't fight back. I've not only seen this happen multiple times, but have had it HAPPEN to me multiple times. Even worse, there are no "real" ways to report these players, or "stop" them from playing in a match with you again.
- Team Play. Yep, this is another con. Just because YOU understand how to work as a team, and be a team player, does not mean you will be paired with other, like minded people. Your team of...oh, lets say 6, could easily loose, because you have 2 players that just go off and do their own thing, while the enemy team works together. Or vice versa.
- Extremely unbalanced. Like I said, sadly the game is extremely unbalanced. Players will almost always play one of 4 ship types, because, bluntly, other ships just don't work. Sure, they have great concepts...but they can't FIGHT off these other ships. Snipers, Assassins, Brawlers, Hunters. These four ships are the single most used types in Fractured space. Snipers, because of the sheer amount of high damage destruction they can wreck, and then run without being hit. Assassins, because they can "stealth" becoming completely invisible until they attack you (and they get a bonus for stealth attacking by the way, letting them deal massive damage) Brawlers and Hunters, because their sheer damage output is insanely high, and tends to stack on each other. Healing mines are cool, but doesn't really matter when your trying to hide from a Sniper, and an Assassin decloaks behind you, and kills you, or forces you into the open, where the sniper/assassin takes you out.
- Teamwork, but not with friends. You can play with 1 friend. No more. So if you want to play with more, you can't sadly. This was a big one for me, because I usually play games with 3 or 4 of my friends, and...sadly we can't here.
- Microtransactions/pay2win. While not "Truly" pay to win, as the premium ships aren't that much better then their equal level counterparts, it also isn't a large advantage, due to you not having the experience to know how to Handle those ships. The reason that's on ere, is because DE are trying to already including Microtransactions. Its a Beta. Get your♥♥♥♥♥♥together, fix your coding, and for the love of all things holy, at least TRY to listen to your players, instead of "internal review". But, Microtransactions. That tells me that they consider the game "finished".
Sadly, the cons, for me, garner the negative recommendation. Its just not fun for me to play a game, where I have to play on the same maps, against the same ships, and it turns into a slugfest of "who kills who fastest".
If you enjoy highly competative, minorly tactical Moba's, you may like this. I thought it was going to head in the right direction, and sadly, it did not.

I tried the game because I was curious about it's story which was interesting and a lot deeper than I thought it would be. There are different ways to go through the game although there are some missions that you have to fulfill in order to progress, the side quests are also fun. In addition, the extra widgets (and mini-game) and the fact that you can change the colour of your UI are little details that make the game's fun increase.
The music is the one thing that I both liked and didn't like. While it fit the atmosphere when you're playing, it can get distracting at times (especially when a part of the mission is time-sensitive). Maybe if it was softer or you had the option to use your own tracks it would be better. There were also some bugs I encountered while playing causing me to restart the game twice. The first was an error wherein it told me thtat the mission I just completed wasn't finished and I couldn't progress through the game (as it was a main mission). The second one was a similar issue later on. A simple restart of the game fixed it and I didn't have any trouble with it afterwards.
The graphics are simple and easy on the eyes and so is the font although I wouldn't mind if it was a teensy bit bigger.
The gameplay is simple and after a while, the commands are easy to memorize. I enjoy the puzzle aspect of the game and there are different ways to play through. One challenge (and perhaps my next playthrough) would be playing the whole game simply in terminal mode to see if (1) it's possible, (2) how fast I can do it, and (3) how challenging it is.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in programming whether just beginning (as it helps teach focus, critical thinking, and memorization) or already pretty in deep (cause it's fun!). It's a great game and pretty cool to play around your friends.

This game is more buggy than XCOM: Enemy Within.
Despite that, I feel that it is absolutely a superior game, especially when it comes to playing on the highest difficulty.
PROS (compared to XCOM:EU)
- Steam Workshop support
- Procedurally generated maps
- More varied mission objectives
- Missions are not an Overwatch-fest
- More opportunities to recover from setbacks, allowing for more risk-taking
- Each soldier class has at least three builds useful for various purposes on Legendary, as opposed to XCOM:EU's one or maybe two. More builds become viable as the AWC endows soldiers with out-of-class skills. Except for psionic soldiers -- and I haven't fully explored the new SPARK class yet.
- No useless options in strategic layer, which is more than I can say for XCOM:EU
- Better strategic layer BY FAR despite what other reviewers are saying. Enemy Unknown definitely had a formula for the most optimal choices and was completely predictable from game to game. Impossible difficulty pretty much meant, "always choose engineers, probably give up South America to the aliens." In XCOM 2, even on Legendary, I may take completely different research paths depending on what resources I find, what AWC does for my soldiers, the distribution of alien facilities, whether or not my hacks pick up Insight or Enemy Protocol or reduced Scanning Times, where the power cores are located in the Avenger, what's available from HQ or Black Market on a given month, what Dark Events I have to contend with.... etc.
- Game music better fits the tone and narrative. I also like how it cross-fades between an "XCOM" and "Alien" track.
- More interesting and likeable characters with better-written dialogue and better delivery on the voice acting
- Did they take out "moving at the speed of death" from Run and Gun? I think they did. Gah that was such a cringe-worthy line.
CONS (compared to XCOM:EU)
- Bugs, largely aesthetic. (Programmer-speak: I think when they pre-calculate the outcome of an action, they load stuff up into asynchronous queues that may get out of order, and the engine gets confused as they are dequeued. This leads to the world as the player sees it having incongruities, like windows or terrain being destroyed without any apparent cause.)
- I cringe a little when soldiers say, "What's over there?" Haderp!
- The music is better, but unlike XCOM:EU none of it gives me visions of my soldiers competing in a roller derby :((( lol
- Was released at a point in life where I have less time for games ;_;

This is a beautiful game, I remember playing each and every single Metal Slug back when I was a kid, used to visit my cousins in summer whenever I got time off from school and since they didn't have any sort of consoles, or anything, we used to go to the arcades near our houses and just spend all of our hours and all of our money, into this games.
Marathons that lasted around seven hours each session, Stapled! trying to figure out enemy patterns, counting how many lives remaining we had, noticing why we were exactly failing in some spots.
It was a glorious time that I still hold dear close to me.
Not that the trilogy it's available on Steam, i've gotten the chance to relive some of that again, and tho I may not have my innocence nor a part of my generosity from that time, I still feel an incredible feeling coming back whenever I get the chance to visit this type of games again.
They were, and are, incredible games in every way, they hold up perfectly up until today, and the pc versions wreck any other "modern" version that i've played, (ps3,ps4,even ps2).
This version has a limited set of settings but all of them are the ones that I feel are necessary for providing an actual faithful experience to the original arcade games, you can play the games at fullscreen resolution, even making them occupy your entire screen, this might not seem as much but I can assure you, it's a wonderful feeling to have a version that finally allows you to that, the Ps3, and the Ps4 version of the games still have some black bars, or alternatively some strange background that in my opinion does nothing more than to just cloud and distract you from part of your screen.
The important thing for me about this version too, it's the options, you're able to change how many lives your character can have, or if alternatively you would like to "free play" the game, meaning have unlimited lives, not LIFE, but LIVES, like unlimited retries, you can also have that.
Besides that there's also multiple difficulties selection that change how much health some bosses have.
Overall this is a great version of a great game that still holds up perfectly today, the gameplay it's amazing, everything has a lot of character and insanity poured into it, and frankly all of the Metal Slug games that are available for NOW, on Steam, are incredible, that is the first one, X (this one), and Metal Slug 3 which is my personal favorite, and the one that is widely considered to be the best.
They are incredible games that do justice for what games used to be, this type of games just don't exist anymore, they were and are games that were souly made out to make you had fun, in an age when gaming hadn't hit the mainstream, and hadn't been both, homogenized, as well as banalized in what the potential for this medium holds up and it can do.
There were games like this one that shined, games made with actual purpose, or at the very least, with multiple ones, not only with the one to go out and make a profit, but with the one to go out, and do something that people might enjoy.
And I did, back when I played, them, and now once again, enjoy this games, a lot.

Ok real review time.
this may seem late but after all i actually needed to upgrade my computer to play this game because its not on console and I can't really figure out why that is but I digress. I guess the biggest point is that if you played X-COM enemy unkown then you arent really missing anything by not buying this especially if you bought the enemy within expansion.
this game is absolutley filled with unskippable dialogue that interrupts gameplay constantly, Central is always screaming about the objective on every ♥♥♥♥ing mission like a child that didnt get the toy they wanted on christmas morning. Dr. Shen's daughter is always painstakingly stating the obvious like telling me the power generators generate power for the base, she's always going on about not trusting Dr. Tygan and about her dead father. what is your problem with Tygan? the man is also annoying but at least he seems to pull more than his own weight around here, and as for your father i miss him too. because at least he knew not to bore me with repetive dribble every time I entered the room. as for Dr. Tygan he never shuts up about Advent hamburgers which i couldnt care less about even if I tried.
The game itself functions exactly like the previous game for the most part you still have your scouts, your heavys, snipers , and medics.
the scout since the last game has been given a sword which is practically useless for him since they have a shotgun for close range and the only time a sword will ever be useful is the incredibly rare occasion when there is only a single enemy left, nobody can shoot the alien, and your scout is out of ammo. the scout can either specialize in or between two extreemes. Ninja or Samurai.
the heavy is also functionally the same but instead of a rocket launcher they get a grenade launcher instead which is much less satisfying than a rocket launcher even though it fulfills the exact same purpose. they instead tacked a rocket launcher to a suit of armor instead. which I will admit, it is fun when you can absolutley blow an entire battalion of aliens to kingdom come with a barrage of rockets and grenades, it just takes a while to get there. the heavy can also be given perks to boost their proficiency with either explosives or their minigun.
not much to say about the sniper really its exactly the same in almost every way. you can either upgrade them to be a fantastic sniper or be a♥♥♥♥♥♥sniper but also do stuff on the frontlines worse than everyone else.
the support has probably seen the most changes meaning that they have been given this little floating robot which gives the support some new abilities and now you can upgrade them to either be a medic or a mad haxzor who will arbitrarily fail hacking something when you really need it to succeed or arbitrarily succeed when there is nothing at stake.
if you want mechs you need to cough up 10 more dollars for dlc.
on the campaign map you are constantly being timed as the aliens march ever closer to completing "The Avatar Project" and you need to stop them. most of the missions in the game are either protect the thing, or destroy the thing, or escort the VIP, or capture the VIP and all of these are under a turn limit. most of these missions dont even make much sense when you think about it.
like why are the aliens just shooting this one device one at a time? also why is this device out in the middle of nowhere if its so important? and if this actually was one of our bases, then why arent there corpses of the resistence littering the ground and advent citizens just wandering the area like nothing even happened? what did advent really have the courtesy to bury their dead enemies before completing their objective? was the base just kind of undercover or something? then I dont know how you could put a giant machine in the middle of a local grocery store and expect people not to take notice?
also in the missions where you are tasked with capturing an advent VIP, why do my men get captured if i dont complete the mission within the time limit? exactly how important is this guy? is advent sending and entire ♥♥♥♥ing armada to deal with 4 or 5 or maybe six guys? was advent going to send this armada of airships regardless of if i showed up or not. or are they just logically sending a dropship and my soldiers are just so thick that they cant tell the difference between their dropship and the enemies?
there are also terror missions like in the last game but they dont make sense because all these people the aliens are killing are unarmed and dont know how to use cover even though they are resistance fighters.
you also have advent bases which are the best because they actually allow you to take your time and actually take advantage of the new concealed mechanic for once.
back on the campaign map you can't choose which contienent you start on anymore neither do you start with a home base continent bonus. in order to recieve a continent bonus you need to make bases on all the sections of the continent which is much harder than it sounds, and then they tell you that you need to make a huge radio towers for each of them and then they'll ask you to make pack lunches for them, danced for them in an animal costume, and sacrificed your first born son, only then will they accept that you are worthy of +5 power to your base. on top of that the resistance likes to place your monthly supplies as far away as possible from your current position and then it takes a full 72 hours to pick up said supplies. what? are we all just guffawing at one poor soul as he loads hundreds of pounds of supplies onto the ship for three days while we picking our noses instead of helping him and getting it done in couple hours? it wouldnt be a problem if you werent interrupted every day by a new event or mission. which happens so often you'll actually start thinking that spot on your wall really could look so much better  with a head shaped hole in it.
but if you liked the first game then you should totally buy this game if you just want more X-COM and you've played the original to death, or you could just not care what i think. afterall I'm just a guy with steam account and a keyboard, you have no reason to listen to me. but then again I dont have to do or care about anything either. so if you'll excuse me I'll be lying on the floor making burbling noises with my lips.

XCOM Enemy Unknown was a game I beat the first try, but with heavy casualties.
X-COM: UFO Defense had me only barely winning the war for Earth with over 70 casualties.
XCOM 2 destroyed my squad one by one then killed Shen in a derelict lab, only 4 hours in.
XCOM EU had me taking all high cover, setting up flanking positions for every battle.
X-COM UFOD had me staggering the position of my soldiers to minimize explosive impact and get ready to auto-shot at any incoming Snakemen that could come from the barn door before sending in Rk. Expendable to open it up and trigger any reaction shots.
XCOM 2 had me breaking out a sweat as my whole strategy, hinging on my Sniper shooting an ADVENT Officer to break supression, missed and left my Demolitionist for certain death in the next turn by the hands of a Faceless he couldn't run from.
XCOM EU sent countries into panic but with the right strategy and a bit of luck, I managed to hold the world together.
X-COM UFO D was something I made it out of with a wing and a prayer, as countries formed secretive pacts with the aliens and gave up on X-COM one by one.  I mortgaged half my base to afford the trip to Cydonia.
XCOM 2 had the world doomed before the game even began, and the aliens can shut you down with a single command.  And they will.  And they have.  Twice.
XCOM 2 is everything EU was, but even better.  You're now the Guerilla side, but with aliens far superior in technology.  They have the upper hand, and you don't even have a chance.  While your soldiers are much more powerful than before with slightly improved technology and brand new classes, along with powerful new skill trees and passive bonuses per class, the aliens counter this with reinforcements, armies, and advantages you can't compare with-- but you can certainly dent them and make a mark.  This is a game I'll spend 400 hours or more in without succeeding once.
Everything from the aesthetic, the soundtrack that puts a new twist on the original game (you can clearly hear the influence of GMGEO1.mid and TACTICAL on some of the songs), and the behavior of AI makes the game feel oppressive and brutal, making it all the more amazing when-- sorry, if-- you pull off a perfect operation.
I'd talk about the ending, but I can't-- mostly because I haven't made it anywhere in the game.
Good luck, 'commander.'  You're going to need it, but you certainly won't get it.

TL:DR :  While not really feeling true as a sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unkown/Within, XCOM 2 is far from a bad game. With exciting new plotlines, crisp graphics, and a tone achieved by gameplay and exciting sequences that leaves little to be desired, XCOM 2 is one of my favourite games to drop an afternoon struggling to defeat.
XCOM 2 was one of the most anticipated titles for me that was being realeased this year. In fact, I skipped buying Fallout 4 last year in favor of it. I purchased Fallout 4 later, and out of loyalty played more of that title to finish it, but few games made me as happy and angry to play as XCOM 2. This game is hard. Very hard. I do not recommend casually playing this game. I guarantee you any complaints people have with this game derive from how frustratingly hard the game is. Every minute decision is costly and dangerous. There are missions that are required that can throw your whole strategy in wreck, and the natural tendency to build up forces and prepare is completely thrown out of whack as you probably won't be waiting in one area more than a few days. All together, it was really exciting to play, and I routinely restarted missions because I knew the cost for success was too dear.
VISUALS:
Let's start here. XCOM 2 blew me out of the water on this one. What a spectacle. Heavy on the loading screens, which made me restless the first time, but shocked me when I saw how crisp each of the maps looks. Everything is an advantage. Height, defence, location, range, environment, and surprise. It's definitely a lot easier to see what is good cover and what isn't. I would say I expected good graphics, but I think what they gave us was definitely either satisfying to expectations or even just a pleasant surprise. The characters adapt certain features and characterisms that aren't switched off on each of the missions. If you customise the crap out of someone, and they look and act a certain way, you can guarantee they look and act like that when you zoom out across the map. I guess that's my main love of this: attention to detail. I appreciate not having generic maps and zones to navigate. The first XCOM had several maps and configurations, but I still got duplicates even with the expansion. I've had to restart XCOM 2 twice now, and barring a couple essential missions, I have yet to get a repeat map.
GAMEPLAY:
It's XCOM. Get the first, enjoy this one just the same. Jokes aside, there are several new mechanics that I don't want to spoil here, but they are hardly gimmicky and once you get the hang of it, they appear essential to you and become second nature. I love the newest mechanic that you get at the very beginning and if you can master it, it is insanely helpful. Altogether, the gameplay upgrades really make it stand out from XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within, and worthy of a purchase by any fan of those games.
And yes, I got really attached to my characters...And yes...they do die...A lot....
STORY:
YES. Just YES. Some people complain about the plot (It assumes you basically lost the last game...no comment), but it really takes the idea that XCOM is some super organization and turns it on its head. In the last game, you had the world on your side. Sure, you were civilization's last hope, but you had resources, monthly staff increases, and confidence. That music oozed confidence! This game? You are on the fringes of society. The world is lost. You are humanity's last hope...again, but now you have nothing. A ship, skeleton crew, an XCOM squad that really seems and acts like the bottom of the barrel in terms of staff, and your wits are your greatest weapon. I feel this all comprises the tone which really struck me deeply. I felt like every decision counted, like I could lose everything in one battle. The enemy continual sends reinforcements...almost like they had an innumerable army at their command. It all compiles to make you feel scared, lost, and worst of all: alone. You are truly alone in this game. Even Epic Voice Guy (same guy from Honest Trailers, Jon Bailey) doesn't help you much. XCOM 2 gripped me and latched on right from the start. If only the game wasn't so hard....
CONCLUSION:
I could hardly recommend XCOM 2 enough. I got it on a 20% sale for about $45 USD, and at that price point, it's very fair. Anything better, I can honestly say you will enjoy yourself for the cost.
I wish you the best of luck....Commander.

For the moment, I can't recommend this game. If future patches fix the existing bugs and optimize the games performance, it may well be a game worth playing. I certainly hope so, because I have long been a fan of the seriees. However, I would currently go so far as to claim that the product I recieved is not the product that I was told that I was purchasing.
My PC is no powerhouse. It's not as though I was expecting to play this on ultra. But my computer either exceeds, meets or falls very slightly short of the "recommended" system requirements. For the record CPU: Intel i7-4770 @ 3.4ghz (Better than). RAM: 8G(same as) Video Card: GTX 760 (slightly below). All well above the minimum system requirements. I didn't expect mindblowing, but I did expect smooth and playable.
In order to achieve an acceptable framerate (and by acceptable I mean not having half second pauses every three or four seconds) I have to set the graphics settings to the lowest possible, across the board. Even then, I experience texture pop ins at remarkably close range, inexplicable framerate drops and stuttering (especially in cutscenes, oddly).
At lowest settings the game is playable, on a machine which meets the recommended system requirements. To me, meeting the recommended requirements ought to mean that I have a computer which is capable of delivering, more or less, the experience that the developers intended. If my experience is that which was intended then... AC: Unity is not a game you want to play. And if I, running at a system fairly close to the "recommended" system, am experiencing these kinds of problems (at low!), I can only imagine the experience of those who purchased it for play on systems which only meet the "minimum system requirements"
Bottom Line: There are people playing on machines far, far superior to mine reporting substantial graphical issues. And I, with a decent PC, can only run this game well on the lowest settings. As a fan of the AC series... Don't buy it. And possibly send an angry letter to Ubisoft.

It's been a while since I wrote a review on Starbound and I'm going to do another because my attitude has changed and I feel that my previous recommendation isn't correct anymore and might lead some people unexpectantly into buying it.
So I will start with my recommendation. Do not buy the game right now. I'll say it again do not buy this game while it is in development. Now you may be asking yourself well why would I say that with having played 80 hours of it and I'm going to explain why my stance is what it is now. I'll try to keep it in bullet format and simple to read so you can pick out the pros and cons and decide more easily for yourself. Also I apologize for my grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors.
Firstly I want to say that Starbound as it is right now is playable and enjoyable to a point, but the reason that I believe you shouldn't purchase it at this time isn't because of the game itself rather the developers and PR behind it which I will get into later.
Pros
Extremely playable, simplistic and fun for short bursts of playing time.
Not necessarily a unique take on the genre, but if you played Terraria I'd argue that you would like this game.
Interesting race concepts and art style
Decent crafting though a bit lacking has it's moments
A variety of biomes to run in and Dungeons to play through keeping some of the worlds you visit fresh and interesting driving
you to continue exploring at least for a while.
Cons
For the cons section I'll follow each bullet with my belief on the validity of the con and whether it should influence your purchase. I am no means a video game expert and all of this is my opinion I'm simply trying to help you understand why my recommendation is what it is.
Though it's marketed as a Beta in this writers opinion it is an Alpha with Beta stability. I'll go in depth with this a bit more to make my reasoning clear, I believe a Beta should be feature complete and be testing for bugs. Some may not agree, but as I stated this is my opinion not a fact. One avenue where I believe this shows itself best is that most if not all of the content dealing with progression, npc interaction, and questing is garbage and it's been this way for coming up a few months shy of a year now. This isn't permenant just current state now.  "In my opinion this is a decent sized con, but I don't believe it should be what you determine your purchase on. Though it does suck a bit now it will get better, but it takes time and work to get through this."
As I mentioned above the game is playable and enjoyable in short play sessions, but it ends at about 2 hours if that. Now you can play and build entire cities if you'd like which isn't bad, but when it comes to enjoyability I like progression and steady game play through to the "end" of the game. "This shouldn't effect your purchase unless you are kind of like me and enjoy progression, questing and npc interaction."
Though there are different biomes after about an hour or so they all blend together, I love their heating system for colder planets don't get me wrong, but the driving force of the game is to gather x ore from x lvl planet and make x lvl armor and ship upgrade to go to the next level. There is no drive to build a base, no drive to colonize anything, and no drive to try to discover anything at all other than dig straight down get your ore then go back to your ship/base to build the next upgrade. "To sum it up these last three cons can all be placed within the Alpha vs Beta con. Just understand that getting into this there are parts missing entire sections that seem boring and will be that way for several more months if not a year more. which brings me to my last con."
The biggest con and the reason that I'm recommending you to not buy this game until it is finished is Developer/company interaction, PR, and feedback to customers. I want to go into detail about this one because it is the damning factor in a lot of the arguments about whether the game is a worth while investment. When I first purchased Starbound the promises from Chucklefish were actually quite different than they are now which brings me to my first complaint. Chucklefish has the worst time with release dates and due to this they change what they say. For instance when I purchased the game there was a quote stating that all funds would go directly to the game and that the more money they got towards it the faster the game would be released. This was followed by a company move and publishing multiple titles for other companies on top of starting another game without having finished their first game. This wouldn't have been so bad had they explained that with the money from Starbound they were in fact not going to hire more programmers and increase the release speed, but rather promote and further their company. Not so bad, but a form of false advertisement on top of a pile of them. Quick releases went to slow releases then releases on a nightly possibly broken status exc. I'll sum this up by when I read what the developers have to say now as they ask for your purchase on steam only a few shards of it are the same as they were when I bought into this and when you argue this point it will get thrown back in your face stating that it is an early release, but I would argue an early release is still promising certain things in the effort to get you to invest in a product so most if not all promises made by a company need to be held accountable no matter the status of the promise. This isn't a kickstarter this is a product being sold on future content or development practices you are promising your customer.
When confronted with the lack of communication back when updates were slow and given between three to four websites developers responded angrily with customers. Through passive aggressive hints or even out right blaming customers for lack of production in certain areas because they were "complaining too much." Let me rephrase I say developers, but TiY is actually the only developer I remember with this. There might have been more, but TiY stands out as having done it the most. "These two points though terrible when talking about a company and a consumer are not so bad, but lead into my final con which is the one that truly drives my recommendation."
Over the past few months when I've visited the forums I've watched as some of the most overzealous moderators delete, censor and close any forum dealing with negative feedback with no other reasoning than "everyone should know better" quote from Izzabelle (The one who locks) < guessing self made title. When questioned about it the moderators continue to delete, censor and act irresponsibly to customers due to the anonymity of their interaction. This behavior though rude and obnoxious can't all be placed on the developer except that it's been happening for months and anyone watching the forums for a length of time know that speaking ill of the game comes with the chance of being banned anywhere from 2 weeks to permanently because "they said so". This would bring one to assume that this type of interaction is not only acceptable to Chucklefish, but applauded by the frequency of these types of responses. Customer censorship is shameful.
Though the game and what it's shaping up to one day be look amazing, Terrible customer interaction, Terrible forum moderation, Lies, Misscommunication and Blaming have ultimately turned me off of this company and any/all of it's future games. My recommendation is to buy the game when it's finished or don't buy it at all, because the moment you have something negative to say you no longer really matter. They got what they needed from you after all.
When the game is out I will switch the recommendation and rewrite the review to explain why in it's finished version it's worth buying, but that any looking to buy need be wary of early access from Chuckle.

I'm very disappointed in the older users of this game as well. Or the ones who spend money often. Not because I envy them or anything, but because they seem to have no consideration for the new users. A lot of the older users, or users who spend real money, are rich in-game, so they're blind to the negative effects of the new updates. They say things like "I love this update! It lets me earn stuff that only someone who has already earned all the best emblems/ gear/ etc could worry about! I'm unaffected by the changes, so you should stop complaining! "
This is how it affects new players. In the very last update, yesterday, they changed the order in which we receive caches from challenges. It originally went like this: Part one gives 2 caches, part two gives 2 caches, part three gives 1 dragon coin. But now it's reversed. Part one give 1 dragon coin, part two gives 2 caches, part three gives 2 caches.
Dragons take 4 coins per soul. You need 75-100 souls for each dragon. Dragons give a small bonus to stats. So people want them. So that's why dragon coins are useful. But the first 2 caches giving money out was far better for a noob than getting 1 dragon coin. Why? Because if a noob doesn't even have money to upgrade their gear so that they can survive in the areas the challenges take you, why do they even care about some dragon bonus stats? The dragons require super rare materials that most people end up BUYING with flux, rather than spending 99% of their Trove time searching for. So now, new players are kinda forced put combat on hold, as they have sucky gear, and all they can do is farm for dragon materials to get those bonus stats. So yes, older players benefit by gaining more dragon coins. THEY have time to earn other things. But newer players needed that small amount of money the challenges use to give.
I was fortunate enough to have obtained most of the classes before they were paid. Back then they could be bought with cubit points. (Curency you earn every day by doing a few dungeons.) Because it allows me to complete the challenges as the bonus class, which completes the challenge in a shorter amount of dungeons. But even as the bonus class, I only complete the first 2 parts of the challenge. 40 dungeons... Because 99 dungeons is bull shet. Nobody does that unless they already have gear high enough to quickly kill the highest difficulty dungeons. I've tried it on a lower level, where we don't receive a bonus multiplier. I absolutely destroyed the lower level dungeons, but the time it took to fly to 99 dungeon alone, was too much time to complete the challenge. Each challenge lasts 20 minutes. 99 dungeons in 20 minutes is a godly expectation that only end game professionals can do.
So now you see that new players are limited to doing the first 5 dungeons and getting 1 dragon coin, but NO caches (Which contained money. Enough money to slowly earn for better armor by spamming the challenge every hour.) Or I guess they could find some way to make freaking 100,000 flux to buy new class coins. Huehue.
The few friends I've introduced to trove are discouraged from even playing it when they see that it's an immediate grind-fest. There use to be a grace period, where newer players could easily get into the game and start earning money to upgrade their gear, but not now. Now you either begin your long journey to get dragons, or you find another way to leech off of higher players by following them to higher area farming. (I'm guilty of doing this currently. I'm maxxed out, yet still need the help of other maxxed out players JUST to make a few bucks. As in, if i wanted to make a new class and upgrade its armor, it's going to take twice or three times as long as the first character I made before the pay to win updates.
You can go to hell, Trion/ Trove. I'm only here because I've developed a tolerance for grinding, and gained some knowledge of income methods in-game. But for how long? A player who is completely unequipped for the difficulty we're at, will follow me around, pretending to help with their puny damage, as we farm away. I sympathize 100%, and have no problem with them. Now... before I start this, probably meaningless, review off, I would like to say that I do enjoy the difficulty of the game. For the same reason I enjoy other games like Xcom. Its fun to be in high stakes battles, and the the game delivers spades in that particular department. While it is down to random chance, the fights feel beefy while still avoiding the pitfall of having "bullet spongy" enemies. The bosses are unique, and while at times frustrating, are extremely satisfying to kill. Its a fun game...
However...
This "however" isn't about the new dlc, in fact I don't even own it. No, this is about a certain radiant quest added as free dlc that snuck its way into my save file called the Brigand Vvulf, along its associated town event.
Lets start off with the basics, It is a level 6 end-game content level of difficulty, and yet it can trigger if you have at least four level 5 characters. It pops up a menu about "If you don't comeplete this mission the town will be damaged!" without specifying "how" much your town will be damaged.
Spoiler alert! it's two upgrades, but you would've never known that unless you've checked online...
It's a mission similar to the final level as in, "If you abandon this quest we'll randomly kill one of your party members even If your only at the start, because REASONS"
It's trash mob's are slighlty more annoying versions of the standard endgame enemies, mixed in with weaker level one enemies, and the boss isn't too shabby either being a cool mix of the prophet and brigand eight pounder. It seems fun... If your at the endgame. If your not, and are... lets say roughly sixty percent through the game? like I was, then your not going to have a good time.
I didn't know anything going into the fight, but initially, I thought that If I didn't then all my buildings would lose all thier upgrades, as that would seem the logical outcome given the games track record. I went in with level 5 guys, mostly un-upgraded to top tier due to me trying to get my other guys geared up. I went in, and got mostly destroyed, but I persevered and got all four of my party members to the boss so I could go and do something more fun. I got mostly destroyed, but I was able to kill the boss, after of course three of my party members become paranoid freaks. I was ready to move on and- wait... why arn't his summoned guys dispersing?

EDIT2.0: It's been a LONG time and yet still none of the promises were expanded upon, and the game's current population are fanboys or people who are angry, still waiting for a product.
-REVIEW-
Starbound is very linear, with no real goals on what to do other than: 'Collect stuff, make better stuff.'
There is no real incentive to play beyond that, as building is mostly pointless as you will leave worlds behind, as you should be travelling across the whole galaxy of space and whatever.
The quest system is very under-utilized ( as of which, they have stated that they will add more for 1.0 )
and even if they do add more quests, the question changes to: 'Will it ever be worked on far enough to be interesting and add value to the game?'
Outside of it's initial charm, which comes from the 'immersive' part of the game, the game can get old rather quickly, as there currently isn't enough material to keep you interested in the lore of the game, and there isn't enough quests/dialogue to keep you wanting to stay around the towns/villages/airships, which again, comes down to lack of content. There are plenty of descriptions, which are a nice touch to the 'immersion' factor, and the player will actually move as if they were talking. There's also a ton of references, which will entertain some. Some references are VERY obvious, while others are a bit more subtle, however, still obvious.
But that isn't enough to keep players interested for long.
There's survival elements into this game that require you to eat, be warm, and of course, remain in good health ( so nothing completely ruins your day ).
However, this adds to the linear part of the game.
You make armor, it protects you, you make better armor, it protects you better, and now you are a bit more warm. As for food, you can get food almost anywhere, making it more of a annoyance than an actual survival element. And I do mean anywhere, you can kill animals on the moon if you needed to.
The combat works in a good concept, it's actually better than Skyrim. You'll need to actually attempt to stay alive, as enemies are dangerous enough to overwhelm you, until you are geared.
There are various types of weapons in Starbound.
Spears - Good for poking
Swords - Good for stabbing
Guns - Good for shooting
Bows - Good for Hunting
and various other tools of violence, all at your disposal.
Currently, the enemy isn't programmed far enough to actually require tactical use of the weapons.
The best use is simply to get a ranged weapon and kite the opponent.
If an opponent could require certain use of weapons, ( perhaps teamwork )
then this would be very interesting.
Shooting a monster, while it turns to deflect you, while an ally stabs it in the back with a spear, avoiding it's protruding spikes and toxic clouds.
There is the standard mining. Not much to explain there.
Cutting down trees actually falls over. Rather than combusting. +1 Immersion.
Items; they are everywhere.
There are plenty of items and upgrades within Starbound that really change the game.
However, your luck is based on whether you go to the right planet or not.
Whether you got lucky with the RNG, or maybe you looked for a good planet on the internet, there will still be many pointless planets in which you do nothing but look for a giant monster that has red particles near it. Then you kill it and get a weapon with special properties, which are pretty fun to use. My personal favorite was the bonehammer, which let you slam with a melee attack, while at the same time, launching bones at the enemy.
Speaking of items and upgrades( called techs ); there are some pretty cool finds that let you do certain things.
Using a quick dash, or maybe creating a bubble to help you levitate, those help with the game's combat, adding a bit of excitement. But, again, there simply isn't enough to use, losing out on any potential diversity.
The game's modding scene is extremely good, but, as this is a review of the base game, we will not discuss mods as part of the game. The modders of Starbound have done some excellent work and have added many things that players have wanted. If you did pick up Starbound and regret it, you may have a chance using the player created mods, which would help you gather some value out of the game.
Now, you have all of those cool stuff in a sci-fi world. 'What more do I need?' - No one, ever.
There's the giant problem of the game not being finished, and not currently having enough meta-game. The lack of content really strains the game, a moment where dynamic missions would be very influential. Right now, the only real content there is, is based on the sole existance of player creativity, and mechanics. Once a player has exhausted either, ( which they will, unless you have a never-ending supply of drugs. ) they will then have nothing to do. Yes, there are quests, but how long will those really last the player? Will they be lengthy enough to continue playing, and will they successfully hook the player? The lack of a true meta-game really shows after just beating the first boss, and is very evident after you get to the last sector.
'Oh, you can uh-uh-uh build a b-b-base!'
But what purpose does it serve me, other than for more storage?
Other than searching for dungeons ( then raiding them after hopefully finding one )
and beating all of the bosses in the game and crafting the linear-upgrades of items, what more can you REALLY do?

If you'd like to see my (very condensed) stream-through of this game for the first time, feel free to click on the link below.  WARNING:  I swear frequently.
I'll preface this by saying that I'm a huge Dark Souls fan.  However, I'm extremely critical of all games that I play, including those dear to my heart like the Souls series.  All of my experiences playing this game are as a lightly armoured Rogue.  Apparently, the game is much different (easier) for heavily armoured Warriors, but I lack the experience to comment on that.  Scroll to the very bottom for the TLDR-style conclusion.
REVIEW
This game is the only one in several years to crash on me.  My PC should be able to handle it without a hitch on High, maybe even Ultra settings, yet I was forced to turn off all the extra effects and go Medium just to make it playable.
I don't remember anything about the soundtrack.  Voice acting is stiff, but sometimes to comical effect.
The story is dull, the characters are forgettable and the writing is flat out bad.  I for one can actually appreciate the comedic potential of bad writing, but most people won't be so forgiving.  The majority of the story is told through collecting Audio Logs.  This is a nice touch, as it lets you understand the setting while you continue exploring.
Combat is... all over the place.  Sometimes combat is fluid and makes sense.  Other times enemies will immediately counterattack and stun you without an animation, making you sit through free damage.  Many enemies have giant shields, and just like in a Souls game, they're extremely monotonous to fight.
The pacing of combat is very slow compared to either Souls game, where your fast roll feels like something between a medium and fat roll from DS1.  I wouldn't say the change in pace is a good or bad thing, just different, and Souls vets will definitely take time to adjust.
Boss fights drag on with huge health bars and little variance in attacks, making them a chore after the first few moments.  They do, however, use a 'phase' system similar to bosses in MMOs, which can make the fights more interesting.
The game uses a combo system that encourages you to chain attacks together for increased damage and poise breaking.  This sounds great on paper, but in practice, you'll rarely be given an opportunity to use them because...
...poise is an absolute mess in this game.  When staggered, enemies will often break out of the stun to continue attacking you, which defies any sense of game logic.
I didn't use magic to comment, but the gauntlet - a ranged magic weapon - feels extremely forced into the game, as if it was something for the devs to tick off their checklist.  Same thing with destructable items.
While the graphics are very good and well detailed, the game world is tiny and forces you to backtrack so much that one can only assume there were budget restraints.  The game tries to emulate the joy of Souls shortcuts, but for every one that makes sense, there are ten that don't... or ask you to come back much later in the game.  On foot.
There's really not much selection in weapon types, especially considering you'll be locked to your stat of choice.  Agility, for example, has daggers, shortswords and staves, along with one axe that feels slow and heavy like a Strength weapon.  You can socket items similar to Diablo games, but in similar fashion you'll be using the exact same gems every time to min/max.
Finally, let's talk about bugs.  Crashes.  Animations being skipped.  Enemies standing still and attacking you from bizarre angles.  Invisible enemies.  Frequently absurd hitboxes.  And yes... this game has almost been out for a year.
CONCLUSION
Lords of the Fallen is a shorter, buggier and often nonsensical version of Dark Souls 2 but with superior graphics and an art style reminiscent of Warhammer.  While I wouldn't call it a terrible game and did enjoy my playthrough at least somewhat, there's a lot of barriers blocking the way for 'fun'.  Impatient players and Souls players in particular will be rubbed the wrong way by this game.  I cannot recommend this game in good faith simply because you can buy Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin for the same price, a game that is superior in almost every way.  Only consider this game if you can get it at a very reduced price and are prepared to muscle through bugs and poor optimization.  What I will say, however, is that it's very important that this game exists, because it shows that companies other than From are willing to take a shot at Souls-likes.  Let's hope the next attempt is a better one.

I initially started this game expecting it to play like Darksiders however it was quite different.
In essence the combat is more like Monster Hunter. Especially when wearing heavy armor your character is quite slow which takes some time to get used to.
My first attempts failed miserably due to the fact that I wasn't accustomed to the game mechanics. Even the very first enemy took me considerable effort to defeat.
However, after you get past that 'hill' and start getting familiar with the controls and how the character behaves the game becomes incredibly fun!
The atmosphere of the game is awesome: a dark and gritty monastery in which you uncover one horror after the other. Throughout the game you'll find pieces of lore which help you put the puzzle of the story together. My only gripe here is that in the beginning you get dumped into the game without any hook into the story i.e. you have no clue what's going on.
You can find a huge amount of different weapons and armor, each with different stats and abilities and all of them look incredibly cool! The game is also loaded with many secrets which can be uncovered like special equipment, hidden treasure chests, special Portals after defeating bosses etc.
The boss fights (i.e. the Lords) are a mix: some of them are quite easy while others are extremely hard. It takes time to learn their attack patterns and to equip yourself appropriately. Especially the final boss was a tough nut to crack. However, I have to add it never felt impossible i.e. even for the difficult fights you will manage to do a substantial amount of damage so that gives hope that it can be pulled off on a next attempt.
Saving is done by means of checkpoints. So when you die you start back at a previous point and all enemies are back. Initially I didn't like this until I understood this is the core of the game: you have to redo parts in order to get more XP so you become more powerfull for the later game.
When the game is completed you can start a new game +. This allows you to carry over all equipment of your previous playthrough. In addition it allows you to select a new school of Magic. So in this way you can eventually level up in all three schools which is quite nice.
To conclude a couple of minor points which I found:
- There is no Quest log, so it's hard to keep track of some side Quests. Taking notes is required.
- There is no map, so you have to have a good memory where everything is located.
- Most of the secrets in the game are not hinted at by the in-game lore. So some you will find by chance while the rest you can only find by looking at forum posts or youtube vids. It would have been much nicer if this info could be gathered from the game itself.
- Even after finishing the game I'm still strugging sometimes with the controls (using Controller). In most cases this is caused by the fact that sprinting, rolling and jumping is one and the same button. So more often that not when I want to sprint to perform a heavy leap attack ... my character just rolls and bounces against the enemy only to get pounded. When wanting to jump over a gap ... my character just rolls and fall in the depths. These nuisances could have been avoided by a better control sheme.
My final verdict is that it's a great game. It takes some time getting into it, but when you remain persistent (and patient) it becomes an awesome game!
Note: After upgrading to Windows 10 I always got a crash when starting a new game. Disabling the NVidia Turbulence fixed this issue.

I would highly recommend you stay away from Fallout 4 for a 4 main reasons.
1. The entire game is focused on gunplay and will very rarely have any quests with choice or diplomacy involved. It's also oversaturated with copy and paste quests with objectives that boil down to "kill x amount of enemies" or "retrieve x by doing a dungeon". Combat encounters are also not interesting because there are only a handful of enemy types and 90% of them just shoot you, which means the only thing that separates a radier from a super mutant is how much you have to shoot them. The gunplay may be better than it's predecessors but it's not enough to hold up an entire game.
2. The writing and quests are incredibly bland. Even though the game has "4 endings" it only truly has 2 ending states. 1 is blowing up the evil scientists and 2 is siding with the evil scientists. If you're a long time fallout fan you should know that in just about every fallout game previous you would get a complex ending depending on what actions you did in many parts of the game. You only get rewarded with one prerendered cutscene which is basically the protagonist talking about everything you already know, things completely unrelated, and saying that "war never changes" in the end. I should also mention that you have a voiced protagonist, less dialouge options (yes, yes, explain, and sarcastic yes). You also have no skills, tag skills, traits, or even skill checks, which takes the RP out of RPG.
3. No character buliding. Since they've done away with stats and the like all the rpg elements are resigned to your special stats and the "perks" that go along with them. Perks do not function as they have in any other fallout game because they not serve the purpose of having a leveling system. Every level you get 1 perk point to put into any of the perks you have available. But you'll end up ignoring most of the semi-interesting ones to put it into gunplay or modding your weapons, because almost all of the quests invole shooting people. The way they make you upgrade your weapons skills is also very annoying. Your weapon upgrades are not based around making weapons types better (guns, energy weapons, melee, unarmed) but having the upgrades only effect certain weapon firing types (auto, semi-auto, etc) which sucks any variety the gunplay still could have had. That means if you found a really cool gun you can only viably use it if it fires the way that corresponds with what you put your perk points into. It's confusing for new players, and annoying for all players.
4. Bloatware and Paid Mods. For those unaware bloatware is a type of software that takes up a large amount of hard drive space. And with the new paid mods it earns that title. Because their new paid mod initiative (that is patched into every game now) installs all of the mods that are available to purchase, your harddrive is going to be full with useless data. Not to mention that paid mods are one of the scummiest things to come out in a long time. I don't think bethesda understands that mods are made out of love for a game, not to bleed consumers dry. Even if you're ok with everything above I wouldn't buy this game because you'd be supporting this terrible buisness practice.
I would not recommend anybody play this game. With the 60 dollars this game costs you could buy every other game in the fallout series. If you're more of a fan of shooter games buy the new DOOM, it's miles better than this and you can even make your own levels with their snapmap mode. And if you want to play the settlement mode (that isn't even worth mentioning) just ♥♥♥♥ing buy Minecraft, it's a fraction of the cost and updates are free. Go buy yourself a nice dinner or 10 of everything mcdonalds value menu, because you'll get more enjoyment out of that than playing Fallout 4.
TL;DR: Gameplay is boring, writing is bland, it has paid mods, it's bloatware, go buy something else.

Steer clear of this.
I've spent nearly 1000 hours modding and testing, never once finished the game.
This is a typical sandbox shooter that just happens to be in the Fallout setting.
It's an alternate 50's timeline where the world has been devastated by nuclear war.
Still, it's more technologically advanced than today with handheld lasers and nuclear fusion in your pocket.
For once, they've taken hints from the modding community and included crafting of weapons and settlements.
But you need DLCs to really take advantage of this. So consider that thoroughly.
You will spend the entirety of the game lugging around trash you need to build weapon/armor modification and building "blocks".
If you're a packrat, then you will also spend most of this time encumbered. Slowly walking wherever you go.
You are given the title of General of the Minutemen, if you so choose.
Being a general does not mean you command anything.
Other factions also gives you fancy titles, but in the end...
You are told what to do and go do it as a lackey for some no-name idiot, and to adopt the ideology of the faction you represent.
In the end, not a single npc recognizes your efforts, so it's a thankless task you do because killing stuff gives experience.
It's a blatant standardized method of leveling. Thin, soulless, mindless.
Indirect methods of solving quests are non-existant.
The main quest of finding your kidnapped son is totally diminished and ends up being something to steer towards once you're done with everything else. This is you being a parent.
But hey. You get'a shoot stuff, so no need think.
As a wasteland sandbox shooter with the Fallout feel, it's ok. But it doesn't have the essence of Fallout.
It's a brainless shooter directed at the console generation with little depth and attention to story.
You're pretty much forced to join a faction if you really want something out of this, and then be told what to do.
So you get to be a glorified janitor to clean up the wasteland and fix lodgings for mindless idiots that has been living in the wasteland their entire lives, yet cannot defend themselves without your explicit help.
Even when you have a fully defended settlement, settlers still manage to get kidnapped.
And there is only one that could possibly do this daring rescue.
Not the settlers that defend. Not the minutemen. Not anyone but you.
So, in essence, there is no sense to this game.
But then again, it's what we expect from Bethesda. A skeletal game that needs to be fleshed out and bugfixed to be successful.
Hence the creation kit that comes with every Bethesda release, and the plethora of tools and mods following in its wake by the modding community.
Verdict:
By itself, the game is a soulless framework.
It feels bugridden and rushed at every turn, but it's easily overlooked because there's always more to shoot.
It is thanks to the modding tools and the modding community that this game gets a fan base.
And the modding community makes this game great.
This game isn't worth much without DLCs and mods to fix and enrich the game.
I would give it a weak thumbs up if it wasn't for the microtransactions. Thanks a bunch Bethesda.
