Wow, Hacknet is one immersive command line game.
You get to pick up the left overs of a now dead hacker, following in his footsteps, slowly taking on harder challenges and making a name for yourself.
Hacknet offers a tight narrative (which is completely text based) and enthralling 'hacking'
Pros:
- presentation. I know a lot of people will be turned off by a CL interface game. but heck (huehue), it's beautiful, intuitive and well designed. plus you can download more UIs from servers and people you hacked
- gameplay. it's relatively easy, requiring (so far, I'm roughly 4 hours into the game) simple management skills, a keen eye and some reading and prioritizing. the hacking is served well, not letting you button mash, but rather focused on the finer points such as: reading emails for usernames and passwords, changing websites headers into vulgarities, finding the right tools and balance, covering your tracks.
a lot of the gameplay is indeed done over a command line interface, which, exactly, means you type out what you wanna do. there's helps, and little tools making it a lot easier than real life hacking could ever be.
- Story. it's a pretty cool mix of paranoia, technology and a weird form of justice. no one talks, no fancy cutscenes. it's all in your head, buddy
- immersion. yeah, the computers you hack are rather empty, but what is on there is hilarious and often gives small hints to connections between the hackers you 'meet' (I think, at least
- music. absolutely perfect.
Cons:
- uhm, let me think ... hmmm ... no, it is exactly what it says it is. and then some
Verdict:
You like hacking/hacking movies or just recently discovered Mr Robot or the deep web?
Well, come on in. this is a perfect supplement to your diet.
Hacknet is pretty (for CL standards :D as I work in IT I actually find it gorgeous), fun and fast paced. It will test your patience, but mostly your ability to read and type properly.
But nothing is keeping it from delivering the best hacker game since Uplink, if not even a tick better.
And it is totally worth the price tag

If your looking for a review on Fractured Space you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

This game is not what I thought it was going to be, BUT it blew my expectations out of the water! I'm having loads of fun playing it! In a world of Shooters and Strategies, this game puts SHOOT in the background, and emphasizes Strategy. If you don't come up with a good plan, and just "Run and Gun", you will DIE. Another term you won't find among the best laid plans in this game is "Spray and Pray" HA! The level of customization of weapons, soldiers, your team/teams, even your base is amazing. On another level even. If you want to purchase a game with a lot of replay value, a game where planning ahead is a MUST, this is a game I would definitely recommend.
The GOOD: The levels of customization in this game from your single soldier, to your whole team, to your entire base is staggering. Also, a lot of games that emphasize "Thinking Ahead" can get old, and repetitive, but each level, each zone requires some new kind of thinking which makes sure the playing never gets stale.
The BAD: The entirety of the game you have a timer running with a bar of how far along the aliens are coming with their "End Game", and the choices you make about which levels you do effect, or delay, their plan. It can get stressful trying to gather supplies, healing your team/best players, building your base, etc while this bar gets stronger. Make sure you save A LOT.
The UGLY: Could be considered the WORST part of the game is the save dynamic. You can save at ANY point in the game... This means that in a game requiring an entirely higher level of thinking and strategics you can save, play, die/screw up, restart, play again and beat it. Cheating? Or cheap tactics? OR tactics period? You be the judge! HA!

GAHHHHHH. So many things to like about XCOM 2 but unfortunately it has one crippling flaw that can literally ruin all gameplay. LOS is still totally broken months after release. Almost every mission I'll get instances of randomly getting shot or grabbed through a wall/floor. In a game where cover and positioning is everything, this is utterly gamebreaking.
People do complain a lot that the RNG is broken. Whatever, I don't think so, it sucks sometimes but imo that makes the game more intense and interesting (also kinda more realistic). But for Line of Sight to be broken makes the game a literal luck simulator. Taking cover behind a wall? Trying to stay out of an alien's LOS by flanking around behind walls/cover? Too bad, the enemy saw you through two solid walls and killed Johnny Flanker through said walls.
It's hard to explain how crippling this is to the gameplay without actually playing the game, but anyone familiar with any strategy games should understand that LOS is a critical element to playing smart. If it can't be relied upon to be consistent, then you never know if you're putting your soldiers in amazing cover or a killzone. Kinda important distinction there. WIth it being broken, it just doesn't make any sense to even call this a strategy/tactical game...
So you saw the "Difficult" tag for the game? Want a challenge? Wrong game then, this is actually an anxiety simulator.

It's funny. I see a lot of people hating on this game for reasons such as grinding, seeing your heros dieing in horrible ways and the RNG system dealing low blows now and again.
Here's the thing for anyone interested in this game: It is not a friendly hand holding experiance like most triple A titles these days. Darkest dungeon is grueling and cruel in how it will toss things to beat your heros into dust and pulp, but it's YOUR job as the player to learn when odds are impossible, when things have gone sideways and you've got to cut your losses. You have to take the punches and learn how to react to them. It's all about the long haul instead of the here and now. It will not hand you anything on a silver platter, period. Most of the tricks and strategies you will have to learn on your own or, if you want to sully the experiance, look up. Many of these tricks are hidden values so, when you do play the game, you need to expariment; toss people into the grinder and see what works and what doesn't.
As for a review of the game in a more.....proffessional light, it has it's flaws: the game will prey on your attatchment to recruits, your drive to clear a dungeon and push through the light, but that is what sets the game apart from the sea of utter garbage floating around these days. The visuals are always jarring, but may waver after you've killed certain foes many times because they just won't stay dead, but the narration is almost soothing even if you've been playing for hours on end.  The dev team is also rather flexible and responsive, putting out options to dial back the brutal nature of the game and sprinkling shoutouts and praise to the more dedicated playerbase who stick with the original options.
Before you do get into the game however, you must ask yourself one burning question: how far are you willing to go, how many lives will you throw away to see yourself victorious?

Quick summary: great DLC but flawed in many ways, recommendable to those with huge passion to original game plus Lovecratian horror. For everyone else, wait til it goes on sale and/or Red Hook fixes the broken parts of the game.

The good: new class, new monsters, new boss, new items, new area, new part of Hamlet. All pretty good. The set trinkets are hit or miss, some incredibly awesome, others not so great; The new class is very unique and plays quick differently from everyone else, quite powerful but also feels very limited in his roles. New monsters are designed well, both in terms of funcationality and graphics. The new areas of the Hamlet allow us to spend heirlooms and buff hero abilities.
The bad: the curse, the nerfs. The curse itself felt OK, when monsters swarm every single corner of all arenas, it is almost a guaranty to get the curse every time you head out. The problem is, the curse acts pretty much like an affection that's nigh impossible to deal with or get rid of (until much much much later). You can try to maintain it at passive, but craving, wasting and blood lust all lead to affected heroes to act out on their own or refuse actions or stress everyone like crazy. On top of the penalties and the fact that your heroes can (and WILL) die from this BS, it becomes incredibly frustrating to deal with. Eventually you gonna have an entire town with the curse and it's kinda like having permanent afflictions. Also, I honestly want to ask RedHook's logic behind nerfing the Hound...the Hound Master was already under-powered, now you guys decreased his first bleed attack's DOT down to 2???? Are you out of your minds? Did you guys all get a resolve check and turned up Irrattional? Right now there is only ONE use for the Hound - against the Flesh. In almost every other situation they become UTTERLY and completely useless, period. As soon as I beat champion level Flesh, I'm gonna toss my two hounds out and never look at them again. Once a balanced class, now worse than that pile of excrement left on the floot by the Swine Prince. Thanks RedHook, you did us a solid.

No seriously, I wouldn't do that. But seriously this game is good enough to make me want to do that. I'll admit the KB+M controls are a bit odd to get used to, but I found them more reliable than a controller. Perfectly playable either way and would recommend the controller for the QTE prompts. I gave it a first run playthrough using KB+M though and other than not being able to press keys with my fingers as fast as I can controller buttons with my thumbs, I have no complaints. I do wish it was more obvious when gameplay was about to start as a cinematic transitions into it, and I wish the opening sequence hadn't dragged on as long as it did, but trivial nit-picks at best. This is Platinum Games at it's finest and it stuns me they've only been getting better since. I doubt Nintendo will allow even a "Nintendo content stripped out" version of Bayonetta 2 on PC, but I would buy it at even $60 if they did. Otherwise I'll have to use alternative means to play it.
What? You've not heard of Platinum Games? Well, this studio that made this game and many other great action games before and since is probably the singular BEST studio at making action-combat games in the industry right now. They mostly make hack'n'slash and brawlers, but have done at least one 3rd-person shooter as well. This game for as little as it sold is probably the game that made them famous. Not for how great the gameplay is though, but for the controversy of how "objectified" Bayonetta is. Let's set that record straight: SHE IS NOT OBJECTIFIED!!! Not at all. At least not in the game; can't say the same for all the fanfic out there... Bayonetta is a female protagonist that is characterized to own her sexuality. She's not abusing it to get what she wants, she taunts and flaunts with it like any self-respecting woman does. It's taken to a comedic extreme sure, but that's to counter-balance how exaggerated male protagonists are in mainstream games. You cannot go wrong with Platinum Games starting here. If you like Hack'n'Slash or Brawlers, even as old as this is now, it'll still easily make anyone's top ten in those genres.

I was really, really impressed by this game. While incredibly old by this point, I still consider Uplink to be the pinnacle of hacking "simulation" games. While other games sometimes offered more technical depth to the hacking procedures than Uplink, they didn't manage to immerse you in the story like Uplink did. They didn't make me disconnect from the internet out of paranoia like the first time I played Uplink. And while I can't say that Hacknet made me disconnect from the internet (mostly due to knowledge and experience gained over the past 14 years), it made me fall in love with the genre all over again.
While the basics of the game are straightforward (connecting to nodes, overloading proxies, hacking ports, erasing logs, etc...), you are rewarded for being curious. Finding helpful programs, extra information on your targets, or the hilarious IRC logs that are included from
are just some of the things you can find. Some of the later levels are quite challenging despite the simple mechanics. And there is an immense sense of accomplishment when you back-hack someone who wrecked your system, only to get all of their information, hack them, and completely wipe their terminal.
There are a ton of references to all kinds of hacker related media. Movies, games (with plenty aimed at Uplink), nerd culture, prominent authors, and some well-known security groups all get nods from this game. On top of that, some of the information you gain access to while on contracts is absolutely hilarious. Sure, there are a few grammatical/spelling errors here and there, but the content of the game is still outstanding.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who played Uplink, or is a fan of computers and computer security in general. No, it's not realistic, it's not accurate, it's not perfect...but it is damn fun.

This game is very, very good. On the surface it seems like a hacking game somewhat in the style of games like Uplink, but with a huge amount of polish. However, when you actually get in to it, its better described as a really clever puzzle game with a very compelling story, wrapped in a layer of hacking. The music and the visuals are fantastic, the whole package is put together to make it feel less like you're loading up a game from steam, and more like you're logging in to a VM and stepping in to the story.
Prospective buyers need to know that this game requires you to learn and use command line functions in order to do most stuff. It does an adequate job of explaining these to the user, however if I had one criticism it would be in this area.  Had I not had command line experience in the past, I would have found the game much less accessible. I feel the game could have done a better job of introducing these concepts to a command line novice.
With that said, if you like puzzle games, if you like a good mystery, if you have any interest in hacking or computer security, and the idea of a command-line interface doesnt put you off, this game is a must buy.

As a semi-realistic hacking game, Hacknet delivers one of the most enjoyable experience available. While rich in things to do, it doesn't get overly complicated.
The storyline doesn't prevent you from taking your time, except of course when you've breached into a well secured node and a tracer is upon you. Overall you feel like a real baddass hacking your way into the many servers available, private or corporate. I've made a second playthrough immediately after finishing the first, only because I wanted to test different approches to the multiple contracts you get. Note that some side missions won't be accessible anymore after you complete certain story missions, so if you like to be thorough, get these done first. From a gameplay perspective, it might get a bit repetitive to some players, but the music, the interface, the hidden secrets and the number of programs available make it, I feel, quite an immersive experience.
The real joy of it is that you can (almost completely, if you feel like it) play it all using only your keyboard. This wasn't possible with previous games of that genre.
If you are into 'hacking' stuff and believe you can be at ease learning some basic Unix commands, you'll certainly enjoy Hacknet!

When I first played this game I hated it. I thought that it was extremely complicated and impossible to beat. This is likely the feeling most people get when they first play a Dark Souls game. Dark Souls is not a game that you can just give up on. It rewards your persistence, makes you work hard, and teaches you how to play a game proactively rather than reactively. Most other games focus on quick-time events, cutscenes, and gameplay mechanics that we have seen to much of. Dark Souls breaks this idea of what a game should be by making us strategize, learn how to create our own builds, think ahead, and forge the best tactics through the most creative processes in order to achieve greatness. I was ignorant to dismiss a game due to it's difficulty. I accept my mistakes and have moved past them. Dark Souls III has become one of my favorite titles that I have played, and I look forward to play the games that came before. Give this game a chance, and when it breaks your leg, use your crutch as a weapon in the end.

If you played XCOM, you'll probably like this one, too.  The core squad-based tactical combat remains the focus for the game but they smoothed it out with angle adjustments and an AI that constantly tries to get around to your flanks.  Moreover, they fixed my two biggest criticisms with the first game: the reverse learning curve and the staggering difficulty of coming back after you lose a mission.
Instead of the cheesy difficulty curve of XCOM, which peters off as soon as you get a colonel, XCOM 2 consistently releases new, brutal aliens to fight you right up until near the very end of the game.  If your combat tech lags behind or you delay too long in pursuing the story goals, you'll find yourself being overwhelmed.  I just completed my first campaign on veteran (read: normal) difficulty on ironman- it took me about 20 tries.  I'm a fairly casual gamer but from my perspective, this is one of the most challenging games around.
In XCOM, when you lose a mission, you not only lose your elite squad of super soldiers but suffer devestating campaign penalties which quickly lead to strategic failure.   In XCOM 2, you'll still lose your soldiers but the campaign penalties are sufficiently light that it is possible, if challenging, to come back.  They even added an abort option for most missions so you can leave mid-scenario if it looks like you are just going to get wiped out.
In addition to these points, XCOM 2 provides a larger variety of missions and objectives, more characterization for the story characters, and sharpened a lot of the mechanics from the first game.
Of course, there are issues.  Graphical glitches and occasional fatal errors are a real concern but for the most part, this game is clean and gameplay challenging and fun.

I bought this in a bundle for puzzle-platforming games and I am so glad this was in a bundle. This game is simplistic in its design, but the gameplay mechanics is not. I'm not saying the gameplay is difficult (finished it in ~90 mins with 100% completion - so anywhere from 1hr-3hrs for this game). Rather, it takes a simple idea of changing the direction, that which your avatar (force) travels in, and flips it as you try to collect the orbs. Yes, a handful of puzzles really stumped me at first. However, a few trial+error runs and you can solve the puzzle easily. The majority of the puzzles are simple enough that by seeing them and what options you have to change the gravity, you will know what to do. One thing that constantly aggravated me during gameplay is how fast force (can move/moves) during the game (hmm the force is strong with this one). However, that's what makes the game a bit harder as you need to control your movements precisely. Plus, the beady little eye on the character is simply amusing to watch as you make it run across the map.
Aside from the game, the acheivements didn't proc'ed correctly the first time around so I had to play a few rounds in each chapter to register that yes, I did collect all of the orbs in each chapter.
Overall, very nice puzzle-platforming game. Highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys puzzle-plaform genre games. 9/10.

Assassin's Creed Unity is a game that would be more enjoyable, with a few tweaks and fixes.
I've managed to stack about 32 hours into this game now, and have tried a bit of everything; the campaign is finished, and I have put time into the side content as well. From the experience I've had so far, I believe that the game isn't too bad. The story and the characters were pretty decent overall. I enjoyed Arno and Elise, and the wry humour in the interactions between the two. The story fleshes out fairly similar to the rest of the Assassin's Creed games, acting about in a tested formula that allows for a satisfactory experience. The problem, however, lies within game mechanics, performance, and lack of access to content. These issues combined may drain some enjoyment out of your game time.
First of all, the game mechanics. This will be mainly focused on character control, as most of the issues lie here. In terms of combat, I believe the movement is quite fluid. It has built over the previous combat system, and ensures that you will avoid biting off more than you can chew in a fight, unless you have a death wish. Too many enemies will leave you overwhelmed, putting you in a tough situation very quickly. Actual exploration-style movement, however, is a great hindrance when playing. The animations themselves roll nicely, but when it comes to trying to move Arno in the direction you wish, he just doesn't seem to want to listen. He will stumble off in another direction, or fail to climb something you have just moved towards. Climbing through windows will take you more than a few times before actually going through the window. Trying to jump over an object near the edge of a roof will have you falling to your death after an unexpected and unwarranted leap over the edge. All in all, Unity has a very clunky movement system, and as a result, gameplay can sometimes be frustrating.
Secondly, the game's performance. From what I have read in the other reviews, performance is appalling, making the game unplayable for many. I have fortunately not had issues of the severity that the majority of the reviewers here seem to be reporting. However, I have had to deal with light to moderate FPS lag/stuttering. However, even a small amount of stuttering can completely hinder you in-game for many activities. Lockpicking, and trying to land the cursor inside of the small rectangle to open the lock is nearly impossible, with the unpredicable stuttering. Combat will be especially awful, causing parrying to often miss completely. I've had one application hang, which seemed to be of no apparent reason. Even after the driver updates for our video cards, it appears that there is some work to do on Ubisoft's part.
Lastly, the lack of access to all content. Although I use this app myself, the Unity Companion ultimately proves to be fairly irritating. Getting through the "missions" (better to be called chores) require having units be stationed at jobs for what can be many hours before the next. Even after beating the campaign, I have not finished the first set of missions yet. Another frustation is the fact that most of the Legendary end-game content is locked to Club Competitions. Now, the game itself is playable without this content, but for a completionist such as myself, not being able to get this content through my efforts alone make trying to completely finish the game an annoying task. I want to have the best gear, but I don't want to have to rely on forming or joining a club to make that happen.
The game itself isn't entirely bad. I enjoyed playing the campaign, and the Co-op missions were pretty fun. Honestly, I can still recommend it. I'll probably keep playing the game, and work on finishing the game 100%. What Ubisoft needs to do is to work on releasing some patches and fixes to keep this game from becoming any more frustrating. The game-breaking problems need to be addressed as soon as possible, and I personally think that making multiplayer optional would take off some of the frustation as well. In conlusion, enjoyable game, just needs to have it's problems addressed.

This game is risk management, bad things will happen at the worse possible time, and you need to be prepared for that. Wether you do well depends on your ability to pick good team compositions, pack the right items (and correct quantity), and select trinkets that complement your setup (stacking damage trinkets with stress penalty is risky, you will have to focus stress dealers for example). I do mostly dark runs (no torches, so enemies crit chance and accuracy go up, and you take way more stress), and the only time that I've lost people was to the shambler mini boss because I got too cocky (my team didn't have the dps to kill it quickly). I highly recommend beating the game on Radiant mode first, the actual gameply is still the same, but the character/item management is cheaper and more forgiving (aka game same difficulty, but less grind needed when you ♥♥♥♥ up).

This game is a long one.
There are 5 locations, 4 of which you will visit frequently as you play, only one if you wish to beat the game.
Each location has multiple bosses, each boss having 3 versions of it, each deadlier than the last.
Heroes will die.
Parties will be wiped.
This is to be expected.
Your hero that has the best trinklets, equipment, and buffs can be destroyed be the powers that be.
You could take the greatest caution to not have a hero die, and still lose them.
This game is not like D&D, where the DM wants everyone to live, but face a challenge, this game wants you and every one of your members dead.
By playing this game over the 2 hour mark, you accept this, and will suffer.
But risk brings reward, and the game acknowledges that.
You can reduce the light level, which will make the monsters you fight more accurate and deadly, but also give more loot.
Anything you interact with can curse, poison, or cut you, while at the same time give prizes for being lucky.
Using the right item on a curio (or interactable object) will provide good results... most of the time.
Just because you got a party wipe does NOT mean the game is bad. It just means you were unlucky.
Besides, you never acknoledged the time you got 3 crits and dodged 3 attacks in a row.
This game gives, and this game takes.

Bayonetta may be a relatively old game but it's still damn good fun to play. Who'd have thought it would be fun to beat up groups of angelic eldritch horrors as a witch who can literally summon demons with her hair?
While the plot of the game is pretty serious, Bayonetta herself looks like she's having fun while taking down various creatures with different weapons and combos. And this game is ridiculous fun. There is a lot of charm and charisma and all the characters are well-written.
Graphics wise, it's very well-rendered and the usually muted background colours help to make the foreground colour (where all the action is happening) pop out but they're also not too distracting. Character models are well rendered and wonderfully animated, especially Bayonetta herself. Nothing particularly negative to point out here.
Sound wise, the soundtrack is very well put together. Atmospheric in places but also oozes a lot of charm and charisma when it needs to. Very well crafted and puts the tension in the right places. The only complaint I really have is that the battle music can get a tad repetitive but that's me being incredibly nitpicky.
Now onto the meat: the gameplay. I did play the original console version before this and the combos feel very fluid, although some of the more important mechanics (such as Dodge Offset) aren't very well explained. However, combat does feel very satisfying and the various weapons you can get all pack their own punch. The addition of auto-aiming on lower difficulty settings, as well as assistance with the trickier combos, is very good and doesn't take away from the overall skill too much (some skill is still required to get big combos even on lower difficulties but it still works). The torture attacks were fun and the end of boss fights (Climaxes) were well done. Only complaint is that some cutscenes did have a few too many QTEs but aside from that, all very good.
Controls felt okay if you're using a keyboard and mouse, but I ended up havign to put the sensitivity quite far up. However, using a controller make everything feel like a dream. It is playable on keyboard/mouse but I highly recommend using a controller to play. Much more fun.
I had such fun with this game and I cannot recommend it enough. Definitely on my must-play list.

The Short:
Its a Dark Souls clone.
You say it like its a problem.
The Long:
Lords of the Fallen is a game that takes heavy inspiration from the Souls games, but does enough on its own that it can be rightfully called its own thing. From the spellcasting being closer to that of a traditional RPG (hurray for mana bars!) to the way the characters and enemies feel, I find it to be just as fun as any Souls game.
Fiords of the Lawnmower (one internet cookie should you get that reference) has a very pleasing visual style. and by pleasing I mean everyone looks bad@$$. Skulls and flames are on basically everything and while it may get old after alittle bit, I still find it to be much more exciting than Dark Souls traditional medieval gear. Everyone has pauldrons the size of a small city and the detail in the armors and weapons are gleefully over designed.
The graphics are absolutely gorgeous even with a medium spec'd rig such as mine. It runs very well outside of the occational open area where the framerate noticably dips, but it never becomes unplayable. Particle effects and such are everywhere; sparks flying when an attack bounces off a sheild, snow swirls, and ash sprouting from flaming weapons and torches make sure it looks extra pretty.
Combat is very weighty, even with the light weapons. All of them feel like they have weight to them and it feels wonderful, especially when you bring a mighty greathammer down on a cowering enemy and watch as they are crushed and the screen shakes from the shear force of it all. Your attacks feel like they're going to do something as your character grunts from the strength needed to heave an axe with the head as large as one of your pauldrons over his shoulder and into an enemy.
The controls on keyboard and mouse a great (I'm looking at you, Dark Souls) as are the ones using a controller. The buttons can all be remapped to your liking, but the default ones should be just fine.
The gameplay is similar to all the Souls games, with you exploring a castle (or 2), fighting enemies, getting loot, and dying. Alot. However the game is easier than Souls, due to it not punishing you as much when you do inevetably kick the bucket. Another thing is how experience is gained. every time you kill an enemy you gain an experience multiplier. The more enemies you kill, the higher the multiplier gets and the more XP you get per kill. However, whenever you go back to a checkpoint to refill your potions, level up, and save; the multiplier is reset so weighing whether or not you want more XP or to live is a key point. The game also encourages multiple playthroughs allowing you to select an additional spell tree on each go. This allows you access to weapons you may not be able to obtain on other playthroughs. From my research an average playthrough takes around 15-20 hours.
Overall, this game is a great pick for those who finished up the Souls games and want to have a game that plays much the same or for someone who wants to get eased into this style of gameplay and found the Souls games too unforgiving.

Good attempt at a logical platformer that utilizes gravity to make you think. I enjoyed the game quite a bit but found it too short for my liking, more on that below.
Pros:
- Smooth gameplay
- Precise platforming controls
- Levels are simple and yet complex enough to have you think through the "game plan"
Cons:
- Intro and ending are waste of time, no point to them
- The menus are somewhat too simple, adding labels would have helped a bit but they work as intended
- Only 50 levels that can be powered through relatively fast (completed the game in 44min and that includes getting all achievements)
- Levels range from dead simple to I have to stop and think for a bit, but never posed any real challenge
- I never died more than a couple of times at any level (had to manually get 25 deaths in a single level achievement), mostly due to the difficulty being fairly low. Adding expert mode that makes all the levels twice as hard after finishing the normal game would have address this.
Get it on a discount for a quick and fun gameplay if you enjoy puzzlers. 5/10

If you played XCOM, you'll probably like this one, too.  The core squad-based tactical combat remains the focus for the game but they smoothed it out with angle adjustments and an AI that constantly tries to get around to your flanks.  Moreover, they fixed my two biggest criticisms with the first game: the reverse learning curve and the staggering difficulty of coming back after you lose a mission.
Instead of the cheesy difficulty curve of XCOM, which peters off as soon as you get a colonel, XCOM 2 consistently releases new, brutal aliens to fight you right up until near the very end of the game.  If your combat tech lags behind or you delay too long in pursuing the story goals, you'll find yourself being overwhelmed.  I just completed my first campaign on veteran (read: normal) difficulty on ironman- it took me about 20 tries.  I'm a fairly casual gamer but from my perspective, this is one of the most challenging games around.
In XCOM, when you lose a mission, you not only lose your elite squad of super soldiers but suffer devestating campaign penalties which quickly lead to strategic failure.   In XCOM 2, you'll still lose your soldiers but the campaign penalties are sufficiently light that it is possible, if challenging, to come back.  They even added an abort option for most missions so you can leave mid-scenario if it looks like you are just going to get wiped out.
In addition to these points, XCOM 2 provides a larger variety of missions and objectives, more characterization for the story characters, and sharpened a lot of the mechanics from the first game.
Of course, there are issues.  Graphical glitches and occasional fatal errors are a real concern but for the most part, this game is clean and gameplay challenging and fun.

What is Gravity Error?
Gravity Error is a short platform puzzle mix. You are playing in rectangular rooms that only fill a screen each, using placeable arrows to influence gravity.
Gameplay
The gameplay consists of the strategy and the action phase, as I will call them. In the strategy phase, you place the arrows. There are four arrows: Up, down, left, right. Each arrow makes gravity pull the protagonist in the direction it shows. You can place them on the whole playfield, with some exceptions. You can't place them into other objects (orbs are exempt from this). You want to collect all orbs and then reach the exit, so you must plan a bit ahead, but only in one level was it actually interesting to figure out how to do it. Many times you have more arrows than you will need.
The game consists of five sets of ten levels each.
Achievements
There are ten achievements that unlock as you progress while collecting all orbs. As the developer currently is moving, he will fix the achievements when he is able to, he says on the forums!
Music
The music is very nice, it's very catchy. The sound effects are sparse and fitting, but of a bit a low quality.
Controls
The controls are working fine, but have two big issues to me. First the protagonist does not steer well. He oversteers easily, running further than he should. This can become tedious later on.
Second the protagonist goes on the 2D plane in the direction of the key you press. Now this might be a matter of taste, I would actually like him to always jump when you press up and accordingly go for the other keys, so for example pressing left is going right when the gravity points up.
Graphics
The graphics are very basic, there are few different graphics. The game feels just like a series of chambers you go through, which it is, and does not build any graphical atmosphere.
Overall you get a small nice game, one I can actually recommend if you got it from a bundle or cheaply. Since you get only around an hour of entertainment until you 100 percented everything (except of course the broken achievement), you should keep that in mind when buying.
Recommended: If you get it cheap

The walking dead is a great interactive story. I've never read the comics or seen the tv show, but I really enjoyed this game.
Given the nature of this game, you should know that the narrative in this game is really top-notch quality. I've only seen one of the endings at the time of writing but the story line I followed was great. The design and stories for all of the characters are also very good.
The design of the game, in terms of how choices are laid out is very good, and the point-and-click method helps to keep a high emphasis on the story. The highlighting is also good at preventing "click everything until it works" syndrome, which I have seen in other games.
I found that this game has a good balance between "leaning back" and watch the events unfold, and the actual interactions the player makes. When needed, the keyboard controls for movement work well, although in certain scenes I did find that the map's camera angle meant that ties between "W for forwards" and actually moving forwards was a bit off.
The graphics in this game are really nice, following the style of the comics, but still managing to be three-dimensional. Some of the graphics could have been made at a bit higher of a resolution though, especially the ones that you'll get close-ups on.
The music and sounds in this game are very good in terms of ambiance, and the voice acting is also very good. This is important in a game like this, and telltale did a good job choosing voices.
This game is definitely worth a buy if you want a good story, and I'm sure you'll love it if you are already a fan of the walking dead.

I'm fairly new to the XCom series having only beat XCom and XCom 2 over the past month. So consider this review as a "casual" or "intermediate" player's perspective.
Graphically the game is an improvement if not a giant leap over the original. Sadly it still has many of the clipping issues and janky animation that was seen in the first game. The performance also leaves a lot to be desired. I use a GTX 1080 and even with SMAA scaled back to x2, my frames were still fluctuating between 70 to as low as 20 FPS (even lower during animations sometimes). However this is a turn based game with no real time elements so this issue isn't a deal breaker, but it does need to be mentioned.
No real compaints in the sound department. Everything seems fine and the mundane chatter on the Avenger screen can be interesting. The repeated "advice" from Bradford can get annoying, especially during scans and retaliation missions however this can be disabled using mods.
The gameplay is just as addictive as the previous games with far more combat and infiltration options available. HOWEVER... This is undermined by arbitrary time limits that are forced into most missions causing a "ticking clock" element and favouring rushed play over meticulous and careful planning. Personally I utterly despise forced time limits and luckily there are mods available to make this feature more lenient or even eradicate it almost completely. Whilst this may not be a huge issue for XCom veterans, it is bound to impact the enjoyment for newer players. RNG also feels more unreliable than ever with even 95% chance shots missing more often than they should. This can be infuriating however the common rule still stands that a failure should never hinge on a chance shot.
Base management has been simplified so that there is less micro management involved. You will still have to "make contact" with various countries however success no longer hinges on building satellites and is done more for the purposes of earning income and continent bonuses. Facilities are now upgradeable which also streamlines the experience. All in all, the emphasis is on scanning various sites and managing your research rather than worrying about interceptions.
In terms of lifespan, the sequel has definitely taken cues from "The Long War" mod that was created for the first game. There are more story missions however this time it is more beneficial to take your time and build your equipment up before rushing through the campaign. This makes the game feel less frantic and allows a lot more choice early rather on compared to the previous race to build satellites. There is a timer in the form of the "Avatar Project" however this can be kept in check by infiltrating various facilities and completing certain story missions. Personally I didn't find it to be much of a problem. However the added emphasis on resources does mean that the last third of the game was made particularly easy and did mean that I was able to steamroll every mission once I had the best equipment and missions, without much care on my part. Personally I enjoy being OP and smashing everything in my path but XCom veterans may want to up the difficulty level.
In summary, this game is a very a good sequel and worth your time if you enjoyed the first XCom. Whilst the time limits and especially random RNG can feel like a very arbitrary and lazy way of increasing the difficulty, the various improvements make up for those faults. The extensive mod workshop support means that even if you dislike certain elements, chances are there are options to change them to your liking. Performance is quite inconsistent and would render a real time game almost unplayable, however isn't a big deal in a turn based strategy.
Recomended, although newer players may want to utilise the mod workshop.

This is the 3rd review I'm writing for this game, and honestly, when talking about this game, I am both bored and felt that it ended too soon.  The game is short, mind you.  It takes about 5 to 6 hours to complete.  Most of this time is spent fannying about, doing the games' equivilent of 'go there, kill 10 of these things', as the game frequently breaks you away from the main story/context to have you perform side missions, that usually boil down to 'hack x, delete y.'
Why am I recommending this game, saying it ended too soon?  I say this because the last two missions are two of the most cleverly crafted puzzles I've ever seen.  'Project Junebug' and 'Bit Foundation' are stellar works of glory.  I'll focus on Project Junebug, as the Bit Foundation is the final story mission (the story ends spectacularly, by the way).   Obvious spoiler alert for ahead.
The game's side missions usually work as a sort of key insert thing.   Hack 4 ports, using 4 specific commands you get earlier in the game, Port Hack, boom, in, done.  No challenge, besides when there's a tracer, but simply disconnect and reconnect, and you're good as gravy.
Project Junebug was shaping up to be another one of those things.  As I hacked the medical terminal, I thought it was clever, having to use intuition to find the IP for a heart monitor, to kill a guy.  Connecting to said IP, I found that it required access to Port 104, where up until that point I only found stuff for ports 22, 25, 28, 1433, and 88.  Not wishing to go further, it required me to hack several computers slightly hinted at, and it was brilliant, as it forced me to use inginuity and my brain to track it down.
Note to Developers:  If you made the game more like THAT, other than the slog through Entropy and CSEC, then you'd have my full support.  Say utilize the 'find and replace' skill more, or maybe give us some way to hack to second computer by using the first.  Just suggestions.

For me my experience with darkest dungeon has been an interesting one.. I only played xcom 2 immensely, for years and that gave felt extremely rng heavy. Every gunshot was an average 40-70% chance to hit and then it's another random generated number...
This game isn't that. It's base numbers, with their values added, or reduced, given the
number everytime for a target instead of a ballpark range. This game is far deeper than big numbers. After careful planning of a selection of heroes, you have to use their skills uniquely to deal the most damage out of the various enemies. So it's not the same scenario setup you're trying to optimize each situation.
I love that it is
but not
. If you're having a decent game, lets say lets two runs go AWFUL, your 8 best picks just landed 6 feet under the grave, stuck with rooster of newbies. Despair? Hardly, pick a lower difficulty mission and tread carefully. There are even chances you'll have them back... I am also happy there is a fair retreat mechanic. You can run from any fight, or dungeon (on chance) and take your obtained loot with you. No casualties. No empty coffers. Of course there are ramifications to make retreating the not ideal option, however
.
Bottom line, I love this game it and it is addicting. It's satisfying to land in the worst scenario's and see my heroes pull through, make it home, and bring home the bank. The threat of death of a real one.

First of all, let me tell you that i've played this game on both PS4( friends house) and PC( My game)
The difference between consoles and PC version are obvious: Lagg.
Some may say there are more glitches in the PC version then the console version, but that may not be true.
The reason why less glitches and bugs may be encountered in consoles in comparison to PC is that most are caused by the lagg, example:
The scale down a building pretty fast once you got the hang of the new parkour controls, when suddenly your game laggs for maybe 3 seconds. When the mists of lagg clear and you're eager to continue, you notice Arno floats mid-air in his gliding position, not able to move or anything. Starting Coöp or fast traveling may fix this, yet if you're in the begin missions, this may turn you into a rage devil.( consult a doctor before raging, tables will be flipped.)
A pro about the PC version is that the online experience is free of cost, in comparison to PS4 and XboxOne.
Lagg doesn't occur for me most of the times(mind you that the only thing not being 'optimal' is my vid card.)
making the online experience one of the best gameplay features of Unity.
Just for those who would still consider buying it. I strongly suggest you don't when your pc can't handle the weight this game will bring with it. If your video card is from Nvidia, is a ' generation too less' and it's the only thing not optimal for Unity, you might want to take the risk to try it, if you're willing to go through 30 minutes of hell first in the begin missions.
Conclusion: For the average old gen pc user, i don't recommend buying it. For those with a 'weaker' vid card, i'm suggesting you consider well before taking the risk to try it. But a life without risk, is a life not lived.

I couldn't be happier to see one of my all-time favorite Tower Defense games having it's equally amazing sequel FINALLY make it's way to Steam.
The amount of determination this small team has shown, to re-create this game from SCRATCH, to be able to bring it to the Windows platform, shows what kind of devotion Ironhide has towards it's games. And it does show. The same polish and charm the first game had, fully remains.
This sequel has the exact same feel as the original Kingdom Rush; clean and consistant gameplay, yet balanced and challenging. They found a way to completely re-create all 4 tower types with exciting and interesting ability trees. All new enemies with equally interesting abilities, a large array of unique Heroes to choose from, intimidating bosses and ultra challenging bonus levels (and bosses) once the compaign is complete (to be added in an update).
The game and the others in the series are perfect, in my eyes. I couldn't recommend this more, ESPECIALLY if TD is your thing and you like a good challenge (play Veteran:)
I should note i Beta tested the game, so i may be a bit biased. But of course i'm biased, the game is amazing.

This just came out today and I thought I'd give it a try. As a Unity Developer myself I'm extra picky about these kinds of games but I was pleasantly impressed by this one. Very smooth, creative, cute minimalistic side-scroller that lets/makes you set up the level before trying to survive it. Gets very challenging later on. It reminds me of VVVVVV with the amount of dying-by-spikes. Decent soundtrack. Excellent physics. Gameplay is thought out and set up so you get to try and experiment with different setups as you play... without having to restart the level... which is refreshing. Has an Angry-Bird-Esque scoring system that's blissfully free of any time limits. Advancement is based on collecting powerups, however these powerups can be hard to see in the first world due to the bright background. Doesn't seem to be an issue though once you progress and the game gets darker. My kids love watching me play. Gonna say it was worth the $5.

So, I really wanted to like the game. I've played it through, five times now, and while the second time through had some nicer features, it still feels broken. Being a big fan of the original, and seeing as how this is basically the only game in the genre, when it finally came on sale for like, 30 dollars, I was super happy to finally get to play the game.
And boy, it was a big let down. In a lot of ways. My honest opinion is that it's not worth 60 bucks. Buy it on sale, hopefully 30 bucks or less. It feels less like a new game, and more like a horrible mod. It's only saving grace is the community modder base who can make it 10 times better (reccomend Long war perk pack among all of them), so here I go. While I ultimately have a positive view of the game, it is fundamentally flawed. I've had fun with it but I don't know whether or not I hate it or love it. I had an even bigger review written up but due to the 1000 charachter limit, this won't work. So, here's a list of problems with it.
-Line of Sight is fundamentally screwed up. You find yourself eitheir glitching through walls or simply "triggering" aliens by taking 1 step to the left, in places it doesn't even make sense. Or not being able to shoot aliens right in front of you etc. As a LOS based tactics game, screwing up this part of the game just makes it feel broken and honestly, it almost makes it unplayable in some areas.
-Everything is random, the game is balanced on you getting things like new ammunition or armor mods, or the right weapon upgrades and so on, but these things are completely random. It's fun when you actually get to play certain aspects of the game but this is so incredibly rare as to be almost irrelevant. I didn't even know that UFO missions existed until my second play through, that's how rare and random some of the features are. You will sometimes not get any of them.
-The timers are horrific. Not only do you have a razor thin amount of time to complete missions, but even the logistics system "month" is only 21 days, and you have to spend 3 days to collect your money. Yeah. You don't instantly get new money, you have to wait hovering over stuff for it. So, good luck spending 18 days doing♥♥♥♥♥♥and getting constantly interrupted. Honestly, this is the most broken element of the entire game, as it forces you to abandon your tactics and strategies and instead get from point A to point B without any real strategic goal. As a defensive game (you want aliens to discover you, rather than you discover them, in order to win) this pretty much breaks the game. I reccomend "true concealmet" and "configurable timers" as mods to make this more enioyable.
-The maps are tiny and you tend to accidentally bump in to 6-9 aliens at atime. Not even kidding you, nearly every time you move when you're near an alien another pod of aliens will be within 2 tiles of them. So, moving 2 tiles means now you have to fight 9 guys. Given that you are legitimately weaker in this version of the game (until you get super powers later on which just feels cheap, like doing double damage every turn), you're far more likely to die than in the original. And random mobs will pop up and attack you out of your control, acting like landmines. It's just overall too random and the clustered maps feels broken considering that xcom is about not discovering aliens too quickly.
-The game's style and story are lackluster. Notably, they removed Etherals and added in the Archon and Andromedon, two new aliens that make 0 sense to be in the game. The style clashes with itself and honestly it feels like they tried too hard to make the game feel like portal or overwatch. It ends up being bleh. I reccomend playing it without sound.
-The loading times are atrocious. For a game where you go back and load old saves due to perma deaths, it can take up to 5 minutes to for the load screen to open, then another 5 minutes to actually click on the load thing, then another 5 minutes to get it. Oh, and if you accidentally glitch again by having a guy see through a wall or something stupid like that, it's back to load it again! Honestly, it's the most frustrating thing of the game. Even with a great computer and mine is great, it's super slow. Even loading a mission or returning home adds needless minutes to your game. I'd honestly say that 10-20% of the game is just waiting for the loading timers. When it's fun, it's fun, when it's bad, it's REALLY bad. If you like watching paint dry or grass grow, this is the game for you. Good luck trying to play if your game glitches a lot.
-Concealment only lasts for the start of the mission. New items are completely random and you never get to choose the one's you want (which yes, is as stupid as it sounds). Pretty much all the new features add almost nothing to the game at all. This was a huge bummer to me as I thought they really stood a chance to change the gameplay logistics and instead it was a throway gimmick that you get once at the beggining of a mission. Really dumb concealment mechanic. Why take the trouble of designing it in to the game and then only have it once? I don't get it.
-The aliens are really overpowered and you are really underpowered, and later on in the game this switches. They give you special magical abilities like doing double damage later on but, it just feels broken. I don't mean that it's hard, I mean that the aliens take forever to kill and can kill you in one hit. If you don't attack the enemy without getting attacked once every play through, you pretty much can expect 14 day waiting periods where you're totally inept or for someone to die. Rather than fix this by rebalancing the game, you just get more powerful items and powers that allow you to do so much extra damage it becomes too easy. So later on, now you are too powerful. The game feels like it has almost no balance. It's more of a rock-papers-scissors thing, as you need certain classes to destroy the armor of certain units, certain classes to stun other units and so on, rather than playing the one's you want. Oh and, it's all completely random so, good luck playing through if you don't get two grenaiders. You might as well re-roll if you don't have at least one grenaider, it will be impossible to play without shredder.
The real simple issue of the game could be described as two sets of game mechanics that work in opposite directions. One of them wants you to play defensivley, and one of them forces you to complete things in a certain amount of time or instantly lose the game. The mish-mash of awkward styles, mechanics and the sheer randomness make it not very fun. I enjoy a challenge, I've played X-Com and xenonauts and all the originals, but, this game sucks. It's not that it's too hard, it's that it's broken. It's barely playable and, if it wasn't for the mods, I would have quit it a long time ago. Seriously, invest in to the mods.

Kingdom Rush Frontiers arrives on Steam at last, and it's a welcome sight!
The original Kingdom Rush is one of the best Tower Defense games out there, and Frontiers works hard to stand out while still being true to the original. The advanced Towers have all changed, which is both a blessing and a curse (no more spamming Tesla Towers for easy wins!), and the enemies have been switched around as well to present you with whole new challenges. You'll face tribal shamans who can make their allies all but impervious to specific damage types, enemies with multiple forms, necromancers galore and all manner of tricky foes that will need smart planning to defeat.
Frontiers feels a lot harder than its predecessor, in no small part due to the need to counter all manner of enemy casters that wander down your lanes. Thankfully, you can always lower the difficulty if things get overwhelming.
If you're new to Tower Defense, try picking up the original Kingdom Rush first. For people who've played that and want more, Frontiers is happy to provide!

Writing this review saddens me. I have been a fan of Bethesda’s games since Morrowind, which, like Oblivion, I bought twice (once in a store and once on Steam). My opinion of Bethesda was so positive that I preordered both Fallout 4 and the season pass. I trusted Bethesda enough to pay money for a game that had not been released yet. To date, that is the only time I have preordered a game. That is how much respect I had for Bethesda.
Fallout 4 itself is a good, but disappointing game. As I played it, I thought, “Man, I wish they had done more here,” far too often. For example, in the scene with Nick Valentine at the end of the Dangerous Minds quest, Bethesda hinted that continuing to travel with Nick might be a bad idea. That is why I kept him around. And I was disappointed. Nick went back to being just Nick. Bethesda hinted at a possible source of tension, a potential reason for the player to become invested in the story, and then they dropped it.
They did the same thing with Cait’s storyline. Rather than telling the story of a junkie’s slow and painful road to recovery, they invented a magical machine that cured her drug addiction forever. No tension. No reason to care.
And again with Piper. Talking with her reveals that she is worried that her younger sister will turn out to be just like her. But consoling Piper is enough to belay her fears. All the tension is gone. No reason to care. Another opportunity Bethesda wasted.
Et cetera. Et cetera.
Despite this, I still enjoyed Fallout 4. Bethesda’s greatest attribute has always been it’s ability to create amazing worlds. And the world of Fallout 4 is amazing - once you decide to ignore Preston Garvey and his idiotic radiant quests and just wander around the Commonwealth, that is. When you ditch all quests and just get lost in the world, Fallout 4 shines. The world Bethesda created in Fallout 4 tells a story far better than any of their quests do. There is a moment in every Bethesda game where I think, “Alright, show me something I have not seen before.” And Bethesda has never failed to do just that.
But, and this is a big but, finding that moment in Fallout 4 was harder than in any other Bethesda game. They seemed to be doing their utmost to keep players from wandering too far from their vision for the game. You can try to do your own thing, but the main questline will keep getting in your way. For example, completing Curie’s quest without first doing the Main Quest Dangerous Minds is impossible without using the console.
It feels as if Bethesda, for some insane reason, decided that it alone knew what players wanted. And if anyone dared to question their decisions (even the players themselves), then he/she was just wrong. Think about everything Bethesda has done since the release of Fallout 4...the mess that surrounded the unveiling of their mod service (I left the name out on purpose)...the underwhelming content provided in the beta release of their “club” (name omitted on purpose, any advertising is good advertising)...Bethesda thinking that it was okay to download this paltry collection of “curated” content onto people’s computers without being purchased… These are the actions of a company that has lost touch with it’s community, a community that turned Bethesda into the success it is.
This is why I cannot recommend Fallout 4. This is why Bethesda needs to repair the damage it has done to it’s community before I will buy another one of it’s games. They managed to turn this loyal fan into a cynic. Only Bethesda can remedy this. But I doubt they care. That is how low my opinion of them has fallen.

Without a doubt a contender as my favorite game of the seventh generation and even of all time. PlatinumGames really created a masterpiece here and i'm really looking forward to playing the sequel.
Graphics

It's the best action game ever. To me this beats out Devil May Cry and God of War and Rising Revengeance with having the most satisfying and craziest combo system ever. It seems like every button corresponds to a combo combine that with the vast amount of weapons and abilities has me replaying this game non stop till I get the best ranking.
Controls
Perfect, especially with a controller
Story
Too be honest the story isnt anything special but what made it so enjoyable was how nonsensical and over the top and self aware the game was but the actual plot itself is without a doubt the weakest aspect but made more enjoyable by the characters in the story.
Buy this game it's worth it especially for $20 and no microtransactions or DLC in sight which is always a plus

I won't comment on graphics or anything of the sort, It's a beautiful game that runs very well on my PC. What I will comment on is how every sells this game as the perfect game if you are craving a Dakr Souls feeling. I disagree.
First off:  It seems everyone says that the combat feels heavy, like you're really hitting something with a big hammer. I think it feels unbareably slow. I loved darksouls for the fast paced, heart pumping action, where that next role counts, that next slash is the big one, the one you have been waiting to go for for so long. In LotF you know if you are about to lose, you see the killing hit coming a mile away and there isn't a thing you can do about it. Roling doesn't matter becuase all roles ar fat roles, so dont even bother. Blocking is next to useless since if they do enough damage it practically negates the use of your shield. You feel helpless to do anything but watch as the great sword slams into your skull.
Second off:  I got barely into the game before I ran into an enemy that I could not beat. He hit harder than me, he blocked more than me, he had more health than me. No matter what I do I can't kill him. I have come to the fact that I'm not supposed to kill him, which angers me to no end. In darksouls the point is that you can win no matter what the odds. Even if I could kill him fighting him is so tedious. I spam my ability and hit him in the back, than rinse and repeat. This way of fighting becomes the standard. In Dark Souls you need to change the wa you fight the boss to beat him, in LotF It's the same thing over and over and over again. A big boss that you kill by using your ability 800 times and smacking him. It got to the point where I didn't WANT to progress through the game.
The armour is really cool, and I enjoyed the story that I experienced, but if you are looking the comments that are saying it's just like Dark Souls than re think what you loved about darksouls.
If you loved the feeling after killing a boss, than yes, this is great, you feel like you accomplished something.
If you are willing to sacrifice satifying, heart pounding combat, and the feeling that with enough energy you can do anything, than buy the game. I'm not willing to sacrifice thet combat experience, maybe i'll come back to the game and see  the good in it, until than, it isn't for me. I'm recommending it none the less because to some this game will be great, but if you are like me, I'd stay away.

People that say this game is "nothing but RNG", and that "your skill doesn't matter" don't know what they are talking about. This game is risk management, bad things will happen at the worse possible time, and you need to be prepared for that. Wether you do well depends on your ability to pick good team compositions, pack the right items (and correct quantity), and select trinkets that complement your setup (stacking damage trinkets with stress penalty is risky, you will have to focus stress dealers for example). I do mostly dark runs (no torches, so enemies crit chance and accuracy go up, and you take way more stress), and the only time that I've lost people was to the shambler mini boss because I got too cocky (my team didn't have the dps to kill it quickly). I highly recommend beating the game on Radiant mode first, the actual gameply is still the same, but the character/item management is cheaper and more forgiving (aka game same difficulty, but less grind needed when you ♥♥♥♥ up).

I have really tried to like this game, and in a masochistic manner I have returned to crawl through the Darkest Dungeons time and again but ultimately I have to say this game is broken. It's simply impossible to level up your characters effectively to handle the higher level dungeons because you never earn enough money to keep improving your characters as needed for these dungeons. And when money is the main thing holding you back from advancing in a game that game is broken.
Add in the fact that the enemies are far too buffed no matter the level and it's far too easy to drive your characters crazy no matter their level and you've got a game that feels like pulling teeth to play. I really wanted to like Darkest Dungeons, it has a great look about it, some cool characters and story elements and overall is a great idea for a game, but when you're simply sending your characters in to die over and over again the game becomes no fun at all.
Oh, and I forgot to mention the one thing that really burns my butt- you don't get to keep the stuff you found in a dungeon unless you finish the dungeon! Why wouldn't my characters be able to carry out their loot if they abandon a quest? This contributes to the lack of funding for your party, and makes the whole thing so stupid when you realize you're not going to be able to survive the dungeon you're currently in.
So unless you like watching your heroes die no matter how much you've improved their skills don't bother with this broken game!

Each location has multiple bosses, each boss having 3 versions of it, each deadlier than the last.

Your hero that has the best trinklets, equipment, and buffs can be destroyed be the powers that be.
You could take the greatest caution to not have a hero die, and still lose them.
This game is not like D&D, where the DM wants everyone to live, but face a challenge, this game wants you and every one of your members dead.
By playing this game over the 2 hour mark, you accept this, and will suffer.
But risk brings reward, and the game acknowledges that.
You can reduce the light level, which will make the monsters you fight more accurate and deadly, but also give more loot.
Anything you interact with can curse, poison, or cut you, while at the same time give prizes for being lucky.
Using the right item on a curio (or interactable object) will provide good results... most of the time.
Just because you got a party wipe does NOT mean the game is bad. It just means you were unlucky.
Besides, you never acknoledged the time you got 3 crits and dodged 3 attacks in a row.
This game gives, and this game takes.

The recent surge of zombie culture is possibly at a climax. From zombie movies, comics, games and merchandising.. the undead are anything but. They are seen in every facet we'd like to healthily admit they are in. The zombies have invaded our desktops, our conversations, our jokes and even our televisions. They've even travelled across the atlantic ocean and settled in Europe and are spreading beyond control. So when another game, based on a tv show that is based off a comic book of more zombies comes up, we say.. "meh". At least I do, that I'm sure of. Except this time, this time I think they've struck gold.
The Walking Dead video game is a breath of new life to a dieing topic. It pulls out all of the bits and pieces that we've forgotten in our ever continuing thirst for entertainment in the zombie genre. It brings us back to our roots of what the zombie culture is all about, and what it should be like. Survival, safety, kinmanship, distrust, compassion and every other human quality and emotional disregard all fight together and mix up worse than oil and water in a world torn apart by the undead and chaos. Upon starting the game, you'll be drawn into the cell shaded world of "The Walked Undead: Season 1", and immediate realize that this is a story driven game. Pay close attention to how you respond to other characters, your future might depend on it.
Lee Everett is a man who has a bad run in with the law. On his way out of the city to prison, the vehicle runs into a silhouette of an unknown person on the freeway and the car overturns into the forest. You're quickly given the controls and theme of the game when you must use keystrokes to perform animated actions inorder to escape the mangled vehicle. In pain and in need of medical attention, you quickly understand the true desperateness of your situation while basic human instincts tell you to run.
After escaping your ordeal, you'll soon meet the real star of this show, "Clementine". A young girl, wise beyond her years is stuck in this new world and needs your protection. You mission in life is now clear, and you must do everything in your power to ensure you don't fail.
"The Walking Dead: Season 1" is a story driven adventure about survival and friendship in the face of despair and death. In this point and click adventure, almost every choice you make will have consequences and the outcome is never very clear until they happen. Experience zombies like you've never experienced them before in this riveting and memorable tale. A must buy for anyone who loves stories and pc games. Do not miss this.

Kingdom Rush Frontiers continues the story that ended in the original. After Vez'nan demise, evil mage Lord Malagar gets his hands on Vez'nan's staff and steals powerful Hammer of Ages. You, unknown hero, have a task to retrieve it before Lord Malagar can use it for his evil plan. That proves to be a difficult job as you are chasing him across the desert, jungle and underground caverns. During your journey, you are gonna encounter new, powerful enemies but you will also get help from (unexpected) allies.
KRF's gameplay isn't any different from original. There are 15 levels with 3 game modes - Campaign, Heroic and Iron. Also, there are 3 difficulty options - Casual, Normal and Veteran. Completing levels will grant stars that can be spent on upgrading towers and spells. Using Hero during levels will make him more experienced and you can use that experience to make him more powerful.
Downside of KRF is that there is no checkpoint or fast forward system thus making game a bit tedious on multiple replays but it's balanced by having relatively short levels and plenty of easter eggs.
Fun gameplay, interesting story and upgrade system makes this journey worthwhile of your time.

XCOM:EW was a breath of fresh air when it was released. Yes it was an old game being remade (which I also played and loved), but I think that as it was essentially an afterthought by Firaxis it surprised many people with its playability, particularly as a console release. As for XCOM 2, after having loved the first so much, I was really looking forward to its release, watching every trailer and press release giving any new details, and I certainly was not disapointed.
Now I think that first I should point out that the game is certainly not perfect, but I feel that the pros still massively outweigh the cons.
The graphics have been given an upgrade, sharpened and polished, and some new ideas and concepts have been brought in. Animations have become slightly less predictable. I could tell in EW from the units cut scene if they were going to miss or not.
The gameplay has remained the same mostly except that getting up close and personal with the enemy has become somewhat more focused with dedicated troops for this. We see the removal of the Mecs and Gene lab, however some new ideas have come in to replace that although arguably these do not make up for the loss. I can not help thinking, much like I did with EW that I would like to be able to manage multiple bases around the world each with their own crack team, like in the original games, I would also like to see more attacks on my own base, or in this case ship.
I personally found the introduction of so many timed missions to be frustrating, and would often force me into making errors or strategic saves when not playing ironman just to see what is around the corner. That being said they did mean that I was often put under pressure and certainly lost more units than I did in EW.
Overall I love this game, I would recommend getting the DLC to allow for a more rounded game, There is also a big modding scene for this game now which will help to keep things fresh. I would like to see some more elements brought into the game to break up the missions which can be hard work if you get a run of them while you are waiting for new tech. All told I think this is an excellent addition to the series and I look forward to future games.

I learned to love many Tower Defence Games over the years. The original Kingdom Rush on
was amongst my favorites, thus I did not hesitate to buy its updated version as a fullpriced game on Steam. Seeing this successor made me wonder if the quality could hold up to my expectations; after about an hour of gameplay I have the feeling that I will indeed love this game- as it builds upon the strengths of its predecessor while adding some improvements.
I will first speak about the Kigdom Rush Series as a whole, before getting into detail with Kingdom Rush Frontiers.
First of all the lovely art and sound design; if you are able to bear the sight of a comic look you will notice that the drawings may not be at the peak of 2d-graphics (probably due to the games flash/mobile origins) - but that they do have a decent style on them that makes them distinguishable from other TD-Games. The sound itself is a combination of a decent background music (neither is it outstanding,nor is it irritating) and wonderful catch-phrases by your troops/towers.
Kingdom Rush is that kind of TD-Game where the path of the enemy units can not be influenced by your towers as you are building them next to the walking-path at specific locations (therefore: no mazes and no towerspamming till the map is full). However, one of the four towers you can build is a "melee-tower" which spawns three soldiers at a location you can can choose within its influence area - this gives you the opportunity to block enemies on the road with a fight - while your towers are tearing them apart. Micromanaging the spawning locations ofthese troops - as well as your powerfull hero character and your two spells - while planning your tower upgrades makes for a pretty intense experience in which you will forget that there is no button for fast-forwarding; as you are much more actively involved into the gameplay as you usually are in a TD-Game.
First and foremost it is the leveldesign that was improved; while the first 6 stages offered a nice variety of artstyle it is the uniqueness of some gameplayelements in those maps, that made them really distinguishable -  without any spoilers: new paths are created and there are more interactive objects than before.
The heroes feel more powerful and unique than in Kingdom Rush.
That - as always - depends on your experience with Kingdom Rush and TDs in general and of course the price of the game.
If you played Kingdom Rush and liked it you will like this one too. If you like TDs in general but never played Kingdom Rush - give the original a try. If you do not like TDs but are still reading this review I really do question your priorities.

I should start this off by saying I bought this game because I adored The Wolf Among Us and Telltale Games also did The Walking Dead. Telltale games also says this one is similar to TWAU. So I decided to give it a shot.
Don't get me wrong, I love the story and the decisions you have to make when facing the zombie apocalypse. The characters are diverse and great. (I love the whole dynamic of dialogue choices affecting how the other characters view the protagonist as a person.)
The thing that gets me, and personally makes this game unenjoyable, is the gameplay. The camera is questionable at times, and it isn't always clear about what you're supposed to do or if you can even look to the right or left. (For example, in the prologue, it's hard to see the little dot to call for help off by the horizon.) Secondly, if you click on something and your viewpoint zooms in. I've found ones (if it's not what you're supposed to do at that very moment) you can't back up out of it and I actually had to restart the game. Talk about interrupting the moment. The combat is okay, but it's not as smooth as it could be.
