In it's current form, this game is an absolute mess.
I've read and watched a lot after spending some time with it and there is obviously a lot of "covering of asses" that will continue for the foreseeable future. As it stands, it feels like what will eventually be an enjoyable, playable, more realistic assassin's creed experience eventually, but at the moment it's a $60 Beta with terrible performance and hilarious bugs and glitches throughout.
The combat is better than before, certainly offering more challenge, but once you realize there are actually only 3 weapons with various skins and stat upgrades, it's simply a means to an end. The cover system is barely acceptable and at times frustrating to maneuver, but at least they added stealth to what should have always been a stealth game, right? Meh.
The story is okay, but there rarely seems to incorporate the time-period save for a few late-game missions and a few interesting French Revolution-based Murder Investigations. Arno is an okay protagonist, but it's clear from the start that he's essentially a less interesting Ezio with a love interest in his first game rather than his third. By the time new characters are introduced, or in this case grow up, you are just expected to care about them. Your only insight into any of the characters' backstory is to assassinate them, so getting attached to a target is entirely meaningless, as you're unaware of your motivation for doing so until after they're dead. The large assassination mission structures, while diverse enough, lack any sort of tension because honestly, who cares if Templar A, B, or C has a backstory once they're dead, on to the next one. The modern-day story has become even less detached from significance. With Desmond gone and Black Flag getting away from a named protagonist, who needs to even play a character anymore? It's some of the laziest writing and gives you no clue as to what is even going on in the world any more, or if you should even care.
Side missions may be the most interesting part of the game. While the murder investigations weren't extremely challenging, they tied well into the time-period and some were extremely significant to the French Revolution. The lack of interesting in-game anecdotes led to my own research, which is telling to the level of care put in around the margins of this game, it is lacking significantly. The various other fetch quests and Co-Op missions are okay, and are useful if you're bored of single-player. At the end of those though, it's quite obvious, Unity is good at things it wants to be good at, it's okay at things you think it should be good, and it's terrible at things it needs to be good at.
In some form, optimized and fixed, and on sale, this game will be worth picking up, but skip it for now.

Take no notice of the bad reviews. These are mostly from people that don't want to put the time and energy in that's required to learn how to play OMSI2. Many of them claim to have decent machines to play OMSI on, well they don't because buses that jump and down only happen on low-spec PCs.
This is a simulator and not some kind of dirt rally driving game. This is as realistic as it gets as far as bus simulators go and to be honest, this really is the only one of its kind out there at the moment.
You have to learn how to select your route and line (Bus) number. You have to learn how to operate the buses because nearly every switch and button is modelled to work like the real buses. You have to learn how to use the ticket machine e.t.c. In other words, you have to read the PDF manuals and watch YouTube videos to help you familiarise yourself with the game.
The physics and sounds of the bus models are pretty darned good with suspension and the buses rattle and shake when driving over rougher roads with broken tarmac and pot-holes just like in real life. There are automatic announcements on some routes and you can even download the current real-world weather to drive in.
There is quite a lot of paid DLC to expand with more routes and more buses including lots of freeware maps too.
The game is of course pretty old now and is not really optimised for todays PCs as it's only 32Bit and limited to 2Gb of RAM which is why you need to download the seperate 4Gb patch but its still a perfectly good working game and lot's of fun.

Short Version: Is it worth playing? YES. Is it worth the full price? HELL NO!
Long Version:
(WARNING: I will compare this game to Darksouls games a lot since it's obvious that it tries to mimic it's mechanisms and gameplay style.)
PROS: 1. Semi-Darksouls action combat - If you like the way Darksouls I & II handles combat chances are, you'll probably like the way this game handles it as well. The difference is that the combat in Darksouls is faster and more flashy.
2. Beautiful Graphics - Although the graphics are brilliant and beautiful (scenery, armor, weapons, you name it...) some of them are a bit "samey". (More on that in CONS)
3. The story - Unlike Darksouls where you have to scrape the story from item descriptions and where most of it you decide and invent for yourself, the story here is way more accessible. You are a convicted criminal whose crimes are tattooed on your face and your mission is to redeem yourself by destroying a fallen god. Sounds fun! There are more hidden lore bits found out from the few NPCs and much more numerous log files.
4. Performance - I only played the game after the latest patch and can confirm that on my system (i5 3,5 GHz, Nvidia 770GTX, 16GB ram, SSD disk, every graphics setting maxed out) the game held a stable 60fps 99% of the time with maybe 2-3 times dropping to 45-50 FPS and only on specific places.
5. Bugs - with the recent patches most have been squashed. Haven't really noticed any during my gameplay.
6. Game Mechanics - There is a risk-reward system implemented in the game that works really well. The more enemies you slay before resting at a checkpoint the more it increases your exp. multiplier which in turn increases the exp. gain from other enemies. But if you are killed, that exp. will slowly drain away until you either collect it back or it drains completely. The only real big difference from the darksouls games.
MEH: 1. Difficulty - Harder than most games, way easier then Darksouls II. To be honest I was expecting a more challenging game, but I guess this decision makes the game appeal to a broader audience.
2. Enemy variations - too little variations. Same enemy models reused through the game. Most of the bosses resemble ordinary units only bigger in size.
3. Customization - Oh my GOD. Everyone is overusing steroids in this game. From the main character to the lowliest mob. Want to role-play a squishy mage? Nope, here's a mage that bench presses 200 kg. Want to play as a sleek and agile rogue? Nope, here's a rogue with 140 kg of muscle. I prefer the big warrior class but to have the option to at least customize the face and a few sliders wouldn't hurt the game one bit.
CONS:  1. Lack of NPCs - There are maybe 3 worthwhile NPCs in the whole game.
2. Dialogue - The dialogue with the said 3 NPCs is sometimes strange and somewhat out of place.
3. Replay value - Whereas I've played Darksouls I and II with multiple characters for months, After I finished this game, I'll probably finish it once more from the beginning this time trying to get all the collectables and the special weapons from the bosses. After that I'll probably delete the game never to play it again.
4. Game duration - It's too short. It took me probably 15 hours to finish.
5. "Samey" world design - Remember how in Darksouls you have very distinct and different environments? Well there's no such thing in Lords. The whole game is one big dungeon and castle interiors mixed with a bit of snowy exterior. It looks great but it's the same most of the game. And since it's all interconnected (something I like very much, reminds me of how Darksouls I handled it's world and shortcuts to bonefires) it results in being lost quite often, trying to find how to progress further into the game (something I hate very much).
Overall Score: 6.5/10
Verdict: Buy the game if you are a darksouls fan, but get it when it's on discount.

Bayonetta is honestly one of the most fun video games I've played in longer than I can remember. Oddly enough I've never enjoyed these beat em up type games clearly in the vein of Devil May Cry. I even bought the newer DMC reboot near the end of the Xbox 360 era and really didn't like it. If my DMC memory serves they share quite a bit of DNA so It's hard to put into words why Bayonetta works so well for me but man does it work.
The puzzle solving and moment to moment combat are a bit stale but the game throws enough mini bosses at Bayonetta on a frequent basis that you're kept on your toes or heels I guess. Bayonetta just feels great to control. Bayonetta feels  lethal and incredibly powerful yet fragile as glass. It's an incredibly tricky balance to strike but the game pulls it off masterfully. The real thrill of Bayonetta is taking on collossal bosses with well timed combos. Button mashing is unfortunately possible but you'll carve angels up with style and look competent doing it if you take the time to learn the combos and master witch time. I feel like I'm sailing through the game but I also keep replaying levels which is really stretching out my playtime. You're ranked on your performance in each fight and an overall score at the end of the level. I can't really wrap my head around why I keep replaying these levels to get gold or platinum scores but it's just so much fun to become more and more dangerous.
The story is whatever to be honest but the characters are all pretty funny. The game is pure schlock but the self aware nature of the game makes it more charming than groan worthy. I found myself laughing way more than I'd like to admit and whenever I wasn't laughing I just had a big stupid grin on my face. Bayonetta makes no excuses for what it is and I think that's why it works. Even if the campy nonsense style of the game doesn't work for you it's worth playing just for the fun combat and all the cutscenes are skippable. I have to say I think you're doing yourself a huge disservice to pass on the cutscenes but I can see how the jokes and story aren't for everyone.
The graphics hold up pretty well for a game nearly 8 years old and it holds at a solid 60fps. At $20 this game is easily worth every penny but being a relatively new release on steam I'm sure it'll go down lower in the future. I'd highly recommend picking it up during a sale if not at full price. Hoping to finish up soon and run through again on a higher difficulty if beating the game unlocks more challenging settings. I don't know if 2009 me would have enjoyed this game but I'm glad I picked it up when I did.
I'd comfortably give Bayonetta 8.5/10 and I'll be looking forward to future titles in this franchise.

I'm always finding myself coming back to this game every now and again.  It's a different take on a brain exercise; definitely not your crossword or Sudoku mental exercise.  Granted that I'm a simple guy who is easy to please with games, provided there's what I view as a good story and at least a good attempt at making it asthetically pleasing.  I know there are a lot of hardcore gamers on here who will diss a game over the simplest of things, so this review might end up displeasing those kinds of people.  Oh well, can't please them all, right?
Anyway, with the expansions they made from the prequel XCOM, it's more of a death sentence to just haphazardly send soldiers without direction.  The time limits also give a sense of realism to the missions; strike forces in real life don't run on an everlasting clock.  To some degree, it provides a sense of urgency and prompts you to continue moving even if you just aren't completely ready or confident enough to do so.
It's true that there are some things technical-wise that can be improved on.  There are a few glitches that aren't game-breakers but somewhat annoying if you're a stickler for games needing to be played without mechanical interruptions.  However, there is one glitch revolving Chrysallids which will ruin your current save file; if you are a save scum, don't try to load a game where the Chrysallids have been revealed and burrowed underground.  It will forever lock that file with no hope of opening it.  I don't know if it's been fixed at the time of this posting, but just a bit of heads-up for you lovable save scums out there!
If you're a person who lets the little imperfections and occasional glitches get in the way of a good gaming experience, then this won't be for you.  Although to be honest, there is no one game that is completely glitch or problem free.  That and to say you won't recommend it after clocking in over 100 or so hours of gameplay seems like a bad claim to a non-recommendation stance.  Otherwise, this game is one I love and would recommend.  It allows for easy difficultly if you just feel lazy in the planning department all the way up to extreme difficultly if you feel particularly self-sadistic.  It's great for all skill levels with the difficultly ramped up accordingly regardless of what the starting difficulty level is.

This is a review of a full playthrough of the game on normal difficulty.
To clear things up real quick: I reloaded mid battle, time and time again. I do not know what it is like losing your troops over and over again due to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ percentages. This is however based on the design of the spotting system where suddenly the entire enemy squad that you just spotted starts moving all over the place, combine this with having spotted them with your last unit and you just turned from decent battle to half dead team with a single move. This is actually the worst part about the battle system in my opinion.
The game is famous for making you miss 95% chance hits, but looking at it realistically that did indeed only happen 5% of the time to me. I think people overestimate the misses because they actually DO lose units and not cheat like me.
What I always loved most about both this game and the first part is the arms race. You develop new technologies based on what you can grab from the aliens and then use that knowledge to get more powerful armor and weapons and it FEELS SO GOOD, when you just got the plasma sniper rifle and witness a beam like a deathstar shredding through the puny enemies, nothing can beat that feeling.
Meanwhile the aliens put more and more powerful units on the field, both by buffing the HP and by introducing entirely new types of foes. (where the berserker at though? I saw like 2 throughout the entire game)
I also like your own unit variety, you can have experts in melee combat, slicing through the enemy with swords and shotguns, or the heavys, that carry enough explosive rounds to take out the enemy team by themselves as well as a minigun. Perhaps the deathstar sniper, sitting out of danger while being the danger is your style. Or the unusual psionik warrior, using mind control to force new friends?
Storywise it is...meh. Aliens have conquered the earth so now take it back by turning earth into vietnam. Predictable and not memorable.
The looks are pretty damn sweet in my opinion, particularly the effects of laser based weaponry and all that.
The music fits into the background and gets the job done, thats it.
Among the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ spotting system I also found myself strongly disliking the camera. Often it just didnt give the perfect view of the battlefield now matter how I turned it. Even worse though is the increase in frequency of crashes. The farther you got the more often you had to reload after a complete crash. This was already an issue in the first game.
The duration you should expect for a single playthrough, if you reload a lot like me, is about 40 hours. Is that worth 50 Euros/dollars/whatever ? Probably not. I reccomend waiting for a very big sale. All in all though if you liked the first part you will like this one as well. If you didnt play the first part you might wanna check that one out first, it should be cheaper and is just as good.
Tl:dr: good game for its genre

DISREGARD WHINERS. This game is an instant classic. The people whining about RNG are ridiculous. The game tells you from the first moment it's an outlast disaster game, where your town/party management is the key to success or failure.
- This game is challenging, but the challenge is rewarding, and there is ample opportunity to improve if you have a bit of patience and understand that you must accept and learn from the death of your favorite characters. It's the people that don't get that aspect that go salty on the RNG, missing half the point of the whole game.
- The art is perfect. Maybe I appreciate the hand-drawn style games more than the next guy.... this game is a sure example of unique art done right in a way that contributes immensely to the mood of the game.
- THE VOICE ACTING! Oh god yes I love it when I hear "Executed with impunity!". Along with the art, the voice makes this game... and then you notice afterwards that ALL the audio is great, but most is eclipsed by the awesomeness of the narrator.
- Mechanics: The light and stress mechanics are a fresh treat for my strategy taste buds. Camping skills add some great management aspects into the middle of all but the short expeditions. Characters have sets of well-thought skills of which you can choose to have half active during an adventure. Resistances are meaningful and balanced enough to play a more obvious role. Skeletons are nearly immune to bleed. Fungi creatures have high blight resistance. Damage over time becomes important with enemies with high protection... And always and forever it's all about that tough choice. Should I heal? Reduce nearly topped stress? Or hope for a critical to end that last enemy before they can strike a deathblow. Just damn fine all around strategy/management mechanics.
- RNG cuts both ways, and it is not as all-encompassing as detractors claim. Everything touched by RNG has at least one mechanic available to improve chances. Most characters have a high base chance to hit, and a variety of buffs and debuffs are available for clever use to change the odds.
To sum up, Red Hook acted upon a solid vision, and created a game that stands out and above in every way, engaging and challenging from the first moments. Darkest Dungeon rewards the resilient with great satisfaction.

This is a review of the base game, without mods, which I bought 6 months after game release.
Summary:
Playing this game was like drinking a nice soda and finding a hornet in the bottom of the glass!
Pros:
Good UI
Minimal game-engine problems
Good to great graphics
Interesting soldier mechanics and play styles
Explosives
Cons:
The Plot
Pacing.  The Avatar timer mechanic in particular
Characters, or lack of them.
Shallow and relatively obvious tech tree
Utter lack of surprise at anything
Save files that balloon in size
The cutscene before the final mission causing actual computer crash when equipping WAR suit.
A game that feels way too short and unfinished without DLC
I had a feeling Firaxis would make a mess of this game... and I was right.  I decided to play the vanilla game, mod-free, without any DLC.
Getting to a good balance of difficulty was tough.  I eventually settled on veteran, then realized once you know how to play this game most of the mechanics are largely irrelevant.  There's a more or less simple solution to every problem.
The missions are fairly repetitive.  Some require more stealth than others, and some require killing all enemies and other requires soldiers to evac out.  My basic playstyle of XCOM1 was totally fine: lots of heavies and snipers, with supports and assaults carrying rifles.  Explosives destroy cover and shred armor, everyone else gets shots at exposed targets.  Robotic enemies are nasty... until you realize that your supports are absolutely OP against them.  Again, kind of typical of the laziness on Firaxis' part - create an enemy with an insta-counter.  Heck the biggest risk is that you don't level up early supports because you think they're useless.
The overall missions were fun, especially once I got 6 colonel ranked soldiers and started blowing everything up.  I didn't ever deploy a single psionic soldier, and it was no big deal at all.
Anyways, the cutscene before the final mission literally crashed my computer!  It resembled a power cycle (and this happened 3 times at exactly the same point in the cutscene)... people on the internet have also experienced it... mine was solved by removing the WAR suit from the soldier who had it in the loadout scream, which apparently caused a graphics glitch.  That is unacceptable, Firaxis!  A known, full-crash bug that still hasn't been addressed.
In sum, I think the fun factor of this game is probably in the mods... however it speaks poorly to the creators that the best thing about their game is that other people can make it better.  I am not a modder, I believe games should be good as sold, and that they should not suck in general.

Second in the line of totally awsome Kingdom Rush TD games, Frontiers is a damn near total refinement and improvement of the original across the board!
The Hero system has been totally refined and expanded upon, no longer do heroes level to max in each battle and then lose their levels after you win. Now, heroes have persistent levels and abilities you can assign skill points to in whatever order you wish! Leveling heroes is fairly fast (especially when you play on later levels) so don't worry about there being a grind!
Level 4 Tower upgrades are all new and more interesting than in the original game! Now, the Mage towers can become the Necromancer or Archmage! Necromancer raises skeletons to block and fight for you when enemies die near the tower and the Archmage can store up to 3 high-damage shots to really blast enemies! Of course each level 4 Tower also has special abilities you can buy such as the Necromancer's Death Rider that is a powerful fighter and buffs nearby friendly skeletons and the Archmage can summon forth a Twister to damage and push back enemies!
All of the levels are top-grade stuff too with many having special features. One level has "Tuskan Raiders" up on a cliff shotting at targets that come near, another has man-eating plants that can gobble up friend and foe alike and yet another has a band of friendly dwarves (with unique Towers!) setup to aid you! These are only a few examples!
Truly great Tower Defense game and a worthy sequel to the first!

Imagine Dark Souls, but with enemies that have unlimited stamina, hit extremely hard (1-2 shot anything other than heavy armored, high vitality Knights) and you got no shield break. Then, about 25-40% into the game, enemies with shields appear that almost never put their shield down (remember, no shield break like in DS) and hit REALLY hard. I mean every enemy after the second boss/third boss hits hard but those... And the best part is this: enemies can adjust their strikes mid-swing. You cannot. You cannot circle around them and hit them, because they will always look straight at you and when they swing and you move, they will adjust. There are maybe 1 out of 3 attacks that leave them open for a bit of damage.
To put it shortly for everyone who played Dark Souls 2: Remember those knights dual-whielding two shields in the Undead Crypt? And also remember those big, black knights in the Dragon Shrine with the hammers? Fusion them and you got the big Rhogar that appear mid game in Lords of the Fallen. Unpenetrateable shield and hard, staggering strikes.
At some point I got so sick of the regular enemies that I put on the heaviest armor and some sort of staff and just mashed attack, hoping to hit them before they hit me (it worked btw, finished the game pretty easily).
Now, I tried assasin - everything one shots me after the third boss.
I tried cleric - everything two-shots me after the third boss which is easy because they stagger me (poise useless).
Btw your roll is terrible in this game. I think you can only roll in 4 directions and if you roll left/right you won't be able to hit the enemy because either your roll is too far or your strike is too slow or your weapon is too short.
Now one thing about the bosses. Especially the first two ones. They have patterns which is absolutely fine Dark Souls has that, too, and I really like the game, however the have exactly one or two out of X attacks which leaves them vulnearable (because you can attack their back). The bosses in this game are about as entertaining as the first Dragonrider. But unlike that one, who you can attack whenever you can reach his back or left side and even parry his strikes, in Lords of the Fallen you have to wait for this one particular attack which gives you time to reach their backs and attack.
Perfect Example is the second boss:
He has an attack-patter where he strikes to times horizontally and creates a shockwave-cutting blast. Even when you stand right in front of him and dodge to the right as he strikes the first time, he instantly turns around 90° and strikes again - you HAVE to doge both. But then he has 2 attacks that leaves his back wide open.
The bosses are actually a joke compared to the Rhogars with the shields, or the charging-assasin-like ones or the fat bow shooting ones.
I know I heavily compare this game to DS but it is definitely what inspired the whole game however it fails. Especially at the balancing which DS isn't - or was - really great at but at least other "classes" or builds were fine to play. Here, as noted, there is a HUGE difference between heavy armored tank and an agile assasin (that basically does the same damage but dies after 2 hits). And of course: Shield Break. You may think that's not a big deal but if you play a game in which every big guys has a shield and won't let you attack him you will realize why it IS a big deal.
Now I could go on and say "this game looks sooo great" but I couldn't care less in an action-RPG about anything, if the ACTION part, the fighting is terrible.

This review is quite in depth, so here is the summarisation, but for some who are new or want the in depth review, please see below.
OMSI 2: 6/10 or 64%. Would recommend to the right person, but overall I can't, as base price is way to high as well as the several add-ons. You have to invest yourself into the game almost as much as me, to get some fun out of it.
Personally I find it to be fine.
-Quick Notes
This game is a massive mix of the good and the bad, as many negatives, link to positives. If you read on, it will make more sense... and just to summarise, despite what is seen below, I recommend this game, but only to hard core simulation fans.
I'm not just going to pour out the negatives, as I've been playing this for hundreds of hours, so I'll get the good stuff out first and I only have the X10 and Three Generations addons, so the positives and negatives only reflect them.
-The Actual Review
1. The Buses
The buses that come with the base game, the MAN SD200, SD202, NL202 & NG272 (I think its called that) are well made and rarely have any issues. They're fun to drive and smooth, with the exclusion of the NL202 (partially) the NG272.
(see negatives below)
The X10 Addon bus, the MAN Lion's City DD (AKA DL05, 07,08 & 09) are well made too.
2. The Worlds
The base Spandau map, is distinct and well created, with rarely any glitches, but it does lead to an issue.
Berlin in the X10 Addon takes place primarily in the south west of Berlin, with the famous Berlin Zoo and the town of Zehlendorf being immersive and well made.
3. The Community
Ever since the original was released in 2011, many players of OMSI have made add on buses, maps, repaints and more for free, which really has increased the longevity of the game and has allowed OMSI players other the world to come together. Not to sound flowery, but its nice to see others adding content to the game based on their hometown, so there is a varying degree of maps and buses to utilise and explore. Again, there are negatives to this.
4. The Game's Exisitence
The game existing is a good thing, due to the lack of well made bus simulators, which this definitely is. Amongst older simulators like the Bus Simulator series and even the really old Bus Driver from SCS software, it stacks up pretty well.
Whilst, yet again, this is a good thing, it leads to an negative.
1. The Buses
SMALLER ISSUES
As stated before with the NL202, there is a tiny nitpick and this can also be stated for the 'Three Generations' addon of the 2013 Citaro C2 bus.
The braking is quite tight, even if you don't apply too much pressure, which can lead to passengers complaining. adn on the C2 bus, a jerky ride. The NG272 has a larger problem. I understand the point of the swaying connector of the bus, hence the 'articulated' name, but the squeaking noise it makes when turning corners can be quite annoying, especially on the more corner heavy route: the 5 (or 130).
The Lion's City DD can also have texture errors, as the bus is quite demanding, meaning that sometmes textures don't load, leaving the windows opaque, preventing anything to be seen from the inside.
BIGGER ISSUES
The more prevalent negative however, is the fact the range of buses is quite poor for both the base game and the X10 addon. Only 2 double deckers with slight variations and 1 single and articulated bus for the base game, as well as only 1 single decker for the X10 addon. Its pretty poor, which leads to many (me as an example) paying for addon buses to use in the maps.
2. The Worlds
BASE SPANDAU MAP
I appreciate the effort placed into recreating many cities around the world for players to explore, but in the long run, these efforts will be forgotton and people will wonder why there isn't more.
For example, the base Spandau map in all honesty has only 2 day routes: the 5 and 92.
I don't count the 130 and 137, just because they take place in a different time period, its essentially the same as the original, except for the extension of the 137 form Freudstr. to Falkensee Bahnhof.
I'm sure players have seen the AI routes like the 13, 54, 94 and 97 routes (for example) and though why they aren't fully playable. I don't see why a revisit to these routes to extend them to their actual destinations would not be considered.
To make it a free or even a £5 at most fee would be great and would leave the map feeling more complete and open world. This is a feature that more average gamers to the genre will likely find an annoyance, and drops its recommendation value quite low.
X10 ADDON
I don't have every DLC, but I know the same can be said for the X10 Addon, as only 2 Berlin buses (the 115 and X10 are full routes)  and 2 routes (I think the 626 and another route) in Teltow ( a town in the Brandenburg area (or county as I'd relate it to) is fully playable.
Lots of routes like the 110, 285, 601/X1, 621, 623 & 625 buses are only partially playable and it can be quite blatant.
For example, the 285 travels from Dahlem Waldfriedhof to S+U Rathaus Steglitz in real life and the destination blinds even state Steglitz, but (and this is especially apparent when selecting the Appenzeller terminus, as the same thing happens) the route ends abruptly ends on a road called Wupperstr. in Zehlendorf, making the route quite short, shorter than the 5 or 92 from the Spandau map.
This is a let down, as the route tends to use a double decker from time to time and using it can seem unnessecary depending on the time of day and amount of passengers spawned in the world.
Despite the long paragraph detailing the 285, this occurs with the 110, which is almost criminally poor in how the route's terminus (Grunewald Roseneck) is a lie, as you see it at its real terminue (U Oskar Helene Heim) when driving commonly the 285, but possibly the 115, 623 and X10. But I'll leave it at that.
3. The Community
-TO BE CLEAR
The community isn't the issue, but they are used by the developers, to create less add- on content, or relieve the feeling of leaving consumers underwhelmed, with the high price to pay for so little. The communities and their products to average consumers can be a minefield to understand, as downloading and learning where to store add on buses can be a cinch, but downloading maps and some repaints can be hard to understand and find out where to place them, leaving the consumer alienated and helpless. Believe me, this has happened to me and its not usually creator's fault, as they try to explain what to do for installations, but sometimes their native language is different.

The various communities have varying buses with varying quality. Some can be excellent amd some can be poor. I've come across a few which fail to work normally, or have a slight issue that can't be resolved, which again, makes things tough for the consumers. The lack of double deckers, is quite apparent, as the only double decker fan made bus, is a Lion's City DD, that has a few issues, but an official version, as mentioned before, can be used with the X10 pack. Single deckers make up around 80% of the fan buses, which can be an issue to those who wish to drive a new or different double decker on a longer, busier route. Articulated buses are fine, but tend to be less reliable with high density passengers than double deckers.
-MAPS
Fans have gone as far to recreate Spandau in a fictional and interesting way, (New Berlin- Spandau Map) as it utilises the many AI routes, but completely change the routes for some, which can be seen as a positive or negative. Assets have had to be reused from the original map, which is noticable sometimes, but is acceptable. The map however, for me at least rarely works and the text of issues relating to the map and any others that occur, tend to be in German, so English and other language speakers will have an annoying time tryong to figure and work it out.

This game is incredibly pretty to look at, and the way your weapons and armor impact your movement and fighting style is something I wish more games would implement. The attack animations of heavy weapons like the Cleric's hammer definitely feel well done -- you can practically feel the impact of them in your chair. From a purely visual feast standpoint this game is at least an 8 out of 10.
All of the good, unfortunately, pales in comparison to the bad. And there is a lot of bad going on in this game. Thankfully, the first boss does a terrific job of calling attention to most of the problems.
The collision/hit detection is terrible. When combined with the frustrating way that enemy attacks track you despite dodging/rolling (making them largely pointless as defensive abilities go), you will be taking a lot of damage even when you were sure you had successfully evaded an attack. An enemy in the midst of the downward stroke of a massive overhead two-handed axe attack will rotate with you while you roll, so an attack that you think will impact the floor at 12 o'clock will follow you as you roll all the way to 3 o'clock. You'll take damage, and likely curse a bit.
Add in the incredibly clunky, unresponsive controls and fighting becomes even more of a challenge because you're fighting both the monsters and the controls. The attack animations for your character are very well done, and you get ample opportunity to appreciate them because when you start one you are committed to it until it finishes or the monster(s) knock you backwards on your butt. There is no breaking off an attack for a quick roll, parry, or block. You'll take more damage than you do, and probably curse a bit. This leads to a lot of stick and move fighting which is a terrifc way of making fights more realistic than standing toe-to-toe hacking away at each other, but that kind of fighting relies heavily on spot-on, responsive controls, which Lords of the Fallen falls woefully short on delivering.
Now, a positive of this game is that it does provide a challenging "Souls"-like game, which is a nice refreshing change of pace in a world of games that seems to practically want to hold your hand from the starting line to the finishing line. However, when I think of challenging games, I think of things that make me use my head, employ strategy, evolve what I'm doing to overcome a new obstacle. I don't consider bad controls and cheap AI trickeration as a legitimate part of making a challenging game. Imagine climbing Mt. Everest with an anvil chained around your waist while abominable snowmen fire rockets at you that never miss.
You'd die, and probably curse a little bit. But you might enjoy that more than playing Lords of the Fallen.

Reading about Concerned Ape's vision for this game is really what makes the final product clear. The goal is to refine a genre that was previously underexploited and whose potential was not fully met. In this case, refering to the popular farming simulator (and so much more) Harvest Moon. This game is truly a labour of love, one I never saw myself liking at first but that I fell in love with. The genuine nature of the world makes it too charming to remain cynical about. Sure the game isn't perfect, and some design choices I'm not really a fan of, but this isn't something whose parts you can pick and choose. Similarly to its characters and to anyone playing the game, nothing is perfect, we all have our flaws but love is about accepting those flaws and the visibly rushed brushstrokes on a usually otherwise beautiful painting. The feeling of playing this game defies explanation. Do yourself a favor and take some time to dive into this jewel, it will be worth every minute.

This is an alright game albeit short.  It's one part detective, another part cartoony.  This game neither recommended nor a game to avoid.  It's somewhere in the middle where you can give it a shot if you're interested in what you think it brings to the table.  If this game goes on sale, all the better to give it a try.
There are two modes in which you will have to play to complete the entire Part 1.  Detective mode allows the player to interact with the environment and put pieces together to solve a case.  Action mode is where you shoot baddies and chase them.  Control features change if you are in a particular mode.  When you play a level, it will only be in one mode, detective or action.  This format is interesting although not entire new.
Some positives to the game is the environment.  I like the 40's noir look especially in an insect universe.  With references and jokes about insects, it feels you are entering this world for the first time.  The city looks nice but it's too bad that the game isn't an open world that we can discover its environment.  Voice acting is done well, too.
There are some flaws to the game that felt frustrating at times.  In the beginning, there should've been some tutorial.  Mostly everything is basic but I didn't know that I can double jump.  I didn't even see it under the controls section or anywhere that tells you to double jump on to the next building.  I had to watch someone's playthrough to figure it out.  Also, the platforming mechanics aren't great.  Even a short drop can literally kill you.  Sometimes you have to jump at pipes that can make you slide off.  Even though the ground or roof top is walkable, and you are just several feet above, one slip, you still die for some reason.
The game is simplistic in a lot of game sense.  There aren't many enemy types; most (if not all) action mode are designed the same way; weapon choices are few; and there are just a handful of main characters.  But this shouldn't detract from the game's major selling points.  The crime solving aspects, even in its simplicity, is still engaging.  Also, exploring the cartoony, bug universe is interesting.
It's unfortunate that part 2 didn't get converted into Steam even though "part 2" or the second half can be played on the Nintendo DS.  If players are interested in what happens after part 1 ends, there are cinematics on Youtube or even a continuous gameplay on Nintendo DS if you look hard enough.

Played XCOM: Enemy Unknown and loved it! But I love this even more!
Every mission is definitely exciting, you'll never know what could happen especially in limited-turn missions. Definitely improved gameplay, not only graphics but in terms of mechanics as well. New upgrades to experiment, such as items that gives certain type of boosts, weapon mods (e.g. gives chance to 1-hit even a full health Sectopod unit, I'm not sure if this is OP but is definitely useful), skill paths, and etc.

I can't have a mission without atleast one - a stealthy scout that can give you sight ahead to better strategize your positions or an aggressive finisher that can deal massive crit or slice enemies. DISREGARD WHINERS. This game is an instant classic. The people whining about RNG are ridiculous. The game tells you from the first moment it's an outlast disaster game, where your town/party management is the key to success or failure.
- This game is challenging, but the challenge is rewarding, and there is ample opportunity to improve if you have a bit of patience and understand that you must accept and learn from the death of your favorite characters. It's the people that don't get that aspect that go salty on the RNG, missing half the point of the whole game.
- The art is perfect. Maybe I appreciate the hand-drawn style games more than the next guy.... this game is a sure example of unique art done right in a way that contributes immensely to the mood of the game.
- THE VOICE ACTING! Oh god yes I love it when I hear "Executed with impunity!". Along with the art, the voice makes this game... and then you notice afterwards that ALL the audio is great, but most is eclipsed by the awesomeness of the narrator.
- Mechanics: The light and stress mechanics are a fresh treat for my strategy taste buds. Camping skills add some great management aspects into the middle of all but the short expeditions. Characters have sets of well-thought skills of which you can choose to have half active during an adventure. Resistances are meaningful and balanced enough to play a more obvious role. Skeletons are nearly immune to bleed. Fungi creatures have high blight resistance. Damage over time becomes important with enemies with high protection... And always and forever it's all about that tough choice. Should I heal? Reduce nearly topped stress? Or hope for a critical to end that last enemy before they can strike a deathblow. Just damn fine all around strategy/management mechanics.
- RNG cuts both ways, and it is not as all-encompassing as detractors claim. Everything touched by RNG has at least one mechanic available to improve chances. Most characters have a high base chance to hit, and a variety of buffs and debuffs are available for clever use to change the odds.
To sum up, Red Hook acted upon a solid vision, and created a game that stands out and above in every way, engaging and challenging from the first moments. Darkest Dungeon rewards the resilient with great satisfaction.

Back again, it’s time for the next game in the great Kingdom Rush series to arrive on steam. I will add a TL:DR at the end.
Kingdom Rush: Frontiers (KRF) currently has 15 levels or 45 if you count iron and heroic level variations, 41 different enemies, 4 base towers each with two different specializations, and 9 different heroes. There are 3 different difficulties to play on which include casual, normal, and veteran so you can choose whether to make every hero movement and tower purchase count, or take it easy and perhaps experiment with different heroes and strategies.
Just like in the previous title in the series you unlock heroes as you complete more levels. There is a story about your adventure which you can read on each level, and as you beat more levels and level variations you get upgrade points to use on the upgrade screen. The towers now have different specializations than in the older title and they allow you to rethink your strategy, and find a way to effectively use these new towers along with new heroes to beat the levels and challenges which are presented before you.
The variation within heroes is quite large allowing you to have a character for whatever playstyle you prefer, however the leveling works quite a bit differently than before. Now your main hero Alric will start at level 1, but levels are kept throughout the game meaning once he becomes level 2 he will stay level 2 in the next level. When the hero levels up you can go into the hero room to choose which upgrade to give them, whether that is Alric’s sand warriors, Deirdre’s holy light, or even Ashbite’s feast you can choose which upgrade you put those skill points into and can reset it with no problems.
As you advance further I previously mentioned that more heroes are unlocked, however they don’t start at level 1 like Alric, but rather are of a higher level to allow them to be useful in the point where you unlock them throughout the campaign.
The same beautiful art is present again, the great artstyle that makes Kingdom Rush, well, Kingdom Rush. The map is animated and every little detail is great to see, you can even see the locations of the soon to be added levels.  The designs of the new towers are great and the enemies are unique to Frontiers.
The music works very well to give into the atmosphere of the game and add to it.
+ Breath of fresh air in a familiar setting
+ Hero and enemy variety
+ Good replay value
+ Easter eggs
+ Interesting story
+ New upgrade choices
+ No microtransactions
- Hero reliability (this is not a con for everyone, but it is for some where in later levels it is impossible to win without the use of a hero and so those who think that since KRF is a tower defense it should have the option to be beaten with only the use of towers may find great difficulty in that task)
- Tower usefulness with baracks in question (It seems baracks lack usefulness after a certain stage because they are supposed to be body blockers first, and that is taken away through the great skill of the necromancer tower and if you do need baracks you usually never need to upgrade it to a specialization because it will usually be more optimal to upgrade an Artillery, Mage, or Archer. There is also the case of Templars (one specialization) being discussed as a worse investment compared to its counterpart the Assasin)
I was one of the lucky individuals allowed the opportunity to beta test this game, to perfect it for its release on steam. I’ve seen bad bugs and great bugs and all of them fixed. For someone like myself it’s amazing to get to play Kingdom Rush again. A while ago I checked to see if KRF was coming to steam and I saw a huge notice saying that it would sadly never make its way here. Happily, it’s not the case, the future is here, and so is the next game in a beautiful series. This improves upon the original KR amazingly and honestly if you played the first KR, I don’t think you can hate on this game. I am a huge fan of KR since I owned all the games on mobile and beat them repeatedly while waiting at the airport or bored during the day. It’s truly amazing to see this game come to steam (here’s to hoping for Origins to come onto steam as well). This game has less currently as compared to KR, but more is going to be added (for free). That includes enemies, heroes, and levels.  If you never played a game in the Kingdom Rush series before and enjoy tower defense games with humour and story, then whether you start at KR or go to KRF I would say you will enjoy it.
The second coming of Kingdom Rushing has arrived. If you liked the last one, you will most likely enjoy this one. If you are uncertain whether KRF is for you then go onto a site such as Kongregate and check out the much, much more limited flash version to get an idea of what the game will be like. When you return here I like to think you will want to buy the vastly superior version.

You've read all about how hard the DS series is, I'm sure. Truth is, it's not that hard. It simply has a different game mechanic. One that is based on trial & error, and dying a lot while doing it. You never permanently lose anything on dying, and because of the soft caps on stats, most people end their leveling on lvl ~125 anyway (both to be matched against others in PvP, and because more levels than that don't really pay off in PvE much either). That's something you'll reach on a single playthrough, even without grinding. And this game is ALL about NG+. So the only thing you lose while dying are your souls, which are the game's currency for shop and leveling. And you'll have more than enough of those anyway.
With that out of the way, I can't possibly list the numerous things this game has going for it. You should google for those. The game has a lot of meta in it but its relatively easy - even if time consuming - to learn most of it. Besides, with the ability to do NG+ endlessly and respec your character 5 times each playthrough, you can't really make permanent wrong choices beyond picking your class. The difference between endgame stats for different classes is negligible, but it is there. So if you're a minmaxer, be warned and check out your ideal starting class early.
Anyway, you came here to check whether DS3 is any good. I myself, some of my friends, and some of my colleagues even all agree that this is one of the best, if not THE best game ever made. It's a bit quirky at first, but once you get the hang of it there's nothing like it.
Be warned though, the series suffers from lazy console porting. Technically the game works perfectly, but all the in-game controls are given for a gamepad even if you're using a keyboard & mouse. It's a hassle to learn to play with KB&M but well worth it if you just ride it through (especially casters benefit immensely from mouse's freeaim capabilities). The game also suffers from an infestation of twinks in sub-45 lvl PvP, so if you're going to play embered (you'll learn what that means ingame), be sure to summon aid and get used to the idea of dying anyway. By infestation I mean that basically literally every PvP invader is a twink before that level, meaning they take 20x more to kill and hit 5x harder than you do, and are also far, far better at the game. So bear in mind, if you don't ember, you cannot be invaded.
The DS3 world is harsh, and unforgiving, but also more rewarding than anything made in at least a decade, if not longer.

Half Life is a game most people have probably played in their lives. I've played bits of it as a kid, but I think I found it to scary so I never played it properly back then. Over the time I just never really cared for it so I didn't play it.
Thanks to the Valve sales, I decided to buy it and play it.  Considering the low price, it was worth it. 10 hours spent well.
It should be noted that the game was quite innovative for its time, and did a lot for its genre. Playing it now, most of it is lost on you, so you just take it for what it is now. Did it age well? Yes it did, aside from enemies taking too many hits at times and every bullet hitting you for sure. Thanks to Quick Save/Load, that's not a problem, you just avoid taking lots of damage, as you can recover health after every bigger section. So I'd say the action is good and not that much broken.
However, platforming can be a bit tricky, as the player movement doesn't seem to have been designed for platforming. Kinda like having to jump on platforms in a Call of Duty game. It's just weird, and often you end up missing or jumping on it and falling off. Quick Save/Load fixes this issue as you can just save before tricky jumps.
Quick Saves. They are your best friend in this game, but at the same time you might hate yourself for using them. They make the game too easy as you can save anywhere and anytime you want. Dangerous enemies in the next room? Quick save. Took out one of the big ones without taking much damage? Quick save and attack the next one.  It just makes the game easier than it should be, so the challenge is kinda low thanks to it. It's basically "legal' save states. Finishing the game without them would be a nice challenge.
Can't talk much about difficulty differences as I played on normal. I don't know how difficult this mode even was, as Quick saves take you right back into the latest action.
The story was more subtle in this game. You are just a scientist that got involved in a mess. Most of the story you hear from other NPCs (you can't pause the game while they are talking, otherwise the audio gets canceled) and observing what's going on.
After 10 hours of fun, I have to say that the ending was really disappointing in my case. It was just a short dialogue with you getting to choose between a good and bad ending. So it's kinda pointless.
Overall, I'll rate this game 7/10, it's worth giving a try, and the game looks really nice with the HD texture pack.

Full disclosure; I have done several things to make the game as easy on me as possible. Many of the ingame options includes disabling certain features, including debuff chances and monster corpses (Which can mess with your attack formations) to name a couple. Alongside that, I’ve utilized the workshop and downloaded several quality-of-life mods that include bigger inventory (and thus higher payouts at the end of quests, if you nab enough things), Stronger Start (which effectively buffs your starter two heroes), and level restriction removal which allows me to bring higher level people on lower level missions which would help “Carry” new characters. There’s several more but nothing quite so severe as what I have done to XCOM2. If you people only knew...
You’ve probably already heard about Darkest Dungeon. It’s one of the very few Early Access success stories. What we have here is a roguelike turned based roleplaying game. For those just joining us, “Rogue” was an older game, effectively inventing its own genre of difficulty and progression. Roguelikes tend to be punishing, destroying your early game while slowly earning currencies and upgrades that continually aid you in your further attempts.
In the story, some nobleman got some gold fever and started digging around his lands and unleashed a literal eldritch abomination which cast a swath of land into darkness, turning the whole place into a hellscape. I don’t know what matter of character we, as the player, plays as but we lead a band of mercenaries across these lands to explore dungeons and forests. You scrape up gold and treasure, eventually upgrading your township and champions so you can take on higher challenges. The overarching goal is to assault the Darkest Dungeon itself, which I’m sure is full of good times and parties.
That’s the baseline concept but there are a ton of nuances that go into the game. I for one am happy to have some turn based combat in my life again, the last memory of which was Final Fantasy X which I enjoyed greatly in my teenage years. There may be a reason the genre faded in the background as it’s a bit of a flow-breaker, which had no place in a world of Call of Duty’s and Halo’s and Arkham’s. Darkest Dungeon makes the concept really work, with an interesting art style that makes it look like you’re reading an ancient tome with plenty of pictures to go along with the legend, helped by the narrator who occasionally spouts antiquated language like “Perched at the very precipice of oblivion...” You really do feel like you’re playing through an interactive book at times.
If you’ve played a Dark Souls or any roguelike game, you probably know the score. Your people will die. If they don’t die, they might get to a point where you can no longer tenably sustain their negative quirks and high stress levels. Quirks and stress (stress being comparable to any insanity mechanic in a Call of Cthulhu RPG or Amnesia game) bring your heroes down constantly, from easily ignored to debilitating. I don’t care if my tank has -3 speed, but I do care when someone gets a tapeworm which doubles their food consumption. That’s basically♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥my money away. At a certain point, characters become so stressed, they gain an affliction which is usually much harsher. A healer of mine once became “Paranoid”, not only fleeing to the back of the group but sometimes wrestled control away from me on her turn, using her own decision making to pop a heal or attack without my command. These can be cured for high sums of gold in your township but most players choose to abandon the character.
Thankfully, retreating is a possible option. You don’t get the high payout quest rewards but you do keep everything you acquired in the dungeon itself. If you made it past 80% of the dungeon but all your people are at 10% health, one of them is bleeding, one of them is paranoid, it might just be better to flee, take your earnings, and send some of the worse-off characters on their way. I’ve probably abandoned quests more often than I’ve completed them, but I’m still making some progress in the game and that’s what matters.
Now, I’m a fairly casual scrub player. I like my games fun and easy if at all possible but there is something positively enchanting about Darkest Dungeon. The combat is incredibly intense, and I can feel my heart skip a beat every time I see “dodge” or “miss” pop up. Every time my people don’t land a blow, it opens me up for another attack and that frightens me to a decent degree. The game’s tone is dreadful but it works in its favor with its highly stylized... style. I just like looking at the game, which is impressive because I find myself thinking about it when not playing it. Due to the steam summer sale, I also was able to get Watch Dogs 2, but this game is drawing more of my attention than any triple A game at the moment and that’s always a good sign.
If I had a complaint, it’s probably the same complaint you might have seen while skimming over other reviews. The random number generator aspect of the game can be seen as a detriment. People like to progress, and we also like having our decisions matter in the grand scheme of things. Other times, it feels hopeless. I once equipped a character with a -25% stress trinket only to have a very harsh fight with a Madman enemy constantly unload high stress on the entire team before I was able to take him out. It’s moments like that, that give me the sense of “Why did I even bother?”
I do believe that’s how some of this is supposed to work. Retreating from dungeons more often than completing them makes it all the more satisfying when I am actually able to complete one and see that sweet, juicy 4500 gold enter my theoretical bank account.
Still, there can be a bit of that old “nothing I do matters” feeling that creeps up while you play. I certainly get that from time to time but I’m doing my best with some of the easiest settings cranked up and I find myself enjoying the experience anyway.
Would I recommend this game? As usual it depends on what you look for in games. It has plenty to offer for challenge seekers, with a lot of gear management, loot, and town upgrading to cater to any RPG lovers. The general consensus across the internet can be very mixed, with every update having a vocal outcry on things being too easy or too hard. I wasn’t there during many of these updates, I’ve come in two years later into their development and I’m probably experiencing one of the most refined versions of this game and as it is, I’m enjoying it. I’m as surprised as anyone.

You are the owner of the hamlet with an obsessive need to find its secrets. The people who come to raid are either greedy, or adventurous, or evil, or looking for redemption, or for some other kind of personal gain. You do not care about them, only about your hamlet. Send a team to the dungeons without any torches or provisions. Let them go crazy or get injured as long as they bring back treasure to rebuild the hamlet. If they become too damaged, you dismiss them and find another sucker to take his/her place. This is how you play this game. It is about the hamlet, not about the adventurers.
If people are looking for a highly stress inducing, teeth grinding, scream filled gaming experience in a simple 2D game, then Darkest Dungeon is the game for you. I have never come across a game in my entire life that solely depended on RNG. In a way, I consider this a tiny Dark Souls like game, except you can't control everything in the Dark Souls games, such as dodging, landing hits, and encountering/avoiding enemies. This is by far one of the most challenging and yet highly satisfactional experience I have ever had playing Darkest Dungeon, if you have the fortitude/patience to outlast your own stress.
Honestly the negatives depend and vary from player to player. If i was to point out something i disliked that would be the lack of inventory space on long quests. Also this game is sometimes dependent on luck i have lost heroes in the most unfair scenarios possible. In addition, the boss battles are abosolute hell. They are not a walk at the park it will take a few deaths to know how to win them.

This game will truly test your stress control and patience. A careful, methodical player who takes time to set up each run and adapt to new situations as best he/she can will prosper, though everyone will eventually be confronted with the fact that heroes, even if well-managed, are ultimately only human.
I would definitely recommend skimming through a couple videos seeing how people prepare for different areas, and how well it goes. You can find detailed spreadsheets giving outlines for what to bring where. Youtuber Baertaffy has played this game so much, and at the start of his videos he explains who and what he's bringing where and why. Maybe watch the first few minutes of a handful of his DD videos to get an idea of how to prepare. If you're unsure on what to bring, overpreparation is a safe bet. Bring lots of food and shovels.

My Fallout 4 review: (I've played this game on ps4 for over 200hrs)
Massive downgrade from the prior games.
Major Cons:
-Your character now has a voice, meaning that you loose actual dialogue choices and stuck with a mass effect kind of dialogue wheel. No matther what you say it won't change the outcome of the game.
-No in depth story that has any form of decisions other than 3-4.
-No unique weapons of any kind. It's now been replaced by a legendary loot drop system.
-The perk system has now been dumbed down, focusing for a more broad skill set which is inferior to it's prior games.
-All side-quests have been made based of a single idea that was talked about in the Bethesda office. Resulting in all side-quests having little to no depth at all.
-The game "requires" you to get a season pass to get a DLC which will allow you to be the bad guy.
-Optimisation issues, bug ridden "quests" and overall lack of polish but thats Bethesda for you.
-Workshop mode is a great feaure but lacks essential parts and unfortunatly to get them you'll need to buy the DLC's (or the season pass) dedicated to workshop mode.
-The game focuses too much on the workshop mode and less on dialogue.
-Vanilla side quests often become incredibly repetitive; go to a settlement, run across the map to kill one major ghoul etc.
-Creation Club.
-Bethesda made this and not a developer that can create and actual RPG.
Major Pros:
-Gunplay is great, however due to this V.A.T.S becomes pointless, unless you plan on using your critical.
-The style of the game is a major improvement overall, making you feel more immersed.
-Graphically it's a huge upgrade from it's prior games. Whilst not great to modern games it's still nice to look at, sometimes.
-The game's life is easily prolonged thanks to the great people who decide to create FREE content. (Modders)
-Sound design is nice and clear.

TLDR: Overall, moments of entertainment locked behind odd design choices and unresolved glitches that makes it impossible to recommend.
EDIT: And I feel bad for not being able to recommend it because I did have some good fun and effort was clearly made.
First the good:
-The character/monster/environment designs are well done, it's all massive muscles, massive armour and massive weapons but if you don't mind that it's nicely done.
-When the combat works, it can be fun.
The mixed (subjective):
-The armour sets are well designed, as mentioned above, but the standard as you go through set progression is inconsistent. For light armour for example, you get the best designed armour about half way through then get sets that seem much more 'vanilla' or are (I believe) reskins of previous sets.
-The story isn't terrible, but I'm still unsure about the premise. Why exactly is Adyr the god considered a 'villain'? I may have missed an audio log that explains this, but then it is still missable.
-There is a universal cooldown on spells, use one and they all go on cd (at least the ones from the same school do, can't verify whether it applies to other schools). On some combinations this may make sense, on others it seems overly restrictive. Keep in mind that without massive xp investment into faith (magic), the mana cost of each spell is likely prohibitive of chain casting anyway. Not impossible mind you, but when you factor in the cast time of each spell and the likelihood of interruption by enemy hits, a gcd seems superfluous.
-Combat staggering seemed unpredictable across the board, both on you and the enemies. There seemed no way of knowing ahead of time whether Harkyn would get staggered by any given enemy's attacks or whether they would be staggered by his.
-Certain classes may seem underpowered, mileage may vary. Rogue class definitely could have used some life steal baked in to a spell.
-Majority of voice work is bland, not all but a lot of it.
-The rune/crafting system seemed inconsistent. The game features a system where you can invest xp into locked runes  to increase the likelihood of better quality buffs but the return on this seemed very disappointing. Possibly rectified with better 'Luck' character stats but that's uncertain.
The bad:
-The hit detection is suspect. Weapon strikes simply may decide not to land, spell hits may just not register.
-Enemy projectiles may not hit you when they should and may seek you out through walls.
-Equipment stats are confusing. You are given numbers without context. Conversely some items have only 'fluff' descriptions.
-The camera may decide to snap to a completely obscured perspective during 'backstabs'.
-Spell effects may also overwhelm your vision.
-The gauntlet is intrusive and frequently redundant. It seemed underpowered no matter which class or loadout was used, an enemy could always be reached to melee them anyway, using it costs mana that would 9 times out of 10 be better used on spell casting and it is unalterably bound to the stance swapping button which gets in the way during combat.
-The physics are unbelievable in a bad way. Enemies may do a U-turn mid leap, defying momentum. The enemy also has a bad habit of tracking your motion during weapon swings that would likely snap their bones, also rendering combat maneuvering futile. This becomes more of a problem with the more fragile classes.
-Pathing is incompetent. Enemies may get stuck on corners or non existent obstacles, may reset and speed off to their original point (no, not that one demon dog who is scripted to do something similar).
-Harkyn's magic is wildly unreliable. Magic may simply not do what it is supposed to. Direct damage spells may just not land despite hitting the mark. Buffs may drop off before their proper duration or not do as described. Bad pathing also applies here.
-Even after hours of play time, the cumbersome nature of the spell casting can still be infuriating. Enemy AI is unreliable as to attacking during casting, they may knock you out of it or stand there and wait. A hit the wrong side of a millisecond may interrupt a 'complete' cast.
-Controls are unreliable, Harkyn may simply ignore commands. The most frequent suspect for me was the running shield bash attack, it simply didn't happen about 40% of the time and would land Harkyn in hot water each time. Dodges may simply not occur either.
-Saves may not be complete, by which I mean you can save your progress at a checkpoint or even move to a new area and quit and when you reload, the game may simply not have saved to that point. On a whim.
-Desktop crashes. Frequent and exacerbated by the above problem.

If you ever played a harvest moon like game and liked it, you will love this. This is defenitely made by people who really love the genre, and that love really shows in the game.
Obviously it's a farming game. You can farm, fish, harvest wild resources, mine, fight and interact (and eventually marry) villagers. So there are plenty of things to do, and you'll soon find the 13,5 minutes each ingame day lasts isn't nearly enough to do everything you planned to do every day. You can upgrade the farmhouse, and build and upgrade lots of other buildings, machines and tools, and can create fences and paths, sprinklers and lots of other things to improve and personalize your farm.
Another thing I liked about Stardew Valley compared to Harvest Moon; no stupid hurricanes! In the Harvest Moon games I played there occasionally comes a hurricane that just about destroys all the crops. Nothing as cruel as that in this game.
So let's talk about the downsides. First thing is the graphics. It looks pixally. At first this was kind of annying, but I quickly got used to it and didn't even notice it after a while. Some people even seem to like it with the retro feel of it, at first I didn't but now I do. Another downside is that when playing the game at a certain point it feels like you're done. And at that point the game starts feeling monotous. This is after a long time playing, but it happens eventually. When it does you take a break from the game, then start a new game, there are different farm maps and ofcourse several different love interests. So there's plenty of replayability. And there is an active mod community to make a second (or third or fifth) run still entertaining.
In the end what really makes the game in my opinion is the overall vibe. I really got that idyllic feel of moving to the countryside, making friends with the village and living the good life (even though my toon worked his butt off). All in all I feel very confident that if you like Harvest Moon, you'll definetely love this. And if you never played a game like Harvest Moon I would still recommend it. It's an awesome game.

Avoid Metal Slug 2 fps and play this version of Metal Slug 2 instead. Metal Slug 2/X introduces more level variety, weapons, powerups, humor and two new playable characters compared to Metal Slug 1. Besides fixing the framerate/peformance or Metal Slug 2 (Even on Steam) Metal Slug X remixes the orginal. On Steam Metal Slug 2's port lacks online/local COOP but other than that here's a list of differences based on what I could find when comparing the two:
-Much of the music has been slightly remixed/altered. It is made to sound more clean, sweeping and/or epic.
-Many stages had the time of day changed. Instead of being simply at day or at night, the stages take place at dusk, twilight, sunset and dawn.
-Different Boss placement.
-Entirely new mini bosses.
-The Harrier Boss is now only a mini boss in the level it appears in.
-It is now possible for your character to become fat in every stage after Mission 2, while it was only possible in Mission 4 previously.
-There is less slowdown than in Metal Slug 2, especially in COOP.
-All levels contain increased and different enemies, as well as a different boss in the first mission.
-Vehicle types and locations are usually changed.
-There are generally more power ups, prisoners, and items, particularly food, which are often hidden and must be shot to obtain.
-The action is more unusual, with many environmental elements doing things such as exploding with unexpected results or randomly spewing out items or enemies.
-Original (Super pixelated) art for Metal Slug is shown at the end of the game while the credits are rolling, instead of a black screen used in Metal Slug 2.
-Apparently people swear that Metal Slug 2 is brighter color wise but I can't see any difference on Steam.
-Removed airplane taking off.
-Aliens appear earlier. (Spoiler?)

In the same fashion, like in many games, before attacking, the ennemies gives off a visual cue, a "flash". To tell you when to use your perfect dodge.. But no. Some attack will give off the cue one entire second before you need to dodge, some will at the exact moment you need to dodge. So the visual cue doesn't serve any purpose, since you need to watch the animation anyway.
The game in itself is very good, but full of inconsistencies that can ruin your gameplay.
However, it has it's price going for it, wich is what makes me recommend it.

Bayonetta is one of those games you can't help but buy multiple times, because it's just so damn good. If they made a version of this for the Tiger
, I'd buy 50 copies. I was unlucky enough to have popped my Bayo cherry on the PS3 version of the game, which is still considered one of the worst ports of any game ever made. I got to play it a second time on the Wii U when it was bundled with its equally-amazing sequel (which will never get a PC port because Nintendo sucks and has to keep everything for itself), and I just couldn't resist dropping $15 just to experience this game one more time on the superior gaming platform. It's amazing how much better this game is on the PC, running at an unfettered 60 frames per second. A fast, combo-driven action game deserves only the best in terms of performance and playability, and even though it took Platinum 8 years, it's better late than never.
The combat is the star of the show here- the movelist is bigger than some fighting games I've played, and the underlying mechanics are easy to pick up, but devilishly difficult to master. In many ways, perfecting your skills here isn't unlike picking up a character in a fighting game, and once you've truly mastered the game, it becomes an absolute spectacle to play and watch (as many combo video makers on YouTube have proven for years).
I've played a lot of character action games, but this one might be the best one I've played next to its older sibling, the almighty Devil May Cry 3. It's still a damn good game, even after nearly a decade. You can tell that everything here is the result of years of experience from Hideki Kamiya's long career in the games industry- the whole thing is fine-tuned to be the best game it can possibly be, and I'll be surprised if Platinum or some other developer somehow manages to top it.

Where should I start.  My background is in hacking, and Hacknet annoyed me.  I already know unix commands, I felt entitled enough at the start to scoff at the simulated terminal's shortcomings.  No top? No df/du? No ability to create directories even? Pfft.
But then I stopped and listened.  I remembered the kick♥♥♥♥♥tunes in the best hacking films of yesteryear, particularly Hackers, and I stopped expecting realism and just tried to enjoy the game for the atmosphere.  And there were moments during my first play through where I actually, uncontrollably, smiled like a kid at christmas.  You see, the beauty in this  game is that thinking like a hacker gets you places, and it's rewarding to once more feel that, even if just for a short time.  I won't spoil the game for anybody, but there were 3 points during my playthrough where I felt ridiculously happy.  The rest of it was entertaining but would have been bland if not for a compelling story and surprisingly good characterisation, given the short nature of the game.  But that's also my greatest criticism.  I can forgive the subset of 'nix commands, the hokey visualisations that accompany your hacking tools and the ultra cheesy faux corporation names, but the real problem it the game leaves you wanting a hell of a lot more when it's over.  There is a multiplayer version in the pipe (see what I did there), but I wasn't able to find much on upcoming features other than the dev is currently working on ports for mac and linux, which is fine but doesn't interest me since I mostly game on windoze.  But I want more plots, more things to hack, more tools.  I want modding, I want more of that amazing retro-themed music (particularly that ONE track, again, no spoilers. If you've completed the game, you know the one).  I want that track to kick in more than once a play-through, when I'm doing something crazy important and urgent in the game.
TL;DR? Ex-hacker got nostalgic playing indie hacking game, had feels, loved it enough to write a review.
5/10 for replayability of the game as it is currently.
10/10 for some obvious and not-so-obvious references to Hackers and other hacking esotera.
Overall, 10/10 if, and when, RPG-like elements like upgrading equipment, infinite procedural mission/story generation, and bouncing connections/more advanced tracing dynamics are introduced.  I know, I'm demanding.
For now? 8/10 for the most fun 6 hours of a game I've had since Portal 2.

So one day me and my cousin were looking through steam games, trying to find one we should try out. I told him "Hey, there is this adventure game that has been out a while and is pretty popular. It is like minecraft, but with more adventure." So he got excited, and we both tried it out. I played about 20-30 hours ahead of him, and I too stopped because of repetitiveness. I do come back every once in a while to check on the new updates, and try to grind a little bit more towards my goal of getting a radiant bow.
PROS:
There's enough gameplay to keep you playing quite a while.
You can be a dragon.
You can GLIDE on wings.
You can hatch 3 invincible chickens to fight for you for 30 seconds.
You can raise a giant skeleton to fight for you until he dies.
There are a lot of character options.
CONS:
The gameplay will get repetitive after a while, before you get some of the highest tier stuff.
You cannot flap to gain altitude while flying with your wings.
Getting different classes were screwed up, it is not as easy.
The new power level really screws the feel of the game.
You will crash quite a bit. Not a ton, but too much for any normal game.
The new updates feel to take away from some of the classic aspects of the game, instead of adding to them.
Overall, I rate it 6/10. It is not terrible, and you can have some good hours of fun, especially if you play with a friend.
